papers.node_id: 52uchilrev903!!ARTICLE: Beyond Promissory Estoppel: Contract Law and the "Invisible Handshake".
papers.title: ARTICLE: Beyond Promissory Estoppel: Contract Law and the "Invisible Handshake".
papers.authors: Daniel A. Farber; John H. Matheson
papers.abstract:
As every law student knows, promissory estoppel is based on detrimental reliance.  Law students share this idea with the American Law Instituteand with treatise writers.Indeed, promissory estoppel is one of the few points of agreement between the critical legal scholars on the left and the law and economics writers on the right.  Both agree that reliance has been the foundation of promissoryestoppel,and both accuse the courts of incoherence in applying the doctrine.
We have recently surveyed over two hundred promissory estoppel cases decided in the last ten years.Our conclusion is that reliance is no longer the key to promissory estoppel.Although courts still feel constrained to speak the language of reliance, their holdings can best be understood and harmonized on other grounds.
Part I of this article reports the results of our survey.  It documents the declining role of reliance in establishing liability and determining remedies.  It also suggests that most cases denying recovery, purportedly for lack of reasonable reliance, can be readily explained on other grounds.  Part II explores the implications of these findings.  We believe that a new rule of promissory liability is emerging from the courts' encounters with an economy in which Okun's "invisible handshake" is increasingly important.  The rule isquite simple: any promise made in furtherance of an economic activity is enforceable.
Our proposed rule unifies promissory estoppel and other exceptions to the consideration requirementwith consideration doctrine itself.  In each instance, the underlying legal policy is to protect the ability of individuals to trust promises in circumstances in which that trust is socially beneficial.  Traditional consideration doctrine allows trust to function in contexts such as sales, leases, insurance, and loans -- key economic arrangements that could not function effectively without legal enforceability.Promises involving firm offers, sureties, and options are enforceable without consideration because some economically useful transactions would otherwise be difficult to structure.  Promissory estoppel fills a similar function by enforcing promises in other settings not amenable to traditional bargaining transactions, in which reliance is beneficial both to the promisor and to society as a whole.
In our view, the expansion of promissory estoppel is not, as some have argued, proof that contract is in the process of being swallowed up by tort.Rather, promissory estoppel is being transformed into a new theory of distinctlycontractualobligation.Wealso think, for reasons that will appear more fully in Part II, that our proposed rule not only harmonizes many otherwise inconsistent cases, but also furthers the often divergent values proclaimed by the law and economics writers and the critical legal scholars. Besides serving the interest of economic efficiency, our proposed rule also furthers the important moral value of mutual trust.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49hastingslj1191!!ARTICLE:Rescuing Reliance: The Perils of Promissory Estoppel
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Rescuing Reliance: The Perils of Promissory Estoppel

shared_topics.topic: the centrality (and decline) of detrimental reliance in promissory estoppel
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate whether detrimental reliance remains the doctrinal foundation of promissory estoppel — Paper A surveys historical and contemporary critiques that call the doctrine's essential nature into question, while Paper B presents empirical evidence that courts now often decide promissory estoppel cases on grounds other than reliance.

shared_topics.topic: whether promissory estoppel has expanded or contracted as a mechanism of promissory liability
shared_topics.justification: Both articles assess shifts in the scope of promissory estoppel over time — Paper A frames the post-1980 period as a possible decline from an earlier high-water mark and surveys critiques of the doctrine's widening, and Paper B argues the doctrine is expanding into enforcement of promises that further economic activity.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between promissory estoppel and consideration/contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the doctrinal interface between promissory estoppel and traditional consideration rules — Paper B proposes unifying promissory estoppel with consideration-based enforcement as part of a single policy to protect socially beneficial trust, and Paper A examines how reliance-protection fits within the broader law of promissory obligation.

shared_topics.topic: normative justifications for enforcing promises (economic utility and trust)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat the social-policy rationale for enforcing promises: Paper B explicitly grounds enforcement in economic efficiency and the moral value of mutual trust (the 'invisible handshake'), while Paper A discusses the practical and symbolic importance of promissory estoppel for enabling reliance and sustaining contractual expectations.

shared_topics.topic: judicial incoherence and the need for doctrinal reassessment or harmonization
shared_topics.justification: Both works respond to perceived inconsistencies in court decisions and scholarly commentary — Paper A offers a reassessment of the doctrine in light of critiques and changing practice, and Paper B uses case-survey data to diagnose incoherence and to propose a unifying rule to harmonize disparate holdings.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between enforceable promises and gratuitous gifts (consideration vs promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts are enforcing promises beyond traditional consideration—often via promissory estoppel—arguing for a rule that enforces promises made in furtherance of economic activity; Paper B traces the doctrinal and historical debates over consideration and gift promises, showing how courts draw (and struggle to draw) the line between enforceable contracts and unenforceable gifts.

shared_topics.topic: the declining/unstable doctrinal role of reliance and consideration in enforcing promises

papers.node_id: 56galrev423!!ARTICLE: BOOM OR BUST: ENSURING THE GEORGIA STATE-WIDE BUSINESS COURT FULFILLS ITS CONSTITUTIONAL PROMISE
papers.title: ARTICLE: BOOM OR BUST: ENSURING THE GEORGIA STATE-WIDE BUSINESS COURT FULFILLS ITS CONSTITUTIONAL PROMISE
papers.abstract:
On January 2, 2009, the Atlanta Hawks traveled to East Rutherford, New Jersey, to play the New Jersey Nets, who at the time had lost seven of their last eight home games.The Hawks were poised to win their seventh game straight, for the first time since 1999.Early on, the Nets had a rough game: the team consistently missed open shot after open shot, Coach Lawrence Frank received two technical fouls and was ejected from the game, and the Nets were one for seven from three-point range by the half.But as the Nets entered the second half, the tide turned, and they put thirty-two points on the board in the third quarter.Then, in the fourth quarter, Devon Harris drained a three-pointer, overcoming a twenty-point halftime deficit to give the Nets a two-point lead.In overtime, the Hawks enjoyed a one-point lead with 5.3 seconds left on the clock, but the Nets had possession.The final in-bounds pass intended for Vince Carter was deflected into the backcourt, putting him too far from the basket.Carter recovered the ball, planted himself at thirty feet, and put up a long three-pointer at the buzzer to seal the deal.
Carter delivered the Hawks a disappointing buzzer-beater that night. But each team played the game by its rules, and the Nets, with the help of Vince Carter, fairly took their place as winners, ending the Hawks' six-game winning streak.The next year, in a different type of court, the Georgia Court of Appeals delivered the Hawks another epic loss. InTurner Broadcasting System, Inc., v. McDavid, the court held that the expiration of a letter of intentexecuted by the parties addressing David McDavid's intent to purchase the Atlanta Hawks, Atlanta Thrashers, and certain operating rights at Philips Arena did not preclude McDavid from holding Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. (TBS) liable for breach of an oral agreement.This time, the Hawks thought that they were on the winning side of a buzzer-beater deal, and the ultimate loss felt like the referee just missed a few contractual interpretation play calls.Nothing foreign to Georgia sports fans.While in sports it is a loss on a team's record, a missed chance at a national title, or a missed bonus on salaries, for TBS it was $ 281 million in damages.
In the deal world, material terms are constantly in limbo. It is imperative that the parties are able to negotiate and can appropriately bargain to meet the demands of each side so that all are satisfied in the end.Months-long negotiations and puffery are commonplace, and the understanding that material terms are notfinal until written and signed in an agreement is routine, especially in high-value transactionslike the sale of two major league sports teams and the operating rights to an arena in the commercial capital of the Southeast.
Many factors impact the trajectory of a given case: the questions of law at issue, the scope of discovery, the necessity of expert evidence--the list goes on.In matters of complex commercial and corporate disputes, complicated legal issues and extensive discovery are consistently in the frontcourt.Accordingly, to better address the complex issues embedded in business disputes, many states have incorporated specialized business courts within their state legal systems.The American specialized business court modeloriginated with the Delaware Court of Chancery,the nation's leading forum for corporate matters.Accordingly, every business court in the country is geared toward accomplishing one goal: providing an efficient, specialized forum for complex business disputes.But these courts differ significantly in jurisdictional reach, creating a high degree of variation in the number and kind of cases that reach each court's docket every year.Some courts annually accept cases in the low hundreds, while other courts, such as the Circuit Court of Cook County's Chancery Division in Chicago, accept up to 3,700 cases a year.Some courts mandate particular subject matter requirements, certain amount-in-controversythresholds, or more specific criteria and duties outlined in enabling legislation and local rules.
The basic limitations outlined in the different jurisdictional models employed by American business courts can be summarized in three categories: (1) courts with specific subject matter requirements and a specified amount-in-controversy requirement (the Baseline Model), (2) courts with complex business or commercial subject matter classification requirements (the Gatekeeping Model), and (3) courts following rules as outlined by enabling legislation and corresponding authority but with discretion to allow non-mandatory business cases onto the docket (the North Carolina Model).
The Georgia State-wide Business Court (GSBC) received approval from Georgia voters through a constitutional referendum in 2018.Shortly thereafter, the Georgia General Assembly crafted and passed the GSBC's enabling statute, and the court began officially hearing cases on August 3, 2020.The GSBC loosely follows a fusion of the Baseline Model and the North Carolina Model.The GSBC mandates specific subject matter requirements but provides supplemental jurisdiction over claims falling outside the statute's defined limitations, as well as an established amount-in-controversy requirement.
At the time of theTurnerdecision, Georgia did not yet have a statewide business court. Years later, in a joint hearing of theGeorgia House and Senate Judiciary Committees on August 14, 2019, the committees unanimously, and with bipartisan support, confirmed the appointment of Judge Walter W. Davis as the inaugural judge of the GSBC.Judge Davis began his term on January 1, 2020, making history as the first and, to date, only judge of the GSBC,a court with statewide, but limited, jurisdiction.The Georgia General Assembly included many restrictions within the GSBC's enabling statute "aimed at ensuring that smaller, less complex cases, among others," do not land on the court's docket.In creating the GSBC, the Georgia legislature intended for the court to balance having the "objectivity and predictability" of hearing cases focused on the enumerated subject matter requirements with the "subjectivity and flexibility" of determining which cases are "complex" commercial matters falling within its discretion.While the GSBC strikes a balance in terms of jurisdictional limitations encompassed by the three basic business court models, the GSBC deviates from the North Carolina Model on one foundational element: the Georgia court is a voluntary forum.This Note argues that the two-party consent rule in the GSBC's enabling statute-- which limits the GSBC's ability to exercise its subject-area expertise to only those instances in which both parties agree to litigate in the GSBC, without any judicial input in that decision--frustrates the GSBC's purpose by leaving cases with complex contractualinterpretation issues like those inTurnerto whichever court one party fancies.
Part II of this Note reviews the rationale for adopting specialized business courts in state court systems generally, highlighting the unique challenges involved in complex commercial and corporate disputes. Part III provides an in-depth review of the history and current structure of the GSBC and explores different limitations that litigants will face if the court's current voluntary structure remains unchanged. Part IV analyzes both the judicial and business interests that a statutory amendment allowing courts to transfer cases to the GSBC's docket sua sponte, regardless of the parties' desires, would offer. Part IV also discusses how cases such asTurnerare better resolved in specialized forums like the GSBC and the positive impact that this statutory amendment would have on business negotiations and investments in the state of Georgia. This Note concludes that the Georgia General Assembly should amend the GSBC's enabling statute to establish a more predictable business court that is able to use its expertise to the fullest, ultimately encouraging more businesses to choose Georgia as their home.

questions.question: Does making participation in a statewide specialized business court voluntary (requiring both parties' agreement) undermine the court's ability to resolve complex commercial disputes efficiently and predictably?

Would authorizing courts to transfer cases to a specialized business court sua sponte (without party consent) improve judicial efficiency, expertise-driven outcomes, and consistency in complex business litigation?
Does greater, predictable access to a specialized business court increase business confidence, investment, and the quality of commercial negotiations in the state?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: legal predictability and its importance for commercial transactions and investment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how automation and synchronous execution in smart contracts transform the nature of promises and affect forward‑looking obligations, raising concerns about predictability and enforceability, while Paper B foregrounds predictability and objectivity as key rationales for a specialized business court to foster reliable dispute resolution that encourages business negotiations and investment in the state.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Promissory Basis of Section 90.

papers.node_id: 39flastulrev563!!ARTICLE: BRINGING ORDER TO CONTRACTS AGAINST PUBLIC POLICY
papers.title: ARTICLE: BRINGING ORDER TO CONTRACTS AGAINST PUBLIC POLICY
papers.abstract:
"When they argued this case . . . it was said there was no consideration, and if there was it was illegal. . . . If it be illegal, it must be illegal either on the ground that it is against public policy, or against some particular law. I, for one, protest . . . against arguing too strongly upon public policy;-it is a very unruly horse, and when once you get astride it you never know where it will carry you. It may lead you from the sound law. It is never argued at all but when other points fail."
Judge Burrough's enduring "unruly horse" metaphor for the public policy defense to contractappears in contract literature,in contracttreatises,and in case law.When a party asks a court to refrain from enforcing an otherwise valid bargain on the grounds that it would offend public policy, the party asks the court to do something out of the ordinary. Instead of requesting the court to apply a traditional common law defense, the court is being asked to discern public policy, or possibly pronounce public policy. This can compel a court's reliance on statutes,regulations,prior case law proclaiming public policy serving as precedent,or as troublingly described by M.P. Furmston, reliance "on reasoning not convincingly or completely adumbrated."
This Article tests the "very unruly horse" metaphor to see if the description remains valid wisdom nearly two centuries later. No existing contracts literature empirically evaluates the content of the cases involving the public policy defense in a systematic manner. I attempt to partially fill that gap in the literature here. I hope to contribute to a more elegant structural understanding of the public policy defense by importing the case law as we find it, rather than by just providing a study of the "leading cases,"as some of the literature does. Essentially, this Article aims to provide another view of the defense-a view based on what courts are routinely doing, not based on what the most famous or leading cases say or what the Restatement (Second) of Contracts attempts to restate or prescribe.
Generally, I set out in this Article to find a simpler, more predictive way of categorizing the cases-to address, among other questions, whether some types of a challenge to enforceability on public policy grounds were more successful than others and whether certain categories were more orderly or "unruly" than others.

questions.question: Whether courts' refusal to enforce otherwise valid contracts for public-interest reasons is applied inconsistently or unpredictably across cases.
Whether some types of public-interest challenges to contract enforceability are more likely to succeed than others.
Whether routine judicial decisions refusing contract enforcement on public-interest grounds can be organized into a simpler, more predictive categorical framework based on empirical case patterns.

matched_themes: Are courts' refusals to enforce contracts on public-interest grounds applied predictably, and which categories of public-interest challenges are most likely to succeed?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 36wmmarylrev1379!!ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS
papers.title: ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS
papers.abstract:
0000*1379 Every American law student is well acquainted with the writing and thought of Benjamin N. Cardozo, the fox of American contract law. For over seventy years, his opinions have formed the basis for many discussions of doctrine, method, and policy in the traditional first-year curriculum.The current generation is also becoming well acquainted with the hedgehog of American contract law -- Richard A. Posner, whose opinions have been entering the domain of the core first-year curriculum in the past decade.
With the 1989 publication of the second edition of their casebook on contracts, Professors Calamari, Perillo, and Bender announced that, as a partial reflection of continuing changes in law and legal analysis, "the number of opinions by Richard Posner reproduced in this volume outnumber those of Benjamin 0000*1380 Cardozo."In 1988, Professors Farnsworth and Young had done the same thing, though without the fanfare.In 1992, Professors Hamilton, Rau, and Weintraub also quietly fell in line.While nine other contracts casebooks published since 1989 have kept Cardozo in the lead, a number of opinions by Judge Posner appear in most of them.Undoubtedly, Posner has made a mark on contracts scholarship and is increasingly making significant contributions to the doctrinal shape and texture of the contract law taught each year to virtually every law student across the country.
Despite Posner's growing reputation, however, Cardozo remains the judicial cynosure of contracts, having displaced Oliver Wendell Holmes as the avatar of the American common law of contractsand having exerted an influence on the law and teaching of the subject unmatched by any other modern jurist, including Stanley Fuld, Learned Hand, and Roger Traynor. Indeed, Posner recently published an elegant meditation on judicial eminence confirming that Cardozo is a judicial titan, the reasons for which Posner elucidated with characteristic erudition.Posner identified his work as a new genre called the critical judicial study, which he urged others to undertake.Posner's book, along with his own prominence in the law and teaching of contracts, provokes this comparative critique of the leading contracts opinions written by Judges Cardozo and Posner, each of whom has contributed significantly to the law and teaching of contracts.
0000*1381 Cardozo's judicial contributions to the law and teaching of contracts, including the good faith obligationand the doctrine of substantial performance,were achieved using a thickly textured doctrinalism involving conscious mediation amongst the competing values at stake in the law of contracts. His opinions reveal a capacious juridical framework capable of harmonizing the many contending concerns of contract law, including commercial certainty, freedom of contract, good faith, protecting the reasonable expectations of parties, and forfending interparty exploitation. Cardozo was at once master of the incremental evolution of the common law and servant of the imperative to adapt law to the needs of those it governs, evincing in his contracts opinions a fluid sense of doctrine and an animating principle of justice broadly conceived.The hallmark of his contracts opinions is balance. He was an intellectual fox.
Posner, of course, is still making contributions to the law of contracts, and it would be foolhardy to predict how important those contributions will turn out to be. Given his swift rise to prominence, however, his contributions likely will be important. In many cases, however, Posner's views are opposed to Cardozo's, or at least in tension with them. For example, whereas Cardozo minted the implied covenant of good faith in the performance of contracts,Posner is averse to any such implication and strongly resists recognizing any obligation of good faith, even where it is imposed by statute. Posner's contracts opinions are far less textured than Cardozo's, showing a reluctance to mediate amongst the many contending values contract law has traditionally implicated and instead putting into the mix only one primary concern -- efficiency through freedom of contract. Posner is an intellectual hedgehog.
0000*1382 Because the Posnerian framework is stricter and less capacious than the Cardozoean framework, this comparison of Cardozo and Posner is primarily a study in contrasts, as a matter of doctrine, theory, and style. Contracts opinions by Posner and Cardozo resemble one another in their creativity and ingenuity, but they employ the judicial craft within very different frameworks and with distinct normative ends. Cardozo and Posner are judicial antipodes. Indeed, were Posner's contributions to the law of contracts to rise to the level of Cardozo's, many of Cardozo's contributions, both substantive and textural, would have to be jettisoned. Although attempting to forecast the future path of contract law is replete with obvious and insurmountable problems, one thing is clear. Should Posner's contributions to the law of contracts achieve the broad acceptance and application that Cardozo's have, the texture and substance of contract law will be very different indeed.
Whether that evolution of contract law should be welcomed or thwarted ultimately depends on one's own normative views. For example, and at the risk of oversimplifying, one may prefer a conception of contract that limits itself to interests in freedom of contract and efficiency, one that presupposes that people behave, or can be made to behave, as rational economic actors and therefore prefer a Posnerian approach. Or one may prefer a conception of contract that seeks to balance values, such as good faith, fairness, or reasonable expectations, in addition to freedom of contract and efficiency and that conceives of people as socialized actors and therefore prefer a Cardozoean approach. It should be recognized, however, that such preferences entail significant consequences for the way contract law is understood and taught and that the widespread and continued reproduction of Posner's opinions in the casebooks stands both to reflect and shape that understanding. This comparative critique is written in the spirit of opening up perspectives about such consequences.Along the way, moreover, this discussion is also an opportunity to explore many interesting aspects of contract doctrine and theory, 0000*1383 treated in very different ways by two of this century's most luminous judges.
Before beginning the comparative critique, Part I first presents statistical evidence of Cardozo's and Posner's prominence in the law and teaching of contracts. This evidence is drawn from a survey of contracts opinions reproduced in contemporary contracts casebooks.It shows that Cardozo is the most important judge in the law and teaching of contracts, followed by Roger Traynor and then Posner.Cardozo's lofty perch and Posner's ascendancy make comparative critiques like the one that follows Part I particularly important.

questions.question: How do two contrasting judicial philosophies-one that balances multiple normative values and another that prioritizes efficiency and freedom of contract-differ in their doctrinal, theoretical, and stylistic approaches to contract law?

How prominent are these two judicial voices in contemporary contract law education (as reflected by the selection of opinions in casebooks), and how might their relative prominence shape the way contract law is understood and taught?
What would be the likely substantive and pedagogical consequences for contract law if the efficiency-focused judicial approach were to displace the multi-value balancing approach?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How do casebook selection practices and pedagogical choices (e.g., using multi-issue appellate cases or emphasizing litigation realities) shape students' understanding of contract law and practice?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81notredamelrev747!!ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW AS AN ITERATIVE PROCESS: A PRELIMINARY INQUIRY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW AS AN ITERATIVE PROCESS: A PRELIMINARY INQUIRY

shared_topics.topic: limits and influence of judicial discretion in shaping common law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the common law's iterative, path-dependent structure constrains the systemic significance of individual judges' discretion, while Paper B compares Cardozo and Posner to show how differing judicial styles and choices can nonetheless have durable, doctrinally transformative effects in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: how precedent and path-dependence produce continuity and constrain change in doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a theory of the common law as an iterative, path-dependent process where initial cases constrain later outcomes, and Paper B documents and theorizes how longstanding authorities (e.g., Cardozo) versus emerging voices (e.g., Posner) shape the trajectory of contract doctrine over time.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between underlying social norms/values and doctrinal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that social norms are absorbed into the common law and can drive non-self-similar departures from prior rule applications, while Paper B contrasts Cardozo's balancing of norms like good faith and fairness with Posner's efficiency-centered approach to show how normative commitments affect contract decisions.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms and forms of doctrinal change (incremental evolution versus decisive shifts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explains change via concepts like self-similarity and judicial bifurcation that allow the system to shift course, and Paper B contrasts Cardozo's incremental, textured doctrinalism with Posner's more parsimonious, potentially paradigm-shifting framework in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the empirical and interpretive role of case selection and case law study in understanding legal development
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for close, case-by-case study to apprehend the common law's complexity and rhythms, while Paper B uses empirical analysis of contracts casebooks and reproduced opinions to trace which judges and decisions influence teaching and doctrinal trajectories.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 32connlrev1699!!SYMPOSIUM: An Uncertain Trumpet: A Gloss on Kirksey v. Kirksey
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: An Uncertain Trumpet: A Gloss on Kirksey v. Kirksey

shared_topics.topic: judicial reasoning and opinion style in contract decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the doctrinal and rhetorical styles of Cardozo (nuanced, balancing reasoning) and Posner (economics-driven, narrower reasoning), while Paper B close-reads the terse rhetoric and idiosyncratic phrasing of the Kirksey opinion to reveal how judicial voice and brevity shape outcomes and perceptions of legitimacy.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of familial or gratuitous promises (consideration versus reliance and implied obligations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats debates over when courts should recognize implied duties or obligations (e.g., Cardozo's willingness to protect expectations and imply duties versus Posner's resistance), and Paper B examines Kirksey as a paradigmatic dispute over whether a family promise is a mere gratuity or supported by consideration/reliance and therefore enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: the role of canonical cases and casebooks in shaping first-year contracts pedagogy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical evidence about the frequency of Cardozo and Posner opinions in contemporary contracts casebooks and their influence on teaching, while Paper B explicitly discusses Kirksey's status as a memorable family-correspondence case in first-year curricula and its treatment in casebooks and treatises.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formalist doctrine and equitable/justice-oriented outcomes in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames Cardozo as a justice- and balance-oriented judge versus Posner's formal efficiency focus, and Paper B highlights the Kirksey majority/dissent dynamic as an instance of conflict between strict doctrinal refusal to enforce a promise and a morally sympathetic, justice-driven willingness to find consideration or remedy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev947!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: The Democratization of Contract Law: The Case of Mutual Promises
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: The Democratization of Contract Law: The Case of Mutual Promises

shared_topics.topic: judicial role in developing contract doctrine (how judges create and shape doctrines like good faith, substantial performance, and consideration)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Cardozo's and Posner's judicial craft and methods in producing major contract doctrines, while Paper B traces early judicial decisions that established mutual promises as valid consideration, showing both papers focus on courts as primary agents of doctrinal change.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for enforcing promises — party autonomy/trust and fairness versus efficiency and freedom of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a debate between a Cardozoean balance of good faith, fairness, and reasonable expectations and a Posnerian efficiency/freedom-of-contract approach, and Paper B defends enforcement of mutual promises as democratizing by crediting party trust and autonomy, engaging the same normative fault-lines.

shared_topics.topic: historical shifts in what contract law enforces (from property/service/formalism to enforcement of mutual promises) and the consequences for modern doctrine and teaching
shared_topics.justification: Paper B documents the sixteenth-century move away from property-based limitations to enforcement of reciprocal promises, and Paper A documents contemporary shifts in doctrinal emphasis and pedagogy (e.g., Posner displacing Cardozo in casebooks), so both examine doctrinal evolution and its pedagogical or institutional effects.

shared_topics.topic: the courts' role in protecting parties' reasonable expectations and preventing exploitation through doctrines that give effect to bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Cardozo's concern with protecting reasonable expectations and guarding against interparty exploitation via doctrines like good faith and substantial performance, while Paper B emphasizes how enforcing mutual promises empowered parties and validated their reciprocal expectations, connecting both works on the protective function of contract doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68ohiostlj71!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Myth of Precontractual Reliance
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Myth of Precontractual Reliance

shared_topics.topic: judicial opinions as primary drivers of contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how a single judicial decision (Hoffman v. Red Owl) was taken as doctrinal touchstone and how courts actually apply promissory estoppel in subsequent decisions, while Paper B compares the doctrinal influence of major judges (Cardozo and Posner) and how their opinions have shaped the substance of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of case selection and publication in shaping legal education and perceived law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes how Hoffman’s prominence in casebooks and commentary has distorted practitioners’ understanding of precontractual reliance, and Paper B empirically examines which judges’ opinions (Cardozo vs. Posner) appear in contracts casebooks and the implications for teaching and doctrinal perception.

shared_topics.topic: doctrines that enforce expectations outside a formal bargain (promissory estoppel and implied obligations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on promissory estoppel and the circumstances under which courts will impose liability for precontractual reliance, while Paper B discusses doctrines such as the implied covenant of good faith and contrasts Cardozo’s willingness to recognize implied obligations with Posner’s resistance—both engaging the question of when courts should enforce nonbargained expectations.

shared_topics.topic: methodological approaches to discovering and justifying contract rules (case-by-case balancing vs systematic/efficiency frameworks)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates reading cases systematically rather than inferring doctrine from isolated rulings and scrutinizes factual narratives underlying judicial decisions, while Paper B critiques and contrasts Cardozo’s value-balancing, contextual method with Posner’s efficiency-driven, principled approach to judicial reasoning in contract disputes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45wakeforestlrev607!!ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: efficiency‑oriented versus balancing/contextual interpretive frameworks in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A juxtaposes Posner's efficiency‑and‑freedom focus against Cardozo's capacious, value‑balancing approach to contract doctrine; Paper B frames the debate as a choice between acontextual/formalist rules and high‑context interpretive strategies that incorporate social, economic, and relational factors.

shared_topics.topic: expansion or contraction of judicial discretion and variability of outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows Cardozo's methodology as permitting broad judicial mediation among competing values while Posner's framework narrows the considerations courts will weigh; Paper B argues that adopting high‑context analyses expands judicial discretion and increases outcome variability in contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal choices' effects on bargaining power and protection of vulnerable parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Cardozo's doctrines (e.g., good faith, protection of reasonable expectations) as protective of weaker parties with Posner's libertarian/efficiency tilt that can favor stronger repeat players; Paper B contends that contextualist doctrines are often motivated by — and will produce — shifts in bargaining power toward disadvantaged classes like consumers, employees, and franchisees.

shared_topics.topic: role of implied obligations and extralegal/contextual factors in interpreting and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the implied covenant of good faith (Cardozo's innovation versus Posner's resistance) as a central doctrinal divide over reading obligations beyond explicit terms; Paper B analyzes the use of party status, trade usage, performance circumstances, and other extralegal context as grounds for enforcing the parties' 'real' bargain rather than only the paper terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103nwulrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretive methodology and its normative grounding
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly compares Cardozo's capacious, balancing doctrinal method with Posner's efficiency-driven, narrower framework, while Paper B analyzes how competing interpretive theories (originalism, construction) and theories of legitimacy determine how judges should construe constitutional text.

shared_topics.topic: when and whether judges should imply terms or obligations into written texts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on Cardozo's invention of implied duties (e.g., the covenant of good faith) versus Posner's reluctance to imply obligations, and Paper B treats the distinction between express and implied-in-fact terms and whether background assumptions may be used to supply implied content to constitutional provisions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of background assumptions and extra-textual values in fixing meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether contract law should incorporate values like good faith, reasonable expectations, or solely efficiency, whereas Paper B critiques the use of historical background assumptions to determine original constitutional meaning and explores when such assumptions legitimately inform interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: consequences of judicial approaches for doctrinal development and legal practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how differing judicial philosophies (Cardozo v. Posner) would reshape contract doctrine and legal education if one approach predominates, and Paper B examines how differing theories of construction and legitimacy produce divergent long-term effects on constitutional doctrine and governance.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recent Defenses of Consideration: Commodification and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: competing normative justifications for contract law (efficiency/freedom of contract versus moral/balancing approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly contrasts Posner's efficiency- and freedom-of-contract-centered framework with Cardozo's balancing approach that emphasizes good faith, fairness, and reasonable expectations; Paper B engages the same fault-line by weighing instrumental/economic reasons for enforcing bargains against Kantian moral accounts (Markovits) and other moral considerations that might counsel different enforcement rules.

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope of enforceability of promises (when the law should enforce bargains versus nonbargain/ donative promises or imply duties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes doctrines that expand or limit enforceability (e.g., Cardozo's implied covenant of good faith and substantial performance versus Posner's resistance to such implications), while Paper B directly debates whether donative promises should be enforceable under the requirement of consideration and whether legal sanctions should be withheld from gifts.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules affect or should respect social and moral practices (e.g., commodification of gifts, reasonable expectations, good faith)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B raises the worry that enforcing donative promises would 'commodify' the world of gift and undermine social practices around giving, and Paper A discusses Cardozo's concern for protecting reasonable expectations and preserving relational/moral dimensions of contracting (good faith) as distinct from a strictly commodifying, market-oriented approach.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of judges and scholars in shaping contract doctrine and pedagogy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides empirical and doctrinal discussion of how Cardozo's and Posner's opinions shape teaching and the substantive texture of contract law, and Paper B is a scholarly engagement with influential academics (Eisenberg, Markovits) whose novel arguments seek to reconceptualize core doctrines like consideration, thereby aiming to influence doctrine and debate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 120pennstlrev477!!ARTICLE: Charitable Pledges: Contracts of Confusion
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Charitable Pledges: Contracts of Confusion

shared_topics.topic: when courts should imply or enforce obligations in the absence of explicit contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Cardozo's readiness to imply doctrines like a covenant of good faith and substantial performance with Posner's resistance to implied obligations, while Paper B examines courts' readiness to enforce ambiguous charitable pledges (via contract doctrines, unilateral-contract theories, or promissory estoppel) despite lack of clear, explicit promise language.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate normative framework for adjudicating contract disputes (efficiency vs fairness/balanced values)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the debate as Cardozo's balanced, justice-oriented approach versus Posner's efficiency/freedom-of-contract focus, and Paper B criticizes current doctrines for producing unfair results (and perverse incentives for charities), proposing a reform that better respects donor intent and equity rather than purely enforcement-maximizing rules.

shared_topics.topic: judicial creativity, fictions, and doctrine-shaping in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how different judges' styles and methodological choices (textured doctrinal mediation versus streamlined economic reasoning) shape contract law, and Paper B catalogs and criticizes the 'twisted legal theories' and judicial fictions courts use to make charitable pledges enforceable, showing how judicial reasoning constructs doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of empirical evidence to assess and motivate doctrinal critique or reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents empirical survey evidence about which judges' opinions are reproduced in contracts casebooks to demonstrate doctrinal influence, and Paper B provides new empirical data on pledge-form language prevalence (≈95% ambiguity) to document the practical scope of the problem and motivate a change in enforcement rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78valrev1045!!ARTICLE: THE PROMISSORY BASIS OF PAST CONSIDERATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PROMISSORY BASIS OF PAST CONSIDERATION.

shared_topics.topic: why courts enforce certain promises (promissory enforcement vs restitutionary grounds)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes cases where courts enforce promises made in recognition of moral obligation and argues that courts are enforcing the promissory commitment itself rather than an underlying restitutionary claim; Paper B engages this question more broadly by contrasting judicial philosophies (Cardozo vs Posner) that drive why judges accept or reject particular bases for enforcing contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal versus policy frameworks that guide contract law (balancing values vs efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes prevailing restitution-centered accounts and proposes a promisor-focused, contract-theory explanation for enforcement choices, while Paper B explicitly contrasts Cardozo's value-balancing, doctrinal approach with Posner's single-minded efficiency/freedom-of-contract policy lens, showing how different frameworks produce different outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of expectation interests and remedies (expectancy vs reliance vs restitution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds Fuller and Perdue's expectancy and reliance interests and documents that courts often award expectation damages even in 'moral obligation' or Section 90 cases, whereas Paper B highlights Cardozo's emphasis on protecting reasonable expectations (and doctrines like substantial performance) versus Posner's skepticism, tying judicial theory to remedial consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the judicial role in shaping enforceability through case law and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how courts use doctrines (e.g., Section 90, promissory estoppel, moral-obligation cases) and judicial screening to decide which promises to enforce, and Paper B is a comparative study of two judges whose opinions (Cardozo's and Posner's) have materially shaped contract doctrine and thus the enforceability of promises.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68iowalrev699!!ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications

shared_topics.topic: judicial adaptation of contract doctrine to unforeseen, real-world circumstances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts have evolved rules (e.g., relaxing the preexisting-duty rule and invoking the Restatement) to allow post-contract modifications when unforeseen events make original performance impractical, and Paper B contrasts Cardozo's capacious, incremental judicial approach (adapting doctrine to meet parties' needs) with Posner's more constrained framework, thereby directly engaging the question of how judges should adapt contract law to real-world change.

shared_topics.topic: the role of good faith and doctrines to deter opportunism or extortionate demands
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on distinguishing legitimate renegotiation from extorted promises and the law's interest in discountenancing opportunism, while Paper B treats the implied covenant of good faith as a core doctrinal battleground (Cardozo favoring good-faith protections and Posner resisting them), so both examine how doctrines like good faith operate to police opportunistic conduct in performance and modification contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the conflict between formalist rules (consideration/preexisting-duty) and flexible equitable standards (Restatement fairness, substantial performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the rigid preexisting-duty/consideration rule and discusses courts' move toward flexible standards (e.g., Restatement (Second) permitting modifications in unanticipated circumstances), and Paper B contrasts doctrinal styles—Cardozo's flexible, value-mediating holdings (e.g., substantial performance) versus Posner's stricter rules—thereby engaging the same debate over formal rules versus equitable, pragmatic standards.

shared_topics.topic: competing normative frameworks for enforcement: efficiency/freedom of contract versus fairness/reasonable expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames enforcement choices in terms of promoting planning and efficient reliance while warning against enforcing extorted transfers that merely reallocate wealth, and Paper B explicitly frames Cardozo and Posner as embodying competing normative visions (balancing good faith and reasonable expectations versus prioritizing efficiency and freedom of contract), so both grapple with how normative commitments should shape contract enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58ucinlrev1283!!ARTICLE: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: conflict between an efficiency/law-and-economics approach and doctrines emphasizing good faith, fairness, or relational obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Posner's efficiency-focused, law-and-economics approach with Cardozo's emphasis on good faith, reasonable expectations, and balancing multiple values; Paper B treats law-and-economics (neoclassical contract) as one of the major competing frameworks and analyzes how relational, critical, and other theories challenge its dominance.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial opinions and scholarly theory shape contract doctrine and legal education
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents the growing presence of Posner's opinions (versus Cardozo's) in contracts casebooks and traces judges' influence on teaching and doctrine; Paper B argues that competing contract theories fundamentally reframe the content and practice of contract law, affecting how scholars, judges, and practitioners understand and teach the subject.

shared_topics.topic: the methodological debate over doctrinal pragmatism versus systematic theory in resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A juxtaposes Cardozo's 'thickly textured doctrinalism' and incremental common-law reasoning with Posner's call for critical judicial study and theory-driven efficiency analysis; Paper B examines the broader proliferation of abstract contract theories and the backlash from proponents of pragmatic, flexible doctrine, treating this as a methodological crisis in legal scholarship.

shared_topics.topic: the normative consequences of adopting different theoretical frameworks for contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that widespread acceptance of Posner's framework would substantially alter the substance and texture of contract law (e.g., reducing doctrines like implied good faith), while Paper B argues that choosing between neoclassical and alternative theories has deep implications for what problems are recognized and how contract law should be reformed.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 70washlrev1019!!ARTICLE: WHAT TO DO WHEN THERE'S NO "I DO": A MODEL FOR AWARDING DAMAGES UNDER PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHAT TO DO WHEN THERE'S NO "I DO": A MODEL FOR AWARDING DAMAGES UNDER PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL

shared_topics.topic: judicial lawmaking and the courts' role in shaping contract doctrine and remedies

papers.abstract: I am told at times by friends that a judicial opinion has no business to be literature.

papers.node_id: 2020michstlrev547!!ARTICLE: CHALLENGING LAND CONTRACTING ON THE BASIS OF DISPARATE IMPACT AFTER TEXAS DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING AND COMMUNITY AFFAIRS V. INCLUSIVE COMMUNITIES PROJECT, INC.: A VIABLE OPTION OR A DEAD END?
papers.title: ARTICLE: CHALLENGING LAND CONTRACTING ON THE BASIS OF DISPARATE IMPACT AFTER TEXAS DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING AND COMMUNITY AFFAIRS V. INCLUSIVE COMMUNITIES PROJECT, INC.: A VIABLE OPTION OR A DEAD END?
papers.abstract:
When Clyde Ross purchased his home in the North Lawndale neighborhood of Chicago in 1961, he saw it as the last step in his journey toward the American dream.Ross, a Black man, moved toChicago from Clarksdale, Mississippi to escape the terror that governed the lives of people of color in the South.When he arrived in Chicago, he attempted to get a Federal Housing Administration (FHA)-backed mortgage but was told there was no financing available.When he found his home in North Lawndale, he purchased the home "on contract," meaning the seller kept the deed for the house until he paid the contractual monthly payments in full.Per the terms of his contract, if Ross missed a single payment, he would immediately forfeit his $ 1,000 down payment, all of the monthly payments he made on the contract, and all of the money he spent improving and maintaining the property.Unlike most contract buyers, Ross eventually made every required payment on his contract and came to own his house in full; however, in the end, he had paid $ 27,500 for a home that the previous owner--a white man who peddled similar contracts around predominantly Black neighborhoods in Chicago--had bought for $ 12,000.
Fifty years later, in 2011, another Black man named Zachary Anderson saw a "SALE" sign in the front yard of a small bungalow in Capitol Park, a predominately Black neighborhood in Atlanta.He had always wanted to own a home but could never qualify for traditional financing or save enough money for a down payment.A representative from Harbor Portfolios, the owner of the property, gave Anderson the key to a lockbox on the property and told him to take a look around.He noticed that the house needed some work but felt like he could make most of the improvements himself.The representative told Anderson he could purchase the home, which Harbor Portfolios said was worth $ 46,750, by paying a $ 1,000 deposit and signing a contract.The contract provided that if he missed a single payment, he would forfeit all the money he had paid to Harbor Portfolios.Furthermore, it also said that he was responsible for all taxes and expenses for the property--all while Harbor Portfolios retained title to the house.A year later, after falling behind on payments while he was hospitalized after being injured at work, Anderson received an eviction notice from Harbor Portfolios.Determined to keep the valuehe had added to the home, he caught up on his payments, but he continued to struggle to stay current while paying for the maintenance and improvements of a home he did not actually own.Anderson will not actually own his home until he makes the last payment on the contract.
Land contracting, which allows contract sellers to retain title to a piece of property until a contract buyer makes a certain number of monthly payments, is not new.During the second wave of the Great Migration between 1940 and 1970, thousands of families of color in the Midwest who fled the Jim Crow South, like Clyde Ross and his family, fell victim to predatory land contracts because they were systematically excluded from the legitimate, government-backed housing market.Discrimination in both private mortgage lending and government agencies tasked with insuring mortgages made the traditional American dream of home ownership nearly impossible for people of color.Decades later, predatory land contract sellers continued to target low-income families of color through the 2000s.The void left in predominately minority neighborhoods following the foreclosure crisis and Great Recession in 2008 created a ripe environment for predatory land contracts to reappear as a device that disadvantages low-income people of color like Zachary Anderson.
In the midst of land contracting's resurgence among low-income and minority communities, the Supreme Court decidedTexas Department of Housing & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.In deciding whether the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs's allocation of housing tax credits had a disparate impact on Black residents of Dallas, the Court announced that disparate impact claims were cognizable under the Fair Housing Act.Some Fair Housing advocates and scholars cautiously celebrated the ruling as a victory, saying that the ruling presented a return to a progressive interpretation of the disparate impact doctrine.While the ruling solidifiedclaimants' ability to bring disparate impact claims under the Fair Housing Act, it is unclear whether it gave them any greater chance of being successful because of how the Court interpreted the traditional burden-shifting test used in disparate impact claims.This interpretation of the test requires that after a plaintiff shows a prima facie case of discriminatory effect, a defendant can rebut the prima face case by showing that a challenged practice is necessary to achieve a valid interest.Under this iteration of the burden-shifting test, nearly any viable interest can serve as a reason for enacting a practice that may have a discriminatory effect on minorities.These "cautionary standards" set forth inInclusive Communitiesmake it difficult for disparate impact claimants to win and weaken the ability of the doctrine to remedy covert discrimination.
With land contracting returning to the national spotlight and continuing to have a disproportionate impact on low-income people and minorities, challenging the practice on disparate impact grounds seems like a logical fit.Fair Housing nonprofits, governmental actors, or land contract buyers could sue land contract sellers under the Fair Housing Act on disparate impact grounds.Despite the Supreme Court's recent ruling inInclusive Communities, however, litigants face an uphill battle bringing a disparate impact claim.They face this battle in part because the burden-shifting test the Court applied inInclusive Communitiesmakes it nearly impossible for disparate impact claims to survive summary judgment.
TheInclusive Communitiestest is not the first test the Supreme Court used to apply the disparate impact doctrine.Previous iterations of the burden-shifting test, such as the test set forth in the 1975 employment discrimination caseAlbemarle Paper Co. v. Moody, placed a greater burden on disparate impact defendants to show that a practice disparately impacting minorities was absolutely necessary to achieve its goals.While claimants challenging land contracting on disparate impact grounds would not likely succeed under theInclusiveCommunitiestest, they could succeed under a framework similar to that set forth inAlbemarleif courts applied that framework to a disparate impact claim under the Fair Housing Act.TheAlbemarletest, which places a greater burden on the defendant than the test inInclusive Communities, would give claimants who challenge land contract practices on disparate impact grounds better chances of success and would better comply with legislative intent behind the Fair Housing Act.Furthermore, using this test could create precedent that could effectively address the racially discriminatory nature of predatory land contracting and stop the practice on a large scale.
This Comment explores how land contracts operate as a racialized practice in the modern legal landscape and how the resurgence of the practice mirrors its racially discriminatory roots.Additionally, it discusses whether challenging land contracts on a disparate impact basis is a viable litigation strategy afterInclusiveCommunities.In Part I, this Comment provides background and historical information about what a land contract is, how buyers and sellers have used land contracts in the United States, and the predatory nature of land contracts.In Part II, this Comment provides context about the development of the disparate impact doctrine, discusses its evolution in several key Supreme Court cases, and explores the evolution of the burden-shifting test prior to the Court's most recent interpretation inInclusive Communities.In Part III, this Comment analyzes whether challenging the practice of land contracting on disparate impact grounds under the Fair Housing Act is viable given the current state of the doctrine.Part III then argues that returning to a burden-shifting test similar to the one the Court applied inAlbemarlewould allow a disparate impact claim under the Fair Housing Act against land contract sellers to survive.

Whether courts applying a more plaintiff-favorable standard-one that forces defendants to justify that a challenged practice is truly necessary-would materially increase plaintiffs' chances of prevailing against predatory land contract sellers and better remedy racialized harms.

papers.node_id: 2016michstlrev1267!!ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?
papers.title: ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?
papers.abstract:
It seems obvious that we should apply the law of gifts to charitable donations. Unfortunately, this obvious approach has caused disasters in situations involving naming rightsover charitable buildings and other properties.
For example, in one case, a court's choice of gift law over contract law allowed a donor who contributed only $ 50,000 of the initial $ 150,000 needed to build a university dormitory to recover over $ 1.2 million from the school when the school removed the donor's name.Even more disturbing, this donor contributed nothing to a $ 2.5 million renovation of the dormitory,and this donor had enjoyed the exclusive naming rights for eighty years.
In another case, an elderly donor contributed her life savings to a hospital.She expected the hospital to establish a lasting tribute to her deceased grandfather in connection with the donation,but she failed to express that intent at the appropriate time. Under the law of gifts, the court concluded that the hospital could keep all the money without honoring the donor, her grandfather, or anybody else, in any way.Despite noting the hospital's "callousness" and its failure to "take great care to see that [the donation] was adequatelyrecognized," the court concluded that under the law of gifts it could not provide any remedy for the elderly donor or her family.
Also, in a headline-grabbing story, a sophisticated charity's failure to negotiate a reasonable duration for building naming rights cost the charity and its patrons dearly. In 1973, Lincoln Center was renovating its philharmonic hall. It accepted a $ 10.5 million donation from Avery Fisher, and it granted him perpetual naming rights.In 2002, when Lincoln Center needed to renovate the hall again, the Fisher family threatened legal action to prevent renaming.The end result was that Lincoln Center delayed the renovation for over a decade while thousands of patrons, and many performing artists, endured the outdated, shabby facilities. In addition, when the parties finally settled in 2014, Lincoln Center paid the Fisher family $ 15 million along with various perks.Amazingly, soon after the settlement with the Fishers, Lincoln Center made the same mistake again. It agreed that a new donor contributing approximately 20% of the cost of the concert hall's renovation in 2015 would haveperpetualnaming rights over the renovated concert hall.
This Article asserts that for these transactions the parties and the courts should embrace contract law, rather than the law of gifts, to minimize disputes and reach more reasonable results. Charitable naming rights are controversial. They are very popular with charities. Behavioral-economics research indicates that "publicity [sharply] increases charitable giving in [the] aggregate"and that "anonymity . . . causes low contributions."On the other hand, moralist and armchair philosophers criticize the practice. These critics assert thatpublicity "contaminat[es] the spirit of philanthropy,"and they maintain that anonymous giving is more virtuous.Others stake out a middle ground, such as the art columnist who wrote, "[I]n the nine circles of hell that are nonprofit fundraising, surely the mildest sin is allowing benefactors to attach their names to parts of buildings . . . . [W]hat real harm is done by giving these donors a lift?"
Despite some criticism, the practice has exploded since the mid-1990s.Today, perhaps "less than one percent of [substantial] charitable gifts are anonymous."Surprisingly, there is scant legal scholarship on the negotiation and enforcement of these popular arrangements.
The judicial treatment of charitable pledges and naming rights has been controversial and confusing.Commentators often criticize Justice Cardozo's landmark opinion on this topic.Courts may treat these arrangements as gifts, charitable trusts, or contracts.The legal characterization can turn on the intentions of the donor, and those intentions can be multifaceted, opaque, or indecipherable.
Charities and donors sometimes appear perplexed when structuring these financial transactions.For example, charities frequently offer and grant perpetual naming rights for properties that will need to be renovated in twenty or thirty years, setting the stage for a conflict among the parties and their successors when the charity needs to grant naming rights to a big donor to underwrite a substantial part of the renovation.Also, donors and charities frequently fail to specify exit mechanisms if the misdeeds of thedonor, a related person, or the charity render the arrangement embarrassing for one side.
This Article focuses on the choice between contract law or gift law in structuring and enforcing these arrangements. In a future article, I plan to reconcile the treatment of these arrangements as contracts for state law purposes with their treatment as tax-deductible gifts for federal income tax purposes. A scholar has already examined the application of trust law principles to older charitable naming rights arrangements when the donor has made all the promised donations, but the charity wishes to remove the donor's name.Accordingly, this Article will discuss trust principles sparingly.
Part I of this Article briefly describes the creative,controversial, and expanding charitable naming rights market. Offering naming rights as a fundraising tool has spread from educational organizations to all types of nonprofits including hospitals, museums, zoos, social service organizations, and even our national parks.Naming opportunities seem limited only by the boundaries of human imagination. Donors emblazon their names on all sorts of real and personal property from the otter playground at the Louisville Zooto the restrooms at Harvard Law School, the University of Colorado at Boulder, and the Museum of Modern Art in Manhattan.Donors name even the quarterback or linebacker positions on college football teams.
Part II analyzes when courts choose to classify charitable naming rights transactions as (i) gifts or (ii) contracts. The focus is on the largely ignored case law categorizing these transactions. This Part also discusses the case law from other honor or glory markets, including the baby-name market in which money is paid for the right to name a child, and the embarrassing secrets market in which hush money keeps secrets under wraps.
Part III explores negotiating opportunities for charities and donors structuring charitable naming rights contracts. It also explores options for courts in resolving disputes. The Part focuses on the practices and doctrines available under contract law that can avoid the disasters encountered with the law of gifts.
The conclusion highlights potential benefits for charities, donors, and courts in choosing contract law and practices in this area. Contract practices can introduce flexibility in structuring key terms such as the duration of naming rights for property that will eventually need renovation and morals clauses for when the donor or the charity threatens to tarnish the other's reputation. Also, courts would have greater flexibility in resolving disputes. For example, if the parties fail to agree on an important term such as the duration for the naming rights to a building, under contract law the court may be able to supply a reasonable duration mechanism.

questions.question: Should charitable naming-rights transactions be legally characterized and enforced as contracts rather than as gifts?
Does treating naming-rights transactions as contracts (instead of gifts) reduce disputes and lead to more reasonable, flexible remedies and outcomes for donors and charities?

What contractual design and negotiation practices for naming-rights arrangements (e.g., duration limits, exit mechanisms, reputational clauses) best minimize future conflicts between donors, charities, and their successors?

matched_themes: Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When and how should charitable pledges be enforceable?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How should the law characterize and enforce charitable pledges and naming-rights transactions: as enforceable contracts, as gifts, or via a special doctrinal category?
Does treating naming-rights, charitable donations, or licensing transactions as contracts rather than gifts or property promote better outcomes for donors, charities, or collaborative communities?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: whether charitable fundraising arrangements (naming rights, pledges) should be characterized and enforced as contracts rather than gifts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that naming-rights transactions should be governed by contract law to avoid the inequities and rigidities of gift law, and Paper B similarly critiques current judicial fictions and proposes enforcing pledges only when they are binding under ordinary contract/promissory-estoppel principles or when the donor clearly intended enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: the role of donor intent and evidentiary standards in determining enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that donor intentions in naming-rights deals are often multifaceted and indeterminate and that courts' reliance on intent produces inconsistent outcomes, while Paper B proposes a clear-and-convincing evidentiary rule to identify when a pledge-maker intended legal obligation.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrines and legal fictions used to enforce charitable commitments (consideration, promissory estoppel, trusts)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts invoke doctrines like consideration, promissory estoppel, and trust principles to uphold or recharacterize charitable gifts and pledges, and both criticize these doctrines as producing confusing or unjust results in the charitable-fundraising context.

shared_topics.topic: contract drafting, disclosure, and institutional practices to reduce disputes and perverse incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends using contract techniques (duration clauses, morals clauses, exit mechanisms) when negotiating naming-rights, and Paper B presents empirical evidence that pledge forms usually fail to disclose enforceability and proposes reforms to drafting and disclosure to eliminate incentives to mislead donors.

shared_topics.topic: policy consequences of current legal treatment for donors and charities (perverse incentives, litigation, and harms to charitable missions)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles document concrete harms from the existing approach—e.g., costly litigation, donors recovering disproportionate sums, delayed renovations, charities using vague pledge forms—and argue that clearer legal rules would better protect donors, charities, and the public purposes they serve.

shared_topics.topic: reliance on contract doctrines to supply terms, remedies, or fill gaps in transactions

shared_topics.topic: normative question of whether courts should adopt or defer to particular doctrinal frameworks

shared_topics.topic: the need for clearer transactional drafting, negotiation, or legislative/doctrinal reform to avoid disputes

shared_topics.topic: critical case‑law analysis as the primary method for diagnosing doctrinal failures
