papers.node_id: 120pennstlrev477!!ARTICLE: Charitable Pledges: Contracts of Confusion
papers.title: ARTICLE: Charitable Pledges: Contracts of Confusion
papers.abstract:
"The law of charitable [pledging] has been a prolific source of confusion."
Imagine that Transparency-Challenged Charity ("T.C. Charity") provided its donors with a multi-year pledgeform that fails to state whether the pledge is legally binding. New empirical evidence developedfor this Article indicates this occurs 95 percent of the time.If Generous Giver ("Generous") signs the pledge form and makes the first pledge payment, in which of the following situations will Generous be legally obligated to make all of the scheduled pledge payments?
a. Investigative reports reveal that T.C. Charity officials have been billing the charity to fund their outrageously extravagant lifestyles.Generous, who has supported T.C. Charity for years, feels betrayed, stops funding T.C. Charity, and begins supporting a different charity.
b. T.C. Charity owns and operates a hospital, and a new survey reveals that it provides a disturbingly small amount of charity care for the poor and aggressively tries to collect its fees from low-income individuals.Generous is disappointed and would prefer to support a more merciful hospital.
c. T.C. Charity owns and operates a high school, and when Generous signed the pledge the high school was in an area accessible for inner-city youths. T.C. Charity subsequently relocates the entire high school campus to an affluent suburb miles away.Generous would prefer to support a high school accessible to inner-city youth rather than supporting a high school catering to wealthy families.
d. T.C. Charity owns and operates an all-female college, and Generous made the pledge because the school did a fine job educating her eldest daughter. News reports recently reveal that many all-femalecolleges are welcoming transgender individualsbut T.C. Charity is not among them. Generous stops contributing to T.C. Charity and instead makes an identical pledge to support a more inclusive college.
e. Generous made the pledge when her youngest daughter was attending the local high school owned and operated by T.C. Charity. Subsequently, Generous' job requires that she and her family relocate. Her daughter now attends a different high school, and Generous would prefer to donate to her daughter's new high school.
f. T.C. Charity's mission is to feed the poor, but a new survey reveals that T.C. Charity incurs significantly higher administrative and other overhead costs compared to other charities performing the same function. Generous would prefer that her donations support a charity providing greater benefits to the poor.
g. T.C. Charity conducts medical research on a disease, and Generous made the pledge when she was still grieving the death of her mother from that disease. Now, Generous realizes she would prefer to support a different charitable mission.
The vast majority of U.S. courts would conclude that Generous Giver is legally obligated to pay all future donations under the pledge form despite T.C. Charity's failure to disclose that the pledge is legally binding.Furthermore, T.C. Charity's board of directors likely has a fiduciary duty to sue Generous in court for any missed payments.
A U.S. court likely will enforce Generous' pledge to T.C. Charity under one or more of the following twistedlegal theories:
. It is a binding bilateral contract supported by consideration because under its articles of incorporation the charity must use all funds received for charitable purposes.
. It is a binding bilateral contract because other donors pledged.
. It is a binding unilateral contract because T.C. Charity actually used Generous' initial donation for charitable purposes.
. It is enforceable under the doctrine of promissory estoppel because T.C. Charity substantially relied to its detriment on the pledge.
. It is enforceable under a modified promissory estoppel theory approach in, regardless of whether T.C. Charity relied on the pledge.
This is an unfortunate result in many respects. Generous likely feels duped. The pledge form failed to honestly disclose that Generous was legally obligated, circumstances changed, and she chose to support a different charity. At the same time, T.C. Charity's governing body may feel like ingrates when suing someone who made an initial contribution and subsequently preferred not to donate because of changed circumstances. And courts frequently complain about having to apply the artificially contrived legal rules of charitable pledging which defy logic,common sense, and fundamental principles of common law.
This practice of U.S. courts enforcing almost all charitable pledges likely encourages charities to use laconic pledge forms that mislead donors.This Article demonstrates the prevalence of this problem with new empirical research indicating that approximately 95 percent of standard charitable pledge forms fail to clearly state whether the pledge is legally binding, and 85 percent fail to provide even a clue about whether the pledge is binding.
The current U.S. approach disregards the donor's intent. This Article proposes a new approach that will enforce a charitable pledge only if: (i) it would be binding under noncharitable legal principles normally applied, specifically under contract law or the promissory estoppel doctrine; or (ii) the donor manifested an intent that the pledge would be legally enforceable by clear and convincing evidence.
Part I of this Article traces the legal fictions U.S. courts often use to enforce charitable pledges, including standardcharitable pledges. This discussion will demonstrate that a donor could reasonably believe that a standard pledge to make future charitable gifts would not be enforceable either as a matter of common sense or based upon an understanding of basic legal principles. Indeed, English common law and a handful of U.S. cases refuse to enforce standard charitable pledges for persuasive reasons.
Part II describes new empirical evidence created for this Article that indicates approximately 95 percent of standard charitable pledge forms are sneaky; they fail to disclose that the charitable pledge is legally binding like a debt.
Part III proposes a new two-prong test for enforcing charitable pledges. Under the first prong, charitable pledges would be enforceable under normal legal rules. In the modern era of fundraising, normal contract analysis may enforce most significant dollar pledges because the donor receives valuable charitable naming rights.When a transaction involves a part-bargain (such as a naming right) and a part-gift, traditional contract analysis finds sufficient consideration to enforce the entire transaction.In addition, normal promissory estoppel doctrine could enforce other significant dollar pledges when the donor knew or should have known the charity was relying on the pledge in beginning constructionon a project or in other ways.The second prong proposes a change in the law that would enforce other charitable pledges when there is clear and convincing evidence that the donor intended the pledge to be legally binding.
Part IV concludes that this Article's proposal would encourage charitable fundraisers to honestly disclose legal enforceability and reduce the current economic incentive to deceive donors. Additionally, this proposal will free charity's directors from suing donors who can realistically claim they were misledand will eliminate artificial judicial concoctionsimposing liabilities on donors with bona fide claims of deception.

questions.question: Do courts enforce donors' multi-year charitable pledges as legally binding obligations when the pledge forms do not disclose whether the pledge is legally enforceable, including after changes in the charity's conduct or the donor's circumstances?
How common is it for standard charitable pledge forms to fail to disclose or give any indication about whether the pledge is legally binding?

Would an enforcement rule that requires either ordinary transactional indicia of legal obligation or clear and convincing evidence that the donor intended to be bound better align outcomes with donor intent, reduce deceptive fundraising practices, and limit needless litigation?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
How should law allocate evidentiary burdens in disputes over assent and formation to protect against unfair bargains?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
How do systemic institutional changes (deregulation, litigation costs, ADR, transnational codes) affect contracting behavior and the relation between law and practice?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
What procedural or evidentiary features of an intermediary-based arrangement distinguish genuinely serious, enforceable gift commitments from casual promises?

When and how should charitable pledges be enforceable?
What defenses should a promisor be able to raise to block enforcement of a contract by a non-party beneficiary?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do market and institutional features affect whether informative 'cheap talk' will arise privately or require legal intervention to induce accurate precontractual communication?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev1016!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Pillans and Rose v. Van Mierop and Hopkins: The Worst Way to Win
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Pillans and Rose v. Van Mierop and Hopkins: The Worst Way to Win

shared_topics.topic: the justificatory and functional role of consideration in enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally debate whether and why consideration should be required to enforce promises: Paper A criticizes Lord Mansfield's dismissal of consideration in Pillans and analyzes consideration's evidentiary, cautionary, and channeling functions; Paper B documents how courts sidestep or manufacture consideration to enforce charitable pledges and proposes limiting enforcement to situations where normal contract consideration or clear intent exists.

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel and reliance as substitutes for consideration
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with courts using reliance-based doctrines to enforce promises absent consideration: Paper A critiques the appellate judges' speculative reliance reasoning in Pillans and notes later rejection, while Paper B catalogs promissory estoppel and modified reliance theories as frequent bases for enforcing charitable pledges and proposes tighter limits on such doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: judicial law‑making and doctrinal stretching / legal fictions to reach enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both criticize judges for stretching doctrines or inventing legal fictions to produce commercially or morally desired results: Paper A accuses the Pillans court of labeling mercantile custom and equating promises with acceptance to justify enforcement, and Paper B shows how U.S. courts employ a variety of contrived theories to hold donors to pledges despite ambiguous forms.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and formal role of writing and disclosure in determining enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how writing, formality, and disclosure affect enforcement: Paper A analyzes Mansfield's claim that a written promise satisfies the evidentiary need for consideration and contrasts writing with seals and the Statute of Frauds, while Paper B presents empirical evidence that pledge forms usually fail to disclose enforceability and proposes requiring clear manifestation of intent (writing/clear evidence) before enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the need for clearer rules or statutory reform to reduce uncertainty in promise enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both propose or note the desirability of clearer doctrinal or statutory solutions: Paper A laments 220 years of uncertainty after Pillans and observes later statutory/theoretical resolution (UCC letters of credit), and Paper B offers a two‑prong test and disclosure rules to bring predictability to charitable pledge enforcement.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends using contract techniques (duration clauses, morals clauses, exit mechanisms) when negotiating naming-rights, and Paper B presents empirical evidence that pledge forms usually fail to disclose enforceability and proposes reforms to drafting and disclosure to eliminate incentives to mislead donors.

shared_topics.justification: Both articles document concrete harms from the existing approach—e.g., costly litigation, donors recovering disproportionate sums, delayed renovations, charities using vague pledge forms—and argue that clearer legal rules would better protect donors, charities, and the public purposes they serve.

shared_topics.justification: Each article analyzes courts stretching or substituting equitable doctrines for classical contract principles—Paper A discusses courts invoking promissory estoppel and various fictions to enforce pledges lacking consideration, while Paper B examines courts softening forfeiture through equitable protections for purchasers—highlighting doctrinal conflict and instability.

shared_topics.topic: protection (or neglect) of vulnerable or unsophisticated parties and its doctrinal consequences

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules create behavioral incentives for private actors and risk of exploitation

shared_topics.topic: availability and choice of remedial alternatives beyond strict enforcement

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: enforcement of promises under information asymmetry using contract and equitable doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when nondisclosure should affect contractual obligations and exceptions, while Paper B examines how courts enforce charitable pledges through various contract theories and promissory estoppel despite donors' informational deficits and unclear intent.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats relationships of trust and confidence as a distinct ground requiring disclosure, and Paper B discusses charities' governing boards, fiduciary duties (including the duty to sue for missed pledges), and how the donor–charity relationship affects enforcement and fairness.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames disclosure rules by balancing a default duty to disclose against efficiency costs and exceptions, and Paper B proposes legal reform to reduce charities' incentives to use ambiguous pledge forms that mislead donors while preserving enforceability where appropriate.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IS MORE PARENTAL LEAVE ALWAYS BETTER?: AN ANALYSIS OF POTENTIAL EMPLOYEE PROTECTIONS FOR LEAVE OFFERED OUTSIDE THE FMLA

shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when promises made by organizations (charitable pledge forms in Paper A; expanded parental leave policies in Paper B) become legally enforceable, evaluating doctrines like contract (including unilateral-contract theory) and promissory estoppel as potential bases for enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: reliance/performance by an individual as a trigger for organizational obligation
shared_topics.justification: Each paper focuses on individual acts (making an initial pledge payment in Paper A; taking parental leave in Paper B) as the critical reliance or performance that could create or should create binding obligations on the organization.

shared_topics.topic: harms from ambiguous or misleading institutional communications and the need for clearer disclosure
shared_topics.justification: Each article documents how ambiguous institutional representations (laconic pledge forms in Paper A; potentially ambiguous or superficially generous leave policies in Paper B) can mislead individuals and create perverse incentives, arguing for greater clarity or stronger legal safeguards to prevent abuse or unfair outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: AALS SECTION ON CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM EMPIRICAL SCHOLARSHIP: WHAT SHOULD WE STUDY AND HOW SHOULD WE STUDY IT?: Go Out and Look: The Challenge and Promise of Empirical Scholarship in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: the use of empirical evidence to inform and justify doctrinal reform in contract law

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FREEDOM NOT TO CONTRACT.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:The American Provenance of the UNIDROIT Principles

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?

shared_topics.topic: legal characterization and doctrines for enforcing charitable commitments (contracts vs. gifts/trusts vs. promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts classify and enforce charitable promises—Paper A examines the assorted doctrines courts invoke to enforce standard charitable pledges (contract, unilateral contract, promissory estoppel), while Paper B analyzes when charitable naming-rights arrangements are treated as gifts, contracts, or trusts and argues for treating them as contracts to avoid harmful outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: role of donor intent and evidentiary standards for enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both articles focus on the centrality of donor intent in determining enforceability—Paper A proposes enforcing pledges only when intent to be legally bound is clear (or under normal contract/promissory-estoppel rules), and Paper B repeatedly notes that ambiguous or unexpressed donor intentions produce harsh results under gift law and advocates clearer contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: importance of explicit terms and contractual design (duration, morals clauses, exit mechanisms, naming-rights scope)
shared_topics.justification: Both works stress that lack of explicit terms produces disputes and poor outcomes—Paper B emphasizes negotiating duration, morals clauses, and exit mechanisms for naming-rights deals, while Paper A documents how vague pledge forms mislead donors and proposes clearer legal standards to govern pledge terms and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape fundraising incentives and organizational behavior (perverse outcomes from current doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique current legal treatments for creating undesirable incentives—Paper A shows empirically that vague pledge forms persist because courts enforce pledges and thus charities benefit from obfuscation, and Paper B shows that treating naming rights as gifts can produce perverse results (e.g., blocking renovations, costly settlements) and argues contract law would better align incentives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34umemlrev499!!ARTICLE: Origins of Promissory Estoppel: Justifiable Reliance and Commercial Uncertainty Before Williston's Restatement
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Origins of Promissory Estoppel: Justifiable Reliance and Commercial Uncertainty Before Williston's Restatement

shared_topics.topic: the role and scope of promissory estoppel / justifiable reliance in enforcing non‑traditional promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts apply promissory estoppel to enforce charitable pledges (often expanding the doctrine) and proposes narrowing enforcement to cases meeting normal promissory estoppel or clear evidence of intent; Paper B traces the historical development of justifiable reliance, showing courts long used reliance doctrines to enforce commercial promises that did not fit classic contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: how courts circumvent or adapt classical contract doctrines (consideration, offer and acceptance, preexisting duty) to make promises enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents judicial fictions (e.g., finding consideration via corporate articles, other donors, naming rights) used to treat pledges as contracts, while Paper B analyzes nineteenth‑century decisions where courts circumvented strict rules on definiteness, mutuality, and consideration to enforce flexible commercial arrangements.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of reliance and party intent in determining enforceability of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes donor intent and reliance as central to whether a pledge should be enforced and proposes a clear‑and‑convincing intent standard alongside normal reliance analysis; Paper B centers on justifiable reliance as the doctrinal basis courts historically used to grant relief and adapt promises to uncertain commercial conditions.

shared_topics.topic: critique of judicial remedial choices and their policy consequences for private ordering and economic incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts' broad enforcement of pledges for creating incentives that mislead donors and generate unfair litigation, and Paper B critiques doctrinal histories (e.g., Williston's account) and explains how reliance remedies functioned as policy tools to address commercial uncertainty and the harshness of formal doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61ukanlrev591!!ARTICLE: Assent Is Not an Element of Contract Formation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Assent Is Not an Element of Contract Formation

shared_topics.topic: the role of consideration and equitable doctrines in enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate when a promise becomes legally enforceable, with Paper A debating whether charitable pledges should be enforced under normal contract principles or promissory estoppel, and Paper B arguing doctrinally that consideration (and related equitable tools) is the foundational inquiry that subsumes notions like assent when determining enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal clarity and the misuse of legal fictions
shared_topics.justification: Both authors criticize current judicial and Restatement practices as conceptually confused: Paper A catalogs courts' ‘twisted’ legal theories used to enforce pledges, while Paper B argues that treating assent as a separate element is doctrinally superfluous and contributes to confusion.

shared_topics.topic: how to assess parties' intent/manifestation to form binding obligations
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with the problem of discerning whether a party meant to be bound — Paper A presses for clear-and-convincing evidence of donor intent before enforcing pledges, and Paper B shows that questions about assent/intent are properly resolved within the consideration analysis rather than as a freestanding element.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between doctrinal rules and policy/fairness concerns (reliance, deception, defenses to formation)
shared_topics.justification: Both pieces connect doctrinal choices to policy outcomes: Paper A highlights reliance, donor deception, and charities' incentives as reasons to reform pledge enforcement, while Paper B situates formation defenses (fraud, duress, mistake, unconscionability) as rationales that operate by undermining consideration and protecting fairness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev7!!SYMPOSIUM: GILMORE'S GRANT (OR THE LIFE & AFTERLIFE OF GRANT GILMORE & HIS DEATH)
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: GILMORE'S GRANT (OR THE LIFE & AFTERLIFE OF GRANT GILMORE & HIS DEATH)

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and role of consideration in enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A chronicles and critiques the ‘demise of consideration’ in classical contract doctrine (tracing Holmes, Williston, Beale, and Gilmore's attack on formalist bargain theory), while Paper B analyzes how courts nonetheless invoke consideration (or find substitute consideration via naming rights or corporate charters) to enforce charitable pledges.

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of doctrinal fictions or stretched doctrines to achieve enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes Langdellian formalism and the ways courts and treatise-writers create or sustain doctrinal rules despite exceptions, and Paper B documents and critiques courts' use of multiple legal fictions (contract, unilateral contract, promissory estoppel, corporate charter obligations) to enforce pledges in ways the author calls ‘twisted’ or artificial.

shared_topics.topic: the mismatch between formal contract rules and real-world expectations or intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes Gilmore's theme that classical contract theory often fails to describe or serve the realities of modern transactions, and Paper B shows this concretely in charitable giving—donors' expectations about whether pledges are binding often diverge from how courts treat them.

shared_topics.topic: proposals for doctrinal reform to better align law and practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with whether Gilmore's critique implies a need to reconceive or reform contract doctrine and pedagogy, while Paper B advances a concrete reform (a two‑prong test requiring ordinary contract/promissory‑estoppel standards or clear-and-convincing evidence of intent) to govern enforcement of charitable pledges.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1988dukelj609!!ARTICLE: VAGUENESS AND THE RULE OF LAW: RECONSIDERING INSTALLMENT LAND CONTRACT FORFEITURES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: VAGUENESS AND THE RULE OF LAW: RECONSIDERING INSTALLMENT LAND CONTRACT FORFEITURES

shared_topics.topic: legal vagueness and doctrinal unpredictability that harms transactional parties
shared_topics.justification: Both papers diagnose widespread vagueness in governing doctrines—installment-contract forfeiture law in Paper A and charitable-pledge enforcement in Paper B—and argue that imprecision produces unfair surprise, reliance costs, and inability of parties to plan their affairs reliably.

shared_topics.topic: judicial extension or fabrication of doctrines to achieve equitable outcomes, producing confusion
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for stretching forfeiture law and treating installment contracts like mortgages to protect purchasers, while Paper B documents courts resolving pledge disputes through a hodgepodge of fictions (contract, unilateral promise, promissory estoppel, fiduciary duty), with both authors arguing these judicial maneuvers create doctrinal incoherence.

shared_topics.topic: overlap and interaction of multiple remedies/theories that complicate enforcement and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Both articles show how a proliferation of available remedies or legal theories—forfeiture, rescission, breach, specific performance in Paper A; contract doctrines, promissory estoppel, and fiduciary claims in Paper B—interact unpredictably and can undermine the policy goals of the governing regime.

shared_topics.topic: proposals for clearer, rule-based reforms (including disclosure) to align expectations and curb opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Each paper concludes with concrete reform suggestions favoring clearer rules or tests—Paper A recommends narrowing and clarifying forfeiture rules so vendors and purchasers can rely on them, and Paper B proposes a two-prong enforcement test and clearer disclosure to prevent charities from misleading donors and to reduce opportunistic litigation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33houslrev1103!!ARTICLE: CARDOZO'S ALLEGHENY COLLEGE OPINION: A CASE STUDY IN LAW AS AN ART
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CARDOZO'S ALLEGHENY COLLEGE OPINION: A CASE STUDY IN LAW AS AN ART

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrinal construction in charity-law disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Cardozo's Allegheny College opinion as a case study in how judges craft and justify doctrine in a charity-related dispute, and Paper B documents and critiques the doctrinal devices (contract principles, promissory estoppel, and various judicial fictions) that U.S. courts use to resolve charitable-pledge cases.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal legal rules and parties' expectations or intent in charitable pledges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a prominent judicial opinion to explore how judges reconcile legal rules with perceptions of fairness and meaning in charity disputes, while Paper B shows empirically and doctrinally that courts often enforce pledges in ways that conflict with donors' expectations and urges doctrinal reform to better respect donor intent.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial rhetoric, style, and judicially-created 'fictions' in shaping outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Cardozo's writing style and rhetorical choices as central to understanding how an opinion persuades and frames legal issues, and Paper B highlights courts' rhetorical recourse to 'twisted legal theories' and judicially-created fictions when enforcing charitable pledges, arguing that such rhetoric affects both doctrine and real-world consequences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36vandlrev1383!!ARTICLE: The Parol Evidence Rule: Promissory Estoppel's Next Conquest?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Parol Evidence Rule: Promissory Estoppel's Next Conquest?

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel as a substitute for consideration to enforce noncontractual promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies promissory estoppel as one of the principal doctrines courts invoke to enforce charitable pledges absent traditional consideration, while Paper B traces the historical evolution of promissory estoppel from a modest substitute in donative cases to a broad enforcement device and analyzes its expanding role in contract law.

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of equitable/legal fictions to circumvent formal contract requirements and bind parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A catalogs the various legal fictions (e.g., unilateral contract, implied consideration, reliance) U.S. courts use to enforce pledges despite ambiguous forms, and Paper B studies how promissory estoppel has been used to bypass formal rules like the Statute of Frauds and potentially the parol evidence rule.

shared_topics.topic: tension between doctrinal expansion (estoppel) and preserving party intent and predictability in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for enforcing donors' pledges in ways that disregard donor intent and proposes a limiting test requiring clear evidence of enforceability, while Paper B worries that estoppel's expansion threatens traditional contract doctrines (reducing clarity) and examines whether such incursions are desirable or should be constrained.

papers.node_id: 73uchilrev1299!!ARTICLE: Commodification and Contract Formation: Placing the Consideration Doctrine on Stronger Foundations
papers.title: ARTICLE: Commodification and Contract Formation: Placing the Consideration Doctrine on Stronger Foundations
papers.abstract:
People make promises all the time. In the course of a day, we might promise a spouse to complete household chores, a coworker to finish a project by its deadline, and a service provider to pay for a service upon completion. Yet only the last of these promises will generally impose a legal obligation. Whereas the first two statements are mere unilateral promises, the fact that the third promise is exchanged for something of value -- the service -- makes it a contract that can be enforced in courts of law.
This rule is known as the consideration doctrine: the law will not enforce unilateral promises, but promises exchanged for something of value become legally binding contracts. There are many exceptions to this doctrine. Other rules can make a promise legally binding, and not all promises backed by consideration are legally enforceable. Nevertheless, the consideration doctrine remains the most important rule for distinguishing between unenforceable promises and contracts backed by law.
Unfortunately, we lack a sound theoretical justification for the consideration doctrine.Underlying most of contract law is the general principle that parties' intentions should be honored.So why, then, do we refuse enforcement to even those unilateral promises that were clearly intended to be binding?
Existing attempts to justify the consideration doctrine fall into two general camps. First, formalist scholars defend the doctrine as a mechanism for determining parties' intentions. By creating a hoop the parties must jump through in order to make their promises binding, the law creates a mechanism for parties to convey which promises they intend to impose legal obligations. In order to make their promises legally enforceable, the parties need only claim that their promise is being exchanged for something of value. In other words, they need only recite consideration. Yet as Eric Posner explains,
There is no reason to require parties to recite a consideration as opposed to reciting that they want their promise to be enforceable. . . . Efforts to rationalize this practice as a way of ensuring

questions.question: Whether requiring an exchange of value for a promise is an effective mechanism for identifying which promises parties intend to make legally binding.

Whether treating promises as commodified exchanges (i.e., enforcing only promises backed by value) produces better economic or behavioral outcomes-such as reduced opportunism, improved reliance, or greater overall welfare-than enforcing promises based solely on parties' stated intent.

Whether formalistic evidentiary hoops (like demanding proof of an exchange) are necessary for reliable contract formation, or whether simpler means of signaling intent would achieve the same legal and social goals.

matched_themes: Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78neblrev491!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal justification for the consideration requirement in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers substantively engage with why the law requires consideration to turn promises into enforceable contracts: Paper A critiques existing theoretical justifications for the consideration doctrine and seeks a stronger foundation, while Paper B situates mutuality doctrine as a corollary to the mutual promise/consideration rule and defends its normative role within that framework.

shared_topics.topic: when unilateral versus bilateral promises become legally enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the difference between unilateral promises (promise exchanged for performance) and bilateral promises (promise for promise) and how contract formation rules treat each: Paper A foregrounds that only promises exchanged for something of value typically create enforceable contracts, and Paper B analyzes how unilateral contracts are treated differently from bilateral contracts under the mutuality and mutual promise rules.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between mutuality of obligation and the mutual promise/consideration rule
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address how mutuality interacts with consideration: Paper B is centrally focused on defending a (reinterpreted) mutuality of obligation as a corollary to the mutual promise rule, while Paper A engages the broader doctrine of consideration within which mutuality operates and is one of the doctrines courts use to select enforceable promises.

shared_topics.topic: the role of 'value' and adequacy of consideration versus intent or reciprocity
shared_topics.justification: Both confront the question whether enforceability turns on some exchange of value (adequacy) or on parties' intent/reciprocity: Paper A emphasizes the traditional formulation that consideration is ‘something of value’ and questions that rationale, and Paper B explicitly examines and rejects treating mutuality as a doctrine about 'value', treating reciprocity and remedies as the core concerns.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical approaches to contract doctrines (formalist recitals versus purposive/historical interpretation)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage competing theoretical accounts of contract formalities — Paper A critiques formalist accounts that reduce enforceability to recited consideration and seeks a sounder theory, while Paper B advances a historically informed, purposive defense of mutuality as an affirmative, presumptive doctrine rather than a strict formalist rule.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 22geomasonlrev297!!ARTICLE: PAY FOR PLAY: THE COMPENSATED LEISURE FLAW OF CONTRACT DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PAY FOR PLAY: THE COMPENSATED LEISURE FLAW OF CONTRACT DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: economic foundations of contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers use economic reasoning to critique existing rules and propose reforms: Paper A questions the theoretical (including economic) justification for the consideration doctrine as a gatekeeper for enforceability, while Paper B applies labor-economics concepts (reservation price, labor/leisure tradeoffs, diminishing marginal utility) to redesign damage rules for service contracts.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal coherence and internal inconsistency in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both identify incoherence across contract doctrines—Paper A highlights the mismatch between the principle of honoring parties' intentions and the rigid consideration rule, and Paper B exposes the inconsistent treatment of goods versus services in damage awards and the resulting unfairness.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between formal bright-line rules and individualized adjustments
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between administrable, formalist rules and more tailored fact-specific inquiries: Paper A critiques recitals/hoops (e.g., reciting consideration) as a blunt mechanism for signaling intent, while Paper B argues for approximations and sliding-scale adjustments (reservation-price estimates, likelihood findings) instead of categorical full-price damages.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate measure of parties' expectations and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how law should measure what parties are owed—Paper A asks why some intended promises are denied enforceability despite expressed intent, and Paper B interrogates whether benefit-of-the-bargain damages properly capture the injured party's real expected surplus (vs. overcompensating compensated leisure).

shared_topics.topic: the role of commodification in turning promises into enforceable obligations and in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both treat commodification as central: Paper A focuses on how exchanging value (commodification) transforms promises into contracts and seeks firmer foundations for that boundary, while Paper B analyzes how treating labor as a commodified service (vs. sale of goods) generates distinct and problematic remedial outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91califlrev1645!!ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: conditions that make promises legally enforceable (doctrinal gates to contract formation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the consideration doctrine as the chief doctrinal mechanism that converts promises into enforceable contracts and questions its justificatory basis, while Paper B analyzes disclosure rules as another doctrinal condition that can determine whether a transaction is fair and therefore legally actionable; both focus on what legal requirements (beyond mere utterance of a promise) should be imposed to create enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: information, signaling, and efficiency as justifications for contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques and evaluates formalist/signaling accounts of consideration (the idea that doctrinal hoops communicate parties’ intent), and Paper B formulates a Disclosure Principle that weighs disclosure obligations against their efficiency costs and the informational investments of parties; both engage substantively with information problems and efficiency-based rationales for contract doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: the need for nuanced, multi‑stranded rules and exceptions rather than blanket doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the consideration rule coexists with numerous exceptions and is inadequately theorized as a categorical test, and Paper B develops a multi‑stranded Disclosure Principle with multiple specific exceptions (adventitious vs. deliberate acquisition, foreknowledge, trust relationships, etc.); both advocate dissecting broad rules into context‑sensitive strands.

shared_topics.topic: how the law should treat parties’ intentions and expectations in formation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the tension between honoring parties’ expressed intentions and imposing formal requirements like consideration, and Paper B addresses when a party’s undisclosed information or the other party’s expectations should be protected (e.g., allocation of risk, notice, reasonable search); both grapple with when subjective intentions or reasonable expectations deserve legal protection in contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58tennlrev367!!ARTICLE: PERFORMATIVES IN SPEECH ACT THEORY: AN INTRODUCTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PERFORMATIVES IN SPEECH ACT THEORY: AN INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: role of parties' intent in transforming promises into legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates why contract law (via the consideration doctrine) refuses to enforce certain promises despite apparent intent, and Paper B explains how speech act theory locates the binding force of utterances in their illocutionary intent, showing a shared focus on how intention in language maps to legal obligations.

shared_topics.topic: performative function of legal language (utterances that bring legal relations into being)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how some promises become contracts when exchanged for value (a linguistic/behavioral act that produces a legal relation), while Paper B develops the notion of performatives (e.g., 'I hereby...') that literally create legal states like marriage, arrest, or contractual commitments.

shared_topics.topic: reliability of formal linguistic or doctrinal markers as signals of enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques formalist defenses that treating recitals of consideration as a sufficient hoop to show enforceable intent, and Paper B analyzes enacting formulas and performative verbs (like 'hereby' or 'enact') as formal linguistic signals whose capacity to mark legal force is under theoretical scrutiny.

shared_topics.topic: institutional prerequisites for speech acts and contract formation (authority, exchange context, status)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B emphasizes that performatives only work within social institutions and require proper authority and status, and Paper A likewise engages with the institutional context of promises—how exchange (commodification) and other legal rules determine when private utterances become enforceable contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77califlrev1077!!ARTICLE: RELATIONSHIP OR BOUNDARY? HANDLING SUCCESSIVE CONTRACTS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RELATIONSHIP OR BOUNDARY? HANDLING SUCCESSIVE CONTRACTS.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and justification of existing contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that prevailing contract doctrines (which treat successive contracts as terminating relationships) inadequately deter opportunism and may produce unfair or wasteful outcomes; Paper B critiques the lack of a sound theoretical foundation for the consideration doctrine and interrogates whether the existing rule is justified as a doctrinal device.

shared_topics.topic: role of information, signaling, and party intentions in contract formation and renewal
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes informational gaps and asymmetries across inception, performance, and renegotiation stages and how party sophistication affects opportunism; Paper B examines how the consideration requirement operates as a signaling mechanism (or fails to) for parties' intent to create enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape parties' incentives and social welfare (opportunism, hold-up, commodification)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how doctrinal boundaries and lack of renewal rules produce hold-up and socially wasteful opportunism and evaluates welfare tradeoffs of mandatory rules; Paper B studies how the consideration doctrine (and the commodification of promises) affects which promises are enforceable and hence alters parties' incentives and social outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: designing alternative legal regimes or doctrinal reforms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares possible regimes for successor contracting (enforceable renewal clauses, implied renewal, mandatory renewal) and advocates rules tailored to party sophistication; Paper B seeks stronger theoretical foundations for the consideration doctrine and thereby supports rethinking or reforming contract-formation rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101columlrev1876!!ARTICLE:THE GIFT BEYOND THE GRAVE: REVISITING THE QUESTION OF CONSIDERATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE GIFT BEYOND THE GRAVE: REVISITING THE QUESTION OF CONSIDERATION

shared_topics.topic: theoretical justification of the consideration doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers diagnose a lack of satisfactory theoretical grounding for why the law enforces some promises but not others; Paper A traces historical and normative accounts of consideration and their stakes, while Paper B critiques existing justificatory attempts and seeks a firmer foundation for the rule.

shared_topics.topic: the line between unenforceable unilateral/gift promises and enforceable contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of which promises (especially gifts or unilateral promises) the law should treat as legally binding, with Paper A examining gift case law and historical debates and Paper B emphasizing the doctrinal rule that only promises exchanged for value become enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: formal signaling role of consideration (the 'hoop' to show intent)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers discuss the formalist account that consideration functions as a device for parties to indicate intent to be legally bound—Paper B explicitly critiques this 'hoop' explanation, and Paper A situates such formalism within broader theoretical shifts that prioritized promise and voluntary exchange.

shared_topics.topic: commodification/market framing of promises and the contracting subject
shared_topics.justification: Both works connect consideration doctrine to a broader picture of commodification and the construction of contracting individuals: Paper A argues the doctrine helped produce an economically calculating subject and demarcate market/private spheres, while Paper B (by its title and abstract) links consideration to commodification as part of the foundation for contract formation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev947!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: The Democratization of Contract Law: The Case of Mutual Promises
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: The Democratization of Contract Law: The Case of Mutual Promises

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal and theoretical basis for the consideration doctrine, especially mutual promises as sufficient consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical emergence and judicial reasoning that reciprocal promises constitute good consideration, while Paper B interrogates the theoretical foundations of the consideration doctrine and seeks a stronger justification for why some promises (including exchanged promises) are treated as enforceable contracts.

shared_topics.topic: when promises become legally enforceable versus mere unilateral promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the shift that allowed exchanged promises to be enforced (democratizing contract law), and Paper B analyzes why unilateral promises are typically non‑enforceable and how the law distinguishes enforceable contracts from nonbinding promises.

shared_topics.topic: the role of party intentions and signaling in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts respected parties' own assessment of the value of their reciprocal promises (their expressed intent), whereas Paper B examines formalist accounts that treat consideration as a signal of intent and critiques whether such signaling justifies enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the commodification/exchangeability of promises and its social/legal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how recognizing mutual promises transformed promises into tradable obligations that expanded access to contracting (democratization), and Paper B (by focusing on commodification and contract formation) engages with the idea of treating promises as economic items whose exchange grounds legal obligation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69fordhamlrev427!!ARTICLE: THE ORIGINS OF THE OBJECTIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT FORMATION AND INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ORIGINS OF THE OBJECTIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT FORMATION AND INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: function of formal doctrinal requirements (e.g., consideration, objective tests) as mechanisms for identifying enforceable promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the consideration doctrine as a formal hoop purportedly used to signal or determine parties' intent to create legal obligations, while Paper B analyzes the objective theory as an analogous doctrinal device that relies on words and conduct (rather than secret intent) to identify when promises become enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical tension between subjective intent and objective manifestations in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions why courts refuse to enforce unilateral promises despite apparent intent, challenging the gap between actual intent and legal enforceability; Paper B traces the historical debate between subjective 'meeting of the minds' approaches and objective (reasonable-person/words-and-conduct) approaches and explains why objective standards predominate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of evidentiary rules and practical adjudication concerns in shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A points to the ease of reciting consideration as a practical signal and critiques formalist justifications, and Paper B shows how changes in admissible testimony and fear of perjury drove courts toward objective criteria—both papers tie substantive contract rules to evidentiary and enforcement realities.

shared_topics.topic: limits and exceptions to when promises become legally binding (doctrinal boundaries of enforceability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys exceptions to the consideration doctrine and asks why some unilateral promises are nevertheless enforced, while Paper B examines how doctrines like the parol evidence rule, mistake, duress, incapacity, and statutory changes affect when a purported promise will be treated as a contract.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2008uilllrev505!!ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: normative justification of the consideration doctrine and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates why the consideration doctrine lacks a sound theoretical justification and surveys attempts to ground it normatively, while Paper B more broadly questions whether contract doctrines (including rules like consideration) can be given a single moral or normative foundation and critiques efforts to do so.

shared_topics.topic: promise vs reliance vs transfer heuristics for determining which promises are legally enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts unilateral promises with promises exchanged for value (consideration) as the dividing line for enforceability, and Paper B systematically analyzes the three descriptive heuristics—promise, reliance, and transfer—as competing bases for explaining which promises the law enforces.

papers.node_id: 75geolj1575!!ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.
papers.abstract:
Since time immemorial, people have made contracts.  For no doubt just as long, the expectations created by these contracts have sometimes been disappointed by subsequent events.  If the disappointing event occurs before the contract has been fully performed by both sides, the question then arises: What is the legal effect of the event upon the unperformed contractual obligations?  Does the disappointing event discharge or only suspend the obligations, or does it have no legal effect?  This question has been with us for centuriesand can be exquisitely difficult to decide.  This article studies the English solutions to the question from late medieval times to the present.
In the law of contracts, cases presenting this question are usually classified under the topic of impossibility, a shorthand reference to the doctrine of excuse for supervening impossiblity of performance.  In England this topic is sometimes called frustration, but this article uses the term "frustration" only to refer to a particular part of the larger topic of impossibility -- excuse for inordinate delay.
English impossibility cases have traditionally played a significant role in the teaching of contract law in American legal education.  Most students in American law schools encounter the English impossibility cases ofParadine v. Jane,Taylor v. Caldwell,andKrell v. Henryin their first-year contractlaw classes.The primary thesis of this article is that the English law of impossibility and its history are often incorrectly taught to law students.Paradine,for example, is usually cited for a proposition for which the case does not stand and which the judge had no intention of establishing.Krellis often taught without appreciation of its surrounding events or subsequent English case law that indicate it was really a creature of unique circumstances rather than the foundation of a new principle of impossibility law.
This study has several additional goals.  First, most of the other discussions of this area pay little attention to the authorities cited in the early English impossibility cases, perhaps because these authorities are relatively inaccessible.  Many times, however, these cited authorities provide valuable clues for interpreting the main cases.  Therefore, this study describes the authorities in detail, usually in the footnotes so as not to burden the text.  Second, when the result of a case seemed puzzling attempts were made to locate additional facts not included in the court's opinion that might serve to explain the case.  These endeavors were not always successful, but some were and have been included.  Finally, this study provides an overview of the English law of impossibility that the reader may compare with its American counterpart to discern similarities and differences in approach between these two common law systems.

papers.node_id: 56depaullrev55!!ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH
papers.abstract:
Should there be legal recourse for bargaining gone bad? Professor Charles Knapp explored this question in his influential article, Enforcing the Contract to Bargain, and courts have continued to struggle with it, despite public policy that supports cooperative processes.Enforcement of "contracts to bargain" or to pursue other cooperative processes creates a conundrum by calling courts to confront intricate difficulties in filling gaps and fashioning remedies for breach.Moreover, these difficulties are now threatening the efficacy and vitality of agreements to participate in mediation and other nonbinding alternative dispute resolution processes, which I refer to as "ADR agreements" to distinguish them from contracts requiring binding arbitration.
Professor Knapp's conception of a "contract to bargain" is a useful framework for exploring the enforcement of ADR agreements because it captures "middle position" situations. In these situations, parties stand at the crossroads between "yes-contract" and "no-contract" by incorporating flexibility and leaving gaps in the terms of their deals. As Professor Knapp has explained, they signify their "willingness to be regarded as 'committed' to the entire proposed exchange" by negotiating and reaching agreement on some terms of the deal, but nonetheless delaying agreement on other important terms.Similarly, parties to ADR agreements commit to an underlying exchange but promise to pursue a cooperative process to resolve any disputes that arise during performance. In both cases, parties expect to cooperate but usually do not specify what that cooperation entails.
Although public policy ostensibly supports ADR, courts have failed to adequately analyze and enforce ADR agreements. Instead of considering the middle-position nature of these agreements, courts jump to the same formalist yes-contract/no-contract conclusions they have imposed on other contracts to bargain. They either assume ADR agreements fall in the no-contract column under traditional, formalist conceptions of so-called "agreements-to-agree," or they mistreat nonbinding dispute resolution processes as binding arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA)or the Uniform Arbitration Act (UAA).Even if the results are acceptable in some cases, problems arise when courts misapply statutes and formalist doctrines to over-or under-enforce ADR agreements.Courts may cut off the parties' contractually preserved access to judicial recourse by using the FAA to jump to the yes-contract conclusion that a binding contract exists. Moreover, the failure of courts and legislators to openly confront the yes-contract/no-contract conundrum of ADR agreements has left parties without adequate contracting guidance.
In a previous article, I critiqued the improper treatment of nonbinding ADR as binding arbitration under the FAA and UAA and invited courts to refresh common-law contractual analysis of ADR agreements.I suggested that courts should enforce ADR agreements flexibly where parties' participation in an ADR process will foster fair settlement or provide other collateral benefits that outweigh the burdens of compelled participation in the process.For example, it may be appropriate for a court to use the common law to order corporate buyers and sellers to negotiate price adjustments under an ADR agreement in an installment sales contract. In contrast, a court might refuse to order an employee to mediate sexual harassment claims against an intimidating or abusive employer.
This Article goes a step further by confronting the tensions and complications courts face when they actually apply such common-law analysis to enforce ADR agreements. The Article shows how Professor Knapp's conception of a contract to bargain captures the middle-position nature of ADR agreements and explains why they are ill-suited for formalist "one-size-fits-all" enforcement.This is because formalist rules ignore the human context of ADR agreements.They undervalue "relational realities" and often fail to adequately redress the parties' harms.Furthermore, rigid enforcement rules create arbitrary and unfair outcomes; these outcomes ultimately cause the rules to become inefficient and less legitimate. A court applying rigid rules, for example, would treat the above-referenced installment sales and harassment claimants the same - regardless of how the parties' relations evolved after they agreed to their original contracts. Although this seems to foster contract law's efficiency goals, such quick yes-contract conclusions may cause parties to suffer emotional harmor reach one-sided settlements, while narrow no-contract conclusions render ADR agreements meaningless.
This Article invites courts to go beyond formalist yes-contract/no-contract conclusions to craft appropriate remedies for enforcing ADR agreements. The Article proposes that courts should separately decide (1) whether there is a valid ADR agreement, and (2) how to overcome obstacles to determine breach and craft remedies for redressing breach. Although this seems to be what courts already do when they decide contract cases, the reality is that courts collapse these questions into one yes-contract/no-contract conclusion to escape the difficulties of defining ADR duties and determining proper remedies. The proposed approach allows for more relational and contextual analysis by asking courts to ease formalist rules that have traditionally limited enforcement of contracts requiring cooperation. The Article also seeks to spark consideration of remedial tools that courts have not adequately utilized in enforcing these agreements in the past.
Part II discusses the yes-contract/no-contract conundrum of contracts to bargain, and how this conundrum has impacted the analysis of ADR agreements.Part III highlights some of the problems with this yes-contract/no-contract conundrum.Part IV discusses the first step of my proposed analysis of ADR agreements, and explains my suggested approach for determining validity of ADR agreements and defining parties' duties to comply with these agreements in good faith.Finally, Part V focuses on the second step of the proposed analysis and addresses how courts may overcome evidentiary hurdles of determining breach and suggests some tools that courts may employ to remedy breach.The Article concludes by inviting consideration of this proposed analysis as a starting point for further exploration into the means for addressing the yes-contract/no-contract conundrum that is threatening the efficacy of ADR agreements and other contracts to bargain.

questions.question: Whether agreements to participate in nonbinding dispute-resolution processes (e.g., mediation) should be legally enforceable, and if so, how courts should determine their validity and the parties' duties to comply.
Whether courts should assess and remedy breaches of such cooperative ADR agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid yes-or-no formalist contract approach.

Whether separating the questions of (a) an ADR agreement's validity and (b) how to define breach and craft remedies leads to fairer and more effective enforcement outcomes than collapsing those questions into a single contract/no-contract determination.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do systemic institutional changes (deregulation, litigation costs, ADR, transnational codes) affect contracting behavior and the relation between law and practice?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How do informal relational norms and repeated interactions govern commercial contracting in practice, and when do these norms supplant formal state-enforced rules?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do parties in ongoing exchange relationships use relational contracting-informal, repeated-interaction arrangements-to govern performance and adapt to change?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: the role of good faith or a duty to negotiate in governing precontractual behavior
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with duties of good faith/negotiation: Paper A notes jurisdictions that impose a duty to negotiate in good faith and considers liability once negotiations are advanced, while Paper B advocates using good-faith and relational analysis to define and enforce ADR and bargaining duties.

shared_topics.topic: designing remedies and allocation rules to redress losses from failed negotiations

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS LIMITING LIABILITY: A PARADOX WITH TACIT SOLUTIONS

shared_topics.topic: weighing public policy/paternalism against private autonomy and positive social benefits
shared_topics.justification: Both articles interrogate the role of public policy in declining to enforce certain bargains: Paper B argues courts focus narrowly on paternalistic harms and should explicitly account for positive societal benefits when assessing liability-limiting agreements, while Paper A urges courts to consider collateral benefits and contextual fairness when deciding whether to enforce ADR commitments.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal uncertainty leading to chilling effects on contracting and inefficiency
shared_topics.justification: Both authors emphasize that current doctrinal vagueness causes unpredictable enforcement that deters parties from making mutually beneficial bargains; Paper A warns that formalist answers render ADR agreements meaningless or oppressive, and Paper B explains that vague public‑policy scrutiny discourages parties from entering liability‑limiting deals that could produce social efficiencies.

The scene is a table at a sidewalk cafe, where a lawyer and a client are sitting down for lunch.The lawyer is Robert Lichten (L), and the client is Carla Marchant (M),the president of Slater Valley Coal Company.  The sun is shining, a light breeze is blowing, and a record album of "Movie Street Noises"is playing softly in the background.  The camera zooms in.
L: How are you enjoying your evening law school classes?

questions.question: Whether and how the law should treat promises or transfers made in commercial contexts differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability (i.e., whether a requirement like consideration should apply differently in commercial vs. gift cases).
What factual, economic, and behavioral factors cause parties and courts to classify an exchange as a commercial transaction rather than a gift, and how does that classification affect legal outcomes.

papers.node_id: 62ukanlrev315!!ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses
papers.title: ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses
papers.abstract:
The common law defenses to contract formation - duress, misrepresentation or fraud, mistake, and unconscionability - are best justified historically, doctrinally, logically, and from the standpoint of policy, as a response to the plaintiff's showing of consideration. The next-best alternative, assent, justifies too little.
This thesis is proved in two parts. Part I addresses doctrinal history. The defenses existed in the law long before assent became part of the doctrine. When the defenses developed, consideration was with promise the primary touchstone of contractual liability. The formation defenses were often formulated explicitly with reference to the doctrine of consideration, a facet of the defenses that continues in many statements of them today.
Part II addresses logic and policy. Part II.A begins with a discussion of the policy grounds for the consideration doctrine and, incidentally, defends the doctrine. Part II.B shows the logical, doctrinal, and policy coincidence of consideration and the defenses. The defenses all show more than lack of assent, but they fully respond to, and coincide conceptually with, the plaintiff's allegation of consideration. Part III briefly concludes.
This Article is the second of two addressing the primacy of consideration and the resultant superfluity of assent doctrines in contract formation law. The first article, Assent Is Not an Element of Contract Formation,showed that assent as an element of formation merelyduplicates a function already performed by the doctrine of consideration. One can have assent without consideration, but one cannot have consideration without assent.Because consideration is required, assent was and is already required as part of the consideration analysis. There is therefore no need for a separate element of assent. The first paper shows that the assent doctrines' true function is merely to determine when consideration was given; the assent doctrines show the time of formation when that is important, not whether formation occurred.
This second article shows the doctrinal and conceptual primacy of consideration and resultant superfluity of assent doctrine with respect to the formation defenses. Commentators commonly suggest that the formation defenses exist because they undercut assent. This assertion is made with regard to each defense - duress,misrepresentation,mistake,and even unconscionability.Fortunately, this mistake is not universal.
not claiming that the defenses do not undercut assent. They do. A primary point of Assent Is Not an Element of Contract Formation is that consideration, as both a concept and a legal doctrine, includes assent. One cannot have consideration without assent. Duress and misrepresentation or fraud, for example, undercut assent not just incontract law but also in other areas of the law.Inasmuch as duress and misrepresentation undercut assent, they also undercut consideration. But as the defenses are phrased and as they function in contract law, they undercut more than assent. Assent therefore does not "occupy the entire area"it is said to cover. It fails to exercise "normative authority over"the defenses. It therefore does not "in fact function[] as a justification"for the formation defenses. Something other than assent shapes the defenses' form and function. That something else is consideration.
These conclusions combined with the historical, doctrinal, and logical arguments presented in Assent Is Not an Element of Contract Formation show that, of assent and consideration, consideration is elemental. Assent, on the other hand, is not elemental but is subordinate and dependent on the consideration doctrine.
