papers.node_id: 27setonhalllrev490!!ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY
papers.abstract:
"Under the existing legal system no legal relation is deemed contractual in the absence of certain voluntary acts on the part of two contracting parties. What acts are those which will cause society to come forward with its strong arm?"
To be enforced, bargain promises must be supported by consideration. As a consequence, consideration tests the divide between "freedom from contract" and contractual obligation.The full significance of the rule's location at this threshold of enforceable exchange, however, has been obscured by a long tradition reifying the requirement as "something given in exchange." The importance of consideration as a meaningful act, not a thing, committing a person to exchange has been inadequately developed. The relevance of consideration as a means to establish grounds of liability for promise has been lost. Instead, consideration has been treated as a troublesome and unnecessary appendage to the contract doctrine and common links between enforceable promises and other forms of liability for civil and criminal wrongs have been ignored.
Understanding consideration as a form for the relinquishment of autonomy forces a reconceptualization of what consideration does. Rather than a senseless, illogical, historical anomaly that should be abolished by judicial decision or legislation,the gathering of act, intent, andnexus of inducement compressed in consideration doctrine emerges as a means of attribution comparable to the more familiar requirements in torts or criminal law. Consideration establishes grounds of responsibility for bargain. As such, it functions not trivially to ban enforcement of promises which should be enforced, or merely formally as a cautionary or evidentiary means to assure promises are seriously intended,but foundationally to construct in everyday acts of exchange the social relation of autonomy on which the economic and social life of a market society depends.
Using the techniques of critical or scientific realism,this essay proposes to explain the doctrine of consideration as an expression of a mechanism for the relinquishment of autonomy. Insofar as it shows how and why the requirement of consideration exists, it constitutes a challenge to widespread attacks throughout the last century on the necessity or coherence of this doctrine. To the extent it argues that consideration involves a requirement of substance - a commitment to relinquish autonomy - it constitutes also a challenge to prevailing contemporary interpretations that suppose to explain the rule as a function of the form of bargaining only. Additionally, insofar as it distinguishes between a mechanism for the relinquishment of autonomy and other mechanisms involving, for example, reliance or modification, it provides a basis for evaluating proposals for reform. Moreover, it also explains why fashionable calls for abolition of the doctrine have been strikingly ineffective while other reform proposals, notably Restatement 90 and UCC 2-209(1), have met with success.Similarly, applications assumed to be more or less incoherent under traditional explanations can be given straightforward and consistent interpretation.
By way of overview, Part II explores the conditions presupposed by the operation of the doctrine of consideration. The form of argument used here is retroductive. The use of this approach, basic to scientific practice, suggests the need for me to frame my argument as a tentative of social science. This is done in Part III where I make clear the orientationson which I rely. Part IV identifies and analyzes the mechanism underlying the doctrine of consideration and locates this mechanism in a structure of social relations I characterize as relations of "interdependent autonomy." In doing so the analysis shows how, as a matter of individual agency, promises may become the subject of legal obligation and why, as a matter of social reproduction, they do come to form an institution of social and economic importance. On this foundation it is possible to establish which promises, as a matter of attribution and personal responsibility, may be fairly enforced against individuals who promise. Part V establishes the boundaries of inquiry by showing limits to the bargain mechanism and provides also a brief conclusion.

questions.question: Whether the enforcement prerequisite that a promise be accompanied by an exchange-related act functions to create a personal commitment to relinquish autonomy that justifies legal enforcement of the promise

Whether that enforcement prerequisite operates as a general attribution mechanism for assigning responsibility for promises, analogous to the grounds of liability used in other areas of civil wrongdoing
Why efforts to abolish or reform the enforcement prerequisite have met with differing success - i.e., why abolition attempts have been ineffective while some reform measures have been adopted

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?

When and to what extent should post-contractual promises (e.g., promises for additional payment to induce performance already owed or post-sale statements) be enforceable as warranties or modifications?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 50ucdavislrev405!!ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract
papers.title: ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract
papers.abstract:
At the core of a criminal conspiracy lies an agreement.It serves both to define the crime and justify it. If A and B agree to distribute drugs, for example, they are at that moment guilty of a crime: federal criminal conspiracy to distribute drugs.Even if they do not actually distribute the drugs, indeed, even if they take no steps to distribute the drugs, they can be prosecuted and convicted of the crime of conspiracy because of the agreement.The law of conspiracy attaches criminal liability far earlier than an attempt, which requires the defendant come dangerously near to committing the crime,or at least take a substantial step toward that crime.
Conspiracy comes close to punishing thoughts and speech alone,unlike most other crimes, which proscribe actual conduct.But courts justify criminal conspiracy on the grounds that the agreement is itself an act.The agreement shows the conspirators are serious,and theagreement itself makes it more likely the conspirators will commit the crime than if one of them simply resolved in his own mind to commit a crime.Sometimes the conspirators fail in their objective, or change their minds; courts still punish them because the agreement itself is the harm and deserves punishment.
Much rests, therefore, upon this agreement. And yet statutes, courts and jury instructions almost never define what constitutes the required agreement.We may at first glance argue that the term "agreement" is clear enough. But when we consider the wide range of meanings the term takes in ordinary English, we discover that our instructions to juries, and our rule of conspiracy law on appeal, create a concept both ambiguous and vague.
For example, "agreement" can essentially mean a contract,entailing an exchange of promises or some kind of commitment or obligation to perform. But "agreement" can also refer to mere harmony of opinion,as when we say, "experts agree smoking causes cancer." This second meaning of agree involves no obligation or promise between the experts but merely similar beliefs arrived at independently. With these two distinct meanings, the term agreement becomes dangerously ambiguous.
Courts have compounded the uncertainty inherent in the plain meaning of "agreement" in conspiracy cases. On the one hand, many courts say the agreement in a conspiracy differs from that in a contract. These courts say conspiracy does not require a "meeting ofthe minds,"at least strongly suggesting they are rejecting a meaning of agreement based upon promises or obligations. On the other hand, other courts insist that a conspiracy does require a "meeting of the minds."As the Ninth Circuit repeated last year, the "essence of a conspiracy is "meeting of the minds.'"Courts leave us somewhat at sea when they disagree over whether a conspiracy requires a "meeting of the minds," especially when that term itself has been repeatedly criticized."
Perhaps worse, courts dilute whatever meaning agreement has, often substituting "understanding,""shared criminal intent,""common purpose,"or worst of all, "slight connection."This last test, for determining when a person has joined an existing conspiracy, seems to read "agreement" out of conspiracy statutes entirely.With these unclear and diluted definitions of agreement in hand, juries routinely convict defendants for mere association or presence,such as ridingin a car with others who possess drugs.The rule for conspiracy has migrated from the impressive platitudes of appellate courts - that we may safely punish conspiracy because the agreement is the act - to an effective rule at trial that makes a person guilty of conspiracy for proximity to criminal activity.
Indeed, scholars often attack conspiracy law for punishing mere speech or association.But they have devoted no attention to "agreement" beyond simply identifying that the phrase is vague.Instead, they tend to repeat the same stale formula that the "agreement is the act."And just like the courts, they often completely disagree with each other whether a conspiracy does require the "meeting of the minds" required in contract law.
This Article tackles the problem with the definition of agreement head-on and argues we should define "agreement" in conspiracy to mean an exchange of promises to commit a crime. More precisely, in the paradigmatic case, the prosecutor should have to prove that the defendant promised to further the criminal goals in exchange for theother's promise to do the same.This exchange of promises creates a sense of obligation,in the eyes of each conspirator, to follow through.
This definition restores meaning to the term while making clear that "harmony of opinion" and other valid plain meaning definitions of agreement do not suffice in this context. My definition follows naturally from the key rationales courts regularly adduce to support recognizing conspiracy as a crime.
, courts assert the agreement shows the seriousness of the parties' intent.If someone makes a promise, especially in exchange for another promise, that promise shows this serious intent, as contract law makes clear.
, courts assert the agreement makes it more likely the conspirators will commit the crime.If the conspirators have exchanged promises, they have committed to following through, making the crime more likely. Each will also follow through to avoid retaliation.
, defining agreement as mutual promises eliminates or greatly reduces vagueness and uncertainty. Of course juries may still find implicit agreements, or secret agreements, and they may find these agreements based upon circumstantial evidence.My proposal does not change how agreements are proved from an evidentiary point ofview; rather, it simply clarifies the standard of agreement against which this evidence must be weighed: promises.
Finally, my definition best explains why we may punish criminal conspiracies consistent with the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment, as explored below.
Despite these straightforward principles of support, my proposal departs quite radically from existing doctrine. Courts do not define agreement in conspiracy as an exchange of promises. In fact, a review of the pattern jury instructionsfor all 50 states and the federal jurisdictions reveals that courts,in defining conspiracy to juries as an agreement, avoid any use of terms such as promise or obligation.This silence stands in bold contrast to how courts discuss contracts, discussions that are pervaded by notions of agreement,promises,and obligation.
A reader may object that courts treat contracts and conspiracies differently because they are different: society seeks to encourage contracts, but deter and punish conspiracies. But on furtherexamination many of the same principles apply: we enforce contracts because they are serious promises made upon consideration; we punish conspiracies in part because they evidence a defendant's serious intent to commit a crime. In both arenas it is the exchange of promises that further evidences serious intent. Similarly, in both cases the parties want the agreement to succeed, and have entered the agreement with promises or commitments to make that success more likely.
But even if the reader resists defining agreement so concretely - as an exchange of promises - such a definition serves as a crucial thought experiment, a first salvo against which to launch alternative proposed definitions in trying to define "agreement." If not an exchange of promises, what does agreement mean, and does that definition meet the very justifications for conspiracy courts have identified?
This article does not argue we eliminate the crime of conspiracy, as some have argued.Nor does it claim, on the other hand, that my definition of agreement solves conspiracy's shortcomings. Rather, it argues that if we continue to prosecute thousands of conspiracy cases a year,we must define "agreement" to match its justifications and guard against convictions based on mere presence. Defining agreement as an exchange of promises furthers these goals.
Part I summarizes the current definition of "agreement" in criminal conspiracy law. It shows both its inherent ambiguity and how courts and scholars have essentially ignored the problem. Part II defends my proposal that courts should define agreement in conspiracy as an exchange of promises, both for juries and for themselves on appeal.
Part III argues that my definition of agreement best justifies punishing conspiracy consistent with the Free Speech Clause. It alsodiscusses a related issue: the courts' frequent assertion that the conspiracy agreement is the act.
Part IV catalogues the profusion of special legal rules and jury instructions that courts have created just for conspiracy law. This vast superstructure forms a body of law unto itself, created to fix the problems caused by not defining "agreement" rigorously in the first place. My simple definition of agreement as an exchange of promises should eliminate or simplify this structure of ad hoc conspiracy rules.

questions.question: Should the 'agreement' required for criminal conspiracy be defined as an exchange of mutual promises (a binding commitment) rather than as mere shared belief, association, or proximity?

Would defining agreement as an exchange of promises better advance the justifications for punishing conspiracies (by showing seriousness of intent and increasing likelihood of completion), reduce vagueness and wrongful convictions, and be more consistent with free speech protections?

matched_themes: Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?

How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?

papers.node_id: 66washlrev937!!ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTING A NEW ACTION FOR NEGLIGENT INFLICTION OF ECONOMIC LOSS: BUILDING ON CARDOZO AND COASE.
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTING A NEW ACTION FOR NEGLIGENT INFLICTION OF ECONOMIC LOSS: BUILDING ON CARDOZO AND COASE.
papers.abstract:
During the past thirty years, courts and commentators have repeatedly addressed whether an architect, contractor or developer should be liable for a plaintiff's economic lossarising from a defect or delayin the construction of an improvement, when the parties are not in privity of contract and the plaintiff has suffered no injury to person or property other than the allegedly defective improvement.They have arrived at a bewildering array of solutions,none of which is satisfactory.
This issue generally arises in two settings.  First, a contractor or other party involved in the construction of an improvement sues another builder,most often the architect or supervising engineer, for economic loss arising during the construction project.  Second, after the completion of construction, an owner or tenant, or occasionally a party with no direct interest in the property, sues one of the builders.
In either setting, the plaintiff often sues in contract and tort.  The plaintiff alleges that the builder's contractual duties, especially itsimplied warranties, run to the plaintiff despite the absence of privity.The plaintiff also claims that the builder breached a duty not to act negligently or engage in negligent misrepresentations so as to cause economic loss.  The builder typically responds that its duty not to cause economic harm is contractual only and that its contractual duty does not extend beyond the party with which it contracted.  The "economic loss" rule, a doctrine which states that negligence law applies only to injuries to person or property, not to purely pecuniary loss, precludes a negligence or negligent misrepresentation claim.  Therefore, the builder concludes, it has no duty to the plaintiff.
In some cases, if no claim exists against the nonprivity builder, the claimant retains a viable claim against the party with whom it contracted.In many other cases, however, if the claimant cannot sue the nonprivity builder, it will have no claim at all, or at least no economically worthwhile claim.  The statute of limitations may have expired on the contract claim but not the tort claim,the claimant may not have received a warranty broad enough to support a claim,or the contracting party may be insolvent.
According to its proponents, the economic loss rule provides two primary benefits outweighing its deleterious impact on injured parties: the prevention of disproportionate liability;and the protection ofparties' freedom to allocate risks by contract.In support of the former, the more important, courts frequently quote from Justice Cardozo's decision inUltramare Corp. v. Touche,which denied a lender's claim that the defendant's accountants had negligently audited financial statements on which the lender had relied.Justice Cardozo stated, "[i]f liability for negligence exists, a thoughtless slip or blunder . . . may expose accountants to a liabilityin an indeterminate amount for an indeterminate time to an indeterminate class."
As the use of Justice Cardozo's decision from a nonconstruction dispute indicates, the issue whether an injured party should recover in tort for negligently inflicted economic loss arises in many contexts outside the construction setting.  This Article proposes the adoption of a new tort, a hybrid of negligence, negligent misrepresentation, and contract actions, dubbed the "negligent infliction of economic loss." It works effectively in construction-defect cases to provide relief to injured parties without exposing nonprivity builders to indeterminate risks.  It should logically work just as well in any other circumstance of negligently inflicted economic loss.  Economic loss caused by negligent construction apparently raises similar issues as other types of negligently inflicted economic loss.
The argument is developed in four parts.  Part II discusses the development of the doctrines which courts have applied to the construction cases.  These doctrines are sometimes at odds, and unsurprisingly, courts have applied them in many ways.  Part III identifies six distinct, inconsistent approaches adopted by various jurisdictions.
Part IV contains the bulk of the Article.  After determining that any action should protect the injured party's reliance interest,microeconomic analysis, in particular the Coase theorem,is applied to show that Cardozo correctly identified indeterminacy as the major problem posed by an action to recover for negligently inflicted economic loss.  The proposed action is structured to protect injured parties' reliance on the nonprivity builder without exposing the builder to claims by an indeterminate class of possible plaintiffs seeking indeterminate types and amounts of damages for losses caused over an indeterminate period of time.  Finally, Part V recasts the tort into more general terms and illustrates its application to non-construction disputes.16

questions.question: Should the law recognize a new cause of action allowing claimants to recover purely financial losses caused by the careless or defective performance of work by parties with whom the claimant has no contractual relationship, and if so, under what conditions?
How can such a cause of action be structured to protect injured parties' reliance interests while preventing defendants from facing indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?

matched_themes: When should a non-party be permitted to enforce a contract (third-party beneficiaries and non-party recovery)?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Can default liability rules be designed to induce socially optimal precontractual reliance, and what informational burdens would such rules place on adjudicators?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 39arizstlj135!!ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTIVE HAIKU AND THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: Raintree County Memorial Library Occasional Paper No. 3
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTIVE HAIKU AND THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: Raintree County Memorial Library Occasional Paper No. 3
papers.abstract:
More than ten years ago, the legal community was awash with speculation as to the identity of the author of two manuscripts, one which came to light in 1991,followed by a second in 1996.Each contained poems focusing on and illuminating various aspects of contract law. The author's identity was never ascertained even though it appeared that (s)he was a resident of Raintree County, a library user, and well versed in the content of a traditional contract law course.Three library patrons were suspected of being the author but none could be linked with the holographic manuscripts.It was hoped that further clues might be found if another manuscript surfaced, but none materialized. For a decade, the anonymous poet was silent. Then, this manuscript appeared under dramatic circumstances that, unfortunately, I am not at liberty to disclose. The Library Trustees granted me access to this collection on the condition that the circumstances surrounding the discovery remain confidential. I am authorized, however, to confirm that handwriting analysis supports a hypothesis of common authorship.
As for the poems themselves, the three line format has apparently been inspired by the pattern in a 5/7/5 haiku.But there most similarity ends. Very few in this collection conform to that model. And the traditional association with a season is often missing. Having said that, I should also note that, in some of the poems, the evocation of mood is as subtle and dramatic as any language in a more traditional work. The powerful imageryin phrases such as "smile of restitution," "lengthening shadows of sickness," and "trapped in the silence of paper" is undeniable. The pleasure to be derived from these legal gems is great, even when they fail to conform to poetic norms.
In editing these haiku, I have organized them by subject matter and provided captions for the individual verses. Where the author's meaning is unclear, I have suggested possible interpretations. The irregular spacing in some entries conforms to the spacing in the original manuscript.
Finally, a few words about the term "constructive haiku." Lawyers are accustomed to the use of phrases such as "constructive trust," "constructive possession," and "constructive service." All of these phrases are convenient legal fictions which help effect "an adjustment between new situations and an existing conceptual structure."The relationship suggested by use of these terms is, at the same time, both significant and remote. And so it is with these poems which are simultaneously closely related to and far removed from traditional haiku. As one great haiku master is said to have observed, "distance both infinite and infinitesimal unites us for the moment."

papers.node_id: 45wakeforestlrev607!!ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS
papers.abstract:
This Article explores the appropriate role for explicitly extralegal contextual factors in regulating, creating, and enforcing contracts. While contract law appears relatively neutral and acontextual on its face, extralegal factors such as party status; the circumstances of the bargain; performance by the parties; trade usage and custom; and background political, economic, and social contexts and circumstances may sometimes be more determinative of the outcome of contract disputes than the explicit terms and legal rules applicable to the parties' transaction.It arguably follows that courts should expansively use context to enforce the "real" relationship between the parties.
Potentially, expansive use of context may provide courts with a more accurate sense of the parties' subjective agreement.But this possibility is not without risks and limits. While contextual approaches to contract hold real promise as a means of critiquing and understanding contract law, there is little evidence that courts can actually use context to achieve a more accurate picture of theparties' real relation.This inability is due to subjective limits on the quality and validity of the data used in judicial analysis as well as inherent restrictions on judicial methods and capabilities. At the extremes, an open-ended contextualism risks becoming a judicial version of postmodern literary criticism or Monday-morning quarterbacking in which widely varying subjective and subconscious motivations are assigned to the helpless authors of the written contract. Instead of a means for increasing the accuracy or quality of judicial assessments of contract disputes, this Article argues that deliberate attempts to expand the use of implicit contextual factors are better understood as attempts to delegitimate existing contract regimes and shift bargaining power to apparently disadvantaged parties.
The use of high-context analysis to get at the "real" deal between the parties, rather than restricting analysis to the acontextual bargain evidenced by the "paper" terms and controlled by abstract contract rules, is tremendously seductive.High-context contract strategies promise nuanced understandings of the parties' contractual relationship.Compared with the deficiencies of neo-and classically formalist contract doctrinesin which ice-houses are left standing undisturbed,sister Antillico wanders homeless,andMichigan drivers wonder why they bothered paying for uninsured motorist coverage,high-context strategies promise to legitimate contract law by enabling courts to enforce the "real" deal between the parties and making contract law more reflective of actual social understandings and interactions between the parties.
High-context approaches to contract are also seductive for another reason. While specific components of expanded context analysis are relevant to assessing the parties' relative bargaining power, context-based arguments also concern power on a more fundamental level. At their heart, arguments for expanded use of context seek to change or expand the metaphorical field of battle for power in the contract relation - to remove the advantages of the (apparently) strong and balance out the disadvantages of the (apparently) weak.
This shift of bargaining power occurs both at the level of specific classes of contracting parties and at the overall systemic level. At the class-specific level, for instance, contextual claims that courts should acknowledge that franchisees lack bargaining power in contracting with franchisors in turn limit the ability of franchisors to impose exploitative terms on their franchisees.
At the systemic level, expanding the legally salient considerations for assessing formation, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts necessarily increases the scope of judicial discretion and the variability of potential outcomes in contract disputes.Expanded judicial discretion and variability of outcomes in turn systemically shift bargaining power from repeat players that benefit most from consistent application of the abstract rules of law to other classes of contracting parties who can achieve advantage (or minimize disadvantage) only by altering the rules of the game.In this sense, the question of whether courts should adopt relatively high-context strategies for contract dispute resolution is identical in many cases to the question of whether courts should attempt to shift bargaining power from repeat players such as business firms to sporadic contractors such as consumers, employees, and franchisees.
These dual views of context - justice through detail and power through changing the shape of the playing field - are potentially either legitimative or delegitimative of the institutions in which expanded context claims seek to operate. Although the legitimative thesis promises a better quality of judicial contract dispute resolution,it is not clear that high-context approaches improve actual treatments of disputes. In contrast, the delegitimative thesis does not concern the quality of judicial decision making, but rather the contest over relative bargaining power between particular classes of parties or systemically throughout contract law.While there remains significant debate over the relative competence of courts and legislatures to address issues of social policy,the characterization of contextual claims as macrolevel bargaining power contests suggests that these questions should be largelyreserved for legislative action.
Part I of this Article briefly surveys what "context" could mean in contract law. This Part includes arguments that courts should expand their analyses of particular doctrines to respond to particular, not currently salient contextual factors. Contextual arguments also include, however, claims that abstract background factors such as social, political, and economic influences on courts and parties affect contracting outcomes. Both types of context implicitly include a normative argument that courts should recognize and respond to contextual factors in resolving contract disputes.
Part II assesses the use of contextual factors in practice. In particular, this Part introduces the problems that may arise from a highly contextualized inquiry at the dispute resolution stage. Part III assesses the proposition that contextualist analysis is valuable for contract law because it in some sense legitimates contract law by prompting courts to engage in a richer and more nuanced inquiry into the context of disputes. Concluding that this legitimative thesis is potentially incoherent, Part IV examines context as a delegitimating influence on contract law that attempts to effect systemic shifts in bargaining power between classes of contracting parties. This Article concludes that it is questionable whether the legitimative thesis justifies use of high-context contract dispute resolution strategies, but that such strategies may be justified under the delegitimative thesis.

questions.question: Should courts incorporate extralegal contextual factors into decisions about contract formation, interpretation, and enforcement?
Does expanded judicial use of contextual evidence produce more accurate or more legitimate outcomes in contract disputes?

Does judicial adoption of high-context contract strategies systematically shift bargaining power between advantaged repeat players and disadvantaged one-off parties, and should courts (rather than legislatures) be the institution to effect such shifts?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do systemic institutional changes (deregulation, litigation costs, ADR, transnational codes) affect contracting behavior and the relation between law and practice?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How do informal relational norms and repeated interactions govern commercial contracting in practice, and when do these norms supplant formal state-enforced rules?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: critique of classical/formalist contract theory and advocacy for a more realistic or flexible approach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques rigid, classical contractual theory for ignoring motivation, bias, and unequal circumstances and urges elasticity in applying rules; Paper B critiques neo- and classical formalist doctrines and contrasts them with high-context strategies promising richer, more accurate adjudication of contractual relations.

shared_topics.topic: risks, limits, and legitimacy concerns of judicially applying context (subjectivity and increased discretion)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A acknowledges that existing corrective doctrines are limited and discusses practical difficulties of remedying bias through doctrine, and Paper B cautions that high-context approaches risk subjective, post-hoc judicial reconstructions, expanded discretion, variability of outcomes, and potential delegitimization of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: use of remedial doctrines (unconscionability, duress, undue influence, capacity) to address bargaining inequities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly urges broader, more elastic application of defenses like unconscionability, duress, undue influence, and capacity to ameliorate biased bargaining; Paper B considers expanding doctrinal analyses (formation, enforceability) to incorporate contextual factors that would affect the availability and application of such remedial doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91califlrev1645!!ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: how party status and relative bargaining power should affect contractual duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the parties' relationship (e.g., seller vs buyer; trust and confidence) as a central factor in whether a disclosure duty arises, and Paper B analyzes how courts’ use of contextual facts (party status, repeat players vs sporadic contractors, franchisees vs franchisors) functionally reallocates bargaining power and thus should influence contract enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should use bright‑line rules or context‑sensitive standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a multi‑stranded Disclosure Principle that balances general rules with specific exceptions, while Paper B directly debates high‑context approaches versus formalist, acontextual rules and the costs and limits of expanding contextual inquiry in adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: balancing efficiency costs against protective or corrective interventions (e.g., imposing disclosure duties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly conditions mandatory disclosure on the absence of significant efficiency costs, and Paper B weighs the legitimating benefits of context‑sensitive interventions against their systemic costs (variability, expanded discretion) when used to protect disadvantaged parties.

shared_topics.topic: the role of relational context (trust, notice, risk allocation, and improper means) in determining when courts should adjust obligations or enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A lists trust/confidence, notice, allocation of risk, and acquisition through improper means as decisive factors for imposing disclosure duties, and Paper B treats background circumstances, trade usage, bargaining context, and the parties’ relative positions as relevant contextual inputs that courts might (or might refrain from) use to alter enforcement outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev919!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Combating Limits of the Case Method with Quake Construction, Inc. v. American Airlines, Inc.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: II. THE BEST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: Combating Limits of the Case Method with Quake Construction, Inc. v. American Airlines, Inc.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary role of extralegal/contextual facts in contract interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A praises Quake Construction for providing rich factual context that illuminates parties' goals and aids interpretation, while Paper B theorizes and critiques 'high-context' approaches, debating when and how courts should rely on extralegal background (party status, trade usage, social/economic context) to reach outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: ascertaining parties' intent to be bound and the enforceability of preliminary instruments (e.g., letters of intent, promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on whether a letter of intent created a binding obligation and explores conditions precedent and promissory estoppel as means to enforce preliminary commitments; Paper B analyzes the broader project of using contextual evidence to discover the 'real' deal and whether courts can or should use such evidence to determine enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: how multiple contract doctrines interact to answer the core question of enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows, via Quake, that interpretation rules, conditions precedent, promissory estoppel, and fairness doctrines converge on whether a promise is binding; Paper B addresses how formation, interpretation, and enforceability doctrines are implicated when contextual factors are admitted or excluded and how that changes doctrinal application.

shared_topics.topic: institutional limits and pedagogical/procedural implications of relying on context (judicial competence, drafting, and teaching)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that richer factual presentation improves pedagogy and highlights drafting care to avoid disputes courts must resolve, while Paper B raises doubts about courts' competence to reliably use contextual data, warns of expanded judicial discretion, and suggests some contextual policy shifts may be better handled outside adjudication.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44depaullrev1301!!SYMPOSIUM: CULTURAL CONCEPTIONS OF COMPETITION: NOTE: TAX ABATEMENTS AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: A MATCH NOT MADE IN YPSILANTI
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CULTURAL CONCEPTIONS OF COMPETITION: NOTE: TAX ABATEMENTS AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: A MATCH NOT MADE IN YPSILANTI

shared_topics.topic: role of extralegal/contextual factors in enforcing obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes about courts' use of high-context information (party status, bargaining circumstances, social/economic background) when interpreting and enforcing contracts; Paper B confronts that practice in doctrine by applying promissory estoppel and reliance-based, fact‑specific inquiry to bind a corporation after tax‑abatement negotiations.

shared_topics.topic: judicial capacity and limits in making fact‑intensive, context‑driven decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts face subjective and methodological limits when trying to reconstruct parties' 'real' relations from context; Paper B illustrates those limits concretely by narrating and critiquing trial- and appellate-level factual findings about promise and reasonable reliance in the Ypsilanti/GM dispute.

shared_topics.topic: use of equitable doctrines to shift bargaining power toward vulnerable or local parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames expanded contextualism as a strategy that can reallocate bargaining advantage from repeat players to sporadic contracting parties (consumers, employees, franchisees); Paper B advocates using promissory estoppel to prevent a plant closing and thus protect a municipality and its workers against a large corporate counterparty.

shared_topics.topic: appropriateness of courts versus legislature in addressing broad social and economic policy issues
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether context-driven shifts in contract law should be effectuated by judges or left to legislative action; Paper B engages that question in practice by weighing statutory frameworks for tax abatements and debating whether judicial enforcement (via promissory estoppel) was the proper vehicle to secure community economic aims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36wmmarylrev1379!!ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: efficiency‑oriented versus balancing/contextual interpretive frameworks in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A juxtaposes Posner's efficiency‑and‑freedom focus against Cardozo's capacious, value‑balancing approach to contract doctrine; Paper B frames the debate as a choice between acontextual/formalist rules and high‑context interpretive strategies that incorporate social, economic, and relational factors.

shared_topics.topic: expansion or contraction of judicial discretion and variability of outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows Cardozo's methodology as permitting broad judicial mediation among competing values while Posner's framework narrows the considerations courts will weigh; Paper B argues that adopting high‑context analyses expands judicial discretion and increases outcome variability in contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal choices' effects on bargaining power and protection of vulnerable parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Cardozo's doctrines (e.g., good faith, protection of reasonable expectations) as protective of weaker parties with Posner's libertarian/efficiency tilt that can favor stronger repeat players; Paper B contends that contextualist doctrines are often motivated by — and will produce — shifts in bargaining power toward disadvantaged classes like consumers, employees, and franchisees.

shared_topics.topic: role of implied obligations and extralegal/contextual factors in interpreting and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the implied covenant of good faith (Cardozo's innovation versus Posner's resistance) as a central doctrinal divide over reading obligations beyond explicit terms; Paper B analyzes the use of party status, trade usage, performance circumstances, and other extralegal context as grounds for enforcing the parties' 'real' bargain rather than only the paper terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42harvjlgender83!!ARTICLE: ANTI-STEREOTYPING THEORY AND CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ANTI-STEREOTYPING THEORY AND CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should adopt contextualist approaches to remedy social inequalities (including gender)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law should reject rule-exception binaries and embrace a contextual approach that incorporates women's domestic experiences to eliminate gendered bias; Paper B analyzes 'high-context' strategies that expand extralegal factors in contract disputes and evaluates their potential to correct injustices and enforce the parties' 'real' relationships.

shared_topics.topic: contract law as a mechanism that reinforces or redistributes bargaining power and social hierarchies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates how doctrines like consideration, unconscionability, and interpretation have historically privileged an 'economic men' model and marginalized women, thereby reinforcing social hierarchies; Paper B frames expanded contextual analysis as a means to shift bargaining power from repeat players (firms) to disadvantaged classes (consumers, employees, franchisees) and treats context as a site of power struggle.

shared_topics.topic: the use and significance of background social norms, stereotypes, and extralegal factors in contract interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally critiques the role of gender stereotypes and state-reinforced norms in shaping contract doctrines and calls for doctrines that do not entrench traditional sex roles; Paper B surveys extralegal contextual factors (party status, trade customs, broader political/economic/social context) and examines how such background norms influence formation, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: trade-offs and limits of expanding judicial discretion through contextualization (accuracy, legitimacy, and predictability)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates contextualization to achieve egalitarian outcomes but implies significant doctrinal and practical shifts are required; Paper B directly assesses the risks of high-context approaches—subjectivity, variability of outcomes, and potential delegitimation of legal regimes—and questions whether courts can reliably use context without undermining consistency or deferring to legislatures.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 76geolj1949!!ARTICLE: Reinterpretations of 18th-Century English Contract Theory: The View from Lord Mansfield's Trial Notes.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reinterpretations of 18th-Century English Contract Theory: The View from Lord Mansfield's Trial Notes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' intentions and fairness in contract interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates using expanded contextual evidence to discover and enforce the parties' 'real' subjective agreement and to make outcomes reflect fairness, while Paper B shows, from Mansfield's trial notes, that eighteenth-century adjudication likewise prioritized parties' intentions and basic fairness in shaping enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the legitimacy and limits of judicial discretion versus formalist rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the risks and systemic consequences of open-ended contextualism—questioning courts' capacity and legitimacy to reshape bargains—while Paper B documents how Lord Mansfield exercised judicial discretion (but also policed its limits) in developing commercial contract doctrines rather than deferring wholly to formalist rules.

shared_topics.topic: the use of extralegal or contextual factors (custom, circumstances, equity) in assessing contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys various extralegal contextual inputs (party status, trade usage, social/economic background) and debates their proper weight in disputes; Paper B demonstrates historically that Mansfield and his courts relied on equitable considerations, intentions, and quasi-contractual notions (unjust enrichment)—forms of extralegal context—in deciding cases.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract and judicially imposed protective limits (including quasi‑contract/unjust enrichment remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames high-context approaches as mechanisms that can shift bargaining power away from repeat players toward disadvantaged parties (thus limiting pure freedom of contract), and Paper B argues Mansfield contributed to the rise of freedom of contract while simultaneously imposing limits and embracing quasi‑contractual relief to prevent unjust outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75cornelllrev62!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.

shared_topics.topic: judicial discretion and unpredictability in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that expansive use of contextual factors increases judicial discretion and variability of outcomes in formation, interpretation, and enforceability decisions; Paper B grapples with how current doctrines on modification and specific performance create practical uncertainty for parties trying to predict enforcement and litigation outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrine allocates or shifts bargaining power and responds to opportunism/bad faith
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contextualist approaches as mechanisms that can shift bargaining power from repeat players to disadvantaged parties systemically, while Paper B analyzes buyer 'opportunism' (self-help specific performance) and seller bad faith in modification contexts, asking how modification and remedy rules should deter or enable such strategic behavior.

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and relevance of extralegal/contextual factors (parties' conduct, circumstances, and motives) in deciding enforceability of agreements and modifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether courts should consider party status, bargaining circumstances, trade usage, and background social/economic context when enforcing contracts; Paper B considers whether courts should assess seller motives, the circumstances of a coerced modification, and related factual/contextual elements when deciding to enforce or void modifications.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of remedies (specific performance versus damages) in shaping contracting behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally examines how availability or denial of specific performance affects incentives to accept or contest modifications, while Paper A's inquiry into enforcing the 'real' deal and the consequences of expanded contextual enforcement implicates how remedial choices (and their predictability) influence parties' bargaining and expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61hastingslj801!!Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores: The Rest of the Story
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores: The Rest of the Story

shared_topics.topic: the role of extralegal/contextual facts in assessing contract formation and precontractual reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Hoffman v. Red Owl as a paradigmatic instance where courts had to decide whether precontractual reliance justified relief despite lack of a formal contract, and Paper B theorizes more broadly about when and how courts should use extralegal contextual facts (party status, circumstances, performance, customs) to decide formation and enforceability questions.

shared_topics.topic: relational contracting and evolving expectations before formal agreement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its inquiry in Macneil's relational-contract critique of the binary view of formation, showing how parties may develop expectations and rely on an evolving bargain, while Paper B engages with similar phenomena when it considers high-context strategies that attempt to recover the parties' 'real' relationship instead of the paper terms.

shared_topics.topic: how use of context affects bargaining power between parties/classes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the practical stakes of recognizing precontractual reliance (which can protect a relying, often weaker, party), and Paper B directly frames expanded contextual adjudication as a means that can shift bargaining power from repeat players (businesses) to episodic or disadvantaged parties (consumers, franchisees, employees).

shared_topics.topic: limitations, risks, and legitimacy of judicial fact-finding when courts adopt contextual approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how appellate opinions and trial records selectively present facts and how fuller factual investigation can change assessments of a case like Hoffman, while Paper B critiques the subjective limits and risks of open-ended contextualism—arguing that courts may lack the competence or impartial data to reliably reconstruct the parties' true intent without risking arbitrariness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33sandiegolrev175!!ARTICLE: Living Without the Avoidable Consequences Doctrine in Contract Remedies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Living Without the Avoidable Consequences Doctrine in Contract Remedies

shared_topics.topic: whether and how courts should use extralegal/contextual evidence (party conduct, background circumstances) to adjust contractual remedies or interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts must account for the benefit a plaintiff obtains from breach (often revealed by the plaintiff's failure to mitigate) when calculating expectation-based damages, effectively treating such noncontractual facts as offsets; Paper B directly debates the propriety of expanding judicial reliance on extralegal contextual factors (party status, bargaining circumstances, performance, social background) to determine formation, interpretation, and enforcement of contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the proper normative goal of contract adjudication (formal expectation interest versus contextual justice or redistribution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the expectation interest and contends that doctrines like avoidable consequences are consistent with avoiding overcompensation under that norm; Paper B contrasts aformalist, rule-based approach with a high-context, legitimative project that would use context to achieve more equitable outcomes or to reallocate bargaining power.

shared_topics.topic: drawing inferences from party behavior (e.g., failure to mitigate, performance choices) to infer private valuations, intent, or offsets in remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally claims that a plaintiff's decision not to mitigate reveals her valuation of benefits from breach and justifies subtracting avoidable losses as an implicit offset; Paper B considers using parties' conduct and performance as part of a high-context attempt to reconstruct the parties' 'real' agreement and underlying bargaining dynamics.

shared_topics.topic: limits on judicial capability and discretion in valuing benefits and applying contextual factors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes courts' difficulty in directly recognizing or valuing the benefits conferred by breach and offers the avoidable-consequences inference as a practical solution, while Paper B criticizes high-context approaches for producing subjective, unreliable inquiry and for expanding judicial discretion in ways that risk inconsistent or illegitimate outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 49hastingslj1191!!ARTICLE:Rescuing Reliance: The Perils of Promissory Estoppel
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Rescuing Reliance: The Perils of Promissory Estoppel

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal expansion of reliance-based remedies (promissory estoppel) beyond classical bargain theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces and debates how the Restatement and later developments expanded promissory estoppel and reliance-protection beyond traditional contract-formation doctrines, while Paper B treats expanded contextual inquiry (which can include reliance and informal understandings) as a broader move beyond formal, paper-based bargains.

shared_topics.topic: legitimacy and normative justification for expanding contract-law intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses whether promissory estoppel should remain part of contract law given critiques of its scope and utility, and Paper B questions whether high-context approaches legitimately improve judicial outcomes or merely change the field of battle for policy and power.

shared_topics.topic: judicial discretion, indeterminacy, and the limits of courts in applying expansive doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A responds to critiques about promissory estoppel's viability and potential overreach (implying concerns about judicially created liability), and Paper B analyzes the epistemic and methodological limits that make contextualist doctrines prone to subjectivity and unpredictable judicial discretion.

shared_topics.topic: use of doctrinal expansion to alter bargaining power and protect disadvantaged parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the practical and symbolic importance of reliance-protection (which often benefits promisees who relied to their detriment), and Paper B explicitly argues that contextual or expanded doctrinal approaches function to shift bargaining advantages toward sporadic or disadvantaged contracting parties such as consumers, employees, and franchisees.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev1016!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Pillans and Rose v. Van Mierop and Hopkins: The Worst Way to Win
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Pillans and Rose v. Van Mierop and Hopkins: The Worst Way to Win

shared_topics.topic: judicial lawmaking versus legislative rulemaking in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that expansive, context-driven judicial decisionmaking effectively changes the rules of the contracting game and that many such redistributive choices are more properly made by legislatures; Paper B criticizes the judges in Pillans for inventing rationales and shows how uncertainty from judicially created rules persisted until statutory reforms (e.g., UCC) filled the gap.

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of extralegal context or labels to evade or reinterpret formal doctrines (e.g., consideration)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts invoke extralegal contextual factors to enforce the 'real' deal and warns that open-ended contextualism risks post-hoc storytelling; Paper B documents Lord Mansfield and colleagues using labels like 'mercantile transaction,' custom, and writing to sidestep the consideration requirement without adequate evidentiary support.

shared_topics.topic: distributional and systemic effects of doctrinal choices on contracting parties and commercial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that adopting high-context doctrines can shift bargaining power between repeat players and sporadic parties (consumers, franchisees, employees) and has systemic distributive consequences; Paper B traces how the Pillans decision (and ensuing confusion) altered commercial norms around letters of credit and produced long-term effects on international mercantile practice and legal predictability.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary, cautionary, and predictability functions of formal requirements and the risks of abandoning them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether replacing formal, acontextual rules with contextual inquiry actually improves accuracy or instead undermines predictability and judicial competence; Paper B discusses Wilmot's articulation of consideration's evidentiary/cautionary/channeling functions and criticizes Mansfield's dismissal of those functions as careless, showing concrete risks when courts discard formal safeguards.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2000byulrev1363!!ARTICLE:Nachfrist Was Ist? Thinking Globally and Acting Locally: Considering Time Extension Principles of the U.N. Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods in Revising the Uniform Commercial Code
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Nachfrist Was Ist? Thinking Globally and Acting Locally: Considering Time Extension Principles of the U.N. Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods in Revising the Uniform Commercial Code

shared_topics.topic: the role of extralegal and background context in interpreting and applying contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates whether courts should use social, economic, and relationship-based context to determine the 'real' deal between contracting parties; Paper B warns against reading international uniform texts through domestic lenses and examines how importing concepts like Nachfrist brings civil-law contextual doctrines into U.S. contract practice.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal choices shift bargaining power between contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that expanding context-sensitive doctrines can systemically reallocate advantage from repeat commercial actors to sporadic or disadvantaged parties, and Paper B considers how adopting CISG-style rules (e.g., Nachfrist) or applying international norms could change liabilities and strategic positions for domestic buyers and sellers.

shared_topics.topic: whether substantive change in contract law should occur through courts or through legislative/codification reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that broad contextual reform raises judicial discretion and that many power-shifting questions are better resolved legislatively, while Paper B explicitly evaluates revising the Uniform Commercial Code to incorporate CISG/Nachfrist principles rather than relying on case-by-case judicial adaptation.

shared_topics.topic: concerns about uniformity, predictability, and variability of contractual outcomes across different legal regimes or interpretive approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that high-context adjudication increases variability and undermines predictable application of abstract rules, and Paper B addresses the CISG’s mixed success in producing uniform results across diverse legal systems and the risks of unexpected liability when different doctrinal frameworks interact.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73uchilrev1299!!ARTICLE: Commodification and Contract Formation: Placing the Consideration Doctrine on Stronger Foundations
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Commodification and Contract Formation: Placing the Consideration Doctrine on Stronger Foundations

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formalist rules and contextual/intent-based approaches in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the consideration doctrine as a formalist hoop purportedly used to identify parties' intent and questions whether reciting consideration is any better than explicitly stating enforceability; Paper B directly contrasts acontextual/formalist doctrines with high-context approaches and evaluates the merits and risks of expanding contextual inquiry to better capture parties' real agreement.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal devices as mechanisms for signaling intent and controlling enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes consideration as a doctrinal device that allegedly signals which promises parties intend to make legally binding, while Paper B discusses how expanding or contracting the set of legally salient contextual factors serves as a tool that courts can use to determine when promises and terms are enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: normative justification for contract rules and limits on judicial competence to implement alternatives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues there is a lack of sound theoretical justification for the consideration rule and critiques existing rationales, and Paper B questions whether courts possess the epistemic and methodological capacity to use rich contextual evidence reliably, thereby challenging normative claims for expanding context-based adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: standards and criteria for contract formation and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on what should count as effective consideration and why some unilateral promises remain unenforceable, and Paper B examines which extralegal contextual factors ought to be treated as legally salient when assessing formation, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90tullrevonline1!!ARTICLE: Third-Party Beneficiaries and the Nature of Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Third-Party Beneficiaries and the Nature of Contract

shared_topics.topic: what contractual formation actually creates — the nature of the obligation (e.g., a right to performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly interrogates how formation, interpretation, and enforceability doctrines should be understood when contextual facts are introduced, and Paper B focuses on whether contract formation creates a distinct kind of obligation (including whether it confers a right to performance), using third‑party beneficiary doctrine as diagnostic evidence.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation and doctrinal tools in defining and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the merits and risks of courts using expansive contextual inquiry (and the discretion that entails) to interpret and enforce agreements, while Paper B analyzes how courts' remedial and interpretive doctrines (including third‑party beneficiary rules) reveal or shape the legal character of contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal choices reallocate rights and bargaining power among contracting parties and third parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contextualist interpretive choices can shift bargaining power between repeat players (firms) and sporadic contractors (consumers, employees, franchisees), and Paper B shows that resolution of puzzles about third‑party beneficiaries has concrete consequences for which parties obtain enforceable rights and protections.

shared_topics.topic: whether core contract doctrines should be revised and by what institutional actors (courts vs legislatures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether courts should expand contextual inquiry or leave structural shifts to legislatures, and Paper B engages the normative question whether we should reconceive foundational doctrines (e.g., abandonment of a right to performance) or adopt more modest theoretical reforms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52amjcompl513!!ARTICLE:Impossibility and Changed and Unforeseen Circumstances
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Impossibility and Changed and Unforeseen Circumstances

shared_topics.topic: use of extrinsic 'context' or changed-circumstances to justify judicial modification or excuse of contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the historical doctrine of changed circumstances (and its relation to impossibility) as a basis for courts to relieve parties when external events alter the character or value of performance; Paper B directly debates whether courts should incorporate extralegal contextual factors (circumstances of the bargain, performance, trade usage, background social/economic context) when creating, interpreting, or enforcing contracts.

shared_topics.topic: when performance-affecting events (impossibility, hardship, dramatic price shifts) should excuse or modify obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on impossibility and dramatic changes in market value as triggers for doctrines that excuse or alter performance; Paper B lists performance by the parties and the circumstances of performance as central contextual considerations in determining enforceability and judicial relief.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and coherence of doctrinal explanations for contract relief doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques historical and modern jurists for failing to provide coherent rationales for Roman impossibility texts while praising medieval explanations of changed circumstances; Paper B questions whether expanded contextualist doctrines genuinely improve judicial accuracy or instead rest on subjective, incoherent inferences, thereby probing the justificatory basis of doctrinal change.

shared_topics.topic: connection between doctrines that recognize context/relief and shifts in bargaining power or equitable outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses moral and philosophical rationales for giving relief under changed circumstances (implicitly tied to fairness in reallocating unforeseen burdens), while Paper B explicitly analyzes how context-based doctrines can function to reallocate bargaining power between repeat players and disadvantaged contracting parties and may be used to pursue equitable ends.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48tullrev946!!ARTICLE: Rules and Terms--Civil Law and Common Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rules and Terms--Civil Law and Common Law

shared_topics.topic: the role of extra‑doctrinal or contextual sources in contract interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates whether courts should use extralegal contextual factors (party status, social/political background, trade usage) to determine the 'real' deal, and Paper B documents how Common law judges and writers invoked Civil law authorities (Pothier, Code Civil, Roman law) as extra‑doctrinal sources when reasoning about contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriateness and limits of judicial reliance on nontraditional authorities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A assesses the epistemic and institutional limits on courts' ability to use open‑ended contextual inquiry and warns of indeterminacy or postmodern overreach, while Paper B interrogates whether Common law courts were justified in borrowing Civilian analysis and whether such comparative citation sometimes distorted Common law reasoning.

shared_topics.topic: comparative and historical influence on the development of contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates 'high‑context' strategies against the background of formalist contract doctrines and evolving doctrinal debates, and Paper B traces the historical influence of Roman/Civil law on the modern Civil and Common law contract doctrines and how that borrowing shaped nineteenth‑century developments.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between systematizing/formalist rules and pragmatic/context‑sensitive approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a conflict between abstract, consistent contract rules that favor repeat players and high‑context approaches that tailor outcomes to particular parties or classes, while Paper B contrasts the Civilian project of rationalizing and systematizing contract law (Pothier, Code) with the Common law's more pragmatic, case‑driven evolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50ucdavislrev405!!ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract

shared_topics.topic: what legally counts as an 'agreement' — an exchange of promises versus mere concordance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the agreement element in conspiracy law should be defined as an exchange of promises (not mere harmony of opinion) to limit convictions for proximity or association; Paper B examines claims that courts should look beyond paper terms to reconstruct the parties' "real" agreement, debating whether implicit/subjective understandings should control legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role and admissibility of contextual or circumstantial evidence in proving agreements or enforcing obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that juries often infer conspiracy from circumstantial facts and secret/implicit agreements and proposes a clearer standard for what evidence of agreement suffices; Paper B analyzes the epistemic limits and risks of using extralegal contextual factors to infer the parties' intent or real deal, questioning whether courts can reliably use such evidence.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate scope of judicial discretion to temper strict bargain rules in the name of fairness

shared_topics.topic: the role of formalist academic influence and ideological commitments in resisting or promoting doctrinal developments

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of information asymmetries and relative bargaining power in deciding enforceability or relief

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules shape bargaining power and acceptable tactics between parties

shared_topics.topic: appropriate judicial role and limits in incorporating extrinsic factors into contract enforcement

shared_topics.topic: confusion over terminology and the need for clearer analytical categories

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT TEXTS, CONTRACT TEACHING, CONTRACT LAW: COMMENT ON LAWRENCE CUNNINGHAM, CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD

shared_topics.topic: the utility and limits of judicial methods (opinions, fact-finding) for conveying and resolving contextual information
