shared_topics.topic: the methodological contest between formalist/doctrinal approaches and contextual/realist approaches to contract law

shared_topics.topic: skepticism about the evidentiary basis for methodological or pedagogical claims

papers.node_id: 83notredamelrev353!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AS AGREEMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AS AGREEMENT
papers.abstract:
Broad theories of contract law are intentional in nature, whether based upon the rights of the individual as an autonomous actor,the benefits to society of encouraging people to engage in bargained-for transactions,or the justice due those who have relied on the promises and representations of others.No one speaks, for example, of the freedom to be bound by something one did not intend. Bargainsimply volition. Acts in reliance come only after an understanding that someone has made a commitment. However contract law is constructed, at the very least, one would expect it to take as its point of departure the players' actual intentions.
Yet, for generations law students have been taught that the law governing the formation of contracts is by and large objective in nature, although it has some subjective elements. It is the appearance of intent that matters most. Many casebooks say so,as do textsand treatises.The Restatement incorporates a largely objective approach to contract formation as well, although its key provision dealing with the interpretation of contracts is both objective and subjective.While it often refers to mutual assent, the Restatement makes clear that its concern is only with outward manifestations of mutual assent. Such manifestation occurs through promising or performing,and promising is itselfdefined as a manifestation of a commitment.The actual states of mind of the parties are not the subject of legally relevant inquiry.Almost a century after he wrote the opinion in Hotchkiss v. National City Bank of New York, Learned Hand's twenty bishops still make their way into discussion, whether through the case lawor the scholarly literature.While there is some debate about how and when this state of affairs developed,there is little controversy about its existence.
The objective account relies heavily on cases in which an individual makes a statement that is reasonably construed as a promise, and for which he has bargained for something in exchange. When the time comes for performance, the promisor denies having intended to commit himself to the deal. The cases routinely say that it does not matter what he thought.What matters is whether a reasonable person would understand his statement as a promise. If so, then he is bound - even if twenty bishops vouch for him.
Because the promisor is, naturally enough, also bound by his promise in the routine case in which he does intend to be bound, his intent appears to be irrelevant. The law provides the same result regardless of what he was thinking, so long as a reasonable person would construe his statement as a commitment to perform. This confluence has led judges and scholars alike to hypothesize that objective analysis is at the core of contract law.
This Article argues that this objective account emanates from too narrow a vantage point. It ignores certain situations in which it would not be reasonable to construe a statement as a promise, and it fails to take into account the understanding of the promisee, which is an important variable in determining contractual liability. Most problematic for the objective account is that when both parties agree that a commitment has been made, the promisor is bound, and when neither believes that a promise has been made, the promisor is not bound. Objective considerations are irrelevant. Even when a reasonable person would construe the promisor's statement as a commitment, courts will not enforce a statement to which neither party subscribed.By the same token, courts will enforce a promise to which both parties agreed, even if a reasonable person would not have understood it as a promise.
When the additional scenarios generated by considering the promisee's state of mind and additional situations in which it is not reasonable to infer a promise are added to the mix, the objective theory has little explanatory power. A theory at the very least should containa set of principles which, when applied to a core set of fact situations, accounts for their distribution of outcomes. The objective account of contract law fails to do this.
Far more descriptive of the actual array of facts are theories of contract formation based upon mutual assent or the reliance of the promisee. Actual agreement matters in the law of contracts. Promises are enforced when the parties have reached an agreement, and are not enforced when the parties have not actually reached an agreement, unless the promisee actually and reasonably believes that a promise was made even though none was intended. By the same token, objective considerations play a role in the decisionmaking process. However, what is called an objective theory is better seen as a rule designed to handle a particular set of cases, embedded in a larger theory whose basic organizing principle is the actual mutual assent of the parties. I argue in this Article that these cases reflect a preference for reliable evidence of actual subjective intent, and act as a species of estoppel, preventing parties from backing away from the predictable reliance upon their acts of speech.
With this reconceptualization comes some positive consequences. For one thing, it allows for added flexibility in the award of contract remedies. While expectation damages may be an appropriate remedy for breaches when the parties have reached agreement, full benefit-of-the-bargain awards may overcompensate promisees, especially when a promisor inadvertently commits himself, and recognizes the fact before there has been substantial reliance.Seventy-five years ago, Professor Whittier made a similar suggestion in his criticism of the first Restatement.Based on a somewhat broader range of data, I argue here that it is time to resuscitate his analysis.
In addition, once we stop speaking of an objective theory of contract formation, various contract doctrines begin to fit more coherently with one another. Among the advantages are the harmonization of rules governing the formation and interpretation of contracts; a significant reduction in the need for peculiar technical definitions of such common terms as offer, acceptance, agreement; reconciliation of the objective approach and the requirement of a bargain, which contains some indispensably subjective elements; and harmonization of the rules governing contract formation and the rules governing incomplete contracts.
Part I of this Article fleshes out the problems that arise with the objective theory of contract. The argument is a descriptive one: Once the core scenarios are defined, it quickly becomes clear that the objective approach fails to account for about half of them. A more subjective approach - whether based upon mutual assent or upon reliance - better explains the basic array of facts.
Part II provides two alternative explanations for cases generally used to justify the objective approach, in which a person is bound by a statement that he did not intend as a binding promise. First, the rule serves as a proxy for the actual intent of the parties. Judges articulate this rationale with great frequency. By accepting the ordinary meaning of the words used as the intended meaning, courts are likely to capture the intended meaning most of the time, since that is how the words are most typically used and understood. The second justification for the rule disallowing unexpressed subjective evidence of intent is that such a rule serves as an estoppel to protect reliance interests. If an individual makes a statement that (1) a reasonable person would construe as a promise and (2) the promisee actually understands as a promise in the context of a bargained-for exchange, then the promisor may not assert that he did not intend to bind himself. I call this principle formation estoppel.
Part III discusses some of the consequences of a subjective account for contract formation. First, the subjective account permits more flexibility in the conceptualization of contract remedies. Expectation damages may not be appropriate when the promisor did not intend to bind himself and the promisee has not acted in reliance. Second, the subjective account brings the formation of contracts into harmony with the rules governing contract interpretation, consideration, and gap-filling. The result is a far more coherent account of contract law generally. Part IV is a brief conclusion.

questions.question: Should the formation of contracts be governed primarily by outward, objective manifestations of intent or by the parties' actual subjective agreement and the promisee's reliance?
Does enforcing promises based on their outward appearance operate mainly as a reliable proxy for the parties' actual intent or instead function as a form of estoppel protecting reliance?
Would reconceiving contract formation around actual mutual assent and reliance change the appropriate allocation of remedies and produce greater doctrinal coherence across contract rules?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
How should law allocate evidentiary burdens in disputes over assent and formation to protect against unfair bargains?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How should courts resolve agreements founded on mutual misunderstanding: voidness versus enforcing each party's reasonable interpretation?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 87columlrev217!!ARTICLE: PRECONTRACTUAL LIABILITY AND PRELIMINARY AGREEMENTS: FAIR DEALING AND FAILED NEGOTIATIONS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PRECONTRACTUAL LIABILITY AND PRELIMINARY AGREEMENTS: FAIR DEALING AND FAILED NEGOTIATIONS.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of objective versus subjective tests for contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly challenges the dominant objective approach and argues for an account centered on actual mutual assent and the promisee's state of mind; Paper B likewise critiques classic offer-and-acceptance vocabulary as ill-suited to modern multi-stage deals and examines when parties' actual negotiating intentions should determine whether a binding obligation exists.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance and estoppel in binding parties during negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the idea of 'formation estoppel' and emphasizes protecting reliance where promisees reasonably believe a commitment was made; Paper B surveys doctrines (including restitution and remedies for lost opportunities) and argues existing law can and should protect reliance interests when negotiations produce expectations despite no formal closing.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of preliminary agreements, open-term agreements, and 'agreements to negotiate'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how a subjective account brings formation and the treatment of incomplete contracts into alignment, affecting when preliminary understandings should be enforced; Paper B directly analyzes when preliminary agreements and agreements to negotiate should be recognized and enforced under existing contract law and what duties they create.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies for failed or inadvertent commitments in negotiation contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for flexible remedial rules (sometimes less than full expectation damages) when a promisor did not intend to bind and reliance is limited; Paper B examines the range of remedies claimants may seek after failed negotiations—restitution, out-of-pocket costs, and damages for lost opportunities—and how existing doctrines can supply them.

shared_topics.topic: harmonizing formation rules with other contract doctrines (interpretation, consideration, good faith/fair dealing, incomplete contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that shifting from an objective formation rule to a mutual-assent/reliance framework yields greater coherence across interpretation, consideration, and gap-filling; Paper B similarly explores how duties of fair dealing and other established doctrines can be applied across negotiation and preliminary-agreement regimes to create a coherent legal response to modern dealmaking.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75geolj1575!!ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal development of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage in close historical and doctrinal scholarship about how key contract doctrines evolved: Paper A re-examines the emergence and reception of the objective theory of contract formation in case law and Restatement authority, while Paper B traces the development and often-mischaracterized history of the English impossibility/frustration doctrine from medieval times to the present.

shared_topics.topic: judicial role in adapting contract rules to factual complexity
shared_topics.justification: Both articles analyze how courts shape and adapt abstract contractual rules to particular fact patterns: Paper A shows how judges apply or depart from an 'objective' rule depending on parties' mutual assent and reliance, and Paper B shows how judges have fashioned the impossibility/frustration doctrines (and sometimes created case-specific exceptions) when supervening events disrupt performance.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate legal consequences when contractual expectations are upset
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider what legal response is appropriate when the parties' expectations do not match the outcome — Paper A debates whether expectation damages or reliance-limited remedies fit situations of inadvertent or nonconsensual commitments, and Paper B examines whether supervening events should discharge, suspend, or leave obligations intact under impossibility/frustration.

shared_topics.topic: limits of broad, rule-based (objective) doctrines and the need for contextual inquiry
shared_topics.justification: Both works criticize overly general rule-first approaches and emphasize context: Paper A argues the 'objective theory' of formation is too narrow and that subjective assent and promisee reliance better explain results, while Paper B argues famous impossibility cases are often products of unique circumstances and that broad doctrinal labels (like 'frustration') obscure the contextual bases for decisions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38sandiegolrev1!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:FOREWORD Is Reliance Still Dead?
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:FOREWORD Is Reliance Still Dead?

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance in promissory estoppel and whether detrimental reliance is necessary or sufficient
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a formation account that centers on actual assent or the promisee's reliance and rejects a purely objective rule, while Paper B traces scholarship and case law on the ‘death of reliance,’ presenting empirical work showing that detrimental reliance typically remains a required element (but not sufficient alone) for promissory estoppel.

shared_topics.topic: objective manifestations versus actual subjective intent in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the dominant objective approach and defends a theory privileging actual mutual assent (or promisee reliance) over mere outward manifestations, and Paper B examines how courts and scholars treat manifested intention to be legally bound versus mere appearances, distinguishing enforcement reliance from other forms of reliance.

shared_topics.topic: criteria for enforcing non‑bargained‑for promises (what extra 'something' beyond reliance is required)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies cases where courts enforce or refuse enforcement based on promisee understanding and mutual agreement and develops formation‑estoppel reasoning, while Paper B surveys empirical studies and normative proposals (e.g., enforcement‑vs‑performance reliance, section‑style rules) to specify the additional conditions that turn detrimental reliance into an enforceable claim.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies when promises are enforced (expectation versus reliance damages and flexibility of remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that a subjective formation account permits more flexible remedial choices — sometimes limiting expectation damages when promisor lacked intent and reliance was slight — and Paper B discusses the normative implications of reliance versus expectation interests and whether reliance recovery should be the default or fallback in promissory estoppel cases.

papers.node_id: 41loyuchilj175!!Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power
papers.title: Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power
papers.abstract:
Legal scholars and academics draw a distinction between "classical contract" and "modern contract"that, for the most part, turns on the differences between the two systems.For example, the classicalsystem relies on technical and rigid rules, whereas the modern system has shifted to more flexible standards. Modern contract, unlike the classical system, also attempts to effectuate the nor ms of fairness and cooperation. And the list goes on.
Conventional wisdom holds that: (1) modern contract law evolved, at least in part, to remedy problems created or left unaddressed by the classical contract law system;(2) modern contract law is different from classical contract law in ways that make the current system work better than the older regime, that is, in ways that attempt to rectify some of those problems;and, therefore, (3) it is the differences between the two systems that are the most important part of the contract evolutionary story.Whether this conventional wisdom is true depends upon whether modern contract has been successful in correcting the problems produced by the classical system. If it has not been successful, then the conventional wisdom is wrong. And if the conventional wisdom is wrong, then one could argue that at least parts of modern contract law are no better than the classical contract system that it replaced, because whatever problems modern contract perceived in the classical system remain. This Article uses modern contract's expanded "policing doctrines" to question the validity of this hypothesis.
More specifically, modern contract law gives expanded recognition to several contract policing doctrines,namely, unconscionability, economic duress, and misrepresentation.Each of these doctrines focuses on some type of bargaining misbehavior that produces a "bad bargain" for one of the parties. All of these doctrines then attempt to address the bargaining misbehavior by making the contract procured asa result of the misbehavior voidableor otherwise unenforceable in whole or in part.
While the type of bargaining misbehavior targeted by each of the expanded policing doctrines varies, all can be characterized as a form of "coercion," meaning that one party is compelled or forced by another to do what her free will would otherwise refuse.So, for example, unconscionability focuses on one party's improper use of its unequal bargaining power and/or unfair and deceptive tactics;economic duress is directed at conduct where one party causes, or at least takes advantage of, the other party's financial distress;and misrepresentation addresses situations where one party presents (or withholds) material information to (or from) the other party incorrectly, improperly, and/or fraudulently.In each of these coercive situations, the end result - indeed the objective of the coercive conduct - is to procure a "bad bargain."Hence, the act to which a party is "compelled or forced by another to do what her free will would otherwise refuse" is agreeing to the bad bargain.
Since a bad bargain is a necessary part of the coercion problem, it warrants further explanation. An underlying assumption of this analysis is that the contracting parties came together for some reason: Party B has what Party A wants or needs, whether a good or service, and Party A is willing to pay for it. In other words, neither party was forced to come to the bargaining table under false pretenses.Now, let us assume further that the contract terms are fair and reasonable. Given that Party A wants and/or needs the good or service at issue and came to the bargaining table willingly, why would Party B have to coerce Party A to enter that contract? Absent any coercion on Party B's part, there is clearly no legal claim presented on these facts, given that the contract terms are fair and reasonable and no false pretenses were used. An argument could be made, however, that Party B might want the additional sale to Party A at any cost. To realize on the additional sale to Party A, therefore, Party B might employ sales tactics to persuade Party A to enter into the fair and reasonable contract.
So, let us assume that Party B uses sales tactics that, unbeknownst to Party B, constitute actionable coercion,and that those sales tactics coerced Party A to enter into a fair and reasonable contract. Is a legal problem presented? To be sure, there is always the principle at stake, namely, that people should not be wrongfully induced to enter into a contract. In fact, permitting such a situation to occur would violate a cardinal principle of contract law, specifically, that a contract is a voluntary undertaking. In addition, there is nothing in a claim for economic duress or misrepresentation, for example, that explicitly requires something to be substantively wrong with the contract.Legally, therefore, Party A has a claim or, more likely, a defense, against Party B for the latter's coercive conduct.If, however, Party A wants and/or needs the goods or service, and the terms are reasonable and fair, how realistic is it that Party A would end up challenging the contract or not performing her end of the bargain, even in the face of coercive conduct by Party B?More pragmatically, without something substantively wrong with the contract, what attorney would take that case? In either event, it seems highly unlikely that a lawsuit (with Party A as the plaintiff or, more likely, as the defendant) would arise.
The only way coercion presents an actionable problem, therefore, is if it results in a bad bargain. Thus, coercion plus a bad bargain is what the modern contract law system identifies as a problem created, or at least not adequately addressed, by the classical system. This coercion-plus-bad-bargain problem is what the modern system attempts to remedy via its expanded contract policing doctrines.Absent the gap left by classical contract, there would be no reason for modern contract law to adopt the expanded policing doctrines.
The problem is that modern contract's solution to the coercion/bad bargain problem does not work. In fact, the modern system makes the coercion problem worse because the modern system only partially rejects classical contract while retaining key parts of the older regime. Specifically, modern contract law left the core of classical contract, which is contract formation, completely intact. And contract formation, particularly in the doctrine of mutual assent, is where the power in contracting is created, embedded, and, under modern contract law, largely immunized from effective challenge by the contract policing doctrines. By leaving the core of contract intact, modern contract law has ensured that the expanded policing doctrines it adopted will not alleviate, let alone correct, the coercion problem.
Consequently, conventional wisdom, which says, in part, that modern contract law is different from classical contract law in ways that make the current system work better than the older regime, is wrong. Instead, the ways in which the two systems are the same are more critical, because it is this sameness that determines whether modern contract law will be successful in remedying the problems it identified under the classical system. My examination in this Article of modern contract'spolicing doctrines will show that modern contract will not achieve this remedial goal. So, while an exploration of specific proposals to address this deficiency is outside the scope of this Article,I do advance the proposition that the modern contract law system is not working the way it should be.
In Part II of this Article, I set out the evolution of the classical to modern contract law system. In particular, Part II.A describes classical legal thought in some detail, because understanding this older regime is vital as it provides the backdrop against which my discussion of modern contract law takes place. Part II.B focuses on the modern system and, more specifically, on the conventional wisdom, which holds that the differences between the classical and modern systems are the most important part of the evolutionary story.
In Part III, I argue that the modern contract solution to the coercion problem will fail. Part III.A disputes the conventional wisdom of Part II and argues that the ways in which the two contract law systems are the same are actually more critical to understanding whether the modern system will be successful in solving the coercion problem produced by the classical system. Part III.B sets out in detail my theory that the seat of power in contract is formation, primarily in the element of mutual assent. I argue that mutual assent is key because this is where most material terms are decided. This is also where the critical decision of whether to enter into the contract is made. If the parties assent to enter the contract, then a contract is formed.At that point, the state effectively steps in and says that the parties are bound to the contract. "Being bound" to the contract creates a presumption of contract (and term) validity that the coerced party has the burden of overcoming.Unfortunately, this presumption is extremely difficult to overcome, because of what I identify as the "process problem."Consequently, satisfying the elements of contract formation means that a coerced party is literally bound to the bad bargain, one that the state, at that point, will compel the coerced party to either pay to get out of or perform.Modern contract law failed to change formation, except to make it easier to form a contract. By making contract formation easier, I argue that the modern system actually expands one party's capacity to coerceher contracting partner. And, by leaving the core (formation) intact, modern contract law also largely immunizes this expanded capacity for coercion from effective challenge by the policing doctrines it ostensibly adopted to remedy it. In other words, modern contract law's failure to change the core of classical contract serves both to increase and protect one party's ability to coerce her contracting partner during contract formation. Ironically, by preserving the core, modern contract law precludes the policing doctrines from protecting the victims of contractual coercion. Thus, the modern system does not adequately solve the coercion problem. It actually makes it worse.
Finally, I briefly conclude in Part IV with what should be obvious even now, namely, that conventional contract wisdom, which focuses on the differences rather than the sameness between classical and modern contract law, is wrong. Because this conventional wisdom expresses our own beliefs about how modern contract law should work, the fact that the wisdom is wrong demonstrates that modern contract simply cannot work in the way that we assert that it should.

Whether retaining the classical rules governing how parties become bound to a contract undermines the effectiveness of modern reforms and thereby entrenches one party's power in contracting.
Whether changes that make contract formation easier have increased one party's capacity to coerce their bargaining partner and made coercive practices harder to challenge.

shared_topics.topic: whether supplemental doctrines or instruments meaningfully remedy gaps or unfairness in domestic contract law

shared_topics.topic: the role of interpretive and supplementary sources in shaping contract enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats policing doctrines as doctrinal tools courts use to interpret and potentially void contracts alleged to be procured by coercion, while Paper B studies the UPICC's use by courts and commentators as an interpretive/supplementary source to influence how domestic contract disputes are decided.

shared_topics.topic: whether existing contract doctrines and remedies effectively address unfair or coercive transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that applying contract law (with its formation, quality, and remedial rules) better serves and protects participants in open-source transactions than relying solely on intellectual-property remedies; Paper B evaluates modern policing doctrines (unconscionability, duress, misrepresentation) and concludes they fail to correct coercion problems because formation doctrine shields bad bargains.

shared_topics.topic: how allocation of remedial power (e.g., extension-to-cure/Nachfrist) affects bargaining power and protection from coercion

shared_topics.topic: the importance of process (formation and performance procedures) in determining who is bound and what relief is available

papers.node_id: 45wakeforestlrev549!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT IN CONTEXT AND CONTRACT AS CONTEXT
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT IN CONTEXT AND CONTRACT AS CONTEXT
papers.authors: Larry A. Dimatteo; Blake D. Morant
papers.abstract:
The annual Business Law Symposium of the Wake Forest Law Review has a distinguished legacy of noteworthy programs that shed light on seminal issues affecting contemporary business in the United States. This edition builds on that tradition of excellence with a focus on the ubiquitous phenomenon of contracts and bargaining behavior. Contract law appears as a set of policies and rules that provide order for those who transact bargains. Indeed, contract law and the rules that it engenders seemingly facilitate an efficient system of transactional conduct that, on its face, appears objective.
Theoretical premises for the formation of contracts support this view. The genesis of a legally enforceable agreement centers on assentand the requirement of a bargained-for exchange of value.
The seeming simplicity of this formula presumably ensures certainty and predictability.Economic principles also provide justification for the objectivity of contract rules.Conventional wisdom suggests that contract law functions empirically, objectively enforcing the idiosyncratic preferences of those who enter into enforceable agreements.
Mundane bargaining transactions support the appearance of objectivity. Individuals regularly and routinely enter into enforceable contracts for the payments of mortgages or rent; the purchase of supplies, materials, and chattels; or the lease or purchase of a motor vehicle.The frequency of these successful transactions suggests that contract rules operate seamlessly and objectively, thereby facilitating the efficient operation of the contemporary marketplace.
The apparent "empiricism of contract may be little more than an egalitarian facade."Contracts, which are borne of human behavior, reflect the context in which they are formed. A contextual approach to contract presumes that preferences are not entirely preformed, but are influenced and altered by the contractual context and the supposedly neutral set of contract law rules that apply to that particular context. Context not only shapes the substance ofthe bargain, but also provides an analytical template required to interpret the terms of the bargain. The rules of contract seemingly eschew contextual realities that affect bargaining.As a result, one might logically assume that contextual factors are irrelevant in the resolution of contract disputes. Moreover, decision makers - who themselves are influenced by contextual realities such as their beliefs, thoughts, and judgments - further challenge the notion that contract law is purely objective and empirical.
To interpret contractual terms or decide disputes without consideration of the context that framed the bargain is a disingenuous analysis at best. Any meaningful and judicious review of contractual matters requires the application of contract rules within an analytical framework that includes the context in which contracts are formed.
A recent exhibition entitled Art, Media and Material Witness posed a series of questions which, with the transposition of the phrase "contract law" for the words "art" or "media," nicely illuminates the meaning of contract in context.What is the relationship between contract law and the historical, political, and social changes of the time? Do lawyers and legal scholars act as witnesses to changes in that relationship? If so, is their "testimony" as to the interpretation of contract law relevant to the understanding of the relationship of law and change, and the resolution of social-legal dissonance? What form does this legal testimony take? What is the significance of contract law in societal discourse? Can contract law change the manner in which transacting parties interact in the world of business? This Symposium provides a series of articles that innovatively address these mostly rhetorical questions and emphasize the importance of context as an important analytical tool.
The fundamental questions inspired by Art, Media and Material Witness are central given the evidence of rampant one-sidedness in contracts related to the recent financial crises.The overreachingrepresented by the granting of subprime loans, wholesale misrepresentation of financial instruments and their ratings, and the profound asymmetrical information and moral hazard problems associated with the appropriation and selling of risk have often characterized bargaining in the corporate landscape.In the world of home loan decision making, some have observed that "different borrowers … falling along socioeconomic lines, make the home loan decision in different contexts, contexts that influence which cognitive and emotional processes will come into play."The fact that emotion and biases affect decision making requires contract law to play a role in effecting rational and fair bargaining. Contract law requires more than the broad modeling of a market actor who could be susceptible to cognitive errors and biases. This over-inclusive approach does not adequately address the influences of such sociological factors as race, gender, class, and culture.In such contracting contexts, mandatory disclosure rules may not be enough to overcome cognitive errors and discriminatory influences. These errors and influences are often manipulated by the stronger or more sophisticated party.Instead, "choice guidance rules" are needed in certain contexts to ensure a threshold of freedom of contract.
Facilitative (freedom of contract)and context-driven regulatoryfunctions of contract law remain central to most debateson the proper role of contract law in a complex, modern economy.Despite epoch-related characterizations of contract law as more or less formalistic in nature, the tensions between formal and contextual, internal and external,and deduction and induction are constant. Contract law as a rules-based order requires formal application, but context is needed to apply contract rules to evolving transaction types that redefine bargaining relationships. Contract law formulation, in the words of Martha Minow, is part of a process in which law is attached "to the social contexts in which norms can be generated and given meaning."It is these social-contractual contexts that influence contract law's choice between freedom of contract or status-based solutions.
In an increasingly complex economy, contract law's development moves from a general, freedom-of-contract-based body of law to contextual, status-based bodies of specialized law. Instead of a unilateral debate over the power of a unified, formalistic theory that explains contracts as mere abstractions, this introductory Article and others in this Symposium examine whether contract law is best understood as a group of specialized, context-driven bodies of law. This approach incorporates both descriptive and normative features. A descriptive query probes whether contract law can be better understood through the prism of context to reveal its true nature in practice. A view that contract law is influenced by status-based relationships suggests that the examination of context will, at times, more effectively regulate freedom of contract.A prescriptive viewrequires that certain contextual factors be more fully and overtly embraced in contract law application.The recognition of the role of such external factors as race, gender, ethnicity, language, information, and power asymmetries suggests that contract law can gain greater salience if such factors are incorporated within its interpretation and policing functions.
Part II of this introductory Article briefly examines the most popular, unitary theories of law. It questions any one theory's explanatory power over the breadth of contract issues and types of contracts. It supports the idea that each theory of contract can be used to explain certain contract rules, but not contract law as a whole. This Symposium buttresses this idea with the collective view that contract law can best be described and guided through a context-driven inquiry. A contextual theory of contract law recognizes the need for flexible rules for different contractual contexts and the elastic application of those rules across contexts. A contextual theory of contract law also recognizes a number of phenomena. First, contract interpretation, through the lens of context, should be used to regulate influences that question the purity of the freedom of contract upon which most agreements are based. Second, the construct of contract has been creatively applied to areas that are not immediately envisioned within the body of contract law.
Part III then examines the different uses of context that illustrate the relationship between contract law and society. It notes that "contract in context," for the purposes of the Symposium, is broadly defined. This Part provides a taxonomy of contract law in context that includes internal and external perspectives. Part III recognizes that societal context frames contract law, but also observes that contract law can frame the private ordering of society. This two-way flow of context, between the greater socioeconomic-cultural sphere and contract as context, analyzes the relationship of contract types and the contextual interpretation of contracts. It concludes by examining the relationship of context to paternalism and consent. Part IV then notes the role of power and identity in the formation and interpretation of contracts, and contract law's shortcomings in recognizing such influences in the search for contractual justice. Finally, Part V introduces the works presented at the Symposium.

questions.question: Whether the social, economic, and cognitive context in which parties bargain (including power asymmetries, information imbalances, and biases) materially affects the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts.

Whether contract law should incorporate contextual and status-based factors (such as inequality of bargaining power, race, gender, class, language, and informational disparities) through tailored rules or choice-guidance to produce more just and effective outcomes, rather than relying on uniform formalistic rules.
Whether a contextual, flexible theory of contract better explains and guides legal treatment across different types of transactions than a single, unitary theoretical approach.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do market and institutional features affect whether informative 'cheap talk' will arise privately or require legal intervention to induce accurate precontractual communication?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: parental waivers/releases and minors' ability to bind contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally analyzes whether a parent can validly sign preactivity releases and indemnities that bar a minor's negligence claims, while Paper A includes minors and status-based relationships in its broader argument that certain contracting contexts (like those involving vulnerable persons) require special doctrinal treatment.

shared_topics.topic: use of public policy to invalidate or limit contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on the Utah Supreme Court's invocation of a public policy exception to void parental waivers and indemnities, and Paper A argues more generally that contract law must sometimes override formal bargains on contextual and normative public-policy grounds (e.g., to address inequality, bias, or cognitive failures).

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract and paternalistic/protective regulation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B exemplifies the limit of freedom of contract by upholding a rule protecting minors from preinjury releases, and Paper A frames that tension normatively, debating when contract law should favor freedom of private ordering versus status-based protective rules or choice-guidance regulation.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries, information problems, and contextual fairness in bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper B highlights practical imbalances (providers requiring waivers due to insurance limits, potential chilling of claims, and parents' constrained choices) that affect the fairness of the transaction, and Paper A develops a general theory that contextual factors—power, information, race, class, cognitive biases—shape preferences and should inform contract interpretation and policing.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and the role of courts in shaping contractual doctrine through context-sensitive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper B details the court's two-step interpretive analysis and its adoption of precedent to create a rule voiding parental waivers, while Paper A argues that judges and decisionmakers are themselves situated in context and must apply contract rules flexibly to evolving transaction types and social circumstances.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92marqlrev423!!ARTICLE: A MATTER OF TRUST: SHOULD NO-RELIANCE CLAUSES BAR CLAIMS FOR FRAUDULENT INDUCEMENT OF CONTRACT?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A MATTER OF TRUST: SHOULD NO-RELIANCE CLAUSES BAR CLAIMS FOR FRAUDULENT INDUCEMENT OF CONTRACT?

shared_topics.topic: the tension between freedom of contract and public-policy/paternalistic limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames a central debate over whether contract law should prioritize formal freedom of contract or adopt context-sensitive, status-based regulation to correct inequalities and biases; Paper B directly confronts that same tension by asking whether courts should respect parties' autonomous choice to include no-reliance clauses or invalidate them on moral/public-policy grounds when fraud is alleged.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of transactional context in interpreting and enforcing contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contractual meaning and appropriate remedies depend on social, economic, and identity-based contexts surrounding bargaining, while Paper B analyzes how courts actually treat negotiation context (sophistication, boilerplate, negotiation history, specificity) when deciding whether no-reliance or integration clauses bar reliance on precontractual statements.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetries, power imbalances, and their influence on bargaining outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes asymmetric information, cognitive biases, and sociological factors (race, gender, class) that distort bargaining and justify contextual regulation; Paper B focuses on uncertainty, opportunism, multiple agents, and unequal knowledge in complex transactions as drivers of misrepresentations and as reasons parties draft (or litigate over) clauses allocating fraud risk.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formalist/doctrinal rules and the case for flexible doctrinal approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes unitary, formalistic theories of contract and advocates elastic rules tailored to different transaction types, and Paper B surveys and critiques competing doctrinal approaches courts use (categorical refusals, restricted enforcement, or broad enforcement) for no-reliance clauses, arguing for clearer, principled balancing rather than rigid presumptions.

shared_topics.topic: the role and efficacy of contractual devices (integration/merger, disclosure, and no-reliance clauses) in allocating risk and precluding tort claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines disclosure rules and proposes context-aware 'choice guidance' or specialized regimes to protect vulnerable parties, while Paper B provides an in-depth analysis of merger/integration and no-reliance clauses (and parol evidence) as tools parties use to define reliance and limit fraud claims, questioning when those devices should be honored.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev132!!SYMPOSIUM: COGS OR CYBORGS?: BLASPHEMY AND IRONY IN CONTRACT THEORIES
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COGS OR CYBORGS?: BLASPHEMY AND IRONY IN CONTRACT THEORIES

shared_topics.topic: critique of formalist/atomistic models of contract and advocacy for context-sensitive theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques nineteenth-century individualist (Holmesian) conceptions of contract and argues that imagining different kinds of social actors (cogs vs cyborgs) changes how contract law should operate; Paper B explicitly rejects a purely formal, assent/exchange model and develops a 'contract in context' approach that requires applying rules with sensitivity to bargaining circumstances.

shared_topics.topic: incorporation of social values (trust, reliance, reciprocity) versus pure freedom-of-contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Gilmore's prediction that contract law would shift toward valuing trust, reliance, and reciprocity as interdependence grows and examines the persistence of contract ideology; Paper B analyzes the tension between facilitative freedom-of-contract and context-driven regulatory functions, arguing that contract doctrine must often embrace social values to achieve fair bargaining outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: attention to power, identity, and asymmetries (interdependence, class, race, gender) in shaping bargains and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds changing kinds of world-inhabitants and interdependence as shaping contract norms, while Paper B documents how socioeconomic status, race, gender, cognitive biases, and informational asymmetries influence contracting and require doctrinal adjustment.

shared_topics.topic: use of interdisciplinary methods (psychology, sociology, history) to understand and reform contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends interdisciplinary lines of work to reconceptualize contract (e.g., imagining cyborgs) and reads historical shifts in doctrine, and Paper B draws on economics, psychology, sociology, and history to argue for contextualized, empirically informed contract interpretation and regulation.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism about unitary predictive theories of contract and the limits of grand narratives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Gilmore's failed prediction as evidence that grand historical theories misread contract's persistence, and Paper B questions the explanatory power of any single, unitary theory of contract law and promotes a taxonomy of context-specific approaches instead.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 96nwulrev39!!ARTICLE:CONTRACT RECONCEIVED
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CONTRACT RECONCEIVED

shared_topics.topic: the role of contextual factors in determining the substance of bargains and contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers argue that the context in which exchanges occur shapes what is actually exchanged and how terms should be read — Paper A develops a broad socio‑legal taxonomy insisting that race, class, power asymmetries, and transaction context matter for interpretation and enforcement, while Paper B asserts that the 'context of exchange' fundamentally determines contract substance and must be built into doctrinal reconceptions.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of unitary/formalistic theories and the need to reconceive contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both critiques target single, formalist accounts (e.g., pure assent/freedom‑of‑contract models) as insufficient; Paper A calls for context‑driven, specialized bodies of contract law, and Paper B argues for a reconception of the basic doctrinal building blocks to better capture when and why promises bind.

shared_topics.topic: developing a methodological or epistemological framework for contract jurisprudence
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with how to systematize contract theory — Paper A contrasts descriptive and prescriptive aims and urges elastic rule application across contexts, while Paper B proposes analogizing Contract to scientific inquiry and invokes philosophical naturalism to bring greater descriptive and normative precision.

shared_topics.topic: reexamining the foundational elements of exchange (what makes a promise binding) and the limits of current explanations
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate core concepts like assent and bargained‑for exchange, with Paper A questioning whether standard assumptions explain real bargaining behavior and Paper B probing the limits of existing explanations and the need to reconceive the substance and function of contractual elements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58ucinlrev1283!!ARTICLE: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: critique of neoclassical/formalistic contract doctrine and advocacy for alternative theoretical frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys and defends the significance of competing schools (relational contract, empirical contract theory, CLS, metatheory, 'death of contract') as fundamental challenges to neoclassical contract, arguing the crisis in the field stems from mainstream doctrine; Paper B likewise rejects a single formalistic theory, arguing unitary, freedom-of-contract models cannot explain diverse transactional contexts and endorses context-driven or specialized bodies of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: importance of context and extra‑legal social forces (power, identity, historical/political change) for contract formation and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats relational, critical, and ideological theories that emphasize how social relationships and politics shape contract law; Paper B centers a ‘‘contract in context’’ approach, detailing how race, gender, class, culture, and power asymmetries—and historical/political change—alter bargaining, interpretation, and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: normative debate over freedom of contract versus regulatory/paternalistic intervention (choice guidance, mandatory rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues theoretical alternatives have consequences for what contract law should protect and how doctrine should be structured; Paper B explicitly contrasts facilitative freedom‑of‑contract functions with context‑driven regulatory solutions, endorsing context-sensitive interventions (e.g., choice‑guidance rules) where bargaining is distorted.

shared_topics.topic: role of empirical and behavioral evidence in rethinking contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies empirical contract theory as a principal competitor to neoclassical views and treats empirical findings as grounds for re-evaluating doctrine, while Paper B invokes behavioral insights (cognitive biases, emotions) and real‑world evidence from lending and financial markets to argue contract law must respond to how people actually decide and transact.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58lalrev663!!ARTICLE: American Mutual Mistake: Half-Civilian Mongrel, Consideration Reincarnate
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: American Mutual Mistake: Half-Civilian Mongrel, Consideration Reincarnate

shared_topics.topic: genealogical and historical development of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates modern contract law as evolving from unitary, formalist doctrines toward context-driven, specialized bodies of law, while Paper B provides a historical genealogy of the mutual mistake doctrine, tracing how precedents assembled into its modern American form.

shared_topics.topic: competing theoretical foundations for explaining and guiding contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the explanatory power of single, unitary theories and proposes contextual/status-based frameworks alongside formal rules, and Paper B shows that the mutual mistake doctrine is a hybrid borrowing from civil law and pre-classical common law (including consideration), illustrating competing theoretical lineages behind a single doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should interpret and apply contract rules given parties' assumptions and contextual facts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract interpretation must account for surrounding social, cognitive, and power contexts that shape bargains, and Paper B examines the mutual mistake doctrine—which excuses or modifies enforcement when basic shared assumptions fail—addressing how judges should respond to factual and assumption-based misalignments.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal contractual requirements (assent, consideration) and equitable/paternalistic adjustments for fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates freedom of contract versus status-based or paternalistic interventions (e.g., disclosure, choice-guidance) to correct imbalances and biases, while Paper B demonstrates that the mutual mistake doctrine retains elements of consideration and functions as a judicial tool that tempers strict enforcement to achieve equitable outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91califlrev1573!!ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: contextual interpretation of contract terms (including tacit assumptions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract meaning and enforcement must be read through the social, historical, and transactional context in which bargains are formed; Paper B develops rules for 'interpretive mistakes' and 'shared tacit factual assumptions,' treating unexpressed contextual assumptions as part of contract interpretation and grounds for relief in certain circumstances.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry, power differentials, and superior knowledge as limits on freedom of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how race, class, gender, and power imbalances distort bargaining and may justify doctrines that constrain formal freedom of contract; Paper B explicitly conditions relief for mistaken assumptions on whether one party had clearly superior information or otherwise bore the risk, incorporating informational asymmetry into doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: critique of formalist doctrinal categories and argument for functional/normative rule‑making
shared_topics.justification: Paper A rejects a single formalistic theory of contract law and urges a context‑sensitive, specialized approach; Paper B criticizes traditional mistake categories as functionally unhelpful and reclassifies mistakes into functionally grounded types to derive normative rules.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tradeoff between protecting parties from error/bias and preserving transactional security (efficiency vs paternalism/morality)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates when contract law should move beyond disclosure to 'choice guidance' or paternalistic interventions to correct cognitive biases and structural unfairness; Paper B evaluates mistake doctrines by reference to policy propositions—efficiency, social morality, and experience—to determine when relief should be granted without unduly undermining transactional certainty.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev254!!SYMPOSIUM: AFTERWORD:THE SHIFTING DOMAIN OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: AFTERWORD:THE SHIFTING DOMAIN OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: limits of unitary/formal theories of contract and the need for pluralistic or context-sensitive doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that no single theory (formalism, classical assent-based models, or pure economic analysis) explains contract law across varied transaction types and urges a contextual, flexible application of rules; Paper B similarly critiques the ambition of unified theories (including classical doctrine and certain economic analyses) and calls for more diversified doctrinal responses to contemporary contract phenomena.

shared_topics.topic: the perceived shift in the 'domain of contract' from doctrinal, court-centered law toward private ordering and context-driven contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how contract has been extended into varied social contexts and specialized bodies of law, implying a move away from a uniform freedom-of-contract model, while Paper B diagnoses a broader trend toward 'contract in fact' (private ordering, ADR, transnational codification) and predicts less centrality for traditional contract law institutions.

shared_topics.topic: importance of social, cognitive, and power-contextual factors in shaping bargains and interpretations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes race, gender, class, cultural influences, cognitive biases, and power asymmetries as determinants of bargaining and advocates that contract law incorporate these contextual realities; Paper B gestures toward external events and real-world pressures that reshape contracting practices and the need to account for behavior 'in the shadow of contract law.'

shared_topics.topic: the call for empirical and interdisciplinary study of contracting behavior to inform doctrinal change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws on empirical insights about decisionmaking, disclosure insufficiency, and behavioral influences to justify context-sensitive rules, and Paper B explicitly urges development of empirical theories about contract behavior and the use/abuse of contracting practices to guide diversified doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39flastulrev563!!ARTICLE: BRINGING ORDER TO CONTRACTS AGAINST PUBLIC POLICY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BRINGING ORDER TO CONTRACTS AGAINST PUBLIC POLICY

shared_topics.topic: how courts use contextual factors or public policy to modify contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that judges and decision makers inevitably bring contextual realities (beliefs, social conditions, identity, power) to contract interpretation and thus should apply contract rules with attention to context; Paper B empirically studies how courts invoke the public policy defense to refuse enforcement, examining the doctrinal and factual contexts in which courts depart from ordinary enforcement.

papers.node_id: 75lalrev127!!ARTICLE: Contract Law and the Hand Formula
papers.title: ARTICLE: Contract Law and the Hand Formula
papers.abstract:
Contract law is largely about negligence.Through the direct and indirect use of a "reason to know" or "reason to believe" standard in many of the black letter rules in theRestatement (Second) of Contracts, contract liability can often be traced to a party's failure to exercise reasonable care under thecircumstances.TheRestatement, however, fails to adequately explain when a person has reason to know or reason to believe something. In other words, despite being largely about careless behavior, contract law fails to adequately explain the standard of care expected of parties.
This Article proposes that negligence law's Hand formulabe applied in contract law to determine whether a person has "reason to know" or "reason to believe" something. As will be shown, using the Hand formula explains the relevance of facts traditionally considered irrelevant under a contract-law analysis, but which intuitively seem relevant.
Part I of this Article explains how contract law is largely about negligence. Part II discusses theRestatement's "reason to know" and "reason to believe" standard and shows that theRestatementfails to adequately explain it. Part III discusses negligence law's famous Hand formula. Part IV maintains that the Hand formula should be used to determine when a party is negligent under contract law's "reason to know" and "reason to believe" standard. Part V provides examples, through the use of well-known cases, of how the Hand formula would apply in cases involving the standard.

questions.question: Whether a negligence-derived cost-benefit balancing approach should be used to determine when a contracting party 'has reason to know' or 'has reason to believe' a fact (i.e., to define the standard of care in contract disputes).
Whether adopting that cost-benefit approach would alter which factual considerations are treated as relevant in assessing party care and thus change outcomes in contract liability cases.

matched_themes: Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the Restatement's 'reason to know / reason to believe' language fails to explain when contracting parties are expected to exercise care, while Paper B contends that corporation law and market rules do not adequately explain or protect investors' expectations (e.g., why investors accept nonvoting shares) or ensure returns to shareholders.

shared_topics.topic: importing non-legal theoretical frameworks to reconceptualize legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes borrowing the Hand negligence formula (burden-probability-loss) to set contract-law standards, and Paper B uses Marcel Mauss's anthropology of gift exchange (and complements from behavioral economics) to reinterpret equity markets and shareholder relations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contextual, social, or cultural norms in shaping standards of reasonableness in transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that facts traditionally treated as irrelevant in contract analysis become relevant under a Hand-formula account of what parties 'reasonably' should know or believe, and Paper B argues that investment and corporate practices (like buying nonvoting shares) are best understood as embedded in an 'equity culture' of social expectations rather than pure individual rationality.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE NOTION AND FUNCTION OF OFFER AND ACCEPTANCE UNDER FRENCH AND ENGLISH LAW.

shared_topics.topic: objective versus subjective standards for attributing assent, knowledge, or belief in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates applying negligence's Hand formula—an objective cost‑benefit test—to determine when a party 'has reason to know' or 'reason to believe' under the Restatement, while Paper B directly contrasts the French focus on inner will/consent (subjective) with the English emphasis on objective inferences from parties' acts in offer-and-acceptance doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal critique and the search for clearer legal standards governing when contractual obligations arise or when parties are blameworthy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the Restatement for failing to explain its 'reason to know/believe' standard and proposes a concrete analytical replacement (the Hand formula), and Paper B surveys historical and contemporary treatments of offer and acceptance to highlight conceptual gaps and divergent analytical frameworks between legal systems.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of parties' conduct (acts/statements) versus mental states in establishing contractual liability or formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links contract liability to a party's failure to exercise reasonable care as judged by observable risk/probability factors (shifting focus to conduct and its foreseeable consequences), while Paper B examines how both systems treat parties' expressions or conduct as the basis for offer and acceptance—contrasting an act‑centered English approach with a will‑centered French approach.

shared_topics.topic: criteria and boundaries for when promises give rise to legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses when facts should make a contracting party liable by translating 'reason to know/believe' into a negligence-style cost–benefit test, and Paper B addresses which promises (bargained-for versus donative) the law should enforce and analyzes policy and moral reasons for drawing those enforcement lines.

shared_topics.topic: use of extra-doctrinal frameworks to revise or explain contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A imports an established tort/negligence tool (the Hand formula) to fill gaps in contract standards, and Paper B examines and critiques non-contractual frameworks—socioeconomic 'commodification' arguments and Kantian philosophical 'collaboration'—as bases for defending the doctrine of consideration.

papers.node_id: 75cornelllrev62!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.
papers.abstract:
Professor Subha Narasimhan's provocative recent article points out the similarities between a contracting party avoiding the enforcement of a contract modification after the other party performs and obtaining specific performance of the original contract.Suppose, for example, that a seller of goods, without stating a reason, insists on a price increase before performing an agreement.  The buyer, who needs the goods, agrees; the seller delivers the goods, but the buyer then refuses to pay more than the original price.  If the seller is unable to enforce the modification, the buyer obtains the goods and pays only the initial price.  Because the buyer achieves performance of the original agreement in this way, Professor Narasimhan calls the buyer's efforts "self-help specific performance."
Professor Narasimhan sees a potential problem with this result.  She reasons that remedies for breach of contract typically do not include specific performance and that a contract promisee therefore does not usually pay for that potential remedy in the contract price.The buyer in our example might therefore gain a windfall by agreeing to the modification and later successfully contesting it, instead of seeking damages for the seller's refusal to perform the original contract.  The buyer might secure the seller's actual performance without paying for the specific performance remedy.
Professor Narasimhan worries that current law restricts specific performance and liberally overturns contract modifications and thereby encourages buyer "opportunism" via self-help specific performancein our example.She therefore bemoans theorists' and courts' one-sided focus on potential misconduct by the seller.  In fact, she seeks to discount the problem of the seller's refusal to perform without a modification by characterizing the seller's duty under the contract as nothing more than a choice to perform or to breach and pay damages.She also insists that current modification law cannot combat seller bad faith in any event, and may actually deter sellers from entering beneficial modifications.For these reasons, Professor Narasimhan proposes a "bright-line" rule that would preclude a buyer from contesting a modification except when the buyer could have obtained specific performance of the original contract or when specific performance was the "theoretically superior" remedy but was unavailable for discretionary reasons.Under her approach, then, a modification might be enforceable even when current law would hold that a seller wrongfully extorted it.
My views differ significantly on many of the issues raised by Professor Narasimhan's interesting article.  In Part I, I argue that a buyer, confronted by a seller's demand for a modification, will encounter significant difficulties attemting to predict whether the law would grant specific performance, to evaluate the likelihood of defeating a contract modification, and to measure the other costs and benefits of the self-help strategy.  In addition, if the buyer were able to penetrate the doctrine, the buyer would learn that courts increasingly grant specific performance and enforce most contract modifications.  Contract law therefore actually disfavors buyer opportunism through self-help specific performance.  I also assert in Part I that current law adequately polices buyer opportunism in the unlikely event that it should come to pass.
In Part II, I assert that we should not be concerned even if current law permitted buyers to achieve self-help specific performance when that law would deny court-ordered specific performance.  In developing Part II's argument, I dispute Professor Narasimhan's view that a seller has a "right" to breach and pay damages and that abuyer can gain a windfall via self-help specific performance.  Professor Narasimhan's approach, I contend, deflects the analysis from far more important issues involving misconduct by the seller.
In Part III, I rebut Professor Narasimhan's claim that today's modification law cannot help deter misconduct by a seller and will only dissuade sellers from agreeing to a modification.  I also contest her assertion that when confronted with seller bad faith,a buyer's options should be tied to contract law's current approach to contract remedies even if those remedies are found wanting.

questions.question: Does the legal treatment of contract modifications enable opportunistic behavior by a party who agrees to a modification and later repudiates it in order to obtain the original contract's performance without paying for equitable enforcement?

Do current rules governing contract modifications and remedies effectively deter bad-faith modification demands by obligors, or do they create incentives for misconduct and unjust enrichment of the other party?
Should a party's ability to challenge a contract modification be limited to situations where a court would have been willing to order performance of the original agreement?

matched_themes: Do existing rules on contract modification and remedies deter bad-faith modification demands or instead create incentives for opportunism and unjust enrichment?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?

When and to what extent should post-contractual promises (e.g., promises for additional payment to induce performance already owed or post-sale statements) be enforceable as warranties or modifications?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev125!!ARTICLE: WHEN DOES THE "FAT LADY" SING? Although this phrase probably originated in the opera setting, one of its more interesting uses occurred in the battle between Pennzoil and Texaco for the Getty Oil Company. When Texaco's Chairman, John K. McKinely, asked Getty Oil's Chairman Sidney Peterson whether Getty might still be available even though an "agreement in principle" had been entered into with Pennzoil, Peterson responded that "the fat lady had not yet sung." Pennzoil Co. v. Getty Oil Co., No. 7425, slip op. at 46 (Del. Ch. Feb. 6, 1984). For a further discussion of the Texaco-Pennzoil case, see infra text accompanying notes 60 to 63. : AN ANALYSIS OF "AGREEMENTS IN PRINCIPLE" IN CORPORATE ACQUISITIONS.
