papers.node_id: 69tullrev715!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTS LIMITING LIABILITY: A PARADOX WITH TACIT SOLUTIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS LIMITING LIABILITY: A PARADOX WITH TACIT SOLUTIONS
papers.abstract:
The concept of "freedom" or "liberty" maintains significant roots within the lexicon of contract law."Freedom of contract"signifies that parties to an agreement have the right and power to construct their own bargains.The Supreme Court's landmarkopinion inLochner v. New Yorkrecognizes the significance of private autonomy and efficiency in the formulation of specific bargains.Indeed, the notion of "freedom of contract" constitutes a historical concept with philosophical origins.Strict adherence to this ideology would require courts to honor parties' bargains and refrain from tampering with the terms thereof.Some theorists who believe strongly in the notion opine that laws "interfer[ing] with private arrangements" should be invalidated.Irrespective of philosophical differences regarding the extent of adherence to the notion of freedom of contract, the concept may suffer from definitional ambiguities.Critics have noted that the concept lacks sufficient clarity and definiteness.
Although debate regarding adherence to the doctrine continues,modern views of freedom of contract recognize that the concept of "freedom" has limitations.The Supreme Court no longer appears to consider "freedom of contract" a constitutional absolute, at least within the context of labor law.Moreover, the state may legitimately restrict the parties' right to contract if the proposed bargain is found to have some deleterious effect on the public or to contravene some other matter of public policy.Contracts that limit the negligence of others tend to attract such scrutiny.
This Article proposes that the law governing contracts that limit liability, and perhaps all voluntary transactions, should employ a more accurate, uniform, and balanced methodology to evaluate the enforceability of such agreements.The present framework explicitly tends to emphasize public policy concerns related to paternalism.This emphasis should be clarified and expanded to include an evaluation of the possible benefits provided by such agreements.
Public policy concerns, which presently focus on paternalistic goals,should not be narrowly construed so as to thwart potential agreements that maximize the utility of scarce resources and promote overall efficiency.Public policy considerations must encompass the evaluation of the societal benefit provided by the parties' agreement. The inclusion of thesepositive, and perhaps implicit, factors that relate to the concept of "public policy" may already constitute an inherent element in the evaluation of indemnity agreements between common carriers.These notable positive benefits, together with the minimization of certain negative concerns that focus on paternalism,contribute to the validity and enforceability of indemnity agreements between common carriers. Consequently, the benefits of positive attributes should be explicitly incorporated in the evaluation of all contracts that seek to limit liability, and moreover, in voluntary transactions generally. Subsumption of this evaluative factor in the decision-making process should lead to more consistent enforcement of such bargains and afford greater certainty to parties that their original bargains and concomitant expectations will be maintained, thereby causing the economy to operate smoothly.
Part II of this Article presents the conventional model that currently governs the enforceability of contracts limiting liability. This section delineates the present policies relevant to such bargains.Concerns relevant to contracts that limit liability include policy considerations that tend to restrict the enforceability of these agreements. This Article then specifically elucidates the law governing indemnity agreements between common carriers. While public policy considerations concerning adherence to publicduty contribute to the skepticism of indemnity agreements in general, such agreements between common carriers tend to have an enhanced probability of enforcement given the characteristics of the parties and the nature of their bargains.
Part III of this Article analyzes the present law governing contracts limiting liability, closely scrutinizing the public policy factors that fuel concern for paternalism. The present model's preoccupation with paternalism actually focuses on negative factorsthat have been explicitly articulated as a basis for limiting such agreements. In addition to an analysis of the traditional public policy considerations governing indemnity agreements, Part III continues with an examination of policy considerations relevant to indemnity agreements among common carriers.Notwithstanding the negative factors inherent in the explicit concern for paternalism, the seeming tolerance for such agreements among common carriers primarily must be due to a tacit consideration of the residual benefits of these agreements. These benefits or positive factors can often include the probability that the agreement will foster the efficient, and perhaps optimal, use of existing scarce resources.
Ultimately, the decision of whether to enforce contracts limiting liability should include the weighing of both negative and positive factors inherent in such agreements. If negative factors are diminished or alleviated by externalities, i.e., statutory or regulatory control or self-interest of the bargainers, and discernible positive factors truly exist, then agreements imbued with such qualities warrant enforcement. This modification of the traditional model would lead to a more efficacious mechanism for evaluating not only contracts limiting liability, but also other types of voluntary transactions.
Restrictions and caveats placed upon contracts limiting negligence liability contribute to the illusory nature of the freedom of contract notion. The following hypothetical situation serves as illustration.X, a small business involved in the production andsale of homemade widgets, enters into an agreement withY, an adjacent small business owner, for the use ofY's land to transportX's goods.Xseeks to obtain a right-of-way upon a small portion ofY's property to facilitate transportation of its goods.YchargesXa fee for the use of her property and insists thatXindemnify and holdYharmless for any damages or liabilities resulting fromX's orY's negligence.Xseeks the agreement withYas a less expensive alternative that accommodates the transportation ofX's goods.Yreceives not only compensation for the use of her property, but also coverage against any liability exposure incident toX's use of the property. The agreement providesXwith a less expensive alternative for the transportation of its goods and, in all probability, lower market prices and increased accessibility for such goods. The arrangement betweenXandY, which represents a contract designed to limit liability, constitutes a hold harmlessor indemnityagreement.
DespiteXandY's good faith effortsto enter into a bargain that is mutually beneficial to both parties concerning the use of resources and economic interests, the viability of their agreement remains speculative due to anxieties rooted in public policy.Thejudiciary generally views indemnity agreements, such as the one adopted byXandY, with a degree of skepticism and suspicion.Although the more modern rule dictates that the agreement betweenXandYmay be enforceable,public policy constraints,notwithstanding legislative proscriptions in many jurisdictions,potentially limit these agreements.Regardless of the parties' informed intent to formulate such a bargain, agreements between private parties such asXandYremain vulnerable to either strict judicial scrutiny at the very least,or a complete invalidation at the extreme.
This skepticism of indemnity agreements basically reflects a paternalistic concern for bothX, an individual who may feel compelled to accept such an agreement, and the public, which may unsuspectingly experience negative effects of that agreement. These paternalistic concerns include a need to protectX, the indemnitor, who entered the agreement from a perceived disadvantageous bargaining position.The other element of paternalism focuses on the protection of third parties due to theagreement's possible facilitation of reckless conduct byY, the indemnitee.
Courts desire neither to encourage antisocial conduct on the part of individuals such asYwho enjoy coverage under the agreement, nor to give judicial approval of such action.In the hypothetical transaction ofXandY, public policy concerns focus on the agreement's impact upon the public service duties ofYor the possible violation of a statutory duty required ofY.Consequently, the restrictions placed upon indemnity agreements remain rooted in the public obligation to protect third parties from possible reckless conduct on the part of indemnitees.
Curiously, not all contracts that limit negligence liability share as dubious a fate as the agreement betweenXandY. For example,A, a United States municipality, seeks to spur commerce in its inner-city business district.Aalso would like to alleviate its burgeoning traffic and parking problems and reduce air pollution. In an effort to achieve these goals,Adecides to establish a light rail commuter service, such as a trolley or a subway, that would extend into neighboring suburbs. One goal ofA's project would be to encourage individuals to rely less on privately owned vehicles that contribute to traffic congestion and air pollution.Aalso intends toprovide a safe, economical, and efficient mode of transportation into the city.
Aseeks to construct and operate its light rail system in the most efficient and least expensive manner available. Notwithstanding these goals, construction of light rail facilities, which include passenger stations and rail tracks extending into the suburbs, may lead to exorbitant acquisition costs.A's planners observe thatB, a large regional freight railroad conglomerate, has tracks extending to many of the suburbs located both north and south ofA. Given the tremendous acquisition costs of property required to construct passenger stations and tracks,Aattempts to negotiate an agreement withBunder whichAcould utilize either the tracks or property adjacent to those tracks to operateA's light rail service.Bremains apprehensive about this arrangement givenB's exposure to liability in the event of an accident on its property as well as the possibility of suffering damage to its own property as a result ofA's activities. Consequently,Apromises to assume liability for damages suffered byAorBin the event of any accidents involving the operation ofA's transportation system.B, secure in the belief that its exposure to liability has been limited, executes the agreement withA. Asubsequently constructs its light rail system, a substantial part of which operates onB's property. In effect,A's promise to indemnifyBfacilitates the expeditious and affordable establishment of public transportation in the area.Indeed,AandB's agreement illustrates a contractual arrangementthat, regardless of nomenclature,has been adopted by several major municipal transit systems throughout the United States.
The value of this bargain is manifold for bothAand the entire local community. The establishment of light rail service inA's metropolitan area will provide low cost transportation for area residents. ForA, the agreement obviates costly alternatives such as outright purchase of the property fromB, or the acquisition of required property through eminent domain. Such acquisition costscan be so extensive as to limit or abortA's project altogether.Consequently, the agreement withBmay not only accommodateA's financial goals in establishing its system, but also expedite the establishment ofA's system by avoiding the time consuming modes of acquisition. Given the advantages afforded by light rail transportation,the expeditious and cost effective construction ofA's light rail system should be of significant benefit to the community.Thus, the indemnity agreement betweenAandBultimately allows this public benefit to come into existence.
Unlike the agreement betweenXandY, agreements between parties such asAandB, who are common carriers,appear to foster an enhanced probability of enforcement.Yet given the similarities between the two bargains, i.e., the sophistication of the parties and the potential benefit to the parties and society on a whole, the disparity in the probability of enforcement of the two indemnity agreements raises significant questions regarding the efficacy and reliability of indemnity agreements in general. The key may lie in the residual, positive effects ofAandB's agreement. The societal benefit of accessible and affordable public transportation represents a real and significant by-product of this agreement and, perhaps, serves as tacit justification for its enforcement.
Few individuals would argue with the general concern about agreements that contravene clearly articulated public policy concerns. However, compliance with this amorphous goal not only creates inconsistent results with regard to the enforcement of contracts limiting liability, but also fosters considerable uncertainty among parties who may seek to enter such agreements without fearing the possibility that such policies may be violated. Given the nebulous concept of public policy,the law thrusts agreementsthat limit the liability of others into a virtual abyss with neither certainty nor clear delineation of rules governing enforceability.Notwithstanding an illusion of legitimacy, nearly every indemnity clause faces an uncertain legal future.
Despite the more modern view that contracts limiting negligence liability are possibly enforceable,the strict scrutinygiven these agreements due to the decision maker'sconcern for public policy renders such agreements ineffectual. Certainly, strict scrutiny by the courts may discourage parties from initially entering into such bargains. Parties seeking protection may fear that the agreement would never be enforced and, therefore, may leave themselves unprotected. Consequently, the fate of such agreements rests on the nebulous concept of public policy, a notion imbued with subjective standards that are neither certain nor predictable.Clearly, such a vague standard that governs the scrutiny, if not the enforceability, of contracts limiting liability will lead to inconsistent results and general uncertainty and insecurity among bargainers in the marketplace.Moreover, the present vagueness in enforcement creates barriers that limit parties' ability to strike mutually beneficial bargains, and also potentially stymies agreements that would maximize the utility of existing scarce resources and produce a service or product beneficial to the public.

papers.abstract:
By several measures,Mitchill v. LathandLucy v. Zehmerare "classic contract" cases.For nearly sixty years, they have been prominent opinions in the overwhelming majority of contract-law casebooks.Quite simply, many law professors--who teach first-year students--rely heavily onMitchillandLucyto help explain several foundational principles of contract law. Among other reasons,MitchillandLucyare celebrated because the facts in both cases are remarkably familiar and captivating. In addition, those uncomplicated facts help budding jurists to understand arguably the more complex and less exciting principles of contract of law.
First, consider the most prominent and intriguing facts inLucy v. Zehmer. Welford Ordway Lucy (Lucy) and John C. Lucy were brothers, lumbermen and farmers.They resided in Dinwiddie County, Virginia.Adrian Hardy Zehmer (Zehmer) and Ida S. Zehmer--husband and wife--lived in McKenney, Virginia--where they "operated a restaurant, filling station and motor court."Additionally, the Zehmers owned the Ferguson Farm--approximately 472 acres of land in Dinwiddie County.
On a wintry evening in December 1952, Lucy and his employee visited Zehmer's restaurant."Lucy took a partly filled bottle of whiskey into therestaurant … for the purpose of giving Zehmer a drink."After Lucy and Zehmer consumed a considerable amount of alcohol, the following exchange occurred:Lucy: "I bet you wouldn't take $ 50,000 for [Ferguson Farm]."Zehmer: "Yes, I would too; you wouldn't give fifty."Lucy: "[Yes. I] would. … [W]rite up an agreement to that effect."
Lucy: "I bet you wouldn't take $ 50,000 for [Ferguson Farm]."Zehmer: "Yes, I would too; you wouldn't give fifty."Lucy: "[Yes. I] would. … [W]rite up an agreement to that effect."
Zehmer secured a restaurant check and wrote the following on the back: "We … agree to sell to W. O. Lucy the Ferguson Farm complete for $ 50,000, title satisfactory to buyer."Both Zehmers signed the "memorandum" and gave it to Lucy.In response, Lucy offered $ 5 for the Zehmers' signatures.But Zehmer refused that offer and stated: "You don't need to give me any money, you got the agreement there signed by both of us.""Lucy left the premises insisting that he had purchased the farm."The Zehmers disagreed, and Lucy sued for specific performance.
In their answer, the Zehmers raised several defenses: (1) Lucy's $ 50,000 offer "was made in jest";(2) Zehmer "did not deliver the memorandum to Lucy … [who simply] picked it up [and] put it in his pocket";(3) Zehmer refused to accept Lucy's $ 5 offer after realizing that Lucy was serious;(4) Zehmer "had no intention of selling the farm, [because] the whole matter was a joke";(5) Zehmer claimed that he "was high as a Georgia pine" during the transaction;and, (6) Lucy and Zehmer were just "two doggoned drunks bluffing to see who could talk the biggest and say the most."
The Supreme Court of Virginia rejected the Zehmers' defenses--declaring that the simple memorandum of understanding was a binding contractual agreement.Ultimately, the supreme court ordered the Zehmersto sell the farm to Lucy and his brother.The sale was ordered, even though only a few words appeared in a short, unsophisticated memorandum of understanding. Even more importantly, the Virginia Supreme Court reaffirmed several extremely important principles of contract law: (1) "An agreement or mutual assent is … essential to a valid contract";(2) "[t]he mental assent of the parties is not requisite for the formation of a contract";and, (3) "[an offeror may not assert] that he was merely jesting when his conduct and words would warrant a reasonable [offeree to believe that the offeror was presenting] a real agreement."
Twenty-six years before the Virginia Supreme Court decidedLucy, the New York Court of Appeals decidedMitchill v. Lath.The controversy inMitchillalso concerned whether the specific performance was warranted under an allegedly bargained-for contract.Consider the simple facts in the case. Charles Lath and his business partner owned a farm and wanted to sell it.Lath also owned an icehouse.The latter sat on Lieutenant Governor Lunn's land, which was directly across the road in front of Lath's land.Standing on Lath's land, one could see the icehouse.
Catherine Mitchill approached Lath, looked at Lath's farm and decided to make a purchase.But there was a condition precedent: she wanted Lath to remove the icehouse on the Governor's land, because "the icehouse [was] objectionable."Accepting the condition, Lath "orally promised" to remove the icehouse.Lath'soral, stand-alone promisewas given as considerationfor Mitchill'scontractual promiseto purchase Lath's farm.Therefore, "[relying upon Lath's oral promise, Mitchill executed] a written contract to buy the property for $ 8,400."
As activities progressed, Mitchill received the deed and took possession of the farm, intending to use it as a summer residence.To help achieve the latter goal, Mitchill "spent considerable sums [of money to improve] the property."However, one unexpected development prevented Catherine's residential plan from coming to fruition: Lath breached the oral, stand-alone promise and refused to remove the icehouse.Catherine commenced an action for specific performance in a court of equity.
Before the lower courts and the Court of Appeals, Lath advanced the parol evidence rule as an affirmative defense.Simply stated, the parol evidence rule places limitations on parties' contractual obligations and/or prevents parties from tampering with totally integrated, written contracts.Justice Andrews wrote the opinion inMitchill, and he reaffirmed a settled principle of contract: generally, oral testimony will not alter or contradict the terms of a written contract.Of course, there is an exception to the rule: if parties intentionally fashion one agreement wholly or partly as consideration for a second and simultaneous agreement, the two are "necessarily bound together."Whether a bond between two agreements is sufficiently close, however, can become a major dispute--like the controversy inMitchill.
In the end, Justice Andrews declared that Mitchill and Lath's written, real-estate contract was "a full and complete agreement, setting forth in detail the obligations of each party."To reach that conclusion, Justice Andrews observed: if the parties had fashioned an "icehouse agreement," it would most naturally appear in the real-estate contract.Yes. The oral "icehouse agreement" was "closely related to the subject … in the written agreement."However, the oral, stand-alone promise was a collateral agreement; therefore, Catherine could not introduce it as evidence of an enforceable contractual obligation.
Each September, for nearly a quarter of a century, the author has witnessed a remarkable phenomenon: Interesting cases likeLucyandMitchillencourage first-year law students to fashion exceptionally intelligent, novel, thought-provoking and commonsensical questions. To illustrate, consider an alleged incident that nearly wrecked the life of a twenty-seven-year-old law student ("Jessica").Six years before entering law school, Jessica applied for an apartment in an "upscale-50-plus-residential community."
The two-page, standardized application form contained six paragraphs.One paragraph was a mandatory-arbitration clause.The latter provision banned all trial-by-jury and trial-by-judge lawsuits--requiring tenants to arbitrate all constitutional rights, common law, and civil rights disputes before private arbitrators.Jessica allegedly "forgot to complete and sign the application."Still, the associate-female manager told Jessica: "Don't worry about it."Ultimately, Jessica signed a one-year lease.The contract, however,did not contain a mandatory-arbitration provision.
A few months after Jessica moved into her apartment, the senior male manager allegedly wanted "to spend time" with Jessica and her new baby.Jessica, however, refused the manager's "romantic and fatherly advances."In response, the senior manager allegedly harassed Jessica--"making [her] life hell on earth."Later, the same manager forced Jessica to vacate the apartment, allegedly asserting: "You and your illegitimate child are trespassers. You are not 50-years-old. Leave!"
The then-twenty-one-year-old Jessica contacted an attorney, who concluded that she had viable claims under several federal statutes: The Fair Housing Act of 1968,the Civil Rights Act of 1866--sections 1981and 1982,and the Age Discrimination Act of 1974.Furthermore, the attorney reported that Jessica probably had sound common law assault and breach of contract claims.On several occasions, Jessica considered filing a multi-action lawsuit against the senior-male manager and the residential community.In the end, however, she vacated her apartment and decided not to sue.
When the twenty-seven-year-old Jessica entered law school, she readLucyandMitchill. And, in the course of events, she raised three questions: (1) whether her former fifty-plus standardized apartment application was an enforceable memorandum of understanding--like the controversial memorandum in Lucy v. Zehmer; (2) whether her uncompleted and unsigned lease application was a binding contract, (3) whether the mandatory-arbitration clause in her defunct apartment application was enforceable, absent probative evidence of any bargained-for exchange consideration; and (4) whether--under the parol evidence rule--the provisions in her uncompleted and unsigned application could have altered or amended the terms in her signed lease agreement.
To be sure, during Jessica's tenure in law school as well as today, state and federal courts are still grappling with each question. For example, preliminary agreements appear in many forms.Consequently, judicialsplits continue to evolve over whether parties' precontractual agreements are valid and enforceable contracts.Such conflicts persist even though a rich body of law has developed to answer the question: whether a memorandum of understanding is an enforceable contract.Moreover, even assuming that standardized application forms are not memoranda of understanding or preliminary agreements, one is still left with a pressing question: whether a signed or an unsigned completed application is a valid and legally enforceable contract.
The latter question continues to be timely and important for two reasons. First, like preliminary agreements, standardized application forms are ubiquitous.Furthermore, there are many types: applications for goods, services, employment, membership, prizes, housing as well as applications for one's gaining admission to a multitude of programs and institutions.Arguably,absent the widespread use of standardized applications, face-to-face transactions and interviews would increase dramatically. In turn, efficient operations of most small-to-large institutions, industries and professions would probably decrease substantially and business costs would increase.
Therefore, given the ubiquity and use of applications forms, disputes over whether such forms create legal rights or obligations are exceedingly common. But consider the pressing question in this Article: whether the Federal Arbitration Act of 1925 (FAA)governs the enforceability of arbitration clauses in standardized application forms? Without doubt, this question has generated serious splits between and among federal and state courts.Furthermore, as discussed later and more extensively in this Article, the Supreme Court has fashioned extremely liberal policies--those favoring the enforcement of mandatory-arbitration provisions in binding contracts as well as in non-binding instruments.
Even more disquieting, all too many inferior state courts as well as federal courts have embraced and applied the Supreme Court's "liberal" arbitration policies--without seriously questioning the wisdom of such policies.And in the wake, two adverse consequences have developed: (1) federal courts routinely ignore or refuse to weigh carefully and intelligently states' settled principles of contract law when deciding whether to coerce applicants into binding arbitration; and (2) the Supreme Courts' admittedly and, arguably, excessively pro-arbitration bias has encouraged lower courts to marginalize or ignore consumer protection, antidiscrimination, and civil rights laws, when the latter tribunals are considering whether to enforce arbitration clauses in standardized application forms.
Unquestionably, a few commentators have sounded the alarm--questioning the wisdom of courts' willingness to enforce mandatory-arbitration provisions in applications.Those discussions, however, have been fairlybrief--appearing essentially as statements or conclusion in the literature.Certainly, the FAA covers enforceable contracts.But, completed and signed application forms generally are not contracts under state laws.Like many memoranda of understanding, applications are simply unenforceable written representations or preliminary agreements. Moreover, the FAA's "savings clause" instructs courts to weigh states' contract laws and equitable principles extremely carefully before deciding to enforce arbitration clauses in contracts.
Without a doubt, the question--whether courts should enforce arbitration provisions in standardized applications--is timely and important. Yet, this question has received surprisingly little serious research and legal analysis. Therefore, the purpose of this Article is to present a comprehensive and an interdisciplinary--historical, legal, empirical and statistical--explanation of the pressing and general question: whether federal and state courts are equally more or less likely to apply section 2 of the FAA and enforce mandatory-arbitration clauses in standardized application forms? There is, of course, an equally important auxiliary question: whether state and federal courts allow legal as well as extralegal factors to influence decisions to enforce or not enforce arbitration clauses in standardized applications?
Part I begins the discussion by presenting an extremely brief review of several common law rules regarding the following: (1) the formation of a valid contract, (2) bargained-for consideration and the enforcement of a valid contract, (3) the enforceability of memoranda of understanding and other preliminary agreements, (4) the applicability of the parol evidence rule, and (5) the enforceability of applications for products, services, employment, residential and commercial tenancy, admissions, and membership in various associations, organizations and institutions.
Part II presents an even shorter review of disgruntled applicants' federal and state statutory theories of recovery. Fairly often, in their underlying lawsuits, applicants allege that defendants violated one or a combinationof federal and state consumer protection, civil rights and/or antidiscrimination laws.In those same underlying lawsuits, defendants file motions to compel the applicants/plaintiffs to arbitrate the disputed claims before a private arbitrator.On other occasions, defendants initiate declaratory judgment actions in courts of equity and file motions to compel arbitration.Still, in other instances, defendants file motions only after applicants have commenced underlying antidiscrimination, consumer protection or civil rights lawsuits in courts of law, and served copies of their complaints.Briefly put, the discussion in Part II is a necessary prerequisite for understanding the more troublesome and prevalent judicial conflicts, which are discussed in Part IV of this Article.
Part III discusses the debate surrounding the actual and purported purposes of FAA section 2--the primary focus of this Article. That section has repeatedly fostered numerous motion to compel arbitration disputes involving the following questions: (1) whether an arbitration clause in a standardized application form qualifies as a "written provision in a contract" undersection 2 of the FAA; (2) whether applicants' antidiscrimination, civil rights and harassment claims "arose out of" an enforceable arbitration clause in an employment contract, or "arose out of" an unenforceable employment-application form; (3) whether an applicant's consumer-protection claims "arose out of" an arbitration clause in a financial services contract or "arose out of" an unenforceable application for services; and (4) whether a party's failure to prove sufficient and bargained-for exchange consideration precludes the enforcement of an arbitration clause in preprinted application form. These specific questions have generated judicial splits, which are discussed in Part IV.
Once more, it is important to stress: many federal and some state courts routinely cite and apply FAA section 2 and enforce arbitration clauses in all sorts of applications for employment, services, goods, benefits and memberships.Under the common law, however, standardized and stand-alone applications are not valid and enforceable contracts.Even more importantly, a large body of congressional and historical evidence exists to support two assertions: (1) Congress never intended for the FAA section 2 to marginalize or preempt state principles of contract law; and (2) Congress never envisioned for the FAA section 2 to govern the enforceability of arbitration clauses in standardized application forms.Part III presents the historical and congressional evidence.
Finally, Part V presents a case study. The reported findings are based on an analysis of approximately one thousand federal and state court cases. More specifically, Part V outlines and discusses the substantive and procedural dispositions of motion to compel arbitration disputes--those involving the enforceability of arbitration clauses in standardized application forms as well as in standardized and negotiated contracts. Quite simply, the statistically significant findings reported in Part V reveal several unintended and troublesome consequences: (1) federal courts' motion to compel arbitration rulings muddle markedly settled, common law principles of contract; (2) state and federal courts' decisions undermine or marginalize consumer protection laws; and (3) federal courts' section 2 rulings effectively preempt the application of antidiscrimination statutes, thereby precluding applicants-litigants from securing remedies under those statutes.
Certainly, Congress did not enact the FAA to undermine federal and state civil rights, antidiscrimination, and consumer protection statutes. Therefore, the Article concludes by encouraging Congress to enact a previously proposed statute entitled, "The Arbitration Fairness Act." The evidence in the study strongly suggests that some state courts and most federal courtswill continue to enforce arbitration provisions in all sorts of standardized applications and bar disgruntled applicants' access to courts of law--unless Congress acts.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of preliminary written instruments (letters of intent, standardized applications, memoranda of understanding)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether standardized application forms and other precontractual writings can be treated as binding contracts for purposes of enforcing arbitration clauses, while Paper B analyzes whether a letter of intent and similar preliminary documents can create binding obligations in the construction context (Quake).

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel and precontractual reliance as an independent basis for recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses courts treating preliminary agreements and unsigned applications as potentially binding (and the consequences when arbitration clauses are enforced), and Paper B centers on promissory estoppel and recovery for reliance costs where formal acceptance or a complete contract was never executed.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parol evidence and intent inquiries in deciding whether preliminary negotiations create obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the parol evidence rule and judicial tests for whether oral or preliminary agreements are 'bound together' with written contracts, and Paper B recounts the Illinois Supreme Court remanding Quake to receive parol evidence about the parties' intent regarding the letter of intent.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrinal change (expansion or contraction) and its practical policy consequences for bargaining risk and litigation exposure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques Supreme Court and lower-court doctrinal trends (pro-enforcement of arbitration) that shift litigation and substantive remedies, producing empirical consequences, while Paper B critiques Quake's doctrinal expansion of precontractual liability and warns of increased litigation risk and economic/dispute-cost consequences.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between contract/precontract doctrines and access to substantive remedies in race, discrimination, and public procurement contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how enforcement of arbitration clauses in applications can marginalize consumer-protection and antidiscrimination claims, and Paper B explores how precontractual promises, minority set-aside conditions, and the political context of public procurement affected minority contractors' opportunities and litigation over those rights.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016michstlrev1267!!ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?

shared_topics.topic: when a transaction qualifies as a binding contract versus a non‑contractual instrument (gift, preliminary agreement, or unsigned application)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when charitable naming arrangements are characterized as gifts, trusts, or contracts—focusing on donor intent and formalities—while Paper B analyzes whether standardized or preliminary application forms and memoranda of understanding are enforceable contracts for purposes of arbitration clauses, focusing on formation doctrines like consideration and mutual assent.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial characterization doctrines determine available remedies and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that courts' choice of gift law versus contract law radically changes available remedies (e.g., ability to enforce naming rights or supply terms), and Paper B shows that courts' application of FAA and contract doctrines (parol evidence, integration, formation) determines whether arbitration clauses are enforced or claimants retain access to courts.

shared_topics.topic: the real‑world consequences of doctrinal choices for vulnerable stakeholders and public policy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents harms—delayed renovations, donors or charities disadvantaged—caused by treating naming rights as gifts, while Paper B documents how enforcement of arbitration clauses in applications can marginalize consumer protection, antidiscrimination, and civil‑rights remedies, tying both papers to policy consequences of legal classification.

shared_topics.topic: the need for clearer transactional drafting, negotiation, or legislative/doctrinal reform to avoid disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends using contract law and specific negotiated terms (duration, morals clauses, exit mechanisms) to prevent naming‑rights disasters; Paper B recommends clearer limits on FAA application and potential statutory reform (Arbitration Fairness Act) and warns about drafting pitfalls in standardized applications to prevent coercive arbitration enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: critical case‑law analysis as the primary method for diagnosing doctrinal failures
shared_topics.justification: Both papers perform sustained reviews of judicial decisions—Paper A surveys naming‑rights cases and related trust/contract rulings, and Paper B compiles historical, legal, and empirical analysis of roughly a thousand cases—to demonstrate how courts’ approaches produce problematic outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56depaullrev55!!ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of 'middle-position' agreements (preliminary memoranda, standardized applications, and ADR agreements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally analyzes whether standardized application forms and memoranda of understanding qualify as enforceable contracts for purposes of arbitration clauses; Paper B uses Knapp's 'contract to bargain' framework to examine ADR agreements that occupy a similar middle position between enforceable contracts and nonbinding commitments.

shared_topics.topic: judicial formalism (yes-contract/no-contract) versus relational/contextual/good-faith analysis
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for mechanically applying federal arbitration doctrine without carefully engaging state contract principles, while Paper B rejects formalist yes/no-contract conclusions and advocates for a relational, good-faith approach to defining and enforcing ADR duties.

shared_topics.topic: misapplication of federal arbitration statutes (FAA/UAA) to nonbinding or preliminary instruments and tension with state contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how courts invoke section 2 of the FAA to enforce arbitration clauses in applications—often sidelining state contract doctrines—whereas Paper B warns that courts improperly treat nonbinding ADR processes as binding arbitration under the FAA or UAA instead of applying common-law analysis.

shared_topics.topic: effects on access to judicial remedies and the need for tailored remedial tools when cooperative or preliminary commitments are breached
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that enforcing arbitration clauses in applications can preclude plaintiffs from pursuing statutory consumer-protection and civil-rights remedies in court, and Paper B focuses on how courts should craft context-sensitive remedies (and overcome evidentiary hurdles) to avoid unfairly cutting off judicial recourse when ADR or bargaining commitments are breached.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 79kylj557!!ARTICLE: Default Rules for Contract Formation By Promise and the Need for Revision of the Mailbox Rule
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Default Rules for Contract Formation By Promise and the Need for Revision of the Mailbox Rule

shared_topics.topic: when acceptance or assent is legally effective (receipt vs. dispatch and reasonable diligence)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the mailbox/dispatch rule and argues acceptance by promise should be effective only on receipt (or at least should track parties' expectations and communication technology), while Paper B probes when standardized applications or unsigned documents create binding obligations—a question that turns on when courts deem assent or a 'written provision in a contract' to have arisen.

shared_topics.topic: whether preliminary writings, memoranda, or standardized application forms are enforceable contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the legal consequences of manifestations of willingness to bargain, revocations, and notifications in formation, and Paper B directly examines the enforceability of memoranda of understanding and standardized application forms (including unsigned or preprinted instruments) as contracts that can carry clauses like mandatory arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: judicial splits and inconsistent application of default contract-formation or enforcement doctrines across jurisdictions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents divergences between English and American courts (and among rules for instantaneous vs non-instantaneous communications) over acceptance timing, while Paper B documents persistent splits between federal and state courts—and among lower tribunals—in applying the FAA and settled common-law contract principles to arbitration clauses in applications.

shared_topics.topic: the need to reconcile or reform default contract rules in light of modern contexts or external legal regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the dispatch/mailbox rule departs from reasonable expectations given modern communications and should be revised, and Paper B argues federal arbitration law and recent judicial practices have distorted common-law defaults (and calls for statutory reform) to address harms from enforcing arbitration clauses in standardized forms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69fordhamlrev427!!ARTICLE: THE ORIGINS OF THE OBJECTIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT FORMATION AND INTERPRETATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ORIGINS OF THE OBJECTIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT FORMATION AND INTERPRETATION

shared_topics.topic: objective vs. subjective intent in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B traces the historical and doctrinal basis of the objective theory (words and conduct over unexpressed states of mind), and Paper A invokes that same objective-doctrine lineage (e.g., Lucy v. Zehmer, Mitchill) when analyzing whether applicants' words, signatures, or standardized forms manifest enforceable assent to arbitration clauses.

shared_topics.topic: the parol evidence rule's role in admitting or excluding precontractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes how the parol evidence rule produces objective strictures that can exclude earlier or contemporaneous understandings, while Paper A squarely treats the parol evidence rule as central to disputes over whether application forms or preliminary agreements can alter or supplement later written leases or contracts (and thus whether arbitration clauses are enforceable).

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of preliminary agreements, memoranda, and standardized application forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally examines whether standardized, signed or unsigned applications and memoranda constitute binding contracts or mere preliminary agreements for purposes of enforcing arbitration clauses, and Paper B addresses the doctrinal standards (meeting of the minds, evidentiary limits, objective tests) that determine when provisional or collateral promises will be treated as enforceable agreements.

shared_topics.topic: tension between predictability (objective rules) and party autonomy/consent in enforcing contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper B frames the objective theory as a tradeoff favoring predictability and market efficiency over subjective will, whereas Paper A highlights that applying broad, objective enforcement (especially via the FAA) to standardized applications can override individual consent and state-law protections, raising questions about whether predictability should trump actual autonomy in specific contexts like arbitration and civil-rights claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev219!!SYMPOSIUM: AN UNLIKELY RESURRECTION
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: AN UNLIKELY RESURRECTION

shared_topics.topic: contract law's role in shaping access to justice and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically documents how enforcement of arbitration clauses in standardized applications diverts disputes from courts and can foreclose statutory remedies, while Paper B theorizes how contract doctrine can enable or deny individuals' agency and legal recourse, urging a reconception of contract's procedural and substantive consequences for marginalized actors.

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrine affects marginalized groups (consumers, tenants, women, and sexual minorities)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the impact of enforcing arbitration provisions in housing, employment, and consumer applications—showing effects on plaintiffs bringing civil‑rights, antidiscrimination, and consumer claims—whereas Paper B examines contract's ambivalent effects on women and lesbians and urges attention to how contract rules can perpetuate or ameliorate oppression.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability and interpretation of standardized or context‑specific contractual instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether standardized application forms, preliminary memoranda, and boilerplate arbitration clauses are valid contracts under doctrines like consideration and the parol evidence rule, and Paper B critiques the adequacy of a unitary contract theory—highlighting the need to rethink contract doctrine in specialized contexts (e.g., employment, family, housing) where form and context matter.

shared_topics.topic: advocacy for doctrinal or statutory reform of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends legislative action (e.g., the Arbitration Fairness Act) and criticizes courts' pro‑arbitration doctrines for marginalizing other laws, while Paper B advocates transformative reinterpretation of contract from feminist/postmodern perspectives, both proposing changes to how contract law operates to address injustices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2wmmarybuslrev73!!ARTICLE: FINGERPRINTS OF EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL ON THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FINGERPRINTS OF EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL ON THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: whether preliminary writings, unsigned or standardized application forms, and short memoranda constitute enforceable contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally analyzes whether standardized application forms and memoranda of understanding function as binding contracts for purposes of enforcing arbitration clauses; Paper B examines when informal oral or unwritten agreements (and the writings that fail formal requisites) can nonetheless be enforced, focusing on the Statute of Frauds context and related case law.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal writing requirements (Statute of Frauds, parol evidence rule) and reliance-based equitable doctrines (equitable estoppel, promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally analyzes how equitable estoppel and promissory estoppel can overcome the Statute of Frauds' writing requirement, while Paper A addresses how parol evidence and other formalities interact with courts' willingness to treat precontractual or application documents as binding for arbitration enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the necessity and sufficiency of consideration or bargained-for exchange for enforcing promises in borderline contract situations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether arbitration clauses in completed or uncompleted applications are enforceable absent evidence of bargained-for consideration, and Paper B discusses reliance-based substitutes (promissory estoppel) when traditional consideration or writing formality is lacking.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrinal choices affect parties' access to substantive remedies (e.g., consumer, civil-rights, or fraud remedies) when formalities are relaxed or enforced
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts' pro-arbitration readings of federal law and relaxed treatment of application formalities can preclude access to statutory consumer and antidiscrimination remedies, while Paper B shows how courts' use of equitable estoppel/promissory estoppel to bypass formal requirements changes which promises are enforceable and thus which remedies are available.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.

shared_topics.topic: legal archaeology / historical reconstruction of judicial opinions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A undertakes an explicit historical and congressional reconstruction of the Federal Arbitration Act and its judicial treatment from 1925–2014 to situate modern arbitration doctrine; Paper B advocates the methodological project of ‘legal archaeology,’ urging scholars to reconstruct reported cases by digging into extralegal historical evidence to understand how and why courts decided as they did.

shared_topics.topic: using extralegal historical and legislative evidence to interpret statutes and doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A marshals congressional history and broader historical materials to argue what Congress intended (and did not intend) about FAA §2 and arbitration in application forms; Paper B recommends seeking evidence outside the law library to make sense of cases and thereby to interpret legal rules in their historical context.

shared_topics.topic: importance of factual narrative and contextual facts in evaluating and teaching law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds the concrete facts of classic contract cases (Lucy, Mitchill) and a contemporary anecdote (Jessica) to probe contract-formation, parol evidence, and arbitration issues; Paper B emphasizes that careful attention to factual presentation and reconstruction is essential both for correct doctrinal analysis and for legal pedagogy.

shared_topics.topic: critique of judicial decisionmaking with respect to justice and legal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts (especially federal tribunals) for doctrinally stretching arbitration law in ways that marginalize consumer protection and civil rights remedies; Paper B highlights how close scrutiny of historically reconstructed facts can reveal wrongly decided cases and revitalize concern for achieving just outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27setonhalllrev490!!ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY

shared_topics.topic: the role of consideration (bargained-for exchange) in making promises legally enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes consideration as the act of relinquishing autonomy that grounds enforceable bargains and attributes responsibility, while Paper B repeatedly treats 'bargained-for consideration' as a dispositive issue when deciding whether arbitration clauses in application forms constitute enforceable contractual commitments.

shared_topics.topic: when preliminary writings, memoranda, or standardized application forms become binding contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the boundaries of the bargain mechanism and distinguishes enforceable promises from preliminary or nonbinding representations, and Paper B empirically and doctrinally examines whether memoranda of understanding, unsigned or standardized application forms, and other precontractual instruments should be treated as enforceable contracts (including for arbitration clauses).

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrine allocates legal obligation and access to remedies (i.e., when private acts become justiciable obligations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames consideration doctrine as a social mechanism that converts everyday exchanges into legal obligations and attributes responsibility, and Paper B analyzes how courts' enforcement (or refusal) of arbitration clauses in applications shifts litigants' access to courts and remedies under consumer protection and civil-rights statutes.

shared_topics.topic: interaction and tension between traditional common-law contract principles and other legal rules or statutes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts consideration with alternative mechanisms like reliance and situates contract attribution alongside tort/criminal requirements, while Paper B investigates the tension between the Federal Arbitration Act, state contract doctrines (parol evidence, formation), and federal statutes (antidiscrimination/consumer laws) when courts enforce arbitration provisions.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of preliminary writings and standardized forms as contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally examines whether standardized application forms and memoranda of understanding qualify as binding contracts (and thus can carry arbitration clauses), while Paper B analyzes whether the fishermen's written modification/new contract in Alaska Packers' constituted an enforceable novation or was invalid under existing contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and application of consideration, pre-existing duty, and novation doctrines to contract modifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether lack of bargained-for consideration or preliminary status of an application precludes enforcement of embedded clauses, and Paper B centers on the pre-existing duty rule versus novation (and related doctrines) to decide whether a wage modification was legally enforceable in a labor setting.

shared_topics.topic: how courts' doctrinal choices are shaped by policy/context and can distort classical contract principles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that federal courts' pro-arbitration stance and selective invocation of FAA §2 has led courts to sideline state contract principles and statutory protections, while Paper B explores how labor-context pressures and judges' sympathies or policy concerns influenced the development and application of doctrines like novation and duress in Alaska Packers'.

shared_topics.topic: intersection of contract enforcement with employment/labor or statutory remedies (access to courts and protections)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how enforcing arbitration clauses in applications can preempt access to antidiscrimination and consumer-protection remedies for applicants/employees, and Paper B examines the consequences of applying contract doctrine to labor disputes (wage claims and work stoppages), highlighting how contract rules determine workers' practical ability to secure remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2000utahlrev223!!SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates treating reported cases like archaeological digs—recovering factual and historical context to make sense of legal decisions; Paper B explicitly conducts an interdisciplinary historical and legal analysis (1925–2014), using historical materials and precedent to explain how arbitration doctrine evolved and how Congress and courts understood the FAA.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between facts, factual reconstruction, and doctrinal outcome
shared_topics.justification: Paper A stresses that careful attention to the factual record and reconstruction of events is essential to reach just legal outcomes and to avoid abstract misreadings; Paper B analyzes how courts' factual characterizations (e.g., treating applications as binding contracts or not) and doctrinal choices (parol evidence, contract formation) determine whether arbitration clauses are enforced, often producing contested outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the pedagogical and interpretive role of landmark cases and case narratives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes using individual cases as rich narrative objects that teach students about law in context; Paper B centers canonical contract cases (Lucy v. shared_topics.topic: critique of judicial practices and the need for empirically grounded case analysis to evaluate judicial decision-making
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for 'getting one's hands dirty' in case investigation to reveal assumptions and avoid doctrinal abstraction; Paper B pairs legal argument with empirical analysis of roughly one thousand cases to critique patterns in federal and state courts (e.g., pro-arbitration bias, marginalization of state contract principles and statutory protections) and to show how aggregate judicial practice departs from stated legal principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev32!!SYMPOSIUM: THE TRIUMPH OF GILMORE'S THE DEATH OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE TRIUMPH OF GILMORE'S THE DEATH OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution of contract doctrine and legal change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A undertakes an explicit historical and empirical study (1925–2014) of how the Federal Arbitration Act and subsequent judicial decisions altered contract enforcement; Paper B analyzes Gilmore's account of the birth and 'death' of nineteenth‑century contract doctrine and uses historical narrative to explain broader doctrinal change over the twentieth century.

shared_topics.topic: the judicial role in shifting contract doctrines (formalist vs. realist approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes Supreme Court and lower-court pro‑arbitration rulings for displacing settled common‑law contract principles, while Paper B centrally examines how courts and legal realism displaced classical/formalist contract thinking (Langdell/Williston/Holmes) in favor of more pragmatic adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between contract law and other legal regimes (preemption, tort, statutory protections)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how FAA enforcement of arbitration clauses can preempt or marginalize state contract rules and statutory consumer, civil‑rights, and antidiscrimination remedies; Paper B argues that tort and other nonconsensual doctrines progressively absorbed functions of contract law, showing how contractual boundaries shift relative to other legal areas.

shared_topics.topic: the role of canonical cases and doctrinal pedagogy in shaping contract law understanding
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds canonical contract cases (e.g., Lucy v. Zehmer, Mitchill v. Lath) as pedagogical touchstones and uses them to frame contemporary enforceability questions, while Paper B interrogates the influence of canonical figures and doctrines (Langdell, Holmes, Williston) on the intellectual development and decline narratives of contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 35amulrev547!!ARTICLE: A PROPOSAL TO SIMPLIFY QUANTUM MERUIT LITIGATION. © 1986 Candace S. Kovacic
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A PROPOSAL TO SIMPLIFY QUANTUM MERUIT LITIGATION. © 1986 Candace S. Kovacic

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of preliminary, informal, or nontraditional agreements (memoranda, applications, implied contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when recoveries like quantum meruit apply versus enforceable express contracts, distinguishing implied-in-fact, implied-in-law, quasi-contract and other nontraditional instruments; Paper B interrogates whether standardized application forms and memoranda of understanding qualify as binding contracts and whether arbitration clauses in those instruments are enforceable under the FAA and state contract law.

shared_topics.topic: judicial inconsistency and doctrinal confusion in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents widespread inconsistent terminology and analytic methods in quantum meruit decisions and proposes a unifying two-tier framework; Paper B documents judicial splits and lower-court application of Supreme Court pro-arbitration rules that, the author argues, muddle settled contract doctrines, supported by empirical case analysis.

shared_topics.topic: the role of assent/request/consideration in creating obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A makes the defendant's request (versus unrequested performance) the key element determining entitlement and measurement of recovery; Paper B engages with questions of mental assent, signatures, and bargained-for consideration (and the parol evidence rule) to determine whether an application or memorandum creates enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how contract formalities affect access to remedies (restitution/unjust enrichment versus arbitration and preclusion of statutory relief)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A prescribes remedies—market value for requested services or unjust-enrichment measures for unrequested performance—when formal contract remedies are unavailable; Paper B explores how enforcing arbitration clauses in nontraditional agreements can preclude access to judicial and statutory remedies (consumer protection, civil rights), and urges careful application of equitable/state-law principles.

compared_to.partner_title: NORMAN J. shared_topics.topic: preemption and conflict between a uniform/federal instrument and domestic contract law

shared_topics.topic: defining the substantive scope or 'borders' of a statutory regime governing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether arbitration clauses in standardized application forms fall within the FAA's reach and how courts determine whether pre-contractual instruments are enforceable contracts under federal law; Paper B develops methods for determining which disputes and legal questions fall within the CISG's substantive scope and thus whether domestic law or the CISG governs.

shared_topics.topic: impact on availability and limits of remedies when multiple legal regimes could apply
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how enforcing arbitration clauses can bar access to judicial remedies under consumer-protection, antidiscrimination, and civil‑rights statutes; Paper B examines how importing domestic remedies into CISG cases (or vice versa) can expand or cut off remedies (e.g., notice, limitation periods, measures of damages) and thus affect foreseeability and legal certainty.

shared_topics.topic: role of judicial interpretation and doctrine in promoting uniformity (or producing fragmentation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques Supreme Court and lower-court doctrinal choices that produce a pro‑arbitration, uniform enforcement trend despite state-law variation; Paper B surveys case law approaches and proposes doctrinal tools (including a two‑step approach) for courts to delineate the CISG's reach and preserve uniform international contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41loyuchilj175!!Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power

shared_topics.topic: the central role of contract formation/mutual assent in allocating power and insulating bargains from challenge
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat contract formation and the mutual-assent rule as the doctrinal fulcrum that determines who is bound and how hard it is to undo bargains—Paper A argues that preserving classical formation immunizes coercive conduct from policing doctrines, and Paper B shows courts treat formation (or its formal trappings) as dispositive when enforcing arbitration clauses in applications.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when written preliminaries or standard-form instruments (applications, memoranda) constitute enforceable contracts
shared_topics.justification: Both articles grapple with the enforceability of precontractual writings and standard-form documents—Paper A interrogates how formation doctrine validates problematic bargains even when coercion is alleged, while Paper B empirically examines judicial willingness to treat standardized applications or memoranda as binding (including binding arbitration clauses).

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of contract-law mechanisms and judicial practice to protect weaker parties from coercion or unfair standard terms
shared_topics.justification: Each paper critiques doctrinal and judicial responses as failing vulnerable parties—Paper A argues modern policing doctrines (unconscionability, duress, misrepresentation) cannot overcome formation-based presumptions, and Paper B documents that courts’ enforcement of arbitration clauses in applications marginalizes consumer, antidiscrimination, and civil-rights remedies.

shared_topics.topic: how higher-order legal choices and institutional rules (e.g., federal arbitration law vs. state/common-law doctrines; classical vs. modern doctrinal shifts) reshape enforcement outcomes to the advantage of powerful contracting parties
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how legal regime choices alter enforcement: Paper A shows retention of classical formation within modern contract law entrenches bargaining power, while Paper B shows how the Supreme Court’s—and lower courts’—application of the FAA and pro-arbitration policies can preempt state contract norms and produce similar pro-power outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26wmmarylrev45!!ARTICLE: A CRITIQUE OF THE PROMISE MODEL OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CRITIQUE OF THE PROMISE MODEL OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the role of consideration in determining when promises become legally enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates whether arbitration clauses in standardized applications are enforceable absent bargained-for consideration and how courts treat 'applications' versus contracts; Paper B critically examines the doctrine of consideration as a central discrepancy between the promissory model and contract doctrine, questioning when mere promises warrant legal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability and judicial treatment of standardized or form (adhesion) contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically analyzes courts' willingness to enforce arbitration provisions embedded in ubiquitous standardized application forms, while Paper B discusses how form contracts and unconscionability reveal limits of the promise model and how law sometimes overrides or modifies terms in standard-form agreements.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy (promissory obligation) and community/public-policy interventions (gap-filling, duties of good faith, mitigation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how federal pro-arbitration policy can displace state contract principles and statutory protections (consumer, civil-rights), highlighting conflict between private agreements and public norms; Paper B theorizes the same tension, contrasting a promissory/autonomy-driven model with the role of community values and gap-filling doctrines that alter or supplement parties' promises.
