shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the meanings and relationships of expectation and reliance measures, showing when they converge, when they diverge, and defending use of expectation damages on fairness and efficiency grounds; Paper B treats the expectation vs reliance distinction as a central pedagogical point that shapes how Contracts is taught and how students understand what the law protects.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies reveal the purposes and normative ends of contract law (fairness, compensation, efficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly analyzes how different damage measures relate to the ends of fairness and economic efficiency and what the compensatory purpose of damages should be; Paper B argues that beginning a course with remedies exposes students to the underlying purposes of contract law and uses remedies to explicate what the law seeks to protect and accomplish.

shared_topics.topic: the limits, types, and measurement problems of contract remedies (what remedies typically protect and what they do not)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops theoretical and practical measures of contract damages (including issues like placing the injured party where they would have been and the ‚damage term' parties would have bargained for) and analyzes contexts (market structure, business conduct) that affect measurement; Paper B emphasizes that contract remedies are typically generous in protecting expectation but limited in other ways (e.g., punitive damages are generally unavailable, specific performance is rare), and uses those limitations to justify pedagogical organization.

papers.node_id: 72iowalrev47!!ARTICLE: Damages for Reliance Across the Spectrum of Law: Of Blind Men and Legal Elephants
papers.title: ARTICLE: Damages for Reliance Across the Spectrum of Law: Of Blind Men and Legal Elephants
papers.abstract:
Everyone knows the story of the five wise blind men of India.  Each, when asked to describe an elephant, touched a different part of that animal.  Each then described a different thing.  "It is very much like a tree," said the one who touched a leg.  "It is very much like a snake," said the one who touched its tail.  "Like a rock," said another, and on and on.  All thought they were correct in their description.  All erred.
Legal scholars face a similar problem when they are asked to describe how the law reacts to the following situation:
Amakes a promise toB,reasonably anticipating thatBwill rely upon that promise.Bin fact reasonably relies upon the promise, perhaps expending time, services, or money.  Thereafter,Afails to perform.Bsues, but for a number of reasons cannot successfully assert breach of contract.Different kinds of legal scholars could have vastly different reactions to the facts just described.  A contracts scholar might assert thatBmay recover under promissory estoppel.A franchises and distributorships expert could assert that someone who reasonably relies upon promises of a franchise or distributorship will be allowed to recoup out-of-pocket expenditures if the agency relationship is either never brought to fruition or is terminated on short notice without cause.A torts specialist could say that ifAmade the promise without present intent to keep it,Amight be liable in tort for misrepresentation.The torts specialist also might note, however, that courts sometimes allow tort damages for the failure to keep a promise even if the promise was made with the present intent to keep it.An insurance expert could argue that people who reasonably rely upon promises to procure insurance can recover damages if those promises are not kept.Finally, a trusts and restitution scholar could assert that the law of restitution or constructive trusts protects people likeB.The experts can agree on only one thing:Bis compensated.
Part II of this Article demonstrates that five different substantive areas of law -- contracts, agency, torts, insurance, and restitution or constructive trusts -- have different methods for dealing with the problem of relying promisees.Similar but often inconsistent remedies may exist in these areas of law for compensating promisees who successfully assert the different substantive theories.  Although some scholars writing in these five fields of law have recognized that substantial overlap exists in connection with the substantive principles, the problem created by the overlap of what damages are appropriate has almost completely escaped their attention.  Part II also discusses "flexible remedies" and courts' and scholars' acceptance of flexible remedies in the five substantive areas of law.
The focus of this Article shifts in parts III and IV.  Part III shows that courts generally have not recognized that the various substantive areas overlap in connection with the rights of relying promisees.  Furthermore, it will be shown that although a few cases discuss more than one substantive theory, none recognize the problem of what damages ought to be awardedwhen substantive areas overlap.Part IV concentrates exclusively on one aspect of the damages issue, namely, the flexible remedy in,and shows that many courts are simply oblivious to the idea of flexible remedies in that context.This part of the Article shows that an enormous discontinuity exists between what contracts scholars for the last twenty years have thought was happening in the courts in connection with the flexible remedy in section 90 and what actually was happening.
The Article concludes with a call for a unified theory of damages for relying promisees regardless of the substantive theory used.Being purely an empirical and historical study, however, the Article itself makes no attempt to suggest what that theory might be.  That task is left to others.

questions.question: How do different areas of law compensate people who reasonably rely on a promise when traditional contract recovery is unavailable - specifically, what types and measures of damages are awarded and how consistent are they across areas?

Do courts recognize and manage the overlap between different areas of law in cases involving reliance on promises, and to what extent do they use flexible remedies versus treating each area in isolation?
Is there a gap between scholarly accounts of how flexible remedies for relying promisees are applied and the actual historical and empirical practice of courts?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
How should remedies for misrepresentation be calculated, and can misrepresentation damages be harmonized with contract-law remedial principles?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
When liability is grounded in misrepresentation rather than ordinary promise enforcement, do courts award different compensatory or punitive remedies?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2014uilllrev115!!ARTICLE: MISREPRESENTATION: THE RESTATEMENT'S SECOND MISTAKE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MISREPRESENTATION: THE RESTATEMENT'S SECOND MISTAKE

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap and redundancy among causes of action
shared_topics.justification: Both papers diagnose substantial overlap among distinct legal doctrines that govern similar fact patterns — Paper A shows nearly complete factual overlap between mistake and misrepresentation in contract law, while Paper B documents overlapping doctrines (contracts, promissory estoppel, tort misrepresentation, agency, insurance, restitution) that address relying promisees.

shared_topics.topic: reliance or misconception as the operative harm justifying relief
shared_topics.justification: Both treat the core problem as reliance on a false assumption or promise: Paper A conceptualizes mistake and misrepresentation as producing a failure of consent from misconception, and Paper B centers on promisees who reasonably rely and are injured when the promisor fails to perform.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies for reliance-based losses (restitution, reliance damages, flexible remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of what relief is appropriate when reliance or misconception causes loss — Paper A argues that mistake and misrepresentation should entail the same remedy regime (with a separate treatment for fraud), while Paper B surveys how courts award out-of-pocket/reliance damages and flexible remedies across multiple substantive areas and highlights inconsistencies.

shared_topics.topic: the case for doctrinal unification or a unified theory
shared_topics.justification: Both papers call for greater doctrinal coherence: Paper A proposes combining mistake and nonfraudulent misrepresentation into a single 'misconception' defense, and Paper B concludes with a call for a unified theory of damages for relying promisees across different fields of law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of fault/intent (fraud) in altering available relief
shared_topics.justification: Both consider how culpability affects outcomes — Paper A insists fraudulent misrepresentation should remain distinct so punitive/deterrent remedies can be applied, and Paper B discusses tort-based misrepresentation and distinctions courts draw when promises are made without present intent to perform versus with present intent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 7wmmarybuslrev1!!ARTICLE: KILL THE MONSTER: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AS AN INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: KILL THE MONSTER: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AS AN INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF ACTION

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel's evolving doctrinal role (consideration substitute vs independent cause of action)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how promissory estoppel has shifted from a narrow substitute for consideration to a broader, sometimes standalone remedy — Paper A situates promissory estoppel among multiple doctrines that compensate relying promisees, and Paper B documents and critiques courts treating promissory estoppel as an independent cause of action.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies and damages for relying promisees (reliance vs expectation and flexible remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles grapple with what damages or relief are proper when promisees rely to their detriment — Paper A surveys how contracts, torts, restitution, agency, and insurance conceive of reliance remedies and criticizes courts' use of 'flexible remedies,' while Paper B highlights how expanded use of promissory estoppel can alter available remedies and produce ad hoc fairness-based awards.

shared_topics.topic: impact on and potential erosion of traditional contract doctrines (statute of frauds, parol evidence, predictable bargain rules)
shared_topics.justification: Both works express concern that fairness-driven doctrines like promissory estoppel can displace classic contract rules — Paper B warns of undermining the statute of frauds, statutes of limitation, and parol evidence rule and urges statutory clarification, while Paper A documents discontinuities between scholarly expectations about section 90/flexible remedies and what courts actually do.

shared_topics.topic: overlap and boundary problems between substantive areas of law (contract, tort, restitution, agency, insurance)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine substantive overlap: Paper A systematically maps how five areas address reliance claims and the inconsistencies that creates, and Paper B illustrates how courts' promissory-estoppel decisions import tort-like fairness reasoning into contract law, blurring doctrinal boundaries.

shared_topics.topic: judicial inconsistency and the need for clearer doctrinal or statutory guidance
shared_topics.justification: Both articles highlight varied judicial approaches and resultant uncertainty — Paper A finds courts largely unaware of overlaps and inconsistent treatment of flexible remedies, and Paper B catalogs divergent state and federal case law and advocates legislative action to restore predictability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84neblrev506!!ARTICLE: Evolving Business and Social Norms and Interpretation Rules: The Need for a Dynamic Approach to Contract Disputes
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Evolving Business and Social Norms and Interpretation Rules: The Need for a Dynamic Approach to Contract Disputes

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based remedies and compensation for promisees when contracts fail
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that a dynamic contract approach should let courts tailor remedies to the parties' real expectations and context (including reliance), while Paper B surveys how multiple doctrines (promissory estoppel, restitution, agency, torts) currently provide reliance-based compensation and calls for a unified theory of such damages.

shared_topics.topic: role of extrinsic evidence and interpretation rules in resolving disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes rigid textualist rules (e.g., the plain meaning rule) and urges use of background context and parties' circumstances in interpretation; Paper B documents that reliance doctrines and flexible remedies often require courts to look beyond written contracts and examines how courts handle (or fail to handle) that extrinsic inquiry.

shared_topics.topic: overlap and interaction among substantive doctrines (contract, estoppel, tort, agency, restitution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B maps the overlapping remedies and doctrines available to relying promisees across five areas of law, and Paper A addresses how contract interpretation rules interact with other legal aims and doctrines, arguing for an approach that navigates those doctrinal overlaps dynamically.

shared_topics.topic: equitable concerns for disadvantaged or less-resourced parties who rely on promises or standardized forms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how strict interpretation rules and standardized form contracts disproportionately harm parties with less bargaining power, language or cultural barriers, while Paper B highlights the need to compensate reasonable reliance (often by less-protected promisees) and the role of equitable remedies in doing so.

shared_topics.topic: judicial inconsistency and the gap between doctrinal theory and actual practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents uneven and limited judicial adoption of dynamic interpretive principles versus formalist doctrines, and Paper B empirically shows courts' inconsistent recognition and application of flexible reliance remedies compared with scholarly accounts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1997wislrev943!!ARTICLE: THE NEW REQUIREMENT OF ENFORCEMENT RELIANCE IN COMMERCIAL PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL:
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE NEW REQUIREMENT OF ENFORCEMENT RELIANCE IN COMMERCIAL PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL:

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment of Section 90 promissory estoppel and the evolving reliance requirement
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts have interpreted and limited Section 90: Paper A documents a judicial trend requiring 'enforcement reliance' (a promisee's belief in legal enforceability) in commercial cases, while Paper B examines how courts actually apply Section 90's 'flexible remedy' and how that application departs from scholarly expectations.

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based remedies and damages for promisees
shared_topics.justification: Both engage substantively with remedies available to promisees who reasonably rely on promises: Paper A distinguishes performance reliance from enforcement reliance and the implications for enforceability, and Paper B surveys how different legal domains calculate and award reliance damages and the inconsistencies in those awards.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal classification and overlap between contract, tort, restitution, and agency doctrines in reliance cases
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront whether promissory estoppel functions as a contract doctrine or as tort/restitution-like protection and discuss overlap with other fields (e.g., agency, torts, restitution); Paper A critiques promise/consent theories that recast Section 90 as contract formation, while Paper B maps the overlapping substantive theories and their competing remedies.

shared_topics.topic: empirical gap between scholarly theory and judicial/commercial practice regarding reliance doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both use empirical or case-based analysis to argue that dominant academic claims about the expansion or use of promissory estoppel/Section 90 are inconsistent with actual appellate decisions and commercial behavior — courts and market actors have limited or adapted the doctrine in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52amjcompl513!!ARTICLE:Impossibility and Changed and Unforeseen Circumstances
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Impossibility and Changed and Unforeseen Circumstances

shared_topics.topic: doctrines that excuse or adjust contractual obligations when performance becomes impossible or circumstances change
shared_topics.justification: Paper B traces the doctrines of impossibility and changed circumstances and asks when and why courts grant relief when performance is impossible or its value shifts; Paper A engages this terrain indirectly by studying how nonperformance (promisor failure to perform) is treated across multiple doctrines that sometimes excuse or alleviate contractual burdens for relying promisees.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate remedial response when a promise is not performed (damages, flexible relief, or adjusted obligations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes when and how relying promisees are compensated—examining reliance damages and courts' use (or neglect) of flexible remedies—while Paper B examines historical and doctrinal bases for granting relief (and thus different remedial outcomes) when unexpected events affect the value or possibility of performance.

shared_topics.topic: the need for a unified theoretical account across doctrinal lines for providing relief from nonperformance or changed circumstances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concludes with a call for a unified theory of damages for relying promisees across contracts, tort, agency, insurance, and restitution; Paper B argues that historical understandings of changed‑circumstances doctrine can yield a coherent explanation for when relief (including in cases of impossibility) should be available, effectively seeking a unifying doctrinal rationale.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal analysis to explain modern remedies for disrupted contractual expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly uses Roman, canon, and medieval sources to explain the evolution of impossibility and changed‑circumstances doctrines, and Paper A uses empirical and historical study of recent court practice to show discontinuities between scholarly expectations and how courts actually apply flexible remedies to reliance cases.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64scallrev1!!ARTICLE: LIABILITY FOR MISTAKE IN CONTRACT FORMATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LIABILITY FOR MISTAKE IN CONTRACT FORMATION.

shared_topics.topic: remedies for promisees who reasonably rely but cannot prove breach
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how the law compensates a promisee who reasonably relies on a promise but cannot prevail on a conventional breach claim—Paper A through discussion of promissory estoppel, restitution and related doctrines in failed negotiations, and Paper B by surveying how contracts, agency, tort, insurance, and restitution each offer remedies for relying promisees.

shared_topics.topic: overlap and conflict among contract, tort, restitution, agency, and insurance doctrines in awarding reliance damages
shared_topics.justification: Both articles analyze the doctrinal overlap in compensating reliance losses—Paper A shows tort doctrines (negligent misrepresentation) encroaching on bargaining contexts normally governed by contract, while Paper B maps how five substantive fields provide sometimes inconsistent remedies and calls attention to the lack of coordination among them.

shared_topics.topic: use of negligent misrepresentation/mistake to impose liability for losses in pre‑contractual negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Both papers treat negligent misrepresentation or mistake as a route to liability where no enforceable promise exists—Paper A develops mistake and negligent misrepresentation as justifications for recovery in failed negotiations (e.g., insurance, subcontractor offers), and Paper B explicitly lists tort misrepresentation as one of the doctrines that can compensate relying promisees.

shared_topics.topic: policy/efficiency rationales (allocation of loss, better cost‑avoider) for imposing reliance losses despite lack of formal promise
shared_topics.justification: Both works appeal to utilitarian or loss‑allocation reasons for imposing duties in negotiation contexts—Paper A argues courts allocate losses to the better cost‑avoider and justifies state intervention, and Paper B discusses the practical and doctrinal willingness across fields to fashion flexible remedies to ensure compensation and address reliance externalities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77neblrev756!!ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law

shared_topics.topic: estoppel/promissory estoppel as a substitute for classic formalities (consideration or writing)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how estoppel (especially promissory estoppel) is used to enforce promises that lack consideration or the writings normally required for land transactions; Paper B treats promissory estoppel as one of the doctrines that allows relying promisees to recover when traditional contract remedies are unavailable (e.g., when consideration or contractual formals fail).

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance — whether it is the basis for liability or merely evidence of a promise
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates the debate in contract and property law over whether courts enforce promises because of induced reliance or because reliance proves a communicated intent to be bound; Paper B surveys multiple fields (contracts, torts, agency, restitution) that treat reliance differently and highlights the practical consequences of those doctrinal choices.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies/damages for relying promisees, including 'flexible' relief versus out‑of‑pocket recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that courts sometimes award enforcement of the promise rather than limiting recovery to expenditures made in reliance, producing a range of remedial outcomes in property contexts; Paper B is centrally concerned with what damages are appropriate across doctrines, criticizes courts' inconsistent use of flexible remedies under section 90, and calls for a unified approach to damages for relying promisees.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap and inconsistency across substantive areas in handling reliance claims and the need for a unified approach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that estoppel operates differently in property law than in contract law (e.g., nonverbal acts, successors‑in‑interest), producing doctrinal complexity; Paper B documents overlap among contracts, agency, torts, insurance, and restitution and argues courts have not coherently reconciled those overlaps, urging a unified theory of damages for relying promisees.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64scallrev1!!ARTICLE: LIABILITY FOR MISTAKE IN CONTRACT FORMATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LIABILITY FOR MISTAKE IN CONTRACT FORMATION.

shared_topics.topic: recovery for reliance (promissory estoppel and failed negotiations)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze situations where a promise or representation leads a party to rely and suffer loss even though no enforceable contract exists — Paper A through promissory estoppel and related doctrines across fields, and Paper B through cases like Hoffman v. Red Owl and Drennan that permit recovery for losses from failed negotiations.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap between contract, tort, restitution, agency, and insurance in compensating relying promisees
shared_topics.justification: Both works confront the overlap among multiple legal doctrines (contracts, torts/negligent misrepresentation, restitution/constructive trust, agency, and insurance) that can provide remedies for reliance losses, and both critique how courts and scholars treat the boundaries and interactions of these doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate measures of damages and the use of 'flexible remedies' for reliance losses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with what damages should be awarded when promisees rely — Paper A documents variation and courts' (in)attention to flexible remedies across substantive areas, while Paper B contrasts contract- and tort-based damage rules and warns about expansive tort remedies for reliance losses.

shared_topics.topic: liability for mistakes and negligent misrepresentation in contract formation/negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Both articles address liability arising from mistakes or misleading statements in bargaining (e.g., mistaken offers, mistaken insurance or mortgage handling), with Paper B developing a theory of mistake/negligent misrepresentation and Paper A noting tort recovery for promises made without present intent or other misrepresentations that cause reliance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59clevstlrev693!!ARTICLE: SELLING SEX: ANALYZING THE IMPROPER USE DEFENSE TO CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT THROUGH THE LENS OF CARROLL V. BEARDON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SELLING SEX: ANALYZING THE IMPROPER USE DEFENSE TO CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT THROUGH THE LENS OF CARROLL V. BEARDON

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap between contract law and other areas of law (and the problems that creates)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the intersection of contract enforcement with criminal law and public‑policy defenses (contracts used for prostitution), showing how overlap with noncontract norms complicates enforceability; Paper B documents overlap among contracts, agency, torts, insurance, and restitution in compensating relying promisees and the confusion that overlap creates for remedies.

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of malleable or flexible standards and the inconsistency that results
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes appellate courts' shifting, vague tests in public‑policy/improper‑use cases and how judges shape outcomes via flexible standards; Paper B documents courts' inconsistent use (and frequent obliviousness to) so‑called flexible remedies across substantive fields, producing discontinuities between doctrine and practice.

shared_topics.topic: the role of public policy and normative judgment in deciding enforceability or remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds public‑policy balancing as central to whether courts enforce contracts tied to illicit purposes and shows cultural/political influence on those judgments; Paper B highlights normative choices embedded in selecting remedies for relying promisees across different doctrines and the lack of transparent policy reasoning across cases.

shared_topics.topic: the need for a more coherent, unified doctrinal approach to recurring problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A laments the judiciary's failure to articulate a coherent approach to improper‑use/public‑policy defenses and suggests alternative approaches; Paper B concludes with a call for a unified theory of damages for relying promisees to resolve inconsistent results across substantive areas.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016michstlrev1267!!ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?

shared_topics.topic: remedies for reliance on promises and the availability/shape of damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A maps how different substantive doctrines (contract, tort, agency, insurance, restitution) supply different remedies for promisees who reasonably rely and emphasizes the discrepancies in damages awards; Paper B shows how treating naming-rights donations as gifts rather than contracts can leave donors with no remedy for reliance and argues for contract remedies to produce fair compensation and dispute-avoidance.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal choice/classification (contract vs gift/trust/tort/restitution) and its outcome-determinative effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents overlapping doctrines that can be invoked for the same reliance facts and the inconsistent outcomes that follow, while Paper B analyzes how courts classify charitable naming-rights arrangements (gifts, contracts, or trusts) and demonstrates how that choice decisively changes parties' rights and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and the desirability of flexible remedies or supplied terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts' failure to recognize or apply flexible remedies across doctrinal lines and surveys section 90-type flexibility, and Paper B argues that treating naming-rights deals as contracts would allow courts (or contracting practices) to supply reasonable terms—such as durations or morals clauses—when parties omit them.

shared_topics.topic: the role of donors'/promisees' intent and reliance in determining legal characterization and relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes reasonable reliance and the promisor's intent (present intent or misrepresentation) as central to which doctrine and damages apply, and Paper B highlights the opacity of donor intent in naming-rights disputes and how that ambiguity affects whether courts apply gift, trust, or contract law and the consequent relief.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38flastulrev709!!ARTICLE: SEPARATING CONTRACT AND PROMISE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SEPARATING CONTRACT AND PROMISE

shared_topics.topic: the conceptual relationship between contracts and promises (whether contracts are enforceable promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates the canonical claim that contracts are a species of promise and challenges treating contractual obligations as morally equivalent to private promises; Paper B treats promises as the triggering fact for multiple doctrines (promissory estoppel, tort misrepresentation, restitution) and therefore assumes and investigates the legal consequences of promises across doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based obligations and remedies for promisees
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the communicative commitment involved in promises and the different moral significance of voluntary keeping versus legal enforcement, while Paper B empirically maps how courts and multiple substantive areas (contracts, agency, torts, insurance, restitution) compensate promisees who reasonably rely on promises and the variety of remedies applied.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap and fragmentation in how the law handles promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that treating contract as simply a kind of promise obscures important differences between private moral norms and legal rules, and Paper B documents substantial overlap (and a lack of coherent coordination) among contracts, agency, torts, insurance, and restitution in responding to relying promisees and the resulting confusion about appropriate damages.

shared_topics.topic: the role of promisor intent/voluntariness in allocating liability for broken promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that private promises are defined by voluntary making and keeping and that most contractual promises lack that voluntary character, while Paper B analyzes how courts sometimes base liability on the promisor's present intent (or lack thereof) and how intent affects whether relief is sought in tort, estoppel, or other doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 76geolj1949!!ARTICLE: Reinterpretations of 18th-Century English Contract Theory: The View from Lord Mansfield's Trial Notes.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Reinterpretations of 18th-Century English Contract Theory: The View from Lord Mansfield's Trial Notes.

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based compensation through restitution/quasi-contract versus promissory liability
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how promisees who expend resources based on a promise are compensated — Paper A shows Lord Mansfield relied on quasi‑contract and unjust enrichment (not a promissory fiction) to award compensation, while Paper B maps the modern landscape in which restitution/constructive trust and promissory estoppel are alternative doctrines for reliance damages.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' intentions and fairness in deciding enforceability of promises
shared_topics.justification: Both works treat the mental state of parties and equitable considerations as central—Paper A finds Mansfield emphasized intentions and basic fairness when policing what promises courts would enforce, and Paper B examines how courts across contracts, torts, and other fields consider present intent and reasonableness when awarding reliance remedies.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap and the boundaries between contract, restitution, and other substantive areas
shared_topics.justification: Each paper is concerned with where lines between doctrines should be drawn: Paper A situates Mansfield's decisions at the intersection of contract and quasi‑contract doctrines in eighteenth‑century practice, while Paper B documents contemporary overlap among contracts, agency, torts, insurance, and restitution and the resulting confusion about appropriate remedies.

shared_topics.topic: historical and empirical study of judicial decision‑making and doctrinal development
shared_topics.justification: Both are historical/empirical inquiries into how judges actually decided promise‑related disputes—Paper A through unpublished Mansfield trial notes and manuscripts to reinterpret eighteenth‑century contract theory, and Paper B through empirical/historical analysis of case law to show how courts have applied (or failed to coordinate) reliance remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83washulq471!!ARTICLE: ON DISCOVERING DOCTRINE: "JUSTICE" IN CONTRACT AGREEMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ON DISCOVERING DOCTRINE: "JUSTICE" IN CONTRACT AGREEMENT

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based recovery and promissory estoppel
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question of when a promisee who has relied on a promise can recover absent a traditional contract: Paper A analyzes reliance remedies across contracts, promissory estoppel, tort, agency, insurance, and restitution; Paper B treats promissory estoppel as a doctrinal adjustment that exemplifies how courts expand or refine agreement doctrines to capture reliance-based claims.

shared_topics.topic: the role of justice/fairness and flexible/equitable remedies in contract relief
shared_topics.justification: Both works probe how equitable considerations shape outcomes: Paper A investigates courts' use (and nonuse) of 'flexible remedies' to compensate relying promisees across doctrinal categories, while Paper B argues that conceptions of justice and fairness are central to how courts define agreement and thus determine appropriate remedies in contract cases.

shared_topics.topic: overlap, inconsistency, and the need for doctrinal coherence across legal doctrines addressing broken promises
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront the problem that multiple substantive fields (contract, tort, restitution, agency, insurance) can apply to the same facts and produce divergent remedies: Paper A documents that overlap and inconsistent damages across those fields and calls for a unified theory, while Paper B analyzes how doctrines expand, contract, or spawn exceptions (e.g., promissory estoppel) when existing rules are under- or over-inclusive.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrine is discovered, formed, and applied versus scholarly accounts of law
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the formation and application of legal doctrine rather than just normative prescriptions: Paper A empirically and historically shows that courts often do not recognize the doctrinal overlaps or the flexible remedies scholars attribute to them, and Paper B offers a theoretical account (cognitive/complexity) of how judges and legal actors perceive facts and produce doctrine, explaining why doctrine can diverge from scholarly expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77neblrev756!!ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law

shared_topics.topic: the role and judicial application of promissory estoppel / Section 90
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts actually apply Section 90's flexible remedy and finds courts often oblivious to the scholarly account, while Paper B traces the contested role of promissory estoppel generally and how courts invoke it in property contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between reliance-based and promise-based doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on promisees who reasonably rely and the remedial consequences of that reliance across doctrines, and Paper B directly interrogates whether estoppel enforces promises because of induced reliance or only because reliance evidences an intent to be bound.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies for relying promisees (reliance expenditures vs enforcement/expectation and flexible remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the different remedial regimes across contracts, tort, agency, insurance, and restitution and calls for a unified theory of damages for relying promisees, while Paper B shows that in property cases courts sometimes limit relief to reliance expenditures and other times enforce full promises depending on the strength of corroborating promise evidence.

shared_topics.topic: empirical/doctrinal case-law analysis revealing divergence between scholarly theory and judicial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents an empirical and historical study documenting discontinuities between what scholars believe courts do about flexible remedies and what courts actually do, and Paper B similarly surveys post-1960 case law to descriptively map how estoppel functions in property decisions rather than prescribe reform.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56depaullrev55!!ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of flexible, non‑traditional remedies for failed promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the courts' (lack of) use of the 'flexible remedy' for reliance claims across contracts, torts, agency, insurance, and restitution, while Paper B advocates that courts craft flexible, context‑sensitive remedies (instead of rigid formalist remedies) to enforce ADR agreements and contracts to bargain.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap or 'middle‑position' problems that complicate remedy selection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents substantive overlap among multiple fields (contracts, torts, agency, insurance, restitution) when promisees rely and asks how damages should be allocated across doctrines; Paper B identifies the ‘middle position’ between yes‑contract and no‑contract in ADR/contract‑to‑bargain contexts that produces similar uncertainty about which doctrinal framework and remedies should apply.

shared_topics.topic: critique of formalist yes‑contract/no‑contract analysis in favor of contextual/relational inquiry
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows courts and scholars have failed to account for overlapping doctrines and the realities of reliance when applying rigid categories, and Paper B criticizes courts' formalist binary approach to ADR agreements and urges relational, contextual analysis (including good faith) to define duties and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: how to determine and tailor remedies/relief for parties who reasonably relied on promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on what damages are appropriate for relying promisees across different substantive doctrines, and Paper B addresses how courts should determine breach and fashion appropriate remedies (including when to compel negotiation or decline enforcement) for parties who committed to ADR or bargaining processes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2002utahlrev551!!ARTICLE: Duties Under the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act: Analysis of a Statutory Conflict The author wishes to thank the Honorable Thomas L. Steffen and Professor Boyd K. Dyer for their insight and encouragement in writing this Comment.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Duties Under the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act: Analysis of a Statutory Conflict The author wishes to thank the Honorable Thomas L. Steffen and Professor Boyd K. Dyer for their insight and encouragement in writing this Comment.

shared_topics.topic: party autonomy to modify default legal duties or remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines courts' and scholars' invocation of "flexible remedies" and how different doctrines permit varied compensation for relying promisees, while Paper B analyzes whether LLC members may use operating agreements to opt out of or reduce statutorily imposed duties—both question when parties can contract around default legal rules and what limits exist on that autonomy.

shared_topics.topic: conflicts and overlaps among substantive legal doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents overlapping remedies and inconsistent rules across contracts, agency, torts, insurance, and restitution when promisees rely to their detriment, and Paper B confronts a direct statutory conflict in the URLLCA (and tensions with prior common-law agency principles) that requires reconciling competing norms—each paper addresses how to resolve doctrinal collisions that produce uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of law and the role of courts versus drafters/scholars
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights a divergence between scholarly expectations about how courts handle flexible remedies and what courts actually do, emphasizing judicial practice and recognition, while Paper B uses canons of statutory interpretation to decide between competing legislative provisions—both engage the question of how judges (and legislators) should interpret and apply legal texts when meanings or applications are unclear.

shared_topics.topic: agency law as a foundation for duties and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats agency as one of the central substantive areas that supplies doctrines and remedies for relying promisees, and Paper B traces LLC members' and managers' duties back to the common law of agency (contrasting that background with newly enacted statutory duties), so both substantively engage agency principles in defining obligations and relief.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67bulrev9!!ARTICLE: WARRANTY THEORY, ECONOMIC LOSS, AND THE PRIVITY REQUIREMENT: ONCE MORE INTO THE VOID Copyright 1986 by Richard E. Speidel.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WARRANTY THEORY, ECONOMIC LOSS, AND THE PRIVITY REQUIREMENT: ONCE MORE INTO THE VOID Copyright 1986 by Richard E. Speidel.

shared_topics.topic: compensating economic loss when promises or warranties fail absent physical injury
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how reliance-based losses (out-of-pocket expenditures) are remedied across multiple doctrines when a promisee reasonably relies and suffers economic harm, while Paper B addresses buyers' recovery for purely economic loss from unmerchantable goods under warranty theory and U.C.C. Article 2.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal overlap and the need to reconcile contract, tort, agency, and restitution approaches to damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and critiques the inconsistent remedies that arise because contracts, torts, agency, insurance, and restitution offer overlapping but different paths for relying promisees and calls for a unified damages theory, and Paper B engages the overlap by seeking a coherent rule (abolishing privity) that realigns warranty (contract) principles with product-safety (tort) concerns and distributional realities.

shared_topics.topic: the justificatory role of reliance versus representational theories for imposing liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on promissory estoppel and reliance-based recovery (and contrasts that with tort misrepresentation), whereas Paper B elaborates warranty as a representational theory that can impose liability without proof of actual reliance—both interrogate when reliance must be proved and how that affects available remedies.

shared_topics.topic: duty to foreseeable remote parties, limitations on remedies, and risk-allocation incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts apply or ignore flexible remedies and the practical limits on recovery for relying promisees across contexts, while Paper B argues manufacturers owe a duty to foreseeable purchasers (even remote buyers), proposes abolishing privity subject to Article 2 limits, and grounds that proposal in incentives to ensure product fitness and appropriate risk allocation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61hastingslj859!!Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Limits of the Legal Method
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Limits of the Legal Method

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel and reliance damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze promissory estoppel as the doctrine used to compensate promisees for reliance losses: Paper A surveys how promissory estoppel functions across doctrines and its remedial reach, while Paper B uses Hoffman v. Red Owl to interrogate whether the facts supported promissory estoppel liability and how courts assess reliance losses in that context.

shared_topics.topic: choice and overlap among doctrines for compensating relying promisees (contract, quasi‑contract/restitution, tort, agency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents substantive overlap and inconsistent remedies across contracts, agency/franchise, torts, insurance, and restitution/constructive trusts for relying promisees and calls for a unified approach; Paper B confronts that same doctrinal choice in Hoffman, weighing promissory estoppel against quasi‑contract/restitution and enforcement of preliminary commitments as alternative bases for recovery.

shared_topics.topic: precontractual reliance and the enforceability of preliminary agreements
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the problem of reliance during negotiations and the legal treatment of preliminary understandings: Paper A discusses flexible remedies (e.g., Restatement section 90) and courts' responses to reliance claims arising before a final contract, while Paper B studies the line between 'missing promises' and binding preliminary commitments (Tribune and subsequent cases) and reports empirical patterns of courts denying promissory estoppel in precontractual settings.

shared_topics.topic: discrepancy between doctrinal theory/scholarly assumptions and actual judicial practice (methodological influences on legal interpretation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents a large discontinuity between what contracts scholars believe courts do concerning flexible remedies and what courts actually do, while Paper B attributes divergent readings of the same case to different methodological commitments (law‑and‑economics vs law‑and‑society) and critiques how those approaches shape inferences about judicial decisions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81neblrev839!!ARTICLE: Why Expectation Damages for Breach of Contract Must Be the Norm: A Refutation of the Fuller and Perdue "Three Interests" Thesis
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why Expectation Damages for Breach of Contract Must Be the Norm: A Refutation of the Fuller and Perdue "Three Interests" Thesis

shared_topics.topic: choice among expectation, reliance, and restitution measures of damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally engage the tripartite framework of contract damages—expectation, reliance, and restitution—analyzing when each measure applies and how they relate to compensating promisees; Paper A surveys how different substantive areas award reliance-type recoveries, while Paper B directly defends the expectation measure as the proper norm against reliance and restitution alternatives.

shared_topics.topic: the proper remedy for promisees who reasonably relied on a promise (reliance damages and alternatives)
shared_topics.justification: Both works focus on the problem of promisees who expend resources in reliance: Paper A maps how contracts, tort, agency, insurance, and restitution doctrines address recovery for relying promisees, and Paper B evaluates whether reliance recovery is an adequate or preferable remedy compared with expectation damages.

shared_topics.topic: the role and legitimacy of 'flexible remedies' versus doctrinally fixed measures
shared_topics.justification: Both papers discuss courts’ use (or failure to use) flexible approaches to damages: Paper A analyzes courts’ (lack of) recognition and application of flexible remedies across different substantive areas, while Paper B critiques competing theories and defends a stable expectation rule despite calls for flexibility.

shared_topics.topic: discrepancy between scholarly/restatement theory and actual judicial practice regarding damages
shared_topics.justification: Each article documents a gap between influential academic formulations (and Restatement language) and what courts actually do—Paper A empirically shows courts rarely confront overlapping doctrines or flexible remedies, and Paper B documents that courts persistently award expectation damages despite the influence of Fuller and Perdue’s competing 'three interests' thesis.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58hastingslj61!!Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters

shared_topics.topic: whether non-traditional communications (e.g., advertisements or informal promises) can create enforceable obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that ordinary advertisements can, in appropriate circumstances, function as offers enforceable by acceptance rather than mere invitations to bargain; Paper B surveys a range of contexts in which informal promises (promissory estoppel, pre-contractual assurances, franchise/distributorship promises, misrepresentations) give rise to enforceable obligations or compensation despite the absence of a conventional contract.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reasonable reliance/objective standards in converting statements into legal rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes the objective theory of contracts and a 'reasonableness' rationale to explain when an advertisement should be treated as an offer, while Paper B centers its analysis on cases where promisees reasonably rely on promises and the law provides reliance-based remedies across doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal inconsistency and the need to revise or unify legal rules governing reliance and formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the repeated but inaccurate doctrinal rule that 'an advertisement is not an offer' and argues for correcting entrenched misunderstanding, and Paper B documents inconsistent treatment of reliance claims across contracts, torts, agency, insurance, and restitution and calls for a unified theory of reliance remedies.

shared_topics.topic: how other legal rules, business practices, and remedial doctrines limit or shape relief for relying parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that competing legal rules and commercial practices often prevent courts from applying the 'advertisement-as-offer' conception, and Paper B analyzes how different remedial frameworks (expectation vs. reliance damages, flexible remedies) across substantive areas determine what compensation relying promisees actually receive.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 22cornelljlpubpoly93!!ARTICLE: PROMISES, POLICIES, AND PRINCIPLES: THE SUPREME COURT AND CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION IN LABOR RELATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PROMISES, POLICIES, AND PRINCIPLES: THE SUPREME COURT AND CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION IN LABOR RELATIONS

shared_topics.topic: Enforcing promises that fall outside traditional contract formation (e.g., promissory estoppel vs labor promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when the Supreme Court enforces promises made in the labor-relations context and whether those promises are treated differently from general contract law; Paper B surveys doctrinal routes (promissory estoppel, tort, agency, restitution, insurance) courts use to compensate promisees when classic breach-of-contract claims fail.

shared_topics.topic: How judges resolve tensions between policy objectives and formal legal principles when deciding promise disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly studies the Court's shifting choice between policy-driven balancing (federal labor policy, industrial peace) and principles (freedom of contract) in enforcing labor promises; Paper B documents inconsistent judicial remedies across fields that reflect competing doctrinal aims and implicit policy/principle tradeoffs in deciding what relief a relying promisee should receive.

shared_topics.topic: Doctrinal overlap and fragmentation in the law's response to broken promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper B shows multiple substantive areas (contracts, agency, torts, insurance, restitution) provide overlapping but inconsistent remedies for reliance, and Paper A shows labor-law promises have been carved out and treated differently over time, highlighting fragmentation across doctrinal categories and institutional contexts.

shared_topics.topic: Historical shifts in judicial treatment of promise enforcement and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces a historical shift in the Supreme Court's approach to labor promises from policy-dominant to principle-dominant reasoning across mid-20th century eras; Paper B provides an empirical-historical account of how courts have actually awarded (or failed to award) reliance damages and flexible remedies over recent decades, noting divergence from scholarly expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57uclalrev669!!Article: The Many Faces of Promissory Estoppel: An Empirical Analysis Under the Restatement (Second) of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: Article: The Many Faces of Promissory Estoppel: An Empirical Analysis Under the Restatement (Second) of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: effect of Restatement (Second) §90 on promissory estoppel litigation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers empirically assess whether the Restatement (Second)'s revisions to §90 produced the drafters' intended effects — Paper B by analyzing 300+ post-1981 cases to measure changes in availability and remedies, and Paper A by examining historical and empirical evidence about how courts have actually applied §90 and related flexible-remedy doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: remedies for relying promisees — expectation vs. reliance and 'flexible' damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate what damages courts award to promisees who relied on promises: Paper B documents that courts often award expectation-style (contractual) remedies despite reliance framing, while Paper A surveys how different substantive areas (and courts) employ or ignore flexible remedies for reliance losses.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal characterization (contract vs tort vs equity/etc.) shapes outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Both works analyze how judges' and scholars' conceptualization of promissory-estoppel/reliance claims — as contractual, tort-based, equitable, or hybrid — affects whether plaintiffs prevail and which remedies they receive, with Paper B emphasizing judges' conceptualization in deciding cases and Paper A mapping these differences across contracts, torts, agency, insurance, and restitution.

shared_topics.topic: overlap and tension among substantive areas in compensating reliance losses
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage with the problem that multiple areas of law can provide remedies for reliance (contracts, agency, torts, insurance, restitution), producing overlapping but inconsistent doctrines and recoveries — Paper A treats this as its central topic, and Paper B highlights how promissory estoppel sits at that intersection and is handled variably by courts.
