papers.node_id: 79kylj557!!ARTICLE: Default Rules for Contract Formation By Promise and the Need for Revision of the Mailbox Rule
papers.title: ARTICLE: Default Rules for Contract Formation By Promise and the Need for Revision of the Mailbox Rule
papers.abstract:
The existing default rulesfor contract formation by promise generally conform, as they should, with the reasonable and probable expectations of the contracting parties.There is, however,one exception: the rule that governs when an acceptance is effective to create a contract.  The dispatch or mailbox ruledeparts from the parties' expectations and from a more logical rule which would be in keeping with modern communications technology.  The mailbox rule also fails to parallel existing formation default rules.  For example, unless otherwise stated, an offer, which is a manifestation of willingness to enter into a bargain,has the legal effect of creating a power of acceptance in the offeree only when the offeree actually receives the offer.If the offeror decides to withdraw or revoke the offer, the revocation generally has legal effect only when the offeree receives the revocation.In the absence of negotiation, the individuals most likely would presume that the offeree must receive the communication of the offeror's revocation before that revocation could affect the contract formation.  Furthermore, if the parties had discussed revocation, their agreement with respect to revocation probably would have mirrored the existing default rule.  An alternative default rule would deprive the offeree of a dependable basis for deciding whether to accept the offer.  Afterthe offeror had manifested an intent to revoke, but before the offeree received notice of the revocation, the offeree may have expended or continued to expend resources to determine whether to accept or may have accepted the offer.  At a minimum, the offeror and offeree would want the offeree to be able to rely on the offeror's original manifestation until the offeree received notice of the offeror's contrary intention.
After receiving the offer, the offeree usually determines whether to accept or reject the offer.  A rejection or a manifestation of intent not to accept the offerterminates the offeree's power of acceptanceonly when the offeror has received the rejection.The same rule applies to a counter-offer by the offeree.In the absence of negotiation, the individuals most likely would presume that the offeror must have received the offeree's manifestation of intent not to accept before the rejection or counter-offer would have the legal effect of terminating the offeree's power of acceptance.  Had the parties discussed rejection and counter-offer by the offeree, their agreement probably would have mirrored the existing default rule.  Until the offeror receives a manifestation, that manifestation cannot affect the offeror.  In that regard, the offeror could notrely on the rejection until receipt.  Likewise, the offeror could not understand that the offeree's counter-offer terminates the offeree's power of acceptance until the offeror has actually received the communication.
If, however, the offeree has determined to accept the offer, the offeree must manifest assent to the terms of the offer.Initially,an acceptance by promise requires that the offeree complete every act essential to the making of the promise.In addition to the manifestation of assent, the offeree must notify or communicate to the offeror the fact that the offeree has manifested assent by promise.In the absence of negotiation, the individuals most likely would presume that the offeror actually must receive notification of the offeree's manifestation of assent by promise before either party would be bound to the contract.  If the parties had discussed the offeree's acceptance by promise, their agreement would probably have mirrored their individual expectations that the offeror must actually receive the offeree's promise.  That, however, is not the existing default rule.
Although parties might presume or agree that receipt of the notification of the manifestation by promise is required, absent an express agreement to that effect, most Anglo-American courts have decided that the offeror need not receive the notice in order to create a contract.Rather, the offeree need only exercise reasonable diligence to notify the offeror of the offeree's acceptance.
What constitutes reasonable diligence may differ according to the circumstances.  If the parties are in the presence of each other, courts expect that the offeror will actually receive the notice of the promise.Courts have not had to determine what constitutes reasonablediligence when the parties are in the presence of each other because in such a situation the offeror immediately learns of the manifestation.  In a decision of the Queen's Bench, Justice Denning posited that, in the instantaneous situation, reasonable diligence should not be adequate because it is no burden for the offeree to ascertain whether his acceptance actually has been received.In those instances, he wrote, actual notification should be required.  For example, assume the offeror and the offeree were discussing their bargain at the Ohio State-Michigan football game.  At the precise moment when the offeree said "I promise," assume that the public address system blared out the score (with the Wolverines suitably ensconsed in the lead).  Assume that the offeror did not hear the offeree's words.  Justice Denning would argue that no contract had been formed because the offeree should have been aware that the offeror actually had not received notice of the offeree's manifestation of assent by promise.
If, as is the usual circumstance, the parties are at a distance, the offeree's manifestation of assent by promise is effective as soon as the offeree puts notice of acceptance out of his possession and into the invited or reasonable channel of communication.The current default rule governing acceptance by promise when theparties are not in the presence of each other is labeled the "dispatch rule" or "mailbox rule."The dispatch rule states that as soon as the acceptance is released from the offeree's possession and placed into the channel of communication, the acceptance is effective.Under the existing default dispatch rule, the offeror need not actually receive the notice sent by the offeree.
The English and American courts differ with respect to the appropriate default rulewhen the parties are at a distance and the offeree decides to notify the offeror by telephone, teletype, or other substantially instantaneous methods of communication.In England, the courts have held that when the offeree accepts by teletype, the parties must use the same communication rules as if the parties were in the presence of each other.The English courts hold acceptance by teletype effective only when received by the offeror.American courts, in contrast, have held that an acceptance by telephone or teletype is effective when dispatched by the offeree with no necessity of receipt.
The existing default dispatch rule does not conform with the reasonable and probable expectations of the parties in that contracting parties expect that their communications will have legal effect only when received by the other party.Moreover, the parties expect that the first communication received will have legal priority.These private expectations usually serve the parties well.However, when a dispute arisesand the parties seek legal advice, they learn that the existing legal default rules do not mirror their expectations of what the law will provide.

questions.question: Whether an offeree's remote acceptance should be legally effective upon dispatch (sending) or only upon actual receipt by the offeror.

Whether default rules for when communications affect contract formation should align with parties' reasonable expectations and be applied uniformly across different modes of communication (instantaneous versus non-instantaneous), or whether different communication technologies justify different default rules.

matched_themes: When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
Should default rules for when communications form contracts be uniform across technologies, or should they vary by mode (instantaneous vs non-instantaneous; electronic) and context?
Should an offeree's remote acceptance be legally effective upon dispatch (mailbox rule) or only upon actual receipt by the offeror?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78stjohnslrev131!!ARTICLE: MUST PROFITS MADE IN TRANSACTIONS INVOLVING LATE-DELIVERED GOODS BE DEDUCTED FROM THE INJURED PARTY'S BREACH DAMAGES? IF NOT, WHAT IMPACT SHOULD LATE-DELIVERED GOODS HAVE?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MUST PROFITS MADE IN TRANSACTIONS INVOLVING LATE-DELIVERED GOODS BE DEDUCTED FROM THE INJURED PARTY'S BREACH DAMAGES? IF NOT, WHAT IMPACT SHOULD LATE-DELIVERED GOODS HAVE?

shared_topics.topic: the role and design of default rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes UCC default remedies (cover, lost-volume rules, market-offsets) and how those rules should allocate rights and remedies after breach, while Paper B critiques and seeks revision of the dispatch/mailbox default rule for acceptance — both focus on what default rules should be and how they govern contractual relations absent express agreement.

shared_topics.topic: how timing (of performance or communication) determines legal effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the legal consequences of late delivery (when belated performance should reduce or not reduce damages), and Paper B centers on when an acceptance or revocation becomes effective (dispatch vs receipt); each examines how temporal rules create or extinguish obligations.

shared_topics.topic: aligning legal rules with contracting parties' reasonable expectations and commercial realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates presumptions (e.g., regular dealers, lost-volume buyers) and market-based adjustments to avoid windfalls and to reflect how businesses actually operate, while Paper B argues the mailbox rule departs from parties' reasonable expectations and should be revised to reflect modern communication practices.

shared_topics.topic: preventing economic windfalls or unfair allocations through doctrinal adjustments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes doctrinal refinements (market-related offsets, presumptions about volume dealers) to avoid over- or under-compensation after late delivery, and Paper B similarly seeks to change formation rules to avoid unexpected legal consequences that would unfairly benefit one party due to timing of communications.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 6wmmarybuslrev405!!ARTICLE: COURTS GONE "IRRATIONALLY BIASED" IN FAVOR OF THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT?--ENFORCING ARBITRATION PROVISIONS IN STANDARDIZED APPLICATIONS AND MARGINALIZING CONSUMERPROTECTION, ANTIDISCRIMINATION, AND STATES' CONTRACT LAWS: A 1925-2014 LEGAL AND EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: COURTS GONE "IRRATIONALLY BIASED" IN FAVOR OF THE FEDERAL ARBITRATION ACT?--ENFORCING ARBITRATION PROVISIONS IN STANDARDIZED APPLICATIONS AND MARGINALIZING CONSUMERPROTECTION, ANTIDISCRIMINATION, AND STATES' CONTRACT LAWS: A 1925-2014 LEGAL AND EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS

shared_topics.topic: when acceptance or assent is legally effective (receipt vs. dispatch and reasonable diligence)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the mailbox/dispatch rule and argues acceptance by promise should be effective only on receipt (or at least should track parties' expectations and communication technology), while Paper B probes when standardized applications or unsigned documents create binding obligations—a question that turns on when courts deem assent or a 'written provision in a contract' to have arisen.

shared_topics.topic: whether preliminary writings, memoranda, or standardized application forms are enforceable contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the legal consequences of manifestations of willingness to bargain, revocations, and notifications in formation, and Paper B directly examines the enforceability of memoranda of understanding and standardized application forms (including unsigned or preprinted instruments) as contracts that can carry clauses like mandatory arbitration.

shared_topics.topic: judicial splits and inconsistent application of default contract-formation or enforcement doctrines across jurisdictions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents divergences between English and American courts (and among rules for instantaneous vs non-instantaneous communications) over acceptance timing, while Paper B documents persistent splits between federal and state courts—and among lower tribunals—in applying the FAA and settled common-law contract principles to arbitration clauses in applications.

shared_topics.topic: the need to reconcile or reform default contract rules in light of modern contexts or external legal regimes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the dispatch/mailbox rule departs from reasonable expectations given modern communications and should be revised, and Paper B argues federal arbitration law and recent judicial practices have distorted common-law defaults (and calls for statutory reform) to address harms from enforcing arbitration clauses in standardized forms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 96washlrev51!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: when an acceptance or manifestation of assent becomes legally effective in technologically mediated exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes traditional consent-based formation because smart contracts execute automatically without human receipt or contemporaneous promises, while Paper B analyzes the mailbox/dispatch rule versus receipt rule and how modern communications (telephone, teletype) affect when acceptance is legally effective.

shared_topics.topic: whether existing offer–acceptance doctrines fit new communication and automation technologies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that orthodox, forward‑looking consent doctrines do not squarely fit fully automated smart contracting, and Paper B argues the dispatch/mailbox rule departs from parties' reasonable expectations given modern communications and therefore needs revision.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance and reasonable expectations versus formal assent as the basis for binding obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a reliance (tort‑like) theory to ground smart contract obligations where human assent is absent, and Paper B defends formation default rules (and revision of the mailbox rule) on grounds of parties' reasonable expectations and reliance interests.

shared_topics.topic: how default rules and dispute‑resolution mechanisms should address contractual incompleteness introduced by technology
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights incompleteness in automated smart contracts and proposes decentralized, user‑based ex post dispute resolution, while Paper B examines how default formation rules (like the mailbox rule) fill gaps when parties have not specified communication/receipt rules and thus shape how formation disputes are resolved.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107wvalrev443!!ARTICLE: A Realistic Proposal for the Contract Duress Doctrine
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Realistic Proposal for the Contract Duress Doctrine

shared_topics.topic: when a party's manifestation of assent is legally effective (receipt vs dispatch and voluntariness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when an offeree's acceptance by promise becomes effective (criticizing the mailbox/dispatch rule versus receipt), while Paper B interrogates when a party's manifested assent is legally valid under duress (arguing voluntariness should be framed as 'no reasonable alternative'), so both tackle legal criteria for when assent binds parties.

shared_topics.topic: the role of default doctrinal rules in governing contract formation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the existing default dispatch rule for acceptance and how it departs from parties' probable expectations, and Paper B critiques how courts apply default duress standards and proposes clearer default rules (e.g., 'no reasonable alternative'), so both examine how baseline legal defaults should operate.

shared_topics.topic: balancing predictability/certainty against fairness and freedom of contract in doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that formation rules should mirror contracting parties' reasonable expectations and provide reliable reliance, whereas Paper B examines how duress doctrine has been narrowed by deference to freedom of contract and advocates a clearer fairness-oriented process standard, with both engaging the trade-off between predictability and equitable protection.

shared_topics.topic: advocacy for doctrinal reform to improve clarity, applicability, and judicial decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for revising the mailbox/dispatch rule to align with modern communications and expectations, and Paper B proposes four concrete changes to the duress doctrine to make it workable and to guide courts, so both offer specific reform proposals to improve contract-law doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 87columlrev217!!ARTICLE: PRECONTRACTUAL LIABILITY AND PRELIMINARY AGREEMENTS: FAIR DEALING AND FAILED NEGOTIATIONS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PRECONTRACTUAL LIABILITY AND PRELIMINARY AGREEMENTS: FAIR DEALING AND FAILED NEGOTIATIONS.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of classic offer-and-acceptance doctrines for modern complex negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether traditional offer-and-acceptance vocabulary can handle multi-stage, multi-actor dealmaking and argues that the doctrines can be imaginatively applied to modern negotiations; Paper B critiques a specific classical rule (the mailbox/dispatch rule) as out of step with modern communications and thus questions the fit of historical formation doctrines for present-day contracting.

shared_topics.topic: timing and effectiveness of communications (acceptance, revocation) in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centrally analyzes when an acceptance, rejection, or revocation takes legal effect (dispatch vs. receipt and the problems with instantaneous communications), while Paper A addresses when parties are bound during protracted negotiations (e.g., at closing, upon exchange of signed documents, or not) and the legal consequences when communication fails and negotiations end without executed documents.

shared_topics.topic: the role of default rules in allocating risk during negotiations and preliminary agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines different legal regimes (negotiation, ultimate agreement, preliminary agreements, agreement to negotiate) and how parties can allocate risks through or against default contract rules; Paper B analyzes existing default formation rules (and argues for revising the mailbox rule) because those defaults determine which party bears the risk when the parties have not expressly agreed on communication and acceptance rules.

shared_topics.topic: using parties' reasonable expectations and fair dealing as normative guides for formation rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper B emphasizes that formation default rules should mirror the reasonable and probable expectations of contracting parties (e.g., that communications take effect on receipt), while Paper A investigates the content of a duty of fair dealing and whether doctrines should protect disappointed parties according to fairness and parties' expectations during negotiations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2002utahlrev551!!ARTICLE: Duties Under the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act: Analysis of a Statutory Conflict The author wishes to thank the Honorable Thomas L. Steffen and Professor Boyd K. Dyer for their insight and encouragement in writing this Comment.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Duties Under the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act: Analysis of a Statutory Conflict The author wishes to thank the Honorable Thomas L. Steffen and Professor Boyd K. Dyer for their insight and encouragement in writing this Comment.

shared_topics.topic: whether parties can contract around or opt out of statutory/default rules (scope of private ordering)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether LLC members may use operating agreements to reduce or eliminate statutorily imposed duties under the URLLCA, and Paper B examines how contracting parties can either accept or negotiate around default formation rules (e.g., requiring receipt of acceptance), questioning whether defaults should be defeasible by agreement.

shared_topics.topic: whether default legal rules reflect the reasonable expectations of commercial actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates which interpretation of the URLLCA best accords with commercial practice and member expectations about allocating fiduciary duties, while Paper B argues the mailbox/dispatch rule departs from parties' expectations about when communications should have legal effect and thus should be revised.

shared_topics.topic: how to resolve internal conflicts or inconsistencies in statutory/default rule regimes through interpretive methods
shared_topics.justification: Paper A confronts directly conflicting URLLCA provisions and applies canons of statutory interpretation to determine which provision should prevail, and Paper B highlights tensions between the dispatch rule and other formation defaults (and between common-law expectations and current rules), using normative and doctrinal analysis to propose a coherent rule.

shared_topics.topic: balancing protection of reliance interests against freedom of contract (non-waivable duties vs contractual autonomy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs whether statutory duties should be rigid minimum standards that protect reliance and third-party expectations or instead be subject to waiver by members, and Paper B centers on protecting offeree reliance (and offeror reliance) in deciding whether receipt or dispatch should govern acceptance, contrasting reliance-protecting defaults with rules that favor contractual flexibility.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 74iowalrev115!!ARTICLE: Illegal Contracts and Efficient Deterrence: A Study in Modern Contract Theory
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Illegal Contracts and Efficient Deterrence: A Study in Modern Contract Theory

shared_topics.topic: whether default contract rules should track parties' reasonable expectations and private autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that illegal-contracts doctrine should, to the extent possible, mirror private choices and the autonomy principle rather than operate solely as a blunt public-policy tool; Paper B argues the mailbox/dispatch rule departs from contracting parties' reasonable expectations and should be revised so default formation rules align with what parties likely expect.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for communication failures, nonenforcement, or changed circumstances to the party best able to avoid costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an 'efficient deterrence' account that allocates the risk of nonenforcement to the cheapest cost avoider through graduated relief; Paper B examines which party should bear the risk when acceptances, revocations, or rejections are dispatched but not received, arguing the default rule should assign risk in a way that supports reliance and minimizes wasted effort.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic/efficiency reasoning to design or revise contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly builds a unified doctrine grounded in efficiency (efficient deterrence) to explain and recommend varying remedies for illegal contracts; Paper B uses cost/expectation and efficiency-type considerations (including modern communications costs and reliance) to criticize the mailbox rule and advocate doctrinal revision.

shared_topics.topic: the need to tailor doctrinal rules to factual settings (including technological context and partial performance) rather than applying uniform rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows courts vary relief (voidability, rescission, restitution) depending on factual predictors like partial performance and protected classes and argues for context-sensitive rules; Paper B argues the traditional dispatch/mailbox rule is ill-suited to modern, instantaneous communication technologies and that formation rules should be adjusted to those factual contexts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 99kylj327!!ARTICLE: Expectation Damages, the Objective Theory of Contracts, and the "Hairy Hand" Case: A Proposed Modification to the Effect of Two Classical Contract Law Axioms in Cases Involving Contractual Misunderstandings
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Expectation Damages, the Objective Theory of Contracts, and the "Hairy Hand" Case: A Proposed Modification to the Effect of Two Classical Contract Law Axioms in Cases Involving Contractual Misunderstandings

shared_topics.topic: whether baseline contract doctrines should yield to the parties' reasonable expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the classical axioms (objective interpretation and expectation damages) when their application produces outcomes that do not reflect the parties' expectations in cases of mutual misunderstanding, while Paper B argues the mailbox/dispatch rule departs from parties' ordinary expectations about when communications become effective and should be revised accordingly.

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate treatment of subjective intent versus objective interpretation when communications are ambiguous or misunderstood
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly debates whether contract terms should be interpreted by reference to the promisor's subjective intended meaning in cases of materially different understandings, and Paper B engages the parallel issue of whether an offeree's communicated assent is legally effective before the offeror actually receives it (i.e., how to treat manifestations of assent across imperfect communication).

shared_topics.topic: protecting reliance interests when doctrinal rules about communication or interpretation create unfair risk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes awarding reliance damages as an alternative when objective expectation damages would be unjust due to a misunderstanding, and Paper B emphasizes how the dispatch rule can improperly expose an offeree (or offeror) to reliance losses when revocations or acceptances are in transit and not received.

shared_topics.topic: advocacy for context-sensitive doctrinal reform or exceptions to traditional contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers propose narrowing or modifying entrenched default doctrines—Paper A seeks an exception/modification to expectation damages and the objective theory in misunderstanding cases, and Paper B calls for revising the mailbox/dispatch rule to better fit modern communications and transactional realities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 105dicklrev31!!ARTICLE: Firm Offers Under the UCC and the CISG
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Firm Offers Under the UCC and the CISG

shared_topics.topic: timing of revocation/irrevocability and the role of offeree reliance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when an offer can be revoked and whether an offeree's reliance can render an offer effectively irrevocable: Paper A asks whether an offer that fails formal requirements can nonetheless become irrevocable through offeree reliance and examines limits on irrevocability periods, while Paper B critiques the timing rules (revocation effective on receipt vs dispatch) because they leave offerees vulnerable to reliance before receiving notice.

shared_topics.topic: communication and formality rules for effectiveness of offers and acceptances (writing requirement, receipt vs dispatch, instantaneous methods)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with formal and communicative prerequisites for contract formation — Paper A asks whether a firm (irrevocable) offer must be in writing and what assurances are required, and Paper B examines whether acceptance must be received versus dispatched and how rules should treat instantaneous media (telephone/teletype) as opposed to mail.

shared_topics.topic: need to revise default contract-formation rules to reflect modern commercial practice and international harmonization
shared_topics.justification: Both papers evaluate existing default rules and advocate reconsideration or reform: Paper A compares current UCC, proposed Article 2 revisions, and the CISG to assess appropriate firm-offer rules (and uniformity across jurisdictions), while Paper B explicitly argues the mailbox/dispatch rule should be revised to align with contemporary communications technology and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: alignment of default rules with commercial parties' expectations and transaction-cost efficiency (merchant context, reliance, search costs, globalization)
shared_topics.justification: Both works are concerned with whether default rules serve commercial actors — Paper A grounds the case for firm offers in merchants' need to justify costly investigations and cross-border trading uncertainty, and Paper B emphasizes that acceptance/revocation rules should mirror contracting parties' reasonable expectations to reduce reliance costs and promote predictable commercial exchange.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56depaullrev55!!ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH

shared_topics.topic: how courts should set and apply default rules when parties leave terms unspecified
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the mailbox/dispatch rule as the existing default for acceptance timing and argues it mismatches parties' expectations, while Paper B criticizes courts' rigid yes-contract/no-contract approaches and urges more flexible common-law defaulting to give effect to ADR agreements that leave terms open.

shared_topics.topic: aligning default rules with parties' reasonable expectations rather than formalist doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the dispatch/mailbox rule departs from contracting parties' reasonable expectation that communications are effective only on receipt, and Paper B similarly argues that formalist enforcement doctrines ignore parties' relational expectations in ADR and contracts-to-bargain and should be replaced by contextual analysis.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap-filling and remedial design for incomplete or 'middle-position' contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how default rules (e.g., notice, receipt, reasonable diligence) fill gaps about when acceptance or revocation takes effect, and Paper B focuses on the difficulties courts face in filling gaps and crafting appropriate remedies for breaches of ADR agreements and contracts to bargain.

shared_topics.topic: use of implied standards (e.g., reasonable diligence, good faith) to govern conduct when parties do not specify terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on an implied standard of 'reasonable diligence' (and situational adjustments) to determine when an acceptance not actually received is effective, while Paper B advocates using good-faith and relational standards to define parties' duties and enforce ADR agreements where the contract is silent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41stanlrev661!!ARTICLE: The Jurisprudence of Classification.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Jurisprudence of Classification.

shared_topics.topic: whether doctrinal rules should track parties' reasonable expectations (especially in contract formation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the mailbox/dispatch rule departs from contracting parties' reasonable and probable expectations about when communications take effect, and Paper B treats doctrinal classification (including contract doctrine) as consequential for social expectations, asking whether legal categories reflect or distort real-world practices.

shared_topics.topic: the need to revise or reform established legal doctrines/classifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates revising the traditional mailbox rule to better fit modern communications and parties' reliance, while Paper B analyzes and criticizes existing systems of doctrinal classification and proposes variations to improve how legal categories operate.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal categories and default rules shape legal reality and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how the default mailbox rule produces concrete legal effects (when contracts form) that can diverge from parties' conduct and reliance, and Paper B emphasizes that classification does not merely describe law but helps create the legal reality by structuring reasoning and outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal, rule-based reasoning and contextual/interpretive approaches to doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the formal dispatch/receipt rules with an alternative based on parties' expectations and contexts (presence, communication method), and Paper B contrasts a systematic/formal account of classification with a holistic, paradigmatic interpretive account, examining the strengths and flaws of each approach.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71tullrev1749!!ARTICLE: IN THE TRIBUNAL OF CONSCIENCE: MILLS V. WYMAN RECONSIDERED
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN THE TRIBUNAL OF CONSCIENCE: MILLS V. WYMAN RECONSIDERED

shared_topics.topic: criteria for when a promise creates a binding contractual obligation (moral obligation vs consideration vs intent-to-be-bound)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates the moral-obligation rule and argues that promises should be binding when made with intent to be bound rather than because of moral duty or traditional consideration, while Paper B examines when an offeree's promise (acceptance) legally forms a contract, effectively engaging the same question of what formal criteria and doctrinal rules should determine when a promise becomes enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: default rules for contract formation by promise and the timing of acceptance (dispatch/mailbox vs receipt)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B critiques the mailbox/dispatch rule and argues default rules should track parties' reasonable expectations about when an acceptance takes effect, and Paper A engages this same area indirectly by reassessing a precedent (Mills) that established a default outcome about promissory liability — both papers focus on which default doctrines should govern when promises yield enforceable duties.

shared_topics.topic: judicial development, historical case law, and opportunities for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A performs historical reconstruction of Mills v. Wyman and criticizes the court's legal reasoning and missed opportunity to shape promissory doctrine, while Paper B surveys English and American case law (including Denning and teletype decisions) to argue that courts should revise the existing default mailbox rule; both therefore analyze judicial history to motivate doctrinal change.

papers.title: ARTICLE: Duties Under the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act: Analysis of a Statutory Conflict The author wishes to thank the Honorable Thomas L. Steffen and Professor Boyd K. Dyer for their insight and encouragement in writing this Comment.
papers.abstract:
With the enactment in 2001 of the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act (URLLCA),Utah businesspeople electing to form LLC's are faced with a difficult conundrum regarding the duties they owe to the company and to each other, and whether they may opt out of or reduce those duties. Although the URLLCA provides statutory duties for members and managers,two of its provisions clearly allow members to opt out of those duties and reduce them according to the terms of the LLC operating agreement.On the other hand, another provision very specifically states that members may not reduce their statutory duties.
The Utah Legislature repealed the original Utah Limited Liability Company Act in 2001 and replaced it with the new URLLCA.The URLLCA is longer and more comprehensive than the repealed act, leaving less discretion to the courts. This Comment examines the new way in which the URLLCA addresses the duties of members and managers toward one another and toward the LLC. The repealed act was silent as to duties, completely leaving the standard that governed members' and managers' conduct to the common law of agency. Now, despite (and possibly due to) a lack of case law specifically defining LLC members' and managers' duties, the legislature statutorily imposed enumerated duties on members and managers of LLCs. However, as indicated above, the legislature has included provisions in the URLLCA that both allow and forbid the reduction of members' and managers' statutory duties.
Because well-established canons of statutory interpretation support both sides of this statutory conflict, this Comment will analyze both interpretations, concluding that the better approach would be to allow members to reduce theirduties. But first, Part I of this Comment will give a brief history of LLCs in general. Then Part II will discuss the first of the two possible interpretations of the URLLCA. That is, its statutory duties are rigid minimum standards of conduct that may not be reduced. Part III will then discuss the second of the possible interpretations - that members may reduce their statutory duties. Following that, Part IV will consult canons of statutory interpretation in an attempt to identify which of the two interpretations should prevail over the other.

questions.question: Whether owners and managers of a limited liability company may contractually limit or eliminate the duties they owe to the company and to one another.

papers.node_id: 68iowalrev699!!ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications
papers.title: ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications
papers.abstract:
Once people have entered into voluntary, bargained-for exchanges of promises of performance, those performances are to follow in due course.  If they do not, the result is a breach of contract.  An elaborate remedial system should then place the victim in his precontract position or in the position he would have enjoyed if performance rather than breach had occurred.The breaching party should provide this compensation because he caused the loss that compensation is meant to cure.  Furthermore, the economic pain may act as a deterrent to those who would breach if it were costless to do so.  The idea is to create a structure that will help us plan our futures with some confidence and efficiency by exchanging promises about what will happen in the future.
Unfortunately, the simple black-letter model of the structure called "contract law" very often neither serves nor reflects reality.  Human quirkiness, the impact of ongoing relationships, unforeseen changes in the world surrounding the contract, the demands of economic circumstances, the deliberate limitations, and the imperfections of the remedial system all too often act to make the model seem ridiculous in practice.The model has tried to absorb the demands of reality, as that elusive beast has beenperceived by its users and guardians.  For example, an ancient and elaborate structure of rules and principles about sufficient excuses from having to perform or pay compensation continues to grow.The remedial system evolves.  The idea that only promises made in a bargained-for exchange deserve enforcement has eroded.This Article is an example of the countless nudges, kicks, and cries that are continually directed at the model by its guardians -- judges, lawyers, legislators, and scholars.
The users, too, have their say.  They do the acting that supplies the system's grist and purpose.  The guardians would be speechless without them.  The users make the contracts; they are the ones who perform or do not perform.  They hire lawyers and bring lawsuits and lobby legislatures.  They also do something else: if, after the contract is made, reality looks different than it did at the beginning, they may modify the originally promised performances by making new promises.
These modifications have long bedeviled the model and its guardians.Until fairly recently, contract law insisted that users could do no such thing unless they either rescinded the original set of promises and started fresh or made a new bargained-for exchange in which each party's promised performance was changed.  Otherwise, one party was merely performing his "preexisting duty" and thus gave no consideration for the other's promise of extra compensation.
Sometimes users actually conform to this insistence.  If, for example,ApromisedBon May 1st to dig a cellar ten feet deep forBby June 1st andBin return promised to payA$ 1000 when the digging was complete, and if on May 20thAencountered rock eight feet down, one of the two things insisted upon might occur.  They might look each other in the eye and agree that ifBpaid $ 800 for the work so far, neither would have any further obligation to the other about digging or paying, then turn around and agree thatAwould finish the job andBwould pay another $ 700, for a total of $ 1500.  Or they might agree thatAwould dig a little deeper than ten feet and thatBwould then pay $ 1500.  If so,Awould dig through the rock and finish the cellar.  IfBthen refused to pay more than the original contract price, a court concerned only about the preexisting duty rule would awardA$ 500 on his suit as damages for breach of contract.But ifBjust promised to pay an extra $ 500 ifAwould complete the job without a prior rescission of the original promises or a change inA's performance,B's promise would not be enforced.
That was not satisfactory.Bmight not want to releaseA,fearing thatAwould just walk away with the $ 800.Bmight not want a different cellar, at least not for an extra $ 500.  UnlessAcould convince a court that there had been a rescission or a bargained-for change inA's performance when neither was true,Bwould win the lawsuit.  Next time, unable to get an enforceable promise of an extra $ 500,Amight breach if his performance could only be completed at a loss.B's traditional remedy is to purchase a substitute performance and sueAfor the difference in cost.
Even ignoring possibly uncompensable transaction and litigation costs, however,Bmay be worse off than if he had been able to secureA's performance for the extra $ 500.  He might, for example, be unable to get a substitute to finish the job by the first of June.  Courts began to realize that people in these circumstances sometimes ought to be able to extricate themselves by agreeing that more compensation is due to secureactualperformance.  After all, if the presence of rock below eight feet was unforeseen,it seems fair to allow the parties to adjust the resulting loss.  The performerwould then cover the increased cost and presumably make his anticipated profit.  In return, the recipientwould get actual performance without having to find a substitute or bring a lawsuit.  The law's insistence on "fresh" consideration led to a frustrating inability to modify performance and compensation to meet the needs of the parties in modified circumstances unless they played a game.  That made the law seem ridiculous, and no matter how well the game might be played the recipient might renege and expose it.
Reluctance to enforce modifications is justified, however, whenA's refusal to fully perform without extra compensation can be characterized as extortion.  Suppose that fishermen, hired on in San Francisco, refuse to work when the ship reaches the fishing waters off Alaska unless they are paid higher wages.Unlike the cellar digger, the fishermen have not encountered some unforeseen circumstance that makes their performance more costly.Since they have control of the only available necessaryoutput -- their labor -- they are monopolists.  They do what we fear monopolists will do: raise prices.  A court's refusal to enforce an extorted promise by the captain to pay more leaves a ringing sense of justice in its wake.  The captain was able to secure actual performance by promising to pay the monopolists a bribe and then was able to avoid paying.
The essence of the older rule and its modern partial retention is the desire to discountenance and if possible prevent extortion.Extorted promises do not have the presumptive social utility of allowing and encouraging people to makevoluntaryexchanges.  With voluntary exchanges, people can more or less confidently exchange things they have for the more highly valued things that are possessed by their partner in the exchange, thus increasing the perceived wealth of each.When at least one of the performances is to take place in the future, the social utility is even greater because that allows and encourages relatively secure long-term planning.This simple notion is rightfully prized by nearly everyone as at leastareason to enforce promises.  This notion loses its force, however, when there is a threat to withhold performance of a preexisting legal duty to perform.  A new promise given tosecureperformance already due seems to do no more than transfer wealth from the recipient to the performer without reciprocity.It seems to be extortion, or, as one recent commentator put it, opportunism.But the matter is not so simple.
TheRestatement (Second) of Contractsrecognizes that there are situations covered by the preexisting duty rulein which courts have nonetheless enforced modifications:
A promise modifying a duty under a contract not fully performed on either side is binding
(a) if the modification is fair and equitable in view of circumstances not anticipated by the parties when the contract was made; or

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrine evolves in response to practical pressures and social change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Gilmore's thesis that contract law has undergone fundamental change (the 'death of contract') as broader legal and social forces altered doctrinal priorities, while Paper B traces how courts and the Restatement have modified the preexisting-duty rule to accommodate real-world needs for contract modification.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between formal, black‑letter contract rules and pragmatic, context‑sensitive adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the Langdell/Williston formalism with the legal realists' context-driven approach that Gilmore invoked, and Paper B documents the failure of the simple black‑letter model (e.g., fresh consideration) and courts' pragmatic responses to make modification doctrine workable.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts, scholars, and other 'guardians' in adapting remedial rules and doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how scholarly accounts (like Gilmore's) and doctrinal critiques illuminate processes of legal change, and Paper B focuses on judges, commentators, and the Restatement reshaping enforcement rules for contract modifications and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between voluntary agreement and coercion/opportunism in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the shift away from a pure voluntarist contract ideal toward doctrines that recognize nonconsensual or regulatory intervention, and Paper B examines when post‑formation promises are properly enforced versus when they constitute extortion or opportunism that courts should refuse to uphold.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46flastulrev862!!ARTICLE: SNAPCHAT'S GIFT: EQUITY CULTURE IN HIGH-TECH FIRMS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SNAPCHAT'S GIFT: EQUITY CULTURE IN HIGH-TECH FIRMS

shared_topics.topic: limits of the rational, self-interested actor model in corporate and contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that equity markets and investor choice are better explained by social and cultural logics than by atomistic, utility-maximizing individuals, and Paper B similarly rejects the simple black-letter contract model of bargained promises, emphasizing that human quirks and ongoing relationships often defeat the rational-actor assumptions of orthodox contract theory.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of social and relational norms on the meaning and enforcement of exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses Mauss's theory of gift exchange to show that buying shares is embedded in an 'equity culture' of meanings and expectations, while Paper B shows that parties routinely modify agreements (and courts evaluate those modifications) in light of relational, contextual factors rather than strict bargain formalities.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between formal legal doctrine and actual market/party practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how corporate practices (e.g., dual-class/nonvoting shares) and investor behavior diverge from traditional corporate-law assumptions about shareholder rights, and Paper B documents how the preexisting-duty rule and classical contract remedies have been adapted because they failed to accommodate real-world practices of contract modification and performance.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries, opportunism, and the law's response to coerced or extractive transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how founders and corporate actors retain control through capital structures that leave ordinary shareholders powerless, raising governance and distributive concerns, while Paper B analyzes extorted contract modifications (e.g., hold-up by monopolistic workers) and the doctrinal tradeoffs courts make to deter opportunism while permitting reasonable adjustments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1997wislrev943!!ARTICLE: THE NEW REQUIREMENT OF ENFORCEMENT RELIANCE IN COMMERCIAL PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL:
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE NEW REQUIREMENT OF ENFORCEMENT RELIANCE IN COMMERCIAL PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL:

shared_topics.topic: when courts should enforce promises that lack bargained-for consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes courts' narrowing of Section 90 promissory estoppel and argues commercial non‑bargain promises should be unenforceable absent a clear intent to be bound, while Paper B examines when post‑contract modifications (often lacking fresh consideration) are enforceable under the preexisting duty rule and Restatement exceptions.

shared_topics.topic: the role and type of reliance required to justify enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes performance reliance from 'enforcement reliance' and documents courts requiring a promisee's belief in legal enforceability, and Paper B evaluates when a promisee's need for actual performance or changed circumstances justifies enforcing a modification despite lack of new consideration.

shared_topics.topic: judicial doctrine evolving in response to commercial practices and opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how commercial actors' defensive strategies have prompted courts to reshape promissory estoppel, and Paper B explores how courts balance enforcement against opportunistic or extortionate modifications, leading to evolving rules on when modifications are binding.

shared_topics.topic: balancing enforcement to permit adaptive renegotiation while deterring extortionate or opportunistic behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues courts preserve promisor choice by limiting enforcement to promises showing intent to be bound, reducing opportunistic liability, and Paper B discusses refusing enforcement of extorted promises while permitting fair modifications when unforeseen circumstances make adjustment efficient.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44depaullrev1301!!SYMPOSIUM: CULTURAL CONCEPTIONS OF COMPETITION: NOTE: TAX ABATEMENTS AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: A MATCH NOT MADE IN YPSILANTI
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CULTURAL CONCEPTIONS OF COMPETITION: NOTE: TAX ABATEMENTS AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: A MATCH NOT MADE IN YPSILANTI

shared_topics.topic: enforcing promises absent traditional consideration (promissory estoppel vs contract modification doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on using promissory estoppel to bind a corporation to keep a plant open despite the absence of a conventional bargained-for contract, while Paper B examines the doctrinal shift that allows courts to enforce contract modifications or reliance-based promises even when fresh consideration is lacking (including Restatement exceptions).

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing legitimate renegotiation from extortion/opportunism and assessing reasonable reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether the municipality's reliance on GM's assurances was reasonable and considers defenses like economic necessity, whereas Paper B analyzes when post-contractual demands are coercive (extortion/opportunism) and thus undeserving of enforcement versus when they reflect fair renegotiation that courts should uphold.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' bargaining power and economic incentives affect enforceability of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how public tax abatements and the economic dependence of a community on an employer shape the parties' leverage and the incentives to renege, and Paper B uses examples (e.g., fishermen withholding labor) to show how control over essential inputs and economic leverage complicate whether courts should enforce revised promises.

shared_topics.topic: equitable remedies to secure performance versus monetary compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the use of equitable relief (an injunction) to prevent a plant closure and protect community reliance on promises, while Paper B debates when the law should compel performance or award damages for modified promises and how remedial choices influence parties' incentives to perform or extort.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91washlrev1663!!ARTICLE: AN "APP" FOR THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN "APP" FOR THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES

shared_topics.topic: limits on enforceability of promises beyond the original bargain (who can enforce what)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines when post-contract promises (contract modifications) should be enforced despite the preexisting duty rule, while Paper B analyzes when non-parties (third parties) may enforce a contract, so both probe legal boundaries on who may obtain relief from contractual commitments that were not part of the original bargained exchange.

shared_topics.topic: use of doctrinal standards (intent, fairness, unanticipated circumstances) to decide enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the Restatement test that enforces modifications if they are "fair and equitable" in view of circumstances not anticipated by the parties, and Paper B critiques and retools the intent-focused test for third-party beneficiary status, so both engage questions about which normative criteria courts should apply to determine enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: balancing prevention of opportunism/extortion against permitting efficient adjustments or claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally concerned with refusing to enforce extorted modifications while still allowing fair adjustments for unforeseen hardship, and Paper B aims to provide an analytic framework (APP) to reduce opportunistic suits or surprise liabilities by clarifying when a nonparty can sue, so both weigh deterrence of opportunism against facilitation of efficient contract outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: need for doctrinal clarification and reform to improve predictability in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts the evolution and ad hoc judicial responsiveness to problems with the preexisting duty rule and endorses principled exceptions (e.g., §89), while Paper B argues the third-party beneficiary doctrine is an "analytic mess" and proposes a new APP framework; both call for clearer, more workable rules to guide parties and courts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71fordhamlrev841!!SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:A HISTORICAL APPROACH TO THE CONTRACTUAL TIES THAT BIND PARTIES TOGETHER
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:A HISTORICAL APPROACH TO THE CONTRACTUAL TIES THAT BIND PARTIES TOGETHER

shared_topics.topic: the status of consideration versus reliance/promissory estoppel as bases for enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical and doctrinal split between bargained-for consideration and doctrines like reliance/benefit-conferred (promissory estoppel) and argues for a more unified view; Paper B examines instances where courts enforce promises despite lack of fresh consideration (e.g., modifications and reliance), engaging the same tension between bargain-based enforcement and reliance-based exceptions.

shared_topics.topic: when and why courts enforce contract modifications that lack new consideration (preexisting-duty rule and its exceptions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how doctrines beyond the classic bargain (reliance, quasi-contract) became treated as exceptions to consideration, while Paper B analyzes the preexisting-duty rule, extortion/opportunism concerns, and the Restatement Second's conditions under which non-bargained contract modifications are nonetheless binding.

shared_topics.topic: the role of fairness, equity, and moral considerations in delimiting contractual liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds fairness and equitable conceptions (e.g., Lord Mansfield, Corbin) as central to deciding which promises deserve enforcement; Paper B balances fairness against concern for extortion—arguing that equity sometimes justifies enforcing modifications to secure performance while also warning against opportunistic demands.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of Restatements and doctrinal evolution on contemporary contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically surveys the historical impact of the Restatements (and Corbin's reaction) in fragmenting vs. unifying bases of liability; Paper B invokes and assesses the Restatement (Second) approach to contract modification, treating both papers as engagements with how Restatements have reshaped and continue to shape enforcement rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38sandiegolrev53!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Expectation, Reliance, and the Two Contractual Wrongs
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Expectation, Reliance, and the Two Contractual Wrongs

shared_topics.topic: the relative roles of expectation and reliance interests in contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly frames the symposium around 'Expectation, Reliance, and the Two Contractual Wrongs,' interrogating how those remedial goals should guide contract decisionmaking, while Paper B opens by contrasting the remedial aims of placing victims in their precontract (reliance) position versus their expectation position and critiques how the remedial system actually implements those aims.

shared_topics.topic: when and whether renegotiated promises (contract modifications) should be enforced
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is centrally concerned with the enforceability of post‑contract modifications (the preexisting duty rule, Restatement §89, and exceptions), and Paper A situates expectation and reliance doctrines that bear directly on whether courts should enforce or refuse modified promises under different doctrinal and normative premises.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of unforeseen or changed circumstances in justifying modification or altering remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B treats unforeseeable changes as a key ground for enforcing modifications (the 'fair and equitable' exception), and Paper A’s focus on reliance and expectation addresses how unanticipated factual shifts ought to change remedial calculations and the decision to uphold adjusted bargains.

shared_topics.topic: balancing prevention of opportunism/extortion against allowing parties flexibility to secure performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly weighs the need to discountenance extorted promises (opportunistic withholding of preexisting duties) against the social utility of permitting modifications to secure actual performance; Paper A engages the same tension indirectly by asking how remedial doctrines (expectation vs reliance) should respond to strategic behavior and real‑world bargaining dynamics.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev125!!ARTICLE: WHEN DOES THE "FAT LADY" SING? Although this phrase probably originated in the opera setting, one of its more interesting uses occurred in the battle between Pennzoil and Texaco for the Getty Oil Company. When Texaco's Chairman, John K. McKinely, asked Getty Oil's Chairman Sidney Peterson whether Getty might still be available even though an "agreement in principle" had been entered into with Pennzoil, Peterson responded that "the fat lady had not yet sung." Pennzoil Co. v. Getty Oil Co., No. 7425, slip op. at 46 (Del. Ch. Feb. 6, 1984). For a further discussion of the Texaco-Pennzoil case, see infra text accompanying notes 60 to 63. : AN ANALYSIS OF "AGREEMENTS IN PRINCIPLE" IN CORPORATE ACQUISITIONS.
