shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Nachfrist (extension) doctrine under the CISG and how inserting a similar procedural device into the UCC would change when a party can treat a breach as repudiatory and what remedies are available; Paper B develops a third‑party‑beneficiary technique that is intended to function as a doctrinal bypass to turn otherwise nonenforceable gift promises into legally enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of formalities or procedural devices as signals of serious commitment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines Nachfrist as a formal time‑extension procedure that structures parties' expectations and the consequences of nonperformance, while Paper B assesses seals, reliance devices, and the proposed beneficiary mechanism as formal or evidentiary markers that distinguish serious gift promises from casual ones.

shared_topics.topic: normative arguments for reforming domestic contract doctrine by importing or reinterpreting legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for reconsidering and potentially revising the UCC by importing or adapting a foreign CISG/German concept (Nachfrist) to improve predictability and fairness in domestic sales law; Paper B advances a doctrinal reform—recognizing third‑party beneficiary law as an intentional vehicle—to expand the edge of contract law and permit binding gift promises under specified structures.

papers.node_id: 61hastingslj859!!Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Limits of the Legal Method
papers.title: Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Limits of the Legal Method
papers.abstract:
I learned how to teach Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores, Inc.at the hands of Stewart Macaulay and Bill Whitford. Their casebook was the first to focus on the "missing promise" as the key issue in determining whether promissory estoppel was an appropriate ground for assessing liability against Red Owl Stores for the reliance losses incurred by Joseph Hoffmann.The question that they posed was a direct challenge to the rationale adopted by the Wisconsin Supreme Court in support of its opinion that a "promise" that supports liability under promissory estoppel - here Red Owl's representation that $ 18,000 was sufficient capital to secure a franchise - need not be as definite in its terms as a promise that is the basis of a traditional bargain contract.And, indeed, the court's opinion seemed to be quite inconsistent with the now-dominant view of when courts should use the doctrine of promissory estoppel to protect precontractual reliance. The majority view is expressed in the oft-quoted opinion of the Second Circuit Court of Appeals in R.G. Group, Inc. v. Horn & Hardart Co.: a claim for promissory estoppel for early reliance requires a "clear and unambiguous promise; a reasonable and foreseeable reliance by the party to whom the promise is made; and an injury sustained by the party" who has relied.
My preferred approach to answering Macaulay and Whitford's challenge to look for the missing promise was to focus instead on quasi-contract: here, the argument was that Mr. Hoffmannhad conferred a benefit on Red Owl during the period from January through November 1961 when he opened and then sold his grocery store, and thereafter sold the bakery business and building and purchased an option on a lot in Chilton.All these actions gave Red Owl valuable and beneficial information as to the kind of franchisee that Hoffmann was likely to be and the extent of his commitment to the project. Under the prevailing view, a quasi-contract claim lies either because one party wrongfully induced the other to confer the benefit in question or had the opportunity to prevent the other from conferring the benefit by mistake.This at least put the right question to a court: was Hoffmann wrongfully induced to provide this benefit to Red Owl or was he a "mere volunteer"?
Meanwhile, I had begun to research an article on precontractual agreements focusing on the sea change in the law following the landmark opinion of Judge Pierre Leval in Teachers Insurance & Annuity Ass'n v.Tribune Co.Leval held that parties will have made a "binding preliminary commitment" when they have agreed on certain terms even though other terms are left open and when the best inference from their negotiations is that they have agreed to bargain in good faith over the open terms.In cases following Tribune, a number of courts began to relax the knife-edge character of the common law by which parties are fully bound or not bound at all. Instead, a new default rule emerged holding that parties to such a preliminary understanding "accept a mutual commitment to negotiate together in good faith in an effort to reach final agreement."Thereafter, if the parties could not ultimately agree on a final contract, they were free to abandon the deal.In the course of analyzing this trend toward enforcing certain preliminary agreements, my coauthor Alan Schwartz and I studied a random sample of 108 cases litigated between 1999 and 2003 that directly presented the issue of recovery for precontractual reliance.Our goal was to dis-aggregate the precontractual-reliance cases by categorizing the various commercial patterns revealed in the cases and their legal consequences.
Thirty cases in the sample raised the issue of reliance in the context of ongoing negotiations where the theory of liability was based on promissory estoppel, thus implicitly conceding that the parties had yet to reach any agreement at all.The courts denied liability in eighty-seven percent of these promissory estoppel claims.Based on the cases in the sample, I surmised that many lawyers were bringing suits claiming reliance on preliminary negotiations based on a theory of promissory estoppel, but because they lacked evidence of a "clear and unambiguouspromise," as required by cases such as R.G. Group, Inc. v. Horn & Hardart Co.,they would almost always lose. For me, the irony was that meanwhile an entire new body of law had emerged enforcing certain "preliminaries" that seemed to offer these parties a viable theory on which they might have predicated their claims. Given the earlier skepticism of Macaulay, Whitford, and others about the doctrinal integrity of the rationale of the court in Hoffman,and the fact that the case was not being followed in other jurisdictions,I resolved to study the trial record and the appellate briefs of the parties. In the process, I hoped to find some answers to two key questions: What explained the rather bizarre behavior of Red Owl Stores in not simply breaking off negotiations if, in fact, they were reluctant to go forward with Hoffmann as a franchisee? And, would the answer to that question provide an alternative and more defensible doctrinal basis for the opinion of the Wisconsin Supreme Court?
My efforts convinced me that the best inference to be drawn from the record was that the breakdown in the negotiations between Joseph Hoffmann and Red Owl officials was primarily attributable to a fundamental misunderstanding between the parties as to the amount and nature of Hoffmann's capital contribution to the franchise operation. This misunderstanding cast considerable doubt on the meaning of Hoffmann's statement to Ed Lukowitz, Red Owl's agent, that "I got - approximately eighteen thousand dollars. Will this put me in a bigger operation or won't it?"The meaning of that statement is central to the case because the Wisconsin Supreme Court held that Lukowitz's reply - that there would be no problem with that level of investment - was the grounds for imposing promissory liability.Thus, evidence that the parties never had a shared understanding of what that statement meant would seriously undermine the court's rationale. The Red Owl representatives appeared to mean that Hoffmann would have to contribute equity of at least that amount, and Hoffmann, on the other hand, clearly was focusing on how much cash he would put into thetransaction, whether borrowed or not.Based on the facts as reported in the trial record, I reached the conclusion that Mr. Hoffmann was at least partly responsible for failing to clarify the nature of the contribution he was required to make, and that failure largely explained his frustration with the changing nature of the financial requirements that Red Owl proposed to him.
Bill Whitford and Stewart Macaulay (hereafter Bill and Stewart) have written an excellent article that offers an alternative view of the case.As they suggest, we have different perspectives on the outcome of the litigation. They read the trial transcript as supporting a finding of promissory estoppel liability.My reading of the same transcript convinces me that the misunderstanding over the nature of Hoffmann's capital contribution undermines any promissory estoppel claim. But although there are important differences between our stories, fundamentally we do not disagree about the "facts" of the case as revealed in the record, the briefs of the respective parties, or the opinion of the Wisconsin Supreme Court. Rather, we disagree about what legitimate inferences can be drawn from those facts.In their view, the misunderstanding about the nature of Hoffmann's equity contribution was insignificant (perhaps even a litigation ploy advanced by Red Owl Stores).Rather, they focus their attention on the additional statements made by Ed Lukowitz in October urging Mr. Hoffmann to sell his bakery business and store.In these later statements, ignored by the Wisconsin Supreme Court in its opinion, Bill and Stewart now find the "missing promise" that they challenged all of us to look for years ago.
So, what is a reader to make of all this? Bill and Stewart are at pains to say in their article that it would be a shame if the lesson drawn is that these exercises in legal archeology are wholly subjective, reflecting only the biases and ideologies of the legal analyst.They state, and I certainly concur, that we agree on many points. But we do draw quite different inferences, and in this companion Article I want to use our respective attempts to understand this case as an occasion to think about why that is so. We all bring biases to our work, but I am inclined to think that my desire to vindicate an earlier expressed viewpoint and their desire to vindicate Mr. Hoffmann (whom they see as having been wronged by my account) play only limited roles in shaping our analyses. And certainly ideology in the narrow sense of political preferences offers no explanation. After many conversations with Bill and Stewart, good friends for many years, I know that we share the same set of political preferences. Rather, I will argue that our inferences are shaped much more by our methodological commitments: their commitment to a law-and-society approach to legal issues and mine to a law-and-economics mode of analysis.
The Article proceeds as follows: In Part I, I argue that these different methodologies lead the analyst to deploy, respectively, either a bottom-up (or "contextual") approach to a legal problem or a top-down (or "theoretical") approach to the problem, thus leading the analyst to focus on quite different sets of facts as salient in any controversy. Part II traces the two very different conceptions of "justice" that these two methodologies emphasize; differences that explain the focus on the "result" of the case on the one hand and the "rule" of the case on the other. I conclude that both approaches struggle with the inherent paradox of legal analysis: without context no legal rule can be applied, but with nothing but context no legal rule can be found. For this reason, among many others, it is important for legal academics to appreciate the biases inherent in their methodology of choice and work to correct for them.

questions.question: How do different methodological approaches to legal analysis (e.g., contextual/bottom-up versus theoretical/top-down) affect which facts are treated as salient and the legal inferences and outcomes drawn from the same case record?

Under what factual circumstances should courts allow recovery for reliance incurred during preliminary contract negotiations-that is, when is it appropriate to impose liability or grant remedies for precontractual reliance?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
How do casebook selection practices and pedagogical choices (e.g., using multi-issue appellate cases or emphasizing litigation realities) shape students' understanding of contract law and practice?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
What empirical methods and research designs produce reliable evidence about how contracts operate in practice, and how can scholars avoid common inferential errors?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Is imposing a judicially enforced duty to negotiate in good faith necessary to achieve efficient outcomes in preliminary agreements, or would protecting reliance expenditures suffice?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How should courts resolve agreements founded on mutual misunderstanding: voidness versus enforcing each party's reasonable interpretation?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91califlrev1645!!ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: duties and obligations during precontractual negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when parties in preliminary negotiations incur enforceable obligations (promissory estoppel, quasi-contract, or binding preliminary commitments), while Paper B formulates when a negotiating party must disclose material facts before contracting; both grapple with what legal duties arise prior to a finalized contract.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk for mistaken assumptions in bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on whether Hoffmann or Red Owl bore the risk of misunderstanding about capital requirements and how that affects liability, and Paper B explicitly treats allocation of risk as a key exception to disclosure duties (i.e., when a party is allocated the risk of a mistaken assumption).

shared_topics.topic: when reliance on information produces legal liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores recovery for precontractual reliance (promissory estoppel and reliance losses) and the evidentiary thresholds for such claims, while Paper B links nondisclosure of material facts to prospective contractual choices and lays out when failure to disclose should give rise to legal consequences.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry and its legal consequences in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights factual misunderstandings and informational gaps between negotiators (e.g., nature of Hoffmann's capital) that shape judicial outcomes, and Paper B systematically addresses asymmetric knowledge (the Disclosure Principle) and when the law should correct or leave those asymmetries unremedied.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of relational context (trust, good-faith preliminaries) on duties and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses emerging doctrines enforcing preliminary commitments and good-faith negotiation norms versus voluntariness, and Paper B makes relational status (trust and confidence) a decisive factor that creates affirmative disclosure obligations between parties.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 64scallrev1!!ARTICLE: LIABILITY FOR MISTAKE IN CONTRACT FORMATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LIABILITY FOR MISTAKE IN CONTRACT FORMATION.

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of Hoffman v. Red Owl as promissory estoppel versus alternative doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reexamines Hoffman by parsing the trial record and questions whether the Wisconsin Supreme Court properly rested liability on promissory estoppel given factual misunderstandings, while Paper B analyzes Hoffman as better explained by mistake or negligent misrepresentation and contrasts promise-based enforcement with mistake-based liability.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal basis for recovery of precontractual reliance losses (promissory estoppel vs quasi-contract/restitution vs negligent misrepresentation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares promissory estoppel, quasi‑contract/restitution, and emerging doctrines enforcing preliminary commitments to explain recovery in failed negotiations, and Paper B similarly evaluates when restitution, negligent misrepresentation, or promissory estoppel should allocate losses from negotiation‑stage reliance.

shared_topics.topic: role of mistake or misunderstanding in contract formation and its effect on liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the parties' misunderstanding about the nature of Hoffmann's capital contribution as central to whether a promise existed and thus to liability, while Paper B centers on mistake as a ground for imposing liability in negotiation contexts and argues that mistaken representations can justify recovery.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of preliminary commitments and good‑faith negotiation obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces a judicial trend toward enforcing 'binding preliminaries' and mutual commitments to negotiate in good faith, and Paper B discusses the limited circumstances in which courts enforce agreements to negotiate and when they impose duties during bargaining.

shared_topics.topic: normative and methodological foundations (utilitarian/law‑and‑economics vs contextual/law‑and‑society) for regulating bargaining conduct and choice of tort versus contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts law‑and‑economics and law‑and‑society methodologies in interpreting Hoffman and selecting salient facts and rules, while Paper B invokes utilitarian (cost‑allocation/market‑failure) reasons for imposing duties in bargaining and compares the implications of using tort law versus contract doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2000utahlrev223!!SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.

shared_topics.topic: legal archaeology / historical reconstruction of reported cases
shared_topics.justification: Both papers endorse digging beyond published opinions to reconstruct trial records and surrounding evidence: Paper A performs a detailed re-examination of the Hoffman v. Red Owl record to test competing inferences, while Paper B develops the metaphor of an archaeological dig and argues for the value of such historical reconstruction in understanding how cases actually unfolded.

shared_topics.topic: how methodological commitments shape legal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize that analysts' methodological frameworks influence the facts they treat as salient and the inferences they draw: Paper A contrasts law-and-economics (top-down) and law-and-society (bottom-up) readings of the same case, and Paper B cautions that doctrinal abstraction or pedagogical habits can bias understanding of a case's justice and rationale.

shared_topics.topic: primacy of contextual factual inquiry over abstract rule-following
shared_topics.justification: Each paper argues that accurate legal understanding requires close attention to context and facts rather than relying solely on bright-line doctrinal summaries: Paper A shows how contextual misunderstandings about capital contributions alter doctrinal conclusions, and Paper B warns that law students and lawyers who ignore factual reconstruction risk mistaken readings of legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: legal pedagogy and the value of case-based, investigatory teaching
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with teaching methods that encourage students to ‘get their hands dirty’—Paper A recounts casebook-driven classroom debates about Hoffman and methodological lessons, while Paper B advocates using archaeological-style case reconstruction to reinvigorate students' commitment to justice and to teach careful factual and historical inquiry.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2008uilllrev505!!ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of reliance/promissory estoppel in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys the 'reliance' heuristic as one of the central descriptive bases for when promises become legally enforceable and highlights its doctrinal shortcomings; Paper B performs a close empirical and doctrinal analysis of promissory estoppel (Hoffman v. Red Owl and a sample of cases), showing when courts require a 'clear and unambiguous' promise and how reliance claims are frequently denied in preliminary-negotiation contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between promise-based and reliance-based accounts of enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract theory around three competing heuristics—promise, reliance, and transfer—and asks how adopting one or another supports different normative accounts (e.g., deontological vs consequentialist); Paper B directly engages that tension by asking whether Hoffmann's case turns on a 'missing promise' (promise-based) or instead is better understood via quasi-contract/reliance reasoning, testing which heuristic fits the doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: limits of legal theory and methodological bias in explaining contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that searches for a unified normative theory of contract may fail and insists on recognizing theory's proper, limited role in explaining doctrinal anomalies; Paper B explores how analysts' methodological commitments (law-and-economics vs law-and-society; top-down vs bottom-up) shape inferences about the same contract dispute and thus reveal constraints and biases in legal interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: interpretive difficulties in discerning parties' mutual understanding/consent (the 'missing promise' problem)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasises the ambiguity of contractual 'consent' and the practical problem that doctrine must distinguish consensual from nonconsensual obligations despite fuzzy facts; Paper B examines a concrete instance of that problem—whether parties shared a meaning about Hoffmann's capital contribution—and shows how factual misunderstandings or ambiguous statements complicate application of contract doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 26wmmarylrev45!!ARTICLE: A CRITIQUE OF THE PROMISE MODEL OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CRITIQUE OF THE PROMISE MODEL OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: whether contracts should be conceptualized primarily as promises versus alternative exchange/relational models
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques the 'promise model' and develops an alternative account of contracts grounded in the exchange relationship between parties, while Paper B problematizes the search for a 'missing promise' in Hoffman v. Red Owl and explores whether liability is better explained by preliminary commitments or other non-promissory bases.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal tension between consideration and reliance (promissory estoppel) as bases for enforceable obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the anomaly of the consideration doctrine vis-à-vis the promise principle, and Paper B empirically and doctrinally examines promissory estoppel's requirement of a 'clear and unambiguous promise' versus courts' willingness to protect precontractual reliance.

shared_topics.topic: use of quasi-contract/unjust enrichment as an alternative ground for recovery when a promise is absent or unclear
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts Atiyah’s thesis that promises may only reflect preexisting obligations rooted in harm or unjust enrichment, and Paper B explicitly advances a quasi-contract/unjust-enrichment theory as a principled alternative to imputing a promise in Hoffman.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and community values in 'gap-filling' or modifying parties' obligations when contracts are incomplete or accidents occur
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses judicial and community interventions (duty to mitigate, good faith, unconscionability, gap-filling for contractual accidents) as evidence against a pure promissory account, while Paper B studies how courts have enforced preliminary commitments, how judges infer promises from context, and how methodological lenses shape whether one emphasizes rule-based or context-sensitive resolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85califlrev821!!ARTICLE: The World of Contract and the World of Gift
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The World of Contract and the World of Gift

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance in making otherwise noncontractual promises legally enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promissory estoppel and when precontractual reliance can justify liability for promises made during negotiations, while Paper B treats reliance as a key special principle that can render donative (otherwise unenforceable) promises enforceable and explains why reliance matters doctrinally and morally.

shared_topics.topic: where to draw the boundary between enforceable contract obligations and non‑enforceable promises or preliminaries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the emerging doctrine that some preliminary agreements or commitments can create binding obligations (or obligations to negotiate in good faith) versus the traditional all‑or‑nothing contract rule, and Paper B distinguishes the 'world of contract' from the 'world of gift' to argue why simple donative promises should generally remain outside contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of parties' intentions, mutual understanding, and contextual facts in determining enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how misunderstandings about the nature of a capital contribution undermined a promissory‑estoppel claim and stresses contextual fact‑finding, while Paper B emphasizes the affective motivations behind donative promises and uses context and the nature of the promise to justify different legal treatment.

shared_topics.topic: methodological and normative bases for doctrinal rules (doctrinal vs social/moral justification)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts law‑and‑economics (theoretical/top‑down) and law‑and‑society (contextual/bottom‑up) approaches to justify legal inferences about promises, and Paper B explicitly separates doctrinal propositions from social and moral propositions and uses moral/social reasoning to justify the donative‑promise principle.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71fordhamlrev695!!SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:PARABLES ABOUT PROMISES: RELIGIOUS ETHICS AND CONTRACT ENFORCEABILITY*
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:PARABLES ABOUT PROMISES: RELIGIOUS ETHICS AND CONTRACT ENFORCEABILITY*

shared_topics.topic: whether and how promises should be enforced when there is no traditional consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the common‑law consideration doctrine and the ‘‘moral obligation’’ cases—asking whether moral or religious duty should make otherwise gratuitous promises legally enforceable—while Paper B analyzes doctrines that courts use as alternatives to consideration (promissory estoppel, quasi‑contract, and enforcement of preliminary commitments) in precontractual reliance disputes like Hoffman v. Red Owl.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal change in contract law regarding the bindingness of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces historical shifts (canon law, medieval jurists, Enlightenment) in the legal grounding of promise‑keeping, and Paper B documents and explains a modern ‘‘sea change’’ (e.g., Tribune and subsequent cases) toward enforcing certain preliminaries and relaxing the all‑or‑nothing common‑law rule.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and methodological bases for deciding when promises should be enforced
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores religious and moral sources as grounds for legal enforcement of promises, whereas Paper B explicitly contrasts methodological and normative frameworks (law‑and‑society vs law‑and‑economics) that shape jurists’ and scholars’ inferences about when to impose promissory or quasi‑contractual liability.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of factual interpretation and inference in assessing whether a promise exists or is binding
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on application of the moral‑obligation/consideration doctrine to concrete fact patterns (e.g., humanitarian acts) to decide enforceability, and Paper B revolves around parsing the parties’ statements, mutual understandings, and misunderstandings (the ‘‘missing promise’’) to determine whether promissory estoppel or another doctrine should apply.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 28seattleulrev1!!ARTICLE: Un-Making Law: The Classical Revival in the Common Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Un-Making Law: The Classical Revival in the Common Law

shared_topics.topic: whether courts should enforce informal or preliminary commitments versus a strict formal‑contract rule
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes a classical revival that pushes courts toward formalistic enforcement of clearly formed bargains and away from interventions that impose terms; Paper B analyzes promissory estoppel and quasi‑contract doctrines (and the emergence of enforcement of certain preliminary commitments), contrasting courts' frequent refusal to enforce vague precontractual promises with newer lines of cases that relax the all‑or‑nothing rule.

shared_topics.topic: the methodological tension between formalist/top‑down and contextual/bottom‑up approaches to adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes a revived formalist method for judicial decisionmaking in contract, tort, and property; Paper B explicitly contrasts law‑and‑economics (top‑down/theoretical) and law‑and‑society (bottom‑up/contextual) methodologies and shows how those choices change which facts and inferences analysts and courts treat as decisive.

shared_topics.topic: how to draw and police boundaries among contract, tort, and quasi‑contract and the remedial consequences of those boundaries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the classical revival sharpens and reasserts distinct boundaries among contract, tort, and property (privileging contract/property rules and limiting tort liabilities); Paper B centers on doctrines (promissory estoppel, quasi‑contract) that operate at the margins between contract and other remedies, exploring when courts will treat a dispute as contractual, quasi‑contractual, or tort‑like and the effects on recovery.

shared_topics.topic: recent doctrinal change in the common law and the normative/political forces shaping it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates ongoing rollbacks of twentieth‑century neoclassical developments as a coherent, politically‑inflected classical revival driven by conservative and business interests; Paper B documents changing judicial approaches to precontractual liability (e.g., Tribune and its progeny), evaluates empirical trends in cases, and interrogates how methodological or normative commitments shape doctrinal evolution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72iowalrev47!!ARTICLE: Damages for Reliance Across the Spectrum of Law: Of Blind Men and Legal Elephants
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Damages for Reliance Across the Spectrum of Law: Of Blind Men and Legal Elephants

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel and reliance damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally analyze promissory estoppel as the doctrine used to compensate promisees for reliance losses: Paper A surveys how promissory estoppel functions across doctrines and its remedial reach, while Paper B uses Hoffman v. Red Owl to interrogate whether the facts supported promissory estoppel liability and how courts assess reliance losses in that context.

shared_topics.topic: choice and overlap among doctrines for compensating relying promisees (contract, quasi‑contract/restitution, tort, agency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents substantive overlap and inconsistent remedies across contracts, agency/franchise, torts, insurance, and restitution/constructive trusts for relying promisees and calls for a unified approach; Paper B confronts that same doctrinal choice in Hoffman, weighing promissory estoppel against quasi‑contract/restitution and enforcement of preliminary commitments as alternative bases for recovery.

shared_topics.topic: precontractual reliance and the enforceability of preliminary agreements
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the problem of reliance during negotiations and the legal treatment of preliminary understandings: Paper A discusses flexible remedies (e.g., Restatement section 90) and courts' responses to reliance claims arising before a final contract, while Paper B studies the line between 'missing promises' and binding preliminary commitments (Tribune and subsequent cases) and reports empirical patterns of courts denying promissory estoppel in precontractual settings.

shared_topics.topic: discrepancy between doctrinal theory/scholarly assumptions and actual judicial practice (methodological influences on legal interpretation)

papers.node_id: 61hastingslj801!!Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores: The Rest of the Story
papers.title: Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores: The Rest of the Story
papers.abstract:
A pair of bargainers negotiate but fail to conclude a legally enforceable contract. Has one any rights against the other? In conversation, Ian Macneil, the great theorist of relational contract, said that classical contract law treats contract formation as if it were a light switch. It is either on or off - either there is a contract and the possibility of liability or there is not and the parties are free to walk away withoutobligations to each other.Macneil, however, said that in many cases, particularly where there are strong relational elements, the situation is like a rheostat.It is hard to say when the light is on or off as power is fed little by little to the light as the dial is turned. Relational bargains evolve as the parties work toward a deal little by little. This means that one bargainer may have influenced the other to do something to her detriment that she would not have done but for the expectation that there certainly would be a deal. While courts sometimes bent the rules of formation and found that the parties had concluded a contract when one was responsible for serious reliance by the other,there was no recognized rule providing for recovery by the relying party when the ultimate deal was not concluded. However, over forty years ago things began to change in many states. And ever since then, there has been scholarly debate about the problem.
Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores, Inc.,is the most famous of the cases that founded a new area of contract law by allowing recovery of reliance expenses incurred before a contract had been formed. Hoffman also has been the most influential case in framing the issue of the rights of a relying party. It was also an influential decision giving meaning to the then-relatively new doctrine of promissory estoppel.Hoffman has now become a staple of contracts casebooks,and it is routinely discussed inlaw review articles and textbook discussions about recovery for "precontractual reliance."Some courts in other states have adopted the Hoffman rule while others have rejected it.
We have had the unexpected good fortune to locate and interview Joseph Hoffmann,the plaintiff in this famous case.We have beendelighted to discover that Mr. Hoffmann remains in good health.And despite the many years that have passed since the events involved in the case, he still has a sharp recollection of many of the events leading up to the trial and appeal. Mr. Hoffmann told us many things about the events that provoked the litigation as well as the litigation itself. He raised points not reflected in the decision or in the scholarly literature spawned by the case. We have verified much of what he has told us from the full trial record.We have also looked at the appellate briefs and Red Owl's Annual Reports.
We have decided to tell a fuller story of Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores as we now understand it. Investigating the detailed background of famous cases is now widely accepted as a useful form of scholarship.Among important insights that stories about well-known cases can offer are the following: First, they are almost certain to reveal that the "facts" stated in an appellate opinion are carefully selected and omit events that many would consider highly relevant to an evaluation of the proper outcome of the litigation. These limitations on facts as stated in appellate opinions are not just because the judge or judges writing opinions select what they choose to report, but also because the litigation strategies of the parties, and the evidentiary rulings of the trial judge, keep certain events from getting into the record. Learning about these matters teach important practical lessons about the operation of the legal system. Second, we all like to speculate about the wisdom of a decision, and a fuller explication of the facts can enrich such a discussion. This is especially valuable when the story is about a foundational case likeHoffman v. Red Owl Stores. Although the current vitality of any principle in the area of precontractual reliance perhaps ought to be independent of the wisdom of a decision now forty-five years old, in fact the current assessment of the wisdom of the outcome of the Hoffman case is likely to subtly influence many people's attitudes about the law.
We have an additional reason for exploring the background of Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores. Several years ago, Professor Robert Scott also obtained the full trial record and wrote an article arguing that the case was wrongly decided.We have a somewhat different perspective on the case. We also have additional information to add to the story, mostly gained from several interviews with Joe Hoffmann. While Professor Scott would have a strong argument for his position if the facts were as he assumed them to be, we believe the available information about the events leading to the litigation suggests a story supportive of the ultimate outcome in this litigation, though not necessarily all parts of the Wisconsin Supreme Court's opinion. We have decided to tell the story as we now understand it. Only the most important differences in our story and Professor Scott's account will be noted, mostly in a few footnotes.
After we have related our story in full, in the conclusion we will return to the benefits of storytelling, and indicate what we think we have learned from our study of the full facts of Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores. These findings suggest that the case reached a just result, and one that would be less controversial if facts not previously fully known had been understood in the many discussions of this famous case.

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?

papers.node_id: 59ukanlrev231!!ARTICLE: Honest Confusion: The Purpose of Compensatory Damages in Tort and Fraudulent Misrepresentation
papers.title: ARTICLE: Honest Confusion: The Purpose of Compensatory Damages in Tort and Fraudulent Misrepresentation
papers.abstract:
Suppose that a plaintiff is injured in a rear-end collision car accident. Even though the rear-end collision was not a dramatic accident, the plaintiff incurred extensive medical expenses because of a preexisting medical condition. Through a negligence claim, the plaintiff can recover compensatory damages based on his medical expenses. But is it fair that the defendant should be liable for all of the damages? It is not as if he rear-ended the plaintiff on purpose. Maybe the fact that defendant's conduct was not reprehensible should reduce the amount of damages that the plaintiff recovers.
Any first-year torts student knows that the defendant's argument will not succeed. The defendant's conduct does not control the amount of the plaintiff's compensatory damages. The damages are based on the plaintiff's injury because, in tort law, the purpose of compensatory damages is to make the plaintiff whole by putting him in the same position as if the tort had not occurred.
But there are tort claims where the amount of compensatory damages is not always based on the plaintiff's injury. Suppose that a defendant fraudulently misrepresents that a car for sale is brand-new. The plaintiff then offers to purchase the car for $ 10,000. Had the car actually been new, it would have been worth $ 15,000, but the car was instead worth only $ 10,000. As they have for a very long time, the majority of jurisdictions would award the plaintiff $ 5000 in compensatory damages based on the plaintiff's expected benefit of the bargain.
Courts label these damages "compensatory," but do not treat them like compensatory damages. For instance, even if courts adhere to the majority rule, some would award $ 0 in compensatory damages because the defendant did not profit from the sale and the plaintiff has no out-of-pocket losses.Similarly, the majority of courts would award $ 0 in compensatory damages if the defendant was merely negligent in making the misrepresentation.
Treating benefit-of-the-bargain damages as compensatory has skewed the meaning of compensatory in tort law. If factors other than the plaintiff's injury change the amount of damages, are the damages still compensatory? If so, what does compensatory mean anymore? More importantly, if tort law tolerates undercompensation of parties injured by fraudulent misrepresentation, what's to stop the defendant in a rear-end collision from successfully reducing damages based on his conduct?
Benefit-of-the-bargain damages cannot be compensatory in tort, and none of the practical or theoretical justifications for awarding benefit-of-the-bargain-based compensatory damages for breach of contract apply to tort law. To restore the meaning of compensatory damages in tort law, courts must limit compensatory damages for fraudulent misrepresentation to the plaintiff's out-of-pocket losses. The purpose of benefit-of-the-bargain damages is, and always has been, to punish the defendant because he committed fraud; these are punitive damages in tort.
Part II of this Article discusses the distinct purposes of compensatory damages in contract and tort law. Part III discusses courts' adoption of benefit-of-the-bargain-based compensatory damages for fraudulent misrepresentation. Part IV explores the difficulty in distinguishing contract and tort actions, a difficulty increased due to the similarity in the damages awarded. Part V argues that benefit-of-the-bargain damages are not compensatory as contemplated by tort law. Part VI further argues that the reasons and justifications for awarding benefit-of-the-bargain-based compensatory damages in contract law do not apply to tort law. The last Parts of the Article explore the consequences of awarding benefit-of-the-bargain-based compensatory damages in tort and conclude that benefit-of-the-bargain damages in tort should be awarded only as punitive damages.

papers.node_id: 74iowalrev115!!ARTICLE: Illegal Contracts and Efficient Deterrence: A Study in Modern Contract Theory
papers.title: ARTICLE: Illegal Contracts and Efficient Deterrence: A Study in Modern Contract Theory
papers.abstract:
Contract law generally is based on the principle that courts will enforce agreements into which the parties freely entered.If parties comply with contract formalities,the law typically provides relief in the event of a breach.The doctrine of illegal contracts, which allows parties to avoid their obligations when a contract is "illegal"or against publicpolicy,is a rare limitation on freedom of contract.
Courts have claimed that they effectuate these public policy concerns by characterizing illegal contracts as "void"and denying them all legal effect.They have indicated that withholding judicial relief deters illegalcontracts because parties will shun unenforceable transactions.While thecourts have not articulated their reasoning clearly, commentators have explained that because nonenforcement will be costly to the parties in terms of wasted resources,they will be careful to avoid proscribed transactions.
Despite their broad declarations of the "no-effect" rules, the courts vary their treatment of parties to illegal contracts.Courts sometimes grant a one-sided voidability right, giving one party the option either to affirm or avoid his contractual obligations, but deny any relief to the other party.Courts also may grant a one-sided enforcement right.  Additionally, in cases in which one party has partly performed, courts may grant a one-sided rescission right, plus restitution.Finally, courts can deny enforcement butgrant rescission to both parties.Commentators have detailed the various qualifications to the no-effect rulewithout offering a comprehensive theory to explain why the exceptions exist and how they interrelate.
This article offers a unified theorythat explains why courts, despitethe compelling argument for deterrence, should not apply the no-effect rule uniformly and why they should vary the type of relief according to the factual setting.  It posits that a graduated relief structure will maximizeefficientdeterrence -- allocating the risk of nonenforcement to the cheapest cost avoider, rather than to both parties in all instances.An efficient deterrence scheme will preserve limited personal, judicial, and societal resources without burdening legitimate transactions.  Efficient deterrence theorycan guide the courts to the proper remedy in differing factual contexts.  Importantly, because efficient deterrence may mirror private choices, it also establishes the illegal contracts doctrine as consistent with, rather than an exception to, traditional freedom of contract notions (referred to here as the autonomy principle).
This discussion of illegal contracts joins the current debate about the public vs. private nature of contract law.  Some scholars portray many contract doctrines as reflecting expanding incursions of collectivistic and paternalistic notions which have begun to underminethe essentially private worldof traditional contract law.Other scholars rebut that thesis, suggesting that even "modern" doctrines such as promissory estoppel, perceived to reflect substantive fairness concerns,dovetail with a regime of private autonomy.The efficient deterrence theory suggests that the illegal contracts doctrine is founded upon a private autonomy basis previously unrecognized because of the exclusive emphasis placed on the doctrine's public policy aspects.
Section I describes the efficient deterrence theory and explores the policy and societal goals that support it.It also posits that, given certain assumptions about human behavior,the efficient deterrence theory is compatible with the autonomy principle rather than an exceptional public policy limit on private agreement.Section II documents the impact of certain factual predictors on case outcome and reconceptualizes them in terms of an efficient deterrence theory.Section III reexamines several doctrinal exceptions to the no-effect rule: the antiforfeiture, the protected class, and the collateralness doctrines.It asserts that the doctrinal exceptions fail to account persuasively for the case law outcomes and then suggests that the doctrines can be better explained in terms of efficient deterrence.  Section IV reexamines the efficient deterrence theory and relates it to the principle of contract freedom.

questions.question: Whether courts' varying remedial responses to unenforceable or illegal agreements can be explained by an efficiency-based deterrence principle that allocates the cost of nonenforcement to the party who can most cheaply avoid proscribed transactions.

Whether a graduated relief regime (tailoring remedies to the factual context) produces more efficient deterrence and better preserves private contractual autonomy than a uniform rule of blanket nonenforcement.
How factual features of transactions and parties predict which side bears the risk of nonenforcement and which remedies courts choose in cases involving unenforceable agreements.

matched_themes: Are courts' refusals to enforce contracts on public-interest grounds applied predictably, and which categories of public-interest challenges are most likely to succeed?
What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 66hastingslj1661!!ARTICLE: In and Out - Contract Doctrines in Action
papers.title: ARTICLE: In and Out - Contract Doctrines in Action
papers.abstract:
It is very easy to enter into a contract but extremely difficult to get out of one. I have said as much in several different places.If asked prior to researching and writing this paper, I would have said that this easy in/difficult out structure of contract law was an established part of the contract law canon. After searching for some time, however, I discovered that no one besides me has actually come out and made this claim explicitly. I primarily blame Charles Knapp for this omission, because so much of his work has informed mine.
Charles Knapp is a professor of contract law,which means that he teaches, writes, and thinks about the law of contracts; and he has devoted himself to this role for the past fifty years. Countless students have passed through Professor Knapp's classroom and he has produced a prodigious as well as influential body of scholarship. Knapp's work sometimes focuses on specific doctrines, like unconscionabilityand promissory estoppel.But in other instances, he has turned his attention to understanding and analyzing the evolution of contract law and its implications for modern society.Regardless of the content, his work is always firmly grounded in contract law doctrines and case law.Armed with this knowledge of what the courts are actually doing, Knapp hasconsistently, and often presciently, identified troubling trends and problematic issues that call for careful attention, like the ever-increasing deference courts give to the drafters of contracts and the vanishing requirement of mutual assent.Through it all, his concern for the effect that contract law in action has on the weaker contracting party is evident and purposeful.
If imitation is the best form of flattery, then this Article should do the trick because in this piece I plan to shamelessly copy Knapp, both in terms of substance and format. In terms of substance, I, like him, will evaluate the state of contract law, concentrating here on contract law in the twenty-first century. In terms of format, I will use the Dickensian scheme from A Christmas Carol, which Knapp has employed so well in at least a couple of his articles.
Thus, Part I will look at where contract law has been by examining Knapp's work, focusing particularly on his assertions that contract law defers too much to the document itself and to the drafters of contracts.He argues, in essence, that because contract law privileges written agreements, drafters of contracts can (and do) include a lot of one-sided terms into their contracts, and then end up getting to keep them because contract law makes those agreements binding.Implicit in these assertions is the claim that contracts are very easy to get into but extremely difficult to get out of.
Part II will then analyze case law from trial and appellate courts in the states within the jurisdiction of the Seventh and Ninth Circuits to determine whether the easy in/difficult out claim is accurate. The data from the case law reveal two significant findings. First, the data indicate that part of the easy in/difficult out hypothesis may not be true. Specifically, it may not be so easy to get into a contract - a contract was not actually formed in more than half of the reviewed cases. That said, the other part of the hypothesis, namely, that, once in, it is extremely difficult to get out of a contract is solidly supported by the reviewed cases. The second significant finding from the data is that the party with more bargaining power generally gets the outcome that it wants in a given case, whether the preferred outcome is that a contract was formed or not formed, or a duty was discharged or not discharged. Home loan modifications are used as a specific and problematic example of this phenomenon. In light of the data collected in Part II, Part III will examine the future of contract law by considering the implications of acontracting reality that may privilege parties with more bargaining power and which definitely locks people into their contracts.
