shared_topics.topic: the role of moral obligation and conscience in contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the moral‑obligation doctrine (the 'tribunal of conscience') and whether moral duty can serve as consideration, while Paper B engages the interplay of ethical/natural‑law reasoning with legal standards (via its discussion of the reasonable person and subjectivity), linking moral judgment to contractual assessment.

shared_topics.topic: the judicial role in creating and applying contract doctrine (how courts set standards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts how judges in Mills shaped — and missed opportunities to reshape — promissory liability and highlights judicial law‑making versus jury factfinding; Paper B focuses on how courts apply the reasonable person standard and exercise subjective judgment, thereby shaping doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical foundations of promissory liability and the consideration doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a theoretical critique of the moral‑obligation rule and advocates intent‑based enforceability of promises; Paper B situates adjudicative standards (reasonable person/subjectivity) within contract theory, bearing on when and why promises should be enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: when promises should be enforced versus excused or adjusted
shared_topics.justification: Both papers address the boundary between enforceable promises and situations warranting nonenforcement or relief: Paper A asks when a promise should be legally binding (examining consideration, moral obligation, and intent to be bound), and Paper B investigates when performance should be excused or the parties' obligations adjusted because of impossibility or unforeseen changed circumstances.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys divergent judicial approaches to no-reliance clauses and calls for clearer articulation of the policy tradeoffs courts make, while Paper B critiques the Mills decision and highlights how judicial fact-finding and doctrinal choices produced and perpetuated the moral-obligation rule.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on distinguishing unenforceable extorted promises (e.g., labor refusing preexisting duties to extract pay increases) from fair, unforeseen-cost adjustments, and Paper B engages with the normative question of when the law should enforce promises motivated by conscience or gratitude versus protecting against opportunistic claims.

papers.node_id: 66geowashlrev508!!ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law
papers.title: ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law
papers.abstract:
Contracts casebooks often use a three-step approach in teaching legal doctrines like consideration, offer and acceptance, or the statute of frauds. They first reprint a decision that applies the traditional rule that most courts followed until the middle of this century. Then, for contrast, they include another case that rejects the traditional approach in favor of a new and usu ally more flexible standard. Finally, the casebooks quote a provision from the American Law Institute's Restatement (Second) of Contracts(the "Re statement (Second)") that adopts the more modern view.
Professors E. Allan Farnsworth and William F. Young's Cases and Materials on Contracts,one of the most popular contracts casebooks, con tains several examples of this pattern. For instance, in covering the topic of modification, the authors first reprint Arzani v. People.In that case, a sub contractor named Arzani agreed to pave a road for a general contractor for a fixed price.When a labor dispute arose, Arzani told the general contractor he would need more money to complete the work.Although the general contractor promised to pay Arzani an additional sum, the court held this promise unenforceable.The court explained that the general contractor had received nothing in exchange for his promise to pay more money because Arzani had a preexisting duty to complete the work and that the contractor's promise therefore lacked consideration.
Immediately following the Arzani case, Farnsworth and Young reprint a contrary decision called Watkins & Son v. Carrig.In that case, an excavator agreed to dig a cellar for a man named Carrig.The excavator encountered unexpected bedrock and declared that it would need more money to com plete the work.Carrig promised to pay the additional amount requested, and the court held the promise enforceable.Refusing to apply the tradi tional preexisting duty rule relied on in Arzani, the court concluded that fair ness required enforcement of the promise in view of the unforeseen difficulty of the work.
In notes printed in connection with Arzani and Watkins, the authors cite section 89(a) of the Restatement (Second).Section 89(a) adopts the holding of Watkins, stating: "A promise modifying a duty under a contract not fully performed on either side is binding...if the modification is fair and equita ble in view of circumstances not anticipated by the parties when the contract was made."The Reporter's Note following section 89 describes the section as "new" and cites Watkins as authority.Several other leading casebooks cover the topic of modification using this same three-step approach.
Another example from the Farnsworth and Young casebook concerns the ability of past services to serve as consideration. The authors first reprint Mills v. Wyman.In that famous old case, a sailor fell ill and a man named Mills cared for him.Mills later notified the sailor's father, Wyman, who promised to pay Mills for the services that he had rendered.The court, however, refused to enforce Wyman's promise.It explained that although the father may have had a moral duty to pay for the services, the father had received nothing in exchange for the promise because Mills already had per formed.This case illustrates the traditional rule that "past" or "moral" con sideration generally cannot serve as a basis for enforcing promises.
Following Mills v. Wyman, Farnsworth and Young include Webb v. Mc Gowin.In that more recent case, Webb saved McGowin's life by divertinga falling piece of wood.To show his gratitude for this service and to com pensate Webb for injuries that he had sustained, McGowin promised to pay Webb a small pension for the rest of his life.The court enforced the prom ise even though Webb had not exchanged any new consideration.The court concluded that Webb's past action sufficed in the circumstances.
In a note following these two cases, Farnsworth and Young cite section 86 of the Restatement (Second),which adopts the holding of Webb v. Mc Gowin. Section 86 states: "A promise made in recognition of a benefit previ ously received by the promisor from the promisee is binding to the extent necessary to prevent injustice."The Reporter's Note to section 86 de scribes the section as "new" and cites Webb v. McGowin (among other deci sions) as authority.Numerous other casebooks reprint the same cases, followed by section 86, in discussing the topic of past consideration.
This three-step approach to covering contracts doctrines has several ben efits. It demonstrates to first-year students that the law changes over time. It shows them the typical direction of change that has occurred in the twentieth century. It also informs students of the preferred view of the American Law Institute and, therefore, presumably of the academy in general.
Yet, despite achieving these pedagogic objectives, the approach raises a difficult issue. After working through the pattern on one doctrine or an other, a student invariably will ask whether the new rule that is included in the Restatement (Second) accurately reflects the current law, or instead whether most courts still apply the traditional rule. This reasonable question usually does not have an easy answer.
The American Law Institute's decision to include a rule in the Restate ment (Second) does not mean that a majority of courts have adopted that rule. The Restatement (Second) strives to state the best rules, not necessarily the rules that most courts have followed. As Professor Herbert Wechsler stated in 1969 while serving as the Director of the American Law Institute, "any statement that the law is such and such is more than an empiric finding that decisions have so held....[I]t implies a normative assertion as to whatshould now be held, if and when the question is presented."Professor Farnsworth, who served as one of the Reporters to the Restatement (Second), similarly has explained that "often a paucity of cases or a confusion in the courts' analyses makes it impossible starkly to contrast innovation with tradition."
Most contracts casebooks, for this reason, contain a disclaimer before quoting from the Restatement (Second). They typically caution students that they cannot rely on the work as an accurate statement of the law. For exam ple, Professors Robert W. Hamilton, Alan Scott Rau, and Russell J. Wein traub warn in their textbook: "The Restatement provisions are usually drawn from case precedent, though they do not always reflect the 'majority' view. Sometimes a Restatement provision sets forth what the Reporter and Advis ers think the rule should be even though there is little precedent for it."Professor Steven J. Burton likewise explains in his casebook that the law in some jurisdictions may differ from the provisions of the Restatement (Sec ond), but assures his readers that "the Restatement (Second)...serves as a conventional statement of 'the modern view' of the law, even when it differs from the formal law on the books in a particular jurisdiction."
Disclaimers of this sort seem somewhat inadequate given the prominent role of the Restatement (Second) throughout first-year contracts courses. Stu dents cannot critically think about the legal system unless they have an accu rate understanding of what courts actually do. Accordingly, they need clear guidance on when the Restatement (Second) reflects actual contract law and when it merely states a proposal that has not yet gone into practice.
To address this problem, I recently undertook a survey to determine how courts have received some of the modern rules in the Restatement (Second). My survey considered six important and innovative sections:
. Section 15(1)(b), which states a new rule for determining when a mental illness or defect makes a promise voidable;
. Section 86, which states a new rule for when past services may serve as a basis for enforcing promises;
. Section 87(2), which states a new rule for when reliance can make an offer irrevocable;
. Section 89, which states a new rule on the enforceability of contract modifications in view of unanticipated circumstances;
. Section 139, which states a new rule on when reliance can make a promise enforceable notwithstanding the statute of frauds;and
. Section 153, which states a new rule on when a unilateral mistake can make a promise voidable.
I analyzed these six sections because they typically arise in contracts casebooks used by students during their first year of law school.
The study had an uncomplicated methodology. Almost thirty-five years have passed since the American Law Institute began work on the Restate ment of Contracts in 1963, and more than fifteen years have passed since it published these rules in their final form in 1981.During this time, 241 cases from a wide variety of jurisdictions have cited these six sections.In con ducting the survey, I simply read all of these cases.
The survey produced surprising results. Although the six sections con tradicted long-standing traditional rules - including black letter rules that ap peared in the original Restatement of Contracts(the "Restatement") published in 1932 - courts almost universally accepted them. Only eight de cisions rejected or criticized the rules.The other cases cited the rules favor ably when applying them or discussing them in dicta.
The study does not answer the nagging question about whether the Re statement (Second) accurately states the law in most jurisdictions, but it takesan important first step. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes famously defined the law as merely a prediction about what a court will do when presented with particular facts.Under that definition, the new rules in sections 15(1)(b), 86(1), 87(2), 89(a), 139, and 153 certainly come close to the status of law. In view of the overwhelming support for these provisions to date, it is reason able to predict that most courts will follow them in the future.
Although I initially had sought to determine only how courts had re ceived these new rules in the Restatement (Second), I observed an unex pected phenomenon in reading the cases. In particular, most courts simply deferred to the new rules. In the vast majority of cases, courts gave no rea sons for their decisions to embrace the six sections. They simply cited them as they would cite a statute or code and did not question their authority.
This practice raises an important normative question: Should courts fol low the Restatement (Second) as readily as they currently do? This Article seeks to address that policy issue in addition to describing the survey. It con cludes that, although some arguments counsel against deference to an aca demic work such as the Restatement (Second), on balance, the practice does more good than harm. By deferring to the Restatement (Second), courts have tended to promote uniformity and certainty in the law of contracts and to conserve judicial resources. Although deference to the Restatement (Second) may alter the substance of the law in some jurisdictions, such changes gener ally do not have deleterious consequences.
The remainder of this Article consists of four parts. Part II describes the development of the Restatement and its successor, the Restatement (Second). Part III describes the survey and shows the extent to which courts have fol lowed the six new rules. Part IV evaluates the propriety of judicial deference to the Restatement (Second). Part V concludes by predicting that even more decisions will support the new rules in the future.

questions.question: Whether courts have accepted and applied modern scholarly formulations of contract law in place of older traditional rules
Whether courts commonly cite and adopt rules from influential scholarly restatements without providing independent, case-specific reasoning
Whether judicial deference to influential scholarly restatements produces desirable outcomes (for example, greater uniformity, certainty, and efficiency) and is therefore normatively justified

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How do casebook selection practices and pedagogical choices (e.g., using multi-issue appellate cases or emphasizing litigation realities) shape students' understanding of contract law and practice?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?

When and to what extent should post-contractual promises (e.g., promises for additional payment to induce performance already owed or post-sale statements) be enforceable as warranties or modifications?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 34umemlrev499!!ARTICLE: Origins of Promissory Estoppel: Justifiable Reliance and Commercial Uncertainty Before Williston's Restatement
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Origins of Promissory Estoppel: Justifiable Reliance and Commercial Uncertainty Before Williston's Restatement

shared_topics.topic: development and role of reliance/promissory estoppel in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the nineteenth-century commercial roots of justifiable reliance/promissory estoppel and argues courts historically used reliance to enforce flexible commercial promises; Paper B examines Restatement (Second) provisions (e.g., §§87(2), 139) that formalize reliance-based enforcement and surveys how courts have accepted those modern reliance doctrines.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how courts historically used reliance and equitable reasoning to overcome common-law barriers (like the preexisting-duty rule) to enforce modifications in response to commercial uncertainty; Paper B analyzes §89 of the Restatement (Second), which creates a modern rule permitting modification without new consideration when circumstances were unanticipated, and surveys judicial adoption of that rule.

shared_topics.topic: when past or gratuitous promises can be enforced (past/moral consideration)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the conventional account that justifiable reliance arose from gratuitous/hardship promises with evidence of commercial reliance enforcement, while Paper B studies §86 of the Restatement (Second) (promises in recognition of past benefits) and reports widespread judicial acceptance of that modern approach.

shared_topics.topic: offer formation, unilateral/indefinite/at-will offers, and irrevocability via reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines nineteenth-century problems enforcing unilateral, indefinite, or at-will promises and how courts used reliance to fill doctrinal gaps in offer and acceptance, whereas Paper B addresses §87(2) of the Restatement (Second) (when reliance makes an offer irrevocable) and surveys how courts have applied that rule.

shared_topics.topic: the Restatements' influence on doctrinal history and judicial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques Williston's Restatement for downplaying earlier commercial reliance decisions and argues that Restatement framing shaped later doctrine, while Paper B empirically assesses the Restatement (Second)'s normative versus descriptive role and documents courts' deference to its modern contract rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016michstlrev1267!!ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?

shared_topics.topic: judicial classification of transactions (gift/trust versus contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates when courts treat charitable naming-rights arrangements as gifts, trusts, or contracts and how that classification determines available remedies; Paper B examines how courts have embraced (or rejected) modern contract rules from the Restatement (Second), which likewise reflects courts' choices about which doctrinal framework governs disputes.

shared_topics.topic: reliance on contract doctrines to supply terms, remedies, or fill gaps in transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that applying contract law (and related doctrines like implied terms, duration mechanisms, and morals clauses) can prevent or resolve naming-rights disputes; Paper B analyzes specific contract doctrines (e.g., modification, past consideration, promissory estoppel) and shows how courts adopt them to enforce or adjust promises in situations where formal rules would otherwise fail.

shared_topics.topic: normative question of whether courts should adopt or defer to particular doctrinal frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates as a policy matter that courts and parties should embrace contract law instead of gift law for naming-rights arrangements; Paper B asks whether courts ought to defer to the Restatement (Second) as an authoritative statement of modern contract law and evaluates the policy consequences of such deference.

shared_topics.topic: need for clarity, uniformity, and predictability in resolving private-law disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights confusion and harmful unpredictability when courts apply gift or trust law to naming-rights transactions and recommends contract-based practices to increase fairness and foreseeability; Paper B documents how the Restatement (Second) has promoted uniformity and certainty by supplying widely-cited modern rules and argues that such uniform rules conserve judicial resources.

shared_topics.topic: case-law survey/empirical analysis of how courts treat doctrinal issues
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conducts and synthesizes case law on how courts have categorized and enforced naming-rights transactions to support its argument for treating them as contracts; Paper B performs a systematic survey of hundreds of cases citing six Restatement (Second) sections to measure judicial reception and usage of modern contract rules.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:"Why Infer"? What the New Institutional Economics Has to Say About Law-Supplied Default Rules

shared_topics.topic: judicially supplied implied terms / default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how courts have adopted provisions of the Restatement (Second) that effectively supply substantive rules or fill gaps in parties' bargains, while Paper B theorizes when and how courts should supply implied terms or default rules, offering an institutional-economics framework for that judicial gap-filling.

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based doctrines and enforcement without fresh consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys Restatement provisions (e.g., §§86, 87(2), 139) and case law showing courts enforcing promises on reliance or past performance despite lack of classical consideration, and Paper B analyzes precontractual reliance and when reliance-based interventions (promissory estoppel/option-by-reliance) are justified as law-supplied obligations.

shared_topics.topic: normative justification of judicial rulemaking and deference (efficiency, uniformity, and costs/benefits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether courts should defer to an academic authority (the Restatement) and highlights effects like uniformity and resource savings, whereas Paper B develops a comparative net-benefit/transaction-costs methodology to normatively justify when legal decisionmakers should impose rules rather than leave gaps to private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: contract modification, unforeseen circumstances, and incomplete/long-term contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on §89 and related doctrines that make contract modifications enforceable in view of unanticipated difficulties, and Paper B addresses incomplete contracting—including quantity terms and long-term/subcontracting contexts—examining when courts should or should not fill gaps given unpredictability, asset specificity, and behavioral constraints.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: THE LIFE HISTORY OF AN IDEAL LEGAL TRANSPLANT

shared_topics.topic: the role of Restatements in shaping and legitimizing contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how section 90 of the First Restatement (and Williston's framing) catalyzed the development and diffusion of promissory estoppel, while Paper B empirically studies how multiple provisions of the Restatement (Second) have been cited and treated by courts, assessing the Restatement's practical authority and influence.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the Willistonian estoppel framing unintentionally liberalized and broadened estoppel beyond older formal constraints, and Paper B documents the Restatement (Second)'s replacement of rigid doctrines (preexisting duty, past consideration, statute of frauds formalities) with more flexible, fairness-oriented rules that courts have embraced.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms of legal diffusion and transplantation (including 'reverse' influence and normative authority)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents promissory estoppel as an 'ideal legal transplant' exported from American courts back to English and foreign jurisdictions due to its malleability and utility, while Paper B addresses how the Restatement (Second) functions as an academic-normative vehicle that courts defer to, thereby diffusing model rules across jurisdictions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 16nevlj659!!ARTICLE: Rethinking Promissory Estoppel
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rethinking Promissory Estoppel

shared_topics.topic: the influence of American Law Institute Restatements on the substance of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the ALI's First Restatement (especially Section 90) fundamentally altered contract doctrine, while Paper B empirically surveys how the Restatement (Second)'s innovative sections have been adopted by courts and thereby shaped modern contract law.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that Section 90 eliminated traditional requirements of mutual assent and consideration (promissory estoppel), and Paper B studies Restatement (Second) provisions (e.g., §§86, 89, 87(2)) that similarly relax or replace classical rules by enforcing promises based on reliance, past benefit, or unanticipated circumstances.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the doctrinal legitimacy of promissory estoppel as promulgated by the ALI, and Paper B raises and evaluates the normative issue of whether courts should defer to the Restatement (Second) as an authoritative source, showing many courts simply cite it without independent reasoning.

shared_topics.topic: historical and forensic examination of the drafters' use of precedent in formulating Restatement rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conducts a detailed forensic review of the cases Williston cited to justify Section 90 and challenges those factual/legal claims, while Paper B discusses the Restatement (Second)'s drafting choices (reporter notes, normative aims) and uses case-survey evidence to assess how well the Restatement reflects or advances existing precedent.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recent Defenses of Consideration: Commodification and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of gratuitous or past-consideration promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically examines courts' reception of Restatement (Second) §86 and related provisions that make promises based on past benefits or non-bargained exchanges enforceable; Paper B directly debates whether donative or gratuitous promises should be legally enforceable, critiquing contemporary defenses of the traditional consideration requirement that would bar such enforcement.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies and questions the extent to which courts defer to the Restatement (Second) as an authoritative source that effectively becomes law, while Paper B engages with prominent scholarly defenses (Eisenberg, Markovits) and treats academic theory as a driver of doctrinal justification and potential legal change.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises and evaluates normative policy questions about whether courts ought to adopt the Restatement's preferred rules (weighing uniformity, certainty, and other policy consequences), and Paper B analyzes and rejects specific normative arguments (commodification, collaboration) offered to justify keeping the traditional requirement of consideration.

shared_topics.topic: the shift from traditional black-letter doctrines to more flexible modern rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and analyzes courts' movement from traditional rules (e.g., preexisting-duty rule, strict nonenforceability of past consideration) toward Restatement (Second) reforms (e.g., §§86, 89), and Paper B addresses that same fault line by debating whether the traditional consideration doctrine should be retained or reformed in light of modern theoretical arguments.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Making Contracts Relevant: Thirteen Lessons for the First-Year Contracts Course

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how drafting choices, merger clauses, and summary-judgment practice determine whether businesses get paid or settle, reflecting a practitioner's perspective on how rules operate in commerce; Paper B examines whether the Restatement (Second) reflects or shapes the law that courts apply in practice, and how judicial deference to an academic formulation changes legal outcomes—both probe the descriptive vs. normative status of contract rules and implications for advising clients.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly contrasts expectation and reliance as competing measures of damages and argues reliance is often a pretext to avoid enforcement, and Paper B examines Restatement provisions and case law that shift traditional rules (affecting when expectation or reliance remedies apply) showing courts' movement toward modern standards.

papers.node_id: 58hastingslj61!!Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters
papers.title: Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters
papers.authors: Jay M. Feinman; Stephen R. Brill
papers.abstract:
Courts and scholars uniformly recite the contract law rule familiar to all first-year students: An advertisement is not an offer. The courts and scholars are wrong. An advertisement is an offer. This Article explains why the purported rule is not the law, why the actual rule is that an advertisement is an offer, why that rule is correct, and what it tells us about contract law in particular and legal doctrine in general.
. The Traditional Rule: An Advertisement Is Not an Offer
It is Hornbook lawthat an advertisement is not an offer. Williston self-assuredly declared the rule to be an application of the dividing line between preliminary negotiations and offers:
Frequently, negotiations for a contract are begun between parties by general expressions of willingness to enter into a bargain upon stated terms and yet the natural construction of the words and conduct of the parties is rather that they are inviting offers, or suggesting the terms of a possible future bargain than making positive offers. Especially is this likely to be true where the words in question are in the form of an advertisement [circular, catalog, or the like]. Thus, if goods are advertised for sale at a certain price, it is not an offer, and no contract is formed by the statement of an intending purchaser that he will take a specified quantity of the goods at that price. The construction is rather favored that such an advertisement is a mere invitation to enter into a bargain rather than an offer.
Corbin frequently disagreed with Williston, but not on this point:
It is quite possible to make a definite and operative offer to buy or to sell goods by advertisement, in a newspaper, by a handbill, [a catalog or circular] or on a placard in a store window. It is not customary to do this, however; and the presumption is the other way. Neither the advertiser nor the reader of [the] notice understands that the latter is empowered to close the deal without further expression by the [advertiser]. Such advertisements are understood to be mere requests to consider and examine and negotiate; and no one can reasonably regard them otherwise unless the circumstances are exceptional and the words used are very plain and clear.
Seventy and fifty years, respectively, after original publication, the modern revisions to the Williston and Corbin treatises have barely altered these statements of the rule.In addition, all of their modern counterparts - Calamari and Perillo, Farnsworth, and Murray - concur.Indeed, only Calamari and Perillo regard the doctrine as surprising, though conceding that, "rightly or wrongly, at an early date it was decided and the law is now settled that there is no offer."The Restatement (Second) of Contracts clearly states the rule: "Advertisements of goods by display, sign, handbill, newspaper, radio or television are not ordinarily intended or understood as offers to sell."Both the first and second Restatements provide an identical illustration that confirms its application: "A, a clothing merchant, advertises overcoats of a certain kind for sale at $ 50. This is not an offer, but an invitation to the public to come and purchase."The legal encyclopedias American Jurisprudence 2d and Corpus Juris Secundum agree.Only the author of an American Law Reports article demurs, observing cautiously: "It appears to be a generally accepted proposition that an advertisement for the sale or purchase of goods at a certain price may or may not constitute an offer the acceptance of which will consummate a contract, the issue turning on the particular facts and circumstances of each case."
Scores of cases also recite the rule that an advertisement is generally not an offer.The recitation is typically succinct, deferring to the weight of judicial and scholarly authority. In the well-known case of Leonard v. PepsiCo, Inc., for example, Pepsi's television commercial advertising the availability of a Harrier jet fighter in exchange for the submission of seven million points collected from Pepsi products was held not to be an offer.Judge Kimba Wood's extensive analysis began with the simple proposition "the general rule is that an advertisement does not constitute an offer," citing the Restatement, Corbin, Williston, Farnsworth, and New York cases.
Courts and scholars justify the rule on two principal grounds.The more specific rationale is that a typical advertisement is too general to be an offer, particularly because it contains no notice of to whom it is directed and no limitation on the number of persons who may accept by attempting to purchase the advertised item. If an advertisement wereconstrued to be an offer, "the advertiser could be bound by an excessive number of contracts requiring delivery of goods far in excess of amounts available."Mesaros v. United States exemplifies the problem; the United States Mint was deluged with applications to buy Statue of Liberty-Ellis Island commemorative gold coins, but the quantity available had been limited by the Act of Congress authorizing the striking of the coins.
The quantity rationale extends to a second, broader rationale, which is that an advertisement is reasonably understood as a notice of goods available and an invitation to examine, negotiate, and buy, but it is not reasonably understood as an offer the acceptance of which obligates the advertiser to sell. This rationale is based partly on the general nature of the advertisement and the quantity problem. As Farnsworth notes, "A customer would not usually have reason to believe that the shopkeeper intended exposure to the risk of a multitude of acceptances resulting in a number of contracts exceeding the shopkeeper's inventory."More broadly, this "reasonableness" rationale is grounded in an empirical assumption that both advertisers and consumers typically understand that a general advertisement is a form of publicity and solicitation, and not the penultimate step in the creation of a legal relationship.Therefore, an advertisement is not an offer because the consumer "knows or has reason to know that the person making it does not intend to conclude a bargain."This rationale reflects the objective theory of contracts.
The "reasonableness" rationale also suggests the exception to the rule: Where there are unusual facts such that the reasonable consumer would understand that an advertiser is manifesting willingness to enter into a bargain, the advertisement is an offer that the consumer can accept.This is often the case when the advertisement uses "language of commitment or some invitation to take action without further communication"and when the advertisement contains more than the usual detail.In the classic case Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis SurplusStore, Inc., the court formulated the much-cited test of whether "the offer is clear, definite, and explicit, and leaves nothing open for negotiation."The store advertised "Saturday 9 A.M… . 1 Black Lapin Stole Beautiful, worth $ 139.50 … . $ 1.00, First Come First Served."This advertisement met the commitment requirement because "some performance was promised in positive terms in return for something requested."Since it was much more specific as to subject matter, offeree, and manner of acceptance than the ordinary advertisement, it constituted an offer that the plaintiff could accept by being the first one in the store on Saturday.
Lefkowitz is particularly instructive because, to use the cliche, it is the exception that proves the rule. The first Restatement offered the following hypothetical: "A, a clothing merchant, advertises overcoats of a certain kind for sale at $ 50. This is not an offer, but an invitation to the public to come and purchase."The second Restatement added a variation to the hypothetical in order to conform with Lefkowitz: "The addition of the words "Out they go Saturday; First Come First Served' might make the advertisement an offer."As in Lefkowitz, an advertisement that is more detailed may be an offer. The Restatement demonstrates the application of the rule and also its force; a general advertisement "is not" an offer, and the addition of more details only "might make" the advertisement an offer.
. The Error of the Supposed Rule that an Advertisement Is Not an Offer
Judicial opinions and the scholarly literature are replete with recitation of the rule that an advertisement is not an offer. But the recitation is an instance of Cardozo's aphorism that "the half truths of one generation tend … to perpetuate themselves in … law as the whole truths of another, when constant repetition brings it about that qualifications, taken once for granted, are … forgotten."For three reasons, the proposition that "an advertisement is not an offer" is not the law. First, the cases that recite the proposition do not apply it. Second, other legal rules and other business practices prevent the propositionfrom being applied. Third, the proposition is inconsistent with the basic principles of contract law.

papers.node_id: 66clevstlrev341!!ARTICLE: IS MORE PARENTAL LEAVE ALWAYS BETTER?: AN ANALYSIS OF POTENTIAL EMPLOYEE PROTECTIONS FOR LEAVE OFFERED OUTSIDE THE FMLA
papers.title: ARTICLE: IS MORE PARENTAL LEAVE ALWAYS BETTER?: AN ANALYSIS OF POTENTIAL EMPLOYEE PROTECTIONS FOR LEAVE OFFERED OUTSIDE THE FMLA
papers.abstract:
Netflix did it.Amazon did it.Google, Twitter, Adobe, and Facebook have all done it.It's trendy, popular, and enticing, but also incredibly important for employees and society. Expanded parental leave appears to be an obvious win for employees. It offers parents the prospect of time off (often paid) to bond with their family's new addition knowing that their jobs await them when their leave expires. Employers who offer them also find these leave policies advantageous, garnering copious, positive praise in the media and likely attracting more candidates for open positions.
However, beneath the surface lies a peril that has, until now, remained virtually unexplored in legal scholarship: what legal protections does an employee have if the very act of taking parental leave is later used against him or her? A groundbreaking study has found that employers perceive employees who use flexible work arrangements as less committed when the arrangements are made for personal reasons.Therefore, an employer would negatively view taking extended time off after the arrival of a baby for purely personal reasons. Even an employer who offers the policy is not immune to judging an employee's commitment by their willingness to use the generous leave.Is there any way in which the law protects new parents who happily enjoy the extra bonding time with their babies from later being labeled as uncommitted, subsequently terminated, or treated adversely in some other way on the job? This Article seeks to answer this currently unexplored question. Unfortunately, any protections offered to employees are far from clear, as too often they are rooted in unsettled legal principles that vary by jurisdiction. These protections also offer little comfort to the employee facing the decision of whether or not to take advantage of a company's expanded parental leave policy.
This Article will explore the question of legal protection for those who have taken advantage of a company's expanded parental leave policy. First, the Article will discuss traditional federal protections that employees enjoy under the Family and Medical Leave Act. Next, the Article will examine what expanded leave policies looklike at some prominent companies. The Article will then analyze potential legal protections for employees who may be retaliated against for using parental leave and will examine why such protections are important not only for employees, but for the greater benefit of society. Finally, the Article will propose greater protections for employees using a company's parental leave to add more certainty and predictability to these important policies. Specifically, the Article will argue that courts should treat parental leave policies as unilateral contracts that are accepted upon performance by the employee. In that way, once the employee takes leave, the company would become contractually bound not to retaliate against that employee.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the current vague public‑policy scrutiny that leaves indemnity and liability‑limiting contracts uncertain and urges a clearer, balanced test for enforcement; Paper B similarly highlights unsettled protections for employees using expanded parental leave and proposes treating employer leave policies as unilateral contracts to create predictability and enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: balancing private autonomy (freedom of contract/policy design) against public‑policy constraints and paternalism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts limit freedom of contract on paternalistic/public‑duty grounds when reviewing liability‑limiting bargains, arguing for weighing positive effects as well as harms; Paper B interrogates how legal doctrines (FMLA, retaliation law, public policy) should constrain or support employer leave policies and whether paternalistic protection or deference to employer policy should prevail.

shared_topics.topic: protection of potentially disadvantaged or vulnerable parties in voluntary bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about bargainers in weaker positions (the indemnitor X) and the role of courts in protecting them from exploitative bargains, while Paper B focuses on employees who may be penalized for exercising leave and the legal need to protect them from retaliation or coercion.

shared_topics.topic: weighing societal/public benefits when evaluating private agreements or policies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that positive externalities (e.g., facilitating public transit via indemnity agreements) should factor into enforceability decisions; Paper B likewise notes that parental leave has broader societal benefits and argues legal protections should reflect and support those benefits.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 96washlrev51!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: legal characterization of non‑traditional contractual commitments (e.g., employer policies and smart contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether employer parental‑leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts accepted by employee performance, while Paper B interrogates the legal nature of machine‑formed 'smart contracts' and whether traditional consent‑based doctrines fit them.

shared_topics.topic: gaps and uncertainty in existing doctrine when applied to novel forms of agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes unsettled federal and state protections for employees who use expanded leave outside the FMLA, and Paper B argues that orthodox contract theory and current literature fail to account for the formation and dispute phases of fully automated smart contracting.

shared_topics.topic: asymmetric power, repeat players, and protection of vulnerable counterparties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights employer leverage and the risk that employees who take leave will be penalized despite generous policies, while Paper B raises concerns about repeat players, consumer arbitration, and how automated systems can disadvantage individual users versus institutional actors.

shared_topics.topic: need for doctrinal or institutional reform to ensure enforceability and meaningful remedies/ex post dispute resolution
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes treating leave policies as contractually binding to provide predictability and protection, and Paper B proposes adopting a reliance‑based theory for smart contracts and a decentralized, user‑driven ex post dispute resolution mechanism to address enforcement and incompleteness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56depaullrev55!!ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH

shared_topics.topic: using contract doctrine to enforce nontraditional or incomplete promises (e.g., agreements-to-agree, unilateral promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines ADR agreements as 'middle-position' contracts to bargain and urges courts to treat them under common-law contract principles (including good-faith duties) rather than formalist categories, while Paper B argues that employer parental-leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts accepted by performance so that employees obtain enforceable protections.

shared_topics.topic: criticizing formalist yes-contract/no-contract rules and urging flexible, contextual enforcement and remedial design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts' binary formalism in labeling ADR agreements and calls for relational/contextual analysis and tailored remedies, and Paper B similarly identifies gaps and uncertainty in existing doctrine (e.g., FMLA and traditional contract forms) and proposes doctrinal adaptation to provide clearer protections to leave-taking employees.

shared_topics.topic: tension between public policy support for cooperative practices and legal under- or over-enforcement that undermines those practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes that public policy favors ADR yet courts' misapplication of statutes and formalist rules threaten ADR's efficacy, and Paper B observes that popular employer parental-leave policies can be undermined by weak legal protections or employer retaliation unless the law adapts to secure their benefits.

shared_topics.topic: risk of adverse consequences for participants in employer-offered or cooperative processes and the need for legal remedies against retaliation or harm
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how rigid enforcement can produce emotional harm or one-sided outcomes for parties who engage in ADR processes, and Paper B focuses on how employees who use expanded parental leave may be labeled uncommitted or retaliated against absent clear legal protections and recommends remedial doctrines to prevent such harms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77neblrev756!!ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law

shared_topics.topic: enforcing non-written employer or property promises via contract-like doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that employers' expanded parental leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts (binding once an employee performs by taking leave), while Paper B surveys how courts use estoppel and related doctrines to enforce oral or conduct-based promises in property transfers and servitude disputes where formal writing or consideration is lacking.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance in giving legal effect to promises outside formal requirements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on employees' reliance in taking leave (and the legal consequences if employers retaliate), and Paper B analyzes how reliance functions as evidence of a promise (or as an independent basis for estoppel) in property cases.

shared_topics.topic: using equitable doctrines to fill gaps left by statutory or formal protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates gaps in statutory protection under the FMLA and proposes equitable contract treatment of corporate leave policies to prevent retaliation, while Paper B documents how estoppel operates to supply enforceability where statutory/formal requirements (consideration, statute of frauds/writing) would otherwise defeat relief.

shared_topics.topic: protecting individuals who act to their detriment based on others' representations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned with protecting new parents who suffer adverse employment actions after relying on generous leave policies, and Paper B describes estoppel-based protection for parties (tenants, neighbors, transferees) who suffer harm after relying on another's representations or conduct.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50emorylj1047!!ARTICLE: Contracting With Electronic Agents
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Contracting With Electronic Agents

shared_topics.topic: whether nontraditional promises/acts should create binding contracts when accepted by performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that employer parental-leave policies offered outside the FMLA should be treated as unilateral contracts that become binding once an employee takes leave; Paper B analyzes whether transactions arranged without a traditional offer/acceptance—specifically by electronic agents—should be enforced, examining how performance and agent actions can give rise to contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy of traditional contract and agency doctrines to address novel forms of exchange or promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that existing employment and statutory protections (like the FMLA and retaliation doctrine) are unsettled for expanded corporate leave policies and asks whether contract law can fill gaps; Paper B demonstrates that common law contract and agency principles, and current statutory initiatives, do not clearly resolve enforceability questions posed by electronic agents.

shared_topics.topic: reliance, reasonable expectations, and normative justifications for enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the need for predictability and protecting employees' reasonable expectations when they use employer leave policies; Paper B evaluates normative theories of contractual obligation (will vs. reliance) and highlights protecting individuals' ability to pursue reasonable objectives as a basis for enforcing exchanges arranged by electronic agents.

shared_topics.topic: regulatory or doctrinal reform to protect parties using new mechanisms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes doctrinal change—treating expanded parental-leave policies as unilateral contracts—to provide greater certainty and protection for employees; Paper B discusses potential doctrinal and statutory approaches (including extending agency or personhood principles or new statutes) to govern transactions made by electronic agents and the need for legal adaptation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81notredamelrev747!!ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW AS AN ITERATIVE PROCESS: A PRELIMINARY INQUIRY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW AS AN ITERATIVE PROCESS: A PRELIMINARY INQUIRY

shared_topics.topic: legal uncertainty and the need for predictability in rights and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the complexity and fact-sensitivity of common-law development and the resulting demand for careful case-by-case reading to understand legal outcomes, while Paper B emphasizes that protections for employees taking expanded parental leave are ‘‘unsettled’’ and vary across jurisdictions, creating practical uncertainty for individuals deciding whether to use leave.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation and case-law evolution in constraining or enabling change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the common law as an iterative, path-dependent process in which prior cases and judicial choices limit later discretion (with occasional bifurcations enabling change); Paper B analyzes how courts have (or have not) developed doctrines that protect leave-taking employees and explicitly proposes a doctrinal shift (treating leave policies as unilateral contracts) that would require judicial recognition.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between legal rules and social/organizational norms that shape behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that evolving social norms drive departures from self-similar rule application and can precipitate doctrinal bifurcations, while Paper B documents employer norms (e.g., penalizing employees who take leave) and analyzes how legal protections or their absence affect employer and employee behavior and broader social outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: normative- doctrinal proposals to reform law to achieve predictable policy outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws normative implications about the limits of judicial discretion and the desirability of understanding systemic tendencies toward stability, whereas Paper B advances a concrete doctrinal proposal (treating parental-leave policies as unilateral contracts) intended to produce clearer, more predictable protections for employees.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50ucdavislrev405!!ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract

shared_topics.topic: using contract/promise doctrines to define non‑contract legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers propose importing contract concepts — Paper A argues that a criminal 'agreement' should be defined as an exchange of promises, and Paper B argues that employer parental‑leave policies should operate as unilateral contracts accepted by employee performance.

shared_topics.topic: remedying doctrinal vagueness by adopting clearer legal standards
shared_topics.justification: Each paper diagnoses uncertainty in existing law (conspiracy's undefined 'agreement' and unclear protections for use of expanded parental leave) and proposes a bright‑line doctrinal fix to increase predictability for courts and fact‑finders.

shared_topics.topic: how inferences about commitment or intent from conduct should be treated legally
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how an agreement evidences seriousness of criminal intent and should be proven by promises, while Paper B addresses employers inferring lack of commitment from taking leave and seeks legal rules to prevent adverse consequences from those inferences.

shared_topics.topic: filling statutory gaps with common‑law or doctrinal innovations
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the limits of statutory protections (conspiracy law and First Amendment concerns in A; the FMLA's scope in B) and argue for common‑law or doctrinal adjustments (contract framing, evidentiary standards, or new rules) to protect interests the statutes do not clearly secure.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1985wislrev565!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: MACAULAY, MACHEIL, AND THE DISCOVERY OF SOLIDARITY AND POWER IN CONTRACT LAW.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: MACAULAY, MACHEIL, AND THE DISCOVERY OF SOLIDARITY AND POWER IN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: continuing employment relationships as relational contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats expanded parental leave as a term embedded in an ongoing employment relationship and argues the law should recognize leave policies as binding (unilateral) commitments; Paper B develops the relational-contract framework that emphasizes contracts as parts of continuing relations rather than discrete transactions and analyzes how obligations evolve within such relationships.

shared_topics.topic: power asymmetries and potential employer domination of employees
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how employers may penalize or retaliate against employees for taking parental leave—illustrating employer power to stigmatize and punish leave-takers—while Paper B centrally theorizes domination and hierarchies in continuing contractual relations and how imbalance of bargaining power shapes outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: limits of traditional legal doctrines to address real-world contracting practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents gaps and jurisdictional uncertainty in federal protections (e.g., FMLA) and argues existing doctrine inadequately protects leave-takers, motivating a doctrinal reframing; Paper B argues mainstream contract doctrine is often marginal to contracts-in-action and insufficient to capture the social norms and practices governing real-world contracting.

shared_topics.topic: reconceptualizing legal remedies or doctrine to protect vulnerable relational parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a specific doctrinal reform—treating employer leave policies as unilateral contracts accepted by performance—to create enforceable protections for employees, while Paper B advocates for incorporating relational insights (social norms, solidarity, regulatory tools) into contract law to address inequities and better govern continuing relationships.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2007uilllrev881!!ARTICLE: "LAW &" GRATUITOUS PROMISES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: "LAW &" GRATUITOUS PROMISES

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of promises that are not classic bargained-for exchanges (gifts vs employer leave promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates why gratuitous gift promises are generally unenforceable under the consideration doctrine and examines exceptions (e.g., charitable subscriptions), while Paper B treats employer parental-leave policies as promises that may be enforceable as unilateral offers accepted by performance and asks what legal remedy employees have when relying on those promises.

shared_topics.topic: use of promissory estoppel / unilateral-contract doctrines to protect reliance on promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promissory estoppel as a doctrinal exception that can enforce non‑bargained promises based on reliance, and Paper B proposes treating expanded parental leave as a unilateral contract (or reliance‑based obligation) to prevent employer retaliation after an employee takes leave.

shared_topics.topic: bringing behavioral evidence into legal analysis of promise enforcement and employment decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates behavioral law & economics (BLE) critiques of classical law & economics in explaining why some promises should be enforced, while Paper B cites behavioral studies about employer perceptions of commitment to motivate why legal rules should address the real‑world biases that harm employees who take leave.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should be used to further social policy goals by protecting reliance on socially valuable promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks whether the consideration doctrine’s exchange focus should delimit contract law even when enforcing promises (e.g., charitable pledges) would serve social aims, and Paper B argues for legal protection of parental‑leave takers to encourage bonding leave and achieve broader societal benefits.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91califlrev1573!!ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of one-sided or nontraditional promises (e.g., unilateral offers/firm policies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when parties’ expressed terms and tacit assumptions should bind the other side and when instruments should be reformed to reflect the actual agreement; Paper B argues that employer parental-leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts accepted by performance so that employees who take leave obtain enforceable protection against retaliation.

shared_topics.topic: reliance and allocation of risk as grounds for relief or protection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conditions relief for mechanical and shared-factual mistakes on whether the nonmistaken party justifiably relied on the contract or whether the risk was allocated to a party; Paper B centers on employees’ reliance on generous leave policies and asks what legal rules should protect those who rely on such policies from adverse treatment.

shared_topics.topic: critique of existing doctrinal categories and proposals for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques traditional mistake categories (mutual, unilateral, mistranscription, misunderstanding) and proposes a functional taxonomy and new rules; Paper B highlights unsettled employment-law principles governing leave protections and proposes a doctrinal shift (treating leave as unilateral contracts) to provide clearer remedies.

shared_topics.topic: use of policy considerations (efficiency, fairness, social welfare) to justify legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly develops rules for mistake based on efficiency, social morality, and experience; Paper B evaluates legal protections for parental leave in light of societal benefits and employee welfare and uses policy arguments to justify stronger protections.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45wakeforestlrev607!!ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS

shared_topics.topic: using contract law doctrines to protect employees against employer power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that employer parental-leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts enforceable upon employee performance to prevent retaliation, and Paper B analyzes how expanding contextual contract doctrines can be used to shift bargaining power toward sporadic or disadvantaged parties such as employees.

shared_topics.topic: performance-as-acceptance and the evidentiary role of performance in workplace policies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A anchors its proposed protection on the idea that an employee's use of leave constitutes acceptance of an employer's unilateral offer, while Paper B treats parties' performance as a key contextual factor courts might use to discern the ‘real’ deal between contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of courts versus legislatures in creating worker protections and changing bargaining dynamics
shared_topics.justification: Paper A seeks judicial recognition (through contract doctrine) to create predictable protections for leave-takers, and Paper B questions whether courts should effect systemic shifts in bargaining power through contextualized adjudication versus leaving such policy choices to legislatures.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between legal certainty/predictability and contextualized, discretionary adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes employees' need for clearer, predictable protections across jurisdictions, arguing for a bright-line contract rule, whereas Paper B warns that high-context approaches increase judicial discretion and outcome variability, undermining predictability even if they aim for substantive justice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73uchilrev1299!!ARTICLE: Commodification and Contract Formation: Placing the Consideration Doctrine on Stronger Foundations
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Commodification and Contract Formation: Placing the Consideration Doctrine on Stronger Foundations

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of unilateral promises and unilateral contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why the law generally refuses to enforce unilateral promises and how the consideration doctrine distinguishes unenforceable promises from enforceable contracts; Paper B argues that employer parental-leave policies function as unilateral offers that should be accepted by employee performance (taking leave) and thus be enforceable against retaliation.

shared_topics.topic: the role and justification of the consideration doctrine as a gatekeeper for contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques existing theoretical defenses of the consideration doctrine and seeks firmer foundations for when promises become binding, while Paper B confronts the doctrine's practical limits—asking whether expanded leave policies should create enforceable obligations even when traditional consideration/formalities are unclear.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formalist requirements and parties' intent in determining legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts formalist devices (e.g., requiring recited consideration) with the principle of honoring parties' intentions in contract law; Paper B similarly questions whether courts should look beyond formal doctrinal hurdles to give effect to employers' public leave promises and the employees' expectations when they use those policies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 32arizstlj1283!!ARTICLE: When should Contract Law Supply a Liability Rule or Term?: Framing a Principle of Unification for Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: When should Contract Law Supply a Liability Rule or Term?: Framing a Principle of Unification for Contracts

shared_topics.topic: whether employer-promulgated leave policies create enforceable unilateral contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly argues that expanded parental leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts accepted by employee performance, while Paper B analyzes when courts should supply or recognize contract terms (including unilateral contract doctrines) to give effect to promises made outside formal bargaining.

shared_topics.topic: legal protection for reliance interests arising from non‑negotiated promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on employees who rely on employer leave policies and the risk of retaliation after taking leave, and Paper B develops a comparative net‑benefit framework for when the law should impose liability or terms to protect reliance (e.g., promissory estoppel, reliance in bidding contexts).

shared_topics.topic: the justification and limits of judicially supplying terms/default rules to achieve predictability and social welfare
shared_topics.justification: Paper A seeks judicially cognizable doctrines to provide certainty for employees using employer leave (arguing for contractual binding once leave is taken), and Paper B offers a general instrumental methodology for when courts should supply law‑made terms or liability rules to fill incomplete agreements and promote efficient, predictable outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48stanlrev481!!ARTICLE: Offer, Acceptance, and Efficient Reliance
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Offer, Acceptance, and Efficient Reliance

shared_topics.topic: unilateral contracts and acceptance-by-performance as a basis for enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when an offer becomes binding (including offers that are accepted by performance) and when reliance makes an offer irrevocable; Paper B explicitly proposes treating employer parental‑leave policies as unilateral offers that employees accept by taking leave, creating contractual obligations on the employer.

shared_topics.topic: reliance/promissory estoppel and the efficiency of enforcing non‑express promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an 'efficient reliance' rationale for enforcing commitments (and links it to doctrines like promissory estoppel), while Paper B centers on legal protection for employees who rely on expanded leave—invoking reliance-based doctrines as the mechanism to prevent employer retaliation.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoff between case‑by‑case reliance inquiries and the need for predictable, bright‑line rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether courts should assess reliance efficiency on a fact‑specific basis or adopt bright‑line rules, and Paper B likewise emphasizes the doctrinal uncertainty surrounding protections for leave‑takers and argues for a clearer rule (treating leave as contract) to provide predictability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 66smulrev341!!ARTICLE: Teaching Contract Law: Introducing Students to a Critical Perspective Through Indentured Servitude and Sharecropper Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Teaching Contract Law: Introducing Students to a Critical Perspective Through Indentured Servitude and Sharecropper Contracts

shared_topics.topic: contract law's role in regulating employer-employee/labor relationships
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that employer parental-leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts binding employers once employees perform (take leave), directly invoking contract law to govern workplace rights; Paper B uses historical labor contracts (indentures, sharecropping) to show how contract doctrines have been deployed to structure and control labor relations.

shared_topics.topic: application and limits of contract-formation doctrines (offer, acceptance, consideration) in contexts of unequal power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on formation concepts — particularly unilateral contract acceptance by performance — to propose legal protections for employees who use leave; Paper B teaches and critiques core formation doctrines (offer, acceptance, consideration) by examining how they operated in highly asymmetric indenture and sharecropper agreements.

shared_topics.topic: critical interrogation of contract law as either protective or oppressive and calls for doctrinal/interpretive change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes the assumption that expanded employer benefits always help employees and recommends a doctrinal shift (treating leave as enforceable contractual promises) to protect workers; Paper B urges presenting a critical perspective showing that contract law has facilitated social domination, encouraging students to question orthodox doctrinal assumptions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48sclrev293!!ARTICLE: The Counterpoise of Contracts: The Reasonable Person Standard and the Subjectivity of Judgment
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Counterpoise of Contracts: The Reasonable Person Standard and the Subjectivity of Judgment

shared_topics.topic: the reasonable person standard and the role of subjective judgment in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is explicitly devoted to analyzing how the reasonable person standard mediates subjective judgment in contract law; Paper B relies on similar interpretive questions (e.g., what expectations are 'reasonable') when assessing whether employees' reliance on expanded parental-leave policies should give rise to enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: whether employer-issued policies/promises can operate as unilateral contracts accepted by employee performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues directly that expanded parental-leave policies should be treated as unilateral contracts accepted when an employee takes leave; Paper A examines doctrines (offer, acceptance, and the objective/reasonable-person tests) that determine when promises become enforceable upon performance.

shared_topics.topic: using contract doctrine to protect reliance-based expectations against adverse treatment or retaliation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B proposes using contract concepts to shield employees who take leave from later retaliation, while Paper A analyzes how contract law's balance between subjectivity and objective standards can vindicate or undermine parties' reliance interests and expectations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE GAP-FILLING ROLE OF THE UNIDROIT PRINCIPLES IN INTERNATIONAL SALES LAW: SOME COMMENTS ON THE INTERPLAY BETWEEN THE PRINCIPLES AND THE CISG

shared_topics.topic: the gap‑filling role of non‑statutory or private normative instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how employer parental‑leave policies and common‑law doctrines (like unilateral contract or reliance) can operate to fill gaps left by the FMLA and other statutes, while Paper B examines how the UNIDROIT Principles serve to supplement and fill gaps in the CISG and international commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay and hierarchy between primary legal rules and supplementary norms across jurisdictions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with the tension between federal statutes (FMLA), employer policies, and varying state/common‑law doctrines about employee protections, and Paper B examines the coordination between treaty law (CISG), the UNIDROIT Principles, and trade usages to determine which rules govern international sales disputes.

shared_topics.topic: the need to promote legal certainty by grounding supplemental rules in parties' expectations, intent, or established usage
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances treating employer leave promises as binding upon employee performance to create predictable protections and reliance interests for workers, while Paper B argues the UNIDROIT Principles should supplement the CISG only where consistent with the parties' intent and trade usages to provide predictable, uniform outcomes for international contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75geolj1575!!ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.

shared_topics.topic: when and how a promise or policy becomes a legally binding obligation (including acceptance by performance/unilateral-contract reasoning)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how English contract law has determined when parties' promises become binding or are discharged by subsequent events (examining doctrines that govern when obligations persist or are excused), while Paper B argues that employer parental-leave policies should be treated as unilateral offers accepted by employee performance, creating enforceable contractual obligations not to retaliate.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A retraces historical authority and contends that key English impossibility cases are often misread or poorly taught, urging clearer doctrinal understanding; Paper B critiques the unsettled and varying case law protecting leave-takers and urges courts to adopt a clearer doctrinal rule (treating leave policies as contracts) to resolve inconsistency.
