papers.node_id: 52amjcompl433!!ARTICLE: Mistake in Contract Formation
papers.title: ARTICLE: Mistake in Contract Formation
papers.abstract: A contract would not be binding if it could be repudiated later by a party who found it to be disadvantageous. But the point of a contract is that each party can obtain something of more value to himself than the performance he promises in return. The law reconciles these considerations by providing that sometimes a party who has made a mistake will obtain relief, and sometimes he will not. As we will see, the classical formulation of when he can obtain relief is when he has made a mistake as to the "substance" of the performance for which he is contracting. According to the classical formulation, he cannot obtain relief when he has merely made and error in "motive," that is, in his reasons for wanting that performance. The formula "error in substance" has been rejected or reinterpreted by many jurists because, if it neglects the parties' motives for contracting, it seems irrelevant to what they were trying to accomplish. Thus, they have tried take the parties' motives into account, either by reformulating the concept of an "error in substance" or by rejecting it. At the same time, they have insisted that a mere error in the motive of a party does not matter. The result, as one might expect, has been confusion. We will first examine the efforts that have been made to distinguish the mistakes that warrant relief from mere errors in motive. We will show that these efforts can succeed if we adopt the approach of certain modern French jurists which corresponds to that of older ones who wrote in the Aristotelian tradition. We will then show - paradoxically it might seem - that there are cases in which a mistake in motive by one party should nevertheless warrant relief.

questions.question: When does a contracting party's mistake justify judicial relief from the contract - specifically, how should courts treat mistakes about the nature or substance of the performance being exchanged versus mistakes about the party's reasons or motive for entering the contract?

Can reconceptualizing the substance/motive distinction to take parties' motives into account produce a coherent rule that identifies which mistakes warrant relief, and are there circumstances in which a mistake of motive should nonetheless justify relief?

papers.title: ARTICLE: Mistakes, Changed Circumstances and Intent
papers.abstract:
Suppose a purchaser wishes to buy a vacation home using the Internet. She desires a house in the country where she can escape the sounds and stresses of the city. On the basis of pictures posted on a website, she enters into an agreement to purchase a house that looks like an idyllic country home. During inspection, she discovers a noisy, nearby road. The house looks exactly as it does on the website, but the posted pictures failed to capture the surrounding environment. The purchaser imagined her mornings would be filled with the sounds of chirping birds, not blaring car horns. The noise from the road would not be unbearable to the average homebuyer, but it undermines the purchaser's reason for buying the house. Could our purchaser avoid the transaction? Should she be allowed to?
Contract law requires that in order for promises to be legally enforceable, they must be supported by consideration.A corollary, often referred to as the "bargain principle," provides that bargains will beenforced according to their terms.Stated another way, as long as there is a bargained-for exchange of a legal detriment (or conferral of a legal benefit), courts should not consider the adequacy of consideration. There are, however, situations where the parties have entered into a bargain and then sought either to avoid enforcement or to reform the contract terms. A party seeking avoidance or reformation must prove one or more of several established "defenses" to enforcement.The most common contract defenses are duress, unconscionability, incapacity, fraud, and the "basic assumption" defensesof mutual mistake, unilateral mistake, impossibility, frustration of purpose and commercial impracticability.In this Article, I limit my discussion to basic assumption defenses. Several prevailing rationales explain why a party should be allowed to escape contractual liability despite the sufficiency of consideration where there has been a failure of a basic assumption material to the transaction. No single rationale or principle, however, unifies all basic assumption defenses. Several commentators have noted that similar fact patterns applying a given doctrine often yield inconsistent results.Parties' employment of these defenses, and courts' analyses of them, is often confusing and inaccurate.
This Article proposes that basic assumption defenses can best be explained and analyzed through the prism of contractual intent. Although typically discussed in terms of a singular concept, contractual intent in fact comprises various facets, which I refer to as volitional intent, cognitive intent, and contextual purposive intent. Part II provides an introduction to, and description of, my proposed expanded intent analysis. Part III applies expanded intent analysis to cases involving basic assumption defenses. Part IV addresses possible concerns with using a dynamic approach/expanded intent analysis. This Article concludes that adopting my proposed intent-based analysis has several advantages over the current application of contract defenses. First and foremost, it directly addresses and incorporates contract law's two primary objectives: furthering autonomy and facilitating transactions. Second, because it removes artificial doctrinal distinctions, it eliminates or minimizes confusion and simplifies analysis. Consequently, it provides for greater consistency in judicial decisions. Finally, the approach is flexible, and therefore better accommodates technological advancements, such as the Internet, in the modern marketplace.

questions.question: Under what conditions should a party be allowed to avoid or reform a contract when a fundamental assumption underlying the transaction proves false or circumstances change?

Whether conceptualizing contractual intent as multiple facets (e.g., volitional, cognitive, and contextual/purposive intent) yields a more coherent and predictable framework for evaluating claims to avoid or reform contracts after such failures of assumption?

Whether an intent-based, dynamic framework for assessing contract avoidance/reformation better advances core contract-law objectives (individual autonomy and facilitating transactions) and improves consistency and adaptability to modern market contexts (such as Internet transactions)?

matched_themes: When should courts grant relief for contractual mistake (mutual, unilateral, or induced), and should one unified test govern all mistake cases across legal systems?

Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How should courts resolve agreements founded on mutual misunderstanding: voidness versus enforcing each party's reasonable interpretation?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the 'will' view as a non‑consequentialist account that grounds obligations in the promisor's will and critiques its incompleteness, while Paper B places intent at the center of doctrine—proposing an expanded, multi‑faceted conception of contractual intent (volitional, cognitive, contextual) to explain defenses and enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: when and why contracts should be enforced versus excused or reformed (making vs keeping agreements)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the central twin questions of why people should make agreements and why they should keep them and argues those questions are interlinked, and Paper B examines when parties may avoid or reform bargains (mutual/ unilateral mistake, frustration, impracticability) and offers an intent‑based rationale for permitting non‑enforcement in some cases.

shared_topics.topic: critique of partial doctrinal/theoretical accounts and the need for a more unified explanatory framework
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that singular theories (law‑and‑economics, harm, or will views) are partial and fail to account for both making and keeping agreements, while Paper B criticizes fragmented basic‑assumption doctrines and proposes a unified, dynamic intent analysis to reduce doctrinal confusion and better serve contract law's aims.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of parties' expectations, purposes, and the relational value of agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the value of the agreement‑relation (respect, collaborative community) and how agreements instantiate shared expectations, and Paper B operationalizes similar concerns by focusing on parties' purposive and contextual intentions—how those expectations justify enforcement or excuse when frustrated by changed circumstances.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78neblrev491!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"

shared_topics.topic: the role and sufficiency of consideration in contract enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the bargain principle and the corollary that courts should not probe adequacy of consideration as background for basic-assumption defenses, while Paper B directly interrogates the mutual promise rule and the mutuality-of-obligation corollary, defending a view of consideration that preserves reciprocal promises as the basis for enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: how contractual intent and what counts as a 'promise' determine enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a multi-faceted expanded intent analysis (volitional, cognitive, contextual purposive intent) to resolve mistakes and other defenses, and Paper B analyzes what qualifies as a binding promise (versus intention or illusory promises) and treats presumptions about mutual binding intent as central to doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: doctrines and defenses that permit escape from or reformation of bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A systematically examines basic-assumption defenses (mutual/unilateral mistake, impossibility, frustration of purpose, commercial impracticability) as grounds to avoid or reform contracts, and Paper B addresses when a party's promise fails to bind (mutuality/illusory promise issues) thereby producing non-enforceability or limiting remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the need for doctrinal coherence and the historical development of contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques inconsistent applications of basic-assumption doctrines and advocates an intent-based unifying framework to increase consistency, while Paper B traces 400 years of common-law and equity authority to clarify the proper historical meaning and doctrinal role of mutuality of obligation as a presumptive rule.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58hastingslj61!!Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters

shared_topics.topic: role of intent (objective vs. subjective) in forming and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the objective-reasonableness basis for treating advertisements as offers versus mere invitations, while Paper B develops an expanded intent framework (volitional, cognitive, contextual purposive intent) to decide when parties may avoid or reform bargains—both centrally engage how courts should infer and apply parties' intent.

shared_topics.topic: how modern communications and market practices affect contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how advertising practices and business realities bear on whether an ad should be treated as an offer, and Paper B considers Internet-based listings and modern marketplaces as motivating examples for updating doctrinal rules about mistakes and changed circumstances.

shared_topics.topic: judicial standards of 'reasonable expectations' and their evidentiary application
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on the 'reasonable consumer' rationale (and exceptions where wording creates clear commitment), while Paper B addresses when a buyer's expectations (e.g., about a property's surroundings) justify relief under basic assumption defenses, so both probe when courts should enforce or excuse based on reasonable expectations.

shared_topics.topic: need for doctrinal coherence and reformulation of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that prevailing hornbook rules about advertisements are inconsistent with other legal rules and practice and should be corrected, and Paper B critiques inconsistent applications of basic-assumption defenses and proposes a unified, intent-based analytic framework to achieve greater consistency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59clevstlrev693!!ARTICLE: SELLING SEX: ANALYZING THE IMPROPER USE DEFENSE TO CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT THROUGH THE LENS OF CARROLL V. BEARDON
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SELLING SEX: ANALYZING THE IMPROPER USE DEFENSE TO CONTRACT ENFORCEMENT THROUGH THE LENS OF CARROLL V. BEARDON

shared_topics.topic: defenses to contract enforcement for nontraditional or excusing circumstances (mistake, frustration, illegality/improper use)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers centrally examine when courts should decline to enforce otherwise-bargained contracts—Paper A by analyzing basic assumption defenses (mutual and unilateral mistake, impossibility, frustration of purpose, commercial impracticability), and Paper B by evaluating the improper-use/public-policy defense that can render a contract unenforceable when the parties' intended use implicates illegal or socially disfavored conduct.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' intent and purpose in determining enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes an expanded, multi-faceted model of contractual intent (volitional, cognitive, contextual purposive intent) to explain when defenses should apply, while Paper B scrutinizes how a buyer's intended (illegal) use and the parties' purposes are treated by courts under the improper-use doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal inconsistency and the need for a clearer, coherent framework
shared_topics.justification: Both articles critique the existing patchwork of doctrine—Paper A argues basic assumption defenses lack a unifying rationale and produce inconsistent results, and Paper B highlights muddled tests and lost precedent in public-policy/improper-use cases, calling for clearer approaches.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of public policy, social context, and judicial discretion on contract law outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames enforceability in terms of balancing autonomy and transactional facilitation and emphasizes adaptability to modern contexts, while Paper B explores how cultural attitudes, public-policy considerations, and judicial tone/choice-of-tests shape whether courts enforce contracts involving morally charged conduct like prostitution.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72fordhamlrev595!!ARTICLE:CORBIN AND FULLER'S CASES ON CONTRACTS (1942?): THE CASEBOOK THAT NEVER WAS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CORBIN AND FULLER'S CASES ON CONTRACTS (1942?): THE CASEBOOK THAT NEVER WAS

shared_topics.topic: the role of remedies and purposive aims in shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that an intent-based approach better aligns contract doctrines with the law's core objectives (furthering autonomy and facilitating transactions), while Paper B centers the longstanding pedagogical dispute over starting Contracts with remedies versus formation, highlighting remedies-first arguments that emphasize revealing the law's purposes and stakes.

shared_topics.topic: basic-assumption defenses (mistake, frustration, impossibility, impracticability) and their inconsistent application
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a doctrinal analysis that reinterprets mutual and unilateral mistake, frustration of purpose, impossibility, and commercial impracticability through expanded intent categories; Paper B treats 'basic assumptions' as an explicit topic in Contracts curricula and situates its teaching (and ordering) among other doctrines, showing how these defenses are packaged and presented to students.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of contractual intent/purpose in interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a multi-faceted theory of contractual intent (volitional, cognitive, contextual/purposive) as the key to resolving defense doctrines, while Paper B repeatedly invokes purposive questions—what promises the law will enforce and why—to motivate different pedagogical orders (formation vs. remedies) and to frame how students understand enforcement decisions.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal organization or framing (including pedagogical choices) affects legal analysis and consistency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that current artificial doctrinal distinctions produce confusion and inconsistent judicial results and proposes re-framing doctrines via an intent-focused lens to promote consistency; Paper B demonstrates historically how the organization of casebooks and the decision to teach remedies-first or formation-first reflects and shapes how generations of lawyers conceive and apply contract rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev7!!SYMPOSIUM: GILMORE'S GRANT (OR THE LIFE & AFTERLIFE OF GRANT GILMORE & HIS DEATH)
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: GILMORE'S GRANT (OR THE LIFE & AFTERLIFE OF GRANT GILMORE & HIS DEATH)

shared_topics.topic: limits of the bargain/consideration principle and the significance of exceptions to enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates Gilmore's claim that the classical bargain/consideration model of contract is collapsing (the 'Death of Contract') and surveys challenges to strict formalist enforcement, while Paper B examines those very limits in practice by analyzing basic-assumption defenses (mistake, frustration, impracticability) that allow parties to escape bargained-for exchanges.

shared_topics.topic: the role and conception of contractual intent in governing enforcement and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses debates over Holmesian/bargain theories and the intent foundations of consideration, and Paper B develops an expanded, multi-faceted theory of contractual intent (volitional, cognitive, contextual/purposive) as the organizing principle for resolving defenses and reforming contract law.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal fragmentation/incoherence in contract law and the need for a unifying analytic framework
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the gradual breakdown of classical doctrinal certainties and critiques Restatement/formalist attempts to impose neat rules, while Paper B documents inconsistent results across basic-assumption defenses and proposes an intent-based framework to unify analysis and increase doctrinal consistency.

shared_topics.topic: normative aims of contract law and adaptation to changing transactional contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises broader questions about what contract law is for and whether older formalist doctrines remain meaningful in new eras, and Paper B explicitly balances autonomy and transaction-facilitation as core objectives and argues for a flexible intent-based approach that can accommodate modern developments (e.g., Internet transactions).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27setonhalllrev490!!ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY

shared_topics.topic: the role of individual autonomy in determining enforceability of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconceptualizes consideration as a commitment to relinquish autonomy and treats that relinquishment as the ground for enforceability; Paper B identifies furthering autonomy as a primary objective of contract law and uses an intent-focused analysis to decide when enforcement should yield to avoidance or reformation.

shared_topics.topic: limits on enforcement despite formal sufficiency of consideration (when bargains should be voidable or reformed)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the boundaries of the bargain mechanism and when promises ought not to be enforced despite appearing to be bargains; Paper B analyzes basic-assumption defenses (mutual/unilateral mistake, impossibility, frustration, impracticability) that permit escape from or reformation of contracts even where consideration is present.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal mechanisms as means of attributing responsibility for promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats consideration as an attributional mechanism analogous to tort and criminal requirements that establishes grounds of responsibility for bargains; Paper B develops an expanded contractual-intent framework (volitional, cognitive, purposive) to attribute liability and explain when a promisor should be relieved of obligations.

shared_topics.topic: critique of formalistic, form-over-substance doctrines and advocacy for intent- or nexus-focused analysis and reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the reification of consideration as ‘something given’ and emphasizes act, intent, and inducement nexus as the operative mechanism, using that analysis to evaluate reform proposals; Paper B criticizes artificial doctrinal distinctions among basic-assumption defenses and proposes a dynamic, intent-centered approach to increase coherence and adapt doctrine to modern transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72minnlrev775!!ARTICLE: Paradox Lost.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Paradox Lost.

shared_topics.topic: normative justification for enforcing promises/contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends a utilitarian justification for why promises should generate legal obligations and rejects rival nonutilitarian accounts; Paper B likewise engages normative questions by proposing an intent-based approach to when contracts should be enforced or excused, situating doctrinal rules within underlying justificatory aims.

shared_topics.topic: source of the binding force of contracts — institutional convention versus parties' intent
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promising as a social convention requiring a principle of fidelity to bind individuals, contrasting high- and low-fidelity accounts; Paper B interrogates the evidentiary and normative role of different species of contractual intent (volitional, cognitive, purposive) in determining when parties are bound or may escape obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of expectations, reliance, and basic assumptions in generating or defeating obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates connecting factors such as promisee reliance, acceptance of benefits, and voluntary consent as candidate grounds for promissory duties and finds them insufficient; Paper B focuses on basic-assumption defenses (mistake, frustration, impracticability) that turn on parties' expectations and whether those expectations justify avoidance or reformation.

shared_topics.topic: balancing individual autonomy against transaction-facilitating consequences in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A pits consequentialist (utilitarian) defenses of promissory institutions against rights-based/neoformalist accounts concerned with individual moral claims; Paper B expressly frames its proposed expanded intent analysis as reconciling and advancing contract law's twin objectives of promoting autonomy and facilitating transactions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52amjcompl433!!ARTICLE: Mistake in Contract Formation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mistake in Contract Formation

shared_topics.topic: when a mistake warrants relief (avoidance or reformation) in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze the circumstances under which a contracting party may escape or reform a bargain due to mistake: Paper A surveys basic-assumption defenses (mutual/unilateral mistake, impossibility, frustration, impracticability) and argues for an intent-based test, while Paper B examines the classical ‘error in substance’ doctrine and its limits for granting relief.

shared_topics.topic: the legal significance of parties' motives and intentions in mistake doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with whether and how a party's motives or intentions should affect entitlement to relief: Paper A decomposes contractual intent into volitional, cognitive, and purposive facets and uses that taxonomy to adjudicate mistake claims, whereas Paper B critiques the substance/motive dichotomy and argues for incorporating parties’ motives into the analysis (drawing on modern French/Aristotelian approaches).

shared_topics.topic: the need for a unified doctrinal framework to resolve inconsistent case law on mistake/basic assumption defenses
shared_topics.justification: Both identify confusion and inconsistent results in courts' application of mistake doctrines and propose more coherent analytical frameworks—Paper A via an expanded intent-based approach to simplify and harmonize defenses, and Paper B by reformulating or rejecting the classical rules to achieve clearer criteria for relief.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CASES AND CONTROVERSIES: SOME THINGS TO DO WITH CONTRACTS CASES

shared_topics.topic: using historical case studies to analyze and teach contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for the continuing pedagogical and analytic value of studying canonical and lesser-known contract cases (legal archaeology) to illuminate doctrine, and Paper B applies case-based analysis to existing mistake/changed-circumstance doctrines, testing and explaining them through precedent-level decisions.

shared_topics.topic: seeking doctrinal coherence by synthesizing disparate cases and doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights assembling individual case stories into a recognizable common law of contract, while Paper B proposes an expanded, intent-centered framework to remove artificial doctrinal distinctions and bring greater consistency to disparate basic-assumption defenses.

shared_topics.topic: adapting contract law and its study to technological and modern-market developments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the question of how electronic records and new media affect the transmission and teaching of contract cases, and Paper B explicitly considers Internet-driven transactions and how contract doctrines (and proposed analyses) should accommodate technological change in the modern marketplace.

papers.node_id: 78stjohnslrev131!!ARTICLE: MUST PROFITS MADE IN TRANSACTIONS INVOLVING LATE-DELIVERED GOODS BE DEDUCTED FROM THE INJURED PARTY'S BREACH DAMAGES? IF NOT, WHAT IMPACT SHOULD LATE-DELIVERED GOODS HAVE?
papers.title: ARTICLE: MUST PROFITS MADE IN TRANSACTIONS INVOLVING LATE-DELIVERED GOODS BE DEDUCTED FROM THE INJURED PARTY'S BREACH DAMAGES? IF NOT, WHAT IMPACT SHOULD LATE-DELIVERED GOODS HAVE?
papers.abstract:
In non-commercial situations involving the late delivery of goods, it is often easy to say that post-breach performance by a breaching seller totally obviates the non-breaching party's damages. This is exemplified in the following hypothetical: A agrees to sell a spare bed to B, who plans to put it in his guest room. B pays A, but A fails to deliver the bed by the agreed upon date. If A actually does deliver the bed a month later, before B secures cover, then there is little chance that B would be viewed as having been damaged. This scenario is easily understood. It is also the basis for some courts' initial negative reaction to a non-breaching commercial plaintiff's effort to recover costs or lost profits owing to the seller's initial failure to deliver and also seeking to retain the profits that it made on its subsequent disposition of the late-delivered goods.
Such a reaction, while perhaps understandable, fails to recognize both the state of the law and the fact that in the commercial world, given buyers' frequently more critical needs, late delivery may not cure all.Indeed, viewing the late delivery as totally obviating the non-breaching party's damages would not even be appropriate in the above example of the sale of a bed if A knew that B needed the bed by the specified date, because he was expecting house guests and, as a result of A's breach, B had to rent a bed to accommodate his visitors.
Moreover, in some commercial circumstances, the injured party may have lost volume because of the breach.That the non-breaching party has actually lost volume is certainly apparent where the non-breaching party is unable to cover and, but for the breach, the seller would have resold the goods - or manufactured them into finished products and sold them - and would have still entered into the subsequent transaction, which involved the late-delivered goods.Indeed, to many resellers or manufacturers, the failure of a supplier to make timely delivery may result in a lost opportunity that can never be recovered.For example, if a manufacturer with no inventory needs delivery of twenty tons of aluminum each week to make cars in its factory, which is operating at full capacity, assuming that cover were not possible on short notice, a supplier's failure to make delivery one week would result in the loss of a week's worth of autoproduction that can never be made up without expanding the capacity of the factory.
While a non-breaching party that promptly covers will not likely have lost volume, this does not mean that it should be precluded from obtaining cover damages and also retaining the profit that it made on a subsequent transaction involving late-delivered goods. Indeed, as discussed below, the law indicates that in appropriate circumstances even a covering purchaser must be allowed to retain profits made in any subsequent transaction involving the late-delivered goods in order for it to be in the same position that it would have been in had there not been any breach.The basic correctness of this conclusion is also demonstrated in the introduction and by the illustrations set forth in Part II, particularly by those which indicate that if the amount that the breaching party would otherwise have to pay the non-breaching party were reduced by the profits that the injured party made on the transaction involving the late-delivered goods, for no good reason other than the fact that the plaintiff made a good deal of profit on a transaction that it would have entered irrespective of the breach or the late-delivery, the injured party would not be placed in as good a position as it would have been in had the other party not breached.
Whether or not a covering buyer, or even one that does not cover, must disgorge some or all of the proceeds of a subsequent transaction involving late-delivered goods depends on the same proof as in the lost volume cases. For example, this would include proof that, in the absence of the breach, the non-breaching party would have made both the originally contemplated transaction involving the goods, resale or sale of finished good, and the second transaction that, by happenstance, actually involved the late-delivered goods.While this analysis does lead to thecorrect result, as noted below, similar and sometimes identical results can also be achieved in a less complicated manner simply by examining the effect of the breach on the covering party's total cost of goods for the affected transactions.
. Fertico: Retention by a Covering Plaintiff of the Profits Made in Transactions Involving the Late-Delivered Goods
One case that tried to tackle headlong the considerably more difficult of the two scenarios noted above, namely, the issue of just how, in a commercial context, post-breach performance by the breaching party should affect the damages recoverable by the non-breaching party that has effectuated cover, was Fertico Belgium S.A. v. Phosphate Chemicals Export Ass'n.
In October 1978, Fertico, a Belgian commodity broker, contracted with Phoschem, an American exporter of phosphate fertilizer, for 35,000 tons of fertilizer to be delivered in two lots.As requested, Fertico provided Phoschem with a $ 1.7 million letter of credit, an amount sufficient to cover full payment for the initial shipment.The first shipment of 15,000 tons was to be delivered no later than November 20, 1978, and the remaining 20,000 tons were to be delivered by November 30, 1978.Phoschem was aware that Fertico needed these shipments by those dates so that the bulk fertilizer could be bagged and shipped in sufficient time to satisfy a secondary contract that Fertico had with Iraq's Agricultural Ministry, Altaweed.
Well before the initial delivery date, Phoschem advised Fertico that the fertilizer would not arrive until December 4, 1978, two weeks late.In response, Fertico informed Phoschem that the delay would cause "huge problems" with its contract with Altaweed.Phoschem's impending breach compelled Fertico to act. On November 15, 1978, so as to avoid breaching its secondary contract with Altaweed, Fertico acquired 35,000 tons of substitute fertilizer on the open market at a price $ 700,000 higher than the contract price with Phoschem.
The shipment from Phoschem did not arrive in Belgium until December 17, 1978, and was not off-loaded until December 21, 1978.Despite Phoschem's breach, Fertico took possession of the fertilizer.Fertico believed that it "had no other choice"because prior to Fertico's learning of the breach, Phoschem had already drawn down the $ 1.7 million letter of credit that Fertico had posted.Fertico did, however, cancel the second shipment.
Fertico stored the 15,000 tons that it had received from Phoschem while it sought a buyer for it, and on March 19, 1979, Fertico eventually sold it to another customer, Janssens.Based on the cost of the fertilizer purchased from Phoschem and the price at which Fertico sold it to Janssens, Fertico made a profit of $ 454,000 on the transaction.
Thereafter, Fertico filed suit against Phoschem seeking $ 1.25 million in damages due to Phoschem's breach of the agreement.These damages included the increased cost of cover, $ 700,000, and certain consequential damages relating to increased transportation costs.The jury granted Fertico a verdict of $ 1.07 million.The Appellate Division vacated the award and ordered a new trial on damages.Fertico appealed this intermediate appellate decision to the New York Court of Appeals, which determined that Fertico was entitled to the increased cost of cover plus consequential and incidental damages minus expensessaved.As part of this decision, the Court of Appeals also concluded that Fertico's damages did not have to be reduced by the profits that Fertico made on the sale to Janssens.That is, the Court of Appeals analyzed the subsequent sale to Janssens as a transaction that was separate and independent, i.e., one that would have been made regardless of any dealings with or breach by Phoschem.Stated another way, the majority believed that in the absence of the breach, Fertico, as a dealer in such goods, would have acquired fertilizer on the open market and still made the sale to Janssens.
The court reasoned that "it would be anomalous to conclude that had it not been for Phoschem's breach Fertico would not have continued its trade and upon such reasoning to counterpoise the profits from the … sale against the damages arising from Phoschem's breach."In doing so, and in also granting Fertico the increased cost of cover, the court applied, which directs that the remedies provided in the U.C.C. be liberally administered so as to put the aggrieved party in as good a position as if the other party had fully performed.In this regard, the court stated that "had [the seller] fully performed, Fertico would have had the benefit of the [sale to Altaweed] and, as a trader of fertilizer, the profits from the Janssens' sale as well."In response to a strong dissent, the majority stated that "the dissent's characterization of the recovery by an injured party of damages for a breach of contract as a "benefit' is wrong, since that functionally attributes a kind oflien against the independently pursued benefits derived out of that separate transaction."
The majority's approach was subsequently criticized in Allied Semi-Conductors Int'l, Ltd. v. Pulsar Components Int'l, Inc.,both in dicta, where the court indicated that Fertico should be limited to its "exceptional" and "peculiar" facts,andby commentators cited by the court.In the latter regard, these commentators opined that Fertico had been overly compensated because:
The Code contemplates that the buyer will make a choice - either accept or reject the goods. The solution reached by the [Fertico] majority allows the buyer to have it both ways - profit as if the goods were accepted, and damages as if the goods had been rejected. The fault lies in treating the goods as accepted goods and then using the cover measure of damages as a test of the loss suffered. The [Fertico] majority's solution puts the buyer in a better position than the buyer would have been in had the contract been performed. This result is not warranted either under the generous remedies policy of the Code or by the scheme of remedies it provides.
The view that Fertico's acceptance of the goods automatically extinguished its right to the profits on their resale is not, however, held by a majority of authorities.As Professors White and Summers and the Restatement indicate, whether the Fertico approach is appropriate does not turn on the reasonableness of the late acceptance; rather it turns on whether or not the non-breaching party regularly dealt with the type of goods in question.They point out that if, as the majority assumed in Fertico, Phoschem had performed and Fertico, as a regular dealer in phosphate, would have made both its sale to Altaweed and its sale to Janssens, then the Fertico majority would be correct.They also point out that if, as the Fertico dissent indicated, it was likely that had Phoschem not breached and Fertico, as acompany that did not regularly deal in phosphate, would not have made the subsequent sale to Janssens, then "the dissent [would be] correct."This conclusion is entirely consistent with the citation to Corbin contained in Fertico that "gains made by the injured party on other transactions after the breach are never to be deducted from the damages that are otherwise recoverable, unless such gains could not have been made, had there been no breach."It is also totally in accord with the view set out in the comments to Section 347 of the Restatement that "if the injured party could and would have entered into the subsequent contract, even if the [first] contract had not been broken, and could have had the benefit of both, he can be said to have "lost volume' and the subsequent transaction is not a substitute for the broken contract."
As these citations indicate, the basic lost volume test - whether, in the absence of the breach the injured party would have made both the originally contemplated transaction and the subsequent one which actually involved the late-delivered goods - applies both in the situation like Fertico where cover was effectuated and there is no loss of volume and in the situation where, due to a lack of cover, volume was in fact lost. For this reason, a better way of summarizing this general rule would be to say that in the case of late delivery, absent more, a non-breaching party is entitled to its normal breach damages without reduction for the profit, if any, that was made on any subsequent transaction involving the late-delivered goods. This is only true if, in the absence of the breach, the injured party could and would have entered into that subsequent transaction.
Even though correct as a basic premise, the general rule stated immediately above is, however, only one path to a correct analysis and result. Another is an outgrowth of the outcome in Fertico having been questioned on the facially plausible basis that all that occurred there was that contracted goods, originally targeted to go to Altaweed, simply went to Janssens and the goods that would otherwise have gone to Janssens simply went to Altaweed.As this analysis goes, it is also reasoned that despite the breach, Fertico likely made just as much money as it would have had there been no breachand that the "award of cover damages in addition to the retained profit represents a windfall."This latter conclusion is, however, premised on the assumption that the wholesale price that Fertico paid for the fertilizer actually shipped to Altaweed was the same as the wholesale price at which Fertico would, absent the breach, have purchased the fertilizer that it would have shipped to Janssens.
While the above analysis has an appealing symmetry and seems to make common sense, those characteristics mask a very basic point which calls the analysis into question. That is, it is extremely unlikely that the fertilizer that Fertico purchasedupon hearing of Phoschem's impending breach would ever have been purchased for the transaction with Janssens. There would have been absolutely no need for Fertico to have gone into the spot market in November and ostensibly pay a premium for immediately deliverable fertilizer, when delivery to Janssens would not take place until March or April. Moreover, if, as is very likely the case, Fertico had to pay more for fertilizer on the spot market than it would have had to in the general wholesale market, even under the above analysis, it would be entitled to that extra cost as well as being entitled to retain the profits derived from the late-delivered goods.
While the normal measure of cover, set out in, is the cost of cover less the contract price plus any incidentaland consequential damages minus expenses saved,the real concern raised by the above analysis is whether Fertico's total cost of raw materials for the Altaweed and Janssens transactions increased because of the breach. Simply stated, did the breach put Fertico in a position economically worse than the one it would have enjoyed in the absence of the breach? As the analysis properly indicates, determining if this is the case need not be based on the anomalous application of the lost volume rules to a party that did not lose volume. Rather, damages can be determined simply by comparing the actual total cost that was incurred for fertilizer to accomplish the two affected transactions, the sales to Altaweed and Janssens, to the total cost that it should have incurred for the fertilizer in the absence of the breach. Since the fixed-price cost of goods under the original contract is contained both in the total actual costs for the fertilizer and the total that Fertico should have spent for the fertilizer, that item can be factored out of the comparison, leaving only a comparison between the price at which cover was obtained and the wholesale price of goods at the time that Fertico would have entered the market to purchase fertilizer for delivery to Janssens. Accordingly, the extent to which the cost of cover exceeded the wholesale market price at the time that Fertico would have entered the market to purchase fertilizer for delivery toJanssens is the amount due Fertico from Phoschem.The court in Fertico did not indicate anything specific about the price of fertilizer after Phoschem's breach.Accordingly, it is impossible to know if Fertico was overly compensated or under compensated pursuant to what, for want of a better term, shall be referred to herein as the simplified cover formula.
As discussed in the ensuing sections, the courts and commentators have attempted and, in round about ways, have succeeded, at least in part, in refining the Fertico thesis to avoid overcompensation. The route to achieving that goal, however, is often a complicated one.
. Regular Dealers and Their Need To Prove that the Subsequent Transaction Would have Been Accomplished Irrespective of the Breach
The question in Fertico of whether, in the absence of a breach by Phoschem, Fertico would have made both the sale to Altaweed and the sale to Janssens, is at the center of the controversy that surrounds the case. While a similar question is certainly central in all cases involving cover and the injured party's retention of the profits flowing from the late-delivered goods, other courts have achieved comparable results in a less controversial manner than did the court in Fertico. Notable in this regard is Aluminum Distributors, Inc. v. Gulf Aluminum Rolling Mill Co.,a suit brought by another middleman against a supplier, Gulf Aluminum Rolling Mill Company (GARMCO), for breach of contract.GARMCO had agreed to sell Aluminum Distributors, Inc. (ADI) a specified quantity of aluminum; however, it delivered the goods late.As a result, ADI was forced tocover in order to fulfill its obligations under several resale contracts and to forego the ones for which it could not obtain cover.Under the circumstances, GARMCO argued that ADI was not entitled to cover damages because it had accepted the aluminum or, alternatively, that it should be permitted to offset the profits ADI had made upon its resale of the late-delivered aluminum against ADI's cover damages.The court largely rejected GARMCO's argument.The reason for this is fairly clear from a reading of the case - the court saw that ADI, as a volume dealer in aluminum, would still have made both the original sales and the subsequent ones that involved the late-delivered aluminum from GARMCO irrespective of the breach.To better understand the court's conclusion, one needs to examine the lost volume cases and the rationale that underlies them.
By far the most often discussed of the various lost volume situations is that of the lost volume seller whose customer breached its contract to purchase. This situation can be exemplified as follows: Buyer X agrees to purchase a new automobile from an auto-dealership for $ 20,000. The dealership's cost for the car is $ 18,000. Therefore, the dealer stands to make $ 2000. The model in question is one that is in demand, but the dealership can obtain additional cars through alternative means. Buyer X repudiates the contract. A few days thereafter, however, the dealership is able to sell the car that was subject to X's contract to Buyer Y for $ 20,000, and Y takes delivery on the very same day on which Buyer X was scheduled to do so. The dealership thus earned the $ 2000 in profit that it would have made if it had sold the car to Buyer Y.
Notwithstanding X's assertion that the dealership suffered no loss, in these facts the law is that X is liable to the dealership for $ 2000 in accordance withbecause, absent X's breach, the dealership would have made the sale to Buyer X and would have sold a car to Buyer Y and thus earned a total of $ 4000 in profit. X's breach caused it to lose $ 2000 ofprofit.Thus X must pay the dealership $ 2000 in order to put the dealer in as good a position as performance by X would have done.
A. Application of the Lost-Volume Concept to Resellers and Others
The logic underlying the result in the auto dealership hypothetical has caused it to be applied both explicitly and implicitly in a variety of situations where the non-breaching party is other than a mere re-seller, i.e., to "a multitude of plaintiffs who are neither lost volume sellers, nor jobbers, nor component sellers."For example, in the following hypothetical Professor Farnsworth discusses the concept of lost volume in a context that is much more akin to the circumstances of both Fertico and Aluminum Distributors than is the automobile dealership example noted above.A builder contracts to build a building on an owner's land for $ 100,000. The builder would have made a profit of $ 10,000 by performing. However, the owner repudiates the contract before any work or preparation is performed. The builder promptly enters into another contract to build an identical building for $ 100,000 at a profit of $ 8000. The builder claims that he has lost volume as a result of the breach, i.e., "had the first contract not been broken, the builder could and would have made both contracts."Professor Farnsworth indicates that not only can the builder prevail on this assertion but also that the assertion can also be successfully made by injured parties in other commercial circumstances.
The same claim may be made by a manufacturer in similar circumstances, when manufacture of the goods is not begun,or … by a seller of goods that has bought the goods for resale … [and if the injured party] can show or the court will assume that [he] could and would have expanded [his] business to take both contracts and make [the] combined profit of $ 18,000, but that as a result of the breach … has only one contract (the second one) on which the profit will be $ 8,000, [he] will be allowed to recover $ 10,000 damages on the first contract, with no subtraction for the profit made on the second contract.
B. The Suggestion in Aluminum Distributors of a Better Way To Determine if the Plaintiff Would Have Entered into the Subsequent Transaction
As noted, the Restatement applies the above rule to any commercial plaintiff provided that it could and would have entered into the subsequent transaction even if there had been no breach.Aluminum Distributors certainly did not disturb this proposition.It required the non-breaching party to demonstrate that it could otherwise have purchased a sufficient quantity of goods in time to enter into the transaction for which it used the late-delivered goods.However, Aluminum Distributors also suggests a better way to determine this, and thus whether the plaintiff must disgorge the profits it made on the late-delivered goods.The answer to the ultimate question of whether the non-breaching party would have entered into the subsequent transaction, had there been no breach, is rarely provable with absolute certainty.In addition, any affirmative testimony by the plaintiff is often looked upon by the court as being at least somewhat self serving.Therefore, Aluminum Distributors implicitly suggests that a better first step is to ask the much more manageable question of whether the non-breaching party was a regular volume dealer in the goods.Where questionis answered in the affirmative, provided that there is also a showing that the plaintiff had the capacity and intention to perform both the initial transaction and the subsequent one,the burden would then appropriately shift to the breaching party to demonstrate "that it is more probable than not that the plaintiff would not have had both sales … and thus that the second resale profit … should be used to reduce the plaintiff's recovery."The breaching party would likely try to do so by, among other things, attempting to prove that the injured party, for some reason, would not have acquired goods of the type under contract in the time between the initial breach and the late delivery and thus was able to enter into the subsequent transaction only because it accepted the late-delivered goods. It might also attempt to demonstrate either that, after the breach, the non-breaching party was operating at what was felt to be an optimum volume and that the late-delivered goods merely caused that optimum level to be exceeded or that the level of operations actually achieved upon delivery of the late-delivered goods could not have been reached but for the breach.These arguments, however speculative and difficult to prove, are substantially facilitated where courts, albeit erroneously, have placed the total burden on the injured party to prove that it could and would have had both transactions if there had been no breach.
C. Application of the Regular-Dealer Concept to Plaintiffs Other Than Middlemen
As noted, the court in Aluminum Distributors readily assumed that, even without the breach, ADI, would have performed both the initial transaction and the subsequent transaction.The Fertico majority did much the same thing.Thisassumption was not based on the plaintiff's role as a mere middleman.Indeed, a similar result would have been obtained by a broad spectrum of plaintiffs.The only threshold requirement is a demonstration that the party regularly dealt with significant quantities of the goods, did a substantial amount of work of the type in question, used a substantial volume of raw materials or components of the type in issue to manufacture goods,or had some other continuing involvement with the goods or work of the type in issue.
Take, for example, the situation of a manufacturer who needs large quantities of certain relatively long-lead-time raw materials to make a finished product, which it in turn sells to the general publicand the consequences of a breach by its raw materials supplier. Needless to say, it would be foolhardy for any such manufacturer not to have entered into substantial raw materialsupply contracts well before the date of planned manufacture. Though such foresight would indeed be prudent, the mere existence of such contracts does not guarantee that the supplier will not breach them or that cover at anything less than a high price can quickly remedy the ensuing failure of supply.
In such circumstances, where the manufacturer effectuates cover and can show that, had there been no breach, it had both the desire and the manufacturing capacity to produce the finished products that it made with the cover goods and the finished products it made in the appropriate subsequent period from the late-delivered goods, the manufacturer is entitled to its increased cost of cover and, absent more, the profits that it made on the finished goods manufactured from the late-delivered goods.Indeed, such a remedy should be applied pursuant to the very broad provisions of, Buyer's Damages for Breach in Regard to Accepted Goods. This provision permits the injured party to "recover as damages for any non-conformity of tender the loss resulting in the ordinary course of events from the seller's breach as determined in any manner which is reasonable" and in turn encompasses the lost volume conceptcontained inor as such remedy may be applied pursuant to common law.In either event,profits made on transactions based on the late-delivered goods need not be deducted from the injured party's damages. Indeed, so long as the transaction involving the late delivered goods was neither a substitute for one that would have been accomplished had there been no breachor a bonus, that is, one which would not have been accomplished had there been no breach,the profits made on the subsequent transaction need not be applied in whole or in part to offset damages otherwise due the non-breaching party.
D. Why the Transaction Involving the Late-Delivered Goods Is Not Simply a Substitute, a Bonus, or Other Child of the Breach
The fact that the late-delivery need not be viewed as a substitute can be seen by reference to the hypothetical set out in the Introduction in which the supplier failed to make timely delivery of twenty tons of raw materials - the amount the non-breaching party used in its factory each week. If by the time that delivery is finally possible and accomplished some weeks or maybe months later, the manufacturer did or could have purchased the twenty tons for that week's needs, and perhaps the ensuing fewweeks', from other available sources, no substitution would be involved and the manufacturer need not reduce the damages otherwise due it by the profits that it made in transactions involving the late-delivered twenty tons.That is, for purposes of determining damages due the injured party that obtained cover, the question is whether it is more likely than not that even without the late-delivered goods the factory would still have been able to operate at the same level of production that it did in the period immediately after acceptance of the late-delivered goods.As noted previously, for a regular purchaser of such raw materials the presumption is that, even without the late-delivered goods, it would have secured sufficient material to maintain operations at the same level, the late-delivery was not a bonus and, as Professors White and Summers aptly describe it, the transaction involving the late-delivered goods was not "a child of the breach"requiring that the profits therefrom be offset against damages otherwise due the non-breaching party.
E. The Applicability of U.C.C. Sections 2 - 714(1) andin the Absence of Cover: Back to the Lost-Volume Situation
The applicability ofandand the common law certainly would not change if, in the current hypothetical, the manufacturer was not able to obtain cover at commercially reasonable prices, and the manufacturer was therefore suing for lost profits on finished products that could not be produced because of the supplier's breach.Indeed, on these facts there would appear to be little doubt that an opportunity was missed by virtue of the seller's breach and that the manufacturer is entitled to the profits that it would have made by producing the finished product from the raw materials which the supplier failed to supply and, absent more, the profits that it made in the subsequent production and sale of finished goods.
As noted, there is little distinction between the situations in Fertico, Aluminum Distributors, and that of the manufacturerthat is unable to cover in the above hypothetical. The fact that the compensation sought in the named cases was the increased cost of cover while the manufacturer in the hypothetical is seeking lost profits is of no moment. In fact, part of what ADI sought and recovered in Aluminum Distributors was lost profits.Moreover, while cover damages are more commonly awarded, the fact that lost profits are awarded in commercial cases where cover is not obtainable is not surprising since the increased cost of cover in reality merely represents the decrease in the profits that the non-breaching party made in its subsequent transaction because it had to use higher cost goods than it had anticipated.
The question over which the majority and the dissent argued so vehemently in Fertico was at its root simply the issue of whether or not Fertico was a volume buyer and seller of fertilizer.This issue would have been no different if Phoschem's breach had, in turn, prevented Fertico from fulfilling its contract with Altaweed and thus Fertico had sued for lost profits.The dissent would have said, just as in the hypothetical set out in note 64 supra, regarding a private owner's reselling his car for $ X after the original party repudiated a contract for the same price, that the profit on the subsequent transaction should be used to offset the loss on the first. On the other hand, the Fertico majority would insist that but for Phoschem's breach, Fertico, as a regular dealer in fertilizer, would have made the subsequent sale to Janssens irrespective of Phoschem's performance after the breach. That is, in the ensuing months, with or without Phoschem's performance, Fertico would have secured sufficient fertilizer to enter into the subsequent transaction with Janssens. The court in Aluminum Distributors, of course, would have agreed with the Fertico majority because it too was of the view that, where dealers in goods are involved, post-breach performanceby the breaching party resulting in profits to the dealer equal to or even greater than those that would have been achieved had there been no breach do not, in and of themselves, eliminate the damages of a lost volume dealer.
The damages recoverable by the hypothetical manufacturer would thus seem to turn on whether it is viewed as a volume buyer/processor of the raw material. If viewed in this light, as both Fertico and Aluminum Distributors suggest and as discussed supra, there is at least a rebuttable presumption, taking into account necessary lead times for the manufacturer's post-breach acquisition of raw materials, that its production of finished products in the subsequent period would have been the same irrespective of its supplier's belated performance.Such a rebuttable presumption is entirely consistent with the observation of Professors White and Summers that the outcome in Fertico is a proper one unless the breaching party can show by a preponderance of the evidence that, had the supplier not breached, the non-breaching party would not have produced any more finished products than it did produce at or about the time of the breach and that without the belatedly supplied raw material it would not have produced as much finished product as it did in the subsequent period when late delivery was made.
Unless raw materials at commercially reasonable prices are nearly impossible to obtain from any source or sources at any time during the period between the supplier's breach and its belated performance, the task of the breaching supplier is to demonstrate that it is more reasonable than not that the manufacturer could not have produced as much without the supplier's late delivery. This is an extremely difficult task. This task is, of course, made even more difficult when the lag time between the breach and the belated performance is significant, and the manufacturer has had a long time to overcome the hole in its pipeline created by the breach and by the need to discount anyimpairment of the non-breaching party's financial situation caused by the breach.
. The Aluminum Distributors Approach To Dealing With Any Real or Perceived Windfall to the Non-Breaching Party
Subsequent to Fertico, Aluminum Distributors indicated that an aggrieved buyer who accepts late-delivered goods should be entitled to its breach damages as in Fertico.The court also suggested that Fertico should be limited so as to permit the non-breaching party to retain the profits from the transaction involving the late-delivered goods, in addition to its breach damages, only to the extent that the buyer can demonstrate that, at the time of late delivery, an identical quantity of similar goods was available from another seller at the same price as the late-delivered goods.As both Aluminum Distributors and the commentators indicated, to the extent that the non-breaching party obtained the advantage of goods that were priced below the current market at the time that they were delivered, however belatedly, the breaching party should be allowed to offset the amount received in excess of any which would otherwise have been realized at the time of anticipated performance, against the damages owed as a result of its breach.In Aluminum Distributors, this special benefit was measured by the difference between the market price at which ADI could have purchased aluminumat the time of the late delivery and the price in the GARMCO contract.
More specifically, in Aluminum Distributors, the court agreed with GARMCO and the dissent in Fertico that, because ADI had accepted the aluminum, it could not recover its cover damages underand.As comment 1 to section 2-711 specifically states, the cover remedy available in sections 2-711 and 2-712 applies only to a buyer who has not accepted the goods or "who has justifiably revoked his acceptance."However, the court did concur with the Fertico majority in holding that ADI was entitled to its cover costs underwhich, although rarely utilized,specifically deals with the situation where the buyer has acceptedthe goods.The Aluminum Distributors court did so because it found that "GARMCO clearly knew that ADI had purchased the aluminum for resale and that the late deliveries would render ADI in breach of its contracts with third parties and require it to cover or lose the sales."Because section 2-714(1) specifically deals with the situation where acceptance has occurred, unlike the plaintiff in Fertico, in order to be awarded damages, ADI was not required to demonstrate the existence of circumstances that virtually compelled it to accept the late-delivered goods.The court also held that section 2-714(1) entitled ADI to the profits it lost on planned resales that were canceled as a result of GARMCO's delays.
Quite significantly, the court further concluded that GARMCO could offset profits that ADI made on the resale of the late-delivered aluminum against damages but only to the extent that ADI failed to prove that it received no market-related benefit by obtaining and reselling the late-delivered goods,
We further find that GARMCO may not offset against these [cover and lost profit] damages ADI's profits on the resale of the late-delivered aluminum as costs saved due to the breach, unless ADI fails to prove that it could otherwise have purchased similar aluminum for resale and hence would nevertheless have made these additional sales… . If GARMCO can show that the price of the aluminum ADI would otherwise have purchased to make these additional sales would have been higher than the price ADI paid GARMCO for the aluminum, this difference in price may be deducted from the damages GARMCO owes ADI, as profits ADI would not have earned but for GARMCO's breach.
… ADI is entitled to keep any profits it made on the late-delivered aluminum so long as it proves it could otherwise have obtained comparable aluminum to fill those sales at comparable prices. GARMCO is entitled to offset from the above damages any decrease in profits ADI would have received if it had canceled delivery of the late-delivered aluminum and has instead made the fourth party sales from aluminum purchased from other sources. Such damages will place ADI in the same position as if GARMCO had not breached.
The commentators that recognized the appropriateness of the Fertico approach with the addition of such a market-related limitation did so in order to ensure general adherence to the principle that the aggrieved party should not be placed in a better position than it would have been in had there been no breach.In this regard, it should be noted that in attemptingto do so in Aluminum Distributors, the court indicated that the breaching party may have been entitled to an offset if it could demonstrate that the price of the late-delivered goods was more favorable than goods which the non-breaching party would otherwise have purchased. In that case, "this difference in price may be deducted from the damages [the breaching party] owes [the non-breaching party], as profits [that the non-breaching party] would not have earned but for [the] breach."
The basic soundness of Aluminum Distributors' acceptance of the Fertico approach with the addition of a market related limitation can be demonstrated by the following illustrations, the first of which assumes that the aluminum market remained stable between T1, when the parties entered into their contract, and T2, when late delivery was actually made or, in the absence of any breach, ADI otherwise would have obtained goods for the subsequent transaction.These illustrations show that, with some adjustments, the Aluminum Distributors' approach properly takes into account the difference in the plaintiff's economic status at the end of all relevant transactions and the economic status that it would have enjoyed in the absence of the breach, what White & Summers describe as "the real question."
A. Case 1:

questions.question: Must profits that a non-breaching buyer earns from transactions involving late-delivered goods be deducted from the buyer's breach damages (for example, when the buyer both covers and later resells the late goods)?

If such profits are not automatically deducted, how should damages be measured when goods are delivered late so as to put the injured party in the same economic position as full performance (taking into account cover costs, lost production/opportunity, and market-price effects)?

What factual criteria should determine when profits from a subsequent transaction are an offset to damages (i.e., when the later transaction was merely a substitute or bonus of the breach versus one the injured party would have made irrespective of the breach)?

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of justice/fairness in shaping contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly invokes the UCC's goal of putting the aggrieved party "in as good a position" and debates when courts should offset post‑breach profits to avoid windfalls; Paper B analyzes how conceptions of "justice" and fairness operate as explicit determinants of contract doctrine (notably agreement and remedy) and how idiosyncratic justice judgments become legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: use of presumptions and doctrinal heuristics (e.g., the 'regular dealer' / lost‑volume presumption)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on doctrinal presumptions—such as treating regular volume dealers as likely to have made both transactions absent a breach and shifting burdens accordingly—to resolve damages disputes; Paper B studies how legal doctrine functions as a heuristic device and how such presumptions reflect cognitive shortcuts that structure courts' deployment of contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between statutory rules (UCC provisions) and equitable/common‑law adjustments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes specific UCC provisions (e.g., cover, accepted goods, 2‑714/2‑711) and shows how courts adapt or supplement those statutory measures with equitable tests (market‑related offsets, lost‑volume analysis) to reach fair outcomes; Paper B theorizes how formal legal rules and the justice calculus interact—how law, rules, and moral judgments coalesce to produce doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: reliance on economic/market facts and efficiency considerations in doctrinal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds remedial rules in market realities—comparing cover prices, wholesale prices, and total cost effects to determine damages and to avoid overcompensation; Paper B situates economic analysis (and related empirical facts such as efficiency) as one of the factual substrates that courts discover and treat as determinants of doctrinal choices in contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44hastingslj621!!ARTICLE: Bargaining with Uncertainty, Moral Hazard, and Sunk Costs: A Default Rule for Precontractual Negotiations.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Bargaining with Uncertainty, Moral Hazard, and Sunk Costs: A Default Rule for Precontractual Negotiations.

shared_topics.topic: design and use of legal default rules to allocate risk and fill gaps in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for an off-the-rack default rule to govern preliminary negotiations and to supply substantive obligations and terms when bargaining fails; Paper B evaluates how courts and the U.C.C. supply remedial rules (e.g., cover, lost-volume, offsets) that effectively operate as defaults for late delivery disputes and determine how economic consequences are allocated between seller and buyer.

shared_topics.topic: protection of reliance, transaction-specific investments, and sunk costs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on protecting promisee reliance and transaction-specific sunk investments made during prebargaining; Paper B grapples with compensating buyers or manufacturers for increased cover costs, lost production, or lost profits that arise from suppliers' late performance — all concerns about protecting reliance and investments that are specific to the transaction.

shared_topics.topic: the role of uncertainty, lead times, and opportunism (moral hazard) in creating contracting and performance problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds a model showing how uncertainty, bounded rationality, and opportunism in preliminary bargaining undermine formation of complete contracts and justify legal intervention; Paper B repeatedly emphasizes lead times, market availability, and supplier opportunism (late delivery) as sources of lost volume and difficulty in proving damages, shaping when and how remedies should respond.

shared_topics.topic: use of economic analysis and transaction-cost reasoning to shape contract doctrine and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly draws on transaction-cost economics, Williamsonian and relational-contract theories to motivate a default rule for prebargaining; Paper B employs economic reasoning (lost-volume logic, comparisons of total costs, market-price adjustments) to refine damages rules and to avoid over- or under-compensation in late-delivery cases.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 99kylj327!!ARTICLE: Expectation Damages, the Objective Theory of Contracts, and the "Hairy Hand" Case: A Proposed Modification to the Effect of Two Classical Contract Law Axioms in Cases Involving Contractual Misunderstandings
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Expectation Damages, the Objective Theory of Contracts, and the "Hairy Hand" Case: A Proposed Modification to the Effect of Two Classical Contract Law Axioms in Cases Involving Contractual Misunderstandings

shared_topics.topic: competing measures of contract damages (expectation vs reliance/cover/lost-volume)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how U.C.C. cover damages, lost-volume profit recovery, and alternative total-cost comparisons should be applied when goods are late or accepted after breach; Paper B questions the blanket application of expectation damages in misunderstanding cases and proposes reliance-based or intent-based alternatives when expectation damages yield unjust results.

shared_topics.topic: use of counterfactuals and presumptions about parties' likely behavior to calculate remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly relies on counterfactual inquiries (would the buyer have made the subsequent resale absent the breach?) and presumptions about regular dealers to decide whether resale profits offset damages; Paper B centers on how the parties' intended or reasonably understood meanings (a factual counterfactual) should inform which damages measure is appropriate when the parties attached different meanings to contract terms.

shared_topics.topic: avoiding unjust overcompensation or windfalls when awarding relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grapples with doctrines and formulas (e.g., market-related offsets, simplified cover formula) to prevent a non-breaching party from being placed in a better position than full performance would have produced; Paper B likewise seeks a doctrinal modification to prevent unjust or anomalous awards that result from mechanically applying objective expectation damages in misunderstanding cases.

shared_topics.topic: evidentiary burdens and proof standards for establishing the appropriate remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses burdens of proof and burden-shifting (e.g., when a dealer must prove lost-volume status and when the breaching party must show the plaintiff wouldn’t have made both transactions), while Paper B addresses the evidentiary question of proving a mutual misunderstanding or a party's intended promise and how that proof should affect the remedy.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how promises and conduct during preliminary negotiations can create enforceable obligations or not, while Paper B examines whether profits from subsequent transactions involving late‑delivered goods should reduce breach damages—both probe how transactions surrounding the core deal change entitlement and remedy.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts' use of Restatement Section 90 and the invocation of common‑law rules via UCC §1‑103 in precontractual liability cases, and Paper B scrutinizes UCC provisions, Restatement commentary, and case decisions (e.g., Fertico, Aluminum Distributors) to determine proper damage rules—each interrogates how courts and commentators apply doctrinal sources to commercial disputes.

shared_topics.topic: the centrality of factual commercial practices and evidentiary proof (dealer status, financing composition, market availability) in legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes close factual inquiry (e.g., composition of Hoffman's $18,000, financing steps) to determine whether a preliminary agreement or reliance claim exists, while Paper B stresses proof of regular dealer status, market prices, and lost‑volume capacity to decide whether post‑breach profits offset damages; both show doctrinal outcomes hinge on commercial fact patterns and evidence.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the risk that a buyer who performs after a seller's coerced modification can later contest the modification and effectively obtain specific performance of the original contract without having paid for that remedy; Paper B tackles whether a buyer who accepts late‑delivered goods and resells them can keep the resale profits in addition to cover or lost‑profit damages, and when offsets are required to prevent double recovery.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how rules about enforcing modifications and awarding specific performance affect seller extortion, buyer opportunism, and sellers' willingness to agree to modifications; Paper B examines how the measurement and offsetting of damages for late delivery affect supplier behavior, buyers' cover decisions, and the economic incentives facing regular dealers and manufacturers.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the predictability and application of courts' specific‑performance and modification doctrines and debates proposals for bright‑line rules; Paper B analyzes and refines doctrinal tests (lost‑volume test, regular‑dealer presumption, market‑related limitation) and allocation of burdens for proving whether subsequent transactions would have occurred absent the breach.

shared_topics.topic: the legal consequences of post‑breach acceptance, acquiescence, or continued performance on available remedies and the right to contest modifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates whether a party who agreed to a modification under pressure can later contest it and obtain the remedy appropriate to the original bargain; Paper B addresses how acceptance of late goods interacts with a buyer's right to cover, recover lost profits, or be required to offset profits from resale, distinguishing accepted goods remedies from cover remedies.
