shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly revisits the expectation vs. reliance justification for contract damages, arguing reliance should be the default; Paper A operationalizes that tension in doctrine by asking whether remedies (cover, lost profits) should aim to put the plaintiff in the position of full performance (expectation) or simply to undo reliance costs.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A wrestles with doctrinal refinements (market‑related limitations, offsets) intended to prevent overcompensation when late delivery yields fortuitous profits, and Paper B questions the moral and political justification for using state power to enforce expectation interests that confer private advantages absent compelling social reasons.

papers.node_id: 46ambuslj531!!ARTICLE: Mutual Misunderstanding in Contract
papers.title: ARTICLE: Mutual Misunderstanding in Contract
papers.abstract:
Perhaps the most famous case of mutual misunderstanding is the 1864 English case ofRaffles v. Wichelhaus.InRaffles v. Wichelhaus, the parties agreed in writing to buy and sell cotton arriving in Liverpool "ex Peerless from Bombay," only to discover later that there were two ships answering to that description arriving at slightly different times. The English Court of Exchequer refused to enforce the agreement on account of the latent ambiguity associated with the name "Peerless." Since that time it has been generally accepted in Anglo-American common law that unenforcement is the natural outcome in cases involving mutual misunderstanding.The explanation most commonly given is that a mutual misunderstanding interferes with and precludes the formation of a contract. If this is true, it follows from this explanation that unenforcement is both necessary and inevitable and any agreement either of the parties believed they had reached is void ab initio. There is simply no contract to enforce.
There are some puzzles that emerge from this doctrine on its face. One is that the parties themselves almost always reasonably believe and behave as if they have settled upon an enforceable agreement from the outset. It is typically only sometime later--such as upon the arrival of the second Peerless ship inRaffles v. Wichelhaus--that the mutual misunderstanding comes to light. If a court refuses to enforce any obligations between the parties on the basis that no contract was ever formed, in many cases one of the parties will experience an unexpected windfall and theother an unexpected deprivation ex post as a result of relying on the apparent agreement. A second puzzle is that if a court finds that one party's interpretation should be favored over the other's interpretation then the court will typically enforce the agreement in keeping with the set of terms the court favors. For the party whose understanding is disfavored, enforcement on these terms contrasts sharply with the "no contract" outcome in circumstances in which the court finds that the contract failed to form due to each party equally reasonably understanding they had agreed to differing terms. The sharp discontinuity in enforceability in these circumstances squarely suggests the fiction involved in refusing to enforce--that is, regarding as void ab initio--agreements based on a mutual misunderstanding. Characterizing mutual misunderstanding as a problem of contract formation is convenient, but flawed. This article demonstrates that the common law can do a better job of addressing mutual misunderstanding.
Although unenforcement yields appropriate and not undesirable results in some circumstances, it entails bizarre consequences in others. I present and defend an alternative legal rule that significantly improves upon the efficiency of the results in most, if not all, cases involving mutual misunderstanding. The rule I propose would allow each party to an agreement founded on mutual misunderstanding to enforce his or her reasonable understanding of the agreement vis-a-vis the other party. In other words, it would be as if there were two sets of rights and obligations between the parties, with each party only able to enforce legally, through conventional contract remedies, his or her own reasonable understanding of the agreement. Thus, instead of assuming that there must be justoneagreement that can either be legally enforced or not, the reasonable expectations of the parties would be given effect by allowing each party to seek a remedy on the basis of his or her equally reasonable understanding of the agreement vis-a-vis the other party. The proposed rule preserves the parties' reasonable expectations, promotes reliance on promises, and provides implicit insurance against the risk that a mutual misunderstanding will interfere with the realization of a party's expected contractual surplus. The proposed rule may also improve ex post bargaining by reducing the incentives to litigate where there has been a mutual misunderstanding.
Before indicating how the article proceeds, it is perhaps appropriate to emphasize what this article does not address. This article is not about contractual interpretation per se. There is already a well-developedliterature in law and economics regarding the trade-offs associated with different approaches to interpretation.This literature is tangential to the current issue, namely, what to do about cases involving mutual misunderstanding. Indeed, regardless of the interpretive approach one adopts, it is always possible that one will ultimately be left with an agreement that from the perspective of the adjudicator admits of two equally reasonable understandings of the terms that had been agreed to between the parties. This article is about what to do when two equally reasonable interpretations arise, regardless of how one discovers or comes to recognize that there has been a mutual misunderstanding. The initial diagnosis or determination of a mutual misunderstanding is centrally a matter of interpretation. What to do about it, however, is a remedial issue. Analyzing this residual remedial issue and improving on current efforts is the aim of this article.
This article also does not present an economic analysis of mutual mistake in contract law. Mutual mistake involves somewhat different considerations from those relating to mutual misunderstanding.In mutual misunderstanding cases, the parties understand the terms of the contract differently. In mistake cases, on the other hand, the terms are clearly understood but the underlying factual beliefs about the world of one or both of the parties are, as it turns out, mistaken.Unilateral misunderstandings in contract are dealt with in the common law by binding the party with theunilateral misunderstanding to the objectively appropriate understanding of the parties' interaction (i.e., the court's determination of the meaning of the terms of the contract). Where there are effectively two unilateral misunderstandings in the same interaction--a mutual misunderstanding--this article makes the case that the same approach should apply in an extended fashion.
The article proceeds as follows. In PartII.A I illustrate that there is broad doctrinal consensus in the Anglo-American common law that agreements founded on a mutual misunderstanding fail at the point of contract formation, are void ab initio, and cannot be enforced. Given the broad consensus surrounding the result, there is little surprise that competing justifications exist in support of the conclusion.In Part II.B, I contend that the arguments in favor of the result can generally be crudely classified as being either subjectivist or objectivist. I argue, further, that, while the subjectivist view is intuitively attractive, it is ultimately a mythical basis for contractual enforcement and ought to be rejected in favor of the objectivist approach. Having established the dominance of the objectivist approach, however, I suggest that it does not necessarily lead to the unenforceability result embraced by the common law. Through a failure of legal imagination, the common law has overlooked a superior objectivist alternative. Part III illustrates how the current doctrine surrounding mutual misunderstanding has been applied by the courts in three well-known cases and, in order to generalize the results, a fictional fourth case. These illustrations are intended to show that, although the current rule yields acceptable consequences in some circumstances, in others it leads to results that are inappropriate and inefficient. Part IV presents in greater detail the argument in support of the neglected objectivist alternative. Part V shows how the proposed legal rule would resolve the three well-known cases and the fictional fourth case of Part III and argues that these resolutions dominate those associated with the current common law approach. Part VI concludes.

papers.node_id: 60washlrev217!!ARTICLE: NOTES ON THE RELIANCE INTEREST
papers.title: ARTICLE: NOTES ON THE RELIANCE INTEREST
papers.abstract:
The topic is Contract Damages.  The interests are defined by how we protect them.  Imagine a breaching promisor.  We protect thereliance interestof the promisee by requiring the promisor to put her in a position as good as she would have been in had the parties not contracted.  The other interests are therestitution interest,which we protect by requiring the promisor to give back what the promisee has given him; and theexpectation interest,which we protect by requiring the promisor to put the promisee in a position as good as she would have been in had he kept his promise.  In a sense the reliance interest is intermediate between the other two interests.  A promisee might rely otherwise than by giving the promisor what a restitutionary remedy will make him give back, and she enters a contract expecting to be better off by doing this than she would be by not doing it (unless she would expect, if she did not enter this contract, to enter a contract similar to it).  The definitions of the interests are by Fuller but the secondRestatementadopts them.
My paper is mainly loosely connected reviews of two other papers about the reliance interest.  I talk in Part I aboutThe Reliance Interest in Contract Damages,by Fuller and Perdue.This paper defined the interests and urged us to attend particularly to the reliance interest.  Goetz and Scott, who wrote the other paper, invite us to extract fromThe Reliance Interestthe insight that "reliance is the organizing principle that supports all contractual obligation."The Reliance Interestis our most significant article on contract law.  (We rightly resist adding 'alas', as in Gide's reply "Hugo -- helas!" to the question 'Who was the greatest poet of the nineteenth century?') Macneil speculates thatThe Reliance Interest"may well have had more influence in changing American contract jurisprudence in the past 40 years than any other single article or book."The competition is formidable.  Conceivably Macneil discounts Corbin's treatise on the ground that its influence is an instance of backward causation.  Corbin published it late in his career (1950-51), long after he had established its ideas.
I talk in Part II aboutEnforcing Promises: An Examination of the Basis of Contract,by Goetz and Scott. Goetz and Scott consciously build on Fuller's idea but they disregard the ethical foundation of it in a way I will discuss.  They defend the thesis they attribute to Fuller: protecting the reliance interest is the objective of contract law.  Goetz and Scott are methodologically more sophisticated than Fuller.  Where Fuller applied Aristotelian philosophy and folk economics they use indifference curves.Hudec remarks ofThe Reliance Interestthat its "analysis has served a generation of contracts scholars as a model of how to think about contract law generally."It certainly has done this but the generation of contracts scholars is not quite the current one.
This is a critical study, its affirmative aspect largely implicit.  But Parts I and II share two theses (A and B) -- or a weak and a strong form of one thesis.  A: The expectation interest countstoo.Evidently this is true but it takes through Part II to bring it out.  B:Onlythe expectation interest counts.  B is maybe less interesting because it turns on taxonomy (we identify a transaction as uncontractual if we purposely protect reliance on it).  But the law is prettier if B is true.  To get clear about A/B, recast the thesisEnforcing Promisesattributes to Fuller and defends as C:Onlythe reliance interest counts.Apparently then 'counts' is interchangeable with 'is an organizing principle of contract law', 'is an objective of contract law', etc.  Nothing is novel about A and B.  Goetz and Scott are trying to refute A by asserting C and they think Fuller was too.  Perhaps; but by a better reading Fuller was more circumspect and tried rather to refute B by arguingforthe other side of A: The reliance interest countstoo.E.g., Fuller breaks off advocating the reliance interest to tell us the expectation interest in charitable contributions isrightlyprotected without regard to the promise having been relied on.
Part I has two jobs: be friendly to A/B; explain why Fuller was not more so.  The problem was the reliance interest was theoretically too central to Fuller's analysis to be protected most of the time by tort law.  So he did not make "the assumption, so frequently made, that any liability explicitly directed toward the reimbursement of reliance must rest on 'tort' rather than 'contract'."The reliance interest was too central to Fuller's analysis for two reasons.  He was unequipped to work out the economics of the expectation interest -- he invoked Aristotle instead of Marshall -- so if deprived of the reliance interest he would have had no theory.  Coincidentally Williston andCorbin in their compromise over section 90 of theRestatementcorrupted his data base so he started off calling too many promises 'contracts'.
have organized Part I like this.  Part IAis an annotated outline of Fuller's data.  I start here because Fuller's paper is classically inductive, i.e., Fuller argued that the cases categorized his way make more sense.  The annotations suggest this is anyway not self-evidently so.  Parts IBand ICrespectively address promises bargained for and gratuitous promises.  Fuller taught us the expectation interest in bargained-for promises gets protected in the course of protecting the reliance interest.  Part IBsays the dependency goes the other way.  Part ICbegins with Gilmore's story of Corbin's enthusiastic and Williston's grudging invention ofRestatementsection 90, then assimilates this section to tort law.  Part IDsuggests that Fuller discounted the expectation interest because his reading Aristotle left him unprepared to get the point of protecting it.
The ideas in Part I are big (and vague).  One gets embarrassed by them.  Part II somewhat redemptively makes mostly narrow technical points.The Reliance Interestwas published in 1936;Enforcing Promisesin 1980.  That the forty-four years intervening have made a methodological difference to scholarship partly explains the difference in levels of the analyses.
The technical analysis is largely to the effect that Goetz and Scott get wrong results from or by interpreting their geometry.  Or better, Goetz and Scott get right results but not enough of them.  To correct what they say, I use what Goetz has published elsewhere, but has applied differently.So in a way I am redirecting their insights, not having new ones.  But our differences, despite being technical, are worth inquiring into, albeit everybody has met more exciting arguments.  Benefit side:Enforcing Promisesdepends on being technically right.  Thesis C -- that only the reliance interest counts -- is sensible according to its self-imposed criterion only if protecting just the reliance interest (with some latitude about what counts as this interest) provides an economic optimum.  Goetz and Scott teach us to calculate this interest a new and excellent way.  If my analysis is right, however, protecting the interest calculated this way is sub-optimal.
Perspective is also important.  For instance, Whitehead reminds us: "After all, even during the worst period of the decline of Rome the barbarians were enjoying themselves."The perspective from whichEnforcing Promisesis wrong (if it is wrong) -- that of the theory of economic policy -- is itself valuable.
Part IIAderives beneficial and detrimental reliances following Goetz and Scott.  Part IIBexplains their optimal damage rule based on these reliances.Goetz and Scott celebrate the equivalence of this rule and the Hand test in tort law.  Part IICfinds the rules governing intentional tort, not negligent tort, more nearly equivalent to the optimal damage rule.  Part IICalso discusses how Goetz and Scott use 'reliance' in a way related only tenuously to Fuller's use of it.  Part IIDmostly criticizes the rule ofEnforcing Promisesas economically sub-optimal.  It argues that if we extendwhatGoetz and Scott say, if we take it as true and investigate the consequences of it, then we end up reinventing contract pretty much as we have it, not as they want it to be.  There is something of Russell's argument against ordinarylanguage physics here: 'If it is true it is false, therefore it is false'.
We should judge a damage rule for breach of contract by whether it performs three functions well or badly: compensates the promisee; gets the number of promises made right; and gets the number of promises kept right.  The first function mattered most to Fuller; Goetz and Scott worry about the second; I am interested in the third.  Parts IICand IIDrespectively talk about accomplishing (or failing to accomplish) the first two and then simultaneously all three of the functions.
Finally, which of A/B/C is best matters although the question is abstract.  This area of contract law has been unstable since Fuller published.  Fuller criticized the parts of the firstRestatementabout remedies effectively enough that not much of them survives.  TheRestatementas it is currently written repentantly embraces Fuller's catalogue of interests, likewise his permissive attitude toward protecting them.It is (perhaps consequently) usually unable to tell judges what to do.  This kind of change in the currentRestatementhas been hailed as a desirable shift from rules to standardsbut is still an evil thing.

questions.question: Should damages for breach of promise be designed primarily to reimburse a promisee's reliance losses (costs incurred in reliance on the promise) rather than to secure the benefit the promisee expected from performance?

Do damage rules that calculate and protect reliance-based losses (as determined by economic models of beneficial and detrimental reliance) produce economically optimal outcomes-balancing adequate compensation, the right number of promises made, and the right number of promises kept-compared with alternative formulations?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When and how should charitable pledges be enforceable?
Can default liability rules be designed to induce socially optimal precontractual reliance, and what informational burdens would such rules place on adjudicators?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
Have doctrinal boundaries among contract, tort, and property shifted toward a formalist, market-oriented model?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 11texwesleyanlrev267!!SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY AND THE COMMON LAW: ORIGINS AND DEVELOPMENT:ROBERT J. POTHIER'S INFLUENCE ON THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY AND THE COMMON LAW: ORIGINS AND DEVELOPMENT:ROBERT J. POTHIER'S INFLUENCE ON THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the remedial objective of contract damages: reliance interest versus expectation interest
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the debate whether contract law should protect the promisee's reliance interest or the expectation (or restitution) interest, analyzing Fuller, Goetz & Scott, and the Restatement taxonomy; Paper B engages the same issue by tracing how civil‑law measures (damnum emergens and lucrum cessans) and Pothier's writings were transmitted into common‑law doctrine and the Restatement's measurement rules.

shared_topics.topic: limiting consequential damages by foreseeability / the 'contemplation of the parties' (Hadley rule)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques economic formulations of optimal damage rules and compares them to tort tests (Hand) while assessing rules that constrain recoverable reliance losses; Paper B is a historical and doctrinal account of Pothier's 'contemplation of the parties' test and Hadley v. Baxendale as the common‑law rule for limiting consequential (foreseeable) damages.

shared_topics.topic: methodological foundations of contract doctrine: moral/natural‑law (Aristotelian/Pothier) versus economic/analytical approaches
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts Fuller's Aristotelian, ethical grounding of the reliance interest with Goetz & Scott's indifference‑curve/economic methodology and criticizes the substitution of ethics by economics; Paper B documents Pothier's natural‑law and Aristotelian influences and shows how those moral/philosophical foundations shaped substantive rules that later encountered more objective or economistic reinterpretations.

shared_topics.topic: policy functions of damages—compensation, incentive effects, and regulating promise formation and performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes assessing damage rules by how well they compensate promisees and influence the number of promises made and kept, arguing different theories emphasize different functions; Paper B discusses the social and economic rationale behind limiting damages (e.g., avoiding ruinous liability, stabilizing commerce), and how rules on damages and penalties serve broader regulatory and incentive purposes.

shared_topics.topic: historical transmission and authority of treatises and Restatements in shaping modern contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Fuller's influence and how Restatement revisions adopted or reshaped the catalogue of reliance/expectation/restitution interests; Paper B documents Pothier's widespread, transnational influence on English and American contract law, showing how treatises and codifications (Civil Code, Restatements, UCC antecedents) carried doctrinal principles into modern common‑law practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101columlrev1876!!ARTICLE:THE GIFT BEYOND THE GRAVE: REVISITING THE QUESTION OF CONSIDERATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:THE GIFT BEYOND THE GRAVE: REVISITING THE QUESTION OF CONSIDERATION

shared_topics.topic: where to draw the line between enforceable and unenforceable promises (gifts versus contracts)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally interrogates the consideration doctrine as the mechanism that distinguishes enforceable promises from gratuitous gifts and traces its doctrinal and cultural consequences; Paper B repeatedly confronts the taxonomy problem (when a transaction is treated as contractual versus reliance-based/noncontractual) in debating which interest (reliance, expectation, restitution) the law should protect.

shared_topics.topic: the conceptual primacy of promise in defining contractual obligation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that consideration doctrine privileges a promise-centered conception of contract and thereby shapes who counts as a contracting, calculating agent; Paper B engages the same conceptual terrain by questioning whether reliance or expectation (both promise-related concepts) should be the organizing principle of contract law and by evaluating Fuller's promise-focused framework.

shared_topics.topic: the use of economic analysis to justify doctrines and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A locates consideration doctrine in a broader project of producing an economically rational individual and legitimating market withdrawal of state power; Paper B applies and critiques economic tools (indifference curves, optimal-damage calculations) to assess whether protecting the reliance interest alone is economically optimal and how damages rules perform.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal critique of foundational contract scholarship and the Restatement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A excavates nineteenth- and twentieth-century debates over consideration and gifts to show how classical frameworks persist, while Paper B traces and critiques the influence of key articles (Fuller, Goetz & Scott) and the evolution of the Restatement in shaping contemporary remedies and doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: the purposes and functions of contract law (what interests remedies should protect and why)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links the enforceability distinction to larger questions about what obligations law should recognize and the resultant diminution of state role; Paper B analyzes the aims of damages—compensating promisees, setting the right number of promises made/kept—and debates which protected interest (reliance, expectation, restitution) best serves those functions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78neblrev491!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"

shared_topics.topic: theoretical foundations for enforcing promises (consideration/mutuality versus reliance/expectation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the mutuality-of-obligation corollary to the mutual-promise/consideration rule and examines how mutual promises support enforceability, while Paper B debates whether contract law should rest on protecting reliance or expectation interests and how that choice determines which promises get enforced and how.

shared_topics.topic: the Restatement and doctrinal reform of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the Restatement (Second)'s proposal to abandon mutuality of obligation and critiques recent case law influenced by Restatement formulations, and Paper B analyzes and criticizes how successive Restatements (and section 90) have recast remedies and the catalogue of interests (reliance, expectation, restitution).

shared_topics.topic: remedies and reciprocity between obligation and remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the connection between mutuality of obligation and mutuality of remedy (including equity's mutuality of remedies) to ensure symmetric relief, while Paper B is centrally concerned with damages rules—how reliance, restitution, or expectation protections function to compensate promisees and affect whether promises are kept or paid for.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal interpretation of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both papers undertake historical and doctrinal scholarship: Paper A traces mutuality and mutual-promise doctrines back four hundred years to interpret their original meaning, and Paper B traces Fuller's, Goetz & Scott's, and Restatement-era developments to explain how modern thinking about reliance and expectation evolved.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43buffalolrev1!!ARTICLE: Promises Betrayed: Breach of Confidence as a Remedy for Invasions of Privacy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Promises Betrayed: Breach of Confidence as a Remedy for Invasions of Privacy

shared_topics.topic: using contract doctrines to enforce promises not traditionally thought of as ordinary contractual disputes (e.g., confidences and media promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes plaintiffs suing the press by invoking contract-based breach of confidence theories (including when reporters promise sources confidentiality), while Paper B is centrally concerned with when and how promises should be enforced by contract law and what legal structures protect promisees, so both examine the remedial role of contract doctrines for promises outside classic commercial bargains.

shared_topics.topic: the reliance interest and reliance-based remedies as a basis for recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper B is an in-depth theoretical and doctrinal study of the reliance interest as a protected contract remedy (vs. expectation and restitution), and Paper A discusses plaintiffs’ attempts to recover for invasions of privacy by relying on contract-like assurances and reliance (e.g., confidentiality promises), treating reliance-based contract remedies as a possible path to relief.

shared_topics.topic: adequacy and limits of contract/fiduciary remedies (including damages) versus tort remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract and fiduciary actions often offer limited relief for disclosed private facts due to formal requirements and inadequate damages, and Paper B critically analyzes how different damage measures (reliance vs. expectation) perform and when reliance-based awards may be suboptimal, so both assess whether contractual/fiduciary remedies adequately compensate harms compared to alternative tort remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary and taxonomy between contract, tort, and fiduciary claims for similar harms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys how courts have framed breaches of confidence under contract, fiduciary duty, or tort and the consequences of those classifications, while Paper B repeatedly engages the taxonomy question (e.g., whether reliance protection should be treated as contract or tort) and discusses implications of characterizing remedies within one category or another.

papers.node_id: 48stanlrev481!!ARTICLE: Offer, Acceptance, and Efficient Reliance
papers.title: ARTICLE: Offer, Acceptance, and Efficient Reliance
papers.abstract:
In this article, Professor Craswell explores efficient reliance as an implicit economic rationale underlying courts' decisions in contract formation cases. Contracting parties often fail to express their intentions clearly and courts must later decide what the parties would have wanted ex ante. When negotiations fail, one party (S) may deny ever making a commitment, while the other party (B) may claim to have relied on the first party's statements or conduct. Professor Craswell observes that courts often find a binding commitment by S when reliance by B would have been efficient. After explaining when reliance is efficient, and why the nonrelying party might prefer it, Professor Craswell shows that courts appear to apply an efficient reliance rationale under a variety of common law doctrines. But because the question of whether B's reliance was efficient is highly fact specific, Professor Craswell concludes that bright line rules would not, as a general matter, guarantee a more efficient result.
The problem is a familiar one. Two parties negotiate with an eye to a potential transaction. Discussions are held; documents are exchanged; perhaps a preliminary agreement is reached; perhaps one party even starts performing. Then something happens: The market turns, a better offer comes along, or someone simply has a change of heart. At any rate, one party announces that he or she is no longer interested in the transaction. The other party responds irately, claiming that "we had a deal," and that the time for free withdrawal from the transaction has long since passed. The legal question is whether the first party is indeed free to walk away, or whether the disappointed party is instead entitled to compensation.
While the question is straightforward enough, contract law attempts to answer it with a bewildering array of doctrines. The outcome of the case may turn on whether either party did or said anything the law will interpret as an "offer," and, if so, whether the other party did or said anything the law will interpret as an "acceptance." The law will also ask whether the "acceptance" took the proper form, and whether it came at a proper time (had the offer already been withdrawn? had it lapsed?). Liability may also turn on whether the party now attempting to withdraw said anything the law will interpret as a"promise" on which the other party "reasonably" relied, or whether the disappointed party's preparations conferred any benefits on the other party for which he or she might be liable in restitution.
As scholars have pointed out for at least fifty years, the legal doctrines governing these issues are largely conclusory and question-begging.The law interprets a communication as an "offer" if it is "so made as to justify another person in understanding that his assent to that bargain … will conclude it."An offer of unspecified duration lapses if it is not accepted within a reasonable time, where what is reasonable depends "on all the circumstances existing when the offer and attempted acceptance are made."An offer also expires if the offeree responds by making a counteroffer - unless the purported counteroffer is really a "mere inquiry" or a "qualified acceptance."If an offer has not expired, the offeree's reliance on it may make the offer irrevocable - but only if the offeror should reasonably have expected to induce such reliance.Even then, the offer is irrevocable only "to the extent necessary to avoid injustice."And so on.
A long line of contracts scholarship, running from Arthur Corbinand Karl Llewellynto Melvin Eisenberg,has argued that courts should not simply apply mechanical or formalistic rules to contract formation cases, but should instead decide them to give effect to the parties' most likely intentions. The wisdom of this approach is, of course, contestable,andconsider some of the possible alternatives in Part V. The article's main focus, however, is on how we might implement this approach, assuming that we accept its validity. In Parts I through IV, I argue that if we are to carry out the Corbin/Llewellyn recommendation, we need some way of figuring out what the parties most likely intended, and (in particular) some understanding of why someone would ever want to form a contract. That is, why would a party ever want to commit to a transaction in advance, rather than reserve the right to withdraw until the moment the transaction is consummated?
While there are several possible reasons why such a commitment might be in a party's interest, I focus on the effect of an enforceable commitment on the other party's incentive to rely on the proposed transaction. As Charles Goetz and Robert Scott pointed out in 1980, a legally enforceable commitment may sometimes be the only way to induce the other party to choose an efficient levelof reliance.Building on their insight, I suggest that the legal doctrines governing offer and acceptance can be interpreted to prevent one party from withdrawing in just those cases where an enforceable commitment would have been necessary to induce an efficient level of reliance by the other party. In those cases, I argue, even the party who now seeks to withdraw would have wanted to be committed (if he or she had been asked that question at the time the other party had to rely), precisely in order to induce efficient reliance.
Parts I through III develop this theoretical argument in more detail, explaining when reliance on a proposed transaction is efficient, and showing why a nonrelying party might want to be committed in order to induce efficient reliance. Part IV then surveys the reported cases to show that many decisions can be understood by reference to the efficiency (or inefficiency) of each party's reliance. That is, I show that in cases where the party now seeking to withdraw had a reason to be committed (in order to induce efficient reliance by the other party), courts have been quite willing to find both an offer and quite willing to find a valid acceptance, and quite willing to resolve every other legal issue in favor of an enforceable obligation. I do not claim that courts have consistently decided cases according to this principle: Exceptions and counterexamples are easy to find. But I do claim that considering the efficiency of the other party's reliance provides a principled method of applying these vague and conclusory legal doctrines, in a way that the doctrines themselves cannot.
Finally, Part V asks whether courts should even engage in this inquiry, if doing so requires them to assess the efficiency of one side's reliance on a case-by-case basis. The alternative to case-by-case analysis is increased judicial use of bright line rules. In theory, bright line rules could encourage the parties to decide for themselves when a commitment would induce efficient reliance, and to signal their decision more clearly to the courts and to each other. A bright line strategy could thus free courts from the burden of deciding when one party's reliance would have been efficient. As discussed in Part V, however, a bright line strategy also has drawbacks, which may explain why courts so often revert to case-by-case analysis.

questions.question: Whether courts' decisions to enforce pre-contractual commitments track whether one party's reliance on negotiations would have been socially efficient.
Under what circumstances reliance on a proposed transaction is socially efficient, such that an enforceable commitment is necessary to induce the efficient level of reliance.
Whether replacing case-by-case judicial assessments with bright-line rules would produce more efficient reliance and overall contractual outcomes.

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Can default liability rules be designed to induce socially optimal precontractual reliance, and what informational burdens would such rules place on adjudicators?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 86columlrev269!!ARTICLE: A CONSENT THEORY OF CONTRACT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CONSENT THEORY OF CONTRACT.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance in forming and enforcing contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an efficiency-based account of when one party's reliance should make a commitment enforceable and shows courts often apply such an 'efficient reliance' rationale; Paper B evaluates reliance as one of the competing bases for enforceability and explains how its consent theory treats reliance and seeks to avoid courts having to adjudicate 'reasonable' versus 'unreasonable' reliance.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations for when promises should be legally enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks why a party would want an enforceable commitment (focusing on inducement of efficient reliance) and reads doctrines through that economic rationale; Paper B surveys competing theories (will, reliance, fairness, efficiency, bargain) and proposes a consent-based account as the preferable moral-legal foundation for enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should infer parties' intentions (objective intent and interpretation of offers/acceptances)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how vague communications are resolved into offers and acceptances by reference to what would have induced efficient reliance and the parties' likely ex ante intentions; Paper B explains why the law generally uses an objective approach to intent, when and why it deviates, and how a consent theory explains those interpretive choices.

shared_topics.topic: the choice between bright-line rules and case-by-case standards in contract doctrine
