shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether courts should do fact-specific efficiency inquiries or adopt bright-line rules to govern formation and reliance; Paper B addresses the drafting and harmonization process—how international texts borrow and adapt domestic rules (UCC/Restatement/CISG)—a design choice aimed at producing predictable, transnational contract norms.

papers.node_id: 83washulq471!!ARTICLE: ON DISCOVERING DOCTRINE: "JUSTICE" IN CONTRACT AGREEMENT
papers.title: ARTICLE: ON DISCOVERING DOCTRINE: "JUSTICE" IN CONTRACT AGREEMENT
papers.abstract:
Start from the premise that the object of positive legal analysis is to resolve doctrine into matters of fact. That object certainly explains the common ground between such diverse intellectual enterprises as the economic analysis of law (including its iterations in behavioral decision theoryand "neuroeconomics") and so called "critical theory" (from its various perspectives). Each assumes that there is some fact qua empiricalfact that explains why the Law looks the way the Law looks.That fact may be efficiency,or it may be bigotryor some basic biological imperative that defies normative classification.Once "discovered," the fundamental facts too may lend themselves to construction: One person's efficiency is the other's hegemony; what is racism or sexism from one perspective is respect for the individual from the next. Debate is not so much resolved as moved from the level of theory to fact to, perhaps ultimately, invective. But the object of "legal" analysis remains the same: to reveal the facts upon which the analysis is founded. We trust the ostensible objectivity of facts, and even the subjectivity of objectivity we assert as a discernible fact.
This Essay is a further and inevitable variation on that theme. I pursue here what might be termed "doctrinal jurisprudence": Study of the way facts (including rules) become legal doctrine,specifically here howidiosyncratic perceptions concerning "justice" facts support the development of contract agreement doctrine.
Analysis in terms of doctrine is heuristic in nature. That is, doctrine translates a bundle of data; we explain data (when, for example, a promise is enforceable) by reference to doctrine (when, say, there is "agreement"). But like all heuristics, doctrine is both under-and over-inclusive.Doctrine does not formulate enough cases (and so we may adjust the doctrine or create a new exceptional category, like promissory estoppel), or it formulates and determines the result in too many cases (in which event we refine the doctrine or create exceptions to its operation, like impossibility or frustration). It is doctrine we encounter, normally as the elaboration of rules or a law, when we try to make sense of Law or an area of Law such as contract.
This Essay investigates the relationship between the way we encounter data (including laws, and specifically a contract law) and what we may conclude about the Law, as doctrine, that emerges from that encounter. The study is limited to the contract law not because there is necessarily anything unique about contract so far as our encounter with law as data is concerned,but because the subject is fundamental and generally accessible. Further, in the formulation of contract doctrine you can see quite starkly the operation of forces generally at work in the Law. There isalso something else about contract doctrine that reveals a good deal about our encounter with Law: At several crucial junctures, contract expressly invokes conceptions of morality in the form of references to "justice" and "fairness" in order to resolve recurring sources of controversy. So an appreciation of our encounter with contract doctrine may intimate as well something about the Law-morality dynamic that underlies so much of the Law, or at least so much of the way we talk about Law.
Though the scope of the Essay may seem broad, the goal is really quite modest: to discover a means to describe a structure to depict human agents' encounter with justice-based contract doctrine. The goal is not to describe the constituents or determinants of justice in this or any context - this is not an exercise in consequentialist or deontological theory. There may be nothing more fundamental to contract than the constituents of agreement, and justice is, as this Essay demonstrates, frequently the measure of contract liability. Agreement is the product of a "justice" calculus. At least, that is the case often enough to support the conclusion that you cannot understand what contract means by "agreement" unless you understand the justice component of agreement.
The development and presentation of a structure is crucial to the argument here. A challenge to our current understanding of justice as a determinant of contract agreement is our inability to be certain that we are talking about the same thing when we use the same terms: What you mean by the word "justice" - by which I do not mean, your sense of what is just - may be wholly different from what I intend the term to denote (and connote). A structure helps us assure that we are talking about the same thing (or make sense of our conversation when we are not). Also, once we identify law (or rule), Law, and the justice calculus in the structure, we can better investigate the relationship among them. It is a thesis of this Essay that the relationship among laws, Law, and the justice calculus may tell us more than would simply crafting definitions of each in isolation from the other two.
The ultimate conclusion here is that, notwithstanding its invocation of justice, contract (and perhaps all of Law) is essentially amoral; that is, there is no such thing as a fixed "morality" that can matter in the way Law, specifically the contract law, governs transactor interrelations. That is not to say that there is no such thing as morality. There may well be a phenomenon or network of phenomena that is best described as morality, but that is another thing altogether from saying that that phenomenon or those phenomena can have currency in the sphere of "legal morality" - theconfluence of the coordination, expertise, and efficiency interests that justify Law.I use "legal morality" to describe the moral purposes Law serves.What is crucial about the concept for present purposes, though, is that legal morality pertains only in the case of a relation between or among two or more subjects of Law. Morality simpliciter would pertain no less in the case of an individual actor. Legal morality is a corporate concept that operates just in case coordination, expertise, and efficiency considerations are in play.
The objects here are, admittedly, ambitious, and the course of the argument must effect a certain consilienceto support the observations about contract agreement offered. Extant positive legal theories are not up to the task.They just reveal the incongruities without describing their sources. To make more sense of the Law of contract agreement, it is necessary to invoke conceptions of our encounter with data generally and then to formulate an explanation of what it is that we "see" when weencounter a legal rule. The consilience accomplished here takes advantage of contributions to our understanding of cognitive theory generally as well as our developing appreciation of the "complex."
Part I of the Essay will offer an account of five contracts cases that concern the nature of agreement: Hadley v. Baxendale,Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent,Peevyhouse v. Garland Coal & Mining Co.,Henningsen v. Bloomfield Motors, Inc.,and Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc.While that is not to say that those five cases determine agreement fully and completely, it is to say that we cannot understand what agreement in contract means unless we can account for these five cases and the fit between justice and agreement they present. Four of the cases expressly invoke "justice" as the measure or determinant of contract agreement. The fifth relies on "practical considerations" essentially indistinguishable from the elements of the "justice" calculus relied upon by the first four. The cases are not mined for their sense of justice. The cases reveal the contract law's reliance on justice expressly, even in the course of fixing what may be one of its most prosaic conceptions: the agreement.
That brief exposition of five seminal contract agreement cases will demonstrate the salience of justice in recurring agreement contexts: We have come to understand contract's central agreement doctrine by direct reference to justice as a tool of analysis, not simply as a trope we might apply after the fact to signify our concurrence with a more fundamental analytical criterion. The cases, we will see, do not simply admonish the next court to do what is just or to reach the result consistent with justice. Instead, they hold that the very contours of the parties' agreement is determined by justice. So in order to formulate that agreement, you must appreciate what terms justice would require. The contract law, then, can be no more accessible to us than can be the conception of justice, and is every bit as subject to idiosyncrasy as our conceptions of justice. Part I presents the five crucial cases to make clear the role of justice in contract agreement in order to support the analysis that follows of the structure of the justice calculus: what we can mean when we describe a result as consistent with the dictates of justice.
Justice (as perhaps all constituents of legal doctrine) is the product of cognition. Part II of the Essay first describes a conception of cognitive theory that explains well how we encounter data, including legal doctrine, subject to pervasive heuristic limitations. Our every encounter with data is determined by our prior encounters with data, which ultimately determine what we understand to be our perspective. Our perspectives are dynamic and shift as we are subject to data, and we are constantly bombarded by additional data: We never stand in the same river twice.Over time, certainly, our perspectives become more fixed and more difficult to shift, much as an automobile's fuel efficiency gauge varies more markedly when fewer miles have been traveled than it does after many more miles have been traveled, and just as we learn more in the first year of life than we will ever learn thereafter. Cognitive theory offers an account of our encounter with data and the idiosyncrasies of perception that nonetheless conspire to reveal sufficient consensus for cooperative action, the object of Law. Conceptions of cognition, essentially how we process the constant onslaught of data, can tell us something about how we encounter the datathat is and that becomes Law - for present purposes, the contract agreement law.
Part II then builds on that cognitive theory to offer a depiction of legal rules (the laws that determine, at least in part, what Law is) and describes our engagement with them in terms of complexity theory. The description demonstrates something important about the nature of legal doctrine (here, contract agreement law). I argue that the structure of legal doctrine may be revealed by the same cellular automata complexity theorists use to depict the elaboration of rules in nature. That is not to say that a legal rule is determined in the same way as might be the "pattern" of cells that account for the appearance of natural phenomena (a flower or an animal's markings), but it is to suggest that the analogy to complexity theory's demonstration in cellular automata may offer a useful reconception of legal doctrine and the relationship between doctrine and what we mean by "justice."
The second Part concludes by offering a synthesis of cognitive and complexity theory in terms of the contract law of agreement, and the Conclusion of the Essay suggests the answers that might be provided by the structure as well as the questions that remain. The object is to make more concrete the justice calculus in the case of contract agreement, and the possibility is left open that the structure developed may pertain as well to other analytical settings in Law. The emergent structure is a first step, but an important one.
For clarity's sake, it is worthwhile to present the course of the Essay's argument at the outset:

questions.question: Whether and how idiosyncratic perceptions of justice (the 'justice calculus') determine what counts as an agreement and thus shape the content of contract law.
Whether a formal descriptive structure drawing on cognitive theory and complexity theory can explain how legal actors encounter, form, and apply justice-based legal doctrine about agreements.

Whether invoking justice in legal doctrine yields a stable, determinate moral standard that governs obligations, or whether such invocation is inherently variable/constructed so that contract law functions essentially as amoral or coordination-focused law.

matched_themes: When a seller partially performs, what is the appropriate measure of monetary restitution awarded to the partially performing party?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 46ambuslj531!!ARTICLE: Mutual Misunderstanding in Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mutual Misunderstanding in Contract

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal meaning and contours of 'agreement' in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the concept of agreement is shaped by recurring case law and by an implicit 'justice' calculus (using five seminal cases as exemplars), while Paper B examines how the formation doctrine applies (or fails) in mutual misunderstanding cases and how courts treat the existence or absence of an enforceable agreement.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of parties' subjective perceptions or misunderstandings on enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats justice and legal doctrine as products of cognition and idiosyncratic perception that determine how we 'see' agreement, and Paper B focuses squarely on mutual misunderstandings—how differing, reasonable subjective understandings affect whether and how agreements should be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: critique of existing formation/interpretation doctrine and proposals for reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues extant positive legal theories are inadequate and proposes a cognitive-plus-complexity structural reconception of how doctrine (including agreement) emerges, while Paper B criticizes the common-law fiction that mutual misunderstanding voids contracts and proposes an alternative remedial rule allowing each party to enforce their reasonable understanding.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between subjective and objective standards in contractual interpretation/enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the trust in ostensible objectivity of legal 'facts' versus idiosyncratic subjective conceptions of justice, and Paper B explicitly contrasts subjectivist and objectivist rationales for enforcement, advocating an objectivist alternative that operationalizes reasonable understandings.

shared_topics.topic: efficiency, reliance, and coordination goals as justificatory considerations for contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames 'legal morality' in terms of coordination, expertise, and efficiency as the corporate aims that law serves and that constrain moral claims in doctrine, while Paper B evaluates current and proposed rules in light of reliance, preservation of reasonable expectations, ex post bargaining, and overall efficiency.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42harvjlgender83!!ARTICLE: ANTI-STEREOTYPING THEORY AND CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: ANTI-STEREOTYPING THEORY AND CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the role of justice/non‑economic norms in shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A applies anti‑stereotyping (an equality norm) to show how contract doctrines embody gendered normative assumptions, while Paper B analyzes how explicit invocations of "justice" and "fairness" function as determinants of contract agreement doctrine and shape outcomes beyond pure efficiency analysis.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law doctrines encode and perpetuate social biases (especially gendered assumptions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A demonstrates that doctrines like consideration, interpretation, and damages have historically excluded women's domestic experiences and perpetuated a market/home (men/women) dichotomy, and Paper B shows that idiosyncratic justice judgments and cognitive heuristics produce doctrinal outcomes that reflect underlying social perceptions and biases.

shared_topics.topic: limits of existing doctrinal categories (agreement, interpretation, unconscionability) to accommodate diverse lived experiences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the rule/exception model leaves non‑economic (often female) concerns marginalized and calls for a contextualized contract law, while Paper B interrogates how the agreement doctrine (and related doctrinal categories) both under‑ and over‑include cases because of the embedded justice calculus and cognitive constraints.

shared_topics.topic: reforming contract doctrine informed by normative theory and a structured account of how doctrine emerges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes doctrinal changes to make contract law more egalitarian by rejecting stereotypical assumptions, and Paper B offers a structured (cognitive + complexity) account of the justice calculus aimed at clarifying how doctrine is produced and how it might be rethought.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1984wislrev1373!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF RELIANCE: A HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF RELIANCE: A HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE.

shared_topics.topic: the shift from bargain/consideration to reliance and justice-based doctrines (e.g., promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A historically documents the decline of consideration and the expansion of reliance‑based recovery (promissory estoppel) in contract law and asks why that shift occurred; Paper B situates promissory estoppel and other exceptions within a broader story about how 'justice' and practical considerations reshape the meaning of agreement when bargain doctrine is under‑ or over‑inclusive.

shared_topics.topic: methodological inquiry into how to explain doctrinal change (historical, critical, interdisciplinary methods)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques traditional legal‑historical accounts and advocates using critical methodologies to connect doctrinal shifts to social context; Paper B likewise rejects narrow positivist accounts and develops an interdisciplinary methodology drawing on cognitive theory and complexity theory to explain how doctrines emerge and stabilize.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of extra‑legal factors (social conditions, cognition, perceptions of justice) on the content of contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks how social conditions and broader social processes help explain the growth of reliance doctrines; Paper B analyzes how idiosyncratic perceptions of justice and cognitive heuristics shape courts' formulations of agreement and thus the substance of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: consequences for judicial decisionmaking and legal scholarship (reconstruction, doctrinal interpretation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws implications of the historical inquiry for how judges and scholars should understand and reconstruct contract law (including utopian/critical projects); Paper B offers a structured account of the justice‑calculus intended to inform how judges and scholars should interpret and apply agreement doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91washlrev1663!!ARTICLE: AN "APP" FOR THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN "APP" FOR THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal ambiguity arising from reliance on subjective concepts (intent, justice)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers identify that core contract doctrines depend on indeterminate, subjective concepts — Paper A argues that the third‑party beneficiary rule is plagued by an inherently ambiguous 'intent' inquiry, while Paper B shows that contract 'agreement' is shaped by idiosyncratic conceptions of 'justice,' producing doctrinal indeterminacy.

shared_topics.topic: the need to reconceptualize or reframe doctrinal analysis with a new vocabulary or structure
shared_topics.justification: Both propose replacing or supplementing current doctrinal language to improve clarity — Paper A proposes the 'APP' (additional possible plaintiff) framing to focus analysis on practical notice, and Paper B develops a formalized structure (drawing on cognitive and complexity theory) to explicate the justice‑calculus that underlies agreement doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: focus on practical consequences as a central criterion for doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works argue that doctrinal determinations should be informed by their real‑world effects — Paper A centers the analysis on whether contracting parties had reason to know of an extra potential plaintiff (practical litigation consequences), and Paper B emphasizes that the justice calculus and resulting rules must be understood in terms of coordination, expertise, and efficiency implications for transactors.

shared_topics.topic: whose perceptions or mental states (perspective) should matter in resolving contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with the question of which parties' mental states or perspectives are relevant to doctrine — Paper A asks whose intent (promisor, promisee, or both) should count for third‑party beneficiary status, while Paper B analyzes how prior cognitive perspectives and heuristics shape legal actors' perceptions of justice and thus the content of agreement doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2007uilllrev881!!ARTICLE: "LAW &" GRATUITOUS PROMISES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: "LAW &" GRATUITOUS PROMISES

shared_topics.topic: why some promises are legally enforceable while others (gratuitous promises) are not
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how courts carve out the content of 'agreement' — often invoking justice and ad hoc doctrines — to determine enforceability, while Paper B foregrounds the classic question of why gift promises are generally nonenforceable and evaluates doctrinal exceptions to that rule.

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel and other doctrinal exceptions to the consideration requirement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats promissory estoppel as an example of how doctrine is adjusted when existing rules under- or over-inclusive, and Paper B examines promissory estoppel (alongside charitable subscriptions) as a primary exception that allows otherwise gratuitous promises to be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: the boundaries and meaning of 'agreement'/'consideration' in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the very contours of what counts as parties' agreement are shaped by an underlying 'justice' calculus and doctrinal evolution, while Paper B questions whether the traditional exchange-based conception of consideration should set the limits of contract law and interrogates how the doctrine defines enforceable promises.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of cognitive/behavioral and non-economic factors on contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs cognitive theory (and complexity analogies) to explain how perspectives and heuristics shape legal perceptions of justice and agreement, and Paper B directly compares law & economics to behavioral law & economics, using cognitive and psychological findings to explain why courts treat certain promises as unenforceable.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61dukelj1511!!ARTICLE: WHEN MONEY GREW ON TREES: LUCY V. ZEHMER AND CONTRACTING IN A BOOM MARKET
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHEN MONEY GREW ON TREES: LUCY V. ZEHMER AND CONTRACTING IN A BOOM MARKET

shared_topics.topic: the influence of extrinsic economic and background facts on whether parties are held to a contractual 'agreement'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that conceptions of 'justice' and background facts shape what counts as agreement in contract doctrine, and Paper B shows how the regional timber boom and economic motives would have changed the reasonable-person assessment in Lucy v. Zehmer.

shared_topics.topic: the limits and fragility of formal contract doctrines (e.g., agreement/objective theory) because of perspective, perception, and heuristic constraints
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that doctrinal rules are heuristic and under-/over-inclusive due to cognitive limitations and idiosyncratic justice-calculi, while Paper B demonstrates that the objective theory's conclusions are highly narrative-dependent and thus vulnerable to alternative factual framings.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial narrative, selective fact-presentation, and institutional decision-making in producing and stabilizing contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts invoke justice and construct doctrinal facts to define agreement, and Paper B documents how the Virginia opinion and contemporaneous actors obscured or omitted contextual facts—shaping the court's account and the resulting precedent.

shared_topics.topic: using historical/contextual case-reconstruction to revise doctrinal understandings of contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes a set of seminal agreement cases to reveal how justice operates in doctrine and proposes a cognitive/complexity-based structure, and Paper B performs archival and historical reconstruction of Lucy v. Zehmer to reveal hidden economic context that undermines standard readings of the case.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78stjohnslrev131!!ARTICLE: MUST PROFITS MADE IN TRANSACTIONS INVOLVING LATE-DELIVERED GOODS BE DEDUCTED FROM THE INJURED PARTY'S BREACH DAMAGES? IF NOT, WHAT IMPACT SHOULD LATE-DELIVERED GOODS HAVE?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MUST PROFITS MADE IN TRANSACTIONS INVOLVING LATE-DELIVERED GOODS BE DEDUCTED FROM THE INJURED PARTY'S BREACH DAMAGES? IF NOT, WHAT IMPACT SHOULD LATE-DELIVERED GOODS HAVE?

shared_topics.topic: the normative role of justice/fairness in shaping contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A repeatedly invokes the UCC's goal of putting the aggrieved party "in as good a position" and debates when courts should offset post‑breach profits to avoid windfalls; Paper B analyzes how conceptions of "justice" and fairness operate as explicit determinants of contract doctrine (notably agreement and remedy) and how idiosyncratic justice judgments become legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: use of presumptions and doctrinal heuristics (e.g., the 'regular dealer' / lost‑volume presumption)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on doctrinal presumptions—such as treating regular volume dealers as likely to have made both transactions absent a breach and shifting burdens accordingly—to resolve damages disputes; Paper B studies how legal doctrine functions as a heuristic device and how such presumptions reflect cognitive shortcuts that structure courts' deployment of contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between statutory rules (UCC provisions) and equitable/common‑law adjustments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes specific UCC provisions (e.g., cover, accepted goods, 2‑714/2‑711) and shows how courts adapt or supplement those statutory measures with equitable tests (market‑related offsets, lost‑volume analysis) to reach fair outcomes; Paper B theorizes how formal legal rules and the justice calculus interact—how law, rules, and moral judgments coalesce to produce doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: reliance on economic/market facts and efficiency considerations in doctrinal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds remedial rules in market realities—comparing cover prices, wholesale prices, and total cost effects to determine damages and to avoid overcompensation; Paper B situates economic analysis (and related empirical facts such as efficiency) as one of the factual substrates that courts discover and treat as determinants of doctrinal choices in contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev49!!SYMPOSIUM: THE AFTERLIFE OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE AFTERLIFE OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the role of "justice" or legal morality in defining contract agreement and liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes how conceptions of justice and "legal morality" are explicitly invoked to determine the contours of agreement in contract cases; Paper B repeatedly examines how equitable, policy, and justice-based considerations (as opposed to pure formalism) have shaped contract doctrine historically and in debates between Williston, Gilmore, and later commentators.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between doctrinal formalism and realist/critical (or law-and-economics) critiques of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes doctrinal heuristics and how rules over- and under-inclusive readings map to competing theoretical accounts (economics, critical theory); Paper B surveys the Gilmore–Williston debate and the rise of realism, Critical Legal Studies, and law-and-economics, showing how those schools contest classical formalist accounts of contract.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of political economy and ideological rhetoric (laissez-faire / market ideology) on contract doctrine and interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates economic analysis of law and critical theory as competing factual explanations for why law looks the way it does; Paper B documents the practical and rhetorical resurgence of laissez-faire thinking (e.g., The Contract With America, Posner-style law-and-economics) and traces how those ideological commitments shape doctrinal choices and the framing of contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy and the role of non-legal factors (perspective, rhetoric, empirical practice) in shaping contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses cognitive and complexity theory to explain idiosyncratic perceptions and emergent structures that make doctrine indeterminate and contingent on perspective; Paper B emphasizes how narratives, rhetoric, and empirical sociology (Macaulay) reveal that case law and doctrinal outcomes are influenced by extra-doctrinal practices and political storytelling.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72iowalrev47!!ARTICLE: Damages for Reliance Across the Spectrum of Law: Of Blind Men and Legal Elephants
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Damages for Reliance Across the Spectrum of Law: Of Blind Men and Legal Elephants

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based recovery and promissory estoppel
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question of when a promisee who has relied on a promise can recover absent a traditional contract: Paper A analyzes reliance remedies across contracts, promissory estoppel, tort, agency, insurance, and restitution; Paper B treats promissory estoppel as a doctrinal adjustment that exemplifies how courts expand or refine agreement doctrines to capture reliance-based claims.

shared_topics.topic: the role of justice/fairness and flexible/equitable remedies in contract relief
shared_topics.justification: Both works probe how equitable considerations shape outcomes: Paper A investigates courts' use (and nonuse) of 'flexible remedies' to compensate relying promisees across doctrinal categories, while Paper B argues that conceptions of justice and fairness are central to how courts define agreement and thus determine appropriate remedies in contract cases.

shared_topics.topic: overlap, inconsistency, and the need for doctrinal coherence across legal doctrines addressing broken promises
shared_topics.justification: Both papers confront the problem that multiple substantive fields (contract, tort, restitution, agency, insurance) can apply to the same facts and produce divergent remedies: Paper A documents that overlap and inconsistent damages across those fields and calls for a unified theory, while Paper B analyzes how doctrines expand, contract, or spawn exceptions (e.g., promissory estoppel) when existing rules are under- or over-inclusive.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrine is discovered, formed, and applied versus scholarly accounts of law
shared_topics.justification: Both examine the formation and application of legal doctrine rather than just normative prescriptions: Paper A empirically and historically shows that courts often do not recognize the doctrinal overlaps or the flexible remedies scholars attribute to them, and Paper B offers a theoretical account (cognitive/complexity) of how judges and legal actors perceive facts and produce doctrine, explaining why doctrine can diverge from scholarly expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44iowajcorpl649!!ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority

shared_topics.topic: historical emergence and evolution of private-law doctrines in Anglo‑American law
shared_topics.justification: Both papers trace how specific private-law doctrines developed over time — Paper A reconstructs the 18th–19th century emergence of apparent authority in agency law, while Paper B traces the doctrinal development of contract agreement through landmark cases and doctrinal shifts.

shared_topics.topic: the shift from subjective intent to objective standards in interpreting parties' relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that apparent authority arose as part of a movement from subjective to objective reasoning (reasonable third‑party perceptions), and Paper B examines how contract doctrine relies on shared, often objectified, conceptions (e.g., justice/fairness and practical considerations) to determine agreement.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of commercial practice/custom and coordination needs on legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates agency doctrine within commercial and mercantile custom and a body of commercial rules, while Paper B foregrounds Law's coordination and efficiency functions (legal morality) and analyzes contract cases where commercial/practical considerations shape doctrinal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: use of doctrinal devices and exceptions (e.g., estoppel, promissory estoppel) to fill gaps or correct over/under‑inclusiveness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether apparent authority is best understood as an equity estoppel or an independent doctrine, and Paper B discusses how doctrines (and doctrines like promissory estoppel) are created or adjusted when existing rules under‑ or over‑include cases of agreement.

BAXENDALE:HADLEY AND THE COMMON LAW: ORIGINS AND DEVELOPMENT:ROBERT J. POTHIER'S INFLUENCE ON THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT

papers.node_id: 44vandlrev221!!ARTICLE: Opportunism and Trust in the Negotiation of Commercial Contracts: Toward a New Cause of Action
papers.title: ARTICLE: Opportunism and Trust in the Negotiation of Commercial Contracts: Toward a New Cause of Action
papers.abstract:
In a complex economy, many business transactions take place sequentially -- one party performs in part or in full before the other side executes its side of the bargain.  Sequencing has many advantages, but it creates an unfortunate incentive.  Having received its benefit from the bargain, the party who is to perform last may be tempted to renege on its obligations.  Law and economics scholars often describe the conduct of a reneging party in these situations as "opportunistic."The reneging party, perceiving an opportunity to increase its gain, yields to temptation and refuses to perform.  The law of contract helps to diminish the danger of opportunism by providing assurance to those performing first that their contracting partners can be held accountable if they renege.Accountability reduces the risk of entering business transactions and facilitates an atmosphere of confidence conducive to exchange.
Recently, scholars have explored the dangers of opportunism even after a contract is formed.If performance under the contract requires one side to invest in assets specially tailored to the transaction,the other side may be tempted to exploit this postcontractual situation by renegotiating the original terms to capture more of the bargaining surplus.The same postcontractual opportunistic incentives exist when one side becomes dependent on unique skills or knowledge acquired by theother side after performance has begun.
This scholarly interest in postcontractual opportunism has not extended to the precontractual stage of business dealings.Law and economics scholars have assumed that parties in the precontractual stage are not likely to invest heavily in contract-specific assets and that the costs of finding suitable substitutes for performance are relatively low.More traditional doctrinal scholars likewise have failed to explore the concept of opportunism in their analyses of precontractual legal regulation.Both groups' approaches reflect traditional doctrinal distinctions, which sharply differentiate between precontractual and postcontractual dealings.
This Article challenges the assumptions of law and economics scholars regarding precontractual opportunism and seeks to fill a significant gap in the doctrinal analysis of commercial negotiation.  First, the Article argues that the dangers of opportunism arise in the precontractual stages of business relations more frequently than law and economics literature has recognized.Opportunism often is more subtle in initial negotiations than in long-term contracts, and precontractual losses usually are more modest than those in the postcontractual cases.  Nevertheless, a case survey reveals recurring fact patterns that point strongly toward the presence of opportunism in the initial negotiation of agreements.
, as a normative matter, the Article posits that legal doctrines regulating the precontractual stage can be made more precise and effective by directly introducing the concept of opportunism into the law.  Third, the Article argues that regulation of precontractual opportunism is appropriate because opportunistic behavior during bargaining undermines one of the fundamental psychological conditions for the successful coordination of complex commercial transactions --interpersonal trust.Social psychologists,sociologists,economists,philosophers,and legal scholarsall have recognized that trust is central to the efficient coordination of human goals.  Once trust is established, commercial parties are better able to take risks that are necessary to coordinate transactions.Without trust, parties must resort to costly mechanisms such as simultaneous exchanges, precontractual contracts, or deposits to reduce suspicion of one another's motives to manageable levels.If these mechanisms are unavailable, parties may forego transactions altogether.
Until now, scholarship regarding the relationship between law and trust has been lacking.  Legal economists have discounted trust in their analyses of legal regulation.At the opposite extreme, more traditional scholars have treated trust as a self-evident necessity of commercial dealings without examining the social psychological mechanisms for creating and maintaining trust.  This Article addresses the shortcomings of both law and economics theorists and traditional scholars.  It does so by exploring theoretical and empirical research on trust from the fields of sociology and social psychology and linking that research to the judicially imposed legal penalties for precontractual opportunism.
Part II of this Article first discusses and defines commercial opportunism.  Part II then describes the landscape of complex commercial negotiations.  By exploring the wide variety of doctrines that courts have manipulated to compensate victims of precontractual opportunistic conduct, this section demonstrates that transaction-specific investments are common in complex negotiations.  Part III explores why precontractual opportunism is socially and economically undesirable.  Part III examines sociological and social psychological literature on the dynamics of interpersonal trust and asserts that precontractual transaction-specific investments are part of a vital trust-building process that undergirds many commercial relationships.  Part IV looks at the role of law in supporting the construction of trusting commercial relationships.  After analyzing nonlegal methods of deterring opportunistic conduct and reviewing the costs of legal intervention, Part IV concludes that legal rules proscribing opportunism in negotiation are justified as a means to reinforce and support the process of building trust.  Part IV then extends this analysis by suggesting a new cause of action to improve deterrence of precontractual opportunistic conduct.  Part V concludes with a summary and a suggestion for further research.

questions.question: Whether opportunistic behavior by one party during precontractual commercial negotiations occurs frequently enough to cause meaningful losses to the other party.
Whether legal regulation that recognizes and deters precontractual opportunism is justified as a means to preserve interpersonal trust and thereby promote efficient commercial coordination.

Whether creating enforceable legal remedies (a cause of action) against precontractual opportunism would effectively deter such conduct and reduce transaction costs relative to nonlegal or informal safeguards.

matched_themes: When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How do informal relational norms and repeated interactions govern commercial contracting in practice, and when do these norms supplant formal state-enforced rules?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
Is imposing a judicially enforced duty to negotiate in good faith necessary to achieve efficient outcomes in preliminary agreements, or would protecting reliance expenditures suffice?
How do market and institutional features affect whether informative 'cheap talk' will arise privately or require legal intervention to induce accurate precontractual communication?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 34umemlrev499!!ARTICLE: Origins of Promissory Estoppel: Justifiable Reliance and Commercial Uncertainty Before Williston's Restatement
papers.title: ARTICLE: Origins of Promissory Estoppel: Justifiable Reliance and Commercial Uncertainty Before Williston's Restatement
papers.abstract:
Between the early 1860s and the 1926 proposal for a promissory estoppel section in the Restatement of the Law of Contracts (Restatement), American courts, with some regularity, granted justifiable reliance relief on commercial promises designed to adjust to uncertain conditions. While some commentators overlooked, or chose not to acknowledge, these early commercial reliance-based decisions, other writers forthrightly rejected the doctrinal propriety of allowing recovery. The denial that nineteenth century courts had bound commercial promisors on the grounds of justifiable reliance reflected the conventional belief that the origins of justifiable reliance relief resided in nineteenth century hardship decisions involving gratuitous promises.
Contrary to that accepted account, the following legal history of the justifiable reliance doctrine documents that courts regularly granted commercial promisees relief from reliance hardship for many decades prior to the first Restatement. More often than not, these reliance-based decisions provided a means to overcome doctrinal obstacles to enforcement of novel promises crafted to deal with uncertain economic conditions. Much has been written about the development of justifiable reliance relief subsequent to Williston's inclusion of a promissory estoppel section in the Restatement; however, except for the generalizations of the authors of the Restatement, or restaters and their contemporaries, surprisingly little legal history has been written about the development of the justifiable reliance doctrine prior to the Restatement.
The story begins around the early 1860s as business planners found it increasingly necessary to incorporate greater flexibility into their agreements to contend with economic unpredictability in the context of longer-term relationships. Promissory innovations in the form of open-ended language, unilateral contract offers, at-will relations, and the more frequent need to modify contract terms butted up against traditional contract doctrine developed during earlier, more static times. Strict common law demands fordefiniteness, mutuality, reciprocity of bargain and the related preexisting duty rule scuttled attempts for more malleably structured agreements.
Mounting cases of reliance harm, caused by doctrinal barriers to these unorthodox arrangements, stimulated nineteenth century courts to ameliorate the harshness otherwise generated by traditional rules applicable to contract formation, modification, and termination. Courts justified granting reliance relief through extensions of theories found both at law and in equity; the theories in support of this relief were typically an admixture of legal and equitable notions. Archaic principles opposed to flexible promises fueled growth in the role of justifiable reliance in overcoming resultant unfairness. Justifiable reliance recovery would be a harbinger of twentieth century reforms of some aspects of the inflexibility of formal doctrine.
This study of the commercial roots of promissory estoppel begins in Section II with an extension of this Introduction as a means to furnish background regarding the early sources of the justifiable reliance principle existing at law and in equity prior to the mid-nineteenth century. Section III focuses on Williston's justifications, and the constraining consequences thereof, for the Restatement's sections on bargain consideration and promissory estoppel. Section IV provides evidence, contrary to Williston's claims, regarding the types of transactions in which justifiable reliance recovery was available during the seven or so decades prior to the first Restatement. Williston's denial that commercial reliance relief had previously been given has had a dampening effect on justifiable reliance relief to this very day. The present examination is comprised of case law analysis of reliance recovery granted on commercial promises from around 1860 until Williston unveiled the promissory estoppel section in 1926. These commercial promises were structured to deal with uncertainty in forms incompatible with principles applicable to offer and acceptance and to contract modification. Section IV addresses the obstacles found in the doctrines of offer and acceptance and of consideration to enforcement of offers that were unilateral, indefinite, or at-will. The enforcement of contract modification promises is also examined in Section IV.

questions.question: Did American courts between the 1860s and the 1920s routinely give relief to commercial promisees who reasonably relied on flexible, uncertainty-responsive promises that would not meet traditional contract rules?
Was the historical origin of reliance-based relief primarily commercial (responses to economic uncertainty) rather than arising from gratuitous or purely charitable promises, as is commonly asserted?

How did courts during this period adapt or extend existing legal principles to avoid unfairness when enforcing (or refusing to enforce) novel, malleable commercial arrangements under traditional contract formation and modification rules?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do systemic institutional changes (deregulation, litigation costs, ADR, transnational codes) affect contracting behavior and the relation between law and practice?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do parties in ongoing exchange relationships use relational contracting-informal, repeated-interaction arrangements-to govern performance and adapt to change?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?

When and to what extent should post-contractual promises (e.g., promises for additional payment to induce performance already owed or post-sale statements) be enforceable as warranties or modifications?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 72minnlrev775!!ARTICLE: Paradox Lost.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Paradox Lost.
papers.abstract:
The fundamental question of contract theory is why a promise gives rise to a legal obligation.  Without promising, the scope of contract law shrinks to immediate transfers of property; and without a justification for promissory institutions, a considerable part of contract law is of dubious normative content.  An analysis of some special feature of contract law, such as consideration requirements, could not aspire to great moral status if promissory institutions could be abolished without apparent loss.
This Article defends a utilitarian theory of promising, under which legal and moral obligations to perform promises are justified by the felicific consequences of a convention of promise keeping.  Utilitarian theories, once accepted as providing the most plausible normative support for the economic analysis of law, fell into disfavor about ten years ago.The rejection of utilitarianism now seems premature because many of the criticisms leveled at it do not withstand close scrutiny.This Article does not seek to defend utilitarianism in general, however, but rather to demonstrate the inadequacy of rival, nonutilitarian theories.  It does so through an analysis of contract theory, for if utilitarianism alone offers a persuasive account of so fundamental a legal institution as contract law, lawyers will find rival theories difficult to accept.
The first rival theory, identified most closely with JohnRawls, is referred to as a low-fidelity theory because it does not invest promising with a moral status.  Under this theory promissory obligations ultimately rest on morally compelling connecting factors between individuals and morally neutral institutions.The institution of promising is not ethically desirable in itself.  Rather, the connecting factors alone have moral force.
Under high-fidelity explanations, in contrast, the duty to support promising arises as a consequence of the institution's desirability.  Examples of high-fidelity theories include both utilitarianism and neoformalism,which is utilitarianism's second rival.  Neoformalism defends promising on the basis of the moral value of a right to promise.  As a high-fidelity explanation of promising, neoformalism seeks to provide a justification for the institution of promising and is not simply a theory that, on principles of rights, promises made in a promissory society are binding.  Although neoformalists are rights theorists, not all rights theorists are neoformalists, for in promissory matters a rights theorist might subscribe to a low-fidelity theory.
Neoformalism today attempts to recapture private law institutions from a perspective of rights.  Like the earlier formalists, neoformalists analyze legal institutions with little regard to their end-state consequences.  Unlike their predecessors, however, the neoformalists' defense of contract law is more self-consciously philosophical, with principles of moral choice derived from deontological theories which exclude evidence of the remote consequences of acts.  The neoformalists' readiness to bring forward the Kantian heavy artillery may be seen as a compliment to the strength of their adversaries, the nihilists and consequentialists, for whom no justification, or only one that looks to end states, is possible.
Neoformalist theories attempt both to explain and to justify legal rules and institutions by reference to the moral values they serve.  The two endeavors are quite different, for thedescriptive exercise of identifying the values courts find underlying contract law differs from the justification of the institution's ways to man.  The descriptive project is a crucial part of any theory of contracts, for if the institution that is defended does not resemble the accepted regime of contract law, some otherwise valid contracts will not generate an obligation of performance.  This would be a serious failure, for a normative theory would be unattractive if adherence to it came at the cost of jettisoning one class of binding agreements.However, the discovery of that value which underlies every valid contract does not of itself generate a moral theory of contracts.  Unless it is assumed that the value is ethically desirable, its explanatory power is on the same moral plane as my decision to organize my library by author and not by subject matter.  Thus, a justification of promising must be a normative theory which at the same time can account for the circumstances when promises are in fact binding.
While promissory theories would be unpersuasive if they claimed that valid promises did not oblige, they need not seek to explain every kind of bargaining activity.  Promissory theorists are therefore free to focus on contract as promise.Evenwhen restricted to contract as promise, however, promissory obligations cannot be understood except by reference to a preexisting convention or institution that permits obligations to be incurred in this way.  Although the moral status of promissory obligations distinguishes promising from more trivial institutions, conceding a moral value to the imperative does not explain how an individual may have an obligation to perform a promise.  If commands are issued by a convention, how do they command me?  A justification of promissory institutions requires a principle of fidelity by which the convention's moral imperatives ought to be regarded as binding on a particular individual.
This Article argues that a principle of fidelity can be derived only by assuming the moral worth of the convention, but it does not seek to demonstrate that promissory institutions ought to exist.Instead, it assumes that promising is morally desirable and asks what conclusions follow therefrom.Part I examines promising as a convention, following the well-known discussion of conventional rules by John Searle and JohnRawls.Because promising is conventional, the obligation to perform a promise must rest on a principle of fidelity to promising by which the convention's rules bind individuals.  Two kinds of duties of allegiance are distinguished.  Under low-fidelity obligations, the principle of allegiance requires a morally compelling connecting factor between the individual and a convention.  High-fidelity duties, on the other hand, base fidelity requirements on the duty to support just institutions, dispensing with special connecting factors.
Part II considers whether principles of low fidelity to promising may satisfactorily be generated through connecting factors.  Various explanations of promissory institutions, based on different connecting factors, are examined from this perspective.  Although voluntary consent by the promisor, acceptance of benefits, and promisee reliance might all be proffered as possible links between individuals and institutions, none of these provides an adequate account of promising.  A successful defense of fidelity requirements must therefore assume the moral value of promissory institutions.
Part III examines what the values of the institution might be in high-fidelity theories.  The first high-fidelity theory discussed is neoformalism, which prizes the institution for permitting individuals to exercise a right to promise.  Like low-fidelity theories, neoformalism is unpersuasive.  While promising might at first seem desirable from a libertarian perspective, the institution is neither a necessary nor a sufficient condition of a free society.  As a consequence promissory institutions cannot be justified on abstract libertarian norms but must instead be defended for the special values of a regime of promising.  Neoformalism, however, is unable to identify the ethically desirable attributes of promising and therefore must be rejected.  Giventhe failure of neoformalism, contract theorists must choose between consequentialism, which accords a moral status to the consequences of adopting a promissory regime, and nihilism, which does not.  This Article concludes that only utilitarianism provides a satisfactory defense of the institution of promising.

questions.question: Whether legal and moral obligations to perform promises are best justified by the consequentialist (utilitarian) benefits of adopting a convention of promise-keeping.

Whether promissory obligations can be justified without assuming the intrinsic moral value of promising-for example by grounding obligations in individual connecting factors such as voluntary consent, acceptance of benefits, or promisee reliance.
Whether a rights-based account that posits a moral right to promise can adequately justify promissory institutions and fidelity obligations compared to consequentialist (utilitarian) explanations.

matched_themes: Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2008uilllrev505!!ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: competing normative frameworks (consequentialism/utilitarianism vs deontology/neoformalism vs aretaic ethics) as foundations for contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages this debate by evaluating low‑fidelity (Rawlsian), neoformalist (rights/Kantian) and utilitarian accounts and ultimately defending utilitarianism as the best justification for promising; Paper B surveys and criticizes the three dominant normative modes (consequentialist, deontological, and aretaic) as attempts to ground contract doctrine and examines their limits.

shared_topics.topic: the 'contract as promise' heuristic and the principle of fidelity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promising as a social convention and develops the need for a principle of fidelity to explain why promises generate obligations; Paper B treats the promise heuristic as one of the central descriptive models (alongside reliance and transfer) and interrogates whether treating contract as promise can serve as a reliable normative guide.

shared_topics.topic: the requirement that normative theories fit extant contract doctrine (descriptive vs justificatory demands)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that any normative defense of promising must account for the kinds of agreements courts actually treat as binding and not abandon whole classes of valid contracts; Paper B similarly stresses that heuristics and normative accounts must fit doctrinal practice and uses that fit (or lack thereof) to critique unified theoretical projects.

shared_topics.topic: institutional or conventional bases and connecting factors for promissory obligations (consent, reliance, acceptance of benefits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines various 'connecting factors' (voluntary consent, acceptance of benefits, promisee reliance) and finds them inadequate to generate promissory fidelity without assuming the institution's value; Paper B likewise explores institutional/historical explanations (including transfer and property analogies) and the role of institutional contingency in explaining why some promises become legally enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: whether a single unified normative theory of contract is possible or desirable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that only a utilitarian, high‑fidelity account satisfactorily defends promissory institutions as a unified justification; Paper B asks whether searches for a single, comprehensive normative theory of contract are doomed to fail and treats the discovery of that failure as a valuable explanatory result.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 87marqlrev297!!ARTICLE:RED OWL'S LEGACY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:RED OWL'S LEGACY

shared_topics.topic: reliance as a justificatory link for enforcing promises (promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates promisee reliance as one of the 'connecting factors' (low-fidelity explanations) and finds it inadequate to ground promissory obligations in general, while Paper B centers on Hoffman’s reliance on Red Owl’s assurances and examines the Supreme Court of Wisconsin’s use (and misfit) of promissory estoppel to enforce reliance-based loss.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for imposing legal obligations on promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an explicit theoretical defense of utilitarian grounds for why promises should generate legal duties (rejecting low-fidelity and neoformalist accounts), and Paper B interrogates the normative basis by questioning why the Red Owl court imposed liability absent contract and whether promissory estoppel or a tort-based justification better explains that imposition.

shared_topics.topic: the proper doctrinal boundary between contract remedies and tort duties in precontractual negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how promissory obligations must be tied to conventions and examines which links (consent, benefits, reliance) can justify obligations, while Paper B analyzes whether Red Owl was rightly treated under promissory estoppel or better understood as recognizing a precontractual tort duty to negotiate in good faith.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and legal doctrine in creating or shaping promissory institutions and protections for vulnerable parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats promissory obligations as institutional conventions whose moral force must be justified and whose legal content matters, and Paper B documents and critiques how the Wisconsin court’s Red Owl decision used judicial doctrine to extend protections to prospective franchisees, thereby shaping the practical contours of promissory liability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58washlrev343!!SYMPOSIUM ON ENERGY ISSUES IN THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST: UNCONSCIONABILITY IN A COMMERCIAL SETTING: THE ASSESSMENT OF RISK IN A CONTRACT TO BUILD NUCLEAR REACTORS.

shared_topics.topic: moral and legal justification for enforcing promises and contractual obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops competing normative theories (utilitarianism, neoformalism, low-fidelity accounts) to explain why promises generate binding obligations, while Paper B confronts that enforcement question in practice by asking whether a harsh contractual clause (the "hell-or-high-water" provision) should be judicially unenforceable on unconscionability grounds.

shared_topics.topic: the sufficiency of consent/assent and connecting factors to create binding duties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether voluntary consent, acceptance of benefits, or reliance furnish the necessary connecting factors to ground promissory fidelity and finds them wanting; Paper B foregrounds that the utilities' assent may have been invalidated by a failure to disclose risk information, undermining the parties' ability to give informed consent and thus the clause's bindingness.

shared_topics.topic: procedural fairness and nondisclosure as a basis for invalidating contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers procedural connecting factors (consent, reliance) as candidates for justifying promissory obligations, while Paper B applies procedural-unconscionability analysis—specifically the failure to disclose risk not reasonably available to the counterparty—to argue a commercial clause should not be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: the role of consequences and risk allocation in determining whether contractual institutions should be upheld
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances a consequentialist/utilitarian defense of promissory institutions by assessing the felicific consequences of adopting promise-keeping norms, and Paper B examines how extreme risk allocation (placing virtually all risk on utilities) and the practical consequences of noncompletion affect whether a contractual commitment should be sustained.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO:PARABLES ABOUT PROMISES: RELIGIOUS ETHICS AND CONTRACT ENFORCEABILITY*

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of doctrinal connecting factors (consideration, reliance, acceptance of benefits) to ground enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the common-law doctrine of consideration and the moral-obligation cases as a basis for enforcing promises, while Paper B systematically evaluates connecting-factor explanations (consent, acceptance of benefits, promisee reliance) and finds them insufficient to explain promissory obligation.

shared_topics.topic: the debate between consequentialist (utilitarian/high-fidelity) and deontological/religious or neoformalist justifications of promising
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates students' intuitions about promise-keeping within religious and philosophical (including Kantian) traditions, and Paper B frames and defends that debate explicitly, contrasting utilitarian high-fidelity defenses with neoformalism (Kantian/deontological) and low-fidelity accounts.

shared_topics.topic: focus on 'contract as promise' and the enforceability of private-party promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A limits its inquiry to promises between private parties and how religious ethics bear on contract enforceability, and Paper B centers its analysis on 'contract as promise,' asking what justifies treating private promises as the foundation of contract law.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE FREEDOM NOT TO CONTRACT.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a normative defense of utilitarianism over neoformalism and low-fidelity accounts to justify contract institutions, and Paper B considers whether observed shifts in case law (e.g., reliance-based enforcement or ignoring disclaimers) reflect a move away from the normative promise model toward alternative justificatory frameworks.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Squaring Undisclosed Agency Law with Contract Theory.
