Whether different types of remedies-those grounded in private agreements or special relationships versus remedies based on a general duty to protect privacy-are practically effective and recover meaningful relief.
Whether these confidentiality-based remedies can withstand constitutional free-speech scrutiny and thus be constitutionally permissible when applied against speakers or the press.

matched_themes: When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
When liability is grounded in misrepresentation rather than ordinary promise enforcement, do courts award different compensatory or punitive remedies?
Can confidentiality-based remedies (e.g., injunctions, nondisclosure orders) withstand constitutional free-speech scrutiny when applied to speakers or the press?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 22cornelljlpubpoly93!!ARTICLE: PROMISES, POLICIES, AND PRINCIPLES: THE SUPREME COURT AND CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION IN LABOR RELATIONS
papers.title: ARTICLE: PROMISES, POLICIES, AND PRINCIPLES: THE SUPREME COURT AND CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION IN LABOR RELATIONS
papers.abstract:
When the U.S. Supreme Court decides which promises made in the labor relations context should be enforced, and how to interpret those promises, has the Court treated those promises differently from the way the legal system has generally treated promises? Specifically, have policies (in particular, federal labor policy and its goals of wealth redistribution and industrial peace) played a predominant role, or have principles (in particular, notions of freedom of contract and the autonomy and will of contracting parties) played a predominant role?
This Article maintains that the Court's treatment of labor relations promises from the Wagner Act's passage in 1935to the Warren Court era's end in 1969 was consistent with Professor Grant Gilmore's famous "death of contract" thesis regarding contract law,as well as the predominant legal thinking of the time, the "legal process school."Specifically, during this time period, whether the Court enforced a particular labor relations promise, and how that promise was interpreted, was determined by balancing competing policies, with federal labor policy being themost important. And if Stewart Macaulay was the "Lord High Executioner of the Contract is Dead school,"the Warren Court was the Lord High Executioner of the "collective bargaining agreements are dead" school, with the high-water mark reached in 1964 in John Wiley & Sons, Inc. v. Livingston.
But in the early 1970s - starting in 1972 with NLRB v. Burns International Security Services, Inc.,soon after the "legal process" consensus was shatteredand Gilmore asked whether contract law would be resurrected- the Court shifted to treating principles (specifically, freedom of contract and the autonomy and will of the parties) as the primary bases for enforcing labor relations promises. This shift coincided with the rise of freedom of contract arguments by legal scholars arguing from both principles-based positions - scholars such as Charles Friedand Randy Barnett- and policy-based positions - scholars such as Richard Posner.The shift also coincided with the revival of libertarianism in political philosophy, spearheaded by Robert Nozick's 1974 publication of Anarchy, State and Utopia.
Part I of this Article explores legal thinking about contract law from the late nineteenth century to the present. Part II discusses those situations in which the Supreme Court has jurisdiction over labor relations promises. Part III discusses how the Court has treated promises made in the context of labor relations since the mid-1930s. Part IV addresses whether the Court's treatment of labor relations promises from the mid-1930s to the late 1960s is more consistent with congressional intent than the Court's treatment of labor relations promises from the 1970s to the present. Finally, this Article concludes that the latter approach is more consistent with congressional intent.

questions.question: Whether the Supreme Court's enforcement and interpretation of promises made in the labor-relations context has been driven primarily by competing public policy objectives (for example, redistribution and industrial peace) or by principles of contractual autonomy, and whether that balance shifted across historical periods.

Whether the Court's treatment of labor-relations promises in different historical eras more closely aligns with the underlying intent of the legislative actors responsible for the relevant statutory framework.

How broader intellectual and political shifts in legal and moral thinking influenced the Court's choice between policy-oriented and principle-oriented approaches to enforcing promises in labor relations.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Are courts' refusals to enforce contracts on public-interest grounds applied predictably, and which categories of public-interest challenges are most likely to succeed?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?

papers.node_id: 97harvlrev678!!ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND JUDICIAL METHOD
papers.title: ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND JUDICIAL METHOD
papers.abstract:
ONE of the most significant developments in contract law in the past half-century has been the rise of promissory estoppel-- the enforcement of unbargained-for promises that induce reliance.  Despite initial judicial reluctance to apply the doctrine after its formulation in section 90 of the firstRestatement of Contracts (Restatement)in 1932,courts and scholars have come to recognize promissory estoppel as a principle of wide application.Associated with the expanded use of promissory estoppel have been dramatic changes in the theory and method of contract jurisprudence.  The inclusion of section 90 in thefirstRestatement-- a work that was in most respects the high-water mark of classical contract law -- signaled the impending transformation.  Since the publication of theRestatement,liberal scholars and judges have pressed a broad-based attack on both the traditional substantive principles embodied in theRestatementand the methods by which, according to the traditional view, judges were supposed to apply such principles.At the same time, these jurists have attempted to reconstruct contract law in response to their own critique.
This Article reports and interprets the results of a canvass of the case law of promissory estoppel over the past fifteen years, and relates recent developments to broader changes in contract law.Part I chronicles the evolution of promissory estoppel against the backdrop of the classical conception of contract law and the attack on that conception.  Part I then examines the ways in which courts have applied the elements of the doctrine of promissory estoppel and suggests that such applications pose continuing problems for contract law.  Part II explores and criticizes the doctrinal applications as manifestations of competing methods of contract adjudication.

questions.question: How have courts in recent years treated and enforced promises that were not part of a formal bargain but that induced reliance, and what problems do those judicial applications create for traditional contract principles?

To what extent do different judicial decision-making methods (for example, formalist/doctrinal versus policy-oriented or corrective approaches) explain variation in outcomes when courts enforce reliance-based, non-bargained promises?
How have broader shifts in contract theory and jurisprudential method influenced judicial reasoning and outcomes in cases involving enforcement of reliance-based promises?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 56clevstlrev37!!ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND THE PROTECTION OF INTERPERSONAL TRUST
papers.title: ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND THE PROTECTION OF INTERPERSONAL TRUST
papers.abstract:
Promissory estoppel developed in order to protect reliance on a broken promise in the absence of a contract.Reliance lies at the core of the doctrine. However, reliance necessarily implicates another core concept--trust. The central importance of trust has been recognized by the courts, including the Michigan Supreme Court which observed, "It is the value of trust that forms the basis of the entitlement to rely."This paper examines the role of trust in promissory estoppel and the extent to which the law should protect trust when a promise is made. In order to do so, however, an important distinction must be drawn between two types of trust: (1) interpersonal trust between the promisee and the promisor; and (2) the promisee's trust that the promise will be enforced (which will be referred to as "enforcement trust" in this paper).
Interpersonal trust is about the trust that one person (the promisee) reposes in another person (the promisor). It is about the personal relationship between two people. Trust in the enforceability of a promise, on the other hand, is about the trust that the promisee has in the legal system to enforce a promise.A promisee maychoose to rely on a promise even if she does not trust the promisor because she has trust that the legal system will provide a remedy for a broken promise.
This distinction between the two types of trust is important because it frames the discussion concerning the extent to which promissory estoppel should protect a promisee. This distinction also mirrors the difference between contract and promise, which was discussed in Professor Seana Shiffrin's recent article in the Harvard Law Review.Professor Shiffrin observed that a "promise establishes rules for formalizing trust in interpersonal interactions; [while] contract establishes rules that help to enable a flourishing system of economic cooperation for mutual advantage."
The protection of interpersonal trust is closely allied with the elevation of the role and protection of promise. Those who exalt the importance of promise would argue that a promise is sacred and that a promisee's trust in a promise and the promisor is entitled to the maximum level of protection.The protection of trust in the enforceability of a promise, on the other hand, expresses the view that a promise must rise to the level of contract in order to be enforced.
Although interpersonal trust and enforcement trust are two distinct concepts, they are inextricably bound together (even in ways that appear contradictory). For example, if the law's goal is to protect a promisee's trust in her promisor no matter what, it can be argued that the enforceability of a promise must be maximized. At the same time, if the law's goal is to encourage a promisee to rely on a promise made by someone she does not trust, the law must also provide maximum security of enforcement. On the other hand, if the law's goal is to cultivate trust and a promisee's ability to decide whom to trust, it can be argued that the law should provide something less than maximum protection in order to prevent overreliance by promisees on untrustworthy promisors. Less than maximum protection places a burden on promisees to choose their promisors carefully. And where does thisbalance lie or where should it lie? To what extent should the law protect interpersonal trust and trust in enforcement of a promise? Such questions are the subject of this paper.
The discussion of reliance overshadows the discussion of trust in the typical Contracts class. Nonetheless, there is a school of thought that trust is so paramount and necessary in human interaction that the law should protect and promote trust, no matter what and no questions asked. Indeed, a body of scholarly work has developed to promote the idea that the availability of promissory estoppel should be expanded in order to encourage complete trust in promisors and their promises. One of the most advanced and cited works of this kind is an article from 1985 in the University of Chicago Law Review by Professors Farber and Matheson, who stated, "Our proposed rule is simply that commitments made in furtherance of economic activity should be enforced."In proposing this rule, they argued against the need to show reliance because all that mattered in their view was the enforcement of the promisee's trust in the promise. They went so far as to state that the protection of trust is "the core concern of contract law."
These are grand, sweeping statements. If a complete stranger promises a business opportunity, should the law encourage the promisee to trust the promisor no matter what? The Farber and Matheson view would answer, "Yes." It would also brush aside questions of the following sort: What was the relationship between the promisor and the promisee? Did the promisee have any reason to trust the promisor, other than the promisor's promise? Should the promisee have trusted the promisor? Instead of focusing on such questions, the Farber and Matheson view is that the promisee trusted the promisor, and that is that.
Surprisingly, the notion of trust as an absolutely desirable trait or state seems to have gone unchallenged in large part. It is as if trust is such an ideal virtue that it is beyond question. This exaltation of trust as an unquestionable virtue, however, is contrary to common sense and universal human experience. Parents strive to instill the notion of trust in their children. Yet, all parents tell their children not to talk tostrangers--notwithstanding the importance of trust. The reason is obvious. There are limits that need to be placed on trust, and trust is not a pure good that should be promoted no matter what. In fact, too much trust can be dangerous and destructive. Despite the shared intuitive understanding that trust should have its limits, there has been relatively little discussion as to where the limits should be drawn.
To be sure, trust deserves protection. However, this Article contends that the law should not engage in the maximum protection of interpersonal trust, but should instead concern itself with promoting and protecting an optimal level of trust.Trust, no matter what and however much, should not be the focal point of judicial inquiry. A promisee should not prevail simply because she trusted the promisor. Taken to its extremes, the literature seems to encourage contracting parties to engage in self-destructive acts of casual trust. Instead, the law should ask whether the trust was reasonable and whether it was appropriate. Those who engage in a reckless level of trust should not be protected. The promotion of the optimal level can be justified on the basis of such disparate rationales as morality (at one end of a spectrum) and economic efficiency (at the other).
The obvious question raised by this approach is how to determine the level of trust that should trigger judicial protection. This Article proposes a modest solution. It attempts to establish the endpoints of the continuum along which interpersonal trust should be evaluated. At one end are the situations where trust should be entitled to maximum protection. At the opposite end are the situations where trust should not be protected, and, indeed, should be discouraged.
Part II of this Article summarizes some of the scholarship discussing the nature and role of trust. In particular, it discusses the role of trust in a market economy, and the related role of trust in Contracts law. Part III examines whether there is a difference between trust and reliance, and whether it matters. To put it differently, does a discussion of trust add anything to what has already been generated by the literature's discussion of reliance? Part III further asserts that a separate discussion of trust is beneficial because it has the potential to guide and inform internal decision-making in a way that is not possible by simply focusing on outward reliance. Part IV of this Article discusses the role of trust in the doctrine of promissory estoppel. Among other things, it reviews the scholarly literature's incorporation of trust into the promissory estoppel analysis, and examines the intertwined relationship of trust and reliance.
Part V sets forth why the law should promote an optimal level of trust, as opposed to a maximum protection of trust no matter what. It discusses the need forpromisees to exercise self-reliance and self-protection in order to avoid overreliance. To guide the determination of the optimal level of trust, this Article suggests that the protection of trust should be viewed along a spectrum with one end being defined by the cases where trust should be protected to the maximum extent and with the polar opposite end being defined by cases where trust deserves no protection.Part VI identifies the types of cases where trust should be protected. Such cases include ones where the promisee is engaged in a transaction that she cannot avoid, where she has no control over the structure of the transaction, and where she has no choice but to trust the promisor (or more accurately, trust the legal system to enforce the promise). This Part includes a discussion of cases involving insurers and insureds. Another type of case where trust should be protected includes cases where the parties have developed a long-standing, pre-existing relationship to the point where the promisee has developed a reasonable basis to trust that the promisor will act in a manner consistent with that relationship.
Part VII presents the polar end of the spectrum where trust should not be protected. This part proposes that trust should not be protected if: (1) the promisee could have determined that the promisor was untrustworthy at a low cost to the promisee; or (2) if the promisee could have avoided the harm resulting from a broken promise by taking preventive measures that cost less than the amount of the potential harm. This part includes a detailed discussion ofUniversal Computer Systems v. Medical Services Ass'n of Pennsylvania,which this Article contends may be the most wrongly decided promissory estoppel case ever. It also includes a discussion of the role of lawyers concerning a promisee's self-reliance. Part VIII concludes the Article.
In summary, this Article does not promote or encourage trust to the maximum limits. However, trust is not the only societal interest that deserves protection under the promissory estoppel doctrine. There are other equally deserving and meritorious interests, such as: (1) an interest in discouraging naive, self-destructive behavior--i.e., blind trust; (2) an interest in avoiding misallocation of resources caused by overreliance and misplaced trust; and (3) an interest in avoiding the waste, disappointment and rancor caused by broken promises and lawsuits--in other words,parties would be better off avoiding bad situations, as opposed to trying to sort out in a courtroom the aftermath of an unfortunate act of misplaced trust.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the illusory-promise rule and characterizes mutuality of obligation as a presumptive, defeasible principle (not absolute), and Paper B argues for restricting promissory-estoppel protection to an 'optimal' level—protecting reasonable trust but denying relief for reckless or easily avoidable reliance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev989!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Sherwood v. Walker: Replevin for Rose Redux
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Sherwood v. Walker: Replevin for Rose Redux

shared_topics.topic: how the law should evaluate parties' subjective beliefs and reliance (probabilistic beliefs vs reasonable trust)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes Sherwood for treating the parties' beliefs about the cow as a binary fact and urges recognition of parties' probabilistic beliefs in mistake analysis; Paper B centers on the promisee's reliance and distinguishes interpersonal trust from enforcement-trust, arguing the law should evaluate whether such trust/reliance was reasonable and deserving of protection.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role and standards for courts in applying contract doctrines (factfinding versus lawmaking)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the court usurped the jury by treating a factual dispute about belief as a legal question and misapplied the mistake doctrine, while Paper B analyzes the judicial role in promissory estoppel—advocating doctrinal limits and a spectrum approach that defines when courts should enforce promises to protect trust.

shared_topics.topic: when and to what extent courts should grant remedies for mistaken beliefs or broken promises (thresholds for rescission/enforcement)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the doctrine of mistake and the reciprocal implications of rescission (e.g., fertile vs barren cow scenarios), highlighting problems with binary thresholds; Paper B develops a continuum for promissory estoppel protection, specifying endpoints where trust should receive maximum, minimal, or no protection and proposing tests for when remedies are appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the use of normative and economic reasoning to justify contract rules (efficiency, morality, and optimal protection)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the binary legal logic and invokes probabilistic reasoning (and notes economic-modeling responses to Sherwood) to argue for better doctrinal framing, while Paper B explicitly weighs moral and economic-efficiency rationales in arguing for an ‘optimal’ rather than maximal legal protection of trust and reliance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38casewres1!!ARTICLE: "Reliance" or "Common Honesty of Speech": The History and Interpretation of Section 2-313 of the Uniform Commercial Code
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: "Reliance" or "Common Honesty of Speech": The History and Interpretation of Section 2-313 of the Uniform Commercial Code

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal tension between reliance and alternative bases for enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts traditional reliance-based promissory estoppel with a conception of protection grounded in trust (including enforcement-trust) and debates how far estoppel should extend; Paper B analyzes why the U.C.C. replaced the Uniform Sales Act's reliance requirement with the amorphous 'basis of the bargain' standard in §2-313 and what that change means for warranty enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of the promisee's subjective state (belief, trust, or attention) for remedying broken assurances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally examines whether a promisee's interpersonal trust or trust in enforcement should by itself trigger legal protection and whether such trust must be reasonable; Paper B asks whether a buyer must have actually relied on or believed a seller's affirmation (or whether recovery can occur even without subjective reliance) when treating representations as part of the 'basis of the bargain.'

shared_topics.topic: interpretation and historical/drafting origins of doctrinal language governing promises and representations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates its argument within prior scholarly and judicial treatments of promissory estoppel and critiques competing theoretical framings (citing major scholars and cases); Paper B traces the drafting history and the intentions of U.C.C. drafters (Llewellyn and Mentschikoff) to explain the emergence and meaning of the 'basis of the bargain' phrasing in §2-313.

shared_topics.topic: policy trade-offs about how broadly to enforce promises (protecting trust and reliance versus preventing overreliance and inefficiency)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs moral and economic rationales for protecting an 'optimal' level of interpersonal trust while rejecting maximal protection that encourages risky reliance; Paper B interrogates Llewellyn's problems with reliance—implicit policy concerns about when representations should create liability—and how those concerns informed a different doctrinal balance under the U.C.C.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58tennlrev367!!ARTICLE: PERFORMATIVES IN SPEECH ACT THEORY: AN INTRODUCTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PERFORMATIVES IN SPEECH ACT THEORY: AN INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: Whether and how speech acts (promises, statutes, declarations) function as performatives that create legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the notion that performative utterances (e.g., baptismal formulas, statutes) literally bring institutional facts into existence and can be primary speech acts; Paper B treats promises as speech-act-like moves that the law may enforce via promissory estoppel even absent a contract, i.e., as utterances that can generate legal obligations through reliance.

shared_topics.topic: The importance of institutional authority and social context for speech acts to have legal effect
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that performatives succeed only within social institutions and when the speaker has requisite authority; Paper B distinguishes interpersonal trust from trust in the legal system and centrally analyzes when legal institutions should step in to enforce promises, thereby engaging the role of institutional authority and context in making speech legally effective.

shared_topics.topic: How linguistic form and encoded intent relate to legal enforceability of commitments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes illocutionary force, the relation of propositional content to force, and how intent can be encoded in linguistic structures; Paper B interrogates whether and when a promisor's statement (and the promisee's reliance on it) should be treated as legally binding, focusing on how the communicative act and perceived intent bear on enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: Contextual criteria and limits for when a speech-based act merits legal protection
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies contextual and status conditions required for performatives to succeed (appropriate status of participants, institutional rules); Paper B proposes concrete limiting criteria (reasonableness of trust, avoidability, cost of precautions) for when the law should protect reliance on promises, i.e., when speech-based commitments deserve judicial enforcement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 146upalrev1235!!ARTICLE: AN EXPRESSIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT: FROM FEMINIST DILEMMAS TO A RECONCEPTUALIZATION OF RATIONAL CHOICE IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN EXPRESSIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT: FROM FEMINIST DILEMMAS TO A RECONCEPTUALIZATION OF RATIONAL CHOICE IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the protection of reliance (and trust) as a justification for enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promissory estoppel as a doctrine rooted in reliance and distinguishes interpersonal trust from trust in enforcement, arguing about when reliance-based protection should apply; Paper B identifies protection of reliance interests as one of the central reasons (beyond bare choice) for giving legal significance to contractual commitments.

shared_topics.topic: normative limits on enforcement — balancing autonomy/choice against protection from harm
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues against maximal protection of trust and advocates an 'optimal' level of protection that discourages reckless or naive reliance, while Paper B frames feminist dilemmas (e.g., surrogacy, separation agreements) that require balancing respect for choice/autonomy against protecting parties from harmful choices made under inequality.

shared_topics.topic: differentiation of enforceability and remedies across types of promises/contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a spectrum situating cases where trust should receive full protection versus none and identifies contextual categories (insurers, longstanding relationships, avoidable reliance) for differing protection; Paper B argues that recognizing reasons for enforcement (reliance, convention) will produce a contract law that treats different kinds of contracts and remedies differently, preserving commercial core but altering enforcement outside it.

shared_topics.topic: the salience of relational and contextual factors (power, long‑term relationships, social norms) in assessing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds interpersonal trust, pre-existing relationships, and the promisee's control over transaction structure as key to whether trust merits legal protection; Paper B engages relational and feminist critiques showing how inequality, social roles, and relational context affect whether choices should generate enforceable obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2000utahlrev223!!SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.

shared_topics.topic: importance of factual and contextual inquiry in resolving disputes and shaping doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that promissory estoppel and the protection of trust must be evaluated case-by-case—examining the parties' relationship, whether the promisee could have avoided harm, and other factual indicia—while Paper B advocates 'legal archaeology' and historical reconstruction to recover the factual and contextual matrix behind reported cases so that doctrinal judgments are properly grounded.

shared_topics.topic: normative critique of judicial decisions and the use of cases as a basis for reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly critiques existing promissory estoppel decisions (identifying some as wrongly decided) and debates how courts should balance protection of trust, whereas Paper B urges close reexamination of reported cases to expose faulty assumptions and to assess whether outcomes were just, using that critique to inform legal understanding and reform.

shared_topics.topic: tension between abstract legal rules and case-specific justice (limits of doctrinal abstraction)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions blanket, maximalist rules (e.g., enforcing promises regardless of context) and argues for an 'optimal' trust-protection standard sensitive to circumstances, while Paper B warns that treating law as abstract doctrine risks obscuring injustices and calls for digging into the particular facts and history behind decisions to achieve just results.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103nwulrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS

shared_topics.topic: how contracts differ from non‑contractual legal instruments (promises, constitutions) in legitimacy and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts promises and contracts, asking when a mere promise should be treated like a contract for enforcement purposes (enforcement trust vs interpersonal trust), while Paper B directly contrasts constitutions and contracts to argue that constitutional legitimacy and enforceability cannot be read the same way as consensual private contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of background assumptions, trust, or reliance as sources of legal meaning or grounds for enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes interpersonal trust from trust in legal enforcement and debates when a promisee's reliance/trust should trigger judicial protection, and Paper B analyzes whether the shared background assumptions at enactment should shape constitutional meaning, distinguishing background assumptions from express text and implied terms.

shared_topics.topic: normative limits on judicial protection or construction to avoid overreach and promote legitimacy/efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for protecting an 'optimal' level of trust (not maximal) to prevent overreliance and misallocation of resources, while Paper B argues that original background assumptions should not automatically constrain constitutional construction because constitutions lack the private consent that justifies treating assumptions as binding.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39arizstlj135!!ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTIVE HAIKU AND THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: Raintree County Memorial Library Occasional Paper No. 3
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTIVE HAIKU AND THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: Raintree County Memorial Library Occasional Paper No. 3

shared_topics.topic: the role of 'trust' as a doctrinal and conceptual category in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a jurisprudential taxonomy of trust (interpersonal vs. enforcement trust) and argues about how and when the law should protect trust in promises; Paper B repeatedly invokes trust-related imagery and explicit doctrines such as the 'constructive trust,' using poems to probe how trust figures into remedies and relationships under contract law.

shared_topics.topic: how 'constructive' doctrines and legal fictions adapt legal categories to new factual situations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats promissory estoppel as a doctrinal device that fills gaps where formal contract protection is absent and debates the proper scope of that adaptation; Paper B centers on the family of 'constructive' concepts (constructive trust, possession, service) and frames them as legal fictions that adjust existing conceptual structures to novel circumstances.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of language, metaphor, and conceptual framing on interpreting and applying contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that drawing distinctions (e.g., trust vs. reliance) and framing protection along a spectrum affects judicial decisionmaking about promises and enforcement; Paper B foregrounds poetic language and metaphor as tools for re-describing contract concepts, illustrating how wording and imagery shape practitioners' and scholars' understanding of doctrinal issues.

papers.node_id: 59arklrev841!!ARTICLE: Promissory Estoppel and Wagging the Dog
papers.title: ARTICLE: Promissory Estoppel and Wagging the Dog
papers.abstract:
Few concepts in contract law have received more attention, both positive and negative, than has the doctrine of promissory estoppel.The doctrine has been seen both as an avenue to making contract law more responsive to the needs of contemporary practices,and as an erosion of contract doctrine.And, significantly, there is debate about whether it is in fact a contract doctrine at all, or whether it is more appropriately viewed as a tort concept.This article will suggest that the issueis not whether promissory estoppel is a contract or a tort theory, but whether cases decided under the doctrine are contract or tort cases, or whether they are something else.It will examine promissory estoppel as a doctrine whose application has expanded from very limited circumstances, explainable under established principles, into a doctrine that goes too far in its attempt to deal with difficult fact patterns in order to reach a "just" result.While doing justice is indeed a lofty goal, in a system of stare decisis an exhortation to do justice, without more, contributes little to the development, the certainty, or the predictability of legal rules. This is especially problematic in contract law, which deals with enforcing private agreements between parties.Crucial to a system of private agreement is the ability to know at what point an agreement is made,what the terms of that agreement are,and what the repercussions of non-performance might be.Further, where the concern is not with private agreement, but with the promotion of some publicpolicy, the policy should be defined in a way that allows parties to model their behavior accordingly.
submit that courts have used promissory estoppel unadvisedly to remedy perceived ills - righting tortious "wrongs" or avoiding the application of the statute of frauds or the parol evidence rule, for example - in ways that undercut the policies involved, skew the appropriate remedies, or hamper the development of the relevant substantive law. Rather than continuing to expand the doctrine, those cases that primarily deal with addressing harm should be decided as tort cases, and those that deal with other doctrines, even other contract doctrines, should be decided under those doctrines.If the more relevant doctrines do not serve the cause of justice, they should be reconsidered for all cases under that doctrine, not just those that arguably fit under the promissory estoppel umbrella.
The remaining cases can be characterized as promissory estoppel cases. The term "promissory estoppel," which seems to have been only reluctantly accepted to describe the doctrine, actually serves nicely to describe and classify its proper use.Promissory estoppel should be limited to situations in which both the promise and the estoppel are respected. The cases that are appropriately promissory estoppel thus tend to fall into one of two categories. First, they may be unequivocal contract cases, with the focus on the promise and the required reliance operating as something very similar to, if not actually, acceptance. In such cases the focus is promise, and the "estoppel" is an estoppel to deny consideration. The contract formed is a contract like any other. Second, they may be more traditional estoppel cases, emphasizing the estoppel, but with thetwist that the defendant is estopped due to a promise rather than a statement of present fact. These are more clearly estoppel cases, with the contract connection due to the context in which they arise. If the former analysis is appropriate, the full range of contract remedies should be available for breach. If the latter, the defensive nature of estoppel will determine the relief.
This article will begin by discussing the impact of the remedial goal on the way promissory estoppel is appropriately viewed. It will examine the consideration requirement and the extent to which it is suspended in promissory estoppel cases. It will explore how a focus on the relationship between substantive goals and remedial ones can add to the analysis of cases in these areas. It will suggest that the confusion in promissory estoppel analysis stems from the desire to have a remedy and then crafting a legal rule that will produce that remedy, rather than beginning with a legal principle and deciding what remedy will best accomplish the goals of that principle. It is in those cases that promissory estoppel becomes an example of "wagging the dog." It is in those cases that promissory estoppel has gone too far and should not be used.
When the principle at stake is the enforcement of promises and agreements, the analysis should be firmly grounded in contract. When estoppel principles are at work, estoppel should be the basis for recovery. When the principle is prevention of harm, the cases are better analyzed as tort cases. When the principle is ensuring that requirements of form, such as the statute of frauds or the parol evidence rule, do not subvert the very policies they are designed to protect, the law should craft exceptions that address those policies, not use promissory estoppel to indiscriminately undercut the requirements. In short, this article will suggest that a clearer focus on the goals involved, and an analysis under the appropriate legal principles, will produce results that are more consistent, more predictable, and therefore more just.

questions.question: Should courts use a broad, flexible reliance-based equitable remedy to reach fair outcomes across disputes, or should each dispute be decided under the substantive legal category whose underlying policy (enforcement of promises, prevention of harm, or protection of formalities) best fits the facts?

To what extent can or should a promisee's reliance substitute for traditional contract-formation formalities in creating enforceable obligations, and how does treating reliance as a substitute affect the scope of available remedies?

Do judges tend to craft or stretch legal labels and rules primarily to obtain particular remedies, and if so, should remedy-driven ad hoc decisionmaking be replaced by principled reform of the underlying substantive doctrines?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
When liability is grounded in misrepresentation rather than ordinary promise enforcement, do courts award different compensatory or punitive remedies?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75geolj1575!!ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Common Law and Uncommon Events: The Development of the Doctrine of Impossibility of Performance in English Contract Law.

shared_topics.topic: limits on doctrinal expansion and appropriate scope of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how specific doctrines (promissory estoppel in Paper A; impossibility/frustration in Paper B) have been stretched beyond their original boundaries and argue for clearer limits on when those doctrines should apply to avoid doctrinal overreach.

shared_topics.topic: proper doctrinal classification of cases (contract vs tort/estoppel vs frustration)
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines whether particular fact patterns are being handled under the correct legal framework—Paper A questions when matters should be decided as contract, estoppel, or tort, while Paper B dissects when events should be treated as impossibility/frustration versus other remedial or doctrinal responses.

shared_topics.topic: use of historical precedent and case-law development to clarify modern doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both works ground their critiques in historical and doctrinal analysis, tracing case law and authoritative precedents to show how the doctrines developed and to correct misconceptions about their proper modern application.

shared_topics.topic: tension between remedial goals (doing justice) and the need for certainty/predictability in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Each paper engages the problem of courts pursuing equitable or justice-driven outcomes—Paper A foregrounds how 'doing justice' can undermine predictability in promissory estoppel, and Paper B shows how unique factual drives behind impossibility cases complicate the formation of clear, predictable rules.

shared_topics.topic: critique of misapplication and misteaching of doctrinal principles
shared_topics.justification: Both articles identify and criticize mistakes in authoritative application or teaching—Paper A criticizes courts for using promissory estoppel as a catchall remedy, and Paper B contends that classic impossibility cases are often misunderstood or misrepresented in legal education and commentary.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36arizstlj257!!ARTICLE: Making Contracts Relevant: Thirteen Lessons for the First-Year Contracts Course
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Making Contracts Relevant: Thirteen Lessons for the First-Year Contracts Course

shared_topics.topic: judicial treatment of the parol evidence rule and merger clauses in commercial disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how judges' handling of merger clauses and the parol evidence rule determines whether sellers can obtain summary judgment and avoid protracted litigation, while Paper B critiques the use of promissory estoppel to circumvent the parol evidence rule (and statute of frauds), arguing that courts sometimes use estoppel to undercut these formal doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: the tradeoff between achieving equitable outcomes and preserving doctrinal certainty/predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues students should learn drafting and litigation practices that produce predictable, enforceable results for clients (e.g., drafting to secure summary judgment), and Paper B warns that judicial attempts to reach just results via expansive promissory estoppel undermine stare decisis and the predictability essential to contract law.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of oral promises, reliance, and the role of consideration/promissory estoppel
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts disputes spawned by oral promises (extensions, warranties) that parties invoke to escape performance, and Paper B analyzes promissory estoppel as the doctrine courts use (or misuse) to enforce promises absent consideration, distinguishing when such reliance-based enforcement is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial classification (contract vs estoppel vs tort) and available remedies shape transactional behavior and litigation strategy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on practical consequences—how drafting, merger clauses, and summary-judgment strategy drive settlements and business behavior—while Paper B argues that whether a case is labeled contract, estoppel, or tort should determine available remedies, and misclassification can distort incentives and legal development.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67bulrev9!!ARTICLE: WARRANTY THEORY, ECONOMIC LOSS, AND THE PRIVITY REQUIREMENT: ONCE MORE INTO THE VOID Copyright 1986 by Richard E. Speidel.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WARRANTY THEORY, ECONOMIC LOSS, AND THE PRIVITY REQUIREMENT: ONCE MORE INTO THE VOID Copyright 1986 by Richard E. Speidel.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal boundary between contract and tort
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze when disputes should be treated under contract law versus tort law: Paper A argues warranty-based (contract) liability should reach remote buyers for economic loss and thereby distinguish product fitness (contract) from product safety (tort), while Paper B criticizes the use of promissory estoppel to produce tort-like results and urges that harms best characterized as torts be decided as torts rather than subsumed under contract doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: reliance/representation versus formal contract formation (privity/consideration)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage with liability doctrines that impose obligations without a conventional bilateral bargain: Paper A defends treating warranties as representational (not requiring direct bargain or actual reliance) to abolish the privity defense, and Paper B examines promissory estoppel as enforcing promises based on reliance where consideration or formal acceptance is absent, distinguishing cases where reliance effectively substitutes for contract formation.

shared_topics.topic: role of remedial goals and limitations in shaping doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both works emphasize that remedial aims and statutory limits should constrain doctrinal development: Paper A relies on the remedial and limitative structure of U.C.C. Article 2 to justify imposing manufacturer duties while containing exposure, and Paper B stresses that courts should match remedies to the underlying principle (contract, estoppel, or tort) and not stretch promissory estoppel to obtain remedies inappropriate to the governing doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: whether to expand or curtail traditional defenses and doctrines (privity, estoppel, form requirements)
shared_topics.justification: Both debate reforming entrenched doctrines to achieve justice and policy goals: Paper A argues for abolishing the privity defense in economic loss/product-fitness cases to reflect distribution realities, whereas Paper B warns against further expansion of promissory estoppel (and advocates addressing problems by reforming the specific doctrines like statute of frauds) to avoid doctrinal overreach and unpredictability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50alalrev63!!ARTICLE: The Teachings of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. and Contract Theory: An Intriguing Comparison
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Teachings of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. and Contract Theory: An Intriguing Comparison

shared_topics.topic: tension between doctrinal rigidity and the need for contextual/flexible application of contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that classical, formalist contract theory is ill-equipped to address real-world bargaining distortions and calls for a more elastic, contextual application of contract rules; Paper B critiques judicial overreach in expanding promissory estoppel but similarly frames the problem as one of choosing when flexibility is justified versus when doctrinal limits should be preserved.

shared_topics.topic: proper scope and role of equitable doctrines and defenses (estoppel, unconscionability, duress, undue influence, capacity) in remedying unfair bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights defenses like unconscionability, duress, undue influence, and capacity as the corrective tools that should be applied more expansively to counter bias and opportunism in bargaining; Paper B focuses on promissory estoppel—an equitable doctrine—arguing for clear limits on its use and for deciding cases under the most appropriate doctrine rather than stretching estoppel to cover unrelated harms.

shared_topics.topic: balancing normative goals of justice/fairness with doctrinal coherence, predictability, and remedy design
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes Dr. King’s justice-centered normativity to justify adjusting contract law to advance fairness for disadvantaged parties, while Paper B warns that invoking a general desire to 'do justice' leads courts to craft ad hoc rules (e.g., via promissory estoppel) that undermine stare decisis and predictable remedial outcomes, arguing remedies should follow clear legal principles.

shared_topics.topic: how factual bargaining context—reliance, motivation, bias, and informational disparities—affects formation, characterization, and enforcement of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines motivational and perceptual factors (bias, prejudice, opportunism, constrained capacity) as determinants of bargaining inequity that should influence contract analysis; Paper B examines how reliance can substitute for consideration in promissory estoppel and distinguishes cases where contextual reliance produces a contract-like obligation from those that are better treated under estoppel or tort principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2000utahlrev223!!SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.

shared_topics.topic: the role of careful factual and historical reconstruction in legal analysis
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates treating reported cases like archaeological digs—recovering facts and context outside the law library to understand how cases actually unfolded—while Paper B stresses that reaching just results requires attention to the factual relationships (promise, reliance, harm) that ground whether a case is contract, estoppel, or tort, rather than relying on a one-size doctrinal label.

shared_topics.topic: critique of doctrinal overreach or judicially crafting rules to obtain desired remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the tendency to abstract away from facts and accept legal rules detached from case realities, and Paper B warns that promissory estoppel has been used unadvisedly to 'wag the dog'—stretching the doctrine to secure remedies instead of applying appropriate legal principles.

shared_topics.topic: the need to match doctrinal classification to underlying legal goals (contract vs estoppel vs tort)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes understanding a case's factual and historical posture to see why a court decided as it did, and Paper B argues for deciding cases under the doctrine that best fits the underlying goal—enforcing promises under contract law, preventing harm under tort, or invoking estoppel where defensive estoppel principles apply.

shared_topics.topic: concern for predictability and development of legal rules (stare decisis) tied to analytical methodology
shared_topics.justification: Paper A suggests deep case reconstruction contributes to a more meaningful understanding of law's evolution, and Paper B explicitly links methodological clarity to stare decisis—arguing that using promissory estoppel as a catchall undermines the certainty, predictability, and coherent development of substantive law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43buffalolrev1!!ARTICLE: Promises Betrayed: Breach of Confidence as a Remedy for Invasions of Privacy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Promises Betrayed: Breach of Confidence as a Remedy for Invasions of Privacy

shared_topics.topic: courts' use of alternative doctrines (contract, tort, fiduciary, estoppel) to obtain remedies outside traditional doctrinal bounds
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how plaintiffs injured by disclosures invoke contract, fiduciary duty, or a tort-like breach of confidence to obtain relief for invasions of privacy; Paper B critiques courts' use of promissory estoppel to reach results better characterized under contract, tort, or other doctrines, warning against doctrinal transplant to secure desired remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the classificatory question whether a claim should be treated as contract, tort, fiduciary, or estoppel and the consequences of that classification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A devotes substantial analysis to whether privacy injuries should be remedied via contract, fiduciary duty, or a novel tort of breach of confidence and how that classification affects available relief and constitutional review; Paper B centers on whether promissory estoppel cases are truly contract or tort/estoppel matters and argues classification should govern the applicable remedies.

shared_topics.topic: tension between remedial aims (doing justice) and the need for doctrinal consistency/predictability

papers.node_id: 16hofstralrev131!!ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL DAMAGES.
papers.title: ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL DAMAGES.
papers.abstract:
The proper measure of damages in promissory estoppel cases is a traditional subject of controversy.During the drafting of section 90 of the Restatement of Contracts,Professor Williston maintained that once a promise was enforced because a promisee had reasonably relied upon it, expectation damages should be awarded, as in other contract actions.Although the original section seemed to reflect thisview,other commentators disagreed, arguing that when a non-bargain promise is enforced because of the promisee's reliance, liability should be limited to the promisee's reliance loss.
Promissory estoppel was initially limited to donative, non-commercial, situations.With the expansion of promissory estoppel to commercial settings, some commentators argue that expectation damages are, or should be, generally available in commercial cases.Other commentators note that a flexible approach to damage awards has evolved in promissory estoppel cases.According to these commentators, there are two sets of cases with different measures of damages: expectation damages in commercial settings and reliance damages in donative settings.The Restatement (Second) of Contracts adopts a discretionary approach: "[t]he remedy granted for breach may be limited as justice requires."Nonetheless most commentatorscontinue to view reliance damages as appropriate in many donative settings.
Views on damages in promissory estoppel cases are linked to a more basic issue: Is the basis of liability in promissory estoppel cases contract or tort?  Commentators who view promissory estoppel as more tort than contract consider reliance the appropriate measure of damages,though in many commercial settings expectation damages may be the best measure of full reliance loss.In contrast, those commentators who view promissory estoppel as more contract than tort view expectation damages as generally appropriate, at least in commercial settings.
This article attempts to describe and explain damages in promissory estoppel cases.  In doing so, I rely on an earlier article, which explained why liability is imposed in promissory estoppel cases.That article suggested that in most promissory estoppel cases liability can be understood as contractual in the broad sense that the promisor intended to be legally bound under an objective standard, even though some traditional formal limit on contract liability -- such as consideration or the Statute of Frauds -- would bar enforcement.There are a few promissory estoppel cases, however, in which liability can be understood only on the basis of tort notions.Inthese cases, liability seems to be imposed because of misrepresentation, even though liability would not always lie under established tort standards for misrepresentation.
In this article, I explain promissory estoppel damages in terms of traditional contract and tort damage rules.  I also consider whether the use of promissory estoppel as a basis of liability, rather than overtly changing traditional contract and tort limits on liability, has affected the measure of relief.Section I analyzes the measure of relief afforded in promissory estoppel cases in which the imposition of liability can be understood as contractual in a very broad sense: the promise was made with apparently an intent to be legally bound.  Although the absence of consideration or the informality of the promise would normally bar recovery under traditional contract doctrines,in the vast majority of these cases, the relief awarded is consistent with traditional contract remedy rules.  In donative settings, expectation damagesor specific performanceare often awarded by courts despite commentators' widely-shared doubtsabout such awards in these cases.Similarly, when promissory estoppel is used in commercial settings, the remedy is consistent with traditional contract damage rules.  Thus, courts routinely award expectation damagesunless those damages are too speculative, indefinite, or otherwise unavailable under traditional contract rules.The many cases in which courts use both promissory estoppel and traditional contract analysis as alternative bases for reliefare not discussed because there is nothing novel or interesting about damages in such cases.
Section II analyzes the measure of damages in those promissory estoppel cases in which courts impose liability on the basis of tort notions: to remedy negligent or reckless promissory misrepresentations.In these cases, courts have tended to impose expectation damages when expectation damages can be calculated.In addition, punitive damages have been imposed in two cases in which the misrepresentation was intentional.Whether the overt use of tort principles to impose liability would have resulted in a different measure of compensatory relief, limiting the plaintiff's compensation to reliance losses rather than expectation damages, is not clear.

questions.question: When courts enforce a promise despite the absence of formal contract requirements, what measure of damages should be awarded - expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) or reliance (reimbursement) losses?
Does the characterization of liability as more contract-like versus more tort-like affect the measure of damages awarded for an enforced promise?

When liability for a promise is grounded on misrepresentation rather than ordinary promise enforcement, does that lead courts to award different compensatory or punitive remedies compared with ordinary promise-based cases?

matched_themes: Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
How should remedies for misrepresentation be calculated, and can misrepresentation damages be harmonized with contract-law remedial principles?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
When liability is grounded in misrepresentation rather than ordinary promise enforcement, do courts award different compensatory or punitive remedies?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_title: Article: The French Subjective Theory of Contract: Separating Rhetoric from Reality
