papers.node_id: 45wakeforestlrev641!!ARTICLE: REASONABLE EXPECTATIONS IN SOCIOCULTURAL CONTEXT
papers.title: ARTICLE: REASONABLE EXPECTATIONS IN SOCIOCULTURAL CONTEXT
papers.abstract:
Llewellyn wrote those words over half a century ago, and in this era of email, text messages, and cell phones, they may be even more true. A globalized marketplace and technological advancements have resulted in greater diversity between and among contracting parties inside and outside the United States. The parties to a contract do not always share the same set of cultural references, vocabulary, or business practices.Technology brings togetherparties of different experiential reference points by greatly facilitating transactions across vast geographical distances. It also increases the likelihood of substantive misunderstandings by creating novel contracting situations that often reveal implicit or unexpressed assumptions held by the parties.
The goal of contract law is often said to be the enforcement and protection of the reasonable expectations of the parties.Unlike the purpose of criminal law or tort law, the underlying purpose of contract law is not enforcement of societal standards or norms (other than the norm that if you make a contract, you should keep it). A contract is not enforced solely or even primarily because the substance of what the parties have agreed to is normatively desirable,nor does contract law force parties into contracts to which they have not agreed, even if those contracts would be socially beneficial. A contract is enforced because the parties have agreed to it.They have consented.One of the main objectives of contract law, then, is furthering personal autonomy - the "freedom to contract."An extension of this idea is that our judicial system may force the breaching party to keep his or her promise - or pay damages for failing to do so - because the other party wants him or her to keep the promise, not because the particular thing the party promised to do is normatively desirable.
There is also a societal benefit and objective in enforcing contracts. In a credit economy, parties must be able to depend uponthe promises made by others.A buyer, for example, who is able to purchase equipment on credit with thirty-day payment terms can generate revenue during that thirty-day period. Credit benefits both the buyer and the seller by greasing the wheels of commerce.
A determination of the reasonable expectations of the parties should capture the intent of the parties in entering into a contract and balance the parties' intent with any countervailing societal considerations. Intent, however, is a multifaceted concept. Elsewhere, I proposed that there are three facets to the concept of contractual intent.Volitional intent captures a party's willingness to enter into an agreement.A party entering into an agreement under duress, for example, lacks volitional intent. Cognitive intent refers to a party's understanding of the proposed contract.A party entering into an agreement that contains terms that he or she does not understand lacks cognitive intent. Contextual purposive intent captures a party's motive for entering into a contract, including the relevant circumstances under which a contract is made.For example, a party who rents out a house on a certain street in order to view a parade has the contextual purposive intent of viewing the parade.
Under the objective theory of contract, courts interpret the intent of the parties in adopting a particular contractual term according to the reasonable meaning of that term, or the meaning that a reasonable person would assign to that term.Courts adopt the objective theory to determine all aspects of the understanding between the parties - from the determination of contract formation, to an evaluation of the meaning of written or spoken terms, to an assessment of contract performance.In a series of articles,Professor Melvin Eisenberg explained how modern contract law evolved from the will theory to the classical model, and from the classical model to a more responsive and dynamic model.This Article argues in favor of such a progression. An objective theory of contract erroneously replaces the parties' intent with a reasonableness standard. Reasonableness should be the product of weighing subjective intent against societal considerations, not a factor used to make such a determination.When one of the parties lacks the requisite subjective intent, a court may nevertheless enforce a contract when a failure to do so would cast doubt on the security of transactions and thus endanger our credit economy.
A dynamic approach better serves a dynamic society. In the modern global and technologically driven marketplace, the objective theory of contract incompletely captures - in fact, in some cases, even undermines - contract law's objective of promoting individual autonomy. This Article further argues that in order for modern contract law to be truly "dynamic," it must take into consideration the social and cultural backgrounds and social identities of the parties.This Article proceeds in four parts. Part I discusses the role that social identity and experience play in contract law and introduces the tension between sociocultural dissonance and anobjective approach. Part II analyzes the difference that culture makes by examining a recent case involving two Korean-born businessmen. Part III analyzes the difference that gender makes by examining a case involving divorce and in vitro fertilization. This Article concludes that courts should consider contextual factors, including the background and identity of the parties, in order to better achieve the goal of contract law - to protect the reasonable expectations of the parties.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the classical distinction between mistakes of 'substance' and mere errors of 'motive' and argues for approaches that take parties' motives into account when deciding whether mistaken parties get relief; Paper B develops a three-part model of contractual intent (volitional, cognitive, contextual purposive) and argues courts should incorporate parties' motives and contextual purposes when assessing formation, interpretation, and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: critiques of the classical/objective doctrine and proposals to reform doctrine to incorporate context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the classical 'error in substance' formulation and surveys juristic attempts to reinterpret or replace it (endorsing a contextual approach from certain French and Aristotelian traditions); Paper B critiques the objective theory of contract as insufficient for a diverse, technologized marketplace and advocates a more dynamic, context-sensitive approach that accounts for sociocultural background.

shared_topics.topic: how to balance individual consent/autonomy against broader societal interests (transactional security) when deciding enforcement or remedies for mistaken or non‑intentional agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the tension between keeping contracts binding and granting relief for mistakes, asking when private mistakes should void bargains; Paper B likewise weighs subjective intent against the societal need for predictable enforcement (e.g., credit economy) and argues that enforcement may be justified even when subjective intent is lacking to protect reasonable expectations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 82califlrev1127!!ARTICLE: Expression Rules in Contract Law and Problems of Offer and Acceptance
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Expression Rules in Contract Law and Problems of Offer and Acceptance

shared_topics.topic: the proper balance between objective (reasonable-person) standards and subjective intent in contract interpretation and formation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze whether courts should interpret contractual expressions using an objective 'reasonable person' lens or give weight to the parties' subjective intent — Paper A critiques the objective theory for displacing subjective intent and harming autonomy, while Paper B examine s how modern interpretive principles already mix objective and subjective elements and questions when objective 'expression rules' are justified.

shared_topics.topic: whether doctrinally standardized 'expression rules' (black‑letter rules about offers, counteroffers, auctions, lapse, etc.) can be justified instead of individualized, contextual interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly isolates and critiques ‘expression rules’ that assign a fixed legal meaning to classes of expressions and argues many lack modern justification; Paper A likewise challenges one-size-fits-all objective rules and argues courts should attend to contextual factors (including culture and identity) rather than mechanically applying standardized doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: the need to modernize or reform classical contract doctrines to account for context, social identity, and changing transactional environments
shared_topics.justification: Both authors argue that older, classical formulations of contract doctrine are insufficient: Paper A calls for a dynamic, socioculturally aware approach that incorporates parties' backgrounds and identities, while Paper B shows that many classical expression rules should be dropped or weakened in favor of interpretation aligned with modern principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev183!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW'S UNITY - AN ESSAY FOR THE MASTER CONTORTIONIST
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW'S UNITY - AN ESSAY FOR THE MASTER CONTORTIONIST

shared_topics.topic: theoretical evolution of contract law (will theory → classical/objective → more dynamic models)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces and argues for a progression from will theory to the classical/objective model and onward to a more responsive, dynamic model that incorporates parties' backgrounds; Paper B revisits and critiques major twentieth‑century accounts of contract (via Gilmore, Holmes, Corbin) and engages the same historiography and theoretical debates about how contract doctrine should be understood and reformulated.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal boundary between contract and other areas of law (especially tort)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts contract law's purposes with those of tort and criminal law to motivate a distinct, autonomy‑focused approach to enforcing promises, while Paper B centers on Grant Gilmore's thesis that contract and tort doctrines have collapsed into one another and uses that overlap to question law's unity and doctrinal limits.

shared_topics.topic: the role of social, historical, and contextual factors in interpreting and shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should incorporate parties' sociocultural identities, gender, and contextual purposive intent when assessing reasonable expectations, and Paper B situates contract doctrine within its intellectual and historical contexts—discussing how scholars' perspectives and historical projects (Holmes, Corbin, Gilmore) have shaped interpretation and development of contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 76cornelllrev197!!ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF RELIANCE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF RELIANCE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the expectation interest / "reasonable expectations" in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the primacy of the expectation measure (placing the promisee in the position had the contract been performed) and criticizes proposals to displace it; Paper B treats protecting the parties' reasonable expectations as a central goal of contract law and critiques the objective theory for failing to capture parties' real expectations in a diverse, modern marketplace.

shared_topics.topic: whether and when reliance should limit expectation-based remedies and the attendant incentive/efficiency tradeoffs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly examines the reliance measure (and the estoppel-exception and law-and-economics critiques that reliance should curb expectation damages) and argues against limiting expectation recovery; Paper B engages the related policy tradeoff by asking when courts should nevertheless enforce expectations (or provide remedies) to preserve transactional security and the credit economy in the face of misunderstandings or lack of subjective intent.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of contextual or background factors (doctrinal history, social identity, culture) on contract interpretation and remedy allocation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes historical and doctrinal roots (Restatement First/Second, promissory estoppel) to argue when reliance/restitution should displace expectation damages; Paper B argues courts should consider parties' sociocultural backgrounds, identities, and contextual purposive intent when construing terms and deciding whether to enforce promises or award remedies.

papers.node_id: 41indlrev9!!ARTICLE: Recent Defenses of Consideration: Commodification and Collaboration
papers.title: ARTICLE: Recent Defenses of Consideration: Commodification and Collaboration
papers.abstract:
Occasionally, the disputes of contract theory begin to appear very old, and each succeeding wave of scholarship seems to be little more than dressing up old ideas in new disguises and rehashing old disputes in new jargon. One cure for this academic variety of Weltschmerz is to encounter and address truly novel arguments about thoroughly familiar issues. In this Article, I wish to respond to two such novel efforts, the first by one of our most eminent and prolific contracts scholars, Melvin Aron Eisenberg,and theby a relatively more recent arrival, Daniel Markovits.
The subject of the innovations introduced by Professors Eisenberg and Markovits is the so-called "requirement" of consideration, although in each case the treatment of the doctrine of consideration is part of a larger project. My own interest in the subject goes back to a study of over 300 consideration cases I published as a pair of articles in the 1990s.I argued that, while the majority of applications of the doctrine of consideration are redundant, the doctrine nevertheless still has more than rhetorical bite, i.e., it still is outcome-determinative in a range of cases.I further argued that contract law, on the whole, would be better off without it.On the positive side, I argued that the reasons commonly advanced in favor of enforcing bargain promises-the facilitation of exchange, the protection of expectations or reliance, or respect for autonomy-could also be mustered in support of the enforcement of promises traditionally classified as gratuitous.On the negative side, I argued that the reasons traditionally advanced for the claim that gratuitous promises are somehow suspicious and unworthy of enforcement were all inadequate.In soarguing, I endeavored to examine all the traditional arguments in favor of and against the requirement of consideration, most of which had been made by multiple authors over a period of decades.Each contribution to the discussion of the issues in question moved the argument to a new stage, but the issues themselves have been contested among scholars for a long time. Accordingly, though I continue to adhere to the views expressed in the earlier articles, I do not propose to revisit them here. Instead, I wish to focus on two quite innovative, albeit partial, defenses of the requirement of consideration.
As it turns out, the set of arguments that can be mustered on either side of contentious issues is never really closed. In an article published in 1997, Professor Eisenberg introduced an argument with no prior analogue of which I am aware. Specifically, he argued that at least one class of gratuitous promises- simple, affective donative promises-should remain unenforceable, as the doctrine of consideration dictates.One reason is that a regime of enforcement would "commodify" donative promises and thereby impoverish what he calls the "world of gift."Another is that a regime of enforceability could not, in principle, accommodate the full range of moral excuses for breaking such promises.
More recently, Professor Markovits has suggested that the traditional requirement of consideration finds some support in a philosophical concept he calls "collaboration."That concept is the most important element in a Kantian reconstruction and justification of the making and keeping of contracts,a reconstruction that draws on more general Kantian foundations to account for both the moral obligation to keep promises and the legal obligations surrounding them.The notion of "collaboration" upon which he elaborates is a technical one, and it has no antecedent of which I am aware in previous debates on the doctrine of consideration.
Ultimately, in my view, neither Professor Eisenberg's argument on the basis of "commodification" nor Professor Markovits's argument on the basis of "collaboration" provides a satisfactory defense of the traditional requirement of consideration. My response to their arguments will proceed as follows. In Part I, I examine and respond to Professor Eisenberg's views. After an initial andmore detailed summary of his argument,I proceed to a more articulated analysis of the concept of commodification on which it depends.I examine several possible meanings of the term "commodification" and several corresponding versions of the claim that enforcement of donative promises would commodify them.I argue that none of them provides the defense of the requirement of consideration to which Professor Eisenberg aspires.I then examine, and ultimately reject, two possible interpretations of his claim that a system which enforced donative promises could not successfully accommodate the range of moral excuses to which such promises are subject.
In Part II, I turn to Professor Markovits's argument based on the concept of collaboration. It is necessary to begin with a rather extended summary of his argument,as it is both innovative and complex. After articulating the moral ideals of respectful community and collaboration that Professor Markovits uses as the basis of promise and contract, respectively,I summarize his argument that the collaborative ideal supports the requirement of consideration in the law of contract.My criticism of that argument proceeds in the following stages. Initially, I observe that, even if one accepts the value of the collaborative ideal, it provides, at best, an argument in favor of granting enforcement to bargain promises, but not an argument for withholding it from donative promises.To the extent Professor Markovits presents a distinct argument for withholding legal sanctions from donative promises, it appears to rely on a claim that the presence of a "passive promisee" destroys the prospect for collaboration.I then dissect his notion of a passive promisee and argue that it is too weak to support that claimand can only be strengthened by maneuvers that ultimately make his argument question- begging.Finally, I argue that, from materials found in Professor Markovits's own theory, one can construct an argument that moral ideals other than collaboration, but at least as valuable, support the enforcement of donative promises at least as well as the notion of collaboration supports the enforcement of bargain promises.

questions.question: Whether the legal system should enforce gratuitous (donative) promises or limit enforceability to bargained exchanges (i.e., should gifts be legally actionable or exempt from enforcement).

Whether two purported justifications-(a) that enforcing gifts would 'commodify' gift-giving and (b) that a moral ideal of 'collaboration' supports enforcing bargains but not gifts-provide adequate grounds for withholding legal enforcement of gratuitous promises.

matched_themes: Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Does treating naming-rights, charitable donations, or licensing transactions as contracts rather than gifts or property promote better outcomes for donors, charities, or collaborative communities?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73califlrev1432!!ARTICLE: Damages for Breach of Contract.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Damages for Breach of Contract.

shared_topics.topic: the justification for enforcing promises: expectation versus reliance
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly engage the debate over whether the law should protect expectation interests or reliance interests: Paper A lists and critiques expectation and reliance (and autonomy) as standard justifications for enforcing promises, especially when considering whether donative promises should be enforced, while Paper B analyzes expectation and reliance damages, showing when they coincide and when expectation damages are preferable.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundations of contract doctrine — moral ideals versus economic efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Both works assess the moral and economic bases for contract rules: Paper A evaluates moral-philosophical defenses of consideration (e.g., Kantian 'collaboration' and respect for autonomy) as justifications for enforcement, whereas Paper B weighs fairness and economic efficiency as the guiding ends for awarding expectation damages and for selecting damage measures.

shared_topics.topic: conceptual and doctrinal scrutiny of central contract-law terms and limits
shared_topics.justification: Each paper probes the meaning and adequacy of core doctrinal concepts: Paper A analyzes and criticizes notions like 'commodification' and the 'passive promisee' in defenses of the consideration requirement, while Paper B interrogates the meanings of 'injury', 'compensation', and 'expectation' and develops clearer measures of contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules interact with social and market practices
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how doctrinal choices shape or respond to broader practices: Paper A worries that enforcing donative promises would 'commodify' gift relations and alter social practices, and Paper B shows that market structure and business conduct are major variables determining the appropriate measure of expectation damages.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 30jlegalstud423!!ARTICLE: Precontractual Reliance
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Precontractual Reliance

shared_topics.topic: when (and whether) noncontractual or precontractual promises should generate legal liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes regimes that impose liability for reliance expenditures when negotiations fail (no-liability, strict liability, and intermediate rules) and asks when precontractual communications should give rise to compensation; Paper B addresses whether gratuitous (donative) promises should be legally enforceable at all, defending or rejecting doctrinal limits (the requirement of consideration) that withhold liability for certain promises.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance/expectations in justifying enforcement of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A builds an economic model of reliance investments and studies how legal rules affect parties' incentives to invest and rely during negotiations; Paper B examines reliance and expectation-protection among the positive arguments for enforcing gratuitous promises and assesses whether such considerations support abolishing or retaining the consideration requirement.

shared_topics.topic: how default legal rules should be designed to shape parties' incentives and behavior
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats different liability rules as default rules and evaluates which default produces socially optimal precontractual reliance and negotiation participation; Paper B treats the consideration doctrine as a default doctrinal rule governing when promises are enforced and evaluates novel justifications (commodification, collaboration) for retaining or reforming that default.

shared_topics.topic: practical/doctrinal limits and informational feasibility of rules that distinguish binding from nonbinding communications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares liability regimes not only on normative grounds but also on courts' informational requirements and implementability (e.g., detecting obstructionist bargaining or measuring optimal reliance); Paper B scrutinizes whether philosophical defenses of consideration can be operationalized by law (e.g., accommodating moral excuses, identifying a 'passive promisee') and whether those defenses provide practicable doctrinal guidance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev777!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PETER LINZER'S "ROUGH JUSTICE"
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PETER LINZER'S "ROUGH JUSTICE"

shared_topics.topic: limits of single theoretical justifications for contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique attempts to ground contract rules in a single coherent theory: Paper A rejects economic or formalist monocultures (e.g., using pure economic analysis to decide relational disputes like Circuit City or franchise cases), while Paper B examines and rejects singular philosophical defenses of the consideration requirement (Eisenberg's commodification argument and Markovits's Kantian 'collaboration').

shared_topics.topic: importance of moral, social, and contextual factors in enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both argue that non‑pecuniary values and social context matter to whether promises should be enforced: Paper A stresses power imbalances, emotional and social transaction costs, and the employee's interests in arbitration cases, while Paper B analyzes moral ideals (gifting norms, collaboration) and moral excuses bearing on enforcement of donative versus bargain promises.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should draw boundaries of enforceability and fill doctrinal gaps
shared_topics.justification: Each paper addresses practical criteria for when courts should impose liability or decline enforcement: Paper A advocates a patchwork of doctrines (reliance, unjust enrichment, tort) to resolve novel or incomplete relational contracts, and Paper B debates whether the consideration doctrine (or alternative moral principles) should function as the bright‑line boundary between enforceable bargains and unenforceable gifts.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism toward formalist/doctrinal unity and support for pluralist or pragmatic decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between doctrinal unity and pragmatic adjudication—Paper A laments rigid doctrinal unity that ignores relational realities and endorses 'rough justice' via multiple strands of doctrine, while Paper B questions whether a single justificatory principle (e.g., collaboration) can or should monopolize the law's approach to enforcing promises.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61hastingslj801!!Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores: The Rest of the Story
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores: The Rest of the Story

shared_topics.topic: enforcing promises without traditional formation or consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines courts' willingness to award recovery (via promissory estoppel) for precontractual reliance when no formal contract or consideration exists, and Paper B debates whether the doctrine of consideration should continue to bar enforcement of gratuitous promises, assessing alternate bases for enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: reliance/detriment as a basis for remedies when bargains fail
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on recovery for expenditures made in reliance on an expected deal (the Hoffman precontractual reliance issue), while Paper B engages the justificatory role of protecting expectation or reliance interests in arguing for or against enforcing donative promises.

shared_topics.topic: normative and doctrinal debates about foundational contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Hoffman v. Red Owl within decades-long scholarly controversy over promissory estoppel and precontractual reliance, and Paper B responds to recent scholarly defenses of the consideration requirement, both contributing to core theoretical disputes about when promises should be legally enforced.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of factual/contextual and moral considerations on legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows how fuller factual narratives change assessments of whether a decision was justified on promissory-estoppel grounds, and Paper B analyzes moral ideas (e.g., commodification, collaboration) to argue how social and ethical values should shape the scope of enforceable promises.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39ambuslj289!!ARTICLE: THE ADVENT OF RECOVERY ON MARKET TRANSACTIONS IN THE ABSENCE OF A BARGAIN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ADVENT OF RECOVERY ON MARKET TRANSACTIONS IN THE ABSENCE OF A BARGAIN

shared_topics.topic: defenses and criticisms of the requirement of consideration as a doctrinal gatekeeper
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly engages contemporary novel defenses of the consideration requirement (Eisenberg's commodification argument and Markovits's collaboration account) and critiques whether those show consideration should bar enforcement; Paper B traces how the redefinition of consideration into a bargained-for form was contested and produced doctrinal difficulties, implicitly engaging the adequacy and consequences of using consideration as the primary test for contract enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: whether and why gratuitous/donative (non‑bargain) promises should be enforceable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the tension over enforcing donative or gratuitous promises, assessing arguments for withholding enforcement (commodification, the passive promisee) and for enforcing such promises; Paper B documents historically how many transactions that lacked bargains lost enforceability and why courts and commentators struggled with whether to enforce non‑bargain market promises.

shared_topics.topic: the rise of equitable and alternative doctrines (promissory estoppel, restitution, moral obligation) to fill gaps left by strict bargain doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses whether moral and justificatory reasons that support enforcing promises extend to non‑bargain promises and evaluates competing moral grounds, while Paper B narrates the historical development and adoption of remedies like promissory estoppel, restitution, enforcement of contract modifications, and the moral obligation principle as responses to the narrowing of consideration.

shared_topics.topic: historical transformation of consideration doctrine into a bargain‑focused paradigm and its doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates its critique and responses within longer scholarly debates about how consideration has been applied and changed over time, while Paper B provides a detailed historical account of the nineteenth–early twentieth century shift toward a market‑bargain definition of consideration and explains the legal and social consequences of that transformation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48tullrev946!!ARTICLE: Rules and Terms--Civil Law and Common Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rules and Terms--Civil Law and Common Law

shared_topics.topic: doctrine of consideration — its justification and doctrinal role in enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally devoted to assessing contemporary defenses of the consideration requirement (critiquing Eisenberg's and Markovits's arguments for why consideration should distinguish enforceable bargains from unenforceable promises), and Paper B explicitly references 'consideration' as a contested doctrinal point in the historical reception of Roman/Civil law into Common law contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: use of conceptual and theoretical frameworks to justify contract rules (e.g., commodification, collaboration, Civilian analytic apparatus)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates novel normative frameworks (the commodification critique and a Kantian 'collaboration' account) offered to justify or reject enforcement rules, while Paper B examines how Common lawyers borrowed Civil law conceptual apparatus and general jurisprudential theories to explain and reorganize contract principles.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between gifts (donative promises) and bargains and their legal enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether donative/affective promises should be enforceable and the normative consequences of enforcing gifts, and Paper B discusses how historical treatises and codes (Blackstone, Pothier, the Code) situated 'gifts' relative to 'contract' and thus shaped differing legal treatment of grants versus bargains.

shared_topics.topic: historical and comparative development of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates its discussion in a longer scholarly and case-law history (referencing earlier empirical work and longstanding debates about consideration), whereas Paper B provides a comparative-historical account of how Roman/Civil law influenced the evolution and systematization of Common law contract concepts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 66geowashlrev508!!ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of gratuitous or past-consideration promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically examines courts' reception of Restatement (Second) §86 and related provisions that make promises based on past benefits or non-bargained exchanges enforceable; Paper B directly debates whether donative or gratuitous promises should be legally enforceable, critiquing contemporary defenses of the traditional consideration requirement that would bar such enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: authority of the Restatement (Second) and academic scholarship in shaping judicial doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies and questions the extent to which courts defer to the Restatement (Second) as an authoritative source that effectively becomes law, while Paper B engages with prominent scholarly defenses (Eisenberg, Markovits) and treats academic theory as a driver of doctrinal justification and potential legal change.

shared_topics.topic: normative justifications for contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises and evaluates normative policy questions about whether courts ought to adopt the Restatement's preferred rules (weighing uniformity, certainty, and other policy consequences), and Paper B analyzes and rejects specific normative arguments (commodification, collaboration) offered to justify keeping the traditional requirement of consideration.

shared_topics.topic: the shift from traditional black-letter doctrines to more flexible modern rules in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents and analyzes courts' movement from traditional rules (e.g., preexisting-duty rule, strict nonenforceability of past consideration) toward Restatement (Second) reforms (e.g., §§86, 89), and Paper B addresses that same fault line by debating whether the traditional consideration doctrine should be retained or reformed in light of modern theoretical arguments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 86columlrev269!!ARTICLE: A CONSENT THEORY OF CONTRACT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CONSENT THEORY OF CONTRACT.

shared_topics.topic: moral foundations for legally enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate the moral basis for turning interpersonal promises into legally enforceable obligations — Paper A develops a consent-based moral account of when transfers of entitlements should be enforced, while Paper B evaluates rival moral/conceptual defenses (commodification and Markovits's Kantian 'collaboration') offered to justify or limit legal enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of gratuitous (donative) promises and the role of consideration
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question whether non‑bargained, gratuitous promises should be legally enforceable — Paper A defends enforcement in some non‑bargain contexts (e.g., nominal consideration) under a consent theory, while Paper B directly examines and critiques contemporary arguments for retaining the traditional requirement of consideration to exclude donative promises.

shared_topics.topic: critique and comparative evaluation of contract doctrine/theories
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critically assess existing doctrinal and theoretical approaches to contract (e.g., will, reliance, bargain theories and the doctrine of consideration), weighing their explanatory limits and arguing for a more adequate framework to resolve contested issues of enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: the accommodation of moral excuses and defenses to promise enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how legal doctrine should treat moral excuses or defenses to breaking promises — Paper A explains and justifies historically recognized contractual defenses within a consent theory, while Paper B analyzes whether enforcing donative promises could appropriately accommodate the full range of moral excuses (rejecting Eisenberg's claim it could not).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69hastingslj119!!ARTICLE: Race Politics, O'Hare Airport Expansion, and Promissory Estoppel: The More Things Change, the More They Stay the Same
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Race Politics, O'Hare Airport Expansion, and Promissory Estoppel: The More Things Change, the More They Stay the Same

shared_topics.topic: legal criteria for enforcing promises absent a formal bargain (consideration versus promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines defenses of the traditional consideration requirement and whether gratuitous promises should be legally enforceable, while Paper B analyzes courts' use of promissory estoppel and letters of intent to impose liability without a completed formal contract.

shared_topics.topic: reliance as a justificatory ground for enforcement and basis for recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses reliance (alongside expectation and autonomy) as a positive rationale for enforcing promises traditionally seen as gratuitous, and Paper B focuses on precontractual reliance costs and promissory estoppel remedies for parties who acted on oral assurances or letters of intent.

shared_topics.topic: policy trade-offs and risks of expanding enforceability of informal promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques novel arguments (commodification, collaboration) that would justify excluding donative promises from enforcement and considers social consequences of enforcement, while Paper B warns that cases like Quake expand liability for thin precontractual reliance and may open litigation floodgates, assessing doctrinal and practical consequences.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between moral/ethical reasons to keep promises and legal doctrines that enforce them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages deeply with philosophical (including Kantian) accounts of promise-keeping and how moral ideals map onto legal rules, and Paper B invokes notions of fairness and Restatement section 90 (avoiding injustice) as moral-legal grounds for recognizing precontractual claims and counsel's ethical responsibilities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36wmmarylrev1379!!ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: competing normative justifications for contract law (efficiency/freedom of contract versus moral/balancing approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly contrasts Posner's efficiency- and freedom-of-contract-centered framework with Cardozo's balancing approach that emphasizes good faith, fairness, and reasonable expectations; Paper B engages the same fault-line by weighing instrumental/economic reasons for enforcing bargains against Kantian moral accounts (Markovits) and other moral considerations that might counsel different enforcement rules.

shared_topics.topic: the proper scope of enforceability of promises (when the law should enforce bargains versus nonbargain/ donative promises or imply duties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes doctrines that expand or limit enforceability (e.g., Cardozo's implied covenant of good faith and substantial performance versus Posner's resistance to such implications), while Paper B directly debates whether donative promises should be enforceable under the requirement of consideration and whether legal sanctions should be withheld from gifts.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules affect or should respect social and moral practices (e.g., commodification of gifts, reasonable expectations, good faith)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B raises the worry that enforcing donative promises would 'commodify' the world of gift and undermine social practices around giving, and Paper A discusses Cardozo's concern for protecting reasonable expectations and preserving relational/moral dimensions of contracting (good faith) as distinct from a strictly commodifying, market-oriented approach.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of judges and scholars in shaping contract doctrine and pedagogy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A provides empirical and doctrinal discussion of how Cardozo's and Posner's opinions shape teaching and the substantive texture of contract law, and Paper B is a scholarly engagement with influential academics (Eisenberg, Markovits) whose novel arguments seek to reconceptualize core doctrines like consideration, thereby aiming to influence doctrine and debate.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 61ukanlrev591!!ARTICLE: Assent Is Not an Element of Contract Formation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Assent Is Not an Element of Contract Formation

shared_topics.topic: the necessity and centrality of consideration for contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper B argues doctrinally that consideration is the irreducible, foundational element of contract formation and that assent is subsumed within it; Paper A engages the same basic question by evaluating novel defenses of maintaining the requirement of consideration and whether that requirement should be retained or rejected.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability distinction between bargain promises and gratuitous (donative) promises

papers.node_id: 49smulrev43!!ARTICLE: Recovering Pre-contractual Expenditures as an Element of Reliance Damages
papers.title: ARTICLE: Recovering Pre-contractual Expenditures as an Element of Reliance Damages
papers.abstract:
SHOULD a person who has made expenditures before entering into a contract be able to recover those expenditures as an element of damages if that contract is breached? This question does not arise in those breach of contract actions where either expectation or restitution damages are awarded. It can arise, however, in cases where the court elects to award reliance damages.
The conventional wisdom among commentators is that it is inappropriate to allow recovery of pre-contractual expenditures as part of a reliance interest-based award,and that the courts, at least in the United States, have generally accepted this proposition and denied such recovery.Closer inquiry reveals, however, that a persuasive argument can be made for allowing recovery of pre-contractual expenditures under the reliance interest rubric, so long as it was in the reasonable contemplation of the contracting parties that those expenditures would be wasted in the event of breach. Moreover, there is some support to be found in the United States case law - and quite substantial support in the British Commonwealth case law - for doing so. This article will present and evaluate that argument as well as review and reassess the relevant case law in light of it.
Part II of this article will briefly summarize the basic principles governing the award of damages for breach of contract. Part III will set forth the argument for allowing recovery of pre-contractual expenditures as an element of reliance damages awards. Part IV will review the BritishCommonwealth and United States case law relating to this question. In Part V, I will propose and discuss in detail a "reasonable contemplation" standard for resolving claims for recovery of pre-contractual expenditures and reassess the case law in light of this standard. Part VI will present a brief conclusion.

questions.question: Should expenditures incurred before entering into an agreement be recoverable as damages when that agreement is breached?
What standard should courts apply to decide when pre-contractual expenditures are recoverable as damages?
How have courts in different jurisdictions treated claims to recover pre-contractual expenditures after a breach?

matched_themes: When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?

Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 21umichjlreform541!!ARTICLE: REFLECTIONS ON FULLER AND PERDUE'S THE RELIANCE INTEREST IN CONTRACT DAMAGES: A POSITIVE ECONOMIC FRAMEWORK
papers.title: ARTICLE: REFLECTIONS ON FULLER AND PERDUE'S THE RELIANCE INTEREST IN CONTRACT DAMAGES: A POSITIVE ECONOMIC FRAMEWORK
papers.abstract:
Fuller and Perdue's classic article, The Reliance Interest in Contract Damages,is regarded by many contemporary contracts scholars as the single most influential law review article in the field.  For those of us who teach and think about contracts from the perspective of law and economics,the consensus would probably be close to unanimous.  The article displays an approach highly congenial to an economic perspective.  The connection goes beyond Fuller and Perdue's explicitly functional approach to law (which law and economics shares with other schools of thought descended from the legal realists) and beyond Fuller and Perdue's focus on commercial policy.  Fuller and Perdue's analysis of the relationships among the various damage interests they identify, and of the social purposes served by their protection, reveals a sophisticated understanding of the role and limits of economic incentives in influencing the behavior of contractual parties.
Fuller and Perdue's article made two major related claims.  The first claim was primarily descriptive or positive: that common-law courts deciding contracts cases had actually been attempting to protect people's reliance expenditures, notwithstanding the fact that the doctrinal focus of the cases was often elsewhere, or that courts often claimed to be protecting people's expectations.  The second claim was primarily normative: that the reliance interest, rather than the expectation interest, was the appropriate object of judicial protection.
It is the first claim on which this Article focuses.  How was it possible for Fuller and Perdue to argue that the courts had really been protecting a different interest than everyone believed?  The key to their explanation was a phenomenon they labeled as the divergence between measure and motive.Because of the economic relationship connecting the reliance interest to the other two theories of damages they identified, it was possible for courts to use a nonreliance theory as a measure or approximation of damages, while having as their real motive the protection of reliance.
This Article will generalize the reasoning underlying this claim, and in so doing will outline a theoretical framework connecting all of the damage measures Fuller and Perdue discussed.  The framework makes explicit the economic relationships among reliance, restitution, and expectation that Fuller and Perdue discussed more intuitively.  It also reveals that Fuller and Perdue's analysis suggests a fourth theory of damages they did not recognize.
The relationship among the four damage principles means that any one of the four damage theories can be used, under the appropriate circumstances, as an approximate measure for the others.  Thus, measure and motive can be uncoupled entirely.  Whether the reliance interest is the most important or fundamental of the four interests is therefore a separate matter which I briefly discuss in the concluding section below.  To the extent that the full logic of Fuller and Perdue's descriptive claim is accepted, though, their argument for the primacy of reliance may be subverted by future scholars using arguments similar to their own.

questions.question: Do courts, when awarding contractual remedies, actually aim to compensate parties for investments made in reliance on a promise even when they apply a different stated calculational measure in the decision?

What are the economic relationships among different types of contract-damage measures (compensation for reliance expenditures, compensation for expected benefits, disgorgement of gains, and any implied alternative), and under what conditions can one measure serve as a reliable proxy for another?

Does the ability of courts to decouple the chosen damage measure from their remedial motive undermine the claim that protecting reliance-based losses should be the primary normative objective of contract damages?

matched_themes: How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law

papers.node_id: 39connlrev1977!!ARTICLE: Regulating Contract Formation: Precontractual Reliance, SunkCosts, and Market Structure
papers.title: ARTICLE: Regulating Contract Formation: Precontractual Reliance, SunkCosts, and Market Structure
papers.abstract:
Suppose four firms compete in a sealed-bid auction for a construction project. Each firm must spend $ 50,000 to prepare its bid. The expected cost of performance is $ 1 million. If precontractual costs become "sunk costs during the negotiation process, and thus do not affect the final bids, competition between the firms dictates that the winning bid should not exceed $ 1 million. If so, how do the firms recover their precontractual costs? This puzzle seems to be of purely economic interest. However, we suggest that the plausible solutions of this puzzle pose a fundamental challenge to one of the cornerstones of economic analysis of contract law-the problem of under-investment in precontractual reliance.
It is a well-known fact that negotiation is costly. Negotiating parties are required not only to invest their time and efforts, which means foregoing other opportunities, but also to pay for information, expert opinions, financial guaranties, and, last but not least, lawyers' fees. Furthermore, in certain cases, submitting the best bid requires preliminary steps toward performance of the yet-to- be-agreed-upon contract (e.g., receiving offers from sub-contractors or preparing preliminary plans).Such expenditures-so-called "precontractual reliance (PCR)-are usually, at least to some degree, relationship-specific, in the sense that they cannot be wholly recovered if the negotiation fails. A party who invests in unrecoverable expenditures cannot credibly threaten ex post to withdraw from the negotiation because of such "sunk costs. For this reason, a negotiating party who does not possess ultimate bargaining power cannotexpect to enjoy the full benefits of her investment in PCR. In some cases, the investing party might even be pressed to agree to a price that does not cover her precontractual "sunk costs (i.e., a "holdup problem is created).Assuming that a party's decision ex ante is based on her prospects of receiving the surplus generated by her investment, under-investment in PCR seems inevitable.
The economic prediction of under-investment in PCR has produced two closely linked lines of legal arguments. First, parties are expected to account for the concern of under-investment in PCR through appropriate contractual provisions, such as termination fees, option contracts, irrevocable offers, and so forth. Second, contract law should be construed to facilitate optimal investment in PCR. The latter argument has become increasingly popular in legal scholarship, especially within the school of economic analysis of contract law. It serves to justify, on an efficiency basis, imposing "precontractual liabilityand contractual liability without consent.Additionally, it plays an important role in evaluating other contract law doctrines, such as disclosure rules,remedies for breach,and the legitimacy of contractual "modification bans.

questions.question: Whether competitive bidding environments in which precontractual expenditures become sunk prevent firms from recovering those relationship-specific costs and thereby cause underinvestment in precontractual reliance.

How market structure (e.g., number of competitors and distribution of bargaining power) affects firms' incentives to make relationship-specific precontractual investments and the likelihood those investments are recovered.

Whether and how legal or contractual arrangements that make precontractual expenditures recoverable alter firms' bidding behavior and investment incentives, and what the efficiency trade-offs of such arrangements are.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
Do existing rules on contract modification and remedies deter bad-faith modification demands or instead create incentives for opportunism and unjust enrichment?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Is imposing a judicially enforced duty to negotiate in good faith necessary to achieve efficient outcomes in preliminary agreements, or would protecting reliance expenditures suffice?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 76geolj1949!!ARTICLE: Reinterpretations of 18th-Century English Contract Theory: The View from Lord Mansfield's Trial Notes.
papers.title: ARTICLE: Reinterpretations of 18th-Century English Contract Theory: The View from Lord Mansfield's Trial Notes.
papers.abstract:
The 1974 publication of Morton Horwitz'sThe Historical Foundations of Modern Contract Lawsparked lively debate in America among contemporary legal historians, a debate that was joined in England by the 1979 publication of P. S. Atiyah'sThe Rise and Fall of Freedom of Contract.According to J. H. Baker, Horwitz and Atiyah each advances "[t]he central legal theme . . . that the consensual notion of contract was almost entirely absent before about 1800."Both Baker and A. W. B. Simpson have criticized this analysis."The difficulty with this approach," writes Baker, "is that all the features of contract theory which Atiyah, and Horwitz, trace to the period after 1770 were present in the law long before."
Central to any study of English contract law in the period around and after 1770 are the opinions of Lord Mansfield, Chief Justice of the Court of King's Bench from 1756 to 1788 and the principal architect of English commercial law.  This article examines Lord Mansfield's approach to English contract law by drawing upon his unpublished trial notesand other manuscript sources.  These sources, as well as published opinions, show that Mansfield emphasized basic fairness and the intentions of the parties as governing principles.  Although his efforts laid the groundwork for the subsequentera of freedom of contract, Mansfield was not an unquestioning exponent of that philosophy.  He policed limitations upon enforceable intentions, and he embraced quasi-contract based more upon a belief in compensation for unjust enrichment than on a fictional extension of promissory liability.
The conclusions made possible by the Mansfield manuscripts have interesting implications for the Horwitz-Atiyah/Simpson-Baker debate.  In order to place this debate in context, a summary of modern views about the evolution of English contract law up to the eighteenth century is necessary before focusing on the manuscript sources.

questions.question: Whether a leading mid- to late-18th-century judge's decisions show that consensual, intention-based notions of contractual obligation and basic fairness governed contract law before 1800.

Whether that judge constrained the enforceability of parties' intentions and instead awarded relief grounded in compensation for unjust enrichment rather than by treating obligations as formal promise-based liabilities.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

When Texaco's Chairman, John K. McKinely, asked Getty Oil's Chairman Sidney Peterson whether Getty might still be available even though an "agreement in principle" had been entered into with Pennzoil, Peterson responded that "the fat lady had not yet sung." Pennzoil Co. v. Getty Oil Co., No. 7425, slip op. at 46 (Del. Ch. Feb. 6, 1984). papers.node_id: 77califlrev1077!!ARTICLE: RELATIONSHIP OR BOUNDARY? HANDLING SUCCESSIVE CONTRACTS.
papers.title: ARTICLE: RELATIONSHIP OR BOUNDARY? HANDLING SUCCESSIVE CONTRACTS.
papers.abstract:
Although the ongoing relationship generated by successive contracts between two parties is quite similar to the relationship generated by a continuing contract that entails a series of consecutive obligations, it receives very different legal treatment. Professor Narasimhan argues that traditional contract law fails to protect adequately the parties' stake in successive-contract relationships against opportunistic behavior. In this Article, she analyzes the role that information plays in creating openings for opportunistic behavior and discusses the costs of failing to deter opportunism. Professor Narasimhan argues that, in the context of successive contracts, gaps in the information available to parties create much friction and foster the manipulative behavior which plagues continuing contractual relationships. She also analyzes the effect of the nature of the transaction and the level of party sophistication on these problems. Professor Narasimhan argues that a system of rules enforcing an obligation to renew contracts should be developed. She discusses three possible regimes--enforceable renewal clauses (opting in), implied renewal clauses (opting out), and mandatory renewal--and concludes that the regime that minimizes opportunism depends upon the level of party sophistication.
To a large extent, contract law has treated contractual relationships as extending in time only between the formation and the termination (whether by successful performance or by breach) of a contract. Consequently, contract law has tended to draw sharp distinctions between one continuing contract governing a series of successive obligations--such as requirements and output contracts--in which long-term relational dependencies are recognized, and a series of contracts between the same parties governing successive obligations in which such dependencies are not recognized.Yet, the relationship and dependencies generated between the parties in these two situations remain similar in many important respects.
The differing treatment accorded to these fundamentally similar transactions permits sophisticated bargainers to structure contractual obligations to achieve particular legal consequences.But the legal fiction of sharp boundaries between contracts governing continuing relationships may also give rise to unexpected results, generating unfairness, opportunism, and waste.
Most of the scholarly discussion of the problems of opportunism generated in continuing or repeated contracting focuses on sophisticated bargainers with large stakes in the relationship. In such cases, the parties may be expected to foresee the possibility of repeated dealings and the opportunism problems generated thereby and may be presumed to have sufficient investment at stake to consider these problems when their relationship begins.Consequently, sophisticated bargainers can use the variety of possibilities generated by the differing legal fictions to customize contracts using standardized terms. Such sophisticated parties, however, represent only one end of a spectrum of possible contracting parties.
In this article, I examine the problem of repeated contracting between parties. In Part I, I shall separate the contractual relationship into three periods: (1) The inception of the relationship--that is, the time the bargain for the initial deal is struck; (2) the period during theinitial contract when performance is due; and (3) the period after the termination of the initial contract during which further negotiations may occur to continue the relationship between the parties.
In this Article, I also examine three types of opportunism--opportunism generated by informational problems, by relational values, and by market values--and the similarities and differences among them in each period. I then compare these findings with the assumptions made in doctrines designed to police contractual opportunism, using a model of contracting in which only a fraction of initial contractors want to repeat. This model is further used to examine the effects of varying degrees of party sophistication and of information available to the parties at the time of the initial contract. This analysis allows me to formulate some of the ways in which the current fiction of termination generates values leading to opportunistic behavior by the parties, and to examine the extent to which current policing doctrine can deter such behavior.
In Part II, I demonstrate that although many of the informational asymmetries plaguing the inception of contracting are absent during negotiations for follow-up contracts, these periods are marked by opportunities for relational opportunism closely akin to those that arise during the period for contractual performance. This potential for relational opportunism in negotiating successor contracts--absent in initial bargaining--can lead to socially wasteful hold-up behavior. Yet, for most policing purposes subsequent negotiation and initial bargaining are treated identically. Thus, parties must often attempt to deter opportunism in follow-up contracting by the way theyinitiallystructure their relationship. Where parties do not have adequate information about possible follow-up contracting at the time they negotiate the initial contract, they are unlikely to be able to avoid these problems of relational opportunism.
Since informational problems are quite likely where parties are unsophisticated, or have smaller amounts at stake in each contract,I argue in Part III that mandatory rules governing the negotiations and allocations of successive contracts might produce a net benefit by reducing opportunistic behavior. Moreover, mandatory rules might be justifiedin some instances for sophisticated parties. Such parties might sometimes prefer to engage in risky hold-up strategies to maximize individual gains at the social cost of fewer cost-effective repeat transactions. Mandatory rules encouraging repeat transactions may be justified where such individual profit-maximizing behavior diverges from socially optimal behavior. I make some suggestions as to the form such mandatory rules might take.
assume throughout this Article that the market in question is competitive (thick) both as to buyers and sellers, thus focusing this Article on the particular form of relational dependencies I seek to study, and the opportunism problems generated thereby.
