papers.node_id: 44iowajcorpl649!!ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority
papers.abstract:
Agents pay a crucial role in coordinating transactions and connecting producer to consumer in today's markets. A significant development in Anglo-American law of agency came with the establishment of apparent authority in the 19th century. In his 1891 article on agency, Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr. explained that "the obvious consequence of the principal's own conduct in employing an agent is that the public understand him to have given the agent certain powers."In this statement, Holmes explained the function of the doctrine of apparent authority. An agent acts with apparent authority when he or she transacts without the express authority of the principal, but the third party has a reasonable basis for assuming the agent has authority. Although this doctrine is well-documented, its intellectual and legal foundations have long been disputed.One strand of thinking links the origins of apparent authority to estoppel: as stated by Webb and Bianco, "if the principal, by words or conduct, represents or holds his agent out as having certain authority, he will be estopped" from denying that the agent had actual authority.A second view seesapparent authority as an independent class of authority. It ties apparent authority to the objective approach in modern contract law where the courts adopt the position of a reasonable person in order to interpret how others would have seen the intention of the parties.This article provides new insights into this debate as it traces the emergence of apparent authority back to its legal foundations.
The Anglo-American law of agents was forged in the 18th and 19th centuries by English judges and legal commentators; it was then adopted and revised by their American counterparts.We argue apparent authority has little or no historical roots in equity as a form of estoppel. Rather, the doctrine began as an independent form of authority as part of the movement from subjective to objective reasoning. The emergence of the objective approach occurred first in agency law, much earlier than has traditionally been thought, and arrived later in contract law. This article begins by providing some background and context on early agency law with a discussion of commercial and mercantile custom as independent from the rules of private law. We then consider the sources of an agent's power and how the courts construed authority. Finally, this article explains how the law of agency - as a distinct body of commercial rules - gathered pace and became accepted in the Anglo-American legal world.

questions.question: Whether holding a principal legally responsible for third-party transactions conducted by an agent is best justified as a reliance-based rule that prevents the principal from denying the agent's apparent power, or as an independent, objective rule that assesses how a reasonable third party would perceive the agent's authority.

Whether the shift from subjective to objective reasoning in assigning liability for agents' acts emerged first within commercial agency relationships in the 18th-19th centuries (and later in general contract law), and what commercial, doctrinal, and institutional factors drove that historical development.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

papers.node_id: 65drakelrev615!!ARTICLE: THE MANY FACES OF CONTRACTUAL CONSENT This title borrows from William N. Eskridge Jr. See William N. Eskridge Jr., The Many Faces of Sexual Consent, 37 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 47, 47 (1995).
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE MANY FACES OF CONTRACTUAL CONSENT This title borrows from William N. Eskridge Jr. See William N. Eskridge Jr., The Many Faces of Sexual Consent, 37 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 47, 47 (1995).
papers.abstract:
The concept of consent lies at the heart of contract law. In theory, it is widely recognized as a powerful concept; in practice, however, courts often struggle to identify, examine, and apply consent.This Article seeks to bridge the gap between consent as a fundamental theoretical concept and its troubled practical application. While it does not endeavor to provide a rigid definition of consent, this Article offers a nuanced description of the concept that could pave the way for a better application of consent in contract law. In light of the current problematic application of consent in contract law, some scholars suggest seeking alternative concepts.Other scholars, facing the complexity of the concept of consent, address only one of the many aspects of consent or focus only on specific type of contracts (e.g., standard form contracts).This Article, in turn, seeks to maintain the primacy of the concept of consent, without disregarding its complexity. It does so by offering a rich, layered model of consent, based on a combination of multiple elements of the concept.
At present, courts ascribe only a narrow meaning to consent, namely, that consent is either informed and freely given, or it is not.However, consent is not simply a "yes-or-no" question; consent is more complex than such an analysis suggests and can be both gradual and continuous. Rejecting a binary framework which views consent as an on-or-off concept, this Articleasserts that consent is better understood as a spectrum that ranges from "no consent" to "solid consent," and that contains many gray areas in between.These gray areas include, but are not limited to, hesitation, deliberation, negotiations, mixed feelings, and reservations. Further complicating the matter is the fact that consent is often contextual.Consent is shaped by the relationship between the consenter and the consentee. Factors of power, intimacy, trust, arm's length relations, and more all differently influence consent. Moreover, consent is socially constructed. Factors such as gender, race, and class directly influence the choices and constraints present for both parties in the background of a consensual decision, as do factors such as social context and policy considerations. As such, consent to a prenuptial agreement, consent to an employment agreement, and consent to a consumer contract must be recognized as distinct from one another, in that they are shaped by their unique social contexts. In other words, consent must be recognized as deriving not only from the individual mindsets of the parties, but also from the relevant public and social circumstances.
Consent has many faces, and this Article aims to develop a more robust understanding of consent by shedding light on its diverse characteristics, and thereby to improve the law's application of consent. By exploring the many shades of consent, this Article may serve as a starting point in the development of a heterogenic, diverse, colorful, and pluralistic concept of consent.
This Article proceeds as follows: Part II of this Article explores the gap between the primacy of consent in contract law theory, on the one hand, and the vagueness of consent in practice, on the other. Included in this exploration is a critique of the narrow and limited framework of consent currently utilized in contract law.
Part III offers a model of consent based on a deeper and more developed understanding of the concept. In addition to the informed and voluntary aspects of consent, this Part analyzes three more aspects of consent: continuum, context, and public policy. The first of these, the continuum aspect, offers a lens with which to view consent as gradual and nuanced, rather than binary and dichotomous. The second additional aspect, context, focuses on three examples - spousal agreements, employment agreements, and standard form contracts - in order to demonstrate the ways in which consent must be viewed as contextual. The third aspect explored in Part III is the connection between public policy and consent. Consent, thisArticle argues, is socially constructed and shaped by public policy considerations that extend beyond the contracting parties' choices, intentions, and relationships. Part III concludes by illustrating the relationship between these three aspects as a series of concentric circles (see: Figure 1). By highlighting the layered approach to the concept of consent, this Article hopes to further develop and enrich the law's understanding and application of contractual consent.

papers.title: Article: The Many Faces of Promissory Estoppel: An Empirical Analysis Under the Restatement (Second) of Contracts
papers.abstract:
Scholars have widely acknowledged that the drafters of the Restatement (Second) made several important changes to § 90 of the Restatement (First) with the intent of making promissory estoppel more available,the role of reliance more prominent,and the remedies awarded to successful litigants more flexible.
But did these changes have their desired effect? This Article examines over three hundred promissory estoppel cases decided across all jurisdictions since the Restatement (Second) was published in 1981 to examine what effect, if any, these changes have had on the way judges have decided promissory estoppel cases. The results are surprising: They suggest that the way promissory estoppel cases are being decided has less to do with the language of the Restatement, and more to do with the way judges are conceptualizing the promissory estoppel cause of action.
Part I of this Article begins by providing a brief history of promissory estoppel. It then explores the numerous ways in which this cause of action has been conceptualized over time - for example, as a contractual theory of recovery, as a tort-based theory of recovery, as an equitable theory of relief, or as something else entirely. Finally, it reveals the importance of this conceptualization by discussing the conflicting work of other scholars writing in this area, many of whom disagree with each other regarding what, exactly, promissory estoppel is and how it should (and does) work in practice.
In an attempt to shed light on this debate, Part II examines over three hundred promissory estoppel cases decided since the Restatement (Second) of Contracts was published in 1981 to test (1) the significance of the promissory estoppel cause of action, (2) the normative basis upon which promissoryestoppel rests (that is, promise or reliance), and (3) the traditional remedies that have been awarded to successful promissory estoppel litigants. My research suggests, first, that promissory estoppel is a much more significant theory of promissory recovery than has been previously thought, and seems positioned to continue to grow in importance in the coming decades. Second, and contrary to the claims made by some scholars writing in this area, the data reveal that promissory estoppel cannot be simply understood in terms of "promise" or "reliance." Rather, most judges require the existence of both promise and reliance before allowing a promissory estoppel claim to proceed, although surprisingly few judges speak in terms of "equity" or "justice." And last, but most significantly for purposes of explaining how judges tend to conceptualize the promissory estoppel cause of action, the data reveal that courts tend to treat promissory estoppel actions as traditional breach of contract actions, in that courts often award the (usually) more generous expectation measure of damages, which is typical in ordinary breach of contract actions, over the (usually) less generous reliance measure of damages, which is often awarded where non-contractual obligations have been breached (for example, in tort law).
Part III of this Article critically examines the manner in which promissory estoppel remedies have been traditionally classified according to the conceptual "expectation" and "reliance" interests, and suggests that by focusing attention on the quantum of remedy received, rather than the label given to that remedy by a scholar or judge, it becomes clear that many judges are treating promissory estoppel causes of action as fully contractual. This means that the litigants are usually at least as well off (in terms of recovery) pursuing a promissory estoppel cause of action as opposed to a more traditional, consideration-based breach of contract claim.
However, because promissory estoppel is sometimes easier to prove than a traditional, consideration-based contract, and because defendants are often not protected by many of the doctrines protecting a traditional breach of contract defendant (for example, the Statute of Frauds and parol evidence rule), some plaintiffs are arguably better off pursuing a promissory estoppel claim because they are often able to obtain the most generous remedy available while remaining subject to the fewest constraints in obtaining this remedy.
Importantly, because a judge's conceptualization of the promissory estoppel cause of action is arguably the most important factor in determining not only whether the plaintiff will succeed, but also the remedy that will be awarded to the plaintiff should he or she succeed, different plaintiffs will fare differently according not to the facts of their case, nor to the elements that must be proven to establish a prima facie claim, but according to the way the judgeassigned to their case happens to conceptualize the promissory estoppel cause of action. This last point not only underscores the importance of contract theory for scholars, practitioners, and judges alike, but strongly suggests that even the most practical judges should be aware of the forces operating beneath the surface of their cases.

questions.question: Whether revisions to an authoritative articulation of the law have made a promise-based cause of action more available, shifted doctrinal emphasis toward reliance, and produced more flexible remedies.

Whether the way judges conceptually characterize the cause of action (e.g., as contract-like, tort-like, or equitable) more strongly determines plaintiff success and the remedy awarded than the formal doctrinal language.

Whether courts award expectation-style (contract-like) versus reliance-style (non-contract) remedies in promise-based cases, and whether plaintiffs recover as much (or more) under this cause of action as they would under a traditional contract claim.

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
Have doctrinal boundaries among contract, tort, and property shifted toward a formalist, market-oriented model?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 85valrev385!!ARTICLE:COMMUNICATION AND COURTSHIP: CHEAP TALK ECONOMICSAND THE LAW OF CONTRACT FORMATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:COMMUNICATION AND COURTSHIP: CHEAP TALK ECONOMICSAND THE LAW OF CONTRACT FORMATION

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel as a tool for imposing precontractual liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promissory estoppel as one of the principal doctrines courts use to impose liability for optimistic pretrade communications in the absence of a formal contract; Paper B empirically studies hundreds of post‑Restatement (Second) cases showing how promissory estoppel is actually invoked and litigated across jurisdictions.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal/ normative basis of promissory estoppel (promise vs reliance vs equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes about whether promissory estoppel should be understood as promise‑based or as a non‑agreement remedy tied to performance and reliance, while Paper B empirically examines how judges conceptualize promissory estoppel (promise, reliance, equity, or contractual) and finds that courts often require both promise and reliance.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and remedies shape incentives in negotiations and dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic model showing how different liability regimes for pretrade talk alter incentives for informative vs misleading cheap talk during courtship, and Paper B shows empirically that the way courts award remedies (often expectation damages) and conceptualize the cause of action affects litigants' practical incentives to bring claims and how parties fare.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability of preliminary communications (offers, solicitations, letters of intent, and bindingness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes when early communications and letters of intent should be treated as solicitations, offers, or binding preliminary agreements and the efficiency tradeoffs of treating them as binding, while Paper B demonstrates that courts, through promissory estoppel, often treat preliminary promises as enforceable and sometimes award contractual‑style remedies, effectively enforcing such communications.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62ukanlrev315!!ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between consideration and non-consideration doctrines (assent, reliance/estoppel) in contract formation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that formation defenses (duress, misrepresentation, mistake, unconscionability) are best understood as responses to a plaintiff's showing of consideration and that assent doctrines are subordinate or redundant; Paper B empirically examines promissory estoppel — a non-consideration-based route to recovery — testing whether promise or reliance controls and how estoppel interacts with traditional, consideration-based relief.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal conceptualization (contractual vs equitable/tort framings) affects outcomes and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A claims that treating formation problems primarily through the lens of consideration (rather than assent) explains the form and function of defenses, while Paper B shows that judges' conceptualization of promissory estoppel (as contractual, equitable, or tort-like) materially alters whether plaintiffs win and which remedies (expectation vs reliance) are awarded.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal development of common-law contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical primacy of consideration and the earlier emergence of formation defenses before assent entered doctrine; Paper B provides a history of promissory estoppel and assesses how changes in the Restatement (Second) have (or have not) influenced judicial treatment since 1981.

shared_topics.topic: the role of equitable doctrines (e.g., unconscionability, estoppel) in supplementing or substituting traditional contract protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats unconscionability and other defenses as part of the formation-defenses landscape that interact with consideration, while Paper B focuses on promissory estoppel as an equitable (or hybrid) doctrine that can substitute for or supplement traditional contractual protections and affect the availability and size of remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1993utahlrev67!!ARTICLE: Expanded Liability and the Intent Requirement in Third Party Beneficiary Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Expanded Liability and the Intent Requirement in Third Party Beneficiary Contracts

shared_topics.topic: expansion of contractual recovery beyond privity/consideration
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze doctrines that permit recovery outside of a traditional, consideration-based contract: Paper A studies promissory estoppel as a vehicle for plaintiffs to recover absent consideration, and Paper B examines third‑party beneficiary standing to allow nonparties to enforce contractual promises.

shared_topics.topic: the role of promise, intent, and reliance as elements for nontraditional contractual claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether courts treat promissory estoppel as grounded in promise, reliance, or both, while Paper B centers its test on the promisee's intent to benefit and the promisor's knowledge — showing both works interrogate what mental/state elements justify recovery.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal framing by courts determines available remedies and liability scope
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that judges' conceptualization of promissory estoppel (contractual vs equitable) predicts whether expectation or reliance damages are awarded, and Paper B demonstrates that how courts characterize intent/ duty in third‑party cases affects whether and how third parties can obtain relief.

shared_topics.topic: balancing contractual expectations against broader policy/public‑protection concerns
shared_topics.justification: Both articles engage the normative tradeoff between protecting the reasonable expectations of contracting parties (and preserving contractual limits) and extending protection to outsiders or the public — Paper A in discussing equitable justifications and remedy generosity, Paper B in explicitly weighing contractual expectations against public‑safety rationales in expanded third‑party liability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2016michstlrev1267!!ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CHARITABLE NAMING RIGHTS TRANSACTIONS: GIFTS OR CONTRACTS?

shared_topics.topic: how courts classify nontraditional promises/transactions (contract vs gift/trust/tort/equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically examines how judges conceptualize promissory estoppel—whether as contract, tort, or equitable claim—and shows that this classification drives outcomes; Paper B analyzes case law on charitable naming rights to determine when courts treat such arrangements as gifts, trusts, or contracts and the consequences of those characterizations.

shared_topics.topic: how the legal characterization determines available remedies and doctrinal protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that when courts treat promissory estoppel as contractual they frequently award expectation damages and bypass defenses that apply to conventional contracts; Paper B demonstrates that treating naming-rights deals as gifts (rather than contracts) has produced extreme, often perverse remedial results and argues contract law would allow more sensible remedial and gap-filling options.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and normative role of promise, intent, and reliance in adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores whether promissory estoppel rests on promise, reliance, or both and reports judges often require both elements; Paper B emphasizes the multifaceted and opaque intentions of donors and how donor intent (versus promised commitments or reliance) influences courts' choice between gift, trust, or contract doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: how parties can and should structure transactions or claims strategically to obtain favorable legal regimes and outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes plaintiffs may prefer promissory estoppel because it can be easier to prove and less constrained by rules like the Statute of Frauds, affecting strategic litigation choices; Paper B offers guidance for charities and donors to structure naming-rights arrangements as contracts (with duration and morals clauses) to avoid the pitfalls courts produce under gift law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2020michstlrev547!!ARTICLE: CHALLENGING LAND CONTRACTING ON THE BASIS OF DISPARATE IMPACT AFTER TEXAS DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING AND COMMUNITY AFFAIRS V. INCLUSIVE COMMUNITIES PROJECT, INC.: A VIABLE OPTION OR A DEAD END?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CHALLENGING LAND CONTRACTING ON THE BASIS OF DISPARATE IMPACT AFTER TEXAS DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING AND COMMUNITY AFFAIRS V. INCLUSIVE COMMUNITIES PROJECT, INC.: A VIABLE OPTION OR A DEAD END?

shared_topics.topic: how judicial doctrinal frameworks/tests determine litigant success and remedy availability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Supreme Court's formulation of the disparate-impact burden‑shifting test (Inclusive Communities vs. Albemarle) affects plaintiffs' ability to prevail against predatory land contracts; Paper B shows empirically that judges' conceptualization of promissory estoppel (promise vs. reliance vs. contract-like) strongly predicts whether plaintiffs win and what remedies they receive.

shared_topics.topic: the role of contract-related doctrines in protecting or harming disadvantaged parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines land contracts as a contract-form that has been used predatoryly against low‑income and minority buyers and considers litigation doctrines to challenge that harm; Paper B studies promissory estoppel, a contract‑adjacent doctrine that can enable recovery for parties excluded from formal contract protections and thus has distributive consequences for vulnerable litigants.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between equitable principles and formalistic legal rules in shaping remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that different doctrinal formulations (more deferential vs. more exacting tests) yield very different capacities to remedy covert discrimination, invoking equity versus deference tradeoffs; Paper B interrogates promissory estoppel's hybrid nature—often framed as equitable yet yielding contract‑style expectation damages—highlighting tensions between equitable relief and formal contract doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal evolution and the need for reform or conceptual clarity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques recent Supreme Court precedent and advocates returning to an older burden‑shifting framework (Albemarle) to better effectuate statutory purposes, while Paper B empirically finds that the Restatement (Second)'s revisions did not produce uniform doctrinal change and calls for clearer conceptualization and possible doctrinal reform.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2000utahlrev223!!SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.

shared_topics.topic: how judges' conceptualizations of doctrinal categories drive case outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that understanding a reported case requires digging beneath doctrinal formulations to uncover the factual and conceptual assumptions that produced the decision, while Paper B empirically shows that judges' differing conceptualizations of promissory estoppel (contractual, tort-like, equitable, etc.) meaningfully determine both liability and the remedy awarded.

shared_topics.topic: the importance of factual and historical/contextual reconstruction for interpreting reported cases
shared_topics.justification: Paper A promotes ‘‘legal archaeology’’ — reconstructing the factual and historical context surrounding a reported case to understand why courts decided as they did — and Paper B relies on close examination of hundreds of reported promissory estoppel decisions to reveal how facts, reliance, and promises are actually treated in judicial practice.

shared_topics.topic: methodological scrutiny of legal scholarship and doctrine (historical vs. empirical approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advances a historical/archival method for studying law and criticizes reliance on abstract doctrinal summaries, while Paper B applies empirical case-analysis to test whether doctrinal changes (Restatement (Second) §90) produced the intended effects, exemplifying a critical, evidence-driven method for evaluating doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: how interpretive choices affect fairness of remedies and the pursuit of justice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A links careful case reconstruction to revitalizing lawyers' commitment to just results by revealing what actually transpired, and Paper B shows that judicial framing of promissory estoppel affects which remedies plaintiffs receive and thus has concrete distributive and fairness consequences for litigants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 42textechlrev913!!ARTICLE: RELIANCE ON ORAL PROMISES: STATUTE OF FRAUDS AND "PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL"
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: RELIANCE ON ORAL PROMISES: STATUTE OF FRAUDS AND "PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL"

shared_topics.topic: use of promissory estoppel to enforce oral promises barred by the Statute of Frauds
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds disputes where oral promises (e.g., employment terms or joint-venture commitments) clash with the Statute of Frauds and discusses courts invoking promissory estoppel or the statute to permit or bar recovery; Paper B empirically analyzes how courts actually apply promissory estoppel—often as an alternative route to enforce promises—and examines how that interacts with protective doctrines like the Statute of Frauds.

shared_topics.topic: the role and standards of reliance (reasonable/foreseeable reliance) in promissory estoppel claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes questions about whether a plaintiff's reliance on an oral promise is reasonable or foreseeable enough to support recovery, while Paper B investigates across hundreds of cases whether judges require and how they assess both promise and reliance, showing that most courts demand evidence of reliance and evaluate its sufficiency.

shared_topics.topic: how promissory estoppel is conceptualized (contractual vs equitable/tort) and the doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises concerns about courts using contract doctrines to block reliance claims and about the legal framing of such disputes; Paper B systematically studies judicial conceptualizations—contract-based, tort-based, equitable—and demonstrates that a court's framing strongly influences liability and remedy outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: remedies awarded in promissory estoppel cases (expectation versus reliance damages) and implications for plaintiffs/defendants
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents factual scenarios where plaintiffs seek to enforce oral promises and hints at the practical stakes of available remedies, while Paper B provides empirical evidence that courts often award expectation-type damages in promissory estoppel cases (treating them like breach of contract), explaining the normative and strategic consequences for litigants.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 35amulrev547!!ARTICLE: A PROPOSAL TO SIMPLIFY QUANTUM MERUIT LITIGATION. © 1986 Candace S. Kovacic
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A PROPOSAL TO SIMPLIFY QUANTUM MERUIT LITIGATION. © 1986 Candace S. Kovacic

shared_topics.topic: measurement of recovery for non‑contractual or quasi‑contractual claims (expectation, reliance, market value, unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how courts measure remedies when plaintiffs recover outside an enforceable express contract: Paper A proposes measuring requested services by market value and unrequested services by the defendant's unjust enrichment, while Paper B shows courts often award expectation‑style damages in promissory estoppel cases and urges attention to the quantum of the remedy rather than labels.

shared_topics.topic: normative basis for imposing liability (unjust enrichment vs promise/reliance/equity)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles interrogate the normative justification for relief absent a formal contract: Paper A distinguishes outcomes based on whether services were requested (grounded in justice to pay) or unrequested (grounded in unjust enrichment), and Paper B empirically probes whether promissory estoppel rests on promise, reliance, or equitable principles and finds judges invoke overlapping bases.

shared_topics.topic: the effect of judicial conceptualization and terminology on case outcomes and predictability
shared_topics.justification: Both works argue that how judges label and conceptualize claims (restitution/quasi‑contract, implied contract, promissory estoppel as contractual/tort/equitable) materially influences whether plaintiffs succeed and what remedy they receive, producing inconsistent and unpredictable results that the authors seek to address.

shared_topics.topic: interaction with traditional contract doctrines and defenses (e.g., Statute of Frauds, parol evidence)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers examine how these substitute doctrines operate alongside or around orthodox contract rules: Paper A analyzes categories such as statute of frauds and third‑party recoveries within quantum meruit, and Paper B documents that promissory estoppel can sidestep protections like the Statute of Frauds and parol evidence rule, affecting plaintiffs' strategic use of alternative claims.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 23geomasonlrev125!!ARTICLE: "PROVE ME WRONG" CASES AND CONSIDERATION THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: "PROVE ME WRONG" CASES AND CONSIDERATION THEORY

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel as a substitute for consideration in enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that 'prove-me-wrong' promises typically lack consideration and therefore should be enforced (if at all) under promissory estoppel, while Paper B empirically analyzes how courts use promissory estoppel in practice and shows it often functions as an alternative route to recovery when traditional consideration-based contract doctrines are unavailable.

shared_topics.topic: the necessity of both promise and reliance for promissory estoppel claims
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that enforceability of prove-me-wrong offers should depend on promissory estoppel elements including the promisee's reliance and the avoidance of injustice, and Paper B finds empirically that most judges require evidence of both a promise and reliance before allowing promissory estoppel claims to proceed.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial conceptualization of doctrines (consideration vs estoppel) affects outcomes and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for treating certain unilateral statements as contracts without properly analyzing consideration and urges reliance on estoppel doctrine instead, while Paper B shows that judges' differing conceptualizations of promissory estoppel (contract-like, tort-like, or equitable) materially influence whether plaintiffs succeed and what remedies they receive.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of performance-conditioned (unilateral/reward-style) promises when traditional contract elements are contested
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on 'prove-me-wrong' and reward-style unilateral promises and argues they often fail the consideration requirement but may be saved by estoppel, and Paper B examines a broad set of promissory estoppel cases—many arising where formal contract formation is disputed—and assesses how courts resolve enforceability and relief in such contexts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 10texwesleyanlrev65!!SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF CONTRACT IN THE MODERN EMPLOYMENT RELATIONSHIP:LABOR DISPUTES IN CONTRACT LAW: THE PAST AND PRESENT OF ALASKA PACKERS' ASS'N V. DOMENICO
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM:THE ROLE OF CONTRACT IN THE MODERN EMPLOYMENT RELATIONSHIP:LABOR DISPUTES IN CONTRACT LAW: THE PAST AND PRESENT OF ALASKA PACKERS' ASS'N V. DOMENICO

shared_topics.topic: the influence of judicial conceptualization and policy preferences on doctrinal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically shows that judges' conceptualization of promissory estoppel (contractual, tort, or equitable) strongly predicts both liability and remedy, and Paper B traces how trial and appellate judges' assumptions and policy concerns (sympathy to workers, worry about coercion) shaped the outcome and reasoning in Alaska Packers'.

shared_topics.topic: the interplay between formal contract doctrines (consideration, pre-existing duty, Statute of Frauds, parol evidence) and equitable or alternative doctrines (promissory estoppel, novation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how promissory estoppel operates as an alternative to consideration-based recovery and how it sidesteps doctrines like the Statute of Frauds and parol evidence, while Paper B centers on the choice between novation/modification and the pre-existing duty rule (and related doctrines) in resolving a labor dispute.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal choice affects plaintiffs' and defendants' practical recoveries and protections
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that courts often award expectation remedies under promissory estoppel—making it sometimes superior to traditional contract claims—whereas Paper B shows that doctrinal rulings about enforceability of wage promises and modifications (e.g., refusing to enforce a modification because of the pre-existing duty rule) directly determine whether workers recover and how much.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of classical contract doctrine for regulating ongoing/relational contexts (especially labor/employment) and the use of alternative doctrines to fill gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues promissory estoppel has grown as a significant route for recovery where traditional contract requirements are troublesome, and Paper B uses Alaska Packers' to illustrate the mismatch between classical contract rules and the realities of prolonged or employment relationships, highlighting resort to other doctrines or doctrinal adaptations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71tullrev1749!!ARTICLE: IN THE TRIBUNAL OF CONSCIENCE: MILLS V. WYMAN RECONSIDERED
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN THE TRIBUNAL OF CONSCIENCE: MILLS V. WYMAN RECONSIDERED

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of promises without consideration (moral-obligation rule vs promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the moral-obligation doctrine as articulated in Mills v. Wyman—where a moral duty was held insufficient for consideration—and argues for binding promises based on intent; Paper B empirically analyzes promissory estoppel (the chief non-consideration route to enforcement post-Restatement (Second)) to see how courts actually enforce promises absent traditional consideration.

shared_topics.topic: the normative foundation of promise enforcement — intent, moral duty, or reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques competing theories of the moral-obligation doctrine and ultimately argues that intent to be bound should govern, while Paper B investigates whether courts ground promissory estoppel in promise, reliance, equity, or some combination, finding many judges require both promise and reliance.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedies for promises enforced outside traditional contract doctrine (expectation vs reliance measures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses what compensation should follow when nontraditional promises are enforced and argues for liability where intent exists, and Paper B systematically examines the remedies courts award under promissory estoppel, showing many courts grant expectation-style damages despite the absence of formal consideration.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial decisionmaking and doctrinal development in shaping promissory liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconstructs Mills and criticizes the court's factual and doctrinal choices, arguing judges missed an opportunity to craft a better promissory liability rule, while Paper B demonstrates empirically that judges' conceptualizations of promissory estoppel — not just Restatement language — largely determine outcomes and remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2008uilllrev505!!ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the promise-vs-reliance debate as the foundational heuristic for contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically tests whether promissory estoppel is best understood in terms of promise or reliance and finds that courts typically demand both elements; Paper B surveys the same heuristic dichotomy (promise vs reliance, plus transfer) as the central descriptive device for mapping doctrinal commitments to normative theories and critiques its limits.

shared_topics.topic: how judicial/doctrinal conceptualization determines remedies and case outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows empirically that the way judges conceptualize promissory estoppel (often as contractual) materially affects whether plaintiffs succeed and whether expectation or reliance recovery is awarded; Paper B analyzes how applying different heuristics or misreading doctrinal facts leads to different theoretical prescriptions and, implicitly, different practical results when the law is applied.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of unified normative theory to explain actual contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A’s empirical results question whether Restatement rhetoric alone explains judicial practice, highlighting gaps between theory and adjudication; Paper B argues more broadly that searches for a single normative foundation of contract law (consequentialist, deontological, aretaic or transfer-based) are likely to fail and that understanding why theory fails is itself instructive.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between contract and other legal categories (tort, equity, property/transfer) and its doctrinal significance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that promissory estoppel has been conceptualized variably as contract, tort, or equitable relief and that those labels affect remedies and constraints; Paper B engages the same boundary question by examining how heuristics (promise, reliance, transfer) map contract to tort, equity, or property paradigms and the normative implications of those mappings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59arklrev841!!ARTICLE: Promissory Estoppel and Wagging the Dog
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Promissory Estoppel and Wagging the Dog

shared_topics.topic: conceptual status of promissory estoppel (contract, tort, or equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically investigates how judges conceptualize promissory estoppel and finds courts often treat it as contractual in practice; Paper B analyzes the same debate normative‑ly and urges classifying cases as contract, tort, or estoppel rather than blurring categories.

shared_topics.topic: the normative basis and required elements: promise versus reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's data show most judges require both a promise and reliance and reject simple either/or accounts, while Paper B engages the issue theoretically, distinguishing promise‑focused (contract‑like) uses from reliance/estoppel‑focused uses and arguing for clarity about which element governs.

shared_topics.topic: remedial classification and available remedies (expectation vs reliance measures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that courts frequently award expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases—treating them like breach of contract—whereas Paper B argues remedies should flow from the proper doctrinal classification (full contract remedies if contractual, defensive estoppel remedies if estoppel).

shared_topics.topic: use or misuse of promissory estoppel to circumvent other doctrines (Statute of Frauds, parol evidence) and the need for doctrinal limits
shared_topics.justification: Paper A notes plaintiffs may prefer promissory estoppel because it yields generous remedies without traditional contractual constraints, and Paper B criticizes courts for expanding the doctrine to avoid rules like the Statute of Frauds or parol evidence rule, calling for limiting promissory estoppel and resolving issues under the more appropriate doctrines.

papers.node_id: 1984wislrev1373!!ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF RELIANCE: A HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE.
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE MEANING OF RELIANCE: A HISTORICAL PERSPECTIVE.
papers.abstract:
A basic theme in first-year contract law courses is the decline of consideration and the rise of reliance as a basis for the enforcement of promises.  Recently I wrote an article describing the evolution of reliance doctrine and the connections between that evolution and broader changes in contract law.The article was a modest variation on a familiar theme: the narrowness of bargain consideration led scholars and jurists to fashion a remedy in promissory estoppel for promises that induce unbargained-for reliance; over the past fifty years, the use of promissory estoppel has expanded dramatically.  The article was exclusively an exercise in intellectual history, focusing on developments in contract doctrine and theory within the legal system.  Having described that internal history, the question that then concerned me in my sometime role as legal historian was why the changes in theory and doctrine had occurred.  That question is addressed in this Article.  How do we account for the growth of reliance-based recovery in contract? Methodologically, what theory of history permits us to connect the doctrinal changes with social conditions?  Because the legal present is the legal history of the future,how should we think about the connection between legal process and social process?
Although the scholarly literature on contracts is probably the richest on any legal subject, historical questions of this sort have seldom been addressed directly.  Accordingly, I draw from a variety of judicial and scholarly sources to present the traditional accounts of the rise of reliance.  Then I offer an unusual illustration having nothing to do with reliance, contracts, or even law, as a vehicle for critiquing the traditional accounts and suggesting the desirability of using critical methodologies to approach the problem.  I use one such methodology to sketch a different account of the history of reliance.  Finally, I draw some implications for legal scholarship and judicial decision from the historical inquiry.
To avoid later disappointment, I should make clear at the beginning my conclusion about the history of reliance: I cannot provide a complete explanation for the expansion of the doctrine.  Nevertheless, I find the process of reaching that non-conclusion extremely interesting for what it tells us about the study of legal history and the making of contract law.  Moreover, the historical analysis is useful in advancing another project, the reconstructive or utopian effort within the critical legal studies movement.

questions.question: Why has judicial willingness to enforce promises on the basis of reliance rather than formal exchange expanded over time?
What social, economic, and intellectual factors account for historical changes in how courts resolve disputes over unbargained-for promises?
What historical or methodological framework best links changes in legal doctrine to broader social processes, and how should that connection inform scholarly analysis and judicial decisionmaking?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 84templrev119!!ARTICLE: THE MISSING ELEMENTS OF CONTRACT DAMAGES
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE MISSING ELEMENTS OF CONTRACT DAMAGES
papers.authors: Mitchell L. Engler; Susan B. Heyman
papers.abstract:
We begin by juxtaposing two classic contract doctrines to expose a striking, unrecognized anomaly of contract law. Our joint analysis of the legendary Chicago Coliseum Club v. Dempseyand Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores, Inc.cases reveals that a party negotiating a deal might be more likely to recover costs made in preparation for the contract when the other side backs out before executing a contract than when the counterparty reneges on a fully enforceable contract. Contract doctrine has developed several mechanisms - including the Red Owl promissory estoppel line - that allow recovery of expenditures made in the absence of a contract. By contrast, Dempsey disallows recovery of precontract expenditures in cases where the parties actually reach a "meeting of the minds" but do not sufficiently fix in advance the return on the contract (an "open-return contract").
We then uncover a related but independent inconsistency in contract law between the recoveries available under two different types of finalized contracts. By comparing the recovery under an open-return contract, as in Dempsey, with the likely recovery under a contract whose return is fixed in advance (a "set-return contract"), we demonstrate that precontract and fixed overhead expenses are treated differently and more harshly under an open-return contract.After unmasking these inconsistencies,we propose a new damage regime that reduces these disparities in treatment, more accurately reflects business expectations, and creates better incentives for efficient behavior.
Consider first the famous Jack Dempsey case.Dempsey contracted with Chicago Coliseum to fight Harry Wills in a heavyweight championship match.Rather than negotiating a straight fee for their promotional efforts, the Coliseum agreed to a percentage-of-the-gate arrangement.Dempsey then broke the contract to fight instead Gene Tunney, thereby altering boxing history forever.Although Dempsey's repudiation prevented the Coliseum from potentially earning substantial revenues, the damage award was insignificant.The court denied expectancy damages for the "too speculative" lost profits, finding that it could not estimate the gate receipts for the cancelled match.Instead, the court limited recovery to only reliance expenditures made after the contract signing and before breach, thereby denying recovery for precontractual promotional costs and fixed salaries to corporate officers.Indisallowing fixed overhead and precontract costs where lost profits were indeterminate (the "Dempsey Rule"), the court reasoned that the execution of the final contract was the pivotal point for determining liability, rather than an earlier time during negotiations when the parties "indicated an agreement between them."
Consider next a variation of the Dempsey case to highlight how the recovery would have differed if a final contract had not been executed and the Coliseum could assert a claim under the Red Owl promissory estoppel approach.Suppose that after Dempsey promised the Coliseum that he would fight Wills in a heavyweight championship match, but before all of the terms of the contract were finalized, the Coliseum reasonably incurred expenses in identifying secondary investors, meeting with other promoters, and locating a suitable venue. Dempsey then refused to finalize the contract with the Coliseum. Under these circumstances, the Coliseum would not be entitled to damages on the contract as there was never a finalized agreement. However, under the Red Owl approach, the Coliseum could likely recover its precontract expenses under the equitable theory of promissory estoppel because Dempsey made a promise on which the Coliseum reasonably relied and acted upon to its detriment.
Dempsey and Red Owl have been extensively analyzed over time, albeit independently of each other. By now jointly analyzing the two, we expose the possibility that the aggrieved party on a successfully negotiated contract might receive a lesser recovery than if he had been unsuccessful in negotiating the final contract! In particular, although Red Owl permits recovery even though final negotiations fail, Dempsey cuts off precontract expenditures when the aggrieved party successfully finalizes the deal.
The main stated justification for the Dempsey Rule is that aggrieved parties do not incur precontract expenditures in reliance on the contract.The argument ignores the fact that some precontract costs might have been incurred in reliance on precontract negotiations or preliminary understandings. The Dempsey "integration" approach, which places great weight on the timing of the ultimate contract, wipes out these reliance-induced expenditures.Moreover, our critical analysis of Judge Posner's opinion in Autotrol Corp. v. Continental Water Systems Corp.reveals yet another underappreciated inconsistency of current contract law. Aggrieved parties generally recover all precontract costs and fixed overhead on finalized set-return contracts without regard to reliance since the set amount recovery subtracts out only postcontract saved costs under mitigation principles. As such, recovery on the set-return contract includes, for example, costs incurred even prior to any negotiations. So although aggrieved parties can recover their costs absent any reliance on set-return contracts, the Dempsey Rule disallows recovery of precontract expenses under open-return contracts. Yet Judge Posner curiously defends the current state of the law as providing "symmetrical" results between set and open-return contracts!
One might attempt to explain the disparate treatment between set-return and open-return contracts on the ground that there is no need to separately determine each recoverable cost on the set-return contract; compensation is built into the ordinary damage remedy. Juxtaposition of Dempsey and Red Owl undermines this argument, because under the Red Owl approach the component costs can be recovered when there has been no contract, even though those costs need to be separately determined. Why, then, should the need to ascertain those costs be an obstacle when the parties have reached an open-return contract? Indeed, the contract price can be even less determinable under the Red Owl line than the Dempsey line given the lack of a contract finalizing the terms. And once again, why should the aggrieved party be treated more harshly when he in fact successfully negotiates a finalized deal? Furthermore, the set-return scenario also can require consideration of component costs since postbreach saved costs reduce the aggrieved party's recovery of the set contract price.
The problem, then, is that current law can treat the aggrieved party of an open-return contract less favorably than the aggrieved party of a set-return contract and less favorably than a party who has made expenditures without ever reaching a contract.This Article will demonstrate that both of these disparities can be best addressed by reversing the Dempsey Rule and allowing recovery of precontract and fixed overhead costs on open-return contracts. Reversing the Dempsey Rule is not merely a matter offairness. The Dempsey Rule also leads to undercompensation of aggrieved parties as well as an increased risk of opportunistic behavior and deterring efficient precontract investments.
One response to the undercompensation problem is to require the breaching party to disgorge profits made as a consequence of the breach. However, disgorgement can lead to overcompensation and the risk of deterring even efficient breaches.Consider another variation of Dempsey, modeled after the movie classic Rocky,to highlight the disgorgement overcompensation problem. Chicago Coliseum, a promoter of sports events, spends several weeks and thousands of dollars seeking the perfect contenders for a boxing match, locating a suitable arena, and hiring assistants to help with promotional efforts and ticket sales for the event. Eventually, Jack Dempsey, a popular club fighter, agrees with the Coliseum to fight another club fighter. A few weeks later, Gene Tunney (Dempsey's Apollo Creed), the undisputed heavyweight champion, offers Dempsey the chance of a lifetime, to replace his original contender who broke his hand and fight for the title. Confident that Dempsey's hometown roots and local popularity would draw a large gate, Tunney offers Dempsey significantly more money to fight for the championship. Since Dempsey cannot take on both fights, Dempsey breaches his original contract for a chance of a lifetime payday and fame. Facing possible serious harm at Tunney's lethal hands, Dempsey greatly intensifies his training regime and "goes the distance" in fifteen grueling rounds with Tunney, albeit in a loss. Even assuming difficulty in ascertaining the Coliseum's lost revenues from Dempsey's breach, we find unsatisfying a disgorgement approach that might require Dempsey to pay the Coliseum his entire take from the fight, and possibly even more.
This Article proposes instead a more moderate solution, which validates the undercompensatory concerns of the disgorgement proposals without going too far in the other direction. It proposes a presumptive recovery for aggrieved parties on open-return contracts equal to their entire investment costs (pre-and postcontract; fixed and variable) plus a risky rate of return on that capital investment for the investment period. This proposed solution essentially extends the well-established presumption in contract law that the aggrieved party will recover at least what his postcontract variable expenditures would have been if the contract had not been breached.Under current law, this presumptive recovery of postcontract variable costs is disallowed to the extent the aggrieved party would not have regained such outlays absent the breach, but the breaching party appropriately bears the burden to prove such a "losing contract," since the breaching party's actions caused the lack of an actual revenue stream from theventure.Drawing upon classic investment principles, this Article demonstrates why this reasoning should be extended to all investment costs in a venture along with a profitable return thereon. The current presumption is too narrow, as it is based on the factually counter-intuitive premise that aggrieved parties would have recouped only their postcontract variable costs.As will be shown, most rational investors realistically expect to recoup, on average, all their investment costs plus some actual profit for the investment period.
Part II of this Article explores the undercompensation of aggrieved parties to open-return contracts, as compared to aggrieved parties who fail to successfully negotiate a contract or who negotiate a set-return contract. Part III.A demonstrates the problems of such undercompensation, for instance, how it creates incentives for opportunistic breaches. Part III.B then considers potential responses to the problem, including disgorgement as a remedy, and demonstrates how such solutions go too far in the other direction, that is, they create a reciprocal problem of deterring even efficient breaches. Part IV suggests a reversal of the Dempsey Rule to allow a presumptive recovery of all reasonable costs, including precontract and fixed overhead, plus a risky profitable rate of return thereon. Such a presumption would more accurately reflect the ex ante business expectations of the parties, would encourage efficient precontract expenditures, and would place the burden of proof on the appropriate party, as it was the breaching party's actions that prevented the aggrieved party from earning an actual revenue stream on the contract.

papers.node_id: 1997wislrev943!!ARTICLE: THE NEW REQUIREMENT OF ENFORCEMENT RELIANCE IN COMMERCIAL PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL:
papers.title: ARTICLE: THE NEW REQUIREMENT OF ENFORCEMENT RELIANCE IN COMMERCIAL PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL:
papers.abstract:
Any comprehensive examination of recent appellate court decisions will disclose that the legal doctrine of promissory estoppel has not become a significant source of commercial contractual obligation. Although commercial promissory estoppel claims are often made, plaintiff victories are very rare. These results are difficult to reconcile with frequent scholarly contentions to the effect that contemporary courts have become more receptive to claims of promissory estoppel and have liberalized its doctrinal requirements. More important, the promisor behavior that is incidentally disclosed in reported opinions also undermines academic arguments that rules providing for promissory estoppel have commercial utility. The decisions suggest that most commercial actors consider promissory estoppel liability as a risk to be avoided rather than as a valuable opportunity to create contract obligations, and that they make efforts to avoid it whenever possible. Indeed, a review of recent decisions shows that judicial sympathy toward these efforts to avoid liability has begun to alter promissory estoppel doctrine. In several jurisdictions a commercial promisee must now demonstrate what can be called "enforcement reliance" - reliance on a reasonable belief in the legal enforceability of the promise - in addition to mere "performance reliance" - reliance on a reasonable belief that the promise will be performed. These decisions require that the promisor not only make a reliance-inducing promise, but also clearly express an intention to be legally bound. This article argues that the new requirement is an appropriate default rule for non-bargain, commercial promises because it gives effect to the parties' most probable motives and intentions concerning enforcement.
This is a story about a revolution that wasn't. Section 90 of the Restatement of Contracts was the first formal expression of promissory estoppel as a contract doctrine of general application.Although theRestatement formulation was derived primarily from cases involving family or charitable gift promises,courts soon began applying the generalized language of Section 90 to commercial promises. In the ensuing years, it was widely expected that promissory estoppel would revolutionize commercial contract law by erasing the familiar demarcations between enforceable and unenforceable promises that had been drawn by the bargain theory of consideration and by introducing the uncertainty of a new form of reliance-based, tort liability into contract negotiations and relationships.These predictions, however, failed tomake allowance for a widespread defensive reaction to the doctrinal novelty.Once commercial actors became aware of Section 90, they responded by implementing legal strategies designed to reduce or eliminate the new risk of promissory liability. Judicial receptivity to this adaptive response has now begun to reshape promissory estoppel doctrine.
This Article reports on the current state of the co-evolution of legal strategy and legal doctrine by analyzing how Section 90 is being interpreted in the courts.For several years now, well-counseled commercial promisors have known how to take legally effective measures to avoid Section 90 liability during the negotiation and performance of contracts.More recently, courts in several jurisdictions have begun to modify the reliance element of promissory estoppel so as to require the promisee to demonstrate a reasonable and foreseeable belief that the promise in question was legally enforceable.As will be seen, this is a difficult hurdle for a commercially sophisticated party to surmount. The concerted effort by lawyers and judges to limit commercial promissory liability to formal contract commitments is returning the commercial world to its pre-Section 90 tranquility.
These developments suggest that a reappraisal of Section 90 is appropriate. If it is conceptualized as a rule of contract law, then promissory estoppel should find its ultimate justification in the mutual benefits it confers on potential trading partners.It should, in other words, be an economically efficientrule that all parties to a transaction would prefer to submit to, ex ante. Yet commercial actors seem not to appreciate the advantages they gain from this doctrine. Judged by their persistent efforts to avoid estoppel liability, and by the absence of anyevidence that they are deliberately using the rule to structure promissory obligations, promissory estoppel does not appear to be an efficient rule. This Article contends that the appropriate rule for commercial parties - one that is suggested by recent decisions - is that a reliance-inducing, non-bargain promise should be unenforceable in the absence of the promisor's clear expression of a specific intention to incur legal liability. In that one narrow exception, however, enforcement seems clearly warranted if the promisee actually relies on the promise.
This thesis directly contradicts prevailing academic opinion, both descriptively and normatively. In the past two decades, several scholars have proclaimed that promissory estoppel has achieved a dominant role in commercial transactions and has done so as a contract doctrine rather than as a tort doctrine. Some theorists claim that Section 90 has evolved into a new mode of contract formation that is free of both the technicalities of the consideration doctrine and the vestigial reliance requirement inherited from equitable estoppel.Other theorists imply that Section 90 has become a method that, like the doctrine of offer and acceptance, commercial parties can use for the deliberate creation of legal obligations.Still others, applying economic reasoning that supports enforcement of bargain promises,contend that enforcement of non-bargain, commercial promises under Section 90, reduces transaction costs and encourages efficient levels of promisee reliance.
These lines of argument all imply that rational, self-interested commercial actors attach a positive value to the capacity to bind themselves by informal, non-bargain promises.But every sign that can be gleaned from the appellate reports suggests that commercial actors overwhelmingly prefer to order their legal affairs via the well-worn channels of formal bargain contract and that they consider their potential liability under Section 90 to be more a dangerous pitfall than a valuable opportunity. The behavior of these commercial promisors casts serious doubt on the virtues of Section 90 as a contract device.
Part II of this Article describes the two forms of promisee reliance that a commercial promise might induce and that Section 90 might protect: performance reliance and enforcement reliance. While the law could theoretically enforce all promises that foreseeably induce a promisee to rely on their performance, such a rule would be overbroad. Virtually all promises in the commercial world are made in order to induce performance reliance but not all promises are enforceable.Promisors and promisees benefit from a legal regime that permits both enforceable and unenforceable reliance-inducing promises to be made, at the promisor's option.
Most published economic analysis of Section 90 tends to assume that legal enforcement will be efficient whenever the promisee's reliance is beneficial or efficient and that the parties would prefer such a rule, ex ante, in order to minimize transaction costs.But this "hypothetical bargain" approach conflicts with empirical evidence of actual behavior. Outside the context of formal bargain promises, commercial promisors are usually satisfied with the simple level of performance reliance that is induced by unenforceable promises. While economic analysis persuasively supports a legal rule that would enable promisors to choose to make designated non-bargain promises legally enforceable, it cannotdemonstrate that efficiency is served by enforcing all of the promises described by Section 90.
Part III considers the claim made by two popular non-economic theories of promissory estoppel that actual reliance is not, and should not be, necessary to a claim under Section 90. The promise and consent theories of contract law each reject the view that Section 90 is a tort-like rule,concerned with deterrence and compensation for promisees who are injured by their foreseeable reliance on broken promises. Instead, they conceive of Section 90 as a contract doctrine,providing an alternative to bargain promise as a way to structure a legal obligation.They contend that contemporary judicial treatment of Section 90 permits the creation of contractual obligation by promise alone, without the necessity of either bargained-for consideration or actual reliance.
Using a survey of all of the promissory estoppel cases reported in 1995 and 1996, I will challenge the descriptive claims that underlie these theories. Contemporary courts rigorously enforce Section 90's requirement that the promise induce actual reliance by the promisee. These courts do not enforce promises that satisfy only the simplifiedgrounds of enforceability proposed by the promise and consent theorists, i.e., serious promises made in furtherance of a commercial objective.
The evidence of contemporary practice that can be gleaned from these cases also casts serious doubt on the normative arguments of the consent and promise theorists, who contend that prima facie legal enforceability of non-bargain, business-related promises would facilitate commercial exchanges and give effect to promisors' actual or probable intention to be legally bound. Contemporary commercial practice instead implies that this suggestion would be an inefficient default rule because most commercial promisors would probably contract around it.
Part IV examines the recent growth of a requirement of enforcement reliance in three commercial contexts in which courts appear to have added to the text of Section 90 a requirement that a commercial promisee show that she relied on the legal enforceability of the promise rather than the likelihood that it would be performed. This trend can be seen in the persistent refusal to enforce oral promises of permanent employment; in the judicial enforcement of disclaimers designed to forestall liability under Section 90; and, in the imputation to commercial promisees of knowledge that some non-bargain promises are formally unenforceable and hence unreliable for Section 90 purposes. By requiring promisees to demonstrate enforcement reliance, these courts preserve a role for the unenforceable commercial promise and preserve promisor choice.
The new requirement that a successful claimant demonstrate a reasonable belief that the non-bargain promise he relied upon was legally enforceable when made threatens to transform Section 90 from a commercially useful rule into a meaningless paradox, akin to a Catch-22. A commercial promisee who is legally sophisticated enough to take Section 90 into account in making a reliance decision would also be expected to know that non-bargain, commercial promises are generally unenforceable. Such a promisee could never satisfy the new test, unless courts also recognize a new category of potential contract obligation. They could do this by enforcing reliance-inducing promises that are made with an expressed intention that they be legally enforceable. A promisee's reliance on that expression would constitute enforcement reliance.
The rarity of successful claims for promissory estoppel in the sample demonstrates a systematic exclusion of promissory estoppel from the commercial world.Far from causing the death of contract, Section 90has itself been virtually extinguished from much of the commercial landscape by the reactive adaptation of the bar and the bench. I contend that there is little reason to regret its demise.
