papers.node_id: 50alalrev63!!ARTICLE: The Teachings of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. and Contract Theory: An Intriguing Comparison
papers.title: ARTICLE: The Teachings of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. and Contract Theory: An Intriguing Comparison
papers.abstract:
At first glance, the speeches and writings of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. appear inapposite to or, at some cognitive level, irrelevant to the traditional law of contract. A cursory inspection of both reveals this paradox. Dr. King's goals and dreams reflect the realism and passion of the sixties' Civil Rights Movement,a phenomenon fueled by social consciousness and the proactive aftermath of the United States Supreme Court's path-breaking decision inBrown v. Board of Education.Judicial action evidenced by theBrowndecision must have influenced Dr. King's omnipresent conviction that societal norms may be altered by means of constructive engagement and deliberate action.
Dr. King's messages present a fusion of justice, hope, andmorality contrasted with the contextual realism of society's struggle with what Dr. W.E.B. DuBois termed the "color line."Realisminfused with optimism typifies Dr. King's rhetoric and plea for racial equality and harmony.His impassioned and immortal speech,I Have a Dream, constituted a striking prototype of the vehicle for his themes.Speaking from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial during the historic Civil Rights March on Washington, D.C. in 1963, Dr. King noted the feelings of hope and joy experienced by African Americans after the signing of the Emancipation Proclamation.He then contrasted this euphoria with the despair caused by racial conditions of the time. He stated:One hundred years [after the signing of the Emancipation Proclamation] the Negro still is not free; one hundred years later, the life of the Negro is still sadly crippled by the manacles of segregation and the chains of discrimination; one hundred years later, the Negro lives on a lonely island of poverty in the midst of a vast ocean of material prosperity; one hundred years later, the Negro is still languished in the corners of American society and finds himself in exile in his own land.Dr. King further underscored the erosion of hope and joy, emphasizing with vivid imagery the African American's limited access to basic American entitlements -- life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.
One hundred years [after the signing of the Emancipation Proclamation] the Negro still is not free; one hundred years later, the life of the Negro is still sadly crippled by the manacles of segregation and the chains of discrimination; one hundred years later, the Negro lives on a lonely island of poverty in the midst of a vast ocean of material prosperity; one hundred years later, the Negro is still languished in the corners of American society and finds himself in exile in his own land.
After focusing on past glory (emancipation from slavery) and the more contemporary malaise of African American disenchantment resulting from the denial of the fruits of that glory, Dr. King then advanced the lofty goal of universal inclusiveness. The "dream" portion of his speech proclaimed: "I have a dream my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by content of their character."He then dramatized this aspired universality with the plea for interracial harmony and unity in an unfathomable 1963 context: "In Alabama, with its vicious racists, with its governor having his lips dripping with the words of interposition and nullification, . . . little black boys and black girls will be able to join hands with little white boys and white girls as sisters and brothers."
Of course, Dr. King's philosophies of universality, hope, and social justice were not confined to hisI Have a Dreamspeech. Many of his other writings and speeches echoed these themes, along with an agenda of proactivism, where responsible persons would embrace and take deliberate action to reinforce hope, dignity and social justice.Before an assassin's bullet felled him on April 4, 1968,at the Lorraine Motel in Memphis, Tennessee,Dr. King authoredWhere Do We Go From Here, one of his last public addresses.This work not only emphasized this poignant charge of hope and dignity, but also expanded his message to include a more transformative agenda.Universal themes of global peace and proactive justice became cornerstone aspirations.Dr. King also tinged his aspirations with theological concepts of morality and abjectly renounced hedonistic individualism.His rallying cry became a moral commitment to alter societal circumstances that exacerbate hopelessness and despair.He augmented this plea with an optimistic call for universal justice and harmony.
Contract law, on the other hand, presents a seemingly starkcontrast to Dr. King's messages of hope and justice. Contract rules possess few semblances of passion, hope or love. Dispassionate principles that presumably provide an efficient system of transactional conduct dominate its character.On its face, the theory of contract is objective,eschewing any notion of societal inequities that girded Dr. King's beliefs.The theoretical basis for contract, and bargaining conduct in general, revolves around the notion of assentand the need for some bargained for exchange of value.The deceptive simplicity of this formula fosters a variety of transactional goals which presumably offer societal benefits.Moreover, economic principles, which offersome theoretical justification for many contract rules, further this seeming objectivity.As such, a superficial examination of contract law reveals resultant rules that function empirically, regulating seemingly objective human transactions. The morality of contract law functions more as a system of abstractions where fungible bargainers utilize "off-the-rack" rules to form binding agreements.Justice, as a tacit force, results from strict adherence to stark rules of bargain formation.
Yet, the objectivity and abstraction fostered by the principles of contractual theory have an illusory quality when viewed in terms of actual human contexts.Because bargainers are affected and influenced by environmental and societal stimuli, their resultant conduct may not conform to the egalitarian goals of contractual rules. Indeed, the very act of bargain formation, i.e., discreet individuals searching out bargains to maximize thegain,represents an interpersonal dynamic that automatically implicates subjective notions such as judgment, information processes, bias, opportunism, and discretion.
This latter, more contextual view of contract theory forms the theoretical bridge between Dr. King's beliefs and teachings and the practical law of contract. Dr. King's humanistic desire for universality, hope and love, interpreted within the contextual realities of pejorative human behavior, such as prejudices, discrimination, and bias, illustrates a theoretical weakness of contract law. Even his accommodations in the segregated Lorraine Motel during the eve of his assassination in 1968 provide a contextual link between his message of universality and positive change and bargaining theory.The problems of bias, prejudice, and reduced acumen due to circumstance, all of which prompted Dr. King and many others to champion the courses of the disenfranchised,canallegorically reveal fallacies within the bargaining context. More critically, these problems expose the inability of contract rules, and the decision makers who interpret and apply those rules, to correct those fallacies. This reality of bargaining behavior shatters contract law's illusion of objectivity. It also commensurately prompts discussion of methods to cure the transitional ills resulting from those problems.
To some extent, contract law has progressed to allow certain defenses to compensate for these transactional ills when bargaining positions are disparate and contractual terms are unfair,as well as when individuals are unduly forced into agreementsor are improperly encouraged to enter into certain deals.The law of contract also provides remedies for those who suffered some cognitive impairment at the time they entered the bargain.However, these correctional tools remain elusive, and only scratch the surface of transactional problems related to greed, prejudice and other forms of negative opportunism. These problems alter bargaining judgment and marginalize disadvantaged bargainers.
My aim in this Article is to utilize the theoretical teachings of Dr. King to underscore the need for a more realistic and contextual application of contract rules. The principal term here is realism-- where theoretical constructs of bargaining relationshipsare deconstructed to allow for more proactive measures to counter pejorative conduct. This exercise is not intended to dismantle the rules of contract. Rules are fundamentally required mechanisms within any transactional enterprise.But contextual realities demonstrate a need to construe and apply contract rules more flexibly, thereby allowing decision makers to take into account such transactional ills as bias, opportunism, and prejudice.
The allegorical use of Dr. King's teachings, which portray the contextual realities of human dynamics, can emphasize the need to take a more expansive, less rigid view of contractual rules. Contextual realities, if employed by both judicial and legislative decision makers, can support remedial efforts that counteract the effects of biased bargaining behavior. This, too, may lend further support to the now recognized defensive tools of unconscionability, duress, undue influence, and capacity.
Part II of this Article utilizes jurisprudential constructs to form an analytical bridge between Dr. King's teachings and contract law. Finally, Dr. King's embrace of natural law will be examined through an analysis of his critical speeches and writings. This examination will be contrasted with the theoretical basis of contractual rules which demonstrate more positivist characteristics. The underpinnings of traditional, classical contractual theory include bargaining autonomy. This policy will be contrasted with the pleas for justice and equality espoused by Dr. King, who does not necessarily reject autonomy outright, but acknowledges its limitations.
Part II will also highlight the failings of rigid, classical contract theory as an idealistic mechanism. In its unabashed and unchecked form, classical contract theory fails to maintain the overall transactional goal of efficiency and marketplace integrity. This, then, provides an appropriate transition into themotivational and perceptual factors which can dictate and influence bargaining conduct. Modern contractual theory fails to overtly recognize the influence of cognitive processes, i.e., motivation, bias, or prejudice, that drive bargaining behavior. But an appreciation of these influences, and the need to neutralize their effects, will provide a foundational parallel between the law of contract and the basic constructs of Dr. King's teachings. They also serve to underscore the need for transactional remedy.
After establishing bargain motivation as a transactional variable, Part III of this Article will then use Dr. King's theories to buttress the need for a more flexible approach to the application of contract rules to transactions colored by bias or opportunism. The Article will debunk the belief that Dr. King's teachings were primarily tenets of natural law. An examination of the full dynamic of his writings reveals a more contextual ideology, one defined more by events of the time. Dr. King's teachings are defined more by circumstance than by abstractions. Despite the more superficial contentions that Dr. King called for judgment by character rather than color, the true essence of his teachings present a more complex agenda that embraced a proactive approach to the resolution of inequity and provision of justice. The contextual examination of his writings illustrates Dr. King's theoretical support for a more elastic application of the rules for contractual remedies such as unconscionability, duress, undue influence, and capacity.
Hopefully, this exercise will expand the conventional applicability of Dr. King's teachings beyond the customary problems of political disenfranchisement.His messages serve as a catalyst to examine the probative value of the effectiveness of contract rules. They also enliven the debate for a less abstract dependence on contractual rules as they relate to bargaining inequities.

questions.question: Whether contract law should be interpreted and applied more flexibly to account for contextual factors (such as bias, prejudice, unequal bargaining power, and cognitive limitations) that distort bargaining and produce unjust outcomes.

Whether the emphasis on formal autonomy and objective assent in classical contract theory fails to achieve fair or efficient outcomes when parties are influenced by social inequalities and behavioral or informational biases.

Whether teachings that prioritize universality, justice, and proactive remedial action can provide a coherent normative framework for reforming contract rules to better protect disadvantaged or marginalized bargainers.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
Do existing rules on contract modification and remedies deter bad-faith modification demands or instead create incentives for opportunism and unjust enrichment?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
What doctrinal categories of threats or coercion should render agreements unenforceable, and how should courts evaluate whether the threatened party had a reasonable alternative?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?

papers.node_id: 66amjcompl31!!ARTICLE: The UNIDROIT Principles as Reference for the Interpretation of U.S. Law +http://dx.doi/org/10.1093/ajcl/avy020
papers.title: ARTICLE: The UNIDROIT Principles as Reference for the Interpretation of U.S. Law +http://dx.doi/org/10.1093/ajcl/avy020
papers.abstract:
When the first edition of the UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts (UPICC) was published in 1994, their Preamble suggested a whole array of potential uses for the non-state codification, but the use for interpretation and supplementation of domestic law was not among them.That use was added in the 2004 edition, in view of the fact that almost half of the known decisions referring to the Principles use the UPICC for this purpose.Today, this describes their most important use.The UPICC are rarely applied on their own, but they frequently are used to supplement the applicable law. This is in accordance with the main function they have acquired, namely that of a global background law.
Countries vary greatly in the extent to which they make of the UPICC for this purpose. Some countries refer to the UPICC a lot, others very rarely. The United States is in the latter category.The UPICC play a very subordinate role in its law. The number of court opinions referring to them is minuscule, as the following analysis will demonstrate. This is so even though both the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) and the Contracts Restatement were amongst the most-used references in the drafting of the UPICC.This raises the question why that is so.
This Report follows the structure of the questionnaire set out by Professors Moreno and Garro. After a brief introduction into U.S. contract law (Part I), it first discusses potential doctrinal openings for the UPICC in domestic law (Part II), following which it takes a closer look at the few decisions in which the UPICC have actually been used (Parts III and IV). In the next Part, it analyzes in more detail the potential use of select provisions of the UPICC for U.S. law (Part V). A final Part analyzes possible explanations for the limited use that is made of the UPICC in the United States (Part VI).

questions.question: To what extent and in what ways are the UNIDROIT Principles used as a reference to interpret or supplement domestic contract law in the United States?
Which provisions of the UNIDROIT Principles are most amenable to being incorporated into or influencing United States contract law?
What institutional, doctrinal, and practical factors explain the limited reliance on the UNIDROIT Principles by U.S. courts and legal actors compared with other jurisdictions?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?

Why do courts and practitioners in the United States rely relatively little on instruments like the UNIDROIT Principles compared with other jurisdictions, and what institutional factors explain that pattern?
How do systemic institutional changes (deregulation, litigation costs, ADR, transnational codes) affect contracting behavior and the relation between law and practice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

shared_topics.topic: how multiple normative sources (domestic codes/restatements vs. broader normative frameworks) interact in shaping contractual outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts positivist contractual rules with natural law and moral teachings, arguing for integrating broader normative considerations into doctrine, and Paper B traces the influence of domestic sources like the UCC and Restatement on the UPICC and analyzes how courts choose between or combine these sources when construing contracts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33sandiegolrev175!!ARTICLE: Living Without the Avoidable Consequences Doctrine in Contract Remedies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Living Without the Avoidable Consequences Doctrine in Contract Remedies

shared_topics.topic: whether general codified principles should be used to interpret, supplement, or displace specific contract doctrines (e.g., duty to mitigate/avoidable consequences)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the avoidable consequences doctrine can be understood as redundant once the expectation interest is properly applied and thus could be dispensed with as a separate rule; Paper B investigates the use of the UNIDROIT Principles as a non‑state codification to interpret or supplement domestic contract doctrines in U.S. law, including whether such transnational principles can fill or reshape gaps in existing doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: how damages and remedy calculations should net out benefits of breach and account for mitigation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a substantive theory that damages should be reduced by the value of benefits the plaintiff receives from breach (the avoidable loss offset) as part of the expectation interest; Paper B evaluates UPICC provisions (and analogous U.S. authorities like the UCC/Restatement) that govern remedies and mitigation, and considers their potential to guide U.S. courts in calculating damages.

shared_topics.topic: reconciling and harmonizing different doctrinal sources (common law doctrines, Restatement/UCC, and international principles) to produce coherent contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconciles the avoidable consequences doctrine with the expectation interest to show internal doctrinal coherence within contract remedies; Paper B analyzes the compatibility and indebtedness of the UNIDROIT Principles to the UCC and Restatement and explores the prospects and limits of harmonizing those transnational principles with U.S. contract law.

shared_topics.topic: judicial practice in applying contract principles and the risk of misapplication or underuse
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques courts' reliance on duty‑language (e.g., mitigation as a 'duty') and the resulting misapplications of the avoidable consequences doctrine; Paper B surveys the scarcity of U.S. judicial citations to the UPICC and investigates patterns and reasons for courts' limited use of those principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 66geowashlrev508!!ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of non-state/academic model rules (soft law) to interpret or supplement domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the UNIDROIT Principles (a non‑state ‘soft law’ code) are used to interpret and supplement U.S. contract law, while Paper B investigates how courts cite and apply the American Law Institute's Restatement (Second) of Contracts as an authoritative guide in domestic cases.

shared_topics.topic: whether such instruments are descriptive statements of existing law or normative proposals for reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the UPICC's role as a ‘global background law’ and questions its fit with U.S. doctrine despite drawing on U.S. sources, and Paper B emphasizes that the Restatement (Second) often states what the drafters think the law should be rather than a strict empirical account, surveying courts' reactions to that tension.

shared_topics.topic: judicial deference, legitimacy, and normative implications of treating academic or transnational instruments like binding authority
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the limited deference U.S. courts give the UPICC and analyzes reasons for that restraint, while Paper B documents widespread judicial deference to the Restatement (Second) and evaluates whether such deference is appropriate given its academic provenance.

shared_topics.topic: empirical case‑law surveys of how courts cite and adopt model rules and explanations for cross‑jurisdictional variation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conducts a structured analysis of the few U.S. decisions that reference the UPICC and probes explanations for limited uptake, and Paper B systematically reads hundreds of cases citing six Restatement sections to measure acceptance and identify patterns and causes of variation in adoption.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 83notredamelrev353!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT AS AGREEMENT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT AS AGREEMENT

shared_topics.topic: contract interpretation and the significance of parties' intent (objective vs subjective approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how the UNIDROIT Principles' interpretation rules might be used to interpret and supplement U.S. contracts (including provisions bearing on intent and meaning), while Paper B directly critiques the dominant objective approach to contract interpretation and argues for a greater role for actual mutual assent and the promisee's understanding.

shared_topics.topic: gap‑filling and the use of default or background rules to supplement domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the UPICC as a global background law frequently used to supplement gaps in domestic law, and Paper B discusses gap‑filling (and how a subjective account of formation affects when and how courts fill gaps), arguing for more coherent defaulting among doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and persuasive role of influential doctrinal sources (Restatement, UCC, and transnational instruments)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that the UPICC drew on the UCC and the Restatement and analyzes why U.S. courts nonetheless rarely cite the Principles, while Paper B engages with the Restatement (and its objective stance) as a central authoritative influence on formation and interpretation doctrine and critiques its adequacy.

shared_topics.topic: harmonization and coherence among contract doctrines (formation, interpretation, remedies, consideration)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents the UPICC as a tool of global harmonization and a means to achieve coherent background rules across jurisdictions; Paper B argues that adopting a subjective/mutual‑assent framework better harmonizes rules governing formation, interpretation, consideration, gap‑filling, and remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 66geowashlrev508!!ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: use of non‑state codifications (Restatement (Second), UPICC) as persuasive authority in interpreting and supplementing domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how the Restatement (Second) functions as a favored statement of the 'modern view' and how courts cite its provisions, while Paper B examines the UNIDROIT Principles' role as a background/global law used to interpret or supplement U.S. contract law.

shared_topics.topic: empirical analysis of judicial reception (how courts cite, adopt, or reject such instruments)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reports a case-survey of 241 decisions assessing how courts have received six innovative Restatement (Second) provisions, and Paper B surveys the (very few) U.S. opinions that refer to the UPICC and analyzes patterns of usage.

shared_topics.topic: normative question of whether and when courts should defer to academic or transnational codifications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly evaluates the propriety of judicial deference to the Restatement (Second), weighing benefits like uniformity against concerns, and Paper B considers whether and why U.S. courts should (or should not) rely on the UPICC and analyzes barriers to their adoption.

shared_topics.topic: variation in uptake across jurisdictions and sources of influence on domestic doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents widespread acceptance of select Restatement (Second) rules across U.S. courts (with few rejections), whereas Paper B highlights cross‑country variation and the notably limited uptake of the UPICC in the United States despite substantive borrowing from instruments like the UCC and the Restatement.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81neblrev839!!ARTICLE: Why Expectation Damages for Breach of Contract Must Be the Norm: A Refutation of the Fuller and Perdue "Three Interests" Thesis
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Why Expectation Damages for Breach of Contract Must Be the Norm: A Refutation of the Fuller and Perdue "Three Interests" Thesis

shared_topics.topic: the role and authority of restatements and non‑state codifications in U.S. contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the UNIDROIT Principles as a non‑state codification and its (limited) use to interpret and supplement U.S. law, explicitly comparing them to the UCC and the Contracts Restatement; Paper B engages the Restatement (Second) of Contracts (and Fuller & Perdue’s incorporation thereof) as an influential secondary authority in the debate over the proper measure of contract damages.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between scholarly/proposed norms and actual judicial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents that U.S. courts rarely invoke the UPICC despite their drafting ties to U.S. authorities, and explores explanations for that limited uptake; Paper B shows that despite extensive scholarly debate (and Restatement language echoing Fuller & Perdue) courts continue to apply expectation damages almost exclusively.

shared_topics.topic: normative and institutional justifications for adopting particular contractual doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether select UPICC provisions are suitable for application in the U.S. legal system and considers doctrinal openings and policy reasons for or against their use; Paper B offers an institutional, normative defense of expectation damages by showing how that measure serves the needs of principal market institutions better than alternatives.

shared_topics.topic: the function of supplementary rules or measures to fill interpretive and remedial gaps in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the UPICC primarily as a ‘global background law’ used to supplement and interpret domestic contracts law where gaps or ambiguities exist; Paper B addresses how different damage measures (expectation, reliance, restitution) operate as remedial tools and critiques proposals for flexible application, thereby engaging with how courts should fill remedial gaps.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38flastulrev709!!ARTICLE: SEPARATING CONTRACT AND PROMISE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SEPARATING CONTRACT AND PROMISE

shared_topics.topic: whether contractual obligations should be understood as promises (moral commitments) versus legal constructs
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes the claim that contracts are a species of promise and teases apart moral features of private promises from legal contractual obligations; Paper B engages the same underlying question indirectly by examining whether courts and commentators import promissory norms (via instruments like the UPICC) when interpreting and supplementing domestic contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of non-state or extra‑doctrinal principles in interpreting and supplementing domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how contract law is saturated with the language and norms of promise (an extra‑legal moral discourse), while Paper B studies the concrete use of a non‑state codification (the UNIDROIT Principles) as a background or supplementary source for interpreting U.S. contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between moral/voluntary obligations and legally enforceable duties, and its implications for party autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the voluntary character of private promises with the often non‑voluntary character of contractual promises; Paper B addresses how adopting or rejecting external principles (like those in the UPICC) can change the normative content of enforceable duties and thus affect parties' autonomy and expectations.

shared_topics.topic: the interpretive influence of doctrinal sources (Restatement, UCC, promise discourse) on shaping contract norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how U.S. contract law represents contracts in promissory terms and relies on that discourse to define obligations, while Paper B analyzes how instruments such as the UCC, the Restatement, and the UPICC function as interpretive references that shape or fail to shape U.S. contract doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev271!!SYMPOSIUM: THE REVOCATION OF OFFERS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE REVOCATION OF OFFERS

shared_topics.topic: rules governing contract formation (offer and acceptance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B gives an in-depth normative and doctrinal analysis of offer-and-acceptance doctrine, including when an offer creates and when a power of acceptance is terminated; Paper A examines whether and how the UNIDROIT Principles' provisions (including those governing formation) can be used to interpret or supplement U.S. contract-formation rules.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of alternative doctrinal sources on domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the UNIDROIT Principles as a non‑state, transnational source that can function as a global background law for domestic contracts, while Paper B traces how historical and doctrinal shifts (classical to modern doctrines) have reshaped the sources and content of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: normative evaluation of what contract rules should be
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly argues about how the law governing offers, revocations, and termination of acceptance ought to be structured, and Paper A engages normatively by assessing whether UPICC provisions should be adopted or relied upon to improve or supplement existing U.S. contract doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1991wislrev247!!ARTICLE: THE RELIANCE INTEREST AND THE WORLD OUTSIDE THE LAW SCHOOLS' DOORS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE RELIANCE INTEREST AND THE WORLD OUTSIDE THE LAW SCHOOLS' DOORS.

shared_topics.topic: use of non-state or extra‑judicial authorities (international principles, restatements, scholarship) to interpret and supplement U.S. contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the UNIDROIT Principles (a non‑state, transnational code) can be and have been used to interpret or supplement domestic U.S. contract law, while Paper B treats Fuller's influential law‑review argument as an extra‑judicial source that shaped doctrinal understandings (expectation/reliance) and legal teaching, i.e., both examine the role of non‑court authorities in forming contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: assessment of doctrinal influence on U.S. case law and reasons for limited judicial uptake
shared_topics.justification: Paper A empirically and doctrinally investigates the very limited number of U.S. court decisions that cite the UPICC and proposes explanations for that limited use; Paper B similarly asks what concrete impact Fuller's 'Reliance Interest' article has had on cases over decades and offers reasons and concerns about its reception in practice.

shared_topics.topic: how legal culture and dissemination make particular contract concepts salient (diffusion of doctrinal ideas across communities)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses variation across countries in referring to the UPICC and characterizes the Principles as a potential ‘global background law’ whose uptake depends on legal culture, while Paper B reflects on 'legal sensibility' and how Fuller's framing made the reliance/expectation concepts salient to scholars, teachers, and judges, i.e., both focus on the processes by which contractual ideas disseminate and gain traction.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41loyuchilj175!!Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power

shared_topics.topic: interaction between competing contract law frameworks and the persistence of older doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how modern contract law retained the classical core of contract formation (mutual assent), arguing that this persistence undermines modern reforms; Paper B examines how a supranational, non‑state framework (the UNIDROIT Principles) seeks to function as a background or supplementary law to domestic contract regimes and why U.S. law has been resistant to that external influence.

shared_topics.topic: whether supplemental doctrines or instruments meaningfully remedy gaps or unfairness in domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates expanded policing doctrines (unconscionability, economic duress, misrepresentation) and concludes they fail to correct coercion because formation rules remain intact; Paper B investigates which UPICC provisions might fill doctrinal openings in U.S. law and why the Principles have had limited success as a tool to address perceived shortcomings in domestic contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: the role of interpretive and supplementary sources in shaping contract enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats policing doctrines as doctrinal tools courts use to interpret and potentially void contracts alleged to be procured by coercion, while Paper B studies the UPICC's use by courts and commentators as an interpretive/supplementary source to influence how domestic contract disputes are decided.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONFRONTING ADR AGREEMENTS' CONTRACT/NO-CONTRACT CONUNDRUM WITH GOOD FAITH

shared_topics.topic: gap-filling and supplementation of incomplete or 'middle-position' contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes 'contracts to bargain' and ADR agreements as middle-position contracts that leave gaps and therefore require courts to fashion duties and remedies beyond rigid formalist rules; Paper B examines the UNIDROIT Principles as a tool for interpreting and supplementing domestic contract law where national rules are incomplete, treating the Principles as a global background law for gap-filling.

shared_topics.topic: use of nontraditional or transnational sources/principles to guide contract interpretation and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A urges courts to refresh common‑law contractual analysis and employ remedial tools (beyond strict formalism) to enforce ADR agreements in context; Paper B explores the UPICC as an extrastate, non‑binding source that U.S. courts could (but rarely do) use to interpret, supplement, or inform domestic contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: judicial receptiveness and limits on courts when applying supplemental norms to domestic contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents courts' failures or misapplications (e.g., treating nonbinding ADR as binding arbitration) and their tendency to collapse difficult questions into yes/no contract determinations; Paper B documents the very limited use of the UPICC by U.S. courts and analyzes doctrinal openings and reasons why courts have been reluctant to rely on such supplemental principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68iowalrev699!!ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of contract modifications and the limits of the preexisting-duty rule
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on when courts should enforce post‑contract modifications (distinguishing fair adjustments for unforeseen circumstances from extorted demands to withhold preexisting performance), and Paper B evaluates whether provisions in the UPICC (and related transnational provisions) could be used to interpret U.S. law on when modifications are binding, thus engaging the same substantive question about criteria for enforcing changes to contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the use of non‑binding normative sources (Restatements, UPICC) to supplement or interpret domestic contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A appeals to the Restatement (Second) of Contracts as reflecting and shaping exceptions to rigid doctrines like the preexisting‑duty rule, while Paper B studies the UPICC’s role as a background or supplementary law and asks how and when courts and commentators use such non‑statutory instruments to fill gaps or guide interpretation in U.S. contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and doctrinal evolution in balancing certainty (predictable enforcement) against flexibility (equitable adjustment)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how judges and courts have modified traditional contract rules to accommodate real‑world needs (preventing extortion yet allowing fair modification), and Paper B analyzes judicial practice in the U.S. — including the limited judicial uptake of the UPICC — as an instance of how courts selectively adopt or resist doctrinal change to reconcile predictability with commercial practicality.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39arizstlj135!!ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTIVE HAIKU AND THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: Raintree County Memorial Library Occasional Paper No. 3
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSTRUCTIVE HAIKU AND THE LAW OF CONTRACTS: Raintree County Memorial Library Occasional Paper No. 3

shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates the UNIDROIT Principles (a non‑state codification) as a source courts and practitioners might use to interpret and fill gaps in U.S. contract law and explains their limited uptake; Paper B treats anonymous poems as an extra‑legal interpretive medium that illuminates contract doctrines, treating literary materials as tools for understanding legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: methods for explicating and teaching contract doctrine beyond traditional casebooks and opinions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages in doctrinal analysis of how UPICC provisions could be read into U.S. law and surveys decisions that reference those provisions as a mode of legal exposition; Paper B organizes and captions contract‑law themed poems and offers interpretive glosses, using poetic form as a pedagogical/interpretive device to convey doctrinal meaning.

shared_topics.topic: the role of background principles and legal fictions (e.g., 'constructive' doctrines) in shaping contract rules and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes the UPICC functioning as a ‘global background law’ that supplements domestic rules and supplies doctrinal content where gaps exist; Paper B explicitly reflects on ‘‘constructive’’ concepts (constructive trust, possession, service) as legal fictions that adjust existing conceptual structures and thereby shape how contract remedies and obligations are understood.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48sclrev293!!ARTICLE: The Counterpoise of Contracts: The Reasonable Person Standard and the Subjectivity of Judgment
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Counterpoise of Contracts: The Reasonable Person Standard and the Subjectivity of Judgment

shared_topics.topic: standards for interpreting contractual obligations (objective 'reasonable person' vs subjective approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally examines the reasonable person standard and the limits of subjective judgment in contract law; Paper B engages this theme by analyzing how the UNIDROIT Principles are used as interpretive tools or supplements to domestic contract rules, i.e., how courts choose and apply standards when construing contracts.

shared_topics.topic: the role of general principles or background norms in supplementing domestic contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the doctrinal/philosophical basis for invoking shared normative standards (the ‘law in us’/reasonableness) to resolve contractual disputes, while Paper B studies the UNIDROIT Principles as a concrete instance of transnational general principles serving as a background law to supplement and interpret U.S. contract law.

shared_topics.topic: judicial decision‑making and doctrinal variability in applying interpretive tools
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores the subjectivity of judicial judgment under standards like reasonableness and its effects on outcomes, and Paper B empirically and doctrinally analyzes U.S. court decisions (and the scarcity thereof) using the UPICC, highlighting variability in judicial willingness to adopt external principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 72fordhamlrev595!!ARTICLE:CORBIN AND FULLER'S CASES ON CONTRACTS (1942?): THE CASEBOOK THAT NEVER WAS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CORBIN AND FULLER'S CASES ON CONTRACTS (1942?): THE CASEBOOK THAT NEVER WAS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how a non-state instrument (the UNIDROIT Principles) and other secondary sources (noting the UCC and the Restatement were used in drafting the UPICC) operate as background or supplemental law for U.S. courts, while Paper B traces how influential secondary materials—notably planned casebooks and the Restatement—shape how contract law is taught and thereby how doctrine is understood.

shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on the pedagogical debate over whether to start Contracts with formation or remedies and the pedagogic consequences of each ordering; Paper A similarly attends to doctrinal openings and the selection/placement of UPICC provisions as potential supplements to U.S. doctrine, i.e., how choosing particular doctrinal framings or provisions affects interpretation and application.

shared_topics.topic: the role of leading scholars and their authored works in shaping U.S. contract law and pedagogy
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on the influence of prominent figures (Corbin, Fuller, Langdell) and their (planned) casebook on teaching and doctrinal emphasis, while Paper A discusses the impact of scholarly-crafted instruments (the UPICC, themselves informed by UCC and Restatement drafters) and analyzes why such scholarly products do or do not penetrate U.S. courts.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62ukanlrev315!!ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses

shared_topics.topic: the use of doctrinal frameworks to interpret and supplement contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the UNIDROIT Principles function as a background or supplementary framework to interpret and fill gaps in U.S. contract law; Paper B reframes core contract doctrines (consideration vs. assent) to show how one doctrinal framework can subsume and thereby reinterpret related doctrines in formation law.

shared_topics.topic: historical, doctrinal, and policy argumentation to justify or critique contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on comparative and doctrinal analysis (and empirical court-use data) to explain the UPICC's role and limits in U.S. law and to assess particular provisions' fit with U.S. doctrine; Paper B uses historical, doctrinal, logical, and policy reasoning to defend the primacy of consideration and critique assent-based approaches.

shared_topics.topic: explanations for doctrinal marginality or redundancy within U.S. contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates why the UPICC have seen limited uptake in U.S. courts and explores structural and doctrinal reasons for their subordinate role; Paper B argues that assent doctrines are redundant (subordinate or superfluous) given the primacy of consideration, explaining why those doctrines do not occupy an independent normative role.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev32!!SYMPOSIUM: THE TRIUMPH OF GILMORE'S THE DEATH OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE TRIUMPH OF GILMORE'S THE DEATH OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the role of extra-judicial sources (scholarship, restatements, and non‑state instruments) in shaping domestic contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how figures like Langdell, Holmes, and Williston—and scholarly accounts like Gilmore's—have constructed and reshaped the doctrine of contract, while Paper B analyzes how non‑state instruments (the UPICC) and domestic syntheses (the UCC, Restatement) function as reference sources that can supplement or influence U.S. contract law.

shared_topics.topic: judicial pragmatism/legal realism as a basis for contract interpretation and gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates Gilmore in the tradition of legal realism, arguing courts decide based on context rather than abstract rules, and Paper B shows courts and commentators using the UPICC pragmatically to interpret or supplement domestic law, illustrating a realist-style, context‑sensitive approach to adjudication.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formalistic, doctrinal constructions of contract and modernizing/transnational alternatives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the nineteenth‑century formalist 'ivory tower' conception of contract and describes its displacement, whereas Paper B examines the UPICC as a modern, transnational alternative and explores why U.S. doctrine has been resistant (or selectively receptive) to such external modernization.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 59arklrev841!!ARTICLE: Promissory Estoppel and Wagging the Dog
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Promissory Estoppel and Wagging the Dog

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the UNIDROIT Principles (a non‑state, transnational code) are used to supplement and interpret U.S. contract law; Paper B examines how courts have used the equitable doctrine of promissory estoppel to supplement, bypass, or remake traditional contract rules to reach outcomes courts view as just.

shared_topics.topic: tension between doctrinal flexibility and the need for legal certainty/predictability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers why U.S. courts have been reluctant to rely on the UPICC—including concerns about fit with established domestic doctrine and predictability—while Paper B argues that expanding promissory estoppel undermines stare decisis and predictability and calls for doctrinally coherent limits on ad hoc remedies.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates potential doctrinal openings in U.S. law and the relationship between the UPICC and domestic authorities like the UCC and Restatement; Paper B focuses on how promissory estoppel has been used to avoid or override formal rules such as the statute of frauds and the parol evidence rule and urges that such conflicts be resolved under the appropriate doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69sclrev479!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT, POWER, AND THE VALUE OF DONATIVE PROMISES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT, POWER, AND THE VALUE OF DONATIVE PROMISES

shared_topics.topic: whether non-state or supplementary principles should be used to fill gaps in U.S. contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates the UNIDROIT Principles as a non‑state 'global background law' used to interpret or supplement U.S. contract law, asking when and how UPICC provisions can fill doctrinal lacunae; Paper B argues for doctrinal supplementation—enforcing certain donative promises absent reliance—as a corrective to gaps in the current enforcement regime for gifts.

shared_topics.topic: how courts receive and apply extra‑doctrinal authorities and doctrines in deciding promise cases
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys the (few) U.S. judicial opinions that cite the UPICC and investigates judicial willingness to adopt or reference external principles; Paper B engages with judicial application of promissory estoppel and reliance requirements, considering how case law shapes which donative promises are enforceable and the practical effects of judicial doctrines.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Expectation Damages, the Objective Theory of Contracts, and the "Hairy Hand" Case: A Proposed Modification to the Effect of Two Classical Contract Law Axioms in Cases Involving Contractual Misunderstandings

shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the UNIDROIT Principles as an interpretive reference for domestic contract law, discussing how an external set of rules can guide interpretation; Paper B directly critiques the objective theory of contract interpretation and argues for recognizing parties' differing subjective meanings in cases of misunderstanding.

shared_topics.topic: modifying or creating exceptions to classical contract doctrines

papers.node_id: 85califlrev821!!ARTICLE: The World of Contract and the World of Gift
papers.title: ARTICLE: The World of Contract and the World of Gift
papers.abstract:
Under the donative-promise principle, a simple, unrelied-upon donative promise is unenforceable. In the past, this principle has been explained largely on the ground that a rule under which such promises were enforceable would involve significant process problems. In this Article, Professor Eisenberg develops two substantive bases for the donative-promise principle: (1) The world of gift would be impoverished if simple donative promises that are based on affective considerations, such as love or friendship, were folded into the hard-headed world of contract. (2) Where a donative promise is based on affective considerations, in the absence of reliance a donative promisee is morally obliged to release a repenting promisor. In the course of the Article, Professor Eisenberg shows why the principles that govern donative promises play a key role in both contract doctrine and the social significance of contract doctrine. For example, developments in the area of donative promises have been instrumental in leading to a new principle of contract remedies, under which the extent to which a promise is enforceable depends on the reason why the promise is enforceable. Professor Eisenberg also considers the major theses that have been put forward in recent commentary on donative promises, including claims that under present law all seriously made promises are enforceable by expectation damages.
An important general principle of contract law is that a donative promise - a promise to make a gift - is not legally enforceable simplybecause it is a promise, although certain kinds of donative promises are enforceable under special principles, like reliance. I will call a donative promise that does not fall within one of these special principles a simple donative promise, and I will call the general principle that a simple donative promise is unenforceable the donative-promise principle. This principle applies no matter how well-evidenced the promise is and no matter how serious the promisor was. Three well-known cases, Dougherty v. Salt,Fischer v. Union Trust Co.,and Schnell v. Nell,illustrate this point.
In Dougherty, Tillie signed a blank promissory note under which she promised to pay $ 3,000, at her death or before, to her eight-year-old nephew Charley "for "value received.'"Tillie handed the note to Charley with the words, "You have always done for me, and I have signed this note for you. Now, do not lose it. Some day it will be valuable."Tillie died with the note still unpaid, and Charley brought suit against her estate. The New York Court of Appeals, in an opinion by Judge Cardozo, held that although Tillie's promise was in writing and recited that value had been received, it was "the voluntary and unenforceable promise of an executory gift."
In Fischer, a father gave his daughter, as a Christmas present, a deed to certain property and also agreed to pay two mortgages on the property totaling $ 8,000.The daughter then handed a dollar to her father. The father died without paying off one of the mortgages. The mortgage was foreclosed for nonpayment, and the daughter sued her father's estate for breach of the promise to pay the mortgage. The Michigan court held that the transfer of the property was a completed and therefore effective gift, but the promise to pay the mortgages was donative and therefore unenforceable despite the written form of the promise and the symbolic delivery of the dollar.
In Schnell, Schnell's wife devised $ 200 each to three legatees, but died without assets.Schnell promised to pay the legatees the amounts that his wife had devised and signed a formal contract which recited that his promise was given "in consideration of one cent" paid by the promisees.The Indiana court held that Schnell's promise was unenforceable even though it was in writing and cast in the form of a bargain: "The consideration of one cent is, plainly, in this case, merely nominal," that is, bargained for in name only, not in reality, and the promise "was simply one to make a gift."
In the past, the major reason given for the donative-promise principle has been that significant process problems would result if simple donative promises were enforceable - for example, it would be very easy falsely to convince a jury that such a promise had been made - and that the substantive reasons for enforcing simple donative promises were too weak to outweigh those process problems.In this Article, I will show that there are also two strong substantive reasons for the donative-promise principle: first, that the world of gift would be impoverished if simple donative promises were placed into the world of contract, and second, that in the absence of special circumstances, like reliance, where a donative promise is based on affective considerations, normally the promisee is morally obliged to release a repenting promisor.
I begin by defining the terms that I will use, starting with the term world of contract. The law often defines contract to mean any legally enforceable promise.The social meaning of contract, however, carries the more restricted connotation of a commercial agreement. I will use the term world of contract in the narrower social sense.
The term world of gift also presents a definitional problem, although of a different sort. I will use gift to mean a voluntary transfer that is made, or at least purports to be made, for affective reasons like love, affection, friendship, comradeship, or gratitude, or to satisfy moral duties or aspirations like benevolence or generosity, and which is not expressly conditioned on a reciprocal exchange.I will use the termworld of gift to include both gifts and promises to make gifts. This departs somewhat from legal usage, because the common law draws exceptionally sharp distinctions between gifts and promises to make gifts: Gifts are irrevocable; promises to make gifts are unenforceable. Gifts are part of property law; promises to make gifts are part of contract law. I will use the term world of gift in a more inclusive way, to include both gifts and promises to make gifts, not because there are no meaningful distinctions between the two, but because the manner in which the law should treat promises to make gifts is intimately related to the nature of gifts themselves.
I next consider the term donative promise. It is useful to distinguish this term from the closely related term gratuitous promise. The latter term is sometimes used to include not only donative promises, but all nonreciprocal promises - even promises that lie in the hard-headed world of contract, like promises to hold an offer open for a fixed periodof time or nonreciprocal promises to modify a contract. Following this usage, I will use gratuitous promise inclusively to mean all nonreciprocal or apparently nonreciprocal promises, and donative promise more restrictively to mean promises in the world of gift.
Another point of terminology concerns legal discourse. The rules of the common law are based on two kinds of propositions: doctrinal and social. By doctrinal propositions, I mean propositions that purport to state legal rules and that are found in or easily derived from textual sources generally accepted as valid sources of doctrine, such as statutes, precedents, and legal commentaries. By social propositions, I mean all propositions concerning the world other than doctrinal propositions - in particular, propositions of morality, policy, and experience. In the short run, a given doctrinal proposition may be justified by reference to other doctrinal propositions. In the long run, however, only social propositions can justify legal rules; that is, in the long run, a legal rule can only be justified on the ground that, after giving appropriate weight to all applicable social propositions and making appropriate choices or accommodations where social propositions conflict, the rule is, on balance, better than competing rules.
The structure of this Article is as follows: I begin in Part I by briefly sketching three waves of American scholarship on donative promises. Part II then considers the doctrinal significance of donative promises and the social significance of donative-promise doctrine. Part III concerns the world of gift, and more particularly the nature of gifts and the differences between gift and bargain in our society. Part IV builds on Part III by developing moral reasons, relating to the nature of the world of gift, why simple donative promises should be unenforceable, and also shows why these reasons are consistent with the rules under which special kinds of donative promises, like those that have been relied upon, are enforceable. Finally, Part V examines the position taken in some recent commentary that simple donative promises are enforceable under current law if seriously made.

questions.question: Whether simple promises to make gifts should be legally enforceable in the absence of reliance or other special circumstances.

Whether making such promises legally enforceable would undermine the social and moral practice of gift-giving (i.e., whether folding affect-based promises into enforceable contract law would impoverish the world of gift).
Whether a promisee's moral obligation to release a repenting promisor provides a substantive justification for leaving affect-based donative promises unenforceable.

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Should the law treat commercial promises differently from gratuitous gifts when deciding enforceability, and what criteria should govern that distinction?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
How should the law characterize and enforce charitable pledges and naming-rights transactions: as enforceable contracts, as gifts, or via a special doctrinal category?
Does treating naming-rights, charitable donations, or licensing transactions as contracts rather than gifts or property promote better outcomes for donors, charities, or collaborative communities?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 90tullrevonline1!!ARTICLE: Third-Party Beneficiaries and the Nature of Contract
papers.title: ARTICLE: Third-Party Beneficiaries and the Nature of Contract
papers.abstract:
What is a contract? As Arthur Corbin pointed out, there are at least two different things this question might mean.The first is entirely familiar: we might be asking, How is a contract created? Here, at least the beginning of an answer would be supplied by the doctrines of contract formation, especially the offer and acceptanceand consideration doctrines. The second thing the question might mean, by contrast, is somewhat more obscure. This is in part because no particular legal doctrine is devoted to supplying an answer. The second thing we might be asking is, What does the formation of a contract bring about? Once the parties have satisfied the requirements of contract formation, what kind of obligation do they now owe each other that they did not owe before?
It is natural to think that contract formation must bring about some kind of new obligation, because the law treats parties who have formed a contract differently from persons who have not. For example, a contracting party's behavior may be condemned as a "breach," and she may be ordered to "remedy" that breach by paying money or performing a specific action. One way to explain the special treatment of contracting parties would be to connect this treatment to a distinctive kind of obligation that contract formation creates.The character of the obligation might be revealed by, for example, the rules of contractual remedies, because the remedies are designed to vindicate the obligation or repair its breach. In this sort of way, various doctrines of contract law, though they do not directly define what the parties owe each other, might supply circumstantial evidence.
Nicolas Cornell's brilliant article,The Puzzle of the Beneficiary's Bargain, uncovers some new evidence of this sort.Cornell notices that the law's treatment of third-party beneficiaries, when considered alongside some other commonplace features of contract law, gives rise to a puzzle. This puzzle is a variation on a much older one that troubled the great contract scholars of the last century. To resolve Cornell's puzzle, we may have to revise our understanding of contractual obligation. Indeed, if Cornell is correct, the required revision is radical: we must abandon the notion that a contract confers a right to contractual performance.
This Response begins by briefly recapitulating Cornell's puzzle and outlining his proposed solution. Because the solution is radical, we may be forgiven for having doubts about it. The Response outlines a few such doubts before suggesting an alternative, less radical, solution. Rather than abandoning the notion of a right to performance in contract law, we should attend to Corbin's distinction between thecharacter of an extant obligation and the way in which an obligation is created.

questions.question: Does the formation of a contract create a legal right to the other party's promised performance?
Does the law's treatment of third-party beneficiaries imply that contractual obligations are rights to performance or should be understood as a different kind of obligation?

matched_themes: When should a non-party be permitted to enforce a contract (third-party beneficiaries and non-party recovery)?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SNAPCHAT'S GIFT: EQUITY CULTURE IN HIGH-TECH FIRMS

shared_topics.topic: the legal nature of entitlements created by legal instruments (contracts vs. shares)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates what kind of obligation contract formation actually creates (e.g., whether it confers a right to performance), while Paper B examines what rights and expectations are created by issuance of equity (especially nonvoting shares), asking whether share ownership really confers the usual ownership claims.

shared_topics.topic: the role of social and cultural context in shaping legal expectations of rights and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes Corbin's distinction about the character of obligations and how doctrines reveal what parties owe each other, and Paper B draws on Mauss to argue that investor behavior and the meaning of shareholding are embedded in an 'equity culture' rather than reducible to individualistic legal entitlements.

shared_topics.topic: using anomalous or difficult doctrinal cases to reassess foundational legal theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the puzzle posed by third-party beneficiary rules to challenge prevailing accounts of contractual obligation, while Paper B uses the Snap IPO and the rise of nonvoting shares as a provocative case that calls into question foundational assumptions in corporate finance and corporate law.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy of legal and market mechanisms to vindicate or enforce claimed rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on contractual remedies and whether they reveal a right to performance, and Paper B analyzes how corporate law, indices, and the market for corporate control may fail to ensure returns or governance rights for certain shareholders, interrogating how entitlements are actually protected in practice.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Disclosure in Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: the nature of the obligations that contract formation creates

shared_topics.topic: inferring or shaping contractual obligations from doctrinal rules and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that doctrines of remedies and breach can reveal the character of contractual obligations, and Paper B frames a disclosure rule whose design and exceptions are justified by policy tradeoffs (and would determine when nondisclosure is actionable), thereby using doctrinal rules to define or enforce underlying obligations.

shared_topics.topic: normative principles for reforming or structuring contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates and proposes alternatives to radical revisions of the concept of contractual rights and obligations, while Paper B advances a general Disclosure Principle and multi‑stranded rule that normatively structures when disclosure duties should be required.

shared_topics.topic: delineating the scope of duties and their exceptions across classes of cases
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores limits and qualifications to sweeping theoretical claims about contractual rights (proposing less radical, more finely drawn accounts), and Paper B develops detailed strands and exceptions specifying the classes of transactions and relationships in which a disclosure duty should or should not apply.

shared_topics.topic: reconciling theoretical accounts of contract with actual judicial practice and doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses an empirical study to challenge a scholarly 'new consensus' about how courts apply promissory estoppel, while Paper B critiques a radical theoretical proposal about beneficiaries and urges attention to doctrinal detail and how doctrines are actually applied to resolve puzzles.
