compared_to.partner_node_id: 33emorylj41!!ARTICLE: MISTAKE AND ERROR IN THE LAW OF CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MISTAKE AND ERROR IN THE LAW OF CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the conceptual nature of contractual obligation (what forming a contract creates)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines what obligations should be enforced when agreements were entered into by mistake and whether enforcement creates morally just duties, while Paper B directly asks what kind of new obligation formation brings about and whether contract law should be understood as conferring a right to performance.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tension between enforcing bargains for stability and relieving unfair bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract-mistake doctrines as balancing stability of bargains against fairness seen with hindsight, and Paper B grapples with whether doctrines (e.g., third-party beneficiary rules and remedies) should be read to prioritize enforcement of agreed expectations or to allow other corrective considerations.

shared_topics.topic: the role and interpretation of remedies/relief in defining contractual rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when relief (rescission or other relief) is appropriate for mistakes, and Paper B treats contractual remedies as evidence of the character of the underlying obligation, using remedial rules to interrogate what rights contracts actually create.

shared_topics.topic: using doctrinal analysis to find a rational, predictable basis for foundational contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares American, English, and French doctrines to seek a rational and predictable basis for mistake cases, and Paper B analyzes third-party beneficiary and related doctrines to resolve puzzles about the nature of contract and to propose principled understandings.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50ucdavislrev405!!ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract

shared_topics.topic: the nature of the obligation created by forming an agreement/contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks what kind of new obligation contract formation brings about (e.g., whether it creates a right to performance), and Paper B argues that an agreement (in conspiracy) should be understood as creating mutual obligations via an exchange of promises.

shared_topics.topic: whether promises or a 'meeting of the minds' are the operative element of 'agreement'
shared_topics.justification: Paper A revisits Corbinian distinctions about how obligations are characterized once a contract is formed, and Paper B directly debates whether 'agreement' in conspiracy law must be an exchange of promises or can be satisfied by looser notions like mere concurrence of views.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal vagueness about the term 'agreement'/'contract' and the need for clearer standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights that no single doctrine defines what contractual formation brings about and treats various doctrines as circumstantial evidence, while Paper B documents courts' conflicting and diluted definitions of 'agreement' and proposes a clearer promise-based standard to reduce uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: using contract-law concepts as analytic tools to shape or justify other legal doctrines and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reads doctrines such as remedies and third-party beneficiary rules to infer the character of contractual obligation, and Paper B imports contract concepts (exchange of promises, seriousness of intent) to justify treating conspiracy agreements as punishable acts and to inform evidentiary and constitutional limits.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75califlrev1969!!ARTICLE: Squaring Undisclosed Agency Law with Contract Theory.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Squaring Undisclosed Agency Law with Contract Theory.

shared_topics.topic: the nature of the obligation created by contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Both papers ask what kind of legal duty a contract actually creates — Paper A applies consent and entitlement theories to explain the obligations implicated by undisclosed-agency transactions, while Paper B interrogates whether formation creates a distinctive right (such as a right to performance) and uses remedial doctrines as evidence of that obligation's character.

shared_topics.topic: the role of promise-based (assumpsit) theories versus consent/entitlement accounts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies the historical doctrine of assumpsit and promise-based contract theory as the source of doctrinal tension in undisclosed agency and promotes consent/entitlement explanations, while Paper B explicitly examines and questions the promise/right-to-performance conception of contract and considers less radical alternatives grounded in distinctions about how obligations are created.

shared_topics.topic: third-party effects and the legal relations among three actors (third-party beneficiaries/undisclosed principals)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles centrally analyze how contracts affect non-signatories: Paper A examines the legal relations among agent, third party, and undisclosed principal (including who can sue and refuse performance), and Paper B focuses on third-party beneficiaries and puzzles about what rights, if any, accrue to persons who are not contracting parties.

shared_topics.topic: using contractual theory to resolve doctrinal puzzles and apparent anomalies
shared_topics.justification: Each paper takes a perceived doctrinal puzzle (the anomaly of undisclosed-agency rules in Paper A; Cornell's beneficiary puzzle in Paper B) and seeks to resolve it by deploying or revising contract-theoretic foundations rather than treating the doctrines as merely ad hoc.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68cornelllrev617!!ARTICLE: AN ANALYSIS OF THE CESSATION OF CONTRACTUAL RELATIONS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN ANALYSIS OF THE CESSATION OF CONTRACTUAL RELATIONS.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract formation creates a distinct right to performance (the nature of contractual obligation and remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly interrogates whether a contract confers a right to contractual performance and how that conception should shape remedies, while Paper A treats enforcement vs cessation (damages versus permitting termination) as confronting the same underlying question about what obligations a contract creates and what remedies are appropriate when performance is disputed.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts in filling gaps and resolving ambiguity in contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes courts' gap‑filling function—ascertaining intent, applying implied terms and fairness norms when agreements are unclear—and Paper B likewise relies on doctrinal inferences (e.g., third‑party beneficiary rules and other contract doctrines) to determine what formation actually generates, implicating the judicial role in construing contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of contractual entitlements and rights (who may enforce, who may terminate, and who benefits)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how contracts (and courts) allocate the right to cease performance, termination clauses, and risk between parties, and Paper B investigates whether and how contractual formation creates enforceable entitlements for nonparties (third‑party beneficiaries), so both papers engage with who holds rights and remedies under a contract.

shared_topics.topic: normative limits on freedom of contract and when courts should override express agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops explicit fairness and public‑policy limits on enforcing parties' express cessation clauses, and Paper B engages the normative implications of potentially revising core doctrines (e.g., abandoning a right to performance), so both assess when doctrinal or moral considerations justify departing from literal party agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45wakeforestlrev749!!ARTICLE: DANCING AROUND GENDER: LESSONS FROM ARTHUR MURRAY ON GENDER AND CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DANCING AROUND GENDER: LESSONS FROM ARTHUR MURRAY ON GENDER AND CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the nature of contractual obligation and what formation creates
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates what contract doctrines (especially contract defenses) imply about parties' obligations and protections, asking normatively whether gender should alter those obligations; Paper B directly interrogates whether contract formation confers a right to performance and how doctrines like remedies and third‑party beneficiary rules reveal the character of the obligation created.

shared_topics.topic: who is included within the scope of contract law (parties, non‑parties, and excluded groups)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how contract law's scope historically excluded or marginalized groups (e.g., married women under coverture) and how doctrines treat subordinated actors (Arthur Murray customers), while Paper B analyzes the legal status of non‑parties (third‑party beneficiaries) to determine when and why rights arise for persons outside the immediate bargain.

shared_topics.topic: using particular doctrines/cases to reveal broader theoretical and normative commitments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses the Arthur Murray cases and contract defenses to show how doctrinal application can embody gendered and paternalistic commitments, and Paper B uses the third‑party beneficiary doctrine (and related remedial rules) as evidence to challenge or refine our theory of what contracts accomplish.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between formal doctrine and underlying values or social context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract rules have been shaped by and reflect social hierarchies and competing worldviews (e.g., efficiency vs gender‑sensitive perspectives), and Paper B treats doctrinal patterns as windows into the normative assumptions of contract law, suggesting that resolving puzzles may require revising those underlying conceptions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56galrev423!!ARTICLE: BOOM OR BUST: ENSURING THE GEORGIA STATE-WIDE BUSINESS COURT FULFILLS ITS CONSTITUTIONAL PROMISE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: BOOM OR BUST: ENSURING THE GEORGIA STATE-WIDE BUSINESS COURT FULFILLS ITS CONSTITUTIONAL PROMISE

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of complex commercial contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that complex contractual-interpretation disputes (e.g., the Turner transaction) are core drivers of business litigation and argues for a specialized court better able to resolve such issues; Paper B analyzes how contract formation creates enforceable obligations and how doctrinal understandings (e.g., third‑party beneficiary rules) shape interpretive outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between contractual obligations and available remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights high‑stakes monetary remedies in business disputes and the need for a forum that can manage extensive discovery and remedial issues; Paper B treats remedies (money, specific performance) as key evidence bearing on the nature of the obligation a contract creates and debates whether contracts confer a right to performance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of courts and doctrinal design in shaping commercial expectations and bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the GSBC's jurisdictional rules and voluntary forum structure affect predictability, negotiation behavior, and investment choices in commercial transactions; Paper B considers how different doctrinal accounts of what a contract creates (and thus what courts will enforce) influence parties' expectations and the normative design of contract law.

shared_topics.topic: critique of existing legal structures and proposals for reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the GSBC's two‑party consent rule and proposes statutory amendment to permit sua sponte transfers to the business court, while Paper B critiques prevailing conceptual accounts of contractual obligation (and considers less radical alternatives), engaging in doctrinal reform of contract theory.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92marqlrev423!!ARTICLE: A MATTER OF TRUST: SHOULD NO-RELIANCE CLAUSES BAR CLAIMS FOR FRAUDULENT INDUCEMENT OF CONTRACT?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A MATTER OF TRUST: SHOULD NO-RELIANCE CLAUSES BAR CLAIMS FOR FRAUDULENT INDUCEMENT OF CONTRACT?

shared_topics.topic: what obligations and rights contract formation actually creates (e.g., whether contracts confer a right to performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages this question indirectly by analyzing how contractual design (especially no-reliance and integration clauses) determines whether pre‑contractual tort claims can vitiate or coexist with contract obligations; Paper B takes this up directly, questioning the orthodox account of what new obligations contract formation brings about and whether it should be understood as creating a right to performance.

shared_topics.topic: the role of express contractual clauses in allocating risk and delimiting legal consequences (no-reliance, merger, and beneficiary clauses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how no-reliance and merger/integration clauses are used to allocate the risk of precontractual statements and to limit tort remedies, while Paper B examines how terms that confer benefits on third parties (or omit them) determine who acquires enforceable rights and how contractual allocation of benefits should be treated doctrinally.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between parties' autonomy/freedom of contract and background public policy or moral limits on enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally debates whether courts should honor sophisticated parties' choices to waive reliance despite moral objections to fraud, whereas Paper B raises parallel normative and doctrinal questions about whether and how the law should recognize parties' bargains (including beneficiary bargains) as creating enforceable obligations rather than importing external policy constraints.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal boundaries of enforcement — who may sue and what remedies are available under contract law (interaction between contract doctrines and tort/privity rules)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A probes how doctrines like the parol evidence rule, integration clauses, and fraud-in-the-inducement interact to permit or bar tort claims tied to a contract, and Paper B probes the boundaries of privity and third-party enforcement, exploring how contract doctrine determines who may enforce promises and obtain remedies.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36wmmarylrev1379!!ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the nature of contractual obligations and whether formation creates a right to performance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how Cardozo's and Posner's differing doctrines (e.g., substantial performance, implied covenant of good faith) reflect competing conceptions of what contracts obligate parties to do, while Paper B directly interrogates whether forming a contract creates a distinctive enforceable 'right to performance,' using the third‑party beneficiary puzzle to probe that question.

shared_topics.topic: remedies for breach (and how remedies reveal the character of contractual duties)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses doctrines such as substantial performance and their remedial consequences under different judges' frameworks, and Paper B treats rules about remedies (money damages, specific performance) as key evidence for understanding the kind of obligation contract law creates and for resolving puzzles about third‑party rights.

shared_topics.topic: the status and scope of implied obligations (particularly good faith) versus contractual freedom
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally contrasts Cardozo's willingness to recognize implied duties like an obligation of good faith with Posner's resistance grounded in freedom/efficiency, while Paper B's debate over whether to reconceive contractual obligations (and potentially abandon a right to performance) implicates whether courts should recognize or deny implied duties in resolving doctrinal puzzles.

shared_topics.topic: judicial/doctrinal method and how interpretive choices shape contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a methodological comparison of two judges' interpretive styles (Cardozo's balanced, value‑mediating reasoning vs Posner's efficiency‑centered approach) and their influence on doctrine and teaching; Paper B engages in doctrinal argumentation (responding to Cornell, invoking Corbin) about how to interpret and revise contract concepts, illustrating how theoretical and methodological choices drive doctrinal outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45wakeforestlrev607!!ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTEXT AS POWER: DEFINING THE FIELD OF BATTLE FOR ADVANTAGE IN CONTRACTUAL INTERACTIONS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly interrogates how formation, interpretation, and enforceability doctrines should be understood when contextual facts are introduced, and Paper B focuses on whether contract formation creates a distinct kind of obligation (including whether it confers a right to performance), using third‑party beneficiary doctrine as diagnostic evidence.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial interpretation and doctrinal tools in defining and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the merits and risks of courts using expansive contextual inquiry (and the discretion that entails) to interpret and enforce agreements, while Paper B analyzes how courts' remedial and interpretive doctrines (including third‑party beneficiary rules) reveal or shape the legal character of contractual obligations.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal choices reallocate rights and bargaining power among contracting parties and third parties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contextualist interpretive choices can shift bargaining power between repeat players (firms) and sporadic contractors (consumers, employees, franchisees), and Paper B shows that resolution of puzzles about third‑party beneficiaries has concrete consequences for which parties obtain enforceable rights and protections.

shared_topics.topic: whether core contract doctrines should be revised and by what institutional actors (courts vs legislatures)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions whether courts should expand contextual inquiry or leave structural shifts to legislatures, and Paper B engages the normative question whether we should reconceive foundational doctrines (e.g., abandonment of a right to performance) or adopt more modest theoretical reforms.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recent Defenses of Consideration: Commodification and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: the nature and content of the contractual obligation (e.g., whether a contract creates a right to performance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates what formation of a contract 'brings about' and whether contracts confer a distinct right to contractual performance, while Paper B engages comparable foundational questions about what kinds of promises the law should treat as creating enforceable obligations when defending or rejecting the consideration requirement.

shared_topics.topic: which promises the law should enforce and the limits of legal remedies (bargain vs donative promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses doctrines like remedies and breach to probe what obligations contracts instantiate, and Paper B debates whether donative (gratuitous) promises should be legally enforceable versus bargain promises, including the practical and moral implications of extending enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between doctrinal rules (formation, consideration) and their normative or philosophical justification
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts contract-formation doctrines with the separate question of what obligations those doctrines instantiate, while Paper B evaluates contemporary philosophical defenses (commodification, collaboration) offered to justify retaining the doctrine of consideration.

shared_topics.topic: critical assessment of recent theoretical revisions in contract theory
shared_topics.justification: Both papers respond to novel scholarly claims — Paper A critiques Nicolas Cornell's radical proposal about abandoning a right to performance and offers an alternative, and Paper B critiques innovative defenses of consideration by Eisenberg and Markovits — each weighing whether proposed revisions are persuasive and what implications they have for contract doctrine.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: using doctrinal rules as evidence of what a contract actually creates (the nature of contractual obligations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that doctrines like third‑party beneficiary rules and remedies provide circumstantial evidence about the kind of obligation contract formation creates, while Paper B studies how modern Restatement provisions (e.g., on past consideration, modification, reliance) change doctrinal rules that define parties' entitlements and obligations.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how scholarly or reformist statements should reshape substantive contract rights and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with Nicolas Cornell's scholarly proposal to reconceptualize contractual obligation (even to the point of abandoning a right to performance) and critiques it, and Paper B evaluates the Restatement (Second)'s role as a scholarly reform that has substantively altered enforceability rules and asks whether courts should accept those reforms.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial reception and deference in the evolution of contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is situated as a response in an academic debate about interpreting doctrinal practice (implicitly implicating how courts apply doctrines), and Paper B empirically analyzes and normatively assesses how courts have deferred to the Restatement (Second), showing how judicial uptake changes contract law in practice.

shared_topics.topic: when contractual obligations arise and what counts to make promises enforceable (formation versus content)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes the question of how contracts are formed from the distinct question of what obligations formation produces, and Paper B surveys Restatement rules (e.g., promissory estoppel, past consideration, modification, irrevocable offers) that explicitly alter when promises become enforceable and thus change the content of obligations that arise.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Teaching Contract Law: Introducing Students to a Critical Perspective Through Indentured Servitude and Sharecropper Contracts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that remedies (damages, specific performance) provide circumstantial evidence about the character of contractual obligations, and Paper B emphasizes historical enforcement practices (how servitude and sharecropping were enforced) to show how enforcement mechanisms determine the real-world impact of contractual arrangements.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Race Politics, O'Hare Airport Expansion, and Promissory Estoppel: The More Things Change, the More They Stay the Same

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: AN UNLIKELY RESURRECTION

papers.node_id: 92columlrev1358!!ARTICLE: THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES. Copyright © 1992 by Melvin Aron Eisenberg.
papers.title: ARTICLE: THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES. Copyright © 1992 by Melvin Aron Eisenberg.
papers.abstract:
All common law rules are or should be based on applicable social propositions -- that is, on those propositions of morality, policy, and experience that it is proper for the courts to take into account.  Accordingly, one ideal for the common law is that every rule should be the rule that would be arrived at by taking into account all applicable social propositions, and making the best choices when such propositions collide.  Call this ideal the standard of social congruence, and call a rule that meets that standard a socially congruent rule.
A second ideal for the common law is that every rule should be consistently followed.  This ideal reflects such important social values as predictability and evenhandedness.  Call this ideal the standard of doctrinal stability.
Any given rule that has been stated by a court may have been socially incongruent when adopted, or may have later become so.  In such cases, the standards of social congruence and doctrinal stability point in different directions, and some accommodation must be made between them.  In the common law, the two standards are accommodated by an institutional principle that once a rule has been stated by a court, it will be followed even if it is not themostsocially congruent rule, as long as it does not lacksubstantialsocial congruence.  Because small differences in the social congruence of competing rules are likely to be highly debatable, difficult to perceive, or both, stated rules would lose all reliability if the courts failed to apply a stated rule just because it was modestly less socially congruent than some alternative.  In such cases, the social values underlying the standard of doctrinal stability outweigh the social values underlying the standard of social congruence.  If, however, a stated rule lacks substantial social congruence, the social values underlying the standard of social congruence will outweigh the social values underlying the standard of doctrinal stability, and the rule will be overturned through overruling, inconsistently distinguishing, or radically reconstructing the precedents in which it was announced.
Because the rhetoric of judicial opinions heavily emphasizes rules that have been stated in the past, it is easy to make the mistake of believing that common law rules are relatively autonomous of social propositions.Reasoning that reflects this mistake is sometimes called formal, but might better be calleddoctrinal.In its extreme form, this type of reasoning first takes certain legal propositions as axiomatic in the sense that the propositions are regarded as self-evident, and then purports to derive other legal propositions by logical deduction from these axioms and to justify those other propositions by that derivation.  As Holmes once put it, "I sometimes tell students that the law schools pursue an inspirational combined with a logical method, that is, the postulates are taken for granted upon authority without inquiry into their worth, and then logic is used as the only tool to develop the results."
Doctrinal and axiomatic reasoning has often been particularly prominent in the law of contracts, and indeed was a central feature of classical contract law, as exemplified by the following passage from one of that school's leading texts, Langdell'sA Summary of the Law of Contracts:
[An] acceptance . . . must be communicated to the original offerer, and until such communication the contract is not made. . . .  It has been claimed that [in the case of contracts by mail] the purposes of substantial justice, and the interests of contracting parties as understood by themselves, will be best served by holding that the contract is complete the moment the letter of acceptance is mailed; and cases have been put to show that the contrary view would produce not only unjust but absurd results.  The true answer to this argument is, that it is irrelevant. . . .
For Langdell, then, "the purposes of substantial justice" and "the interests of the contracting parties as understood by themselves" were as irrelevant to contract law as they were to geometry.
Modern contract law is generally a much more open and supple instrument than classical contract law, but even in modern contract law certain doctrines seem to be treated as if they were autonomous, if not axiomatic.  This problem has been especially salient in the law governing third-party beneficiaries, which for a long period undervalued the rights of third parties, and was eventually turned on its head to overvalue those rights.  In this Article, I examine that body of law historically and analytically, with a view both to illustrating the history of a legal idea and to developing the principles that should govern this important area.
Nomenclature is important here.  I will use the termthird-party beneficiaryto mean a person who is not a party to a contract but who would benefit from its performance; the termpromisorto mean a person whohas made a legally enforceable promise the performance of which would benefit a third-party beneficiary; and the termpromiseeto mean the person to whom this promise is made.Finally, I will use the termcontractto mean an enforceable agreement between a promisor and a promisee the performance of which would benefit a third party, and the termcontracting partiesto refer to the promisor and the promisee, taken together.
In Part I of this Article, I examine the law of third-party beneficiaries as the history of an idea.  I show in this Part that the concept of enforceability by third parties gradually flowed forward until the rise of the school of classical contract law in the mid-eighteenth century; then ebbed under the force of doctrinal objections raised by that school; and then flowed forward once again as the force of social propositions broke through the doctrinal barriers.  In Part II, I develop the principle that should determine whether any given third-party beneficiary should be allowed to enforce a contract.  In Part III, I illustrate that principle and develop its implications by examining its application to some recurring third-party-beneficiary problems.  Finally, in Part IV, I examine the defenses that a promisor should be able to raise against a third-party beneficiary who would have power to enforce the contract in the absence of a defense.

What defenses should a promisor be able to raise to prevent enforcement of a contract by a non-party beneficiary who otherwise would have standing to sue?

Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?

papers.node_id: 28seattleulrev1!!ARTICLE: Un-Making Law: The Classical Revival in the Common Law
papers.title: ARTICLE: Un-Making Law: The Classical Revival in the Common Law
papers.abstract:
The common law -- the law of contracts, torts, and property -- is in the throes of a potentially remarkable transformation.The transformation is pervasive; many changes already have been adopted, more are in process, and still more have been proposed. If they all come to pass, the law will have experienced a once-in-a-century remaking. More precisely, we may be observing the "un-making" of law, to use Stephen Sugarman's phrase,as the principal common-law developments of the twentieth century are rolled back. In this sense, the changes are both radical and regressive, representing a classical revival, instituting in the twenty-first century common law a barely updated version of the classical law that reigned in the Gilded Age at the end of the nineteenthcentury. Even more broadly, the changes in the law and the vision that animates them are part of a more general transformation of American government and society.
This article describes the possibility of a classical revival in the common law and situates the revival in its historical context. Part I sets the stage by briefly summarizing a century and a half of common-law development. At the end of the Nineteenth Century, classical legal thought envisioned a highly systematic body of law through which courts could mechanically apply abstract legal concepts to reach determinate results, producing limited liability in contract and tort law and expansive property rights. Critics beginning with Holmes and notably including Progressives and legal realists attacked classical law as incomplete and incoherent. Their critique was absorbed into the mainstream of the law, and by the 1970s a new body of neoclassical law was dominant.
Part II describes the changes already adopted and currently proposed in contract, tort, and property law -- the un-making of neoclassical law -- and the distinctive structure and method of the classical revival. In contract law, the classical revival aims to reinstate the principle that courts should simply enforce the contracts people make, through formalistic rules of formation and interpretation, and should not impose terms or evaluate the fairness of bargains. In tort, the revival seeks to restore corrective justice based on fault as the prime objective by rolling back the generalization of liability for negligence, narrowing products liability, and reducing the scope of compensatory and punitive damages. In property, the revival focuses on expanding the law of takings to limit the ability of the government to regulate property owners in pursuit of the common good. All the individual changes fit within a broader structure in which the boundaries among contract, tort, and property are sharply defined, the market-focused subjects (contract and property) are primary, and a revived formalist method is prescribed for judicial decision.
The conclusion synthesizes the ideology of law, market, and society that animates the classical revival, and situates the common-law changes in their contemporary political context. The classical revival represents an attempt to resuscitate the long-discredited ideas of classical legal thought. This remarkable fact is best understood in this context: The unmaking of the common law is part of the effort by conservatives and business interests to elevate the market and diminish the government.

questions.question: Whether the common law is undergoing a coordinated 'classical revival' that reverses twentieth-century neoclassical developments across contract, tort, and property law.
Whether recent legal changes reflect a coherent methodological shift toward formalism that sharpens boundaries among contract, tort, and property and privileges market-oriented rules.

Whether the contemporary rollback of neoclassical doctrines is driven by an ideological project to elevate market interests and constrain government regulation (e.g., led by conservative and business actors).

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
Have doctrinal boundaries among contract, tort, and property shifted toward a formalist, market-oriented model?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal boundaries between contract, tort, and property
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with where the lines among contract, tort, and property should be drawn: Paper A describes a classical revival that sharpens those boundaries and elevates market-focused doctrines, while Paper B criticizes promissory estoppel for blurring those categories and argues disputes should be decided under the doctrine that properly reflects the governing principle (contract, tort, or estoppel).

shared_topics.topic: formalism versus discretionary, remedial-driven decisionmaking (certainty and predictability)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the debate over formalist rules versus flexible, justice-driven adjudication: Paper A advocates reinstating a formalist classical method to produce determinate results, and Paper B warns that courts have allowed remedial goals to drive doctrine ("wagging the dog") undermining certainty and insists on principled, predictable legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of courts in enforcing private agreements versus advancing policy or preventing harm
shared_topics.justification: Both examine tensions between enforcing private bargains and using common law to advance public policy or prevent harm: Paper A situates recent changes as part of a movement to prioritize market autonomy and limit judicial or regulatory intervention, while Paper B argues that courts should enforce promises when the principle is private agreement but should use tort or targeted public-policy doctrines when prevention of harm or broader policy is the concern.

shared_topics.topic: limits on doctrinal expansion and remedial reach (avoiding ad hoc exceptions to substantive rules)
shared_topics.justification: Both confront the dangers of doctrinal overreach and ad hoc remedies: Paper A chronicles rollback of twentieth-century neoclassical expansions and a push to reinstate narrower rules, and Paper B documents how promissory estoppel has been extended to evade rules like the statute of frauds or parol evidence rule and urges limiting the doctrine or reforming the underlying rules instead.

papers.node_id: 61smulrev1377!!Article: Uncertainty, Reliance, Preliminary Negotiations and the Holdup Problem
papers.title: Article: Uncertainty, Reliance, Preliminary Negotiations and the Holdup Problem
papers.abstract:
CONTRACT law enforces assent-based contracts because they improve welfare for both the parties and for society.In a world without transaction costs or frictions, parties can achieve optimal outcomes on their own.
In the real world, however, many frictions and impediments interfere with the parties achieving optimal outcomes. Uncertainties of various types impede parties as each decides whether to enter into a contract with another party.Parties lack knowledge about their counterparty, specifically about their characteristics and qualities, including their propensity to act opportunistically.That uncertainty makes it difficult to achieve a contract that expressly controls all of the possible permutations of the risk of moral hazard.
The problem of uncertainty is pervasive in all contract negotiations. Parties do not know what the probability of reaching an agreement is and if so, whether it is worth expending costs to find out and up to what point.Each potential party to a contract has a sense that the contract will improve his welfare (and the welfare of society), and each is therefore optimistic about the possibility of a bargain. But that optimism is tempered by three factors. First, each party knows that it cannot produce joint gains from trade if it gives up too much.The party is therefore uncertain about whether the other side will be asking too much to enter into the deal. Second, each party knows that the success of the collaboration depends on a variety of factors that require predictions as to the future states of the world, including market conditions (or, more broadly, conditions beyond the control of either party) and the decisions and actions of the other party.In general, uncertainty applies to one's own ability to perform, the other party's ability to perform, and states of the world that are unrelated to either party's ability to perform. Third, eachparty is uncertain about its counterparty's particular proclivity to engage in opportunistic behavior but knows that there is some potential for such opportunistic behavior in the general population, as it is a facet of human nature.The presence of certain structural factors affecting the sequence of investment may increase the potential for opportunistic behavior.
The optimism of potential opportunities from joint gains from trade is therefore tempered by the risk that a party will invest in reducing the uncertainty only to find out that a bargain is not feasible, or that a bargain that looked good (profitable) turns out to be bad (unprofitable), or that he has made himself worse off by providing the other party with information that the other party can use opportunistically.The law grapples with this latter risk in precontractual negotiation casesand, in ways that will be explored later, the risk also exists in the reliance on preliminary agreements where parties agree on a sequence of investment.
Some of these uncertainties, particularly those relating to the future, may be resolved by negotiating with another party over time, since time itself may resolve some issues.Parties also can reduce uncertainty by undertaking search costs and making expenditures to acquire information.
Parties can also use the "courtship process" and proceed incrementally to mitigate and resolve some of these uncertainties before they commit to one another.Negotiating has costs, and parties will weigh the costs of negotiating against the benefits to be derived from a deal that may or may not be reached.During this initial period of uncertainty before a contract is formed, each party must decide whether and when to makeinvestments of various kinds. If a deal is never reached, these investments may be lost forever. If a deal is reached, when and if each of the parties has invested will determine how much of the surplus is available for them to split.In turn, that prospect will affect their incentives to invest in future negotiations and contracts.
Traditionally, under the aleatory view,the law took a "knife-edge" approach to compensating for reliance investment that was most likely to occur during this period of uncertainty.That conventional approach denied any compensation for reliance without a contract but granted full enforcement to assent-based explicitly reciprocal contracts with consideration.Absent such a contract, any reliance investment was deemed non-compensable.Parties relied at their own peril in the absence of a bargained-for contract.
Following the adoption of Section 90 of the Restatement (First) of Contracts,courts adopted a more liberal approach to reliance compensation issues. They sometimes found liability when a promisee relied on the promises of a putative offeror despite the absence of a bargain in pre-contractual negotiations without the benefit of any bargained-for agreement.Hoffman v. Red Owlis the paradigm case permitting such recovery. Recently, courts have also begun to uphold reliance claims in cases where parties reached a preliminary agreement together with an agreement to invest simultaneously, one party had invested after the preliminary agreement was reached, and the other party walked away from the deal and refused to agree to a final contract.
Recently, two scholars, Alan Schwartz and Robert Scott, have cast doubt on the liberal theory of reliance recovery.They argue that courts generally deny recovery for reliance in cases involving precontractual preliminary negotiationbut grant recovery in cases involving reliancefollowing a preliminary agreement. In this latter class of cases there is an "emerging legal rule" that makes the promisor who breaches an obligation of good faith "liable for the promisee's reliance expenditures."They identify a pattern in which success is likely and then provide an analytical framework to justify liability. When parties reach a preliminary agreement that also includes an agreement that they both invest simultaneously- what I will refer to as agreements to jointly investigate or explore - and one party strategically delays investment for personal gain, the law permits the investing party to recover for reliance expenditures when the other party walks away from the deal.Courts find the party who exits the deal to be guilty of a breach of the good faith obligation that governs parties' actions in preliminary agreements.
Based on an extensive review of case law, this Article suggests that, contrary to the Schwartz and Scott thesis, courts do grant recovery for reliance expenditures made in precontractual preliminary negotiations even when the parties have not reached "an agreement."The courts' willingness to do so depends on a pattern in which the promisor solicits reliance expenditures to reduce uncertainty or to hedge his bets pending the resolution of uncertainty and the promisee relies, particularly if the reliance investment takes the form of a cooperative investment rather than a selfish investment.Neither the promisor nor the promisee would want the promisor to have what amounts to an option that he does not pay for if it would disincentivize promisees from investing and/or discourage trades.
The risk of holdup is present whenever there is sequential investment. Once one party invests a sunk cost, one of two possibilities exist: either the deal never materializes, in which case the sunk cost is lost, or the deal materializes but the non-investing party shares in the surplus.That need to share part of the surplus renders the investing party vulnerable to holdup and discourages promisees from investing.Thus, this Article suggests that courts are willing to grant recovery for reliance expenditures in both categories of cases: (1) precontractual negotiations with no agreementand (2) reliance that follows a binding preliminary agreement. In each set of cases, their willingness to do so is predicated on a framework in which courts seek to control the problem of opportunistic behavior.Presumably, both parties would want such control because the uncontrolled risk of such behavior would discourage future transactions.That framework connects the results of successful preliminary reliance negotiation cases (the Hoffman v. Red Owltype case) and the successful cases of recovery for reliance on preliminary agreements with an agreement to jointly invest, identified recently by Schwartz and Scott.Whether a court is deciding if the good faith obligation requires compensation for reliance made pursuant to a preliminary agreement for joint investment or if a liability rule for reliance in precontractual negotiations is warranted, the court is concerned with essentially the same problem of regulating the holdup problem.
Schwartz and Scott endorse enforcement of preliminary agreements with concomitant agreements to jointly investigate or explore only where the joint promise to investigate is relatively explicit.By contrast, this Article advocates a legal default rulethat would grant compensation where the promise to investigate jointly is only implicit. An implicit agreement is found where one party would not have invested unless there had been an understanding that the investing party would be compensated if the other party operated opportunistically with respect to thatinvestment or had the ability to hold up the other party based on the sequence of investment.
This Article will provide guidance for courts considering whether, when, and why reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations should be compensated through a default rule.Where one party solicits investments to reduce uncertainty or to hedge the future, and the soliciting party is aware that the other party is relying by undertaking such investment, the reliance should be compensated to prevent both the holdup problem and the consequent under-reliancethat occurs when one party solicits investments and then defers any action or contracting until the investments are made by the first party.
Paying greater attention to how courts take account of the potential for strategic behavior, holdup, and the problem of under-reliance in deciding whether, when, and why to award reliance costs would provide greater certainty to the area of precontractual reliance case law and give a more complete picture of when courts will and should find liability. Precise delineation of the stages of negotiation and agreement and the degree of vulnerability to hold up by the other party may vary, depending on the stage in which the investment is made and on whether the other party is investing simultaneously or has the discretion to defer until later on. These issues are important in resolving whether and when reliance costs should be reimbursed.
This Article proceeds as follows: Part II looks at the overall problem of uncertainty in contracting and its effects on hindering complete contracts, the effect on parties' incentives to invest in the precontractual period given the holdup problem, and the methods for mitigating uncertainty, including the solicitation of reliance investments that can facilitate opportunism. Part III examines the aleatory view of contracting, which denied all recovery for reliance investments if no bargain contract were achieved,and reexamines whether the traditional view makes sense in situations of sequential investment. Part IV details the problem of holdup that occurs when one party invests and is subject to the other party appropriating part of the surplus in such a way that the investing party cannot gain the full benefit of its investment and so engages in suboptimal investment.Part IV also examines cases in which sequentialinvestment may be a cure to strategic behavior. It discusses instances in which the sequential investment may require a legal response to curb a moral hazard problem and encourage investment, at least whether there are reasons to think that the parties would have agreed on such a liability rule were it not for a variety of obstacles to its express adoption by the parties, and where there are reasons to think that requiring parties to expressly adopt a liability rule in each case would be more costly or less effective than the alternative default rule of requiring parties to expressly opt into a liability rule. Part V links the two separate contexts in which reliance may occur: (1) following a preliminary agreement with an agreement to invest simultaneously; and (2) during early preliminary precontractual negotiations.Part V suggests that the two contexts can be linked since there is a risk of opportunism in each setting. It suggests that the analytical framework embraced by Professors Alan Schwartz and Robert Scottshould be extended to cover precontractual negotiation where the risk of holdup is also great. Part VI reexamines recent reliance case law to see if case outcomes are consistent with a rule imposing liability when the risk of holdup is great. The support for such liability refutes the thesis of Schwartz and Scott that the case law rejects recovery on reliance unless an agreement is reached.This Article finds courts willing to find liability even when there is too much uncertainty for an agreement to exist if the defendant has solicited sunk costs to hedge while uncertainty is resolved.
The real question is whether on a comparative cost basis it is a priori irrational to think that sometimes bargaining is relatively more wasteful than law-supplied terms.If so, then a law-supplied liability default rule presumption makes sense in certain sets of cases.

questions.question: Do courts compensate reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations or after preliminary agreements, and what factual patterns determine when such compensation is awarded?

Would a legal default rule that compensates reliance expenditures when one party solicits or benefits from another's sunk investments reduce holdup and under-investment and thereby improve ex ante welfare compared with requiring parties to negotiate explicit contractual protections?

Under what conditions of investment sequencing, simultaneity, and implicit understandings is it efficient to impose reliance-based liability to encourage cooperative investment and deter opportunistic behavior?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
Do existing rules on contract modification and remedies deter bad-faith modification demands or instead create incentives for opportunism and unjust enrichment?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Can default liability rules be designed to induce socially optimal precontractual reliance, and what informational burdens would such rules place on adjudicators?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Is imposing a judicially enforced duty to negotiate in good faith necessary to achieve efficient outcomes in preliminary agreements, or would protecting reliance expenditures suffice?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do market and institutional features affect whether informative 'cheap talk' will arise privately or require legal intervention to induce accurate precontractual communication?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: when detrimental reliance justifies promissory estoppel recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes case law showing courts sometimes award reliance-based recovery for expenditures made during precontractual negotiations even absent a formal bargain, while Paper B surveys the debate over the ‘death of reliance,’ presenting empirical work that finds reliance remains a necessary (but not always sufficient) element for promissory estoppel claims.

shared_topics.topic: liability for reliance in precontractual negotiations and preliminary agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on recovery when parties solicit or make investments during preliminary negotiations or pursuant to preliminary agreements (e.g., Hoffman/Red Owl and joint-investment cases), and Paper B likewise centers discussion on those canonical precontractual cases and how courts treat promises made in negotiation contexts.

shared_topics.topic: whether and how law should supply default rules to govern enforcement of promises and reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a legal default rule to compensate reliance (including implicit agreements to investigate jointly) to mitigate holdup and under-reliance, while Paper B proposes and critiques Restatement-style default presumptions (sections 71A–D and a supplement to section 90) to determine when commercial or other promises should be enforced absent explicit bargains.

shared_topics.topic: protecting parties from opportunism and the holdup problem arising from sequential investment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally analyzes the holdup problem created by sequential/sunk investments and how liability for reliance can deter opportunistic delay or appropriation of surplus, and Paper B engages with parallel concerns—explaining why enforcement doctrines (like promissory estoppel) may be needed to protect reasonable reliance and thereby encourage economic activity despite risks of opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: appropriate remedy for nonbargained promises: reliance interest versus expectation interest
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines when courts award reimbursement for reliance expenditures (as a response to precontractual investment and holdup), and Paper B explicitly debates the normative and doctrinal choice between awarding the reliance interest versus the expectation interest and when reliance damages are an appropriate measure.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that judges and drafters create contract doctrine within social contexts (gender, class, etc.) that shape outcomes, and Paper B analyzes how transactional contexts (uncertainty, sequential investment, holdup risk) lead courts to modify or supply default rules, so both examine how context drives doctrinal change.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of formalist, abstract approaches and the case for context-sensitive or corrective doctrinal responses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes formal equality and abstract formulations of contract law that obscure gendered consequences, while Paper B critiques strict formalist denials of reliance recovery and defends context-sensitive default rules to address opportunism and promote efficient contracting.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SNAPCHAT'S GIFT: EQUITY CULTURE IN HIGH-TECH FIRMS

shared_topics.topic: role of legal rules versus informal norms or cultural expectations in governing exchanges
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates when courts should supply default liability rules (or enforce good-faith obligations) to fill gaps in incomplete precontractual bargains and shape incentives; Paper B argues that 'equity culture' and gift-like social norms in Silicon Valley function as nonlegal mechanisms that structure investor expectations and substitute for, or interact with, formal corporate-law entitlements.

shared_topics.topic: asymmetry of control and surplus division after sunk investments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how the sequence of investments and asymmetric ability to delay or refuse contracting affects surplus division and leads to underinvestment absent legal protection; Paper B analyzes how dual-class or nonvoting share structures create persistent control asymmetries that alter who captures future gains and how ordinary investors are disadvantaged after their capital is committed.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: UNINTELLIGENT DESIGN IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the boundary problem between mere promises and legally enforceable promises (consent and doctrinal incoherence), and Paper B analyzes the enforceability of preliminary negotiations and agreements—distinguishing cases with no agreement from binding preliminary agreements and assessing when reliance liability is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the adequacy and limits of normative or unifying theory to explain contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that unified normative theories of contract (promise, reliance, transfer) often fail and that understanding the failure is itself informative, while Paper B demonstrates how courts develop pragmatic doctrines and default rules (e.g., reliance recovery, good faith obligations) that may diverge from tidy normative accounts to address real-world problems like uncertainty and holdup.

shared_topics.topic: the justification for law-supplied default rules versus pure party autonomy in contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions how far theory can prescribe or justify doctrinal rules versus historical or accidental developments in doctrine, and Paper B argues for and analyzes legal default liability rules (compensating reliance or protecting against holdup) where party bargaining is costly or insufficient, weighing when courts should supply terms rather than insisting on explicit private ordering.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 66smulrev341!!ARTICLE: Teaching Contract Law: Introducing Students to a Critical Perspective Through Indentured Servitude and Sharecropper Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Teaching Contract Law: Introducing Students to a Critical Perspective Through Indentured Servitude and Sharecropper Contracts

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior, exploitation, and the holdup problem
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the holdup problem arising from sequential investments and opportunistic conduct and examines how law can curb moral hazard; Paper B uses historical contracts (indenture, sharecropping) to illustrate how contractual arrangements can produce exploitation and opportunistic domination legitimized by legal enforcement.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs welfare-enhancing enforcement and law-supplied default rules against bargaining costs and private ordering inefficiencies; Paper B contrasts the standard efficiency/facilitation justification for contract law with a critical view emphasizing social dominance and the need for protective scrutiny.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a legal default rule to compensate certain precontractual reliance to prevent under-investment and holdup, highlighting circumstances where law should supply terms; Paper B examines historical instances where courts enforced harsh contractual regimes, raising the question of whether legal intervention should reform or refrain from enforcing particular private agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2002utahlrev551!!ARTICLE: Duties Under the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act: Analysis of a Statutory Conflict The author wishes to thank the Honorable Thomas L. Steffen and Professor Boyd K. Dyer for their insight and encouragement in writing this Comment.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Duties Under the Utah Revised Limited Liability Company Act: Analysis of a Statutory Conflict The author wishes to thank the Honorable Thomas L. Steffen and Professor Boyd K. Dyer for their insight and encouragement in writing this Comment.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a court-supplied default liability rule (compensating reliance) in certain precontractual settings to mitigate holdup and under-reliance, while Paper B analyzes whether the URLLCA permits LLC members to opt out of or reduce statutorily-imposed duties in operating agreements, i.e., whether duties are mandatory or defeasible by private agreement.

shared_topics.topic: legal mechanisms to prevent opportunism and holdup between contractual counterparties
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally addresses holdup risk from sequential investments and promotes liability/compensation to deter opportunistic behavior; Paper B is concerned with statutory duties (and their enforceability) among members/managers that serve to curb self‑dealing and opportunism within an LLC.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial/statutory interpretation in shaping private-ordering obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on case law analysis to show how courts have framed good‑faith and reliance doctrines in precontractual negotiations, whereas Paper B uses canons of statutory interpretation to resolve conflicting provisions in the URLLCA and determine the scope of member/manager obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the application and limits of good‑faith/fiduciary‑style standards in relational agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines courts imposing good‑faith obligations and reliance remedies in preliminary negotiations to protect investing parties, and Paper B examines statutorily defined duties (and their potential reduction) for members/managers that serve a fiduciary‑like function in governing ongoing intra‑firm relations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: reliance as the appropriate legal response to investments and expectation losses
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when courts award reliance-based recovery for investments made during precontractual negotiations or after preliminary agreements to prevent unfair appropriation of sunk costs, while Paper B argues that smart-contract transactions are best understood and remedied through a reliance (tort-like) framework rather than orthodox consent-based contract theory.

shared_topics.topic: contractual incompleteness and the need for law or design to fill gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how uncertainty and transaction costs produce incomplete precontractual bargains and proposes legal default rules to allocate risks and encourage investment, and Paper B highlights the inherent incompleteness of automated smart contracts and the lack of entry points for courts or parties, arguing for institutional or protocol-based solutions to address gaps.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic behavior, holdup risk, and sequential-investment dynamics
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the holdup problem—how sequential or solicited investments create vulnerability to opportunism—and assesses when liability should prevent under-investment, while Paper B raises analogous concerns about opportunism, enforcement gaps, and repeat-player problems in automated contracting and proposes dispute-resolution and trust architectures to mitigate strategic abuse.

shared_topics.topic: the primacy of ex post dispute resolution (versus ex ante bargaining) in solving contractual failures
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes courts’ ex post role in awarding reliance damages and imposing good-faith obligations to correct precontractual strategic behavior, whereas Paper B contends that human intervention will persist chiefly at the ex post dispute stage for smart contracts and proposes decentralized, user-based mechanisms as the appropriate forum for resolving failures.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 91washlrev1663!!ARTICLE: AN "APP" FOR THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN "APP" FOR THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES

shared_topics.topic: when obligations are enforceable by non‑parties (limits of privity and substitute doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when a person who is not a contracting party can nonetheless sue as an "intended third party beneficiary," while Paper B examines courts enforcing promises (e.g., promissory estoppel or liability for reliance) in precontractual contexts where no formal bargained‑for contract exists, so both tackle circumstances in which enforcement arises outside strict bilateral privity.

shared_topics.topic: the role of knowledge/intent/awareness in triggering liability or enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the ambiguity of "intent" in third‑party beneficiary doctrine and proposes focusing on whether contracting parties had "reason to know" a third party could be an additional plaintiff; Paper B likewise stresses the soliciting party's awareness that another will rely (implicit agreement or solicitation of investment) as a key fact justifying recovery, so both treat parties' knowledge/intent as central legal triggers.

shared_topics.topic: using legal rules to deter opportunism and mitigate the holdup problem
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the APP inquiry in terms of practical consequences for defendants and the need to account for potential strategic effects of adding plaintiffs, while Paper B directly addresses holdup and proposes default liability rules (and compensation for reliance) to prevent opportunistic behavior and under‑investment; both concern doctrinal design to curb opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: reforming or clarifying doctrinal standards to improve predictability and align law with practical consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for a new vocabulary and analytical framework to "clean up" an analytically messy third‑party beneficiary doctrine and produce more consistent, practical results; Paper B proposes default rules and a clearer analytic framework for when reliance expenditures should be compensated to give greater certainty in precontractual reliance law—both advocate doctrinal reform to reduce ambiguity and improve predictability.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84templrev119!!ARTICLE: THE MISSING ELEMENTS OF CONTRACT DAMAGES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MISSING ELEMENTS OF CONTRACT DAMAGES

shared_topics.topic: compensation for precontractual reliance expenditures (promissory estoppel vs Dempsey rule)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers grapple with when courts should reimburse expenditures made before a finalized contract: Paper A contrasts the Red Owl/promissory estoppel line (which often permits recovery) with the Dempsey rule (which bars precontract costs for open-return contracts) and argues for reversing Dempsey; Paper B surveys case law on recovery for reliance in both preliminary negotiations and preliminary agreements (Hoffman/Red Owl type cases) and explains courts' doctrinal willingness to award such reliance damages to curb opportunism.

shared_topics.topic: the holdup problem and sequential investment vulnerability
shared_topics.justification: Both works center on the risk that one party’s sunk or sequential investments create opportunities for the counterparty to opportunistically capture surplus: Paper B develops a general theory of holdup in sequential investment and how liability rules can prevent under-investment, while Paper A shows how the current Dempsey rule creates incentives for opportunistic breaches and discourages efficient precontract investments.

shared_topics.topic: the role of uncertainty in negotiation and its impact on remedies and investment incentives
shared_topics.justification: Both articles analyze how uncertainty about future performance, market conditions, or contract terms affects parties' willingness to invest during negotiations and how legal rules should respond; Paper B treats uncertainty as the central barrier that makes reliance investments risky and justifies liability defaults, and Paper A emphasizes uncertainty in measuring lost profits under open-return contracts as motivating its proposed presumptive remedy.

shared_topics.topic: design of default liability/remedies to balance under- and over-compensation and to promote efficient bargaining
shared_topics.justification: Both papers evaluate alternative remedial regimes (reliance recovery, expectancy damages, disgorgement, and law-supplied default rules) and their incentive effects: Paper A proposes a presumptive recovery of investment plus a risky return to avoid undercompensation and excess deterrence from disgorgement, while Paper B defends legal default rules that compensate reliance when holdup risk is high rather than forcing parties to contract explicitly over liability.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Remedies for Imperfect Transactions in Contracts and Torts

shared_topics.topic: Opportunistic behavior, holdup, and strategic postponement as justifications for remedial intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops the holdup problem from sequential investment and opportunistic defection as the core justification for awarding reliance expenditures; Paper B treats misrepresentation and parties' opportunistic changes of mind (imperfect transactions) as conduct that may warrant tort or contract-like remedies to address the same strategic harms.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A considers when liability for reliance should be imposed (including good-faith obligations) and focuses on compensating reliance expenditures in lieu of expectation remedies when no final contract exists; Paper B directly compares tort and contract remedies, argues both can rest on expectation interests, and shows how tort damages for misrepresentation can be computed using contract remedial principles including reliance measures.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that vague conspiracy standards produce wrongful convictions based on proximity or speech and proposes a promise-based rule to reduce uncertainty; Paper B shows how courts compensate reliance or enforce preliminary understandings to mitigate bargaining uncertainty, holdup, and disincentives to invest.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CRITIQUE OF THE PROMISE MODEL OF CONTRACT

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rules and Terms--Civil Law and Common Law

shared_topics.justification: Paper A interprets contemporary case law as courts extending reliance liability beyond formal bargains to resolve practical problems of investment and uncertainty; Paper B analyzes the historical practice of Common law judges and writers borrowing concepts, analyses, and solutions from Civil/Roman law to fill doctrinal voids and make contract law more coherent and commercially effective.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58hastingslj61!!Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Is an Advertisement an Offer? Why It Is, and Why It Matters

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: REAL ESTATE SALES AND THE NEW IMPLIED WARRANTY OF LAWFUL USE.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 66hastingslj1661!!ARTICLE: In and Out - Contract Doctrines in Action
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In and Out - Contract Doctrines in Action

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev32!!SYMPOSIUM: THE TRIUMPH OF GILMORE'S THE DEATH OF CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE TRIUMPH OF GILMORE'S THE DEATH OF CONTRACT
