papers.title: ARTICLE: When should Contract Law Supply a Liability Rule or Term?: Framing a Principle of Unification for Contracts
papers.abstract:
I. INTRODUCTION: JUSTIFYING LAW SUPPLIED RULES AND TERMS
century formalism limited contract enforcement to privately negotiated terms.The twentieth century has witnessed the expansion of several contracts doctrines, such as promissory estoppel and good faith, which have involved courts in supplying terms not expressly negotiated by the parties. The willingness of courts to intervene in incomplete contracts has increased with the recognition that it is difficult and costly for the parties to resolve all mattersex ante, particularly in long-term contracts.Somedoctrines filling in incomplete contracts take the form of immutable or mandatory law-supplied rules;others exist as default rules that supply a term unless the parties opt out of the rule.Because courts (and legislatures) have assumed the role of implying terms,the critical question of justification for such terms arises: when and whyshouldthelawsupply a term or a liability rulethat the parties have not expressly agreed to?
This issue of justification for legal interventions taking the form of a law-supplied term or liability rule is a critical one. "Contention over how lawmakers and their coadjutors--advocates and commentators--do (and should) formulate and explain rules is rarely off the boil and never at less than a rapid simmer."The expansion of judicial interventions in incomplete contracts has prompted scholars to debate the very nature of the role which courts should play in private agreements. Some scholars have viewed the doctrinal developments and the expansion of default rules as a challenge to the fundamental notion that "contractual duties are self-imposed,"since by definition law-supplied default rules are "imposing" rules on the parties and thus constitute a potential infringement on private autonomy.Others have portrayed the advent of these interventions as a reflection of an underlying (but seldom admitted to) truth: that courts have and will continue to function in ways that extend beyond the implementation of private agreements,into a domain that polices the fairness and substance of transactions by external norms.
Other scholars have viewed these doctrinal instances of judicial interventions differently and as consistent with the notion of courts acting to facilitate private agreements. Using rational choice economic analysisthey have justified various legal interventions in terms of the parties' projected intentions and overall efficiency.To implement private intentions and promote efficiency, the law should adopt the rule that most parties would have wanted absent transaction costs.This approach favors majoritarian default rules "by providing widely suitable preformulations, thus eliminating the cost (and the error) of negotiating every detail of the proposed agreement."
Two recent analysts, Professors Ayres and Gertner, have diverged from an interventionist posture and argued that in some cases the promotion of efficiency dictates that the law should decline to supply a term. When incompleteness is due to strategic nondisclosure,courts should diverge from what the parties would have wanted and instead adopt a "penalty default rule"designed to force the disclosure of information.
This Article is written in the tradition of law and economics. It accepts the basic proposition that contract formation and default gap-filling rules should be crafted to achieve efficiency goals and thereby maximize social welfare gains.It argues that by using economic analysis and by identifying the discrete elements of a methodology for legal interventionit may be possible to rationalize disparate pieces of Contracts and contract theories. Although such a principle will not provide a meta-theory for all of contract law, clarifying the efficiency methodology for law-supplied terms and liability default rules would help to determine whether, when and how the law should intervene in a wide variety of contexts.
The failure to clarify such methodology has adversely affected the analysis of whether, absent a bargain, a liability rule should be supplied by a court to govern precontractual negotiations and if so, under what circumstances and with what terms.While current analyses of precontractual liability have benefited from a shift from a doctrinal to an instrumental, economic orientation, such analyses suffer from several flaws traceable to the failure to clarify the appropriate methodology for law-supplied liability rules and thus fall short of their potential. Theseapproaches fail to take sufficient account of the behavioral realities of preliminary bargaining, including precontractual uncertainty,and neglect the critical question of justification.These analytical failures in turn lead to incomplete justifications for, erroneous applications of, and overly restrictive cost benefit analyses for precontractual liability rules. The failure to develop a comprehensive methodology for law-supplied liability rules and terms has obscured scholarly analysis of contract default rules in general. It has also hampered analysis of particular problems in contract law, such as the general contractor's reliance in bidding contexts, and interfered with rationalizing judicial approaches to incomplete contracts.
This Article offers a comparative net benefit methodology for resolving omissions in incomplete contracts.Such a methodology can assess theefficiency of a law-supplied rule in the sense of achieving goals for parties at less cost than private solutions. Such methodology would improve the analysis of precontractual liability issues in the cases, rectify deficiencies in default rule approaches, and resolve subcontractor liability under the famousDrennanrule.Articulation of the theory would unify a variety of seemingly unrelated contract doctrines as diverse as, promissory estoppel, implied excuse, and fiduciary obligation.
The Article takes an instrumental approach to contract formation and other doctrinal issues. It assumes that lawmakers (and parties themselves) are interested in maximizing social wealth.Like all instrumental analyses, it assumes that contract law has a "regulatory role"to play in crafting legal rules. It therefore assumes that liability rules will influence future bargainers' "behavior in ways that will affect social welfare."Assessing a rule's capacity for maximizing social wealth requires inquiry into whether adoption of such rule will hinder or advance that goal, given the way in which people with average behavioral characteristics will respond to the rule.
To demonstrate the need for a unified instrumental framework for deciding gaps and implying liability rules, Part II of this Article will first describe the competing visions of the role of law in contract gap-filling. Although each vision has expanded the ways in which we think about contracts and has offered more realistic models of bargaining, each still fails to offer a unified framework for deciding how courts should decideincomplete contracts. Part III of the Article outlines the methodological framework for unifying judicial approaches to law-supplied terms or rules. The framework will incorporate a: (1) realistic model of human behavior; and (2) a comparative net benefit framework to assess law-supplied interventions. Part IV traces the origin of the unifying comparative net benefit method to new institutional economics. Part IV analyzes how the failure to advert to the problems of uncertainty (and other bargaining impediments) has impaired the development of a complete comparative cost structure outlined in this Article and hampered the analysis of precontractual liability. Commentators compound these problems by employing overly restrictive cost/benefit analyses which fail to provide promisees with the optimal incentives to rely. Current analyses of reliance ignore the important issues of the problem of opportunistic expropriation of reliance investments. Accounting for these issues and applying the suggested methodology to reliance issues would improve results. Part IV applies the theory to several prototypical reliance cases. Part V explores two frameworks for dealing with incomplete contracts: a hypothetical bargain and penalty default rules. Since both approaches lack a comparative cost framework, neither can fully justify a law-supplied liability rule or term. Part VI applies the unified comparative net benefit framework to determine whether and in what fashion the law should intervene to protect the general contractor's reliance on a subcontractor's offer and concludes that the protections ofDrennanshould be modified using the framework outlined here. Part VII uses the unified framework to rationalize a myriad of cases of law-supplied interventions in contract. The section will address Professor Alan Schwartz's theory for explaining judicial strategies of intervention in incomplete contracts.Part VIII offers a final assessment of why a comparative net benefit framework matters and outlines its advantages.

questions.question: When should contract law supply a court- or law-imposed term or liability rule for an incomplete contract, rather than leaving the matter to the parties' private bargain?

Under what conditions (for example, given transaction costs, uncertainty, reliance investments, and strategic nondisclosure) does a law-supplied rule increase social welfare compared with private ordering?

Can a comparative net benefit methodology reliably determine which form of legal intervention (rules that replicate likely party choices versus rules that induce disclosure or reliance-protecting behavior) will maximize efficiency in precontractual negotiations and reliance situations?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Can default liability rules be designed to induce socially optimal precontractual reliance, and what informational burdens would such rules place on adjudicators?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Is imposing a judicially enforced duty to negotiate in good faith necessary to achieve efficient outcomes in preliminary agreements, or would protecting reliance expenditures suffice?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How do market and institutional features affect whether informative 'cheap talk' will arise privately or require legal intervention to induce accurate precontractual communication?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PERFORMATIVES IN SPEECH ACT THEORY: AN INTRODUCTION

papers.node_id: 81neblrev839!!ARTICLE: Why Expectation Damages for Breach of Contract Must Be the Norm: A Refutation of the Fuller and Perdue "Three Interests" Thesis
papers.title: ARTICLE: Why Expectation Damages for Breach of Contract Must Be the Norm: A Refutation of the Fuller and Perdue "Three Interests" Thesis
papers.abstract:
Contract law uses three measures of damages. The expectation measure puts the injured party in as good a position as if the contract had been performed (i.e., not breached).The reliance measure puts the injured party in as good a position as if the contract had not been made.The restitution measure restores to the injured party any benefit the breaching party obtained from his breach at the injured party's expense.
Although the expectation measure has always been the norm,Lon L. Fuller and William R. Perdue, Jr. famously questioned its primary status in an article that appeared in 1936.They began by asserting that each of the measures compensates the injured party for the loss of an associated "interest" in the contract - the expectation measure compensates for the loss of the "expectation interest," the reliance measure compensates for the loss of the "reliance interest," etc. They then ranked these "interests" in what they considered to be the order of their importance, putting the restitution interest first and the expectation interest last:
It is obvious that the three "interests" we have distinguished do not present equal claims to judicial intervention… . The "restitution interest," involving a combination of unjust impoverishment with unjust gain, presents the strongest case for relief. If, following Aristotle, we regard the purpose of justice as the maintenance of an equilibrium of goods among members of society, the restitution interest presents twice as strong a claim to judicial intervention as the reliance interest, since if A not only causes B to lose one unit but appropriatesthat unit to himself, the resulting discrepancy between A and B is not one unit but two.
On the other hand, the promisee who has actually relied on the promise, even though he may not thereby have enriched the promisor, certainly presents a more pressing case for relief than the promisee who merely demands satisfaction for his disappointment in not getting what was promised him. In passing from compensation for change of position to compensation for loss of expectancy we pass, to use Aristotle's terms again, from the realm of corrective justice to that of distributive justice. The law no longer seeks merely to heal a disturbed status quo, but to bring into being a new situation. It ceases to act defensively or restoratively, and assumed [sic] a more active role. With the transition, the justification for legal relief loses its self-evident quality. It is as a matter of fact no easy thing to explain why the normal rule of contract recovery should be that which measures damages by the value of the promised performance.
After thus concluding that "it is … no easy thing" to explain why the expectation measure is the norm, they went on to explore what the reason or reasons might be. They eventually concluded that although there were no good reasons for protecting the expectation interest,there was a good reason for using the expectation measure of damages as the norm: because, they claimed, it generally results in the same recovery as the reliance measure would and is easier to prove.
The Fuller and Perdue article and its "three interests thesis" has had an immense scholarly and academic influence in the United States. Richard Craswell cited over sixty publications treating the three interests thesis in his article on the subject published in 2000.A recent Lexis search of the "Law Reviews, Combined" database revealed twenty-six citations to the article within the last two years.The effect of the article has been to throw the question of the proper measure of damages into doubt. Although it has been convincingly shown that the article's conclusion is incorrect - that the expectation measure generally results in the same recovery as the reliance measure would- so that the article's further conclusion that the expectation measure generally makes a good surrogate for the reliance measure is wrong, no one has yet come up with any other generally accepted reason or reasons for the expectation measure being the norm. The Restatement (Second) of Contracts states the three interests thesis almost verbatim as Fuller and Perdue stated it and offersno reasons for preferring any one of the measures over the other two.No hornbook, treatise or casebook in print offers any such reasons either, and nearly all of them mention the Fuller and Perdue article and comment upon it favorably.
Despite its immense scholarly and academic influence, however, the article and its thesis have had no discernible effect on the law. The expectation measure continues to be the norm,and even in the situations for which the contracts restatements have explicitly suggested a flexible approach to damages, the courts continue to use the expectation measure almost exclusively of the other two.
As demonstrated below, the courts have rightfully used the expectation measure to the near exclusion of the other two measures. Toward that end, Part II of this Article sets forth the principal institutions in a modern market economy in which contracts are used. Part III refutes the Fuller and Perdue three interests thesis by explaining how the expectation measure meets the needs of these principal institutions in four crucial respects, while showing that neither of the other measures meets these needs in even one such respect. Part IV exposes further endemic weaknesses in the three interests thesis. Part V concludes by showing that the three interests thesis is too flawed to be of use for comparing the merits of the three damages measures.

questions.question: Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach of contract rather than reliance or restitution measures?
Do expectation damages better serve the needs and functioning of modern market institutions than reliance or restitution measures?
Is the framework that ranks restitution and reliance interests above expectation a valid justification for preferring non-expectation damages?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2004wislrev309!!SYMPOSIUM: AN OFFER YOU CAN'T REVOKE
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: AN OFFER YOU CAN'T REVOKE

shared_topics.topic: the normative primacy and justification of expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends expectation damages as the proper default remedy for breach, arguing it best serves the needs of market institutions and explaining why Fuller & Perdue's challenge fails; Paper B repeatedly treats expectation remedies as the default Eisenberg embraces for enforced offers and critiques the wisdom and limits of an across-the-board expectation-based rule.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship and tension between expectation and reliance remedies (including promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the debate as Fuller & Perdue's 'three interests' (expectation, reliance, restitution) and analyzes why expectation should dominate, while Paper B engages the same tension when evaluating Section 87(2), Drennan, and promissory-estoppel-type reliance as bases for protecting offerees from revocation and questions when reliance-based protection is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of the Restatements and UCC (specific doctrinal provisions) in shaping doctrines of damages and offer irrevocability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the Restatement(s) for adopting Fuller & Perdue's formulation without offering reasons and traces how courts treat the measures, while Paper B conducts detailed doctrinal analysis of Restatement sections (e.g., 45, 87, 90) and UCC §2-205 in assessing when offers are 'firm' or irrevocable and what remedies follow.

shared_topics.topic: policy versus formal doctrinal reasoning in contract law (modern vs classical approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its defense of expectation damages in the institutional and policy needs of a modern market economy and criticizes alternative theoretical accounts, whereas Paper B situates Eisenberg's proposal within the broader debate between classical/formalist rules and 'modern contract law' realism, scrutinizing the policy trade-offs of simplifying rules of irrevocability and remedy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73alblrev1!!ARTICLE: LEGAL AUTOPSIES: ASSESSING THE PERFORMANCE OF JUDGES AND LAWYERS THROUGH THE WINDOW OF LEADING CONTRACT CASES
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LEGAL AUTOPSIES: ASSESSING THE PERFORMANCE OF JUDGES AND LAWYERS THROUGH THE WINDOW OF LEADING CONTRACT CASES

shared_topics.topic: the norm of expectation damages as the primary measure in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A mounts a substantive defense of expectation damages and documents that courts overwhelmingly apply expectation relief rather than reliance or restitution; Paper B treats landmark contract cases (e.g., Hadley v. Baxendale) that hinge on damages rules and uses those cases to evaluate how damages doctrines are argued and decided in practice.

shared_topics.topic: judicial fact selection and narrative shaping in appellate contract opinions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how courts apply doctrinal rules (including damages measures) in real cases and relies on judicial practice to justify the expectation norm, while Paper B documents how appellate judges compress, slant, or alter factual narratives in contract (and related) cases in ways that doctrinally situate disputes and affect outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between academic critique and actual judicial practice in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights the persistent influence of Fuller & Perdue in scholarship despite courts continuing to favor expectation damages, and Paper B notes that scholarly calls for autopsy-like evaluation of judges and lawyers have had limited uptake even though case studies reveal recurring errors and capability problems.

shared_topics.topic: the use of trial records and case studies to assess doctrinal application and professional performance in contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its refutation of the 'three interests' thesis in an analysis of how contract law operates within modern market institutions and how courts actually measure damages, while Paper B argues for close case-study scrutiny of trial records to reveal how lawyers and judges perform and how doctrinal rules are applied (or misapplied) in contract litigation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 107wvalrev443!!ARTICLE: A Realistic Proposal for the Contract Duress Doctrine
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A Realistic Proposal for the Contract Duress Doctrine

shared_topics.topic: the balance between freedom of contract and corrective/substantive fairness
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how contract law should weigh party autonomy against fairness: Paper A argues duress doctrine must protect voluntariness without unduly encroaching on freedom of contract, while Paper B critiques Fuller & Perdue’s move toward corrective/distributive rationales and defends expectation damages as the norm consistent with market and institutional needs.

shared_topics.topic: the need for clear, practicable doctrinal tests that courts can apply
shared_topics.justification: Both works criticize vague or unworkable standards and propose clearer rules—Paper A urges replacing 'free will' tests with a 'no reasonable alternative' standard and doctrinal separation from undue influence, and Paper B rejects the three-interests framework as analytically weak and seeks a justificatory standard for favoring expectation damages that courts can reliably implement.

shared_topics.topic: the role and influence of Restatements and legal scholarship on contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Each paper engages with the Restatements (especially the Restatement (Second) of Contracts) and prior scholarship as authoritative touchstones to assess and critique prevailing doctrine—Paper A discusses First and Second Restatements in relation to duress, and Paper B notes that the Restatement (Second) echoes Fuller & Perdue’s framing while lacking justification.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal rules and remedies serve broader market and institutional purposes
shared_topics.justification: Both articles ground doctrinal prescriptions in consequential considerations about market functioning and institutional needs—Paper A justifies a workable duress doctrine as promoting reliable, unconstrained bargaining and social welfare, and Paper B argues expectation damages best meet the needs of modern market institutions compared with reliance or restitution measures.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33emorylj41!!ARTICLE: MISTAKE AND ERROR IN THE LAW OF CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: MISTAKE AND ERROR IN THE LAW OF CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: tension between enforcing contractual stability (predictability) and providing fairness-based relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends expectation damages as the norm because they promote predictable enforcement of bargains and serve market institutions, while Paper B analyzes mistake doctrines as sites where courts must balance enforcement of agreements against hindsight fairness and sometimes grant relief.

shared_topics.topic: who should bear losses and risks arising from contractual failures (breach vs mistake)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how damages measures (expectation, reliance, restitution) allocate the economic loss of a breach between parties, and Paper B examines whether, and in what circumstances, a mistaken party or the counterparty should bear the loss when a contract was formed under error.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judicial doctrine and remedy design in making contract law administrable and predictable
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques scholarly accounts and shows courts overwhelmingly apply the expectation measure because it fits institutional needs and is administrable, while Paper B seeks a rational, predictable basis for when courts should grant relief for mistake, highlighting judicial discretion and doctrinal development.

shared_topics.topic: historical and institutional evolution of contract doctrines in commercial economies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the dominance of expectation damages against doctrinal history (Fuller & Perdue) and modern market institutions, and Paper B traces the historical progression from formalistic enforcement to modern mistake doctrine across legal systems to explain how contract law has adapted to commercial needs.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 50ucdavislrev405!!ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Conspiracy as Contract

shared_topics.topic: the normative and doctrinal role of promises/exchange of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the ‘agreement’ for criminal conspiracy should be defined as an exchange of promises, drawing directly on contract concepts; Paper B centers its analysis on promise-based interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) and defends expectation damages as the appropriate legal response to breaches of promise.

shared_topics.topic: aligning legal rules with their justificatory rationales
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes narrowing the definition of agreement so conspiracy law coheres with its stated rationales (seriousness of intent, increased likelihood of completion, First Amendment limits), while Paper B evaluates and defends expectation damages by showing that that measure best serves the institutional purposes and policy reasons underlying contract law.

shared_topics.topic: critique of existing doctrinal formulations and the need for clearer standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts and jury instructions for vague, inconsistent definitions of ‘agreement’ and urges a rigorous doctrinal standard; Paper B critiques the influential Fuller–Perdue 'three interests' thesis and the Restatement's uncritical adoption, arguing for clearer, better-justified doctrinal choice on damages.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of evidentiary and practical proof concerns on doctrinal choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A acknowledges that agreements are often proved circumstantially but insists the standard should be promises so evidence is weighed against a clear benchmark; Paper B engages the claim that expectation damages are the norm in part because they are easier to prove and examines how practical proof burdens affect which damages measure courts adopt.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1992wislrev1755!!ARTICLE: THE PHANTOM RELIANCE INTEREST IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PHANTOM RELIANCE INTEREST IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.

shared_topics.topic: critique and assessment of Fuller and Perdue's 'three interests' taxonomy
shared_topics.justification: Both papers directly engage Fuller and Perdue's 1936 thesis distinguishing expectation, reliance, and restitution interests — Paper A argues the reliance interest is a 'phantom' that has been misapplied and should be abandoned or reformed, while Paper B refutes Fuller and Perdue's ranking and defends the primacy of the expectation measure against their claims.

shared_topics.topic: whether expectation damages should be the default/normal measure
shared_topics.justification: Both articles defend expectation as the appropriate baseline: Paper B argues expectation damages must be the norm and explains why alternative measures fail to meet market institutions' needs, and Paper A proposes consolidating remedies under the expectation interest (with a rebuttable presumption of zero profit) instead of relying on a debased reliance doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical versus doctrinal/practical relationship between reliance and expectation measures
shared_topics.justification: Each paper analyzes how the reliance measure relates to expectation in theory and in courts — Paper A traces the erosion from Fuller and Perdue's 'pure' reliance to an expenditure-based tool that often approximates (or undercuts) expectation, while Paper B examines and rejects the claim that reliance undermines or should displace expectation, arguing expectation typically aligns better with practical needs.

shared_topics.topic: descriptive account of judicial practice and the Restatement's influence on damages doctrine (including promissory estoppel and the certainty problem)
shared_topics.justification: Both works survey and critique how courts and the Restatement (Second) treat the three measures in actual cases: Paper A documents courts awarding expectation even in reliance contexts and connects this to the certainty doctrine and promissory estoppel, while Paper B documents the continued judicial preference for expectation despite Fuller and Perdue and the Restatement's ambivalence.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 67sclrev99!!ARTICLE: WHAT IS A CONTRACT?
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: WHAT IS A CONTRACT?

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations and justificatory principles for contract doctrines

shared_topics.topic: gap between scholarly theory and judicial practice in contract law

papers.title: ARTICLE: You Asked for It, You Got It . . . Toy Yoda: Practical Jokes, Prizes, and Contract Law
papers.abstract: For what seemed to be a simple contract dispute,Berry v. Gulf Coast Wings Inc.garnered an unusual amount of attention in both the legal and popular press.Former Hooters waitress Jodee Berry sued her ex-employer for breaching its promise to award a new Toyota to the winner of an April 2001 sales contest. Berry alleged that her manager, Jared Blair, told the waitresses at the Hooters where she worked at the time that whoever sold the most beer at each participating location during April 2001 would be entered in a drawing, the winner of which would receive a new Toyota. As the contest progressed,Blair allegedly told the waitresses that he did not know whether the winner would receive a Toyota car, truck, or van, but that she would have to pay any registration fees on the vehicle. In early May, Blair informed Berry that she had won the contest. He proceeded to blindfold her and lead her to the restaurant's parking lot. Waiting for her there was not a Toyota car, truck, or van, but a doll of the character Yoda from theStar Warsmovies -- a "toy Yoda." Blair laughed. Berry did not. Berry sued for breach of contract and fraud. Hooters answered that Blair was only joking. While the case eventually settled favorably for Berry,it raised three interesting questions of contract law that merit further discussion, namely: (1) whether Blair's statement was clearly in jest, such that it could not be accepted by Berry's performance;(2) whether Blair's statement, even if not clearly in jest, constituted an offer to form a contract that could be accepted by Berry's performance;and (3) whether Berry gave sufficient consideration to bind Hooters to the terms of Blair's offer.

questions.question: Whether a statement that appears to be a joke can nonetheless be reasonably interpreted and enforced as a binding promise when the recipient accepts by performing the requested act.
Whether an announced prize or reward constitutes a binding inducement that can be accepted through performance (for example, by increasing sales) and thereby creates contractual obligations.
Whether the recipient's performance (e.g., sales efforts) provides sufficient exchange/consideration to make the promised prize legally enforceable.

matched_themes: Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
What procedural or evidentiary features of an intermediary-based arrangement distinguish genuinely serious, enforceable gift commitments from casual promises?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 73tullrev497!!ARTICLE:"Why Infer"? What the New Institutional Economics Has to Say About Law-Supplied Default Rules
papers.title: ARTICLE:"Why Infer"? What the New Institutional Economics Has to Say About Law-Supplied Default Rules
papers.abstract:
The great question confronting judges and legal scholars is, in the words of one of my colleagues, "Why infer?"When and why is it justifiable in contexts involving assent-based obligationsfor the law to supply a term or commitmentto which the parties did not expressly agree?
The issue of justification for law-supplied terms and obligations is an important one. It underlies decisions as basic to law as: Should the law even provide a forum for a dispute?When should the law simply take a "hands off" attitude by refusing to supply terms,and when should it intervene either through default rulesor by supplying a term by implication?
The question of legal intervention in assent-based relations crosses varied subject areas. Although these diverse areas often focuson individual doctrinal issues, the real issue, which often remains hidden, is one of justifying the legal intervention itself. The court must confront the question of whether the law should supply a term or obligation to which the parties have not expressly agreed. It must do this whether it grapples with (1)why and in what circumstances the law should supply a fiduciary "performance obligation" in the principal/agent context,(2)why and when the law shouldor in subcontractor bidding cases,or (3)why the law should imply a commitment in precontractual section 90 contexts.
Despite the centrality of the question of law-supplied obligation, the means of resolution remain elusive. The contractual default rule literature relied on to resolve the appropriateness of a variety of law-supplied terms is flawed.The literature often fails to utilize a framework with realistic behavioral assumptions that can fully resolve whether a legal intervention is justified. In addition, this literature confuses situations that are fundamentally different in terms of the nature of legal intervention involved and subjects them to a unified default rule analysis. Such literature confuses cases in which a court"supplies terms in addition to or other than what the parties have expressly bargained for" with cases in which the legal decisionmaker refuses to add or subtract terms from the express bargain.This confusion diverts commentators from clearly identifying a framework to justify legal intervention in the form of an implied term.
, because authors often focus on the substance of a particular default rule without a recognition that the default rule is law-supplied and therefore must be justified,they attempt to resolve questions of implied obligation without reference to a well developed comparative benefit methodology that is standard in new institutional economics.A comparative benefit methodology compares the costs and benefits of the proposed scheme with various other strategies for achieving common goals.Such goals include maximizing the surplus from tradeby controlling problems such as opportunism.Proposed default rules which lack a comparison of "feasible superior alternatives" remain incompletely justified.
, even when the default rule literature incorporates realistic behavioral assumptions affecting the bargaining process, such as strategic behavior,it fails to incorporate these assumptions into a modelthat can ultimately justify the conclusion that the benefits and costs of legal intervention outweigh the benefits and costs of other approaches the parties might use to achieve common goals, given the barriers to private contract solutions.While recognizing that strategizing may cause inefficiencies,default rule scholars do not explain fully why the presence of such inefficiencies cannot be solved by other cost-effective private methods which do not involve a law-supplied rule.Nor do such authors explain how the presence of strategizing in conjunction with asset specificityand bounded rationalitymay cause inefficiencies which cannot be readily solvedby express contracting.Moreover, they fail to devise a structure for determining how opportunistic hazards from strategizing can be mitigated to maximize joint gains from trade in the most cost-effective manner with the greatest net benefits. Thus they fail to invoke a well-known comparative methodologyfor exploring and comparing a range of possible feasible solutions for persistent problems of uncertainty and sunk costs when express private contract solutions to rent-seeking behavior will be difficult or unattainable.Without that methodology, the literature cannot explain why law-supplied default rules should be preferred over other approaches.
Finally, while the body of literature on transaction cost economics and the new institutional economics remains a potentially rich source of solutions to the problem of justifying an implied obligation, it remains partially inaccessible to the current students of contract default rules. This Article will offer a framework to guide decisionmakers in determining the appropriateness (efficiency)of law-supplied implied obligations,by highlighting the realistic behavioral assumptionsof transaction cost methodology as it isreflected in new institutional economics, emphasizing the "hazard mitigation,"and comparing and assessing the arrangements to determine which will yield the greatest net benefits.
Part II of this Article seeks to remedy defects in current approaches to law-supplied obligation by presenting a methodology derived from the new institutional economics that can be used to justify law-supplied obligations in a second-best world.It adopts a "framework" comparing "alternative feasible forms … with each other"to determine whether the implementation of any law-supplied rule would be efficient in the sense of increasing net gains. In its current formulation, the comparative institutional approach is used primarily to explain why parties have adopted various organizational structures and thus to explain what actually exists.This Article suggests that the comparative net benefit approach of the new institutional economics should be extended to cases where the parties themselves have failed to adopt a term or resolve a matter by contract, and a legal decisionmaker must determine whether supplying terms or liability rules would maximize the joint gains from trade.Law,Economics, and Organization theoryshould set the stage for a new approach to incomplete contracting.
Part III of the Article will examine and critique the current hypothetical bargain default rule literature. At present, it has failed to develop a comparative methodology to justify the presence of a law-supplied obligation. This Part will also suggest that the deficiencies in current theories of default rules, including hypothetical bargain theory, must be modified to include a comparative net benefit standard in order to provide a complete structure for determining what the parties would want.
Part IV will draw on the comparative analysis developed in the first two Parts of this Article to critique the penalty default rule methodology proposed by Ayres and Gertner.This Part suggests that while the penalty default rule methodology helpfully recognizes the importance of strategic behavior in deciding how to craft default rules, it still fails to provide a complete justification for a law-supplied rule because it fails to provide a means of determining whether a suggested law-supplied rule will achieve greater net benefits than other approaches in a second-best world.Moreover, because Ayres and Gertner fail to distinguish between default rules that supply terms and those that refuse to do so,they fail to provide an explanatory theory which can account for the variegated judicial approaches to contractual gaps.
Ayres and Gertner's penalty default rule analysis cannot explain the full range of approaches taken to basic issues of gap filling. They argue that the courts' refusal to fill quantity terms left incomplete stems from an underlying penalty default rule designed to force the parties to reveal information about the quantity ex ante, because doing so will efficiently save the courts the cost of filling in such quantity ex post.However, the penalty default rule does not explain the very different approaches taken to quantity terms in short- and long-term contracts. In long-term contracts the courts are often willing to permit the enforcement of requirements contractsin which the actual quantity is not specified. In such cases, courts recognize thatpersuasive barriers, such as the unforeseeability of the future, may prevent the achievement of ex ante specificity and permit the enforcement of what would otherwise be considered indefinite contracts.
Part IV of the Article also challenges the Ayres and Gertner attack on the "soundness" of the hypothetical bargain rationale. This Article argues that the discrediting of the majoritarian hypothetical bargain depends on a falsely perceived judicial rejection of majority preferences. The results in these types of cases are better explained by the law's disinclination to intervene to implement majority preferences if no barriers prevent the private achievement of such goals. So conceptualized, the cases are still consistent with a hypothetical bargain rationale.
The presence of an underlying hypothetical bargain rationale in these cases has been obscured by the failure of the legal decisionmaker to employ a realistic model of behavioral assumptions and a comparative approach. These failures have hampered the development of a framework for justifying legal interventions. With such a framework, courts could then determine whether a legal intervention is efficient in the sense that "some selected objective … will be achieved at a higher level with the interjection (intervention) than without it, all things (benefits achieved and costs incurred, with the intervention as compared without the intervention) considered,"and is therefore hypothetically preferred. Under this suggested structure one can rationalize rules, such as the Hadley rule in hypothetical bargain terms, although Ayres and Gertner have viewed such rules as antimajoritarian, penalty default terms.
Part V will look at particular instances of law-supplied default rules in precontractual negotiation. It will illuminate the underlying frameworks and assumptions used to justify legal interventions in the form of suggested law-supplied liability rules or terms. This Partsuggests that current justifications for the particular default rules for precontractual negotiation are flawed because they (1)fail to identify relevant structural features necessary to resolve whether a given law-supplied rule will produce "a greater net benefit" and is therefore more efficient than other alternatives,(2)obscure the law-supplied nature of the default rule, and (3)fail to develop a comparative framework.
Those analytical flaws are fundamental. They hamper the efforts of commentators to (1)justify liability rules which they propose,(2)explain the variability in judicial treatment of vague or incomplete contracts,or (3)explain whether and in what circumstances the law should intervene.
Part VI will use Williamsonian economics and the analytical framework developed in this Article to resolve questions about the nature and scope of law-supplied obligations in subcontracting. This Part will suggest that current approaches fail to grasp the behavioral realities of subcontractor bargaining, obscure the law-supplied nature of the implied terms, fail to provide a comparative analytical structure for resolving whether the law should interject an implied term, and therefore reach inappropriate conclusions on when the contractor's reliance should be protected.

questions.question: Whether and under what circumstances the law should supply implied contractual terms (default rules) because doing so increases net joint gains compared with feasible private alternatives, given transaction costs and behavioral frictions.

Whether existing default-rule theories adequately justify law-supplied obligations once realistic behavioral assumptions (strategic behavior, bounded rationality, asset specificity) are incorporated, or whether a comparative net-benefit/transaction-costs framework is required instead.

What decisionmaking framework or comparative institutional methodology judges should use to determine when supplying an implied obligation is efficient (i.e., yields greater net benefits than nonintervention or alternative arrangements).

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How do informal relational norms and repeated interactions govern commercial contracting in practice, and when do these norms supplant formal state-enforced rules?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Can default liability rules be designed to induce socially optimal precontractual reliance, and what informational burdens would such rules place on adjudicators?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do parties in ongoing exchange relationships use relational contracting-informal, repeated-interaction arrangements-to govern performance and adapt to change?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
Is imposing a judicially enforced duty to negotiate in good faith necessary to achieve efficient outcomes in preliminary agreements, or would protecting reliance expenditures suffice?
How do market and institutional features affect whether informative 'cheap talk' will arise privately or require legal intervention to induce accurate precontractual communication?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: legal intervention to mitigate opportunism in incomplete or repeated contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a comparative institutional framework (drawing on new institutional economics) to justify when courts should supply default or implied terms to curb opportunistic behavior in incomplete contracting; Paper B analyzes opportunism in successive-contract settings and evaluates rules (enforceable, implied, or mandatory renewal) intended to deter hold-up and other opportunistic strategies.

shared_topics.topic: information asymmetry and uncertainty as drivers of contractual gaps and opportunism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes bounded rationality, uncertainty, and strategic behavior as realistic behavioral assumptions that create gaps and opportunistic hazards that may justify law-supplied rules; Paper B focuses on informational gaps between parties (especially in follow-up negotiations) as the source of friction and manipulative behavior that legal rules must address.

shared_topics.topic: comparative evaluation of alternative legal regimes (opt-in, opt-out, mandatory) for handling contractual gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes default-rule literature for failing to compare feasible alternatives and argues for a comparative-net-benefit methodology to choose between intervention and nonintervention; Paper B explicitly compares three regimes for renewal (enforceable renewal clauses, implied renewal clauses, and mandatory renewal) and assesses which minimizes opportunism under varying conditions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of party sophistication, transaction costs, and asset specificity in choosing legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its framework in transaction-cost/Williamsonian analysis, arguing that asset specificity, bounded rationality, and strategic behavior determine when law-supplied terms are efficient; Paper B models how party sophistication and the nature of the transaction affect informational problems and whether mandatory or default rules are justified.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev974!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Scapegoats and the Common Law: Pinnel's Case, Cumber v. Wane, and the Legal Duty Rule
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Scapegoats and the Common Law: Pinnel's Case, Cumber v. Wane, and the Legal Duty Rule

shared_topics.topic: when courts should supply or enforce obligations that parties did not expressly agree to
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a comparative institutional/economic framework for when judges should supply implied terms or default rules in incomplete or assent-based contracts; Paper B examines courts' treatment of contract modifications (the legal duty/consideration rule) and the circumstances in which courts enforce or refuse to enforce agreements purporting to change obligations despite the absence of fresh consideration.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and the variability of judicial responses to incomplete or modified agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes why courts sometimes fill contractual gaps (or refuse to) and criticizes existing default‑rule theories for failing to explain heterogenous judicial outcomes; Paper B documents the common‑law history and persistent judicial efforts to evade or soften the rigid Pinnel/consideration rule, illustrating inconsistent case law on modification and discharge of claims.

shared_topics.topic: criticisms of rigid doctrinal rules and the search for better justificatory standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes default‑rule literature for lacking a comparative net‑benefit justification and advocates Williamsonian/new institutional tools to justify law‑supplied terms; Paper B collects and presents the vocal judicial and doctrinal criticism of the legal duty/consideration rule as irrational or unjust and implicitly engages with the need to replace or reinterpret the rule with a more defensible standard.

shared_topics.topic: the role of legal doctrine history and precedent in shaping modern contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how existing theories (e.g., hypothetical bargain, penalty defaults) and judicial practices have obscured the law‑supplied nature of rules and calls for reframing via economic history/organization theory; Paper B traces the historical origins of the legal duty rule (Pinnel's Case) and discusses how precedent has constrained or provoked efforts to reform contract doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52amjcompl433!!ARTICLE: Mistake in Contract Formation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mistake in Contract Formation

shared_topics.topic: when courts should intervene to alter or relieve contractual obligations arising from defective assent (mistake or incompleteness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when a party's mistake at formation (distinguishing 'substance' from 'motive') justifies judicial relief from the bargain; Paper B asks when the law should supply implied terms or default rules to fill gaps or substitute for what parties did not expressly agree, i.e. both address the threshold for judicial intervention in defective or incomplete contracts.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' subjective intentions, motives, or hypothetical preferences should inform judicial gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the relevance of parties' motives versus objective substance in deciding relief for mistakes; Paper B critiques and defends hypothetical‑bargain approaches and emphasizes assessing what parties would have wanted under realistic behavioral assumptions, so both grapple with using subjective intent or counterfactual preferences to justify legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: normative frameworks for justifying judicial gap‑filling or relief (comparative/analytic standards)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes rethinking the classical mistake doctrine via alternative doctrinal traditions (e.g., certain French/Aristotelian approaches) to decide when relief is warranted, while Paper B develops a comparative net‑benefit/transaction‑costs framework from new institutional economics to justify when law‑supplied terms should be imposed; both advance systematic criteria for when courts should act.

shared_topics.topic: issues arising at contract formation and precontractual negotiation that create reasons to supply terms or grant relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on mistakes occurring in contract formation (and when they should lead to relief), and Paper B examines precontractual negotiation and formation gaps (and when courts should imply obligations), so both engage the legal problems that arise at or before formation that prompt judicial gap‑filling or adjustment.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 9geomasonlrev99!!ARTICLE: THE SOPHISTICATED DOCTRINE OF CONSIDERATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SOPHISTICATED DOCTRINE OF CONSIDERATION

shared_topics.topic: when and why courts impose obligations not expressly bargained (law‑supplied or implied terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how sixteenth‑century courts bent or dispensed with the consideration requirement to impose obligations (e.g., promissory estoppel, moral obligation, quasi‑contract) that parties had not explicitly agreed to; Paper B asks the modern counterpart question and develops a new‑institutional‑economics framework for when judges should supply default rules or implied terms in assent‑based relations.

shared_topics.topic: gap‑filling for incomplete contracts and doctrinal mechanisms used to do so
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows historically that consideration was applied flexibly or fictionalized so assumpsit could remedy promises that lacked traditional formalities, effectively filling doctrinal gaps; Paper B addresses contemporary gap‑filling directly, critiquing default‑rule theories and proposing a comparative net‑benefit methodology for judicial gap‑filling in incomplete contracting.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations for enforcing promises (reciprocity/exchange versus efficiency/hypothetical bargain)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the core substantive justification for early consideration doctrine was exchange/reciprocity while also noting broader rationales courts sometimes invoked; Paper B engages the competing justificatory frameworks (hypothetical bargain, penalty defaults, efficiency via comparative net benefits) and defends a transaction‑costs/efficiency basis for when law should intervene.

shared_topics.topic: the role of judges/legal decisionmakers in shaping contract doctrine and limiting private bargaining outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how judges in the assumpsit era actively construed 'consideration' to control which promises were actionable and thus shaped substantive contract law; Paper B scrutinizes judicial gap‑filling and default‑rule choices, offering criteria to guide when courts should infer terms and how they should weigh alternatives.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58tennlrev367!!ARTICLE: PERFORMATIVES IN SPEECH ACT THEORY: AN INTRODUCTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PERFORMATIVES IN SPEECH ACT THEORY: AN INTRODUCTION

shared_topics.topic: statutes and contracts as performative speech acts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that statutes and many contractual formulas function as explicit performatives that bring legal states of affairs into being, and Paper B treats contracts and judicial gap-filling as instances where legal language and rules operate to create or supply binding terms, thereby treating legal texts as action-producing utterances.

shared_topics.topic: institutional authority required to create legal effects
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that performatives only succeed within social institutions and when the speaker has requisite authority (e.g., priest, police, employer), while Paper B analyzes when legal decisionmakers (courts, legislatures) should exercise institutional authority to supply terms or intervene—both focus on who may legitimately produce binding legal effects.

shared_topics.topic: attributing or inferring intent from legal language and conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how illocutionary force and meaning can encode speaker intent (relevant to statutes and contracts), and Paper B centers on whether and how the law should infer parties' intents (e.g., hypothetical bargain, implied terms) when the parties have not expressly agreed—both engage the problem of extracting or imputing intent for legal purposes.

shared_topics.topic: gap‑filling and non‑literal force of legal utterances
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses direct versus indirect speech acts and how illocutionary force can differ from literal semantics, while Paper B is concerned with judicial gap‑filling (implied obligations, default rules) and when the law should supply non‑explicit terms—both examine how legal obligations can arise from non‑explicit linguistic or institutional moves.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic strategic behavior in contracting and how law should deter it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how opportunism and strategic bargaining (asset specificity, bounded rationality) create inefficiencies that might justify law‑supplied default rules; Paper B examines buyer/seller opportunism around contract modifications (e.g., extortionate price increases and ‘‘self‑help specific performance’’) and whether doctrine deters such conduct.

shared_topics.topic: when courts should supply or enforce terms versus leaving parties to private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A asks when judges should supply implied terms or default rules rather than remain hands‑off, proposing a comparative institutional test; Paper B debates whether courts should enforce modifications or allow parties to obtain performance through post‑hoc strategies, effectively weighing judicial intervention against private self‑help.

shared_topics.topic: the role of remedies (specific performance, liability/default rules) in shaping contracting incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques default and penalty rules as law‑supplied interventions that alter parties' incentives and discusses liability rules as alternatives, while Paper B centers on specific performance (and its availability) as a remedy that affects whether parties exploit or resist contract modifications.

shared_topics.topic: costs, uncertainty, and comparative benefit analysis as a basis for doctrinal choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a Williamsonian/comparative net‑benefit methodology to justify implied obligations and compare feasible alternatives; Paper B emphasizes the practical difficulty parties face in predicting judicial remedies and weighs the costs and benefits of pursuing self‑help strategies versus relying on doctrine.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: KILL THE MONSTER: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AS AN INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF ACTION

shared_topics.topic: when courts may supply obligations or implied terms the parties did not expressly agree to
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes courts for effectively creating a free‑standing cause of action in promissory estoppel and thereby supplying enforceable obligations beyond the parties' bargains; Paper B poses the central question “Why infer?” and develops an economic framework to decide when law‑supplied default terms or implied obligations are justified.

shared_topics.topic: use of reliance‑based doctrines (promissory estoppel/section 90) to enforce promises absent consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the doctrine of promissory estoppel as a reliance‑based substitute for consideration and laments its expansion into an independent remedy; Paper B analyzes precontractual contexts (including section 90 and negotiation liability) where reliance is the basis for implying obligations and asks when such interventions increase joint gains.

shared_topics.topic: tension between traditional/formal contract rules and fairness‑based, ad hoc judicial gap‑filling
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how promissory estoppel has been used to sidestep formal doctrines (statute of frauds, parol evidence, limitation rules) in the name of fairness; Paper B critiques existing default‑rule theory for failing to explain the variety of judicial gap‑filling approaches and the circumstances in which courts decline or accept ad hoc interventions.

shared_topics.topic: implications for commercial predictability, transaction costs, and the need for a normative framework or legislative clarity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A warns that eroding formal contract rules in favor of courts' fairness judgments undermines predictability for business and recommends statutory limits on promissory estoppel; Paper B proposes a comparative net‑benefit (new institutional economics) methodology to determine when law‑supplied rules are economically efficient, thereby guiding decisionmakers toward predictable, transaction‑cost‑aware interventions.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44iowajcorpl649!!ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority

shared_topics.topic: justification for law-supplied obligations in the principal–agent context (including apparent authority)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the doctrinal and historical foundations of apparent authority—when third parties can rely on an agent's power without the principal's express grant—while Paper B explicitly treats when and why the law should impose fiduciary or performance obligations in principal–agent relations as an instance of law-supplied terms that must be justified.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and the criteria for supplying implied terms or authority
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how courts historically construed and supplied (or recognized) agent powers, and traces the emergence of rules courts used to fill gaps in agency relations; Paper B critiques existing default‑rule approaches and develops a comparative, NIE‑based framework for when courts should fill contractual or relational gaps with implied terms or liability rules.

shared_topics.topic: use of an objective 'reasonable third‑party' or hypothetical standard to infer obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues the doctrine of apparent authority arose from a shift toward an objective approach—what a reasonable person would infer from the principal's conduct—while Paper B evaluates the hypothetical bargain/majoritarian standards used to infer what parties would have agreed and argues for more realistic behavioral and comparative models to justify inferences.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of commercial practice and transaction‑cost reasoning on shaping substantive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds mercantile and commercial custom as formative sources for agency rules and their judicial acceptance, and Paper B mobilizes transaction‑cost and Williamsonian/new institutional economics reasoning to analyze subcontracting, market practices, and when law‑supplied defaults are preferable to private contracting.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE MANY FACES OF CONTRACTUAL CONSENT This title borrows from William N. Eskridge Jr. See William N. Eskridge Jr., The Many Faces of Sexual Consent, 37 Wm. & Mary L. Rev. 47, 47 (1995).

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of consent/assent in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on assent-based obligations and asks when the law may justifiably supply terms despite lack of express agreement, while Paper B reconceptualizes consent as a spectrum and critiques the binary informed/free framework courts often use.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and implied or law‑supplied contractual terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes when courts should supply default or implied terms (the 'Why infer?' question) and critiques default‑rule theory, and Paper B highlights courts' practical difficulties in identifying consent and the need for more nuanced approaches that can justify intervention when consent is incomplete or ambiguous.

shared_topics.topic: contextual and power factors that shape contracting and the need for legal intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how contract form (short‑ vs long‑term, subcontracting, precontractual negotiation), bargaining behavior, asset specificity, and opportunism affect whether private solutions suffice, and Paper B stresses how social context, power asymmetries (e.g., employment, standard‑form, spousal settings), and identity factors influence consent and thus the appropriateness of legal treatment.

shared_topics.topic: normative frameworks for when courts should intervene (efficiency vs public policy/contextual criteria)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes a comparative institutional/transaction‑cost methodology to justify law‑supplied rules by weighing net benefits against feasible alternatives, while Paper B argues that public policy, contextual considerations, and a layered model of consent should inform when and how the law treats or corrects perceived failures of consent.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 1992wislrev1755!!ARTICLE: THE PHANTOM RELIANCE INTEREST IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE PHANTOM RELIANCE INTEREST IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.

shared_topics.topic: when courts should intervene to supply terms or remedies in incomplete contracting
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a comparative institutional methodology (drawing on new institutional economics) to decide whether the law should supply implied terms or default rules when parties fail to contract; Paper B addresses a parallel question for remedies, asking when courts should award reliance versus expectation measures and criticizing current judicial practices in filling the remedial gap after breach or promissory estoppel.

shared_topics.topic: the normative and doctrinal relationship between expectation and reliance doctrines (including the hypothetical bargain)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques and defends varieties of the hypothetical bargain/default-rule literature (and contrasts it with penalty defaults), while Paper B interrogates Fuller and Perdue's reliance taxonomy and argues that courts in practice collapse reliance into expectation—both papers engage with which theoretical interest (expectation, reliance, or a hybrid) should govern judicial gap-filling and damages.

shared_topics.topic: the effects of evidentiary uncertainty, transaction costs, and strategic behavior on doctrinal choices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes bounded rationality, opportunism, asset specificity, and transaction costs as decisive factors in whether law-supplied rules are efficient; Paper B similarly foregrounds evidentiary uncertainty and litigation costs (how proof of profit affects awards) to explain and reform how courts measure damages.

shared_topics.topic: proposals to reform contract doctrine using comparative economic/analytical frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes adopting Williamsonian/new institutional comparative net-benefit analysis to guide implied-term and default-rule decisions, and Paper B proposes replacing the degraded reliance measure with an expectation-based rule carrying a rebuttable presumption of zero profit—both advance concrete doctrinal reforms grounded in economic or analytical reasoning.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY
