shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes consideration as the doctrinal mechanism that marks which promises should become legal obligations (the act/intent/nexus that grounds liability), while Paper B interrogates when and why courts should supply implied or default terms to turn incomplete or unexpressed agreements into enforceable commitments.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between party autonomy and law-supplied intervention
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames consideration as a commitment to relinquish autonomy that justifies legal enforcement of bargains, and Paper B addresses when judicially supplied terms are justified despite parties' failure to agree, weighing intervention against respecting private ordering.

shared_topics.topic: use of institutional and behavioral theory to justify contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A adopts critical/scientific realist social-science reasoning to explain why consideration operates as a social mechanism, whereas Paper B draws on new institutional economics and transaction-cost/behavioral assumptions (bounded rationality, opportunism, asset specificity) to provide a comparative justification for law-supplied default rules.

shared_topics.topic: evaluating reform proposals and the doctrinal boundaries of enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the functional importance of consideration against abolitionist or purely formal critiques and situates its limits (e.g., reliance/modification), while Paper B critiques existing default-rule theories and proposes a comparative net-benefit framework to decide when judicial gap-filling or reform of implied obligations is appropriate.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CONVENTIONAL MORAL OBLIGATION PRINCIPLE UNDULY LIMITS QUALIFIED BENEFICIARY CONTRARY TO CASE LAW

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and doctrinal choice about intervening vs leaving parties to private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the variability in judicial approaches to filling contractual gaps and critiques default‑rule theories for not explaining why courts sometimes refuse to supply terms, while Paper B documents how courts have chosen to enforce or decline enforcement of past‑benefit promises through manipulation or expansion of consideration doctrine, reflecting similar judicial decisionmaking about intervention.

shared_topics.topic: normative methods for justifying enforcement of non‑express obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates a comparative institutional/new institutional economics (comparative net‑benefit, transaction‑cost) methodology to justify law‑supplied terms, and Paper B uses legal history, natural law, and community‑expectation reasoning to justify a broader moral obligation principle—both engage the question of what normative framework courts should use to validate enforcement beyond formal doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: enforcement of obligations arising from precontractual or past interactions rather than explicit agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses implied obligations and liability rules in precontractual negotiation and other contexts where parties failed to contract explicitly, and Paper B focuses on enforcement of promises tied to past benefits or reimbursements (including benefits to third parties), so both treat obligations that originate from precontractual/past conduct rather than express contractual terms.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A Fish Story: Alaska Packers' Association v. Domenico

shared_topics.topic: when and why law should intervene to supply terms (justification for legal intervention)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions authoritative, context-free readings of appellate decisions that justify judicial outcomes without situating the decision in its broader setting, implicitly bearing on the propriety of judicial intervention; Paper B directly addresses the normative question of when the law ought to supply terms (vs. hands-off), proposing a comparative net-benefit test drawn from new institutional economics.

shared_topics.topic: importance of background economic, social, and behavioral context for understanding judicial decisions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the historical, economic, and social context of the salmon industry and the actors involved changes the interpretation of the Alaska Packers opinion; Paper B insists that realistic behavioral assumptions (asset specificity, bounded rationality, opportunism) and transaction-cost context are essential to justify default rules and explain varied judicial treatments.

shared_topics.topic: critique of orthodox/simplified doctrinal accounts and advocacy for richer, revisionist frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques traditional casebook presentations that strip facts and context and offers revisionist alternative narratives informed by primary transcripts and industry conditions; Paper B criticizes the prevailing default-rule literature and hypothetical-bargain accounts for failing to use comparative institutional analysis and calls for a more sophisticated framework to justify implied obligations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTS LIMITING LIABILITY: A PARADOX WITH TACIT SOLUTIONS

papers.title: ARTICLE:Basic Assumption*:(a poem based on Sherwood v. Walker)
papers.abstract: This poem was inspired by Sherwood v. Walker,the "barren cow" case that is a staple of first-year Contracts. The cow in Sherwood, Rose 2d of Aberlone, had been sold for her beef value on the assumption that she was barren. In fact, the cow was "with calf" and worth almost ten times her value as beef. The Michigan Supreme Court held that the seller could rescind the contract if the cow was sold "upon the understanding of both parties that she was barren, … and that in fact she was not barren, but capable of breeding."[cp10,12] I'll tell you how a man with a cow had a cowbecause his cow had a cow.Here's how.The man with a cow had a cowbecause he sold his cow for just chow.How now?He sold his cow for just chowbecause he didn't know his cow had a cow.Had his cow had a cow it would have been worth a thouand would not have sold for just chow.What now?Well, the buyer said "Wow!"The seller said "Yeow!"And the Court finally said "Come now!How can a cow with a cow worth a thousell like a cow for just chow.Not never, and not now!"So now you know how a man with a cow had a cowbecause his cow had a cow.

papers.abstract:
Introduction:Contract Law, Cheap Talk, and Dealmaking
THE newspapers are filled with stories of business deals and their making and unmaking. Corporate mergers and acquisitions are tracked from the very first tentative talks between potential "suitors" through the announcement of an "agreement-in-principle." Other deals, such as the American Medical Association's agreement to endorse exclusively Sunbeam homecare productsor the complex and exceedingly lucrative compensation packages now routinely offered to sports stars, entertainers, and corporate CEOs have likewise become topics of everyday comment and conversation. More generally, in the "winner-take-all"economy, "stars" in virtually all occupational fields move frequently from one employer to another, always searching for the best the market will bring, and bringing their lawyers with them as they go. One might reasonably claim that never before has the process and outcome of contract formation, or "dealmaking," commanded such widespread public attention.
It is in this light surprising to find that contracts scholars and law and economics scholars in particular have had relatively little to say about either the law governing or the economics driving suchcomplex dealmaking. For the most part, formal economic analysis of contract law has concentrated on explaining the types of substantive terms observed in private contracts and on the efficiency of various legal rules that apply as defaults to govern obligations in the performance, modification, and breach of an existing contract. While there have been some important applications of economics and game theory exploring how the legal rules of contract formation and breach might affect various actions taken during dealmaking,there has as yet been no attempt to analyze systematically the general economic incentives in this process, how those incentives might be expected to vary under alternative market and institutional structures, and, finally, how legal liability might shape those incentives. This Article provides such an account.
My account rests on an understanding of dealmaking (or as I often refer to it, "courtship") as that process by which markets for complex and highly differentiated goods and services are created. Courtship is at the most fundamental level a process by which parties acquire and communicate information to each other in an attempt to discern whether the deal is one which they both wish to make and, if so, on what terms. Regardless of whether the "opportunity" is a corporation (or some part of its assets), an employment position, or a complex good or service, a potential buyer will wish to find out what the opportunity would be worth to it; the seller will wish to determine its opportunity cost of parting with the opportunity, a cost which may depend upon what other potential buyers would be willing to offer. During the negotiation or courtship process, the parties will also be interested to learn what theopportunity is worth to the other party, not only because each may be able to drive a harder bargain when it knows more about the other side's cost or value, but also because continuing to talk is costly and not worth its cost if the chance of ultimately reaching agreement and trading the opportunity is too low. For the negotiations to proceed, it may be necessary for the parties to communicate with each other about the chances of agreement. Many of their communications cost little to send and will affect the value of continuing with the courtship process only indirectly by communicating information about the likely prospect of agreement if the process does continue. Such messages will of course depend on what the sender of the message actually knows when it sends the message. For this reason, even an optimistic statement such as "things look good, we're sure to agree if we continue to talk" will often go unfulfilled. The message might well have been true as a relative statement, conveying information about the sender's position that was accurate when the message was sent. Yet either sender or receiver may become more pessimistic as the process continues even further so that trade may not occur, and the assurance will go unfulfilled.
On this characterization, dealmaking or courtship is a process rife with what game theorists call "cheap talk."It may be costly to continue to deal and talk, but given that one is talking, it is just as costless to say "everything looks great" as it is to say "we are not optimistic." Legal scholars of all stripes have been extremely concerned that unless the law imposes liability for the failure to trade after optimistic or promise-like cheap talk, there will be an incentive for either careless or intentional overoptimism in such talk.Indeed, it is this general concern which generates the near consensus view that the court in Hoffman v. Red Owl Storeswas correct in holding the franchisor liable on a theory of promissory estoppel. But this widely held view reflects an implicit assumption about the courtship or contract formation process: Courtship is mostly about conflict, with each side trying to get the best of the other, to take advantage in whatever way possible of every potential contracting party it encounters. As my brief introductory description indicates, I take this picture to be badly incomplete and hence, misleading. Courtship is, in part, a process by which one party tries to gain a strategic advantage over the other so as to get the best terms possible if a deal is struck. But it is also a process in which the parties have a common interest in learning whether a deal is indeed in their mutual interest. Courtship is costly, and each party has an incentive to incur those costs if and only if doing so will increase the chances of a profitable trade.
Dealmaking is thus a complex process involving both conflicting and common interests. As a general proposition, when the parties have at least some interests in common, even cheap talk - talk that involves no direct cost - may be credible and informative.When a speaker is held legally liable for damages if trade does not occur after the speaker makes a promissory (or more generally) optimistic statement in courtship, that message is, as an economic matter, no longer cheap talk.
From the standpoint of efficiency, whether the law of contract formation gets it "right" depends on whether the law is such that liability is usually imposed only when the risk of liability is necessary to create a private incentive for informative pretrade talk - when, that is, cheap talk would be uninformative. The analysis developed in this Article generates two central results. First, parties' mutual interest in minimizing wasteful expense in investigating and negotiating when there is in fact no possibility of mutually beneficial trade often generates private incentives for informative cheap talk about the likelihood of trade. Even when talk is cheap (and there is no risk of legal liability), private incentives do not systematically favor wildly optimistic assurances that a deal is near. By this same token, optimistic statements that accurately reflect the course ofdealmaking up to the point they were made may often go unfulfilled simply because the parties gather new information and become more pessimistic about the chances of doing the deal. On the other hand, the analysis also shows that there are circumstances which generate incentives for misleadingly optimistic pretrade communication, such as when a seller with relatively high costs (and reservation price) faces potential buyers who have relatively high costs of investigating and bargaining. In these circumstances, potential legal liability for unfulfilled optimistic talk (making that talk no longer cheap) may create an incentive for informative pretrade communication when one would otherwise not exist. However this Article's second central analytical result is that only particular kinds of legal liability regimes are likely to enhance private incentives for informative pretrade talk. In particular, if it is the literal content of a pretrade statement which triggers legal liability, then liability concerns will motivate actors to alter the literal content of what they say. But the equilibrium meaning that rational market participants attach to these statements, and hence the statements' informativeness, will be unaffected. Liability for misleading (or more accurately, concealing) talk - assurances that are literally overoptimistic in light of what the speaker knew at the time she made the assurance - may enhance incentives for informative pretrade communication. But this is true only if the legal decisionmaker is sufficiently accurate in determining whether messages were indeed misleading when sent. When the legal decisionmaker errs too badly in making this determination, liability for concealing talk may actually worsen private incentives.
My approach to the economics of contract formation departs quite dramatically from existing work on this topic. Previous analysis has focused on how legal liability for precontractual reliance expenditures affects the parties' incentives to make such expenditures optimally.What drives this analysis is the supposition that early reliance expenditures may be desirable because they increase the value of the contract to both parties if a contract is indeed made. This analysis recognizes, however, that such expenditures should be made based on the actual probability of agreement at different stages of the process. The expected division of the gains from trade, should trade occur, may affect such incentives, and hence legal liability for wasted reliance expenditures may be justified because a party with a weak bargaining position would otherwise not incur such expenses.As for the form of legal liability, strict liability for failure to reach agreement generally creates too great an incentive to incur early reliance expenditures, so an intermediate liability regime emerges as best.
This literature is part of a well-established tradition in both economics and law and economics, which focuses on how contractual incompleteness and the law remedying that incompleteness with default damage rules of one sort or another affects incentives to make relationship-specific investments that enhance the value of the relationship.This literature does not capture what I believe to be most fundamental in the precontractual liability cases. These cases do involve relationship-specific costs, and they sometimes involve partial performance and an investment in the relationship.But even when pretrade costs are incurred by beginning performance, their primary function is not to enhance the value of performance, but rather, to determine whether there will be a relationship at all, and if so, upon what terms.They are the costs of courtship, incurred to determine whether a match will occur, andwhether the costs will be incurred depends strongly upon the parties' ability to communicate information during the process. None of the work in the existing tradition explores how the law might affect the incentive to communicate during courtship, and how those incentives might affect the efficiency of the courtship process. This Article aims to remedy this gap in the economic analysis of contract law.
The new economic approach to the analysis of the contract formation process developed in this Article has significant and wide-ranging doctrinal implications. Although of great practical significance, the law that determines liability for pretrade communications made while engaged in complex dealmaking has been subject to very little detailed analysis by commentators and is poorly understood by courts and commentators alike. This is indicated even by the terminology used to describe such liability, as involving precontractual negotiations or preliminary agreements labels which on my functional approach tend to put the cart before the horse by presuming that there is not "agreement" rather than equating "agreement" with potential liability.
That this is a muddy area of law is widely and explicitly recognized. In commenting on the relatively undeveloped state of the Illinois case law, Judge Richard Posner recently observed that "one of the most difficult areas of contract law concerns the enforceability of letters of intent and other preliminary agreements."Professor E. Allan Farnsworth lists the expansion of potential liability for precontractual negotiations and preliminary agreements as one of the top three developments in contract law during the 1980s,and yet at the same time observes that this body of law is "unfamiliar to many lawyers, who are steeped in traditional contract analysis" and "relatively undeveloped, even on grounds that are already recognized."Farnsworth argues that there are four legal theories which may ground pretrade liability: 1) unjust enrichment; 2) misrepresentation; 3) promise; and 4) generalobligations arising out of negotiations themselves.He has analyzed in some detail how these different theories may apply to ground liability in a spectrum of situations ranging from those where there is no agreement but just negotiations, to those where there is some form of preliminary agreement, to those in which there is an agreement.
In the analysis below, I cut the cases rather differently. Unsurprisingly, most of the reported decisions involving pretrade liability in complex dealmaking have arisen in the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit and involve New York law, and I therefore focus my analysis below on decisions from that circuit.In analyzing these decisions in light of my functional, economic approach, I have found it most useful to distinguish simply between two theories of liability for pretrade communication: those based on agreement and those that are not agreement-based. At least in this context - that of pretrade liability - I believe that not only misrepresentation and unjust enrichment but also promissory estoppel are theories that attach liability as an alternative to finding agreement. I thus take promissory estoppel to be primarily a form of nonpromissory liability. This view differs markedly from much recent scholarship on promissory estoppel, which has argued that promissory estoppel liability is primarily triggered by a promise under circumstances where consideration and/or offer and acceptance fail for technical reasons.I argue to the contrary that what triggers promissory estoppel-based liability in the pretrade communication context is performance, not talk. Seeing this is crucial to understanding both the surprising efficiency of promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment in this context and the difficulties with the legal test for agreement.
To set the stage, this Article begins in Part I by recalling some quite well known contract formation cases. These cases present a continuum, beginning with the early stages of courtship and progressing to the final stages. At the early stage, the issue is whether a communication is an offer or merely a solicitation. At later stages, when parties begin to incur substantial costs in reliance upon a number of encouraging statements, the legal issue becomes whether reliance itself ought to justify some form of legal relief based on promissory estoppel or unjust enrichment. In the final stages, the question is whether the parties have reached agreement despite their failure to execute a final written agreement. By recalling these cases in Part I, I set the stage for a rather extendedand more general analysis of incentives for informative pretrade communication in Part II. This Part develops a general model of the courtship process and incentives for informative cheap talk in this process. Part II contains a good deal of detail both on cheap talk and on general market structures that are likely to affect incentives for informative cheap talk in contract formation. My discussion of market structure amounts to a brief tour through alternative selling institutions that have been analyzed recently by economists and are widely observed in practice. This Part of the Article uses a simple example to demonstrate how cheap talk may be credible in courtship, and then generalizes from the example by accounting for market structure variables that determine whether private incentives induce informative or concealing cheap talk. It then considers whether alternative forms of legal liability are likely to create an incentive for informative pretrade talk when such incentives would not otherwise exist.
Part III gets to the bottom line by applying the general approach to concrete doctrinal issues. I first apply the approach to explain the doctrinal puzzle of determining whether a message sent early on in the courtship process is an offer or a solicitation. The legal default rules on this question efficiently reflect the economic function served by an asking price in different selling institutions. The exceptions to the defaults, such as Lefkowitz v. Great Minneapolis Surplus Store,are analyzed in a new way, by asking whether they arose under market conditions where there is likely to be a very strong incentive absent legal liability for misleading and uninformative optimism. The analysis then looks at the very final stages of complex business dealmaking and the doctrinal issue of whether liability should be imposed for failure to trade even though the parties have failed to execute the final written agreement. This is an issue that is litigated with increasing frequency and intensity, especially in the context of failed mergers and acquisitions. I extend my economic model to explain why the letter of intent, or agreement-in-principle, is typically used in the late stages of such complex dealmaking, and why its informativeness hinges upon its being nonbinding cheap talk. My model also explains why the letter of intent forecloses a very narrow set of reasons forwalking away from a deal. This economic approach generates both positive predictions and normative perspectives, and I draw some of these out by considering the Second Circuit's relatively rich case law on pretrade liability. I find positive confirmation of the model in the widespread but (for that very reason) uninformative adoption of so-called Texaco clause disclaimers in preliminary contractual documents. As a normative matter, I find that the Second Circuit's approach has been far too broad and uncertain - especially by giving general doctrinal recognition to binding preliminary agreements. Given the magnitude of the gains from trade at stake in large corporate deals, it is unlikely that this uncertainty would have more than a marginal deterrent effect on the size of the market; on the other hand, given that this broad approach likely generates no more information in courtship than would be provided under the no-liability default rule I advocate, the current doctrine amounts to an unnecessary tax on dealmaking, a transfer from stockholders and other stakeholders to lawyers.
Part III concludes by evaluating the application of promissory estoppel and quantum meruit in the pretrade liability context. Central to my analysis is the observation that what triggers liability in this context is not just reliance - such as hiring lawyers and engaging in other costs of courtship - but performance that is common knowledge to both parties. From a functional, economic point of view, the distinction is crucial, for performance is likely to involve significantly higher costs and result only when it is the most efficient means of determining whether trade is likely to occur. The evolving doctrine imposes liability if and only if the speaker has made an optimistic statement, observed that performance follows, and remained silent, failing to discourage further performance. This particular doctrinal approach is, I argue, likely to screen effectively for misleading optimism by making expected liability track the speaker's actual belief as to the probability of a deal. It should thus force such actual pessimists to engage in informative talk when they would not otherwise do so.
In Part IV, I conclude by sketching some other potential applications of cheap talk economics to contract law and by discussing very briefly the relationship between notions of meaning and equilibrium in the economic theory of cheap talk games and similar notions in the philosophy of language.

questions.question: When parties negotiate complex, highly differentiated transactions, do their private incentives lead them to send truthful and informative low-cost (cheap) pre-contractual communications, or do those incentives systematically favor misleadingly optimistic assurances?

Does imposing legal liability for unfulfilled optimistic pre-contractual communications make such communications more informative and improve the efficiency of dealmaking, and how does that effect depend on the type of liability rule and the accuracy of legal fact-finding?

How do market and institutional features (for example, investigation and bargaining costs and different selling mechanisms) affect whether informative cheap talk will arise privately or whether legal intervention is needed to induce informative pre-contractual communication?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
Can computational methods (noncooperative game theory, neural nets) provide substantive tests or empirical support for enforcement decisions and doctrinal choices in contract law?
Do no-binding-effect clauses (express statements that parties do not intend legal obligations) prevent courts from finding enforceable agreements in practice?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Can default liability rules be designed to induce socially optimal precontractual reliance, and what informational burdens would such rules place on adjudicators?
Should courts treat a party's judicial admission that an agreement exists as sufficient to overcome formal writing requirements like the Statute of Frauds?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?
What duty of fair dealing (if any) should govern precontractual negotiations, and what remedies should be available for breaches of that duty?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Is imposing a judicially enforced duty to negotiate in good faith necessary to achieve efficient outcomes in preliminary agreements, or would protecting reliance expenditures suffice?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do market and institutional features affect whether informative 'cheap talk' will arise privately or require legal intervention to induce accurate precontractual communication?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 56clevstlrev37!!ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND THE PROTECTION OF INTERPERSONAL TRUST
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AND THE PROTECTION OF INTERPERSONAL TRUST

shared_topics.topic: the justificatory scope of promissory estoppel (when and why the law should enforce noncontractual promises)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promissory estoppel as the doctrinal mechanism for protecting reliance and trust in broken promises and asks how far that protection should extend; Paper B treats promissory estoppel as one of the principal non-agreement theories that can impose pretrade liability and analyzes when such liability is efficient in the courtship/dealmaking context.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between reliance, expectation/ trust, and legal enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes interpersonal trust from trust in legal enforcement and interrogates whether reliance grounded in either kind of trust should be legally protected; Paper B models how parties' reliance expenditures and optimistic precontractual statements (expectations) interact with liability rules and whether enforcement of those expectations alters incentives to communicate and invest.

shared_topics.topic: the normative tradeoff between protecting promisees and avoiding inefficient/naive overreliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for protecting an 'optimal'—not maximal—level of interpersonal trust to deter reckless or naive reliance; Paper B investigates when imposing liability for unfulfilled optimistic statements reduces wasteful negotiation costs versus when it imposes unnecessary transaction costs or distorted incentives, drawing a similar efficiency-based balancing.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal criteria and judicial tests for imposing liability on precontractual statements or conduct
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys case law and proposes a spectrum of factual situations in which courts should extend promissory estoppel protection (e.g., constrained parties, long relationships) and when they should not; Paper B examines how courts (especially in the Second Circuit) have framed offer/solicitation, letters of intent, and pretrade liability, and critiques which doctrinal rules best screen for misleading optimism.

shared_topics.topic: the role of information costs and verifiability in deciding when legal protection is appropriate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A conditions protection on whether promisees could cheaply discover untrustworthiness or take low-cost precautions, making information/verification central to its test; Paper B explicitly models cheap talk and shows how asymmetric information, investigation costs, and verifiability shape incentives for truthful or misleading pretrade communication and when liability can improve informativeness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 23geomasonlrev125!!ARTICLE: "PROVE ME WRONG" CASES AND CONSIDERATION THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: "PROVE ME WRONG" CASES AND CONSIDERATION THEORY

shared_topics.topic: the role of promissory estoppel as a substitute for consideration in enforcing nontraditional promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats promissory estoppel as a principal form of non-agreement-based liability in pretrade communications and analyzes when it efficiently steps in to enforce or deter misleading optimism; Paper B argues that prove-me-wrong promises typically lack consideration and therefore should usually be enforced (if at all) under promissory estoppel rather than traditional consideration doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: when precontractual statements or conditional promises generate legal liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when optimistic pretrade communications (letters of intent, assurances) ought to trigger liability and how different liability regimes affect incentives for informative talk; Paper B examines judicial criteria for holding prove-me-wrong statements enforceable and whether such conditional promises should be treated as binding unilateral offers or nonbinding statements requiring another doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: reliance or performance as the factual trigger for liability and its evidentiary/functional significance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that actual performance (and its common knowledge) and reliance during courtship often trigger promissory estoppel or quantum meruit liability and serve as a screening device for misleading optimism; Paper B insists that enforceability of prove-me-wrong promises should typically depend on whether the promisee relied (and injustice would result), tying liability to reliance/performance rather than mere verbal assent.

shared_topics.topic: the legal distinction between offers (including unilateral/reward-like offers) and mere solicitations/cheap talk
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the offer-versus-solicitation line in early courtship and how market context and message function should influence that legal classification; Paper B focuses on whether prove-me-wrong promises constitute unilateral offers supported by consideration (analogous to reward offers) or are instead non-contractual assertions.

shared_topics.topic: promises and public statements as credibility signals or informational devices in transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models pretrade communications as cheap talk that can be informative or misleading depending on incentives and legal rules, stressing the signaling role of assurances; Paper B explicitly describes prove-me-wrong promises as attempts to signal confidence in a factual claim and interrogates the legal consequences of that signaling.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41stanlrev661!!ARTICLE: The Jurisprudence of Classification.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Jurisprudence of Classification.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal classification at the contract/tort boundary and precontractual liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a functional taxonomy (agreement-based vs non-agreement-based liability) to sort pretrade remedies like promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment, and critiques muddled case law; Paper B examines the general problem of legal classification with special attention to the contract/tort boundary and how doctrinal categories determine when harms are treated under contract versus tort regimes.

shared_topics.topic: how legal categories and definitions shape parties' incentives and legal outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how rules (e.g., what counts as an offer, when optimistic talk triggers liability) alter negotiating behavior and the credibility of precontractual communications; Paper B argues more broadly that the ways lawyers and courts classify doctrines create realities that structure legal reasoning and the consequences of legal rules.

shared_topics.topic: the legal status and enforceability of preliminary agreements and precontractual communications
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes letters of intent, agreement-in-principle, Texaco-style disclaimers, and when preliminary statements should be treated as binding or nonbinding; Paper B treats the classification of such doctrinal categories (including preliminary contractual forms) as central to resolving disputes about enforceability and the appropriate doctrinal response.

shared_topics.topic: critical assessment and reform proposals for doctrinal practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the Second Circuit's expansive and uncertain approach to pretrade liability and proposes economically grounded default rules and doctrinal tests; Paper B criticizes existing classification accounts and offers alternative paradigmatic approaches intended to improve doctrinal clarity and practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 57uclalrev669!!Article: The Many Faces of Promissory Estoppel: An Empirical Analysis Under the Restatement (Second) of Contracts
compared_to.partner_title: Article: The Many Faces of Promissory Estoppel: An Empirical Analysis Under the Restatement (Second) of Contracts

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel as a tool for imposing precontractual liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promissory estoppel as one of the principal doctrines courts use to impose liability for optimistic pretrade communications in the absence of a formal contract; Paper B empirically studies hundreds of post‑Restatement (Second) cases showing how promissory estoppel is actually invoked and litigated across jurisdictions.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal/ normative basis of promissory estoppel (promise vs reliance vs equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A theorizes about whether promissory estoppel should be understood as promise‑based or as a non‑agreement remedy tied to performance and reliance, while Paper B empirically examines how judges conceptualize promissory estoppel (promise, reliance, equity, or contractual) and finds that courts often require both promise and reliance.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules and remedies shape incentives in negotiations and dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic model showing how different liability regimes for pretrade talk alter incentives for informative vs misleading cheap talk during courtship, and Paper B shows empirically that the way courts award remedies (often expectation damages) and conceptualize the cause of action affects litigants' practical incentives to bring claims and how parties fare.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability of preliminary communications (offers, solicitations, letters of intent, and bindingness)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes when early communications and letters of intent should be treated as solicitations, offers, or binding preliminary agreements and the efficiency tradeoffs of treating them as binding, while Paper B demonstrates that courts, through promissory estoppel, often treat preliminary promises as enforceable and sometimes award contractual‑style remedies, effectively enforcing such communications.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92columlrev1358!!ARTICLE: THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES. Copyright © 1992 by Melvin Aron Eisenberg.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THIRD-PARTY BENEFICIARIES. Copyright © 1992 by Melvin Aron Eisenberg.

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of promises by non‑parties (third‑party beneficiaries and pretrade claimants)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when a person who is not a contracting party should be allowed to enforce a contract (the third‑party beneficiary problem) and develops principles for that enforcement; Paper B analyzes liability for precontractual communications and treats doctrines like promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment as mechanisms to impose obligations on non‑contracting parties during dealmaking.

shared_topics.topic: balancing formal doctrinal stability against social/economic policy and efficiency
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the choice between following stated common‑law rules and updating them according to social propositions (social congruence vs doctrinal stability); Paper B evaluates contract formation doctrine in light of economic efficiency and incentives, arguing the law should allow or limit liability where it promotes informative communication in market dealmaking.

shared_topics.topic: when nontraditional communications or documents (letters of intent, optimistic assurances) become legally binding
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates how classical doctrinal rules have constrained and later expanded nontraditional bases for enforcement (e.g., exceptions to strict privity) and develops principles for when outsiders can enforce promises; Paper B focuses on the enforceability of preliminary agreements, letters of intent, and optimistic pretrade 'cheap talk,' analyzing when such communications should attract liability.

shared_topics.topic: reliance or performance as the trigger for imposing liability absent formal contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines doctrines and defenses that determine when third parties or promisees can obtain relief based on the promisor's obligations (including reliance‑based doctrines); Paper B argues that in pretrade contexts liability is often triggered by observable reliance or performance (not mere talk) and analyzes how reliance/performance should be treated to promote efficient communication.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88washlrev1287!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT STORIES: IMPORTANCE OF THE CONTEXTUAL APPROACH TO LAW
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT STORIES: IMPORTANCE OF THE CONTEXTUAL APPROACH TO LAW

shared_topics.topic: contextual, functional analysis of contract law rather than formalistic rule parsing
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes orthodox, rule-focused contract analysis and develops a functional economic model of precontractual ‘courtship’ that examines market structure, incentives, and facts; Paper B advocates a narrative-contextual pedagogy that situates doctrinal rules within the factual, social, economic, and historical context in which contracts operate.

shared_topics.topic: the role and legal treatment of precontractual communications, preliminary agreements, and letters of intent in real-world dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A gives sustained doctrinal and economic analysis of letters of intent, agreement‑in‑principle, promissory estoppel, and when pretrade talk should generate liability; Paper B stresses teaching contracts through real transactional stories and modern contract practices, aiming to expose students to how preliminary agreements and negotiation practices function in practice and influence legal outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the need to reform doctrine and pedagogy so law better matches practice and market realities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes doctrinal defaults and liability rules calibrated to economic incentives of dealmaking to avoid unnecessary deterrence of trade; Paper B argues for transformative (or at least incremental) reforms in legal education—curriculum, casebooks, and teaching methods—to better prepare students for practical, market-driven contract practice.

shared_topics.topic: bridging doctrinal analysis with interdisciplinary methods to improve understanding and application of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A integrates economics and game-theoretic ‘cheap talk’ analysis into doctrinal evaluation of contract formation and liability; Paper B integrates narrative theory, contextual scholarship, and comparative legal-education models to enrich doctrinal teaching and connect legal rules to empirical and institutional realities.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62ukanlrev315!!ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses

shared_topics.topic: when precontractual communications create legal liability (offer vs solicitation, letters of intent, promissory estoppel, unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on the boundary between mere negotiation and legal obligation: Paper A analyzes when pretrade statements or letters of intent should generate liability (distinguishing offers, solicitations, and non-agreement-based liability like promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment), and Paper B engages the same boundary by examining how formation doctrines (grounded in consideration) interact with doctrines that deny or permit enforcement during formation.

shared_topics.topic: normative and policy justification for doctrines governing precontractual conduct (efficiency, incentives to communicate and investigate)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic efficiency account—when liability should be imposed to create appropriate incentives for informative cheap talk and investigation—while Paper B defends consideration as the proper policy basis for formation rules and formation defenses, assessing which doctrinal rules best serve policy goals in formation contexts.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal relationship and hierarchy among formation doctrines (consideration, assent, promissory estoppel, misrepresentation, duress, mistake, unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze how multiple doctrines interrelate in formation: Paper A distinguishes agreement-based doctrines from non-agreement-based ones (treating promissory estoppel and unjust enrichment as alternatives to finding agreement), and Paper B argues that consideration is doctrinally primary and that other formation defenses should be understood relative to it rather than to a freestanding doctrine of assent.

shared_topics.topic: the significance of reliance/performance as the factual trigger for imposing precontractual liability
shared_topics.justification: Both works identify reliance or performance as central to when courts should attach liability: Paper A emphasizes that observable performance (and common-knowledge reliance) is what typically triggers promissory-estoppel/quantum-meruit relief in pretrade disputes, and Paper B locates the formation defenses and the operation of consideration in factual patterns where reliance/performance and the presence or absence of exchange bear on whether contractual liability should follow.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 9geomasonlrev99!!ARTICLE: THE SOPHISTICATED DOCTRINE OF CONSIDERATION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SOPHISTICATED DOCTRINE OF CONSIDERATION

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel and enforcement of precontractual promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models promissory estoppel as a form of non-agreement-based liability in pretrade communications and analyzes when it efficiently induces informative cheap talk; Paper B traces historical instances where courts effectively enforced promises (what we now call promissory estoppel) by bending or bypassing consideration, showing how such doctrines operated to make promises actionable.

shared_topics.topic: use of unjust enrichment / quasi‑contract to police negotiations and costly reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats unjust enrichment and quantum meruit alongside promissory estoppel as alternative bases for pretrade liability and evaluates their role in constraining misleading optimism during courtship; Paper B documents sixteenth‑century decisions where judges invoked quasi‑contractual remedies or moral obligation to enforce promises despite the absence of consideration.

shared_topics.topic: how contract doctrines shape parties' incentives during bargaining and dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly analyzes how liability rules (or their absence) affect incentives to send informative versus misleading cheap talk and to incur costly investigation or performance during courtship; Paper B argues that the historical flexibility of consideration doctrine operated instrumentally—permitting enforcement in some cases—to shape when parties could rely on promises and thus influence bargaining behavior.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal boundaries of enforceability (offer/acceptance, consideration, agreement) in preliminary negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the offer-versus-solicitation distinction, letters of intent, and when preliminary communications should trigger liability or be treated as nonbinding cheap talk; Paper B analyzes how early common‑law judges used (and at times relaxed) the consideration requirement and mutual‑assent concepts to define which promises were legally actionable during negotiation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71cornelllrev1!!ARTICLE: REAL ESTATE SALES AND THE NEW IMPLIED WARRANTY OF LAWFUL USE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: REAL ESTATE SALES AND THE NEW IMPLIED WARRANTY OF LAWFUL USE.

shared_topics.topic: liability for precontractual statements and representations (misrepresentation, promissory estoppel, unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when and how legal doctrines like misrepresentation, promissory estoppel, and unjust enrichment should attach liability for optimistic or misleading pretrade communications in complex dealmaking; Paper B traces courts' expansion of misrepresentation-based liability in real estate sales and considers replacing or supplementing tort doctrines with an implied contractual warranty of lawful use.

shared_topics.topic: legal rules shaping incentives to disclose information and cure information asymmetries between buyers and sellers
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how legal liability (or lack thereof) for cheap talk alters parties' incentives to communicate during the courtship phase and when private incentives produce informative disclosure, while Paper B examines how caveat emptor, nondisclosure, and emerging duties (including an implied warranty) affect sellers' incentives to reveal unlawful uses and buyers' ability to learn material facts.

shared_topics.topic: normative evaluation of doctrinal design to promote efficient transactions and commercial certainty
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates which liability regimes promote informative pretrade talk and minimize wasteful negotiation costs, yielding normative recommendations about default rules for preliminary agreements; Paper B argues that an implied warranty of lawful use would better reconcile buyer and seller interests, simplify disputes, and produce greater commercial certainty than current tort-based approaches.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance, performance, and remedies for wasted or disappointed expectations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on reliance expenditures and performance as triggers for liability (arguing promissory estoppel often hinges on performance), and examines optimal damage rules for pretrade reliance; Paper B discusses buyers' reliance on existing land uses, the limited relief available under tort doctrines (rescission, restitution, unmarketable title), and how an implied warranty would better allocate remedies for disappointed buyers.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20seattleulrev45!!ARTICLE: The Four Phases of Promissory Estoppel
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Four Phases of Promissory Estoppel

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel as a basis for precontractual liability in negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A maps the doctrine's doctrinal development and case law use to enforce promises and assurances made during dealings, while Paper B analyzes promissory estoppel in the ‘courtship’ context, treating it as a form of non-agreement-based liability that litigates when pretrade assurances and subsequent performance make liability appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance (detrimental reliance) and the choice between expectation and reliance remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces promissory estoppel back to 'reliance consideration' and catalogues how courts award reliance, expectation, restitution or equitable remedies across doctrines; Paper B models how parties incur pretrade reliance costs, explores when liability should compensate wasted reliance expenditures, and evaluates which damage regimes produce efficient incentives.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal classification problem: contract, tort, equity, or hybrid approaches to promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A's central thesis is that promissory estoppel evolved through estoppel, contract, tort, and equity phases and resists simple categorization; Paper B engages the same puzzle in the pretrade setting by contrasting agreement-based theories with non-agreement theories (misrepresentation, unjust enrichment, promise/promissory estoppel) and arguing for a functional taxonomy.

shared_topics.topic: how legal rules about precontractual statements shape parties' incentives to communicate (informative vs misleading 'cheap talk')
shared_topics.justification: Paper B develops a game-theoretic model showing when cheap talk is informative and when legal liability for optimistic assurances improves or worsens information transmission, while Paper A documents how courts and equitable remedies have been used to police assurances and reliance in commercial negotiations, thereby affecting parties' expectations and willingness to rely on precontractual communications.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 88washlrev1287!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT STORIES: IMPORTANCE OF THE CONTEXTUAL APPROACH TO LAW
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTRACTS IN THE REAL WORLD: ESSAY: CONTRACT STORIES: IMPORTANCE OF THE CONTEXTUAL APPROACH TO LAW

shared_topics.topic: contextualizing contract law (economic, market, and factual context)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops an economic, market-structure account of precontractual communications and argues that the informativeness of 'cheap talk' and the proper legal response depend on transactional context; Paper B champions a narrative, contextual approach to teaching contract law that situates doctrines within cultural, economic, and factual settings so students can understand how rules operate in real-world transactions.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal indeterminacy in contract formation and the need for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents muddled doctrine around pretrade liability, letters of intent, and promissory estoppel and proposes economically grounded refinements; Paper B emphasizes the law's flexibility and continuity across eras and argues for pedagogical and institutional reforms to better handle the indeterminacy of modern contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: case-law and precedent as the vehicle for understanding and shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes concrete appellate decisions (especially Second Circuit/New York cases) to evaluate how courts treat offers, solicitations, and precontractual liability; Paper B argues for using iconic and modern cases woven into stories as the primary method to teach how contract rules develop and apply.

shared_topics.topic: connecting contract doctrine to legal practice and real-world transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on high-stakes, complex dealmaking (mergers, letters of intent, M&A) and draws normative implications about how law should structure incentives in practice; Paper B frames reforming legal education and case teaching to better prepare students for the complexities of contemporary contract practice and to make doctrine more practically useful.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38flastulrev709!!ARTICLE: SEPARATING CONTRACT AND PROMISE
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SEPARATING CONTRACT AND PROMISE

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing contract from promise and the consequences for enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly argues for conceptually separating contractual obligations from private promises and examines how treating contracts as promises obscures important differences; Paper A engages this issue empirically and doctrinally by asking whether doctrines like promissory estoppel operate as promise-based liability or instead function as non-agreement-based tools in precontractual dealmaking.

shared_topics.topic: the role of communicative acts (assurances, offers, cheap talk) in creating expectations and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models precontractual communications as cheap talk that transmits information (or conceals it) during 'courtship' and analyzes when such speech is credible or should induce reliance; Paper B likewise focuses on the communicative character of promises and contracts—how commitments are conveyed and how those communications relate to authority and expectation.

shared_topics.topic: when preliminary statements become legally binding (offer vs solicitation, letters of intent, promissory estoppel, unjust enrichment)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes doctrinal tests (offer/solicitation, binding preliminary agreements, letters of intent) and the conditions under which courts should impose liability for pretrade statements; Paper B interrogates the underlying assumption that contractual communication equals a binding promise and thus bears on how and why legal rules treat preliminary statements as enforceable or not.

shared_topics.topic: normative tradeoffs of imposing liability for precontractual statements: moral voluntariness versus efficiency and incentives
shared_topics.justification: Paper B emphasizes the moral importance of voluntariness in private promises and suggests contracts lack that voluntary moral character; Paper A examines the efficiency and incentive effects of imposing legal liability for optimistic pretrade talk, showing how liability can either improve or worsen information transmission and bargaining depending on context.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92valrev1581!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTEMPORARY POLITICAL THEORY AND PRIVATE LAW: ESSAY: CONTRACT THEORY ON AND OFF THE GRID
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTEMPORARY POLITICAL THEORY AND PRIVATE LAW: ESSAY: CONTRACT THEORY ON AND OFF THE GRID

shared_topics.topic: how contract-law rules shape private incentives and the efficiency of dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A models how different liability rules for pretrade communication (e.g., promissory estoppel, misrepresentation) alter parties' incentives to send informative cheap talk and thereby affect the efficiency of courtship and deal formation. Paper B examines whether introducing formal contract rules in developing economies will change agents' incentives to invest and transact, asking if and how contract law can causally influence economic behavior and growth.

shared_topics.topic: the role of enforcement credibility and liability in enabling transactions and market development
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the presence or absence of legal liability for optimistic assurances affects parties' willingness to incur reliance and negotiation costs and thus the probability of completing transactions. Paper B interrogates the importance of a credible third‑party enforcer (contract enforcement) for financial intermediation and broader market activity, questioning the empirical link between enforcement credibility and development.

shared_topics.topic: normative and doctrinal design of contract law institutions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers normative conclusions about which precontractual liability doctrines best promote informative communication and criticizes current doctrinal uncertainty (e.g., binding preliminary agreements). Paper B asks whether contemporary contract theories provide appropriate normative guidance for designing contract-law institutions—especially when transplanting or building such institutions in societies without established Western legal traditions.

shared_topics.topic: context‑dependence: how market structure and institutional context condition the appropriateness of contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that market structure and the specifics of selling institutions determine when cheap talk is informative and when liability improves outcomes, generating context‑specific legal recommendations. Paper B argues that the proper content and desirability of contract law depend on the broader social and institutional context, and that theories from developed‑country settings may not map straightforwardly onto different institutional environments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev132!!SYMPOSIUM: COGS OR CYBORGS?: BLASPHEMY AND IRONY IN CONTRACT THEORIES
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: COGS OR CYBORGS?: BLASPHEMY AND IRONY IN CONTRACT THEORIES

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of reliance and unjust enrichment doctrines in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Gilmore's predictive failures about the decline of reliance and unjust enrichment doctrines and interrogates why contract ideology (including those doctrines) has persisted; Paper B analyzes how promissory estoppel (reliance) and unjust enrichment operate in pretrade contexts, showing when each doctrine efficiently allocates liability and how performance versus mere talk triggers relief.

shared_topics.topic: precontractual communication (cheap talk), assurances, and liability in dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises the doctrinal puzzle of reliance and precontractual obligations as central failures of Gilmore's account of contracting life; Paper B develops a formal cheap-talk economic model of courtship, showing when optimistic assurances are informative or misleading and how legal rules should respond to pretrade communication.

shared_topics.topic: whether traditional contract theory adequately explains modern, interdependent dealmaking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions Gilmore's nineteenth‑century individualist account and argues for rethinking contract theory to reflect interdependence (cogs vs cyborgs) and newer social norms; Paper B critiques standard law-and-economics focus on post‑formation terms and argues that traditional analyses overlook the incentives and informational structure of modern complex dealmaking.

shared_topics.topic: bringing interdisciplinary and economic/game‑theoretic methods to theorize contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for interdisciplinary lines of work and reconceptualizations (e.g., cyborg metaphor) to guide future contract theorizing; Paper B exemplifies that approach by applying game theory (cheap talk) and market-structure economics to doctrinal questions about formation, reliance, and preliminary agreements.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75cornelllrev62!!ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT MODIFICATION AND "SELF-HELP SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE": A REACTION TO PROFESSOR NARASIMHAN.

shared_topics.topic: how legal remedies (damages vs specific performance / liability) shape parties' incentives to communicate, perform, or modify agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how imposing liability for pre‑trade statements (versus leaving them as cheap talk) alters incentives to send informative or misleading communications during negotiation; Paper B analyzes how the availability or denial of specific performance (as opposed to damages) affects parties' incentives to seek, accept, or contest contract modifications and to engage in 'self‑help' strategies.

shared_topics.topic: opportunistic strategic behavior in contracting (seller extortion, buyer opportunism) and the role of law in deterring it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies circumstances that generate incentives for misleadingly optimistic pretrade talk (a form of opportunism) and when legal liability should deter such conduct; Paper B examines scenarios of seller bad faith (demanding a modification) and potential buyer opportunism (accepting then later contesting a modification), and whether the law appropriately deters or channels those behaviors.

shared_topics.topic: when preliminary communications or alterations are legally binding (enforceability of letters of intent, offers, and modifications)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages deeply with the doctrinal line between solicitation, offer, letters of intent, and when promissory estoppel or unjust enrichment should substitute for agreement; Paper B confronts the doctrinal question whether post‑contract modifications are enforceable or defeasible and under what standards a modification can be challenged.

papers.node_id: 96nwulrev39!!ARTICLE:CONTRACT RECONCEIVED
papers.title: ARTICLE:CONTRACT RECONCEIVED
papers.abstract:
The context of exchange determines the substance exchanged, and context is the expression of relation. That conception of the province of Contract reformulates doctrine in a way that implies the operation and cooperation of the elements of exchange in a manner not appreciated by the current models. The revised perspective, a reconception of the substance and function of the basic building blocks of Contract, reveals the evanescent but, paradoxically, substantial foundation of the law governing the enforcement of promises. Principles of philosophical naturalism confirm the coherence of this reconception.
We have a good deal to learn from conceiving of Contract as akin to science - from formulating the fit between Contract jurisprudence and the "scientific" form of inquiry to reveal the limits of our explanations for why and when promises bind.While there is a developed vocabulary to informthe Contracts pedagogy,the lack of descriptive (and prescriptive) precision frustrates efforts to order Contract theory in a manner that would distinguish change from progress.When the object of scientific inquiry provides a template, the fabric of Contract becomes manifest in epistemological patterns that accommodate a richer sense of the fit among the values, principles, and rules that inform resolution of recurring controversies.
You get the sense from Paul Hoyningen-Huene's construction of science:
The following may be said about all science, whenever conducted:

questions.question: Whether and how the context of an exchange (the relational setting in which promises are made) determines the substantive content of what is exchanged and thereby affects when promises are legally enforceable.

Whether conceiving the law governing promises in the epistemological form of scientific inquiry-drawing on principles of philosophical naturalism-provides a more coherent, precise framework for explaining the foundations and limits of contract enforcement.

matched_themes: When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 86marqlrev701!!ARTICLE:CONVENTIONAL MORAL OBLIGATION PRINCIPLE UNDULY LIMITS QUALIFIED BENEFICIARY CONTRARY TO CASE LAW
papers.title: ARTICLE:CONVENTIONAL MORAL OBLIGATION PRINCIPLE UNDULY LIMITS QUALIFIED BENEFICIARY CONTRARY TO CASE LAW
papers.abstract:
The conventional American moral obligation principle supports enforcement of a promise to pay for a past benefit received by a promisor from a promisee when necessary to prevent injustice. In fact, this exception to the past consideration rule adopted byfalls short of the broader moral obligation principle expressed in decisions that have enforced promises for benefits received by persons other than the promisor. A number of legal commentators have suggested that a more expansive principle seems to exist in the case law,but, past that generalization, no study has fleshed out the case law in a systematic way to elaborate the range of qualified beneficiaries covered by the principle as found in American legal precedent of the past two centuries. The interrelated purposes of this study are to first set out the development of the conventional principle adopted by the restaters, and second to demonstrate case law support in legal history for a broader structured principle that encompasses benefits received by third parties. The resistance in some jurisdictions to acceptance of a broader principle resides in unease overits potentially sprawling reach. This study of the wider principle found in decisional law should exhibit to the common law mind that the moral obligation principle is neither as amorphous as its civil law analogue nor as extensive in its application.
It is perhaps understandable that the second restaters were cautious in their articulation of a moral obligation principle, in that the first Restatement's conservative Reporter Williston had not admitted any departure from the reactionary position that appeared in many jurisdictions by the second quarter of the Nineteenth Century.The Restatement Second's enunciation of a principle did aid in bringing along jurisdictions that had not strayed from Williston's position;but the downside was in the potential restraint on jurisdictions that had applied, or would be inclined to apply, a principle broader than that contained in section 86. Fused courts of law and equity had lent ongoing support for a broader principle in concert with natural law and civilian ideas inherited from the early republican period. However, the Restatement Second's limited principle belied this support. Indeed, a myth perpetuated by the restatements was the denial of the extent to which a significant number of American courts have subscribed to natural and civil law ideas in their articulation of contract doctrine.These courts provide a model for courts of other jurisdictions in the realization of their roles as fused republican courts of law and equity.
Undoubtedly, the majority of jurisdictions do not currently support some of the applications of the moral obligation principle covered in this study. The moral obligation ideas drawn from the developing case law are presented here in a manner similar to the approach of the second restaters in section 86. The intent is not to state the principle in terms of majority and minority positions, but rather to set out the structure of abroader principle for modern courts to draw from to realize just results consistent with community expectations.This study is broken down into a legal history of the conventional view, which is followed by an ordered elaboration of decisional authority in support of a more extensive moral obligation principle. Part II pursues the legal history of the conventional principle adopted by the restaters as a means to understanding how a doctrinal reaction to Mansfield's natural law ideas unduly narrowed that principle. That halted development, and indeed regression, will provide a point of departure for the remainder of the study. Part III explores decisions that have applied the moral obligation principle when the beneficiary was someone other than the promisor; binding the promisor was in fulfillment of community expectations of binding reciprocal moral obligations to reimburse promisees for benefits received primarily by promisor's dependents and loved ones. Case law authority was occasionally obscured by judicial manipulation of the doctrine of consideration without admission of any departure from the past consideration rule, but an analysis of the facts will illuminate what in reality is accomplished.

questions.question: Whether promises to pay for past benefits should be enforceable when the benefit was received by someone other than the promisor (i.e., whether moral-obligation-based enforcement should extend to third-party beneficiaries).

Whether historical American judicial decisions support a broader moral-obligation principle-extending enforceability to such third-party beneficiaries-than is commonly articulated in conventional doctrine.
Whether adopting a broader moral-obligation enforcement rule would produce just and predictable outcomes consistent with community expectations without being unduly expansive or vague.
