papers.node_id: 100columlrev94!!ARTICLE:FROM THE WILL THEORY TO THE PRINCIPLE OF PRIVATE AUTONOMY: LON FULLER'S "CONSIDERATION AND FORM"
papers.title: ARTICLE:FROM THE WILL THEORY TO THE PRINCIPLE OF PRIVATE AUTONOMY: LON FULLER'S "CONSIDERATION AND FORM"
papers.abstract:
Lon Fuller's "Consideration and Form" originated a scheme for the analysis of contract questions based on multiple formal and substantive considerations, with "the principle of private autonomy" first among equals. This Article places Fuller's scheme in the context of the critique of the nineteenth-century will theory of contracts and the rise of sociological jurisprudence and legal realism. Fuller built on European legal theory and on civilian contract law solutions that seemed more flexible than those provided by the objective theory of contract formation and consideration doctrine. Fuller's scheme came closer to modern policy analysis than anything in the prior literature. It nonetheless achieved only a partial synthesis, denying any place to what the writers of the time called the "social" dimension of the field and underplaying conflict among the factors he identified. These traits may be explained by the fact that he was breaking new ground and by the center-right ideological agenda he was pursuing within private law theory.
In this Article, I read Lon Fuller's "Consideration and Form"as an incident in the emergence of what I will call the "conflicting considerations" model of legal reasoning. I restrict myself to a single area within this large frame: the development of American contract theory from the publication of Holmes's The Common Law in 1880 up to the publication of Fuller's article in 1941. This will be a study of the writings of legal academics, rather than of case law, of what the Europeans call "doctrine." It will be a major theme that, during this period, American contract theory was continuously responsive to the challenges posed by European legal philosophy and by civilian contract theory, so that what I will be describing is a truly international development.
In brief, my thesis is that the current understanding of American legal academics is that each and every one of the valid legal norms that makes up our legal system (including private, public, and international law) can be understood as the product of what I will call "conflicting considerations." Every rule can be understood as representing a choice in the colloquial lawyers' sense of a "policy question." We resolve such questions by balancing conflicting considerations, and throughout this paper I will categorize these as formal, substantive, and institutional.
Formal considerations have to do with the choice between rules and standards of greater or less generality, arranged in rule/exception or rule/counter-rule configurations. Substantive considerations include conflicting utilitarian or welfarist considerations, conflicting moral principles, and conflicting rights implicated in the decision. Conflicting legal institutional considerations arise from the fact that we address the choice of a legal norm in the context of the separation of powers, federalism, the division of sovereign power among nation states and international organizations, and so forth.
At present in the U.S., I think we all agree that the conflicting considerations that are invoked in public, private, and international law disputes are analogous. There is a single underlying model of policy conflict with which we can easily contrast a model of legal necessity, or deduction, or "law," or straight "doctrine." There is an equally clear contrast with what I will call a "reconstruction project," in which a legal theorist uses preferences, rights, moral philosophy, or democratic theory to develop right answers dictated from an outside normative system.
will refer to all of these modes of arguing - formal, substantive, and institutional - as involving conflicting considerations, rather than using the word "policy," for two reasons. First, the consciousness I want to describe is a particular development of the widespread sense of elite legal academics in the first half of the twentieth century that they should replace something they loosely called "deduction" with something they loosely called "policy analysis." The particular form of analysis that triumphed was the conflicting considerations type, rather than the initially far more popular type in which a (single) policy requires a rule, much as deduction can require a rule, except in the mode of social rather than logical necessity. Second, it seems a good idea to try to avoid confusionwith the more restrictive use of the word "policy" to refer to the utilitarian subset of considerations.
The genealogical question that interests me is how we got to what I am claiming is the nearly universal elite legal academic view that we could indeed resolve all situations where there is a choice of norm by balancing conflicting considerations of one kind or another. Of course, there is a lot of conflict about whether we should balance in cases where we clearly could if we wanted to, about how often we have a choice, and even more about how we should go about balancing and what we should balance when that procedure seems appropriate. As to the significance of balancing for the rule of law, adjudication, or liberal or radical political theory, there isn't even agreement about how to conceptualize the disagreement.
For private law, I will argue, the most important respect in which the situation in 1900 differs from that in 2000 is that, in spite of their complete disagreement about the sources and ends of law, the rival schools of nineteenth -century legal theory were in agreement that there was a single primary basis of legal liability. As Pound argued persuasively in 1917, the main schools of legal theory, including natural rights (Lockean in the U.S.), metaphysical moralism (Kant), idealism (Hegel), historicism in the mode of Henry Maine (status to contract), social Darwinism, and utilitarianism, were in agreement about the crucial characteristics of modern law. The state ought to and largely did in fact define the rules of law so as to guarantee the free exercise of individual will, subject to the constraint that willing actors respect the like rights of other willing actors.This agreement existed whether or not one was a positivist in legal theory. In other words, even if you believed that the only coherent definition of law derived it from the will of the sovereign, you were overwhelmingly likely to believe that the end of the sovereign's commands should be the liberation of the individual will, subject only to the constraints necessary for everyone to have equal freedom.
This Article is devoted to showing how this understanding of contract theory came apart, and was replaced by the conflicting considerations approach. I distinguish between external and internal critiques, and between critiques that used the analysis of formal considerations - considerations of administrability - in undermining the will theory, and critiques that demonstrated the presence of other substantive policies than will within the contract core. I will have practically nothing to say here about the emergence of conflicting institutional considerations as a recognized sub-category within private law theory.
Fuller's contribution in "Consideration and Form" was to the long-term project of moving from the will theory of contractual liability to our conflicting considerations model, by arguing persuasively that, even after the demise of the will theory, a "principle of private autonomy" was and should be the key consideration in private law theory, to be harmonized with, and occasionally balanced against, a small number of counter-principles.His article superceded in a decisive way two earlier approaches to the critique of the will theory, which were either to refute it absolutely, or to subordinate it as a mere means to a "higher" goal, for example, "the social," or the "relational," and then restrict its scope, say, by excluding labor law from its ambit. The first approach annihilated the will theory, while the second left it intact within its restricted domain. Fuller, by contrast, reduced it to the status of "first among equals," even within the private law core.
don't want to claim that these were "firsts" in the sense that they had never occurred to anyone before. I do want to claim that the article is the first to manage to "stand for" these propositions. In the genealogy of the conflicting considerations model, this, rather than factual priority, is what makes an article important.
"Consideration and Form" was, however, no more than a kind of mid-point in the development of the conflicting considerations model. The reason for this is that Fuller achieved a coherent formulation of the new approach, as applied to private law, in part through the device of choosing conflicting considerations that were arguably non-ideological. In order to understand our situation at the end of the century, it would be necessary to take the story forward from Fuller's article, through the process by which the potentially threatening traces of the political that Fuller purged from his version of the core found their way back into it. In this process, the key actors after the Second World War were Friedrich Kessler, Stewart Macaulay, and Ian Macneil.
And then we would have to take up the stage that begins around 1970. At that point, contract theorists moved from setting up the conflicting considerations model to trying to supercede it, either with one or another new normatively cogent integrating model (e.g., rights, law and economics, democracy, republicanism, equality, personhood), or with one kind or another of meta-theory of the conflicting considerations model itself (e.g., critical legal studies). I don't think the common understanding of the role of policy in legal reasoning has changed much as legal theorists have pursued these projects.
Before I begin, I should indicate, although I will not pursue, the partisan orientation behind this work. One of the many themes of critical legal studies over the last 25 years has been the notion that there is such a thing as American legal consciousness, and that it has a history we can trace. Of course, if it exists it has many possible histories. The one thatI've worked to construct has been a Death of Reason narrative (a grand recit of grands recits), in which legal consciousness participates in an even more general or abstract history of American thought that in turn participates in a Western story of loss of faith. It is important that loss of faith is something that happens as an event along a rationalizing work path that transforms whatever discourse we are talking about, so that we lose faith (or don't) in reason in a world that has been transformed by reason, rationalized to the point of arbitrariness, so to speak. This is a familiar Western account; among its various bards perhaps my favorite is Horkheimer, who published his most notable version, "The End of Reason," in 1941, the year that Lon Fuller published "Consideration and Form" in this law review.
The era of reason is the title claimed by the enlightened world.
The philosophy this world produced is essentially rationalistic, but time and again, in following out its own principles, it turns against itself and takes the form of skepticism. The dogmatic or the skeptical nuance, depending on which was given the emphasis, in each case determined the relation of philosophy to social forces, and in the shifting fortunes of the ensuing struggle, the changing significance of rationality itself became manifest. The concept of reason from the very beginning included the concept of critique. Rationalism itself had established the criteria of rigidity, clarity and distinctness as the criteria of rational cognition. Skeptical and empirical doctrines opposed rationalism with these selfsame standards. The left-wing Socratic opposition branded Plato's academy a breeding place of superstition, until the latter moved toward skepticism…
Skepticism purged the idea of reason of so much of its content that today scarcely anything is left of it. Reason, in destroying conceptual fetishes, eventually destroyed itself… None of the categories of rationalism has survived… Since this opinion has pervaded every stratum of our society, it does not suffice to propagate freedom, the dignity of man or even truth. Any attempts along this line only raise the suspicion that the true reasons behind them are either held back or are entirely lacking.
This passage reflects the darkness of the year 1941, a darkness of which the reader will find no trace in "Consideration and Form." Horkheimer and Fuller seem to be characters from different worlds. For the one, the meaning of the moment, suffused in the pain and death inflicted on innocent real bodies in the camps and battlefields of Germany and Russia, is that the "progress of reason that leads to its self-destruction has come to an end; there is nothing left but barbarism or freedom."For the other, the point is that it "would… be unwise, and in a broad sense even impossible" to abolish the doctrine of consideration.
And yet Fuller's resuscitation of the will theory of contracts, which he himself had helped slay a few years earlier, seems in retrospect hard to understand without the background represented by Horkheimer. I mean that Fuller's article is part of the reaction of the liberal intelligentsia against the rise of Nazi and Soviet totalitarianism. Moreover, its politics, I will argue, represent a strand within the reaction, that of the center-right.
There is a second connection. In my mind, the history of American contract theory presents a paradigmatic case of reason unraveling itself, with "the dogmatic or the skeptical nuance, depending on which was given the emphasis, in each case determining the relation of philosophy to social forces."Since around 1970, the question has been what to do with the yarn. But the question is too close to us to permit even an attempt at an answer in the "philosophy of history" mode in which this essay is written.
Part I summarizes "Consideration and Form," introduces the conflicting considerations model, and briefly traces some elements of its history in general legal theory. Part II describes the external critique of the will theory - according to which we should subordinate it to higher values, then restrict it to the "sphere" in which it will operate to achieve those values. Part III takes up two different internal critiques of the will theory. One argues that contract law is more than will, because reasons of administrability constantly lead us to disregard will. The second argues that even if we restrict will to an appropriate sphere, according to higher motives of ethics and utility, there will be substantive considerations other than protecting will at play in deciding on contract rules. Here I explore the historical origins of Fuller's triad of private autonomy, reliance protection, and prevention of unjust enrichment, as the substantive bases of contract enforcement. In Part IV, I argue that Fuller's particular contribution came with a center-right ideological subtext, namely the expulsion of "the social" from the doctrinal core of contract law. The path of development of the conflicting considerations model in contract theory involved the reintegration of this element, understood as threateningly ideological, into that core. Throughout, I argue that "Consideration and Form" deserves its fame not because it contributes to our understanding of legal form or the doctrine of consideration, but because it moved several important incremental steps forward along the path to our present conflicting considerations consciousness, steps that had been very fully prepared by (acknowledged) previous steps.

questions.question: How and why did American contract theory shift from a will-centered account of liability to a model that resolves legal questions by balancing competing formal, substantive, and institutional considerations in the period 1880-1941?

What role did prominent academic interventions play in establishing the conflicting-considerations approach, and how did ideological commitments influence which considerations were foregrounded or excluded?

How did internal (e.g., administrability and competing substantive policies) and external (e.g., subordination to higher social values) critiques of the will-centered model contribute to reframing the core aims and justificatory criteria of contract law?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
How did Roman, Continental, and other civil-law ideas and prominent jurists influence the historical development of Anglo-American contract doctrine?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 62ukanlrev315!!ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Consideration and the Formation Defenses

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal role and primacy of consideration in contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues doctrinally, historically, and on policy grounds that consideration—not a separate element of assent—is the elemental basis for contract formation and for justifying formation defenses; Paper B centers on Lon Fuller’s defense and reworking of the consideration doctrine (and its relation to form), treating consideration as a central legal norm within the evolution of contract theory.

shared_topics.topic: the historical and doctrinal genealogy of the consideration doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A devotes a historical/doctrinal account showing that formation defenses predate and were framed with reference to consideration, while Paper B traces the development of American contract theory (Holmes to Fuller) and situates Fuller’s 'Consideration and Form' within the longer history of how consideration and related doctrines evolved.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between consideration and assent/will/private autonomy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that assent is not an independent element but is subsumed within the analysis of consideration, and Paper B examines the decline of the nineteenth‑century will theory and Fuller’s recasting of private autonomy (will) as one key consideration to be balanced with others, thereby engaging the same conceptual problem of how will/assent relates to consideration.

shared_topics.topic: policy, logic, and administrability as justificatory considerations shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops logical and policy defenses of the consideration doctrine (arguing it better explains formation defenses than assent), and Paper B explicates the 'conflicting considerations' framework—distinguishing formal/administrability and substantive policy reasons—that drove doctrinal choices about consideration and form.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction of consideration with adjacent doctrines (reliance, unjust enrichment, and formation defenses)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how doctrines like duress, misrepresentation, mistake, and unconscionability function in relation to a plaintiff’s showing of consideration, and Paper B places consideration alongside reliance protection and prevention of unjust enrichment as competing or complementary substantive bases for enforcing or denying contractual obligations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45flastulrev974!!ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Scapegoats and the Common Law: Pinnel's Case, Cumber v. Wane, and the Legal Duty Rule
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE BEST AND WORST OF CONTRACTS DECISIONS: AN ANTHOLOGY: III. THEWORST OF CONTRACTS CASES: Scapegoats and the Common Law: Pinnel's Case, Cumber v. Wane, and the Legal Duty Rule

shared_topics.topic: the doctrine of consideration and its doctrinal critiques
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the legal-duty/consideration requirement (and judicial hostility to it) as exemplified by Pinnel's Case, while Paper B analyzes Lon Fuller's 'Consideration and Form' and situates the doctrine of consideration within broader academic critiques and reform efforts.

shared_topics.topic: contract modifications and discharge of liquidated claims (Pinnel's rule / legal duty rule)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses specifically on the rule that a promise to accept less requires fresh consideration (Pinnel's Case and its progeny), and Paper B treats the doctrine of consideration — including its limits and the problems it poses for modifications and partial-payment situations — as a core issue in the move from will theory to competing-policy approaches.

shared_topics.topic: formalism (will-theory/legal duty) versus policy/‘conflicting considerations’ approaches to contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents judicial attempts to escape an allegedly antiquated formal rule (the legal-duty/consideration requirement), while Paper B traces the intellectual shift from the nineteenth‑century will theory toward Fuller's and later scholars' conflicting-considerations model that balances formal, substantive, and institutional policies.

shared_topics.topic: historical genealogy of contract doctrine and judicial/academic responses to perceived injustice or impracticality
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats the history and judicial reaction to Pinnel's Case as revealing doctrinal strain, and Paper B offers a historical account (Holmes through Fuller and beyond) of how scholars and courts reconceptualized contract principles in response to doctrinal inadequacies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of alternative doctrines (reliance, estoppel, unjust enrichment) as responses to the limits of consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how courts have sought ways to avoid harsh results of the consideration/legal-duty rule in practice, and Paper B explicates Fuller's triad — private autonomy, reliance protection, and prevention of unjust enrichment — as substantive alternatives or complements to classical consideration doctrine.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev695!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:ROUGH JUSTICE: A THEORY OF RESTITUTION AND RELIANCE, CONTRACTS AND TORTS*
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:ROUGH JUSTICE: A THEORY OF RESTITUTION AND RELIANCE, CONTRACTS AND TORTS*

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of promises without consideration (reliance / promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on section 90 of the Restatement (promissory estoppel) and the move to make promises enforceable based on substantial reliance rather than consideration; Paper A traces the same doctrinal shift in contract theory, treating reliance protection as one of the core substantive justifications that supplanted or supplemented the classical will/consideration doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: restitution and prevention of unjust enrichment as a basis for liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper B recounts the construction of a substantive law of restitution (and its relation to contracts) in the Restatement of Restitution; Paper A identifies prevention of unjust enrichment as part of Fuller's triad (private autonomy, reliance protection, unjust enrichment) and situates restitution among the alternative bases that challenged the will theory.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal transition from formal will/consideration doctrine to policy‑oriented/conflicting‑considerations reasoning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an explicit history and genealogy of the breakdown of the nineteenth‑century will theory and the rise of a conflicting‑considerations model in contract law; Paper B narrates mid‑twentieth century doctrinal developments (e.g., Williston/Corbin, Restatements) that reflect the same move away from strict formalism toward flexible, policy‑driven remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of scholarly authority and Restatements in reshaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper B foregrounds the Restatement projects and key scholars (Williston, Corbin, Seavey, Scott, Gilmore) as drivers of substantive change; Paper A similarly focuses on the influence of academic writings (Holmes, Fuller, Kessler, Macaulay, Macneil) and doctrinal scholarship in producing the modern competing‑considerations consciousness.

shared_topics.topic: the porous boundary and interaction between contract remedies and equitable/procedural devices (contracts, restitution, torts/equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes how a mix of legal and equitable procedural devices were consolidated into substantive restitution and reliance doctrines crossing traditional boundaries between contracts and equity/torts; Paper A discusses how doctrinal change reallocated issues (e.g., reliance, unjust enrichment) across doctrinal categories and how administrators and courts balanced formal rules against equitable or policy considerations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 96washlrev51!!ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACTING IN THE AGE OF SMART CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance (as opposed to promise/will) in defining contractual liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that smart contracts are better characterized by a reliance-based (tort-like) theory because they are automated and often lack human assent, while Paper B traces Lon Fuller's articulation of reliance protection as one of the core substantive bases (alongside private autonomy and prevention of unjust enrichment) that reshaped contract theory.

shared_topics.topic: whether consent/will-based theories adequately describe novel modes of contracting (e.g., automated or socially embedded transactions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contends that consent- and promise-centered orthodox contract doctrines do not squarely fit fully automated, machine-to-machine smart contracting, and Paper B critiques the nineteenth-century will theory and examines its limits and replacements (e.g., Fuller's private autonomy and the conflicting-considerations model) when traditional notions of will prove inadequate.

shared_topics.topic: the institutional design of enforcement and dispute resolution for contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes rethinking ex post dispute resolution for smart contracts (advocating decentralized, user-based mechanisms and preferring proof-of-work style broad participation), while Paper B foregrounds institutional considerations as a category of legal reasoning — showing how choices about forum, administrability, and institutional allocation have historically shaped the development of contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: balancing formal/administrability considerations against substantive policy goals in contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how technological features (immutability, automation, spot transactions) expose doctrinal incompleteness and administrative limits of existing contract rules, necessitating new procedural and design responses, and Paper B develops the conflicting-considerations model that explicitly weighs formal (administrability) considerations against substantive goals in shaping contract law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 84neblrev506!!ARTICLE: Evolving Business and Social Norms and Interpretation Rules: The Need for a Dynamic Approach to Contract Disputes
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Evolving Business and Social Norms and Interpretation Rules: The Need for a Dynamic Approach to Contract Disputes

shared_topics.topic: formalist/objective doctrines versus contextual/subjective interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes rigid, text-focused rules (e.g., plain meaning) and argues for a dynamic, individualized, context-sensitive approach to interpreting contracts; Paper B analyzes Lon Fuller’s and others’ retreat from nineteenth-century will/objective doctrines toward a model that balances multiple considerations and allows more flexible, non-formalist resolution of contract questions.

shared_topics.topic: balancing private autonomy, fairness, and efficiency as competing objectives of contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract interpretation as needing to serve and balance autonomy, economic efficiency, and fairness—arguing dynamic rules better achieve those goals; Paper B traces the rise of the ‘conflicting considerations’ model in which private autonomy is weighed against other substantive policies (reliance protection, unjust enrichment, social concerns) when choosing doctrinal norms.

shared_topics.topic: role and treatment of standard-form contracts and power asymmetries
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how interpretation rules and standardized form terms disproportionately harm less-resourced or culturally/linguistically marginalized parties and calls for dynamic corrective measures; Paper B grapples with the doctrinal handling of form and consideration, and the marginalization (and later reintegration) of the ‘social’ dimension and power-imbalance concerns within contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: intellectual/historical evolution of contract theory away from the will theory toward pluralistic or dynamic frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates its proposal in debates exemplified by Eisenberg’s ‘dynamic contract law’ and criticizes the static, classical focus on the moment of formation; Paper B provides a genealogy from Holmes and the will theory to Fuller and the emergence of the conflicting-considerations approach, explaining how contract theory evolved to incorporate multiple, sometimes competing, policy considerations.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrine of consideration and its continuing role in American contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the modern American mutual mistake doctrine, though shaped by civil-law forms, retains and enforces elements of the pre‑classical common‑law doctrine of consideration; Paper B centers on Lon Fuller's treatment of 'consideration and form,' tracing how consideration persisted, was reinterpreted, and figured centrally in the shift from will theory to the conflicting‑considerations model.

papers.node_id: 52amjcompl513!!ARTICLE:Impossibility and Changed and Unforeseen Circumstances
papers.title: ARTICLE:Impossibility and Changed and Unforeseen Circumstances
papers.abstract: Suppose that the parties are agreed on what performance each is to make but some event makes this performance impossible, or more difficult, or its market price drastically changes. These problems have been handled by two doctrines drawn from two different sources. Roman law developed a doctrine of impossibility to deal with impossible performances. Canon law developed one of changed circumstances to deal with unexpected events that made a performance of greater or lesser value to each party. In the medieval and early modern period, jurists developed philosophical and moral explanations of these doctrines. With time, these explanations were forgotten or simplified. Today, to many modern jurists, both doctrines seem to defy rational explanation. Nevertheless, if we look at the history of these doctrines, we will find that there is a much to be learned, both negatively and positively. Negatively, we will see, the jurists were never able to develop a good explanation of the Roman texts governing impossibility. Their explanation was that no one could be bound to do the impossible - which simply did not square with the texts. On the positive side, they did develop a good explanation of the effect of unexpected circumstances. It was so good that I believe that if it is properly understood, it can also explain why relief is sometimes given when a performance is impossible.

questions.question: When an unforeseen event makes contractual performance impossible, substantially more difficult, or drastically changes its economic value, should courts excuse performance or adjust the parties' obligations, and under what criteria?
Can the historical rationale for granting contractual relief in response to unexpected changes in circumstances coherently account for cases where performance is impossible?
How have historical legal explanations for excusing or adjusting obligations after unforeseen events evolved, and what lessons do they offer for modern justification of relief?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How did Roman, Continental, and other civil-law ideas and prominent jurists influence the historical development of Anglo-American contract doctrine?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 91califlrev1573!!ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law
papers.title: ARTICLE:Mistake in Contract Law
papers.abstract:
Suppose that A and B enter into a contract that is either based on or reflects some kind of mistake made by A, or by A and B jointly. After the mistake is discovered, A claims that because of the mistake the contract should either be unenforceable, if it has not been performed, or reversible, if it has been.
The problems raised by claims of this kind have been a source of persistent difficulty in contract law. In part this difficulty results from the complex nature of the underlying issues: intuitively, there seems to be a serious tension between the concept that a mistake may be a ground for relief in contractual transactions and such basic ideas of contract law as risk-shifting, the security of transactions, and rewards for knowledge, skill, and diligence. Much of the difficulty, however, results from the use of legal categories and doctrinal rules that are not sufficiently based on a functional analysis. In this Article, I develop the legal rules that should govern mistake in contract law. These rules are intended to be normative rather than descriptive, but by and large they are consistent with the results in existing cases and often explain the cases better than existing doctrine does.
Traditionally, contract law has recognized four categories of mistake, each with its own body of rules: mutual mistake, unilateral mistake, mistranscription, and misunderstanding. Many of the rules that govern these categories turn on elements that are either of limited functional significance or are easy to verbally manipulate. Even the names of the categories generally fail to describe mistakes according to their functional characteristics.
What is needed, therefore, is a functional analysis of the issues raised by mistake. Such an analysis involves two steps.
The first step is to describe the types of mistake that are relevant in contract law on the basis of their character. In this Article I consider five different types of mistake: evaluative mistakes, mechanical errors, mistranscriptions, mistakes in interpretation, and shared mistaken factual assumptions.
The second step is to develop the rulesthat should govern each type of mistake in light of applicable social propositions - that is, propositions of policy, principally in the form of efficiency; propositions of morality, principally in the form of social morality n2; and propositions of experience.
______________ Part I develops the considerations of efficiency, morality, and experience that bear most heavily in formulating the rules that should govern the various kinds of mistake.
Part II concerns evaluative mistakes. Evaluative mistakes arise when an actor who was capable and well-informed at the time he made a contract comes to believe that his choice to make the contract was mistaken due to a change in either his preferences, his subjective valuation of the performances due under the contract, or the objective or market value of those performances. Evaluative mistakes should not provide a basis for relief from a contract.
Part III concerns mechanical errors. Mechanical errors are physical or intellectual blunders that result from transient errors in the mechanics of an actor's physical or mental machinery. Mechanical errors should provide a basis for relief from a contract except to the extent that the nonmistaken party has been injured by justifiable reliance on the contract.
Part IV concerns mistranscriptions. Mistranscriptions are a special kind of mechanical error, in which the drafter of a written instrument that is intended to transcribe an oral contract fails to accurately transcribe the oral contract. In such cases either party should have the right to have the instrument reformed to match the actual contract if he can satisfy a requisite level of proof that a mistranscription occurred.
Part V concerns interpretive mistakes. Interpretive mistakes are mistakes by one or both contracting parties about the most reasonable meaningof an expression the parties have employed, the meaning that the other party attaches to an expression, or both. The general principle that should govern interpretive mistakes is that if both parties are equally at fault, losses should be shared, but if one party is more at fault than the other, the interpretation of the party who is less at fault should prevail over the interpretation of the party who is more at fault. One party may be more at fault than the other either because his interpretation is less reasonable than the other's, or because he knows that the other attaches a different meaning to the relevant expression than he does and he does not make the other party aware of their different interpretations.
Part VI concerns shared mistaken factual assumptions. A mistaken factual assumption is a mistake about the world that lies outside the mind of the party who holds the assumption. Such an assumption is shared if it is held by both parties. It is tacit if it is so deeply embedded that the parties take the truth of the assumption for granted. A shared tacit factual assumption is implicitly part of the parties' contract. Accordingly, if a mistake concerning a shared factual assumption would provide a basis for relief to the adversely affected party if the assumption was explicit, so too should the assumption provide a basis for relief to that party if it is tacit, provided that the assumption is material. Therefore, a party who is adversely affected by a mistaken assumption of this type should be entitled to relief, as a matter of contractual interpretation, unless one of the following conditions prevails: (1) The adversely affected party is consciously aware of the risk that the assumption is mistaken or recklessly disregards facts that put him on notice of that risk. (2) The risk that the assumption is mistaken is contractually allocated to the adversely affected party. (3) One contracting party is in a position to have clearly superior information about the risk that the assumption is mistaken. (4) The mistake concerns a windfall rather than a loss.
In a companion article, I consider unshared mistaken factual assumptions.

papers.node_id: 2000byulrev1363!!ARTICLE:Nachfrist Was Ist? Thinking Globally and Acting Locally: Considering Time Extension Principles of the U.N. Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods in Revising the Uniform Commercial Code
papers.title: ARTICLE:Nachfrist Was Ist? Thinking Globally and Acting Locally: Considering Time Extension Principles of the U.N. Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods in Revising the Uniform Commercial Code
papers.abstract:
The United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods ("CISG" or "Convention")came into existence in 1980 and "established the benchmark for the unification of commercial law in the post-war era."It is generally recognized as the first sales law treaty to be accepted worldwide.The United States ratified the treaty on December 11, 1986.The CISG went into effect on January 1, 1988, among 11 nations.Fifty-seven nations, including most of the major trading states, have ratified the Convention.V. Suzanne Cook notes,
In this time of unprecedented globalization of trade, the [CISG] responds to the need for a uniform sales law with international application and acceptance. When law is at its best, it serves and mirrors the values of society and resolves conflicts in a manner that is consistent with such values and expectations. In the case of CISG, with application in [more than] fifty Contracting States spanning five continents and diverse legal systems and traditions, that is a formidable task.
As business interests in the United States continue to globalize, the importance of familiarity with provisions contained in the CISG will be of greater importance to domestic businesses.The ability of domestic businesses to engage in international commercial activity via electronic commerce ("e-commerce") may also compound problems associated with international commercial disputes.Where the CISG is applicable,domestic businesses must confront the issue of whether the application of the CISG will result in unexpected or unanticipated liability.Even if the CISG is inapplicable (i.e., the CISGdoes not apply to a particular contract, or the parties exclude application of the Convention),determining which law to apply in the absence of a choice of law provision is often a complex problem.Where a choice of law provision has been included, more potential problems arise, including that of bias on the part of a court applying its own national law.
Notwithstanding these various problems occurring in international commercial activity, the CISG provides what its drafters intended it to provide - uniform law "a bit" more accessible and predictable than what preceded it.One of the Convention's more intriguing aspects is its partial amalgamation of common law and civil law principles into one body of law. The incorporation of conflictingprinciples could have rendered the Convention unworkable, a quandary clearly contemplated by its drafters.Camilla Baasch Andersen observed,
Uniformity does not follow automatically from a proclamation of uniform rules. Uniformity is a difficult goal to achieve, as uniform words do not always ensure uniform results, especially where a Convention is in effect throughout countries with completely differing social, economic, and cultural backgrounds, and perhaps most significantly, different legal systems.
Professor John Honnold commented that a partial reason for the failure of the 1964 Sales Convention was the rejection by common law countries of the use of "untranslatable" civil law concepts.Comparative law is not typically a strong focal point of discussion among American scholars.The endeavor of uniformity requires an avoidance of interpreting international text through the "lenses of domestic law."
Just as dangers - and corresponding antidotes- exist in applying uniform international law, such a body of law also offers opportunities for insight into application and potential progress of existing domestic laws. A study of the CISG offers such opportunity for study of the Uniform Commercial Code ("UCC" or "Code"). While the UCC clearly is not a "code" in civil law vocabulary,several works have indicated that some of the UCC's provisions were derived partially from foreign influence, particularly from German sources.The relative success of the CISG, coupled with globalization and other influences, has led a number of commentators to suggest inclusion of some foreign provisions found in the CISG into the UCC through revision.One particular focus of inclusion by these commentators has centered on the concept of Nachfrist, generally meaning "extension," as it was adopted into the CISG from German civil law.
This article examines the Nachfrist concept as it applies to the CISG and considers its potential application to the UCC. Part II provides an overview of the applicability of the CISG to international sales contracts and compares some of the provisions in the Convention with those found in the UCC. Part III discusses the difference between what constitutes breach under the UCC and the CISG and explains when Nachfrist applies to CISG contracts. Part IV takes a closer look at the UCC, considering the need for adding a new provision such as Nachfrist and rethinking some of the current mechanics in light of potential incorporation of the Nachfrist provision. Part V offers suggestions for inclusion of the Nachfrist procedure in light of the reconsideration of these existing provisions.
. Applicability of the CISG and Some Comparisons with the UCC

What specific revisions to domestic remedies and contract-performance mechanics would be required to implement a time-extension/cure procedure effectively.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the Nachfrist (extension) doctrine under the CISG and how inserting a similar procedural device into the UCC would change when a party can treat a breach as repudiatory and what remedies are available; Paper B develops a third‑party‑beneficiary technique that is intended to function as a doctrinal bypass to turn otherwise nonenforceable gift promises into legally enforceable obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the role of formalities or procedural devices as signals of serious commitment
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines Nachfrist as a formal time‑extension procedure that structures parties' expectations and the consequences of nonperformance, while Paper B assesses seals, reliance devices, and the proposed beneficiary mechanism as formal or evidentiary markers that distinguish serious gift promises from casual ones.

shared_topics.topic: normative arguments for reforming domestic contract doctrine by importing or reinterpreting legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for reconsidering and potentially revising the UCC by importing or adapting a foreign CISG/German concept (Nachfrist) to improve predictability and fairness in domestic sales law; Paper B advances a doctrinal reform—recognizing third‑party beneficiary law as an intentional vehicle—to expand the edge of contract law and permit binding gift promises under specified structures.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 77neblrev756!!ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Estoppel in Property Law

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal substitutes for formal legal requirements (consideration, writing, or choice-of-law) to create enforceable obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the CISG and potential incorporation of the German-derived Nachfrist into the UCC would interact with existing U.S. formalities and choice-of-law gaps in international sales contracts, while Paper B examines estoppel as a doctrinal substitute for consideration and for the writing requirement in real property transfers.

shared_topics.topic: mechanisms and remedies that protect reliance and regulate non‑performance (time to cure, reliance recovery, enforcement of expectations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on Nachfrist as a time‑extension/curative remedy and on how CISG/UCC doctrines allocate liability and unexpected exposure for nonperformance, whereas Paper B analyzes how estoppel enforces promises or awards reliance-based protection (including preventing forfeiture) in property contexts.

shared_topics.topic: comparative/functional analysis of a legal doctrine across different doctrinal regimes or contexts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares CISG (an international, mixed civil/common law instrument) with the domestic UCC and considers importing foreign concepts into U.S. commercial law, while Paper B contrasts estoppel's role and operation in contract law versus its more complex and varied application in property law (including effects on successors‑in‑interest).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78neblrev491!!ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: In Defense of Mutuality of Obligation: Why "Both Should Be Bound, or Neither"

shared_topics.topic: symmetry and availability of remedies (mutuality of remedy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A defends the mutuality of obligation as an affirmative, presumptive principle that ensures both parties have reciprocal remedies, while Paper B analyzes how CISG and UCC rules (and the Nachfrist time-extension mechanism) determine when parties may pursue remedies for breach, implicating who may obtain relief and under what conditions.

shared_topics.topic: historical and comparative origins of contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a multi-century historical account of the mutuality doctrine's development in common law, and Paper B undertakes a comparative-law inquiry into the CISG's incorporation of civil-law concepts (notably German Nachfrist) and how foreign influences might inform revisions to the UCC.

shared_topics.topic: timing of performance, formation, and breach (when obligations become enforceable or excused)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes unilateral and bilateral contracts and the point at which promises create executory obligations, while Paper B examines the Nachfrist extension and the different triggers for breach and resulting remedies under the CISG versus the UCC, so both address when duties arise and when delay or nonperformance yields legal consequence.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 75cornelllrev987!!ARTICLE: A DIALOGUE ABOUT THE DOCTRINE OF CONSIDERATION.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A DIALOGUE ABOUT THE DOCTRINE OF CONSIDERATION.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal analysis of foundational contract principles (formation, consideration, breach and remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is a sustained examination of the doctrine of consideration in contract law, interrogating a core formation/enforceability rule; Paper B conducts a doctrinal comparison of the CISG and the UCC, focusing on breach and remedies (e.g., Nachfrist) and how those foundational rules operate in commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: rethinking and revising domestic contract law in light of commercial practice and comparative insights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A uses a conversational critique to question the continuing adequacy of an established common‑law doctrine (consideration), and Paper B explicitly considers importing a civil‑law concept (Nachfrist) from the CISG/German law into the UCC, arguing for substantive revision of domestic rules to better suit modern international commerce.
