shared_topics.topic: historical and intellectual origins of contract doctrine (religious/canon law vs Enlightenment/humanistic influences)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the role of canon law, medieval jurists, and the shift during the Enlightenment in shaping whether promises were treated as morally or legally binding; Paper B likewise situates modern interpretive doctrines against an Enlightenment backdrop (Grotius, Pufendorf) and contrasts those logical theories with the common-law development of contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: whether and to what extent the law should enforce moral obligations to keep promises versus relying on formal doctrinal requirements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly asks whether moral obligation should translate into legal enforceability of promises and critiques the common-law consideration doctrine; Paper B engages the same normative tension indirectly by describing rules (objective theory, parol evidence) that limit contextual/moral inquiry and by questioning whether juries should be allowed to vindicate fairness or redistribute in contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formal, doctrinal rules and contextual or fact-based adjudication (judge-as-law-decider vs jury/contextual interpretation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques rigid doctrinal application of consideration in 'moral obligation' cases where context and moral reasons for promise-keeping are salient; Paper B examines the parol-evidence/plain-meaning rules, the fact/law distinction, and the role of juries in interpreting contracts, highlighting conflicts between formal rules and case-specific, fact-driven outcomes.

papers.node_id: 2001wislrev777!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PETER LINZER'S "ROUGH JUSTICE"
papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PETER LINZER'S "ROUGH JUSTICE"
papers.abstract:
The "minimalist" judge "who holds that the purpose of the statute may be learned only from its language" has more discretion than the judge "who will seek guidance from every reliable source." A method of statutory interpretation that is deliberately uninformed, and hence unconstrained, may produce a result that is consistent with a court's own views of how things should be, but it may also defeat the very purpose for which a provision was enacted. That is the sad result in this case.
In these words, which close his stinging dissent in Circuit City Stores v. Adams,Justice Stevens recently underscored the injustice that flows from inattention to context. Dissenting from the United States Supreme Court's 5-to-4 holding that the Federal Arbitration Act applies to ordinary employment contracts,Justice Stevens bitterly decried the majority's willful failure to acknowledge crucial aspects of the history and social context of the Federal Arbitration Act. He observed:
It is not necessarily wrong for the Court to put its own imprint on a statute. But when its refusal to look beyond the raw statutory text enables it to disregard countervailing considerations that were expressed by Members of the enacting Congress and that remain valid today, the Court misuses its authority. As the history of the legislation indicates, the potential disparity in bargaining power between individualemployees and large employers was the source of organized labor's opposition of the Act, which it feared would require courts to enforce unfair employment contracts. That same concern, as Justice Souter points out [in a separate dissent], underlay Congress' exemption of contracts of employment from mandatory arbitration. When the Court simply ignores the interest of the unrepresented employee, it skews its interpretation with its own policy preferences.
As Professor Linzer shows, courts struggling with complex relationships sometimes approach the exchange solely from the perspective of one of the parties, failing to comprehend the interests of the other. Some may even be persuaded by Eric Posner's suggestion that courts intentionally adopt a passive approach to highly relational contracts.In Adams, however, the majority shows no sign of passivity. It contends that "for parties to employment contracts … there are real benefits to the enforcement of arbitration agreements,"including avoidance of litigation costs. The majority notes the special advantage of such savings where recoveries are likely to be relatively small and litigation costs especially high.However, the court says nothing at all of the disadvantages of arbitration to the employee. The omission is striking.
When it is applied less superficially than in Adams, the work of legal economists adds depth to our comprehension of the economic norm. This is especially useful where there is comparatively full presentation or where just one of the parties has been assigned most of the risks. But in the vast majority of real cases, economic theory by itself falls far short of providing a sound basis for assessing liability or for filling gaps in terms. Such analysis is often highly theoretical, disregarding non-pecuniary values and discounting transaction costs. In real contracts that have come to the courts, transaction costs - not merely financial, but emotional, social, moral, even physical costs - may vastly outweigh what is tallied by the economists. Even if these objections were met, economics lends only one perspective to the complex matter of contractual relationship. It supposes that contracting parties, given full information, will act in ways that are mathematically demonstrable to be rational. This is itself a faulty supposition. Moral, religious, altruistic, and philosophical valuescomplicate the mix; many relationships are interdependent and characterized by a shifting power base. Moreover, psychology teaches us that apparently conflicting motivations typify human behavior. Not even in physics does pure mathematics predict reality without taking account of chaos. Linzer is surely right in his insistence that liability must rest upon something real and that theory must serve practical justice.
However, one suspects the majority in Adams would be impervious to the argument. The majority may have seen only one side because it intentionally embraced a perspective consonant with a particular set of social, economic, and political values. These were apparently considered vital enough to warrant discounting all but one dimension of the contextual particularities. Nothing can be done to cure this kind of determined formalism except to continue to rail against it.
For courts seeking to avoid a one-sided perspective, Linzer's proposal may be of value in the richness of its doctrinal sources. Where the novelty of the relationship or its fact-specific nature deprives the court of guidance from established precedent, judges may inadvertently omit to evaluate the interests of one of the parties. Gillian Hadfield has demonstrated the pervasiveness of such an imbalance in the courts' treatment of franchise agreements.Noting the familial language used informally between the parties and the inevitability of incomplete terms in these deals, Hadfield says that conceiving of the relation as a "method of doing business" misleads courts to apply a "business judgment rule" that "amounts to filling in gaps in the incomplete contract by according the franchiser unfettered discretion, much as it would enjoy if it were a vertically integrated corporation."
For these cases, Professor Linzer offers an approach fashioned from a web of doctrinal strands, no single one of which may suffice, but which woven together make a persuasive case for liability as well as a basis for remedy. The strands include reliance and unjust enrichment as well as tort theory. An advantage of Linzer's approach lies in its flexibility. In cases for which there is little precedent or statutory guidance, "rough justice" may be attained, as Linzer suggests, by such a patchwork of doctrine. Although not elegant in theory, this approach assures attentionto the details of the relationship merely by dint of focusing in turn upon unjust enrichment, reliance, expectation, and tort principles.
Even for cases lying well within established doctrinal boundaries, where the experience of many courts distill the normative system in which the transaction is placed, courts must update or altogether discard doctrine when norms have evolved or when other discontinuities between theory and reality become evident. To do this effectively, they must evaluate the "rough justice" of each decision from a variety of perspectives, even if only informally. Theory never drives reality in real life, nor should it in the courts. "It is not clear that courts have a mandate to uncritically privilege one way of understanding and interpreting the world over another, because such questions are typically at the heart of the dispute."Linzer's thesis insists upon reality, rejecting the fantasy that contract liability rests upon any one coherent theory. As useful and interesting as is Charles Fried's "promise principle,"for example, it has little claim, it seems to me, as an explication of reality. As with many elegant theories, it provides a framework to help organize our understanding of what really happens between parties and in the courts, but it cannot describe it.
Even the Wisconsin Supreme Court, whose opinions are featured in Linzer's article, recently failed to live up to its reputation, retreating to insistence on doctrinal unity in a case in which an at-will employee sought punitive damages for the tort of intentional misrepresentation inducing employment. The majority denied any cause of action for the tort, framing its opinion in terms that emphasize discrete norms, and so discount the parties' entire relationship:
Contract law "is based on obligations imposed by bargain, and it allows parties to protect themselves through bargaining." Contract law does not involve the same broader societal concerns as tort law for "the individual limited duties implicated by the law of contracts arise from the terms of the agreement between the particular parties." Because the law encourages economic exchanges and seeks to foster predictability, punitive damages are not allowed in a breach of contract action; to allow otherwise would chill the formation of contracts and reduce predictability … . Essentially, contract law is based upon the principles of free will and consent, whereas tort law is based upon the principles of risk-sharing and social duties.
In her concurrence, Chief Justice Abrahamson refused to endorse the majority's rule, which she states as follows:
When an employer deliberately and intentionally lies to an at-will employee to induce the employee to continue employment and the employee continues to work relying on those lies, and then sustains damages as a result of reliance on the lies the employee cannot sue in a tort action for damages.

questions.question: Should courts resolve disputes arising from relational or incomplete agreements by applying a flexible, context-sensitive mix of equitable principles and multiple remedial frameworks rather than by strictly adhering to the text or a single theoretical model?

Does reliance on narrow, formalistic or abstract economic approaches to interpreting contracts and statutes systematically disadvantage parties with weaker bargaining power or ignore non-pecuniary transaction costs, producing unjust outcomes?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
How should remedies for misrepresentation be calculated, and can misrepresentation damages be harmonized with contract-law remedial principles?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do systemic institutional changes (deregulation, litigation costs, ADR, transnational codes) affect contracting behavior and the relation between law and practice?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
How do informal relational norms and repeated interactions govern commercial contracting in practice, and when do these norms supplant formal state-enforced rules?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do appellate judges systematically shape factual narratives in published opinions in ways that influence doctrinal placement and case outcomes?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How do parties in ongoing exchange relationships use relational contracting-informal, repeated-interaction arrangements-to govern performance and adapt to change?
When liability is grounded in misrepresentation rather than ordinary promise enforcement, do courts award different compensatory or punitive remedies?
Have doctrinal boundaries among contract, tort, and property shifted toward a formalist, market-oriented model?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 78cornelllrev371!!ARTICLE: LEGAL REALISM AND THE SOCIAL CONTRACT: FULLER'S PUBLIC JURISPRUDENCE OF FORM, PRIVATE JURISPRUDENCE OF SUBSTANCE.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: LEGAL REALISM AND THE SOCIAL CONTRACT: FULLER'S PUBLIC JURISPRUDENCE OF FORM, PRIVATE JURISPRUDENCE OF SUBSTANCE.

shared_topics.topic: tension between formalist/legalistic rules and realist/context-sensitive approaches in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Lon Fuller's apparent split between a formalist 'public' jurisprudence of legality and a realist, functional account of private contract, while Paper B criticizes doctrinal and textual formalism (and narrow economic formalism) and urges judges to attend to contextual, realist considerations when resolving contract disputes.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling and the acceptability of post‑hoc creation of enforceable bargains
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses Fuller's acceptance that judges may need to step in post hoc to make bargains enforceable to prevent injustice, and Paper B endorses a 'rough justice' approach in which courts fill gaps across doctrines (reliance, unjust enrichment, tort) when precedent or statute leave relational contracts incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary and normative role of reliance (and related doctrines) in enforcing agreements
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Fuller's critique of formal criteria and his emphasis on the reliance principle as a basis for enforceability, and Paper B explicitly lists reliance, unjust enrichment, and expectation remedies as key doctrinal tools for addressing incomplete or one‑sided contractual relations.

shared_topics.topic: importance of social context, community norms, and power imbalances in interpreting and enforcing contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A locates contractual enforceability in 'relative and contingent community norms' and functional goals, while Paper B faulted the Circuit City majority for ignoring legislative history and the bargaining power disparity between employers and employees, and stresses transaction costs and non‑pecuniary harms.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between legal/doctrinal reasoning and broader legal or political theory
shared_topics.justification: Paper A aims to connect legal realism in contract doctrine to social contract theory and asks how political theory informs doctrines of legality, and Paper B questions the primacy of single theoretical accounts (economic models or the 'promise principle') and argues that theory must serve practical, doctrinally grounded justice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev965!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY COMMENTS ON WILLIAM WHITFORD'S PAPER ON THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY COMMENTS ON WILLIAM WHITFORD'S PAPER ON THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: the role of parol evidence and contextual information in contract interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the parol evidence rule, ambiguity doctrines, and argues that allowing contextual/parol evidence (and treating interpretation as factual) would change who decides contract meaning; Paper B condemns minimalist/textualist interpretation and urges attention to legislative, historical, and relational context when construing contractual and statutory provisions.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of interpretive authority between judges and juries (and the effects of judicial methodology)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the fact/law distinction and when juries versus judges should determine contractual meaning, while Paper B critiques varying judicial interpretive styles (minimalist/textualist versus context-sensitive judges) and shows how those methodologies shape outcomes in contract-related disputes.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal choices affect parties with unequal bargaining power
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights judicial distrust of juries and the concern that procedural and evidentiary rules (like the parol evidence rule) reflect anxieties about favoring ‘little’ versus ‘big’ parties, and Paper B analyzes how courts’ formalist readings (e.g., of the FAA) can ignore the interests of weaker, unrepresented employees and entrench power imbalances.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of economic analysis for resolving contract interpretation and remedial questions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A cites Eric Posner and reports that economic tools failed to dispel doctrinal confusion in parol-evidence disputes because of too many variables, and Paper B similarly critiques relying solely on economic theory, arguing it neglects non-pecuniary values, transaction costs, and relational complexity.

shared_topics.topic: the need for empirical and context-sensitive inquiry into how contract disputes are actually decided
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for empirical studies (e.g., of jury deliberations and foreseeability determinations) to understand interpretive outcomes, and Paper B likewise invokes empirical scholarship and real-world transaction costs to argue that doctrine should be informed by how contracting relationships and disputes operate in practice.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 71tullrev1749!!ARTICLE: IN THE TRIBUNAL OF CONSCIENCE: MILLS V. WYMAN RECONSIDERED
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: IN THE TRIBUNAL OF CONSCIENCE: MILLS V. WYMAN RECONSIDERED

shared_topics.topic: the role of moral obligation in creating enforceable promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on the 'moral obligation' doctrine (Mills v. Wyman) and whether moral duty alone can constitute consideration, while Paper B criticizes reliance on narrow economic/textual models and emphasizes moral, social, and non-pecuniary values as relevant to how courts should treat contractual entitlements.

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretation and doctrine formation — formalism versus contextualism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A fault-finds the court in Mills for applying formal rules and missing an opportunity to shape promissory doctrine, and Paper B attacks minimalist/textualist judging (e.g., Circuit City) and argues for judges to use broader contextual and doctrinal sources when forming contract law.

shared_topics.topic: alternative bases for enforcing promises beyond classical consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for binding promises based on intent to be bound regardless of traditional consideration or moral-obligation labels, while Paper B endorses Professor Linzer's 'patchwork' approach (reliance, unjust enrichment, tort principles) as pragmatic grounds for liability when bargain-based doctrine is inadequate.

shared_topics.topic: importance of historical and factual context in adjudicating contract disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A reconstructs the factual and historical record of Mills v. Wyman to show how context alters the legal assessment, and Paper B emphasizes the need to account for legislative history, social power imbalances, and the real-world context of relationships when interpreting and applying contract rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2014uilllrev663!!ARTICLE: GIFT PROMISES AND THE EDGE OF CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: GIFT PROMISES AND THE EDGE OF CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: formalism versus contextual/flexible approaches to contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the formal requirement of consideration and proposes using third‑party beneficiary doctrine as a doctrinally grounded way to relax formalism for serious gift promises; Paper B criticizes overly textualist and formalist judging and endorses a contextual, multi‑doctrinal ‘rough justice’ approach when rigid formalism produces unfair results.

shared_topics.topic: using alternative doctrines (reliance, unjust enrichment, third‑party beneficiary rules, trusts) to enforce promises that fail traditional contract formalities
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys exceptions to the consideration rule (promissory estoppel/reliance, merchant firm offers, trusts) and proposes deploying vested third‑party beneficiary rights as a device to make gift promises enforceable; Paper B highlights reliance and unjust enrichment (and tort principles) as strands in a pragmatic, patchwork method for creating liability where classic contract doctrine is incomplete.

shared_topics.topic: the judicial task of updating or filling doctrinal gaps to reflect relational realities and changing norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for expanding the ‘edge’ of contract law to accommodate binding gift promises and give independent significance to third‑party beneficiary law in light of normative concerns; Paper B urges courts to update or discard doctrines when social norms or the facts of relational contracts render established rules inadequate, advocating attention to the full context of parties' relationships.

shared_topics.topic: normative evaluation of when courts should enforce promises (social welfare, fairness, and distributional concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the law‑and‑economics account that consideration focuses enforcement where social welfare is maximized and weighs that against arguments for allowing gift enforcement in some cases; Paper B similarly weighs economic theory against non‑pecuniary values and power imbalances, criticizing doctrines that ignore fairness and the interests of weaker parties (e.g., employees).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41indlrev9!!ARTICLE: Recent Defenses of Consideration: Commodification and Collaboration
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Recent Defenses of Consideration: Commodification and Collaboration

shared_topics.topic: limits of single theoretical justifications for contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Both papers critique attempts to ground contract rules in a single coherent theory: Paper A rejects economic or formalist monocultures (e.g., using pure economic analysis to decide relational disputes like Circuit City or franchise cases), while Paper B examines and rejects singular philosophical defenses of the consideration requirement (Eisenberg's commodification argument and Markovits's Kantian 'collaboration').

shared_topics.topic: importance of moral, social, and contextual factors in enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both argue that non‑pecuniary values and social context matter to whether promises should be enforced: Paper A stresses power imbalances, emotional and social transaction costs, and the employee's interests in arbitration cases, while Paper B analyzes moral ideals (gifting norms, collaboration) and moral excuses bearing on enforcement of donative versus bargain promises.

shared_topics.topic: how courts should draw boundaries of enforceability and fill doctrinal gaps
shared_topics.justification: Each paper addresses practical criteria for when courts should impose liability or decline enforcement: Paper A advocates a patchwork of doctrines (reliance, unjust enrichment, tort) to resolve novel or incomplete relational contracts, and Paper B debates whether the consideration doctrine (or alternative moral principles) should function as the bright‑line boundary between enforceable bargains and unenforceable gifts.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism toward formalist/doctrinal unity and support for pluralist or pragmatic decisionmaking
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the tension between doctrinal unity and pragmatic adjudication—Paper A laments rigid doctrinal unity that ignores relational realities and endorses 'rough justice' via multiple strands of doctrine, while Paper B questions whether a single justificatory principle (e.g., collaboration) can or should monopolize the law's approach to enforcing promises.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 103nwulrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and role of background assumptions or context in interpreting legal texts

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Counterpoise of Contracts: The Reasonable Person Standard and the Subjectivity of Judgment

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes the limits of legal economics—highlighting transaction costs, non‑pecuniary values, and power imbalances that economic models often ignore—whereas Paper B grounds its defense of expectation damages in an institutional/economic account of the needs of modern market economies and evaluates which damages rule best serves those institutions.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A laments formalist judicial methods that ignore contextual realities and lead courts to misapply doctrine in employment and franchise relationships, and Paper B documents that Fuller and Perdue's influential academic thesis failed to alter courts' persistent reliance on expectation damages, analyzing why theory and practice diverge.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE JUDICIAL ADMISSIONS EXCEPTION TO THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS: A CURIOUSLY GRADUAL ADOPTION

shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates a patchwork of doctrines (reliance, unjust enrichment, tort principles) to achieve 'rough justice' when formal contract rules or precedent are inadequate, and Paper B analyzes courts' recognition of exceptions (part performance, full performance, judicial admissions, UCC rules) that allow enforcement of contracts absent a formal signed writing.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes strictly textualist or formalist adjudication that ignores bargaining power, social context, and policy consequences, arguing judges should consider broader purposes and realities; Paper B likewise grounds exceptions to the statute of frauds in the statute's ultimate purpose—preventing fraud—and evaluates when contextual evidence satisfies those policy aims so the formal writing requirement can be set aside.

shared_topics.topic: judicial evolution and gradual adoption of contract-law doctrines in response to real-world practices
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that courts must update or discard doctrines when norms evolve and facts reveal discontinuities between theory and reality, and Paper B documents the slow, incremental judicial development (and occasional reluctance) in adopting the judicial-admissions and other exceptions to the statute of frauds to align doctrine with evidentiary and commercial realities.

papers.node_id: 2001wislrev695!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:ROUGH JUSTICE: A THEORY OF RESTITUTION AND RELIANCE, CONTRACTS AND TORTS*
papers.title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:ROUGH JUSTICE: A THEORY OF RESTITUTION AND RELIANCE, CONTRACTS AND TORTS*
papers.abstract:
years ago Samuel Williston and Arthur Corbin combined to create section 90 of the Restatement of Contracts, the most important event in twentieth century American contract law. That section made promises enforceable without consideration if there was substantial reliance on them by the promisee.About ten years later, Warren Seavey and Austin W. Scott took a hodgepodge of related procedural devices, legal and equitable, and created the substantive law of restitution, in the Restatement of that name.Despite the impact of these achievements, a generation later Grant Gilmore, always the skeptic, suggested that
The two concepts were, indeed, twins … . It would seem, as a matter of jurisprudential economy, that both situations could have been dealt with under either slogan but the legal mind has always preferred multiplication to division … .

questions.question: Should cases where a person acted on another's promise without a formal exchange be treated under the same legal theory as cases where one party has gained at another's expense, or do these situations require distinct doctrinal treatments?

What is the appropriate remedial principle and measure in those situations - should the remedy aim to compensate the person's reliance losses, to strip the beneficiary of unjust gains, or to serve some other corrective or deterrent goal?

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
Should gratuitous (donative/gift) promises be legally enforceable, and if so, under what conditions?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
When does a unilateral communication (advertisement, bid, general offer) become a binding obligation on the communicator rather than a mere invitation to bargain?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?

When and to what extent should post-contractual promises (e.g., promises for additional payment to induce performance already owed or post-sale statements) be enforceable as warranties or modifications?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 100columlrev94!!ARTICLE:FROM THE WILL THEORY TO THE PRINCIPLE OF PRIVATE AUTONOMY: LON FULLER'S "CONSIDERATION AND FORM"
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:FROM THE WILL THEORY TO THE PRINCIPLE OF PRIVATE AUTONOMY: LON FULLER'S "CONSIDERATION AND FORM"

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of promises without consideration (reliance / promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B centers on section 90 of the Restatement (promissory estoppel) and the move to make promises enforceable based on substantial reliance rather than consideration; Paper A traces the same doctrinal shift in contract theory, treating reliance protection as one of the core substantive justifications that supplanted or supplemented the classical will/consideration doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: restitution and prevention of unjust enrichment as a basis for liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper B recounts the construction of a substantive law of restitution (and its relation to contracts) in the Restatement of Restitution; Paper A identifies prevention of unjust enrichment as part of Fuller's triad (private autonomy, reliance protection, unjust enrichment) and situates restitution among the alternative bases that challenged the will theory.

shared_topics.topic: historical and doctrinal transition from formal will/consideration doctrine to policy‑oriented/conflicting‑considerations reasoning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is an explicit history and genealogy of the breakdown of the nineteenth‑century will theory and the rise of a conflicting‑considerations model in contract law; Paper B narrates mid‑twentieth century doctrinal developments (e.g., Williston/Corbin, Restatements) that reflect the same move away from strict formalism toward flexible, policy‑driven remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of scholarly authority and Restatements in reshaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper B foregrounds the Restatement projects and key scholars (Williston, Corbin, Seavey, Scott, Gilmore) as drivers of substantive change; Paper A similarly focuses on the influence of academic writings (Holmes, Fuller, Kessler, Macaulay, Macneil) and doctrinal scholarship in producing the modern competing‑considerations consciousness.

shared_topics.topic: the porous boundary and interaction between contract remedies and equitable/procedural devices (contracts, restitution, torts/equity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B analyzes how a mix of legal and equitable procedural devices were consolidated into substantive restitution and reliance doctrines crossing traditional boundaries between contracts and equity/torts; Paper A discusses how doctrinal change reallocated issues (e.g., reliance, unjust enrichment) across doctrinal categories and how administrators and courts balanced formal rules against equitable or policy considerations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44depaullrev1301!!SYMPOSIUM: CULTURAL CONCEPTIONS OF COMPETITION: NOTE: TAX ABATEMENTS AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: A MATCH NOT MADE IN YPSILANTI
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CULTURAL CONCEPTIONS OF COMPETITION: NOTE: TAX ABATEMENTS AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: A MATCH NOT MADE IN YPSILANTI

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel as a mechanism to enforce promises absent consideration
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts and theorizes how Restatement §90 made promises enforceable on the basis of substantial reliance rather than consideration, and Paper B applies that promissory estoppel doctrine to the GM–Ypsilanti dispute, arguing the municipality reasonably relied on GM's promise after receiving tax abatements.

shared_topics.topic: standards for reasonable reliance and judicial review of reliance findings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys the doctrinal development and doctrinal tests courts use to adjudicate reliance-based claims, and Paper B scrutinizes the trial and appellate courts' factual and legal handling of Ypsilanti's claimed reliance (including claims of abuse of discretion and the reasonable-reliance inquiry).

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal relationship between restitution, reliance, and conventional contract/tort categories
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly analyzes the conceptual overlap and tensions between restitution, reliance-based remedies, and traditional contract/tort frameworks, and Paper B situates promissory estoppel within that family of equitable/restitutionary doctrines when assessing whether municipal incentives created enforceable obligations on GM.

shared_topics.topic: use of equitable remedies (including injunctions) grounded in reliance/restitution doctrines to prevent corporate action
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces how equitable devices and restitutionary ideas were folded into modern reliance doctrines, and Paper B demonstrates that reliance-based relief can include injunctive relief—here, the trial court enjoined GM's relocation based on a promissory estoppel finding and the appellate review of that remedy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36stanlrev1107!!ARTICLE: The Responsive Model of Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Responsive Model of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of promises without consideration via reliance (promissory estoppel/reliance remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts the historical creation of Restatement §90 and the Restatement of Restitution establishing that substantial reliance can make promises enforceable absent consideration; Paper B explicitly treats the law of consideration and argues for reconceptualizing doctrines (including reliance-based enforcement) under a responsive model that balances fairness and policy.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal relationship and boundary between restitution, reliance, contract and tort
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the substantive law of restitution and reliance doctrine overlaps with and interacts with traditional contract and tort categories (and notes critiques that the concepts might be unified), while Paper B addresses remedies and the need to situate restitutionary and contractual remedies within a single functional framework guided by fairness and administrability.

shared_topics.topic: critique of classical/formal contract doctrine and the need to reconceptualize contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A invokes historical shifts (Williston/Corbin, Restatements) and Gilmore's skepticism about multiplying doctrinal labels, reflecting a critical stance toward rigid doctrinal categories; Paper B mounts a systematic critique of the classical, objective/standardized model and proposes the 'responsive model' as a reconceptualization grounded in fairness, policy, and functional analysis.

shared_topics.topic: the role of Restatements and influential scholars in shaping contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on the concrete impact of Restatement §90 and the Restatement of Restitution (and their architects) on twentieth-century contract law, and Paper B situates its argument in dialogue with the Restatement (First), Langdell, Holmes, Williston, Gilmore, and Friedman, treating Restatements and scholarship as central drivers of doctrinal development.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 52uchilrev903!!ARTICLE: Beyond Promissory Estoppel: Contract Law and the "Invisible Handshake".
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Beyond Promissory Estoppel: Contract Law and the "Invisible Handshake".

shared_topics.justification: Both papers focus on reliance as a justificatory ground for enforcing promises: Paper A traces the emergence of Restatement §90 and the restitution Restatement as reliance-based interventions, while Paper B surveys recent cases to argue that reliance has been the traditional foundation of promissory estoppel even as its doctrinal role is changing.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship between reliance-based doctrines and the consideration requirement
shared_topics.justification: Both examine how doctrines like promissory estoppel and restitution function as exceptions or supplements to the classical consideration requirement: Paper A recounts historical doctrinal developments that created reliance- and restitution-based enforcement, and Paper B argues courts are merging these exceptions into a broader, unified rule protecting economically useful promises.

shared_topics.topic: whether reliance-based enforcement is properly contract law or tort/equitable law
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the question of doctrinal identity—Paper A highlights the historical split and commentators’ skepticism about treating estoppel and restitution as distinct species, and Paper B addresses charges that promissory estoppel is turning contract into tort while arguing it is evolving into a distinctly contractual theory of obligation.

shared_topics.topic: the policy rationale for enforcing promises to protect economic activity and social trust
shared_topics.justification: Both papers consider the normative justification for enforcing reliance: Paper A situates the development of restitution and reliance doctrines within legal responses to transactional needs, and Paper B explicitly frames an emerging rule that enforces promises made in furtherance of economic activity to preserve trust and efficiency (the 'invisible handshake').

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACTS AS A WORLD FORCE IN TWO AGES OF REVOLUTION: A CONFERENCE CELEBRATING THE 150TH ANNIVERSARY OF HADLEY V. BAXENDALE:HADLEY AND THE COMMON LAW: ORIGINS AND DEVELOPMENT:ROBERT J. POTHIER'S INFLUENCE ON THE COMMON LAW OF CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the contract–tort boundary and use of equitable legal devices

shared_topics.justification: Both engage the problem of where contract remedies end and tort or restitution remedies begin: Paper A traces the overlap and tensions among contracts, restitution, and torts, and Paper B seeks a clearer line between product-fitness (contract/warranty) cases and product-safety (tort) cases while using non-contractual doctrines to allocate risk.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance, representation, and unjust enrichment in justifying liability
shared_topics.justification: Both works consider reliance and alternative justificatory theories for liability beyond a promise exchange: Paper A foregrounds reliance as a ground for enforcing promises without consideration and the substantive law of restitution, while Paper B evaluates warranty as a representational theory (not necessarily requiring actual reliance) and invokes unjust enrichment to support recovery by remote purchasers.

shared_topics.topic: using relational and distributional realities of modern commerce to shape doctrinal rules
shared_topics.justification: Both papers use the realities of commercial distribution to motivate doctrinal change: Paper A situates restitution and reliance doctrines in broader transactional practice, and Paper B grounds abolition of privity and expanded warranty duties in the relational nature of manufacturer‑dealer‑buyer distribution chains and incentives for product quality.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 86columlrev269!!ARTICLE: A CONSENT THEORY OF CONTRACT.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A CONSENT THEORY OF CONTRACT.

shared_topics.topic: role of reliance and restitution in allocating remedies and obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the development of reliance-based remedies and the substantive law of restitution as alternative bases for enforcing obligations; Paper B critiques reliance theory as an account of obligation while recognizing reliance's practical role and proposing a framework that avoids ad hoc judicial distinctions about reasonable versus unreasonable reliance.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal boundaries and overlap between contract, restitution, and tort
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the historical and conceptual interaction (and possible redundancy) between doctrines of contract, restitution, and tort, noting calls to unify or separate them; Paper B situates contract within a broader system of legal entitlements and addresses when the law should impose obligations—questions that implicate the proper allocation of disputes between contract doctrine and other remedial regimes.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations and comparative critique of contract theories
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with jurisprudential questions about whether reliance/restitution doctrines could be reconceived under alternative labels or unified approaches; Paper B systematically assesses major theories of contractual obligation (will, reliance, bargain, fairness, efficiency) and advances a consent theory as a superior normative foundation.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 12nevlj54!!ARTICLE: Cross Purposes & Unintended Consequences: Karl Llewellyn, Article 2, and the Limits of Social Transformation
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Cross Purposes & Unintended Consequences: Karl Llewellyn, Article 2, and the Limits of Social Transformation

shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the 20th‑century emergence of section 90 (promissory estoppel) and the Restatement of Restitution as alternative bases for enforcing promises absent consideration; Paper B situates Karl Llewellyn's law‑in‑action project (and Article 2) as an effort to decouple contract doctrine from formalistic roots and orient enforcement to real‑world reliance and commercial practice.

shared_topics.topic: the incorporation of legal and equitable devices into substantive contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how procedural, legal, and equitable devices were synthesized into the substantive law of restitution and reliance; Paper B engages with the broader project of using doctrinal adjustments (moving beyond formalist rules) to achieve more realistic and equitable outcomes, implicating the role of equitable principles in shaping remedies and enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: historical scholarship on 20th‑century contract doctrine and Legal Realism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A offers a historical account of key Restatement developments (Williston, Corbin, Seavey, Scott) that reshaped contract doctrine, while Paper B provides a historical and critical reading of 20th‑century Legal Realism—especially Llewellyn and Article 2—tracing how those reform efforts affected modern contract law.

shared_topics.topic: comparative and historical development of contract law principles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces twentieth‑century American developments (Williston, Corbin, Seavey, Scott, Gilmore) in contract and restitution law and evaluates their intellectual genealogy, while Paper B situates the CISG in a global comparative context (common law and civil law influences, German Nachfrist) and considers historical influence on potential UCC revision.

shared_topics.topic: the role of procedural/equitable mechanisms becoming substantive rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how a 'hodgepodge of related procedural devices, legal and equitable' was transformed into the substantive law of restitution, and Paper B engages the substantive incorporation of a procedural remedy‑style concept (Nachfrist/time extension) from civil law into international and possibly domestic sales law, raising similar concerns about turning procedural practices into substantive doctrines.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Commodification and Contract Formation: Placing the Consideration Doctrine on Stronger Foundations

shared_topics.topic: enforcing promises without consideration (promissory estoppel/reliance/restitution)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recounts the emergence of Restatement §90 and the Restatement of Restitution as mechanisms to enforce promises grounded in substantial reliance or restitution rather than consideration, while Paper B analyzes the exceptions to the consideration doctrine that permit unilateral promises to become legally binding, engaging the same doctrinal problem of when promises lacking traditional consideration should be enforceable.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical foundations and legitimacy of the consideration doctrine versus alternative doctrines

papers.node_id: 58villlrev553!!NORMAN J. SHACHOY SYMPOSIUM: ASSESSING THE CISG AND OTHER INTERNATIONAL ENDEAVORS TO UNIFY INTERNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW: HAS THE TIME COME FOR A NEW GLOBAL INITIATIVE TO HARMONIZE AND UNIFY INTERNATIONAL TRADE?: Article: SPECIAL TOPICS UNDER THE CISG: DEFINING THE BORDERS OF UNIFORM INTERNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW: THE CISG AND REMEDIES FOR INNOCENT, NEGLIGENT, OR FRAUDULENT MISREPRESENTATION
papers.title: NORMAN J. SHACHOY SYMPOSIUM: ASSESSING THE CISG AND OTHER INTERNATIONAL ENDEAVORS TO UNIFY INTERNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW: HAS THE TIME COME FOR A NEW GLOBAL INITIATIVE TO HARMONIZE AND UNIFY INTERNATIONAL TRADE?: Article: SPECIAL TOPICS UNDER THE CISG: DEFINING THE BORDERS OF UNIFORM INTERNATIONAL CONTRACT LAW: THE CISG AND REMEDIES FOR INNOCENT, NEGLIGENT, OR FRAUDULENT MISREPRESENTATION
papers.abstract:
THE creation of uniform international contract law, as of uniform law in general, is never all-encompassing. Instead, uniform law instruments are typically limited in their scope, because the uniform provisions on which the drafters can agree are limited or because there is no need to unify neighboring areas of law. The borders of uniform contract law thereby created in turn create their own problems, most prominently among them the need to define the relationship between the uniform law and the rules of non-unified domestic law.
Under the United Nations Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods (CISG), this task is particularly important and difficult when it comes to remedies under domestic law and their applicability to CISG contracts.In such cases, any recourse to local, non-unified law involves the risk of upsetting the balance of rights and obligations of international buyers and sellers that has been laid down in the CISG: whenever domestic law provides a party with a remedy it would not have under the CISG's rules, its concurrent application potentially undermines foreseeability and legal certainty in international trade. The arguably most distinctive CISG features that each party should be able to rely upon are provisions limiting the access to or the measure of its remedies. A buyer's obligation to give notice of non-conformity to the seller within a reasonable time after he has discovered or ought to have discovered it, under CISG Article 39(1), plays a significant role in practice, with Article 39(2) of the CISG cutting off all of the buyer's remedies when two years after delivery no notice has been given.A party may furthermore only avoidthe contract in cases in which the other party has committed a "fundamental" breach of contract, under Article 25 CISG, thereby making the burdensome unwinding of contracts an ultima ratio (remedy of last resort).And the damages that a party may claim for a breach of contract may not exceed the loss which the party in breach foresaw or ought to have foreseen at the time of the conclusion of the contract.
In trying to prevent these and other rules of the CISG from being circumvented, the solution is generally seen in international uniform law's prevalence over concurring bodies of law:"Displacing inconsistent domestic law," so it has been said, "is of the essence of establishing uniform law."The theoretical foundations on which this accepted outcome is based are, on the contrary, not uniform. One approach that could be described as "international" is pointing to the rules of the CISG itself, notably Article 7(1), and arguing that the CISG's international character and the need to promote uniformity in its application require the preemption of domestic law.A different line of argument with a more "national" focus primarily looks to the contracting states' domestic legal order that may explicitly or implicitly grant prevalence to the CISG. An example for the first type of rule can be found in the Australian state of New South Wales, where an express clause in the parliamentary act implementing the CISG clarifies that "[the] provisions of the Convention prevail over any other law in force in New South Wales to the extent of any inconsistency."A non-CISG-specific rule of prevalence is followed in the United States, where reference has been made to the CISG's nature as federal law, which therefore "trumps" state common law and the Uniform Commercial Code.The difference between these approaches may eventually besmall, however, because even the "national" view tends to incorporate an international perspective, referring to the CISG's preamble which stresses that "the adoption of uniform rules which govern contracts for the international sale of goods and take into account the different social, economic and legal systems would contribute to the removal of legal barriers in international trade and promote the development of international trade." U.S. courts have concluded that the expressly stated goal of developing uniform international contract law to promote international trade "indicates the intent of the parties to the treaty to have the treaty preempt state law causes of action,"thereby supporting the prevalence of the CISG's provisions with an interpretation of the CISG itself.
The prevalence of uniform international contract law is, of course, only needed and only justified where and as far as its rules attempt to govern exclusively, and not outside the scope of the CISG's substantive coverage. The borders of the CISG therefore also define the scope of its prevalence and of domestic laws' corresponding preemption. Accordingly, the crucial question is: Where exactly do the borders of the CISG run?
. Defining the Borders of the CISG: A Novel Two-Step Approach
Describing the substantive scope of the CISG is not easily done, both when attempted in the abstract and with regard to a particular question. Commentators have criticized that in many of the pertinent cases decided under the CISG, no detailed reasoning is given why certain issues fall within or outside the CISG's scope of application.In Part A below, two "traditional" approaches that can be identified in case law and legal writings will be discussed, before an alternative approach will be presented in Part B.

questions.question: To what extent should rules of a uniform international contract law instrument displace or preempt concurrent domestic remedies for innocent, negligent, or fraudulent misrepresentation in international sales contracts?

What methodological test or two-step approach should courts use to determine whether a given dispute or remedy falls within the substantive scope (the "borders") of a uniform international contract law instrument, thereby triggering its prevalence over domestic law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev125!!ARTICLE: WHEN DOES THE "FAT LADY" SING? Although this phrase probably originated in the opera setting, one of its more interesting uses occurred in the battle between Pennzoil and Texaco for the Getty Oil Company. When Texaco's Chairman, John K. McKinely, asked Getty Oil's Chairman Sidney Peterson whether Getty might still be available even though an "agreement in principle" had been entered into with Pennzoil, Peterson responded that "the fat lady had not yet sung." Pennzoil Co. v. Getty Oil Co., No. 7425, slip op. at 46 (Del. Ch. Feb. 6, 1984). For a further discussion of the Texaco-Pennzoil case, see infra text accompanying notes 60 to 63. : AN ANALYSIS OF "AGREEMENTS IN PRINCIPLE" IN CORPORATE ACQUISITIONS.

shared_topics.topic: drawing the legal 'borders' of contract coverage (when a set of rules applies to a transaction)

shared_topics.topic: use of supplemental doctrines or domestic law to fill perceived gaps or circumvent formal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques parties' and courts' recourse to domestic remedial rules that might circumvent CISG limits and discusses doctrinal bases for CISG prevalence or gap‑filling; Paper B evaluates alternative doctrines (promissory estoppel, enforceable duty to negotiate in good faith) as means to impose obligations where a definitive contract is absent.

shared_topics.topic: the problem of divergent judicial approaches undermining predictability in commercial transactions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how inconsistent application of CISG versus domestic rules threatens foreseeability and legal certainty in international trade; Paper B documents how the courts' "all‑or‑nothing" treatment of agreements in principle produces inequitable outcomes and commercial uncertainty, arguing for a more coherent approach.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Mutual Misunderstanding in Contract

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' reasonable expectations and reliance in deciding enforcement

shared_topics.topic: interaction between competing legal rules or sets of obligations and the resulting impact on certainty and efficiency

shared_topics.topic: defining the scope and boundaries of a legal regime through interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that political philosophies must be interpreted and applied by fallible actors and that contested interpretations can produce divergent outcomes; Paper B specifically addresses the problem of where the 'borders' of the CISG run, surveying doctrinal approaches and proposing methods for determining whether a given dispute falls inside or outside the Convention's scope.

shared_topics.topic: institutional design, incentives, and the risk of misuse or circumvention by actors
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how certain philosophies may be easy to rationalize, attract opportunists, or be institutionally manipulated—making the prevention of misuse and the visibility of abuses central concerns for applied philosophy; Paper B examines how domestic law or legislative implementation can circumvent or undermine the CISG (e.g., by supplying extra remedies), and how rules on prevalence and statutory design are used to guard against such circumvention to preserve predictability.

shared_topics.topic: tension between universal/ideal rules and local/domestic legal orders
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes assuming that a 'first‑best' normative ideal can govern legal practice without accommodating local informational or institutional constraints, arguing the ideal that should govern practice may differ substantially; Paper B explores the conflict between the CISG's aim at uniform, international rules and differing domestic legal systems, including debates over whether and how the CISG should preempt or coexist with national law.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 48tullrev946!!ARTICLE: Rules and Terms--Civil Law and Common Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rules and Terms--Civil Law and Common Law

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between an external uniform/foreign legal regime and domestic law (displacement vs supplementation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when and to what extent the CISG should preempt or coexist with non-unified domestic remedies (discussing Article 7(1), national implementing clauses, and U.S. federal-preemption analogies), while Paper B examines how Common law courts and writers invoked Civil/Roman law doctrines to bolster or supplement domestic contract rules, highlighting practical instances of foreign law being used to influence or fill gaps in domestic law.

shared_topics.topic: defining the borders and scope of a legal system’s application in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the hard question of where the CISG’s substantive scope ends and domestic law begins (proposing a two-step approach to delimit the CISG’s borders), and Paper B wrestles with the difficult line between invoking a parallel from Civil law and adopting an entire institution—i.e., how far foreign concepts can be transplanted before they change the domestic legal system.

shared_topics.topic: methodological issues of comparative and harmonization projects in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with theories supporting international uniformity and differing national approaches to interpreting and applying the CISG for uniformity, while Paper B surveys the nineteenth‑century practice of borrowing Civilian analysis and the related assumptions about a ‘general jurisprudence,’ both interrogating the methods and pitfalls of comparative legal borrowing and harmonization.

shared_topics.topic: the role of codification and uniform instruments in shaping modern contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies the CISG as an instrument of international codification/unification and its intended effect on predictability and the removal of legal barriers in international trade, whereas Paper B traces how codified Civil law (e.g., the Code Civil, Pothier) influenced and structured modern contract doctrine in Common law jurisdictions, showing how codification drives doctrinal development.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39ambuslj289!!ARTICLE: THE ADVENT OF RECOVERY ON MARKET TRANSACTIONS IN THE ABSENCE OF A BARGAIN
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ADVENT OF RECOVERY ON MARKET TRANSACTIONS IN THE ABSENCE OF A BARGAIN

shared_topics.topic: defining the borders of a primary contract regime and when non-primary law fills gaps
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes where the CISG's scope ends and when domestic law may supply remedies or rules for issues (e.g., misrepresentation, notice, damages), and Paper B traces how the narrowing of bargain-consideration created gaps that courts and equity doctrines (promissory estoppel, restitution) filled for non‑bargain transactions.

shared_topics.topic: preemption versus coexistence of competing legal rules (uniform/international rules vs domestic/equitable doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether and how the CISG should prevail over inconsistent domestic laws or be displaced by them, while Paper B examines the tension between an ascendant formal bargain doctrine and older equitable or local doctrines that survive or are reintroduced to provide relief.

shared_topics.topic: availability and design of remedies when standard contract assumptions fail
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on remedial limits under the CISG (notice requirements, fundamental breach, foreseeability of damages) for misrepresentation or nonconformity, and Paper B investigates the development of alternative remedies (promissory estoppel, restitution, moral‑obligation enforcement) where the bargain/consideration framework would otherwise deny recovery.

shared_topics.topic: tradeoffs between predictability/legal certainty and equitable fairness in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the importance of foreseeability and legal certainty in international trade and concerns that domestic remedies may upset the CISG's balance, while Paper B recounts how rigid formalization of consideration produced perceived injustices that prompted equitable doctrines to restore fairness.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 101yalelj111!!ARTICLE: The Promissory Basis of Section 90.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Promissory Basis of Section 90.

shared_topics.topic: mismatch between doctrinal theory and actual remedies in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that Section 90 is framed as a reliance-based rule but courts routinely award expectation relief and enforce promises, while Paper B analyzes how the CISG's remedial rules (and their policy aims) can be undermined or altered by recourse to domestic remedial doctrines, exposing tensions between stated doctrinal justifications and the remedies actually applied.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of model or uniform instruments (Restatement §90 and the CISG) versus judicial practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates how the Restatement's Section 90 has influenced and been interpreted by courts in ways that depart from its reliance rhetoric, and Paper B examines how the CISG's purportedly uniform rules interact with, are supplemented by, or preempt domestic law, raising the same question of how model instruments fare in practice.

shared_topics.topic: foreseeability as a limiting or screening principle for liability and damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the prospect that a promisor could foresee definite and substantial reliance screens for serious promises and influences enforcement, while Paper B treats foreseeability as a central limit on damages under the CISG (losses recoverable are those the breaching party foresaw or ought to have foreseen).

shared_topics.topic: preserving predictability and the balance of contractual rights through defining substantive scope and remedial borders
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores how courts' choices about which promises to enforce and what relief to grant affect the coherence of contract law, and Paper B focuses on delineating the CISG's borders and preventing domestic remedies from upsetting the balance and legal certainty the CISG seeks to achieve.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92yalelj14!!ARTICLE: Restitution as a Remedy for Breach of Contract: The Case of the Partially Performing Seller
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Restitution as a Remedy for Breach of Contract: The Case of the Partially Performing Seller

shared_topics.topic: remedies for breach of contract: restitution versus expectancy damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly analyzes whether a partially performing seller should be limited to expectancy damages rather than money restitution, while Paper B examines how international contract law (the CISG) allocates and limits available remedies and how domestic law remedies (including restitutionary relief) can conflict with those CISG rules.

shared_topics.topic: normative and theoretical foundations for restricting remedies (efficiency, foreseeability, legal certainty, liberal principles)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates restitution against economic efficiency and liberal principles (arguing restitution for partial performers offends liberal values), and Paper B grounds limits on remedies in principles like foreseeability, legal certainty, and the goal of uniformity when determining whether domestic remedies should be preempted by the CISG.

shared_topics.topic: defining the scope or 'borders' of when particular remedies apply across factual categories
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws fine-grained distinctions (buyer v. seller, full v. partial performance, return in specie v. money restitution) to decide which remedy fits each factual scenario, and Paper B develops a two-step approach to define the CISG's borders and determine when remedies fall inside the uniform law or remain governed by domestic rules.

shared_topics.topic: measures and calculation of monetary recovery for breach
shared_topics.justification: Paper A surveys different measures of money restitution and contrasts those amounts with expectancy damages using a numerical example, while Paper B addresses limits on monetary recovery under the CISG (e.g., the foreseeability cap on damages and remedies for misrepresentation) and the risk that domestic measures of recovery will alter the CISG's remedial balance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 38hastingslj417!!ARTICLE: Private Advantage and Public Power: Reexamining the Expectation and Reliance Interests in Contract Damages.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Private Advantage and Public Power: Reexamining the Expectation and Reliance Interests in Contract Damages.

shared_topics.topic: damages measures for breach of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the CISG allocates remedies for breach (including contract avoidance and damages) under its uniform rules, while Paper B is a doctrinal and normative investigation into the choice between expectation and reliance as the proper damages measure; both thus substantively engage with which damages regimes should apply to contract breaches.

shared_topics.topic: limits on recoverable damages and their justification (e.g., foreseeability/extra-advantage)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses CISG limits on damages (notably the foreseeability limitation and related doctrinal bars) and the policy reasons for limiting remedies in international trade, while Paper B examines what losses should be compensable (distinguishing reliance losses from the 'extra advantage' of expectation) and when public enforcement of such private gains is justified.

shared_topics.topic: normative role of law in shaping remedies and the use of state power to enforce contracts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether and to what extent a uniform international instrument (the CISG) should preempt domestic remedial rules to preserve predictability for international traders, and Paper B asks whether state power should be used to enforce private expectation gains or stop at reliance protection; both probe the proper scope of legal authority and policy in structuring contractual remedies.

shared_topics.topic: practical measurement and evidentiary challenges in awarding remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights practical rules (notice, two‑year cut‑offs, 'fundamental' breach) designed to make remedial outcomes predictable and administrable under the CISG, while Paper B addresses the empirical and evidentiary difficulties in measuring true reliance loss versus expectation and considers when doctrinal presumptions (e.g., awarding expectation) are defensible; both engage with how law deals with measurement problems in damages.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how CISG provisions (e.g., notice requirements, the ‘fundamental breach’ standard, and foreseeability limits on damages) define who can obtain which remedies in international sales, while Paper B examines how tort, criminal, and contract doctrines shaped by white race consciousness structure which plaintiffs or defendants gain access to remedies and are held liable.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on how courts and implementing statutes interpret the CISG (including Article 7 and questions of preemption) to determine the Convention’s borders and uniform application, and Paper B interrogates how judges’ constructions of racial codes and white race consciousness in case law shape the reach and application of doctrines across tort, criminal, and contract law.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between supra‑ or formal rules and local social norms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses the tension between an international uniform instrument (the CISG) and non‑uniform domestic law that can alter outcomes for parties, while Paper B explores how prevailing racial ideologies and local social hierarchies are embedded in and interact with formal legal rules across multiple fields of law.

shared_topics.topic: critique of law’s claimed neutrality or universality
shared_topics.justification: Paper A problematizes the assumption that a uniform convention can be universally applied without displacing important domestic considerations, and Paper B critiques the purported neutrality of legal doctrines by showing how they can reproduce racial hierarchies and exclusion.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that apparent authority arose from a broader shift to objective reasoning about how a reasonable third party would perceive an agent's powers; Paper B repeatedly relies on objective standards in the CISG (foreseeability of damages, 'reasonable time' notice, and uniform interpretation) when delimiting remedies and obligations.

shared_topics.topic: defining the boundaries and scope of specialized commercial law versus other legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the boundary between mercantile/customary agency rules and general doctrines (such as estoppel/equity), and Paper B is centrally concerned with where the borders of the CISG run and when domestic remedies may properly supplement or be preempted by the Convention.

shared_topics.topic: theoretical and interpretive foundations for applying commercial norms across jurisdictions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages in historical and doctrinal analysis to justify the doctrine of apparent authority and its acceptance across Anglo‑American jurisdictions; Paper B analyzes theoretical bases (international vs national approaches, treaty interpretation) for giving the CISG prevalence and for uniform application across contracting states.

compared_to.partner_title: Article: Rethinking Consideration in the Electronic Age

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes where the CISG's substantive scope ends and domestic law begins for international sales, proposing a two‑step approach to mark those borders; Paper B asks whether open source software arrangements should be treated as contracts at all, interrogating whether traditional contract coverage extends to digital licensing regimes.

shared_topics.topic: how concurrent legal regimes should coexist or yield (preemption vs complementarity)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether and when the CISG should prevail over conflicting domestic remedies and the doctrinal bases courts use to displace local law, while Paper B analyzes the proper relationship between contract law and intellectual property law for open source licenses and argues for a complementary contract‑IP framework rather than reliance on IP alone.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on CISG remedial limits (notice rules, fundamental breach, foreseeability of damages) and the risk that domestic remedies undermine predictability in international trade, and Paper B emphasizes that contract doctrines (including remedies) provide clearer enforcement and certainty for open source transactions compared with relying solely on copyright injunctive relief.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A confronts the difficulty of applying uniform international contract rules to diverse legal systems and factual questions (e.g., misrepresentation, scope issues), proposing doctrinal approaches to maintain uniformity; Paper B reevaluates classical doctrines like consideration in the electronic/open‑source era, arguing for doctrinal adjustments so contract law remains administrable and socially useful.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the need for predictability and legal certainty in international trade and discusses preferring uniform CISG rules over divergent domestic remedies to preserve those values; Paper B frames the tension explicitly as a choice between the standard of doctrinal stability (predictability) and the standard of social congruence (policy-driven reform) in shaping contract doctrines.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores competing rationales and institutional mechanisms for having the CISG displace inconsistent domestic law (interpretation under Article 7, legislative prevalence clauses, federal preemption analogies); Paper B analyzes how courts should respond when established common‑law rules clash with social propositions—by overruling, distinguishing, or reconstructing precedents—and thus how to resolve doctrinal conflict.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses courts' move to enforce mutual promises and to fashion bargain-focused remedies, whereas Paper B examines which remedies the CISG supplies or limits (notice rules, two-year cut-off, fundamental breach, foreseeability of damages) and how domestic remedies may or may not be applied.

shared_topics.topic: the role of parties' expectations, reliance, and foreseeability in justifying enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that parties' mutual trust and their own assessment of a bargain justify giving promises legal force, and Paper B focuses on protecting parties' reliance and foreseeability by keeping CISG remedies predictable and preventing domestic-law circumvention.
