shared_topics.justification: Both engage the normative and doctrinal question whether expectation (contract) or reliance (tort/unjust enrichment) measures are appropriate for harms caused by defective promises or misrepresentations, with Paper A arguing about expectation-based rules across contexts and Paper B considering how the CISG's remedial limits interact with alternative damage measures.

shared_topics.justification: Both papers probe the overlap between contract-law remedies and tort or non‑statutory domestic remedies: Paper A compares tort and contract damages for imperfect transactions, while Paper B wrestles with when domestic (including tort) remedies may still apply to international sales or are displaced by the CISG.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights an internal incoherence in domestic contract law between goods and services and urges doctrinal reform to harmonize remedies across contexts; Paper B examines where the CISG's substantive scope ends and domestic law begins, focusing on how to define the borders so the uniform regime's remedial balance is preserved.

shared_topics.topic: delineating the doctrinal boundaries and scope of contract rules

shared_topics.justification: Paper A is explicitly concerned with where the CISG's substantive coverage ends and domestic law begins, proposing approaches to delineate those borders; Paper B engages this issue indirectly by debating which subjects (formation vs remedies) constitute the core of contract law and what promises the law should or should not enforce.

shared_topics.topic: tension between normative theory and practical/legal certainty in applying contract rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses competing theoretical bases for giving the CISG prevalence (international uniformity vs national implementation) and stresses predictability and foreseeability as aims of uniform rules; Paper B examines tradeoffs between normative pedagogic aims (revealing purposes via remedies-first) and practical instructional concerns (student comprehension and formulaic predictability of results).

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Expectation, Reliance, and the Two Contractual Wrongs

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the CISG's remedial regime, including limits on damages (foreseeability), avoidance for 'fundamental' breach, and notice requirements that restrict available remedies; Paper B directly interrogates expectation and reliance as competing measures of remedy and how those doctrines should be applied in contractual disputes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes foreseeability limits and the need for uniform remedial rules to promote predictability in international trade, while Paper B examines how privileging expectation or reliance interests affects predictability and parties' decision-making under contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the delimitation of doctrinal boundaries that determine when particular remedies apply
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned with the borders of the CISG and when domestic remedial rules may or may not supplement or displace it, and Paper B explores the boundary between expectation and reliance remedies (the 'two contractual wrongs'), i.e., how doctrinal choices allocate remedies across different kinds of contractual violations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Paradox Lost.

shared_topics.topic: defining the borders/scope of contract law

shared_topics.topic: sources and legitimacy of contract rules and their authority
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages with competing bases for the CISG's prevalence (an 'international' treaty-based preemption view versus domestic statutory or federal-preemption approaches), and Paper B interrogates the moral and institutional grounds that legitimize promissory obligations (principles of fidelity, utilitarian versus neoformal justification).

papers.node_id: 58washlrev343!!SYMPOSIUM ON ENERGY ISSUES IN THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST: UNCONSCIONABILITY IN A COMMERCIAL SETTING: THE ASSESSMENT OF RISK IN A CONTRACT TO BUILD NUCLEAR REACTORS.
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM ON ENERGY ISSUES IN THE PACIFIC NORTHWEST: UNCONSCIONABILITY IN A COMMERCIAL SETTING: THE ASSESSMENT OF RISK IN A CONTRACT TO BUILD NUCLEAR REACTORS.
papers.abstract:
Eighty-eight Pacific Northwest public utilities in 1976 contracted with the Washington Public Power Supply System ("WPPSS") for the construction of two nuclear power plants.The contract, or Participants' Agreement, contained a so-called "hell-or-high-water" clause which obligated the utilities to pay for the construction of the nuclear plants whether or not any electricity was ever produced.This article explores the possibility that such a clause might be unenforceable because of its unconscionability.
The article demonstrates that, contrary to popular belief, unconscionability has often been found in non-consumer commercial settings.  It considers several common avenues to finding substantive and procedural unconscionability and shows that the most likely defect in the Participants' Agreement was a failure to disclose vital information to the utilities -- not about technical details of design and construction, but about the risks involved.  Thus the utilities may have been ill-prepared to make a rational judgment to assume the risk of noncompletion.  This distinction between technical information and risk information mirrors a similar distinction in such public-policy areas as deciding whether to permit nuclear weapons testing.  The relevant inquiry when determining whether procedural unconscionabilityexists is whether one party failed to disclose facts not reasonably available to the other party, and whether that failure prevented the other party from properly assessing the risks involved.  This is true with both public policy and private contract concerns.  If WPPSS failed to disclose the risk of noncompletion to the utilities, and if the hell-or-high-water clause is found to place virtually all risk on the utilities, then the clause should be found unconscionable.

questions.question: Are contractual clauses that force one party to pay regardless of project completion or outcome unenforceable when they place virtually all risk on that party and the other party withheld critical information about those risks?

Does a party's failure to disclose nontechnical but material risk information about a large commercial project prevent the other party from making a rational assessment of risk and thereby justify invalidating the risky contract term?

Should courts refuse to enforce extreme risk-shifting provisions in commercial contracts even between sophisticated parties when the dominant party controlled and concealed information necessary to evaluate the likelihood of noncompletion?

matched_themes: What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?

To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?

How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
Are contractual clauses that allocate virtually all project risk to one party unenforceable where the other party withheld material information about those risks?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 88califlrev1743!!SYMPOSIUM ON LAW IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY:The Emergence of Dynamic Contract Law
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM ON LAW IN THE TWENTIETH CENTURY:The Emergence of Dynamic Contract Law
papers.abstract:
This Essay has a normative thesis and a positive thesis. The normative thesis is that contract law reasoning should be substantive rather than formal, and that the rules of contract law should, where appropriate, be individualized rather than standardized, subjective rather than objective, complex rather than binary, and dynamic rather than static. The positive thesis is that the twentieth century witnessed the emergence of contract law reasoning, and contract law rules, with just those characteristics.
will call the normative principle that instructs us how to make the best possible rules of contract law the basic contracts principle. This principle has two branches. The first branch describes the content that contract law should have. The second branch describes the manner in which that content should be determined. The two branches are related, because the content that contract law should have depends in part on how that content should be determined.

questions.question: Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, subjective, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
Did contract law and judicial reasoning in the twentieth century actually shift toward more substantive, individualized, subjective, complex, and dynamic approaches?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
Should courts adopt a context-sensitive approach to formal formation requirements (offer, acceptance, consideration) especially in non-commercial settings?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.abstract:
Some will tell you light is goodness And black is grief and sin But white is terror, sickness, burning And dark's the color of my skin Shawna
What I propose here is to examine the impact of notions of racial hierarchy, racial exclusion, and racial vulnerability and availability on nonblacks who held, resisted, explored, or altered those notions . . . to see what racial ideology does to the mind, imagination, and behavior of masters. Toni Morrison
Talking about race has become synonymous with violating the rules.  It doesn't matter how quietly or how eloquently you speak, the policy is Don't Ask, Don't Tell. Lani Guinier

questions.question: Whether and how white race consciousness and raced cultural codes influence the formulation, interpretation, and application of laws in tort, criminal, and contract disputes.

Whether and how narratives of racial hierarchy, exclusion, and vulnerability shape the reasoning, imagination, and decisionmaking of legal actors (judges, juries, attorneys) in civil and criminal cases.
Whether legal rules and doctrines encode and reproduce raced hierarchies so as to systematically advantage white parties and disadvantage nonwhite parties.

papers.abstract: . Introduction: The Place of Expectation and Reliance in Contractual Decision Making

questions.question: Should decisionmakers prioritize awarding the promised benefit of a bargain (protecting expectation) or reimbursing the costs a party incurred in reliance when resolving contract disputes?
In which circumstances is it appropriate to choose reliance-focused relief over promised-benefit relief (and vice versa)?
How do expectation-focused versus reliance-focused remedies affect parties' incentives, behavior, and perceptions of fairness in contracting?

matched_themes: How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.node_id: 38sandiegolrev1!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:FOREWORD Is Reliance Still Dead?
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:FOREWORD Is Reliance Still Dead?
papers.abstract:
One thing I found out when I was a prosecutor is that you should never tell a police officer he cannot do something, for that just serves as an open invitation for him to do it. In recent years, I have learned a similar lesson about legal scholarship which I should probably keep to myself but won't. If you proclaim the existence of a scholarly "consensus," this is an open invitation for academics to try to demolish such a claim.
In 1996, I published an article entitled The Death of Reliance,based on a talk I gave at the annual meeting of the Association of American Law Schools on recent trends in legal scholarship. In it I claimed there then existed a "new consensus" that a "reliance theory" did not explain the doctrine of promissory estoppel.What exactly a "reliance theory" is has never been made clear by those who seemed to advocate it - apart from their insistence that, just as tort law rectified the harm caused by physical misconduct, the purpose of contract law was to rectifydetrimental reliance caused by verbal misconduct.
This claim entails that reliance must exist before there should be any recovery (thereby calling into question the propriety of enforcing executory agreements), and that the normal measure of damages should be the "reliance interest" (thereby calling into question the propriety of awarding the "expectation interest"). Moreover, if the heart of this cause of action was induced detrimental reliance, then whether or not the promisor intended to be legally bound by her promise, or manifested such an intent to the promisee, and whether or not the promisee reasonably believed the promise to be legally binding were wholly immaterial. All this was much debated by contracts scholars in the 1960s and 1970s.
The "death of reliance" of which I wrote was based on the fact that, by the 1980s and 1990s, most contracts scholars who had written in any depth on the subject had concluded on the basis of comprehensive case analyses that: (a) the existence of detrimental reliance was not sufficient to explain when a promissory estoppel action would succeed and (b) the existence of detrimental reliance was not necessary for an action based on promissory estoppel to succeed.
As to the first claim it was shown that a claimant needed "reliance plus something" to prevail in a promissory estoppel action and, therefore, a "reliance theory" of promissory estoppel could not, standing alone, explain what this "something" might be. As to the second claim, some scholars found that courts were enforcing serious, but nonbargained-for, promises in a business context even in the absence of any provable detrimental reliance. In addition I noted that some scholars, though not yet a consensus, had begun questioning whether the "reliance interest" should ever be a proper measure of contract damages, even as a fallback recovery when the expectation interest cannot, for some reason, be computed with adequate certainty.
All this led me to conclude that, as a theory of promissory estoppel, reliance was dead. I did not claim, I hasten to add, that promissory estoppel was dead or dying.This was never even suggested by the scholarship I was reporting, nor have I ever contended that reliance was unimportant as a goal of contractual enforcement. To the contrary, I distinguished between "the tort-like conception of contract in which the inducement of detrimental reliance may be held to justify a remedy to compensate for the detriment incurred"from the quite different concern that "contracts are viewed as protecting one party's right to rely on the commitment of another."That the protection and facilitation of reliance was an important function of contract law was never at issue in this debate. Rather, the "new consensus" scholars denied the claim made during the 1960s and 1970s that a reliance principle could explain the doctrine of promissory estoppel and even supplant altogether the traditional requirement of bargained-for consideration.
The reaction to this thesis was pretty swift as scholarly reactions go, and far surpassed the reaction to the underlying scholarship I had been summarizing and reporting. (Lesson number 2: asserting the existence of a scholarly "consensus" is an excellent way to get yourself cited if it ticks off enough people.) Most notably challenged was claim (b): that the existence of reliance was no longer a necessary element of promissory estoppel. This was effectively refuted by a study ofpromissory estoppel cases by Robert Hillman in which he found that the absence of reliance was dispositive in 25% of the cases in which promissory estoppel claims were denied.These data certainly support the conclusion that a reliance requirement for recovery in promissory estoppel does indeed exist and, in this regard at least, reliance is not dead.
But Hillman's study also suggested that the existence of a promise was as necessary as detrimental reliance to a promissory estoppel action. In 135 cases (50%) a defect in the promise was discussed while in 52 of these cases (19% of the total cases surveyed) reliance was not discussed.As Hillman notes: "The result here should not be surprising if both promise and reliance are prerequisites for recovery on promissory estoppel grounds."In one sense, this seems unremarkable.always said that a promise was needed for promissory estoppel. Indeed, section 90 does not use the term "promissory estoppel" at all, speaking instead of "Promise Reasonably Inducing Action or Forbearance."For that matter, though it explicitly refers to "a promise," the Restatement does not actually use the term "reliance" - instead referring to promises that "induce action or forbearance on the part of the promisee."
But though it should have come as no surprise that the existence of a promise was still a requirement of promissory estoppel, this finding still undercut the old 1960s and 1970s "reliance theory" of promissory estoppel in which reliance on any verbal conduct was to be treated like a form of a verbal tort. According to this approach, Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores, Inc.was the harbinger of bigger things to come. The court in Red Owl had dispensed with the requirement that it actually enforce a promise of a franchise made by the defendant. In the much heralded words of the Red Owl court in response to the objection that the "promise" was not definite enough to merit ordinary contractual enforcement: "We deem it would be a mistake to regard an action grounded on promissory estoppel as the equivalent of a breach-of-contract action."
This was taken to signal that promissory estoppel was not the "substitute for consideration" that Samuel Williston explicitly, and theRestatements implicitly, conceived it to be.That is, it was not merely a substitute for a nonexistent bargain in finding enforceability of a promise that otherwise met all the normal requirements of a contract. Rather, it was a different beast altogether and one that, if properly fed and nurtured, could grow to supplant the bargain theory of consideration entirely. In place of a requirement of reciprocal inducement, by which we establish enforceability and all the other formal requirements by which we assess the existence of assent, would be an omnibus cause of action based upon injuries caused by reliance on the verbal conduct of others, in the same way that tort law compensates for injuries caused by the physical conduct of others. Contracts would not themselves die away, but contract law with its basic principle that contractual duties were the creation of consenting parties would be supplanted by tort law that imposes duties on people whether or not they consent.
Extolling very rare judicial statements in such cases as Red Owl, progressive contracts scholars lobbied for what Grant Gilmore colorfully called the "Death of Contract."And it was this campaign of the 1960s and 1970s that provoked the "new consensus" scholarship debunking the role of reliance. Significantly, as was just seen in the data presented by Professor Hillman, the recent reaction to this "new consensus" scholarship has not undermined the importance of promise.To the contrary, it has reinforced it. Nor has it undermined the claim that the existence of detrimental reliance alone is not sufficient to support an action of promissory estoppel. For one thing, a promise is also required, but more than that may also be necessary.
In an important article published almost simultaneously with Hillman's, Sidney DeLong presented the results of his survey of a similarly massive number of promissory estoppel cases over substantially the same time period.His study confirmed Hillman's finding that detrimental reliance remained a necessary element of an action for promissory estoppel,and to that extent at least the "newconsensus" scholars were wrong as a descriptive matter. But, unlike Hillman, DeLong also tried to discern the factor or factors that might be needed to turn detrimental reliance in the absence of a bargain into a successful cause of action.
According to DeLong, his data suggest the existence of two types of reliance which he called "performance reliance" and "enforcement reliance."Performance reliance refers to the trust that a promisee puts in the promisor to perform his promise. For many reasons, wholly apart from the perception of enforceability, the promisee believes that the promise will be performed. Enforcement reliance, by contrast, refers to reliance on a promise that a promisee reasonably believes to be made with the intention of being legally binding. DeLong suggests a norm may be developing that limits promissory estoppel recoveries to enforcement reliance.If this is so, it means that to succeed in making a promissory estoppel claim you need "detrimental reliance plus something" - and that "something" is a manifested intention to be legally bound.
All this, of course, is purely descriptive (and it is far from clear from his tone that DeLong approves of the judicial trend he reports). It does not answer the normative question of whether promissory estoppel actions should be limited to cases where detrimental reliance can be proved or should extend to any manifestation of intention to be legally bound whether bargained-for or not, and whether relied upon or not. I have suggested elsewhere that this would be a good thing: that contractual enforcement is justified, prima facie, whenever there has been a consent to be legally bound, whether explicit or implicit.
In sum, the existence of a manifested intention to be legally bound is what might, as a descriptive matter, and ought to, as a normative matter, separate the detrimental reliance that justifies legal relief from the detrimental reliance that does not. And no theorist has ever advocated compensating all and every form of detrimental reliance on the words and deeds of another. Instead, they have advocated basing recovery on reasonable, justified, or foreseeable reliance. But the next question immediately to be answered has always been: What exactly (or even approximately) constitutes the circumstances that make reliance reasonable, justified, or foreseeable so as to render the promise enforceable? It cannot be the presence of reliance since reliance is present in all such cases. In other words, a purely "reliance theory" cannot explain when detrimental reliance gives rise to a recovery and when it does not. Reliance theorists have been either silent or vague in their answers to this question.
In the interest of putting some doctrinal meat on these theoretical bones, both in my Death of Reliance article and in the first edition of my casebook, I formulated a series of hypothetical Restatement sections that might provide more guidance to courts than the current sections 71 and 90.The first of these, section 71A, accepted as the starting point the proposal of Farber and Matheson that: "A promise is enforceable when made in furtherance of an economic activity."Any promise made between commercial parties would be presumed enforceable unless there was some expressed or implied-in-fact disclaimer of liability. The second, section 71B, established the reverse default rule in cases of noncommercial promises. Such promises would be unenforceable unless supported by a formality manifesting an intention to be legally bound. In section 71C, I described circumstances in which the existence of substantial reliance would itself indicate to the promisee that a promisor intended her promise to be legally binding. And finally, in section 71D, I proposed that a promise meeting the requirements of sections 71A-C might still be unenforceable if the promisor could show that a reasonable promisee would not have understood the promisor to have intended the promise to be legally binding.
Upon further reflection, I have been persuaded that this scheme runsthe risk of overenforcement.The problem is its starting point: replacing the requirement of bargained-for consideration with the rebuttable presumption that any commercial promise should be enforced. I now think, and Sidney DeLong's study confirms that courts may think likewise, that too many promises not intended to be legally binding or reasonably taken as such by promisees would be enforced if this default rule were adopted. What is needed is not the overthrow of the bargain requirement but, like section 90 itself, a supplement to compensate for the underinclusiveness of section 71 - though one that is more definite and theoretically clear than the extraordinarily open-ended section 90.

papers.node_id: 38sandiegolrev193!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Remedies for Imperfect Transactions in Contracts and Torts
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Remedies for Imperfect Transactions in Contracts and Torts
papers.abstract:
Imperfect transactions are promises or assertions insufficiently supported by the accouterments of formalized agreements to be enforceable as contracts. Lack of mutual consideration, discovery of mutual mistake, fraud, or other misrepresentation, disasters intervening between promise and performance, and illusory promises are the typesof imperfections that shift our attention away from conventional remedies in contract. When the promisor's conduct is also tortious, conventional tort remedies may also be inappropriate. There is no unified theory of remedies for imperfect transactions.
The papers by Professors DeLong, Wonnell, and Kelly in this Symposium address different types of imperfect transactions. Promises that are the subject ofare imperfect in the sense that they lack consideration or are disclaimed in subsequent, formalized, written contracts.Section 90 authorizes courts to find remedies for reasonable but fruitless expenditures induced by parties who make promises on which they should reasonably expect others to rely.Professor DeLong decries courts' formalist strategies for enforcing disclaimers that eliminate these promisors' potential liability for intentionally imperfect transactions.Taking Professor DeLong's analysis of imperfect promises one step further sheds light on his critique of formalist analysis of disclaimers. I will hypothesize a rationale for disclaimers and alternative methods for limiting their application that might be appealing to both Professor DeLong and the formalist courts.
The transactions I have described as "imperfect" are not contracts that are breached. They are transactions that are not enforceable as contracts. Professor Wonnell surveys the reasons why a contracting party might change her mind after promising and before performing in order to consider appropriate remedies for each case.Of his six cases,four are cases of breach and two involve imperfect transactions as I have just defined that term. Professor Wonnell agrees that an expectation-based damage rule is appropriate in all but the two imperfect transaction cases.Since I start with the premise that an expectation-based remedy is appropriate in all cases where the court "enforces" a contract, I will focus my reaction on those two "imperfection" cases. I hope my comments will sharpen the definition of these two classes of cases with which Professor Wonnell is concerned. I will also explain why it is likely to be more fruitful to consider those two cases as examples of imperfect transactions rather than as examples of contract breach.
When one party's misrepresentation causes another to suffer adetriment, the interaction between the two may be described as an imperfect transaction. The misrepresentation may induce the other to assent to an agreement or otherwise rely on the other's assertion. In neither case is there an enforceable contract. Whether the result of the misrepresentation is an unenforceable contract or a less formal transaction, the harm done by the misrepresentation calls for a remedy in tort or contract. Professor Kelly describes remedies for this sort of imperfect transaction in the larger context of comparing tort remedies to contract remedies.As I am in complete agreement with his conclusions, I will make several arguments that I believe strengthen his argument that tort and contract remedies are both based on the expectation interest.I will demonstrate how tort damages may be calculated using remedial rules taken from the Uniform Commercial Code and the Restatement (Second) of Contracts. It is not surprising that Professor Kelly chose misrepresentation as the most likely candidate in tort law for a break from the conventional expectation measure of damages.Misrepresentation results in an imperfect transaction analogous to those involving gratuitous promises, mutual mistake, impracticability, and unconscionability. These are all defective transactions for which there is no coherent unifying remedial theory.

How and when formal disclaimers should limit a promisor's liability for inducing reasonable reliance on imperfect promises, and what rationales or constraints justify enforcing or limiting such disclaimers.
Whether remedies for harms caused by misrepresentation can be calculated using the same remedial principles used in contract law (suggesting a unified remedial approach across contract and tort).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev125!!ARTICLE: WHEN DOES THE "FAT LADY" SING? Although this phrase probably originated in the opera setting, one of its more interesting uses occurred in the battle between Pennzoil and Texaco for the Getty Oil Company. When Texaco's Chairman, John K. McKinely, asked Getty Oil's Chairman Sidney Peterson whether Getty might still be available even though an "agreement in principle" had been entered into with Pennzoil, Peterson responded that "the fat lady had not yet sung." Pennzoil Co. v. Getty Oil Co., No. 7425, slip op. at 46 (Del. Ch. Feb. 6, 1984). For a further discussion of the Texaco-Pennzoil case, see infra text accompanying notes 60 to 63. : AN ANALYSIS OF "AGREEMENTS IN PRINCIPLE" IN CORPORATE ACQUISITIONS.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Counterpoise of Contracts: The Reasonable Person Standard and the Subjectivity of Judgment

papers.node_id: 38sandiegolrev169!!SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:The Phantom Reliance Interest in Tort Damages
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:The Phantom Reliance Interest in Tort Damages
papers.abstract:
The reliance interest has fascinated me for some time.As a measure of damages for breach of contract,it seems theoretically unjustified and flawed in its implementation. In theory, it requires compensation for lost opportunities.In practice, such compensation is rarely provided-unless one counts the expectation interest as a proxy for opportunities lost in reliance on a promise.In theory, it justifies recoveries that may exceed expectation.Yet, even its progenitors refused to endorse that implication.Why, then, does the reliance interest have continuing appeal?
One explanation has emerged from discussions with academics: the reliance interest seems apt to some because it resembles tort remedies. Expectation is available only in contract, not in tort.Tort is perceived as the realm of reliance recoveries. That inconsistency may make people uncomfortable. Scholars who see contract as simply a subset of tort naturally prefer that tort remedies apply in each context.Similarly, scholars seeking unified principles underlying remedies generally might be drawn to prefer the reliance interest in contract.The perception that reliance governs in tort appears to contribute to the continuing popularity of the reliance interest in the face of scholarly challenges.
This Article challenges the assumption that the reliance interest is a tort remedy. To the extent that tort remedies can be broken down into expectation and reliance at all, tort remedies usually resemble expectation more closely than they resemble reliance. The project shall proceed in three stages. It will focus first on misrepresentation, the one tort where the reliance interest makes theoretical sense. Despite the justification for employing the reliance interest, it appears that tort lawdoes not limit recoveries to reliance even in this context. Second, focus will shift to personal injury actions. In these cases, it makes very little difference whether we call the remedy reliance or expectation; the same results will apply in almost every case. In cases where it might make a difference, however, there is no support for the suggestion that tort law prefers reliance to expectation. Finally, the Article will assess the implications of this discussion. Fundamentally, it concludes that the reliance interest does not respond to concerns about remedies at all. Its primary rationale centers on liability. That conclusion may seem familiar. I offered it as a possible explanation in my earlier work.Exploring the analogy to tort remedies reinforces the view that the reliance interest is simply an effort to preclude enforcement of promises where reliance did not exist, even when they are part of a bargain.

questions.question: Do damages in tort cases typically aim to compensate plaintiffs for lost expected benefits (lost opportunities) or to reimburse expenses incurred in reliance on the defendant's conduct?

In cases where a false statement induces a plaintiff to act, are recoveries generally limited to reimbursement of those reliance expenditures or do courts also award compensation for lost expected gains?

When courts award reimbursement for reliance-related losses after a broken promise, is the primary rationale remedial (to address the plaintiff's loss) or is it a liability-limiting device meant to avoid enforcing promises that were not actually relied upon?

matched_themes: How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
How should remedies for misrepresentation be calculated, and can misrepresentation damages be harmonized with contract-law remedial principles?
Is categorizing monetary remedies for breach into the three remedial interests (expectation, reliance, restitution) a useful framework for modern normative analysis of contract remedies?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When liability is grounded in misrepresentation rather than ordinary promise enforcement, do courts award different compensatory or punitive remedies?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45uclalrev1005!!ARTICLE: Probability and Chance in Contract Law For David Eisenberg, UCLA '86.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Probability and Chance in Contract Law For David Eisenberg, UCLA '86.

shared_topics.topic: expectation versus reliance as measures of contract damages
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the debate over whether expectation or reliance should govern damage awards — Paper A advocates expectation-based measurement (e.g., using expected value for lost profits), while Paper B critiques the theoretical and practical basis for reliance damages and argues tort and contract remedies more closely resemble expectation.

shared_topics.topic: measuring damages under uncertainty and probability (expected value, foreseeability)
shared_topics.justification: Both authors treat uncertainty and probability as central to how damages should be assessed — Paper A develops concepts (realm of chance, predictability) and recommends expected-value measures and rules for foreseeability, while Paper B examines how uncertainty affects the choice between reliance and expectation and shows that tort law often delivers expectation-like results despite uncertainty.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship and analogies between contract and tort remedies
shared_topics.justification: Each paper examines how remedial rules in contract relate to or contrast with tort law — Paper B directly compares tort remedies to reliance/expectation doctrines, and Paper A uses foreseeability and uncertainty principles (traditionally salient in tort) to analyze contract remedies and reward/prize cases.

shared_topics.topic: when promises should be enforced versus excluded (reliance as a gatekeeping device)
shared_topics.justification: Both discuss enforceability criteria for promises: Paper A argues that promissory structures meant to increase the probability of exchange should be enforceable even absent reciprocal exchange, while Paper B argues the reliance interest often functions to deny enforcement where reliance is absent, highlighting competing rationales for excluding promises from remedy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 39connlrev1977!!ARTICLE: Regulating Contract Formation: Precontractual Reliance, SunkCosts, and Market Structure
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Regulating Contract Formation: Precontractual Reliance, SunkCosts, and Market Structure

shared_topics.topic: theoretical status and limits of the reliance interest as a damages measure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages the reliance concept by showing how precontractual reliance (PCR) creates economic puzzles about who should bear sunk preparation costs and motivates arguments for reliance-based precontractual liability; Paper B directly interrogates the theoretical justification and practical limits of the reliance interest as a measure of damages, comparing it to expectation and documenting where it does and does not operate in law.

shared_topics.topic: precontractual reliance, sunk costs, and the holdup/under‑investment problem
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on relationship‑specific precontractual expenditures (sunk PCR), the holdup risk and the resulting prediction of under‑investment in bidding/negotiation; Paper B treats reliance as compensation for lost opportunities and focuses on contexts (e.g., misrepresentation and promise reliance) where reliance expenditures precede or accompany transactions, implicating similar concerns about whether reliance losses will be recouped.

shared_topics.topic: use of legal doctrines (precontractual liability and remedies) to shape investment incentives in negotiation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract law (including doctrines like precontractual liability, termination fees, and remedial rules) should be structured to encourage optimal PCR investment; Paper B analyzes how reliance doctrines and the choice between reliance and expectation remedies affect liability and therefore the incentives parties have to rely and invest before agreement.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance in determining liability versus remedy and its effect on enforcement of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A raises questions about whether imposing liability for precontractual reliance (and related remedial rules) is justified to prevent under‑investment; Paper B concludes that the reliance interest functions largely as a tool to determine when promises will be enforced (liability) rather than as a pure measure of remedies, highlighting the same blurred boundary between liability and remedy that affects enforcement of precontractual investments.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92yalelj14!!ARTICLE: Restitution as a Remedy for Breach of Contract: The Case of the Partially Performing Seller
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Restitution as a Remedy for Breach of Contract: The Case of the Partially Performing Seller

shared_topics.topic: the appropriate measure of recovery for breach of contract (restitution vs expectation vs reliance)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze which monetary remedy is normatively and doctrinally appropriate when promises are broken: Paper A examines whether a partially performing seller should receive money restitution or be limited to expectancy damages, while Paper B criticizes the reliance measure and compares reliance to expectation as a permissible damages metric.

shared_topics.topic: normative justifications for remedies (economic efficiency versus other principles)
shared_topics.justification: Both works evaluate the theoretical grounds for awarding particular remedies—Paper A explicitly compares the efficiency properties of restitution and expectancy and rejects efficiency as decisive, while Paper B interrogates the theoretical justification for reliance (versus expectation) and shows that its appeal does not track sound remedial theory.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies interact with liability and enforcement policy (when courts should enforce promises)
shared_topics.justification: Both articles consider how choice of remedy affects whether and how promises are enforced: Paper A argues restitution can improperly compel performance and intrude on personal liberty, and Paper B contends the reliance interest often functions as a device to withhold enforcement where reliance is absent.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of remedies from other doctrines (equitable or tort analogies to contract remedies)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage the question of cross‑doctrinal borrowing of remedies—Paper A treats restitution (an equitable remedy) within contract breach contexts and its incompatibility with liberal principles, and Paper B examines the supposed analogy between tort remedies and contract reliance recoveries and rejects the claim that tort law favors reliance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 66geowashlrev508!!ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Ipse Dixit: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts and the Modern Development of Contract Law

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance in enforcing contractual promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the ‘reliance interest’ and challenges the idea that reliance is a distinct tort-style remedy in contract, while Paper B studies Restatement (Second) provisions (e.g., §§87(2), 139, 86) that rely on reliance-based doctrines to make promises enforceable and documents courts' acceptance of those reliance-based rules.

shared_topics.topic: choice between expectation and reliance as measures of recovery
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly contrasts expectation and reliance as competing measures of damages and argues reliance is often a pretext to avoid enforcement, and Paper B examines Restatement provisions and case law that shift traditional rules (affecting when expectation or reliance remedies apply) showing courts' movement toward modern standards.

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel/reliance doctrines as a bridge between contract and tort
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the perception that tort remedies (reliance) inform contract remedies and interrogates whether tort law truly prefers reliance, while Paper B surveys Restatement (Second) sections that institutionalize reliance-based doctrines (promissory estoppel, irrevocable offers, statute-of-frauds exceptions) and how courts have treated them.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal change becomes accepted authority (sources of legal doctrine and judicial deference)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates doctrinal reasoning behind adopting reliance-oriented doctrines (including analogies to tort) and their justificatory basis, and Paper B empirically traces how courts have deferred to the Restatement (Second)'s modern rules—raising normative questions about when and why courts adopt academic formulations.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 81notredamelrev747!!ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW AS AN ITERATIVE PROCESS: A PRELIMINARY INQUIRY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE COMMON LAW AS AN ITERATIVE PROCESS: A PRELIMINARY INQUIRY

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal categories and analogies between contract and tort shape remedies and liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly interrogates the assumed analogy between tort and contract remedies, arguing that the reliance interest’s appeal comes from its resemblance to tort remedies and challenging the claim that reliance is a tort remedy; Paper B theorizes how doctrinal rules and the application of prior decisions (including analogical moves across doctrinal domains) channel future outcomes, showing how doctrinal categories and analogies influence the evolution of legal rules and remedial practice.

shared_topics.topic: the role of precedent and case-to-case iteration in producing stable yet changeable legal doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A relies on the empirical and doctrinal practice of tort and contract cases (misrepresentation, personal injury) to show how remedial outcomes actually operate over time; Paper B models the common law as an iterative, path-dependent process in which each case’s result becomes input for later cases, explaining systemic stability and the mechanisms by which change (bifurcation) occurs.

shared_topics.topic: constraints on judicial discretion in shaping remedies and enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concludes that the reliance interest functions largely to limit enforcement (liability) despite theoretical critiques, implying that remedial doctrines constrain what courts will enforce; Paper B argues that path dependence and systemic stability in the common law place substantive limits on the systemic significance of individual judges’ preferences, requiring particular mechanisms for doctrinal change.

shared_topics.topic: methodological emphasis on close doctrinal and case analysis to understand legal rules and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A tests theoretical claims about reliance by examining specific tort and contract contexts (e.g., misrepresentation, personal injury) rather than relying solely on abstract theory; Paper B argues that the common law’s complexity demands careful, case-centered study and uses selective case examples to link micro-level decisions to macro-level doctrinal dynamics.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 22cornelljlpubpoly93!!ARTICLE: PROMISES, POLICIES, AND PRINCIPLES: THE SUPREME COURT AND CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION IN LABOR RELATIONS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PROMISES, POLICIES, AND PRINCIPLES: THE SUPREME COURT AND CONTRACTUAL OBLIGATION IN LABOR RELATIONS

shared_topics.topic: when and on what grounds courts enforce promises (reliance versus other doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A investigates how the ‘reliance interest’ is used (or invoked) to justify when contractual promises are compensated or effectively not enforced, arguing reliance functions to preclude enforcement absent reliance; Paper B analyzes when the Supreme Court enforces promises in the labor-relations context, showing the Court’s choices turn on competing doctrinal bases (policy vs principle) that determine whether particular promises will be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: how remedial doctrines (reliance vs expectation) affect substantive liability for promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that reliance and expectation remedies are often conflated and that reliance serves primarily to limit liability rather than to calibrate damages, while Paper B examines how the Court’s preference for policy- or principle-based approaches has concrete effects on the scope of contractual obligations and the remedies available in collective-bargaining and labor disputes.

shared_topics.topic: comparative use of doctrines across legal domains to decide obligations (contract↔tort or contract↔labor policy)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly compares contract and tort remedial doctrines to challenge the view that reliance is a tort-style remedy, and Paper B probes whether general contract principles or labor-specific policy should govern promises in labor law, i.e., whether and when doctrinal analogies or domain-specific rules should control enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of academic and jurisprudential movements on doctrine about promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses how scholars’ inclination to unify contract with tort influences the continued appeal of reliance, and Paper B traces shifts in the Supreme Court’s treatment of labor promises to broader intellectual currents (the legal process school, freedom-of-contract scholarship, and political philosophy), showing both link doctrinal outcomes to scholarly and philosophical influences.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 7wmmarybuslrev1!!ARTICLE: KILL THE MONSTER: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AS AN INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: KILL THE MONSTER: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AS AN INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF ACTION

shared_topics.topic: the normative status and scope of the reliance interest versus expectation damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critically analyzes whether reliance is a theoretically justified damages measure in contract (and whether tort remedies actually reflect reliance or expectation), while Paper B traces promissory estoppel's reliance-based origins and debates when reliance should substitute for consideration and yield remedies instead of expectation damages.

shared_topics.topic: the encroachment of tort-like or fairness-driven doctrines on classical contract principles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the perceived analogy between tort remedies and contract reliance claims and challenges the view that tort favors reliance, and Paper B argues that promissory estoppel and ad hoc fairness-based decisions are dissolving traditional contract rules into tort-style notions of injustice.

shared_topics.topic: reliance-based doctrines (including promissory estoppel) as mechanisms to enforce or negate promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper B focuses on promissory estoppel as an enforcement device rooted in reliance and critiques its expansion as an independent cause of action, while Paper A situates the reliance interest as primarily a tool for determining liability (i.e., when promises should not be enforced absent reliance), thereby engaging the same functional questions about reliance-based rules.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal coherence, predictability, and the practical implications of expanding reliance remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper B emphasizes the business harms from unpredictable, fairness-driven enlargement of promissory estoppel and calls for legislative limits, and Paper A considers the implications of reliance rhetoric for remedy rules and liability allocation, questioning whether reliance doctrines undermine coherent remedial and enforcement frameworks.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 120pennstlrev477!!ARTICLE: Charitable Pledges: Contracts of Confusion
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Charitable Pledges: Contracts of Confusion

shared_topics.topic: theoretical legitimacy of the reliance interest / promissory estoppel as a basis for enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the reliance interest in contract and tort, arguing that reliance is often invoked without theoretical justification, while Paper B criticizes courts' widespread use of promissory estoppel/reliance doctrines to enforce charitable pledges and labels those doctrines legally twisted and empirically problematic.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between contract (expectation/consideration) and reliance-based doctrines in imposing liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centrally compares expectation versus reliance remedies and how tort and contract doctrines overlap or diverge, and Paper B analyzes whether charitable pledges should be enforced under ordinary contract principles (consideration) or instead via reliance doctrines such as promissory estoppel.

shared_topics.topic: judicial use of doctrinal fictions or pragmatic constructions to achieve enforcement outcomes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that invoking reliance sometimes functions as a device to avoid enforcing promises or to reshape liability, and Paper B documents and critiques the array of legal fictions (e.g., implied bilateral contracts, unilateral contract theories, modified estoppel) courts employ to make donors liable for pledges.

shared_topics.topic: the evidentiary role of donor/claimant intent and reliance in determining liability and remedial scope
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats reliance as tied to liability (whether promises should be enforced when reliance is absent), while Paper B focuses on donors' manifested intent and whether clear evidence of intent or demonstrated charity reliance should be required before enforcing pledges.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 44iowajcorpl649!!ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Legal Foundations of Apparent Authority

shared_topics.topic: historical and conceptual foundations of private-law doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical emergence of apparent authority and challenges the traditional estoppel-origin account, arguing for an independent doctrinal genesis tied to an objective turn; Paper B likewise interrogates the assumed pedigree of the reliance interest, rejecting common assumptions about its role in tort and tracing its theoretical justification back to liability concerns rather than remedial policy.

shared_topics.topic: third-party reliance and representation as a basis for legal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when a principal becomes bound because a third party reasonably relies on an agent's apparent authority (and the estoppel account of that reliance), while Paper B examines reliance as the justificatory basis for damages (especially in misrepresentation) and whether reliance functions as the proper ground for recovery in tort or contract.

shared_topics.topic: comparative boundaries and cross-influence among agency, contract, and tort
shared_topics.justification: Paper A compares the development of objective reasoning across agency and contract law and situates agency as an earlier site of that shift; Paper B compares contract and tort remedies (and their analogies), asking whether remedial categories from one branch appropriately migrate to the other.

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing liability rules from remedial doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is concerned with when principals are held liable for agents’ acts (a rules-of-liability question tied to apparent authority), and Paper B argues that what is often framed as a remedial ‘reliance interest’ is better understood as a reflex of liability allocation rather than a discrete remedial theory.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 55fordhamlrev125!!ARTICLE: WHEN DOES THE "FAT LADY" SING? Although this phrase probably originated in the opera setting, one of its more interesting uses occurred in the battle between Pennzoil and Texaco for the Getty Oil Company. When Texaco's Chairman, John K. McKinely, asked Getty Oil's Chairman Sidney Peterson whether Getty might still be available even though an "agreement in principle" had been entered into with Pennzoil, Peterson responded that "the fat lady had not yet sung." Pennzoil Co. v. Getty Oil Co., No. 7425, slip op. at 46 (Del. Ch. Feb. 6, 1984). For a further discussion of the Texaco-Pennzoil case, see infra text accompanying notes 60 to 63. : AN ANALYSIS OF "AGREEMENTS IN PRINCIPLE" IN CORPORATE ACQUISITIONS.

shared_topics.topic: promissory estoppel/reliance as a substitute for formal contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how reliance functions (and is sometimes invoked) to justify or preclude enforcement of promises even absent a bargain, while Paper B examines promissory estoppel and enforcement of obligations to negotiate in good faith as mechanisms to bind parties at the 'agreement in principle' stage when a definitive contract has not been completed.

shared_topics.topic: how courts determine enforceability and the parties' intent in borderline promise situations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges assumptions about tort/contract analogies and emphasizes that reliance often serves as a liability gatekeeper rather than a remedy principle, and Paper B criticizes courts' 'all or nothing' approach to agreements in principle, urging a more nuanced inquiry into the parties' expectations and intent.

shared_topics.topic: how damages/remedies should be measured and the implications of that choice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the consequences of labeling recoveries as reliance or expectation (including concerns that reliance could exceed expectation) and examines doctrinal practice in tort and contract contexts, whereas Paper B devotes a section to how damages should be determined for withdrawn 'agreements in principle' and evaluates the equitable and economic consequences of applying different remedial frameworks.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 92valrev1325!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTEMPORARY POLITICAL THEORY AND PRIVATE LAW: ESSAY: MAKING AND KEEPING CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTEMPORARY POLITICAL THEORY AND PRIVATE LAW: ESSAY: MAKING AND KEEPING CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: normative justification of contract remedies (expectation vs reliance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B directly interrogates the theoretical basis for awarding reliance versus expectation damages in breach of contract and shows how reliance is often unjustified or confused in practice; Paper A treats questions about why promises should be enforced as part of a broader inquiry into the moral grounds for keeping agreements, which bears on what kinds of remedial protection (e.g., reliance or expectation) are normatively appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: the role of harm to disappointed promisees and reliance in explaining contract obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the ‘‘harm’’ account that grounds obligations in the harm done to disappointed promisees and criticizes its narrow focus, while Paper B analyzes the reliance interest as a damages doctrine tied to losses from relying on promises and critiques both its justification and its practical application.

shared_topics.topic: the relationship and analogy between contract law and tort law (the tortification of contract)
shared_topics.justification: Paper B explicitly compares tort remedies to contract remedies and challenges the assumption that tort law favors reliance-based recovery, and Paper A references and critiques the trend of translating tort concepts into contract discourse (the tortification of contract), using that cross-domain analogy to evaluate theories of agreements.

shared_topics.topic: how reasoning about making agreements relates to doctrines used to avoid enforcement or limit liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that reasons for making agreements are intertwined with reasons for keeping them and that theories must integrate both sides of the relation, while Paper B shows how the reliance doctrine functions in part to prevent enforcement where reliance is absent—demonstrating a doctrinal mechanism that links considerations about formation/acceptance (making) to choices about enforcement and damages (keeping).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 7wmmarybuslrev1!!ARTICLE: KILL THE MONSTER: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AS AN INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF ACTION
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: KILL THE MONSTER: PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL AS AN INDEPENDENT CAUSE OF ACTION

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance (reliance interest) versus expectation in awarding contract remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the theoretical justification and practical application of the reliance interest as a measure of contract damages and contrasts it with the expectation interest; Paper B treats promissory estoppel as a reliance-based doctrine that substitutes for consideration and thereby raises questions about when reliance — rather than expectation — should govern enforcement and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary and interaction between contract law and tort principles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges the common assumption that reliance-based recoveries are primarily tort remedies and compares how tort and contract remedies map onto reliance and expectation; Paper B argues that promissory estoppel and other fairness-driven doctrines are causing contract law to be infused with tort-like, ad hoc notions of unfairness, eroding classical contract rules.

shared_topics.topic: how reliance doctrines affect enforcement of promises and liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A concludes that the reliance interest often operates to prevent enforcement of promises when reliance is absent and that its rationale centers on liability limits; Paper B examines how reliance-based promissory estoppel is being used to enforce promises that would otherwise be unenforceable, thereby changing who is held liable under contract law.

shared_topics.topic: consequences for legal predictability and commercial certainty from reliance-based or fairness-driven doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explores theoretical and doctrinal implications of privileging reliance and what that means for coherent remedial rules; Paper B emphasizes the practical harms to businesses and transactional predictability when courts apply promissory estoppel or community-fairness standards instead of traditional, predictable contract doctrines.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2000byulrev1363!!ARTICLE:Nachfrist Was Ist? Thinking Globally and Acting Locally: Considering Time Extension Principles of the U.N. Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods in Revising the Uniform Commercial Code
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:Nachfrist Was Ist? Thinking Globally and Acting Locally: Considering Time Extension Principles of the U.N. Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods in Revising the Uniform Commercial Code

shared_topics.topic: theoretical foundations and limits of contract remedies

papers.node_id: 2000utahlrev185!!SYMPOSIUM: A Fish Story: Alaska Packers' Association v. Domenico
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: A Fish Story: Alaska Packers' Association v. Domenico
papers.abstract:
A persistent criticism leveled against legal education is that it fails to teach cases in context.The lack of context arises in two ways. First, the statement of facts in judicial opinions is extremely truncatedand is usually presented as if the facts of the case are not problematical or in dispute.Second, appellate decisions are presented in textbooks and analyzed in classroom discussion with little or no discussion of the historical, economic, and social context in which the litigation arose and was pursued.
The criticism concerning this lack of context has several facets. By simplifying the factual context and ignoring the larger societal context, legal education gives a distorted view of reality--litigation in a vacuum. Pedagogical research, moreover, suggests that adult learners (a category into which all law students fall) learn more easily and retain information moresolidly when the material is presented in context.Finally, and perhaps not unrelated to the preceding point, students (particularly female students) often express feelings of alienation arising in part from the lack of context in which they feel compelled to learn the law.
At the same time, there seems to be a growing interest among legal historians and scholars in exploring the social and historical background of the litigation that has been reduced to a judicial opinion.I suspect that thisis part of a larger project which seeks to study law within a broader social context. During the same period, for example, we have seen the rise of interdisciplinary approaches to legal study: the "law and" movements such as law and literature, law and psychiatry, etc.
This article explores the context of one of the canonical first year contract cases, Alaska Packers' Ass'n v. Domenico.The case involves a wage dispute between a group of Alaskan Salmon fishermen and their employer, the operator of a salmon cannery. In the first section, I present a traditional, straight-forward analysis of the district and circuit court opinions. I also examine how other legal scholars, relying solely on the written opinions (in fact, apparently relying almost exclusively on the appellate court opinion), have interpreted the case, what it means and what it stands for. In other words, the "traditional" interpretation of the case is explicated.
In the following section, I present the "background story." I attempt to situate the legal decision in the context of the growth of the salmon industry and the formation of the Alaska Packers' Association ("Alaska Packers")--"the fish trust" that operated the cannery at Pyramid Harbor. I also provide details about the cannery operation at Pyramid Harbor, Alaska, which is where the "action" of the case occurs.
In the third section, I propose several alternative interpretations of the case. These alternative interpretations are informed by a close reading of the trial transcriptand by an examination of the conditions of the Alaskan salmon industry at the turn of the century. The alternative narratives I propose cannot help but reflect the context in which I write and thus may say more about the turn of the twentieth century than they do about the turnof the nineteenth. In particular, this article reflects a philosophical bent that questions traditional, authoritative narratives and is open to revisionist accounts.

questions.question: Does situating an appellate contract dispute within its historical, economic, and social context change the interpretation and doctrinal lessons drawn from the judicial opinion?

Can a close examination of trial transcripts and contemporaneous industry conditions produce alternative narratives about the parties' bargaining conduct that challenge the traditional, textbook account of the dispute?
How does the practice of presenting truncated factual narratives in judicial opinions affect legal pedagogy, student understanding, and feelings of alienation among learners?

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
How do casebook selection practices and pedagogical choices (e.g., using multi-issue appellate cases or emphasizing litigation realities) shape students' understanding of contract law and practice?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
Do appellate judges systematically shape factual narratives in published opinions in ways that influence doctrinal placement and case outcomes?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?

When and to what extent should post-contractual promises (e.g., promises for additional payment to induce performance already owed or post-sale statements) be enforceable as warranties or modifications?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?

papers.node_id: 71fordhamlrev623!!SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO: DEDICATION A TRIBUTE TO A GIANT
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO: DEDICATION A TRIBUTE TO A GIANT
papers.abstract:
"Let us raise a standard to which the wise and the honest can repair."
Although George Washington did not have a law professor in mind when he made his famous utterance, can it be seriously questioned that Professor Joseph Perillo has met that standard in his profession and at the school to which he has devoted the greater part of his life? He has enjoyed an illustrious career and may he be blessed with a great many more years of "tilling the soil" in his chosen field, a field in which he has matched in productivity and excellence such giants in the law as Samuel Williston and Arthur Corbin.
Professor Perillo came to Fordham in 1963, after a brief stint in the practice of law and then a Fulbright scholarship at the University of Florence. In a relatively few short years he and his colleague and friend, John D. Calamari, would team up to produce a nationally recognized treatise and case book on the law of contracts. Their books today can be found in every law school classroom and library, and far beyond, helping law students to understand the meaning of a "contract," assisting lawyers in their counseling and advocacy roles, and enabling judges to apply the right principles to difficult factual issues. So many of the School's most prominent graduates credit Professor Perillo for giving them the thorough grounding in contracts which kindled their love of the law and their dedication to the profession. His works have certainly set the standard for "supreme excellence" as encouraged by our first president.
But Professor Perillo's work in the field of contract law is only part of the story. A law professorship carries not only a scholarship responsibility but also teaching and service responsibilities - responsibilities which Professor Perillo has discharged in an extraordinary way.
As a teacher, whether in a classroom or at another podium, Professor Perillo has never yielded to the human temptation to "wing it" or "recycle," so to speak, his notes from the prior year. As great ateacher as he is, he remains a great student, reading every advance sheet and article imaginable to stay current in his field and learn from the insights of others and the controversies which are the grist of a lawyer's work. In all of his teaching he brings boundless energy and enthusiasm, revealing his passion for the law in its grandest tradition.
Professor Perillo's service to his profession and school match his prodigious scholarship and teaching. First and foremost, he has enriched his profession by the quality of his path-breaking scholarship. This has not only been expressed in his own books and articles, too many to mention, but in his undertaking to serve as the general editor of a landmark in the law of contracts. An ordinary person would be content enough just to keep his (or her) own work current - but to do so as well for the work of the late Arthur Corbin is of Olympian proportions.
As for Fordham Law School, Professor Perillo has given a level of service second to no one in the school's entire history. He has taught numerous courses, helping deans whenever asked. In 1981-82 he served as the School's Acting Dean. This is what we said about that service at the time:
An acting deanship is usually an interregnum, a caretaker administration. No one expects anything to be done. Joe Perillo did not behave like an acting dean. Things got done. An innovative Legal Process course was inserted into the first year curriculum. Plans for renovation and expansion of the Law School building proceeded apace. Significant additions were made to the faculty. The law school ran smoothly and well. There were no leftover problems when I arrived on July 1-except the ubiquitous (but, one hopes, not eternal) financial challenges.
Joe Perillo's one year in office will be recorded in the history of the Law School as an acting deanship. In the appreciative minds of the Fordham Law School community, it will be thought of as the Perillo Deanship.
During his almost 40-year career at Fordham, Professor Perillo has chaired or been a member of practically every committee at the school. He chaired the Appointments Committee for a number of years, the self-study committee in connection with an American Bar Association inspection, and numerous task forces and ad hoc committees. For me, he was almost always the first I turned to in moments of urgency and importance. Three particular services stand out - his assuming the directorship of the Stein Institute on Law and Ethics in 1983 when we had no full time scholar and teacher in that field; his taking on the directorship of our law school's first summer program abroad and helping make it in its very first year an historic program, functioning in both Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland; and his acceptance of the moderatorship of the Fordham Law Review until then Professor (now Dean) William Treanor returnedfrom his leave of absence to serve in the United States Department of Justice. In addition, unbeknownst to me, somehow or other Professor Perillo managed to find time to twice be the Cubmaster of Pack 9 of Nyack, covering part of the Cub Scout careers of his two sons. All of these acts of service, in the last period of years alone when the scholarship demands on him were so enormous, qualify Professor Perillo for "sainthood."
Not surprisingly when, in 1997, the Law School was asked to recommend someone to be the first occupant of a Distinguished Fordham University Professorship, the School responded with the name of Professor Perillo. He now occupies that professorship at the School.
Professor Joseph Perillo represents not only the best qualities of the scholar, teacher, and servant of justice but the very best of the Fordham tradition. His high ideals, his great personal integrity, and his concern for others are truly a beacon for all his faculty colleagues and his students. He is what we call "one in a million."
As the citation from his bene merenti medal from Fordham University concluded, I conclude:
"Joe has lived up to his family tradition and to the old Italian proverb that states, "Chi ha tempo non aspetta tempo.' (Literally translated, "He who has time should not wait for time.' - in other words, "Don't put it off - do it now')."
simply add that it is my fervent hope that this seminal year in the life of Professor Joseph Perillo will be followed by many more years of service at Fordham Law School and to the profession we both love. I thank him deeply for his special friendship and for his outstanding contributions to the law school.
