papers.node_id: 32connlrev1699!!SYMPOSIUM: An Uncertain Trumpet: A Gloss on Kirksey v. Kirksey
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: An Uncertain Trumpet: A Gloss on Kirksey v. Kirksey
papers.abstract:
This note briefly explores the theme of "rebellious leadership" with reference to the text of a well-known nineteenth century contracts case, Kirksey v. Kirksey.This is not an examination of the case in its historical context, nor is it a systematic examination of the later history of the Kirksey case as it lives in casebooks and treatises. This kind of inquiry has been undertaken by Professor William Casto and the story of the Kirksey family and the elaboration of the later history of the case must await Professor Casto's discussion. The historical questions opened here are not rooted in archival research, but are suggested simply by my reading of the opinion.
Kirksey contains one of the several memorable pieces of family correspondence in the first-year contracts class. The critical letter reads as follows:
Dear sister Antillico-Much to my mortification, I heard, that brother Henry was dead, and one of his children. I know that your situation is one of grief, and difficulty. You had a bad chance before, but a great deal worse now. I should like to come and see you, but cannot with convenience at present.
do not know whether you have a preference on the place you live on, or not. If you had, I would advise you to obtain your preference, and sell the land and quit the country, as I understand it is very unhealthy, and I know society is very bad. If you will come down and see me, I will let you have a place to raise your family,and I have more open land than I can tend; and on the account of your situation, and that of your family, I feel like I want you and the children to do well.
The court's opinion in the case is very short and can be given here in full.
ORMOND, J. The inclination of my mind, is, that the loss and inconvenience, which the plaintiff sustained in breaking up, and moving to the defendant's, a distance of sixty miles, is a sufficient consideration to support the promise, to furnish her with a house, and land to cultivate, until she could raise her family. My brothers, however, think, that the promise on the part of the defendant, was a mere gratuity, and that an action will not lie for its breach. The judgment of the Court below must therefore be reversed, pursuant to the agreement of the parties.
This is not the sort of opinion which one can treat at length, analyzing the intricacies of argument.Indeed, the opening reference to the inclination of the judge's mind suggests that powerfully persuasive argument and analysis may not even be the foundation of the judgment. Nonetheless, the opinion is of interest. Of its 96 words, 52 are given to a description of the conclusion of the dissenting judge, who is the writer of the opinion. A statement of the majority view is given in 27 words. This action will not lie. No cases are cited, from Alabama or any other jurisdiction.
It is not unusual for contracts cases to be short, ertainly by the standards of constitutional law, but the opinion by John J. Ormond is even shorter than the document containing the original promise. He has, in effect, given equal time to the people and the court. But the last line of the opinion is curious. The decision in favor of the widow must be reversed, "pursuant to the agreement of the parties." What does this mean? They agreed at some point, perhaps to take an appeal. So that it is pursuant to their previous agreement to take an appeal and submit to that decision? But does that require a special statement? The language may even hint at something else, perhaps that the parties could still agree, could still reconcile. After judgment, they could still resume family relations. But this is, doubtless, to read too much into the language.

papers.node_id: 90nwulrev219!!SYMPOSIUM: AN UNLIKELY RESURRECTION
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: AN UNLIKELY RESURRECTION
papers.abstract:
Although many words have been written about Grant Gilmore's The Death of Contractin theyears since its publication, few of those words are women's.A possible explanation for this silence is that feminist theory has so vilified contract that feminist writers consider it dead and buried. Why bother, after all, with one mortally wounded when there are so many other oppressive aspects of law still kicking? Why indeed? Because we are in the midst of an "unlikely resurrection."Lesbian legal theoryis resurrecting contract by advocating that lesbians should seek to use contract rather than be used by it.Lesbian legal theory does this not by ignoring or obscuring aspects of contract that are problematic for feminism, but by confronting ambivalence. That is, lesbian legal theory recognizes thatcontract has the potential both to empower women and to oppress them.
In this Article, I identify lesbian legal theory's resurrection of contract as a response to the shortcomings of feminist theory's approach to contract. Specifically, I argue that feminist theory's extant critique of contract represents an important starting point, but for several reasons is ultimately unsatisfying. First, it suffers from a white, liberal, heterosexual bias; thus it commits the very hegemonic sin it seeks to expose. Second, feminist theory has sought only to describe contract's failings from the margin. Little if any effort has been spent on suggesting transformation from within contract, even though contract is a basic social institution that profoundly affects women's lives. Like persons who look down on a crime from cozy apartments (all the while, of course, decrying the increased violence in society) without venturing into the fray to help the victim, feminist theory's critique falls short of having any real effect on women's lives. Lesbian legal theory can be viewed, in part, as a response to the biases of feminist legal theory. In addition, by resurrecting contract, lesbian legal theory spurs a needed re-examination of women's relationship to contract, a re-examination that squarely faces the ambiguity of contract's role in women's lives.
After surveying feminist legal theory's shortcomings and lesbian legal theory's contributions, I then focus on where women's relationship to contract is presently situated.I begin this analysis by suggesting that contract is a far richer institution than feminist critics have given it credit for. Contract is not dead; nor is it irremediably evil. While contract's commitment to the ideologies of individual autonomy and consent has undeniably had oppressive effects, contract has a deep commitment to other ideologies as well, particularly to those of fairness and connectivity. This divided commitment should be cele-brated, not erased. Contract is in tension with itself, as it must be, given that it often reflects the basic societal tension between individual and community.
To address this tension, I advocate a more inclusive and more ambivalent approach to contract by drawing on postmodern feminist theory.A postmodern perspective, which would view as inadequate any legal theory claiming to speak objectively or universally, can usefully be employed to explain an approach to contract that does not reject contract nor wholly embrace it; one that seeks to play a role inending oppression more than in creating unity for its own sake. Moreover, I reject the idea that the institution of contract itself is inimical to women's interests.Contract has had, and can have, both salutary and harmful effects on women's lives. The task before us is to recognize, rather than ignore, those differences and to grapple with their causes and their meaning.
Interestingly, the position I advance here is congruent with my reading of Gilmore's The Death of Contract. Despite the catchy title, Gilmore did not really believe that contract as an institution was dead.Instead, his lectures told the story of the disintegration of the grand classical theory of contract because of the increasing interplay between contract theory and tort theory and because of the specialization of contract law into fields such as labor, employment, and family law.The death of a theory or the death of the possibility of a particular type of theory is not the death of the institution the theory seeks to address. Despite feminist criticism, contract is alive and well in women's lives. Furthermore, just as I here reject the idea of a unitarytheory of contract that covers all persons and contexts, so did Gilmore: "The conventional idea of a unitary theory of contract, which covers all A's and all B's in all conceivable relationships to each other, is sadly deficient and [we] will be well advised to start thinking in narrower categories."Lesbian legal theory has presented the opportunity to address seriously Gilmore's comments and to take them to heart.

questions.question: Whether mainstream feminist critiques of contract adequately account for intersectional perspectives (e.g., sexuality, race) and offer proposals for transforming contract from within rather than only criticizing it from the margins.
Whether marginalized-group legal perspectives (specifically lesbian legal theory) can reframe and reclaim contract as a tool that empowers women rather than only as an instrument of their oppression.

Whether the institution of contract is inherently inimical to women's interests or instead contains both harmful and beneficial elements (such as fairness and connectivity) that can be harnessed to advance women's social and legal position.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 28seattleulrev1!!ARTICLE: Un-Making Law: The Classical Revival in the Common Law
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Un-Making Law: The Classical Revival in the Common Law

shared_topics.topic: the contemporary status of classical contract theory (revival vs death)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents a movement to revive classical contract doctrines and formalism as a rollback of twentieth-century neoclassical developments, while Paper B directly engages Gilmore's thesis about the 'death of contract' and describes an 'unlikely resurrection' of contract theory within lesbian legal scholarship.

shared_topics.topic: the proper methodological stance for contract law (formalist/unitary theories vs pluralist/realist/postmodern approaches)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A diagnoses and criticizes shifts between classical formalism and neoclassical/realist methods and highlights a proposed return to formalist decisionmaking, whereas Paper B criticizes unitary grand theories of contract and advocates a pluralist, postmodern approach attentive to narrower categories and contextual variation.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary and interaction between contract and tort doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes proposals to re-sharpen the boundaries among contract, tort, and property (privileging distinct categories), while Paper B foregrounds the growing interplay and specialization between contract and tort law as central to the erosion of a single grand contract theory.

shared_topics.topic: how contract law embodies and shapes broader social and political ideologies (market power, gender, and governance)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates the classical revival as part of a conservative, market-elevating political project that reshapes government–market relations, and Paper B examines how contract can both empower and oppress women and lesbians, arguing that contract doctrine is intertwined with gendered and political power structures.

shared_topics.topic: strategies for legal change in contract doctrine (rollback to past doctrines versus internal transformation)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A describes concrete proposals to unmake neoclassical contract law by reinstating older classical rules, whereas Paper B urges transformation from within the institution of contract—resurrecting and reframing contract doctrines to address feminist and lesbian concerns rather than abandoning the institution outright.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 90nwulrev183!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW'S UNITY - AN ESSAY FOR THE MASTER CONTORTIONIST
compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW'S UNITY - AN ESSAY FOR THE MASTER CONTORTIONIST

shared_topics.topic: interpretation of Grant Gilmore's 'The Death of Contract' as the death of a grand theory versus the death of the institution
shared_topics.justification: Both papers engage Gilmore's famous claim and its proper reading — Paper A argues that Gilmore meant the demise of a unitary or grand theory of contract rather than the disappearance of contract as a social institution, while Paper B reflects on and assesses that same thesis as central to Gilmore's contribution and legacy.

shared_topics.topic: the collapse or overlap between contract and tort law (the 'contorts' thesis)
shared_topics.justification: Both pieces discuss the convergence of contract and tort doctrines: Paper A cites the increasing interplay between contract and tort theory as evidence that a single grand contract theory has broken down, and Paper B centers on Gilmore's thesis that tort and contract have collapsed into one another and explores its implications.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of a unitary theory of contract and the need to think in narrower, context-specific categories
shared_topics.justification: Both authors reject a one-size-fits-all theory of contract: Paper A emphasizes feminist/postmodern reasons to abandon a universal account and advocates narrower categories, while Paper B recounts and builds on Gilmore's critique that a conventional unitary contract theory is 'sadly deficient.'

shared_topics.topic: specialization of contract law into distinct fields (e.g., labor, employment, family, secured transactions) and its doctrinal consequences
shared_topics.justification: Both papers note how contract doctrine has fragmented into specialized domains: Paper A points to specialization into labor, employment, and family law as changing the meaning of contract for women, and Paper B highlights Gilmore's own work in secured transactions and how specialization informed his substantive critiques.

shared_topics.topic: Gilmore's influence and legacy in shaping subsequent legal scholarship about contract
shared_topics.justification: Both contributions are part of a symposium on Gilmore and evaluate his impact: Paper A uses Gilmore's insights to reframe feminist approaches to contract, while Paper B offers a personal and scholarly tribute that traces how Gilmore's ideas (style and substance) inspired younger scholars and ongoing debates.

shared_topics.topic: the boundary between contract and tort law (when economic harms should be remedied in contract versus tort)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly addresses the doctrinal line between contract and tort in economic-loss cases, critiquing the economic-loss rule and proposing a new tort to fill gaps where privity and warranties fail; Paper B likewise examines the erosion of a unitary contract theory and the growing interplay between contract and tort doctrines (citing Gilmore), arguing for a rethought role for contract rather than its wholesale rejection.

shared_topics.topic: allocation of risk, liability limits, and protection of reliance/autonomy through legal rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A weighs prevention of indeterminate liability against protecting plaintiffs' reliance interests and parties' freedom to allocate risk by contract (using Cardozo and Coase analyses); Paper B interrogates how contract allocates obligations and risks for women (arguing contract can both empower and oppress) and urges reshaping contractual norms to better protect marginalized actors' autonomy and fairness.

shared_topics.topic: normative critique of existing doctrine and proposals for doctrinal reform
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the disparate judicial approaches to construction/economic-loss disputes and proposes creating a hybrid tort to remedy doctrinal failures; Paper B critiques mainstream feminist legal accounts of contract and advances a constructive, transformative program (via lesbian legal theory/postmodern feminism) to resuscitate and revise contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: use of non-doctrinal theoretical frameworks to justify legal change
shared_topics.justification: Paper A employs microeconomic analysis (Coase theorem) and Cardozo-era policy concerns to design its proposed tort and limit indeterminate liability; Paper B draws on feminist and postmodern theory (and Gilmore’s institutional history) to reinterpret contract's normative commitments and justify re-engaging with contract law as a tool for social change.

shared_topics.topic: the project of reforming contract doctrine from within rather than abandoning it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contests feminist legalism's wholesale rejection of contract and advocates resurrecting and transforming contractal practices to serve marginalized groups; Paper B likewise aims to reconstruct the moral foundations of contract (via a collaborative account) to better justify and reform agreement-based practices.

papers.node_id: 90nwulrev132!!SYMPOSIUM: COGS OR CYBORGS?: BLASPHEMY AND IRONY IN CONTRACT THEORIES
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: COGS OR CYBORGS?: BLASPHEMY AND IRONY IN CONTRACT THEORIES
papers.abstract:
Professor Grant Gilmore described contract as theory "dedicated to the proposition that, ideally, no one should be liable to anyone for anything."In his introduction to The Death of Contract, Gilmore agreed with those scholars who had pronounced the creature dead,but rejected their conclusion that contract theory is no longer worthy of attention. He wrote:
In plotting our course, the best we have to go by is some knowledge of where we have come from. The most lovingly detailed knowledge of the present state of things begins to become useful to us only when we are in a position to compare it with what we know about what was going on last year and the year before that and so on back through the floating mists of time.
Gilmore's stated purpose in writing The Death of Contract was to examine the past as a guide to the future. The book offers an analysis of where we are and have been as a tool for understanding where we may go.
In brief, The Death of Contract presents contract as a theory of life developed by and for a particular kind of being - a nineteenth-century individualist of the Oliver Wendell Holmes variety - and explains the passing of contract as the inevitable consequence of a change in the world's inhabitants.Contract has died, according to Gilmore, because individualists have died. People now are interdependent cogs. We cogs, according to Gilmore, seek relationships andperceive obligations very differently from our atomistic ancestors and thus we develop very different law. Gilmore predicts, then, that contract law will reflect norms of interdependence and will feature values of trust, reliance, and reciprocity.
The Death of Contract has failed in its declared purpose. Its account of the life and power of contract has turned out to be a misleading guide to the future of contract law. Others would argue that this stated purpose was not Gilmore's real purpose, that he actually meant to provoke deeper analysis of contract theory, to lay groundwork for a more complete critique of the work of Oliver Wendell Holmes, or merely to amuse his colleagues, and that the book succeeded in these other goals. That may be so, and I do not wish to contest the contribution The Death of Contract has made. But I do want to focus on its failure as prediction. As Gilmore observed, "it is possible to learn as much from a failed experiment as from a successful one,"and there is much to learn from the failure of The Death of Contract. In addition, Gilmore's predictions clearly invite play with world-inhabiting figures and their ethics, politics, and law, and he's right, it is fun to play.
The first section of this Article discusses two of the most notable predictive failures of The Death of Contract, regarding the doctrines of reliance and unjust enrichment, and suggests that these failures were caused by Gilmore's underestimation of the persistence of contract ideology. The second section features some contemporary contract theories, focusing especially on their understandings of the persistence and meaning of contract. This sampling will be necessarily incomplete, presented as a kind of conversation and offered to fill in some of the silence in Gilmore's analysis. The final section joins with Gilmore's play of world-inhabitants and suggests that it is better to imagine ourselves cyborgs rather than cogs, for cyborgs seek active and multiple connection, while cogs live mind- and spirit-deadening coexistence. In furtherance of this cyborgian search, this section points to two engaging lines of interdisciplinary work that offer direction for future contract theorizing.
. On the Purported Birth of Interdependence: Blasphemy and the Reaffirmation of Contract

questions.question: Whether a societal shift from nineteenth-century individualism to greater social interdependence has caused contract law to transform from an atomistic, liability-focused framework to one that prioritizes trust, relational connections, and reciprocal obligations.
What explains the persistence and resilience of contract ideology despite social and normative changes that seemed to predict its decline?

Whether conceptualizing parties as actively connected, multiple-linked beings (a "cyborg" model of social actors) provides a more accurate and productive foundation for contract theory and reform than models that portray parties as isolated or merely interdependent units.

matched_themes: When should courts enforce oral agreements that fail formal writing requirements because of wrongful conduct or reasonable reliance?
When should a non-party be permitted to enforce a contract (third-party beneficiaries and non-party recovery)?
How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts measure contract damages by expectation (net lost surplus) versus reliance (out-of-pocket expenditures) or restitution, and what principles should guide offsets and mitigation?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should expectation (benefit-of-the-bargain) damages be the default remedy for breach, or should reliance, restitution, or alternative measures be preferred in particular contexts?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONTRACT IN CONTEXT AND CONTRACT AS CONTEXT

shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends interdisciplinary lines of work to reconceptualize contract (e.g., imagining cyborgs) and reads historical shifts in doctrine, and Paper B draws on economics, psychology, sociology, and history to argue for contextualized, empirically informed contract interpretation and regulation.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism about unitary predictive theories of contract and the limits of grand narratives
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats Gilmore's failed prediction as evidence that grand historical theories misread contract's persistence, and Paper B questions the explanatory power of any single, unitary theory of contract law and promotes a taxonomy of context-specific approaches instead.

shared_topics.topic: using doctrinal history to inform normative prescriptions and reform of specific contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Each article uses historical and doctrinal narrative not merely descriptively but to recommend principles: Paper B develops a substantive principle for when third‑party beneficiaries should enforce contracts, and Paper A uses historical failure of prediction (reliance, unjust enrichment) to suggest alternative theoretical framings (e.g., cyborgian interdependence) for future contract theorizing.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Allegheny College Revisited: Cardozo, Consideration, and Formalism in Context

papers.node_id: 68ohiostlj71!!SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Myth of Precontractual Reliance
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: COMMERCIAL CALAMITIES: Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores and the Myth of Precontractual Reliance
papers.abstract:
The conventional wisdom among contemporary scholars is that courts sometimes will impose promissory estoppel liability for reliance investments undertaken prior to any agreement between commercial parties.Evidence ofpromises made and relied upon during the negotiation process together with a "general obligation arising out of the negotiations themselves" are the supposed grounds for imposing liability even for preliminary negotiations that ultimately break down.But even a casual survey of contemporary case law casts significant doubt on the accuracy of the conventional view. Courts actually make some form of agreement a necessary pre-condition to a promisee's recovery. The real issues are: When will a preliminary agreement be found? And how does the nature of such agreement determine when and how a promisee can recover?
These questions have generated a literal flood of litigation that has been virtually ignored in contemporary contract and commercial law courses. The reason that this question is ignored in commercial law is that commercial law courses only teach cases that are decided under one or more provisions of the Uniform Commercial Code and yet many commercial law issues, such as this one, require one to exit the Code via section 1-103 and invoke the common law of contracts. One reason that this question is ignored in Contracts classes is because of the misplaced attention given to the decision of the Wisconsin Supreme Court in Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores, Inc.As a consequence of a fundamental misunderstanding of the law in action, lawyers bring suits claiming reliance on preliminary negotiations and, to their surprise and that of their clients, they lose. Meanwhile, an entire new body of law enforcing certain preliminary agreements has emerged unbeknownst to most lawyers (and legal academics).
The story of this misunderstanding of the law of precontractual liability begins with Hoffman. In Hoffman, the court held that even if two parties had never reached agreement on essential factors necessary to establish a contract, a party who relied on representations made during the negotiations could recover sunk costs based on the doctrine of promissory estoppel as expressed in Section 90 of the Restatement of Contracts.Under this doctrine, the court held that a "promise"-here Red Owl's representation that $ 18,000 wassufficient capital to secure a franchise-need not be as definite in its terms as a promise that is the basis of a traditional bargain contract.
Putting aside for the moment the dubious accuracy of that holding as a matter of contract doctrine, one fact has become clear in the intervening years during which time Hoffman has been ensconced as a favorite in Contracts casebooksand analyzed in numerous law review articles:Hoffman is an outlier; the case has not been followed in its own or other jurisdictions.Indeed, a recent case applying the Wisconsin law that governed Hoffman refused to award reliance damages on a promissory estoppel claim under similar facts.Courts in other jurisdictions have established strict limitationsfor imposing promissory liability based on representations made during the negotiation process.
All of this begs for answers to several key questions: How could the court in Hoffman find liability where so many other courts could not? And, what exactly is the law of contracts in the muddy area of precontractual liability? In this essay, I begin with a close look at the Hoffman case. The transcript of the trial reveals a story far different from the conventional understanding of the dispute between Joseph Hoffman and the representatives of Red Owl Stores.The truth suggests an important lesson for law teachers (and law students): It is dangerous to draw inferences about emerging doctrine from isolated cases, and it helps to read cases systematically if one wishes to recover the law in action. By setting the record straight on what really happened in Hoffman and pointing where the legal rules governing preliminary agreements have evolved in the years since the case was decided, I hope to encourage a more systematic approach to the "discovery" of new legal doctrines.
. The True Facts of Hoffman v. Red Owl Stores
The Supreme Court of Wisconsin relied on an edited transcript of the trial as the basis for its decision.But the complete trial transcript of the casepaints a very different picture of the relationship between Joseph Hoffmanand Edward Lukowitz and the other Red Owl agents headquartered in Minneapolis.This is true even if one endeavors to interpret all facts in the light most favorable to Hoffman, as the appellee holding a jury verdict.
The key to unraveling the true story behind Hoffman is to ignore the red herring. Specifically, let's put to one side a consideration of the various actions taken by Hoffman in reliance on statements made by Lukowitz and the other Red Owl representatives during the negotiation process. Rather, let's focus on a single fact. Hoffman claimed to have "about $ 18,000" available to be set up in a Red Owl franchise.This much is conceded by all. These, then, are the pertinent questions: What was the understanding as to the composition of the $ 18,000? Was it supposed to be all equity, or was it to be cash composed of some equity and some debt? If the latter, from what sources was Hoffman to obtain his encumbered cash? Finally, how reasonable was Red Owl's reaction to the changing sources of Hoffman's prospective $ 18,000 contribution as he moved his assets around between September 1961 and January 1962? While these financing questions are complex, they contain the answer to the puzzle that has perplexed students and commentators for years: What explains the behavior of Red Owl officials who, according to the court, repeatedly increased Hoffman's minimum capital requirements, first from $ 18,000 to $ 24,000, then to $ 26,000, and ultimately to $ 34,000?
A. The Purchase and Sale of the Wautoma Grocery Store and the $ 18,000 "Assurance"
In the fall of 1959, Joseph Hoffman was restless. He had operated a bakery in Wautoma, Wisconsin since 1956, but he wanted to do more.So, in November 1959, Hoffman contacted Sid Jansen, the Division Manager of Red Owl Stores,and inquired about the possibility of acquiring a Red Owlfranchise store. Informal discussions continued but without much progress and, by the fall of 1960, Edward Lukowitz had taken over for Jansen as Division Manager. Around Christmas that year Hoffman had an idea. He thought "it might be a good idea to get a little experience in the grocery business before I go into a bigger store."A friend in Wautoma who was running such a store had suffered a heart attack and the store was available. He called Lukowitz who looked into it and advised him to go ahead.
Hoffman bought the Wautoma grocery store business from his friend for $ 16,000 in February 1961 and assumed the lease on the building.Things went well even though Hoffman was stretched thin in managing both the bakery and the grocery business at the same time. In May, Lukowitz and another Red Owl employee came to the store to conduct an inventory, and they concluded that the store was running a three to four percent profit, which they judged as pretty good under the circumstances.Lukowitz thereupon urged Hoffman to sell the business to his assistant, Edward Wrysinski, in order to free up his equity for the larger Red Owl store. Hoffman was reluctant to sell in June because the summer business in the lake country was historically very brisk (an estimated 5000 tourists would increase the summer population significantly).
At this meeting in May 1961, Hoffman said to Lukowitz and his colleague, "Fellows, you know how much money I got-about $ 18,000. Will this put me in a bigger operation or won't it?"Lukowitz replied that there would be no problem with that level of investment.There was, however, no discussion then (or at any time thereafter) as to the nature of the $ 18,000 investment. Was it to be all equity, or was it to be part equity and part borrowed cash?Hoffman clearly assumed it was the latter. He had no intention of selling his bakery business in order to free up equity for the new franchise. Rather, he hoped to continue that business and operate the new Red Owl Store at the same time.He was thinking of putting together $ 18,000 in cash consisting of his current banked savings of about $ 10,500 and a $ 7500 loan from his father-in-law, Simon Vanden Heuvel, a prosperous local farmer.
Red Owl, on the other hand, regarded a substantial equity contribution from Hoffman as the key to a successful franchise.Indeed, Red Owl officials had reason to believe that Hoffman had more than enough equity to establish a franchise. On September 11, 1961, Hoffman had provided a financial statement to Lukowitz that was passed on to the home office in Minneapolis. This statement represented that Hoffman had business equity of at least $ 28,000, consisting of $ 10,000 in cash, $ 1500 in inventory in the bakery, $ 4500 equity in the bakery building, and $ 12,000 equity in his bakery equipment.Thus, from Red Owl's perspective, Hoffman would have ample equity, provided he liquidated his bakery business.
The Wautoma grocery store was sold to Ed Wrysinski on June 6, 1961 for $ 18,000.At the time he sold in June, many details about establishing Hoffman in a bigger store were unresolved, including which town would be the best location for the new store, the size and site of the store building, fixtures needed for a store, etc.Shortly afterward, Lukowitz suggestedalternative locations for the new store-Lake Mills, Clintonville, Kewaunee, and Chilton. The two of them traveled around looking at these places and finally settled on a lot in Chilton.On August 3, Hoffman acquired a thirty-day option to purchase the Chilton lot for a price of $ 6000 with $ 1000 down on exercise of the option.The plan was that Hoffman would purchase the lot and then resell it at a profit to the contractor who was building the new store, taking back a lease at a rental that reflected the enhanced price the builder agreed to pay.In essence, the sale/leaseback was designed both to capture equity in the lot and to serve as an indirect loan from the builder to Hoffman. The goal was to open the new store by December 1.

questions.question: When will courts impose liability for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations in the absence of a finalized agreement?

Under what factual or legal conditions will a preliminary agreement be found during negotiations, and how does the nature of such a preliminary agreement determine whether and how a party can recover for reliance losses?

When should courts allow recovery for reliance investments made during precontractual negotiations, and what factual patterns determine liability and measure of compensation?
Should legal relationships deliberately created by agreement that do not generate enforceable duties (conferring privileges, powers, or immunities) be classified and treated as contracts?

How do casebook selection practices and pedagogical choices (e.g., using multi-issue appellate cases or emphasizing litigation realities) shape students' understanding of contract law and practice?

When parties attach materially different subjective meanings to contract terms, should interpretation and damages rely on objective standards, the promisor's understanding, or the promisee's reliance interest?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
What default rule should govern precontractual bargaining to allocate risk, protect transaction-specific investments, and promote socially optimal contracting?

What criteria should govern termination powers and cancellations that produce disproportionate forfeiture, and should compensation be mandated?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
When should courts recognize and enforce interim obligations (such as duties to negotiate in good faith) that constrain withdrawal after an agreement in principle?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do appellate judges systematically shape factual narratives in published opinions in ways that influence doctrinal placement and case outcomes?

How have courts and jurisdictions developed enforcement of non-bargained, reliance-based promises (promissory estoppel), why do doctrines differ across places and time, and what effects has doctrinal expansion produced?

Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?

Do formalistic evidentiary requirements (like proving an exchange) remain necessary for reliable contract formation, or could simpler signals of intent suffice?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How should legal systems structure causes of action that protect reliance interests while avoiding indeterminate or disproportionately large liability?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: precontractual reliance and liability for promises made during negotiations
shared_topics.justification: Both articles engage substantively with when and how courts will (or should) impose liability for reliance on representations made in preliminary negotiations — Paper A by asking when a preliminary agreement will be found and how that affects recovery, and Paper B by surveying the preexisting exceptions and arguing that Section 90 improperly generalized those narrow categories.

shared_topics.topic: historical and case-by-case forensic analysis of key precedents that shaped the doctrine

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal instability and litigation consequences generated by promissory estoppel
shared_topics.justification: Each paper describes the uncertainty and proliferation of litigation that followed the rise of promissory estoppel: Paper A documents a 'flood of litigation' and widespread misunderstandings among practitioners and teachers, and Paper B emphasizes the theoretical chaos and instability Section 90 introduced into contract law.

shared_topics.topic: the enforceability of non‑bargained promises (precontractual negotiations vs. gift promises)

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal workarounds and legal devices to secure enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Both papers survey and evaluate doctrinal mechanisms courts and parties use to convert non‑contractual assurances into enforceable obligations: Paper A traces how courts treat preliminary agreements and when common‑law doctrines (like §90) are applied or limited, while Paper B proposes and analyzes a third‑party beneficiary 'bypass' (and notes other devices like trusts and merchant irrevocable offers) to achieve enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: what facts, formalities, or indicators constitute a 'serious' promise for courts
shared_topics.justification: Each article is concerned with the evidentiary and formal markers that distinguish casual statements from legally significant commitments—Paper A delves into the financing arrangements, representations, and contemporaneous document record that courts treat as indicating a preliminary agreement or reliance, and Paper B interrogates seals, irrevocability, third‑party vesting, and other formal signs that a promisor seriously intends a gift to be binding.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A advocates reading cases systematically rather than inferring doctrine from isolated rulings and scrutinizes factual narratives underlying judicial decisions, while Paper B critiques and contrasts Cardozo’s value-balancing, contextual method with Posner’s efficiency-driven, principled approach to judicial reasoning in contract disputes.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts objective rules with scenarios where parties' agreed expectations produce binding commitments, and Paper B focuses on when courts will find a preliminary agreement in negotiation disputes (using Hoffman as a focal point) and how that finding governs the availability of recovery.

shared_topics.topic: choice of remedies (expectation vs reliance) when intent or agreement is unclear
shared_topics.justification: Paper A recommends more flexible remedial rules—sometimes favoring reliance damages over expectation when there was no true intent to be bound—while Paper B centers on the availability and limits of reliance damages for sunk costs when negotiations collapse and agreement is disputed.

papers.node_id: 92valrev1581!!SYMPOSIUM: CONTEMPORARY POLITICAL THEORY AND PRIVATE LAW: ESSAY: CONTRACT THEORY ON AND OFF THE GRID
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTEMPORARY POLITICAL THEORY AND PRIVATE LAW: ESSAY: CONTRACT THEORY ON AND OFF THE GRID
papers.abstract:
FIFTY years ago, development assistance generally involved funding for capital-intensive industrial and agricultural projects, increased education, and introduction of modern technology.In that era, both development scholars and practitioners understood that a society's institutions play an important role in facilitating economic growth.Generally, institutions were not treated as instruments that could be engineered, however.Today, the principal international development organizations consider "building institutions for markets" a priority.According to the staff of theWorld Bank, "without land-titling institutions that ensure property rights, poor people are unable to use valuable assets for investment and income growth[,]" and "without strong judicial institutions that enforce contracts, entrepreneurs find many business activities too risky."
Construe institutions broadly enough, and the view that they play an important role in economic growth now seems to be part of the mainstream of development economics. Whether formal government institutions are required is a separate question.Michael Trebilcock and Jing Leng explore the extent to which connections between formal legal institutions and economic growth are supported by empirical evidence.Looking at the case of contract enforcement, Trebilcock and Leng are not convinced that a connection has been shown:
The existing empirical evidence specifically examining the correlation between a country's economic growth and the state as a credible third-party enforcer of contracts suggests a strong correlation only in the financial sector: better contract enforcement appears beneficial in facilitating financial intermediation. This correlation does not provide strong or unambiguous corroboration of the contract-formalist position more generally, beyond the truism that most rich countries have sophisticated formal contract law and enforcement regimes and many, if not most, poor countries do not. This could equally be said of many otherdifferences between rich and poor countries, indicating little about what is a cause or what is a consequence of development.
The referees of the development agenda, however, seem comfortable moving ahead with institution building without waiting to view the tape.
Suppose that an effective regime of formal contract law does have the potential to promote economic growth in a developing country. On what basis is the adoption of an institution of contract law justified in a society without an established tradition of Western legal institutions?In this Essay, I consider whether contemporary theories of contract law provide significant guidance in addressing that question. I discuss a number of prominent approaches in the absence of a dominant school of contract theory in legal scholarship.I suggest that these contemporary theories tell us very little about the proper content, desirability, or legitimacy of contract law in societies other than those in which Western private law institutions are already well established.

questions.question: Whether contemporary theories of contract law provide meaningful guidance on whether, how, and on what normative grounds a society without an established tradition of Western private-law institutions should adopt formal contract law.

Whether the adoption of formal contract-enforcement institutions in developing or non-Western societies can be justified as a means to promote economic growth, and what empirical or normative criteria should govern that decision.

matched_themes: Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: SEPARATING CONTRACT AND PROMISE
