shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the trial court's use of promissory estoppel to prevent GM from abandoning a community despite no long‑term sale/operation contract, while Paper B argues courts should recharacterize installment land contracts as leases and impose the warranty of habitability—both advocating judicial intervention that reaches beyond the written/formal transaction.

shared_topics.topic: protecting vulnerable stakeholders and community reliance interests
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames the municipality and local workforce as reliance beneficiaries of tax abatements and seeks protection from corporate departure, and Paper B frames low‑equity purchasers/residents as vulnerable actors who need the same habitability protections tenants receive—both center legal remedies on protecting less powerful parties and community welfare.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between public policy/statutory incentives and private contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates promissory estoppel claims against the backdrop of statutory tax abatements (Act 198) and the public policy goal of local economic development, while Paper B grounds its proposal in the public policy behind the implied warranty of habitability and recent statutory/mortgage‑law analogues—both examine how public policy and statutory schemes should shape enforcement of private transactions.

shared_topics.topic: reliance/reasonable expectations as the doctrinal basis for relief
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on whether Ypsilanti reasonably relied on GM's inducements when granting abatements (the core of the promissory estoppel claim), and Paper B emphasizes purchasers' functional expectations (possession like a tenant, risk of forfeiture) as a reason to treat installment contracts as leases—both use reliance and parties' reasonable expectations to justify altering ordinary contract outcomes.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 43buffalolrev1!!ARTICLE: Promises Betrayed: Breach of Confidence as a Remedy for Invasions of Privacy
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Promises Betrayed: Breach of Confidence as a Remedy for Invasions of Privacy

shared_topics.topic: resorting to alternative common‑law doctrines when traditional causes of action fall short
shared_topics.justification: Both papers analyze parties and plaintiffs turning to non‑traditional common‑law remedies — Paper A examines using breach of confidence (and contract or fiduciary theories) as a substitute for a weakened privacy tort, while Paper B explores invoking promissory estoppel to bind a corporation after municipal tax‑abatement incentives failed to secure contractual performance.

shared_topics.topic: enforcement of promises and the elements of reliance
shared_topics.justification: Each paper focuses on courts enforcing promises outside ordinary contract law — Paper A discusses Cohen v. Cowles Media Co. and state‑law enforcement of promises by the press, and Paper B centers on whether GM made a binding promise and whether the township reasonably relied (promissory estoppel elements) to justify relief.

shared_topics.topic: the role and limits of equitable remedies and injunctive relief
shared_topics.justification: Both works engage with equitable relief as a remedy: Paper A assesses whether tort/other actions could yield meaningful damages or injunctions in the face of First Amendment limits, and Paper B analyzes the trial court's injunctive order to prevent GM's plant closure and the appellate court's reversal and standards for issuing such equitable relief.

shared_topics.topic: how doctrinal requirements and formalities constrain access to remedies
shared_topics.justification: Both articles identify specific legal formalities that restrict plaintiffs — Paper A argues contract and fiduciary formulations of breach of confidence are hampered by formal requirements and limited damages, while Paper B scrutinizes promissory estoppel's proof requirements (promise, reliance, abuse of discretion on factual findings) and how statutory and appellate review rules affect relief.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68iowalrev699!!ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Enforcing Extorted Contract Modifications

shared_topics.topic: enforcing promises absent traditional consideration (promissory estoppel vs contract modification doctrines)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on using promissory estoppel to bind a corporation to keep a plant open despite the absence of a conventional bargained-for contract, while Paper B examines the doctrinal shift that allows courts to enforce contract modifications or reliance-based promises even when fresh consideration is lacking (including Restatement exceptions).

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing legitimate renegotiation from extortion/opportunism and assessing reasonable reliance
shared_topics.justification: Paper A evaluates whether the municipality's reliance on GM's assurances was reasonable and considers defenses like economic necessity, whereas Paper B analyzes when post-contractual demands are coercive (extortion/opportunism) and thus undeserving of enforcement versus when they reflect fair renegotiation that courts should uphold.

shared_topics.topic: how parties' bargaining power and economic incentives affect enforceability of promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A studies how public tax abatements and the economic dependence of a community on an employer shape the parties' leverage and the incentives to renege, and Paper B uses examples (e.g., fishermen withholding labor) to show how control over essential inputs and economic leverage complicate whether courts should enforce revised promises.

shared_topics.topic: equitable remedies to secure performance versus monetary compensation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses the use of equitable relief (an injunction) to prevent a plant closure and protect community reliance on promises, while Paper B debates when the law should compel performance or award damages for modified promises and how remedial choices influence parties' incentives to perform or extort.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 69hastingslj119!!ARTICLE: Race Politics, O'Hare Airport Expansion, and Promissory Estoppel: The More Things Change, the More They Stay the Same
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Race Politics, O'Hare Airport Expansion, and Promissory Estoppel: The More Things Change, the More They Stay the Same

shared_topics.topic: use of promissory estoppel to hold corporations to economic-development or procurement-related promises
shared_topics.justification: Both papers center on courts applying promissory estoppel to promises made by large corporations in the context of community-affecting economic decisions — Paper A argues promissory estoppel should prevent a corporate plant closure after tax abatements, while Paper B analyzes Quake's extension of promissory estoppel to a letter of intent in a public procurement/minority-contract set‑aside project.

shared_topics.topic: what constitutes a legally cognizable 'promise' and sufficient reliance in precontractual or incentive contexts
shared_topics.justification: Both works scrutinize how courts identify the existence of a promise and evaluate reasonable reliance — Paper A examines the factual record and appellate review about whether Ypsilanti reasonably relied on GM's assurances, and Paper B discusses ambiguity in a letter of intent, parol evidence, and the thin factual record the Illinois Supreme Court relied on.

shared_topics.topic: policy tradeoffs and consequences of expanding promissory estoppel (litigation risk, economic effects, fairness to communities)
shared_topics.justification: Each article wrestles with the broader implications of permitting promissory‑estoppel recovery for precontractual/incentive promises — Paper A emphasizes community harm and supports equitable enforcement to protect public reliance, while Paper B highlights the danger of opening litigation floodgates and the commercial costs of imposing liability for 'cheap talk.'

shared_topics.topic: the intersection of public incentives, political context, and contractual/promissory liability
shared_topics.justification: Both studies situate promissory‑estoppel disputes within public policy frameworks — Paper A analyzes statutory tax abatements (Act 198) and the municipality–corporation relationship, and Paper B places the Quake dispute in the political and race‑conscious setting of O'Hare expansion and minority set‑aside requirements, showing how public programs shape promises and litigation.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: A PROPOSAL TO SIMPLIFY QUANTUM MERUIT LITIGATION. © 1986 Candace S. Kovacic

shared_topics.topic: use of equitable doctrines to grant relief where no express contract exists
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes quantum meruit, restitution, and quasi‑contract as means to recover for services when an enforceable contract is absent, while Paper B examines promissory estoppel as an equitable device to bind a promisor and prevent a plant closure despite lack of an enforceable contract.

shared_topics.topic: the decisive role of particular claim elements (request/promise/reliance) in entitlement and remedy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its two‑tier framework on whether the defendant requested the plaintiff's performance, affecting entitlement and measure of recovery; Paper B focuses on whether a promise was made and whether the municipality reasonably relied on it to justify equitable relief.

shared_topics.topic: judicial reasoning, inconsistency, and the need for clearer doctrinal standards or review
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes inconsistent terminology and analytic approaches and proposes a unified framework to produce predictable outcomes, and Paper B critiques appellate review and the lower court's treatment of facts and precedent, arguing for a clearer, more consistent application of promissory estoppel.

shared_topics.topic: interaction between statutory schemes and equitable remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses categories like the statute of frauds and how statutory rules affect availability and measurement of quantum meruit recovery, while Paper B examines Public Act 198 (tax abatement authority) and how that statutory context shapes the promissory estoppel claim and available equitable relief.

compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY COMMENTS ON WILLIAM WHITFORD'S PAPER ON THE ROLE OF THE JURY (AND THE FACT/LAW DISTINCTION) IN THE INTERPRETATION OF WRITTEN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: admissibility and enforceability of extrinsic/oral promises (parol evidence vs promissory estoppel)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the parol evidence rule and when extrinsic (including oral) evidence may be admitted to interpret or vary a writing, while Paper B litigates whether municipal assurances tied to tax abatements amounted to enforceable promises under promissory estoppel and thus could be used to bind a corporation despite the absence of a formal contractual term.

shared_topics.topic: the fact/law distinction and allocation of decisionmaking (trial factfinder vs appellate judge)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that contract interpretation and related questions (foreseeability, meaning of terms) are properly factual questions for juries rather than legal questions for judges, and Paper B centers on a trial court's factual finding that a promise and reasonable reliance existed which was later reversed on appeal, raising the same issue of who decides contested factual predicates to contract enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: judicial willingness to enforce, modify, or excuse contractual obligations via equitable doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses doctrines like impracticability, impossibility, and frustration and courts' varying readiness to excuse performance or reshape bargains, while Paper B focuses on promissory estoppel as an equitable mechanism to prevent a corporation from abandoning a community after inducements, debating whether courts should use equitable relief to uphold reliance-based expectations.

shared_topics.topic: policy rationales shaping contract rules (predictability, distrust of testimony, economic/community effects)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes policy drivers behind the parol evidence rule and the objective theory of contract—predictability and distrust of party testimony—whereas Paper B weighs policy concerns about the economic effects of tax abatements, the 'race to the bottom,' and the community-protecting rationale for invoking equitable doctrines, showing both papers ground doctrinal choices in broader policy considerations.

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between economic incentives/market considerations and equitable contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes tax abatements as market/economic incentives and argues for using an equitable doctrine (promissory estoppel) when those incentives produce reliance harms; Paper B critiques market‑centered accounts of contract law and examines when market reasons should yield to other normative doctrines like reliance and consent.

shared_topics.topic: judicial fact‑finding and doctrinal interpretation about what counts as a 'promise'

papers.node_id: 90nwulrev7!!SYMPOSIUM: GILMORE'S GRANT (OR THE LIFE & AFTERLIFE OF GRANT GILMORE & HIS DEATH)
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: GILMORE'S GRANT (OR THE LIFE & AFTERLIFE OF GRANT GILMORE & HIS DEATH)
papers.abstract:
This Story is addressed to theIntelligence of the readerwhich stages things itself.
We are told that Grant Gilmore, like Contract and God, is "dead."And so it is.
A quarter-century ago, Professor Gilmore (then at Chicago) delivered his famous lectures in Columbus, Ohio. Some years later, Gilmore (having returned to Yale) published those revised lectures in his novel little brownbook. Now, nearly 50,000 copies and twenty-two printings later,this Contracts monograph remains one of the best known of American compositions on the topic. Currently assigned in over thirty U.S. schools,its ongoing recognition by commentators is virtually unprecedented in the field. Contract, like Gilmore, may be dead, but The Death of Contract lives on. And so it is.
Is Gilmore's evocative book simply a generational flash in the jurisprudential pan? Or does it retain any conceptual staying power? Is Contract really dead? If so, what does that mean? Do the lessons of The Death of Contract have meaning outside of the world of common-law contracts and torts? Will The Death of Contract retain any meaning in a new era, or will its message become little more than anecdotal? Grant Gilmore's contracted volume on law and life invites us, as the Essays in the Symposium reveal, to consider these and scores of other questions - anew.
Before getting too far along into any or all of these stories, it may be salutary to consider how to begin to read both Gilmore and hisDeath. I venture to do this in what follows by suggesting how Gilmore and his work might be read, but not necessarily how they must be read.(Think of this, if you will, as a peculiar form of literary-legal criticism with biographical shades.) By so venturing, we stand to be the beneficiaries of a marvelous grant, or promise, conveyed by Gilmore. To realize that promise we must, however, tender due consideration to the enterprise, hopeful that our reliance will not be detrimental. This, then, is Gilmore's Grant, leaving us as his "Grantees."
*****Thought is (auto)biographical. Forbehind every great work lies theperson, in all complexity andcontradiction.
In April of 1970, University of Chicago Law Professor Grant Gilmore pointed his Saab toward Columbus, Ohio, where he was to deliver the Law Forum Series Lecture.Though the series was not as renowned as the Storrs Lectures - those would come a few years later upon his return to Yale- the Ohio State College of Law program had already attracted more than its share of legal luminaries. The notables included the much heralded Roger Traynor of the California Supreme Court, Joseph T. Sneed, the respected Stanford Law professor and former president of the Association of American Law Schools, and Telford Taylor, the distinguished Columbia University Law Professor who had earlier served as the chief United States prosecutor at the Nuremberg war crimes trials.
Besides the honor and the $ 1000 honorarium,these lectures were plum because publication in book form was basically assured by the Ohio State University Press. Thus, the sometimes elite-mindedGrant Gilmore had ample incentive to go to Columbus when a former Yale acquaintance, Ohio State property Professor Charles C. Callahan, invited him.According to Professor Merton Bernstein, who was on the Ohio selection committee,"we were looking for a lion."In Gilmore they expected to find a scholarly roar.
And why Gilmore? Simple. He was one of the preeminent "Yale men" (though in 1965 he left in a furious huff). Here was the New Haven bred scholar who journeyed to Cambridge to collect the James Barr Ames Prize. This was the award given for distinguished work in legal scholarship by individuals not on the Harvard faculty, the same award earlier bestowed on Judge Cardozo (1930) and on Professor Corbin (1954). The two-volume, 1500-page treatise, Security Interests in Personal Property, was Gilmore's professional opus, the work he dedicated to his mentor, Arthur Linton Corbin. Grant Gilmore wasalso the man (strange as it may now seem) hand-picked by Oliver Wendell Holmes's executors to complete the definitive biography of the eminent jurist.And this was the same man who, along with his Yale colleague Charles L. Black,coauthored the highly regarded treatise titled The Law of Admiralty (1957).
Additionally, there were the customary highbrow fare of law review articlesin the "best" journals, articles on everything from the International Court of Justice (1946)to and beyond articles on legal realism (1961).Equally true to form, there were the customary ivy-league credentials - A.B. (1931), LL. B. (1942), law journal editor-in-chief (1942),all stamped with the Yale seal. Then there was Gilmore's Ph.D. in French Studies (1936). His 350-page Yale doctoral dissertation, Stephane Mallarme: A Biography and an Interpretation, examined the life and work of the highly unorthodox nineteenth-century French symbolist poet. Afterwards, Gilmore taught French at Yale University from 1937 to 1941. And one more tantalizing item: In 1959 Professor Corbin privately recommended Gilmore (again, a little odd?) to serve as an adviser for the drafting of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.True to Fate, the nod never came, and Gilmore never became a "restater."
By many measures, this was an eclectic and impressive vita. Except for Gilmore's self-imposed but generously compensated exile (1965-73) at the University of Chicago (a place he apparently detested), here was a man who met his moment and was steering fast and far into the future. The next stop in that future was Columbus, Ohio.
Gilmore arrived at Ohio State during the turbulent times of the antiwar student riots of the 1970s. Amid the general tenor of protests over death abroad, the University of Chicago Bigelow Professor turned to the domestic front and reported on the "Death of Contract." He cleared his throat, brushed his flannel suit, and began.
During the course of his two evening lectures (April 7th and 8th, 1970), Gilmore spoke through his mustache with his characteristic tone and aristocratic-like accent. First God, then Columbus, then the Decline and Death, and finally the Resurrection. It was a secular talk with religious intimations. By and large, the Tuesday and Wednesday evening lectures were well and amiably received, though at least one present found them to be "insubstantial," even "disappointing." According to Professor Bernstein, "His oral remarks suggested that the manuscript was certainly not complete when delivered."If so, not to worry: Gilmore would have extensive time to polish his secular sermon. The first publication of The Death of Contract did not come until four years later in June of 1974 - with all future royalties going to the copyright holder, Ohio State University Press.*****There is nothing so suspect as anoriginal thought without a past.
The subliminal idea for the Ohio lectures may have occurred to Gilmore decades before the book's publication. For one thing, there was the 1942 Yale Law Journal article by Columbia Law Professor Arthur Nussbaum, an article titled "Conflict Theories of Contracts: Cases Versus Restatement."In this article, published when Gilmore was an editor on the journal, Nussbaum took Joseph Henry Beale (the noted Harvard Law Professor and Reporter of the Restatement of Conflict and Laws) to task for his views on the "Creation of Contract" as set out in the Conflicts Restatement. In what follows, consider the general similarity between the Gilmore and Nussbaum missions:
1.) Nussbaum challenged Beale's "inflexible rules"along with his "all-embracing, ironclad rule"of contract.
2.) Nussbaum questioned Beale's rejection of the intent theory of contracts.
3.) Nussbaum noted the "demise of consideration"as a legal rule and even hinted at his reservations about other treatise-minded formalists such as Samuel Williston.
4.) Finally, Nussbaum challenged the very enterprise of the formalist brand of a Restatement; that is, he challenged Beale's method of classifying and appraising the cases in a way to produce a neat and categorical rule.
Joseph Beale was Samuel Williston's intellectual counterpart. Like Williston, he "persuaded himself that some sort of necessity controlled law, that there existed a cosmic logical sequence which should be perceived and stated if only one could think aright."Predictably, then, virtually every key point Gilmore advanced in The Death of Contract about Langdellian formalism held equally true for Beale. It was, after all, Beale who first took Langdell's case method gospel to the University of Chicago Law School in 1902.And it was Beale and Williston who championed Langdell's philosophy at Harvard Law School.The two Harvard men were so alike that the Harvard faculty published a book of essays in their honor,printed by Harvard University Press, naturally. Two Harvard law professors, two formalists, two "restaters," two treatise writers - it all proved too much for Nussbaum and Gilmore.
Since Grant Gilmore apparently never wrote publicly about either Beale or the Nussbaum article, one can only speculate about what actual influence the 1942 Yale Law Journal essay had on the young editor. Influence or coincidence,the similarities stand out. In time, those similarities would find even more open expression in a wonderful 1956 lecture Gilmore delivered to the entering Yale LawSchool class.Here too, many of the basic points advanced in The Death of Contract were set out earlier, though in a more general way. The path was being paved, the journey remained.
Years later, some funny things happened on the way from the oral lectures delivered at Ohio to the publication of the work by Ohio State University Press. In 1972 an "unpublished" teaching manual accompanied the 1970 second edition of the Friedrich Kessler and Grant Gilmore contracts casebook. The "Introduction and Teaching Notes" were penned by Gilmore.As Professor Peter Linzer has aptly revealed in his Contracts Anthology,those notes (copyrighted by Kessler and Gilmore) bear a telling resemblance to what would later evolve into The Death of Contract. For example, here are the first three sentences from the Notes:
What might have been called the classical theory of contract is, we have been told, dead. Being dead it is no longer relevant to what is going on in the real world or what we may guess may be going on tomorrow. Being irrelevant, the classical theory is no longer worth studying.
Now the first four sentences from The Death of Contract:
We are told that Contract, like God, is dead. And so it is. Indeed the point is hardly worth arguing anymore. The leaders of the Contract is Dead movement go on to say that Contract, being dead, is no longer a fit or worthwhile subject of study. (p. 1.)
Thus, in a way far more particular than before, Gilmore's Introduction and Notes to the Kessler-Gilmore teaching manual made way for what would follow.
There were, nonetheless, a few significant differences between Gilmore and his coauthor Friedrich Kessler, the much noted German-born contracts scholar. First, Gilmore's personal friend did not altogether accept the "Contracts is Dead" theory; he found it exaggerated.Second, Kessler was not as harsh on Harvard's Christopher Columbus Langdell.Third, "Fritz" Kessler likewise dissented from Gilmore's absolute liability, minimum remedy theory.Fourth, Kessler was skeptical of Gilmore's claims regarding the Holmesian consideration theory and its purported reformulation by Harvard's Samuel Williston.Fifth, Professor Kessler was not a believer in "contorts," at least not as boldly formulated by Gilmore.And finally, in a 1982 memorial tribute to his coauthor, Kessler stated that Gilmore's Introduction to the Teaching Manual "offers a gentle critique of my own introduction in the casebook."Friendly in style, contrary in substance.
Importantly so, there was some apparent agreement on key points. First, and perhaps most important, Professor Kessler registered no express dissent to the following declaration: "It is the underlying thesis of this book that the story of contract law in this centuryhas been the story of the gradual breakdown of the "classical' theory."Next, Kessler appears to have agreed that the "stages of the process of doctrinal disintegration are chronicled in the extraordinary rich literature of the field."Furthermore, Kessler took no formal exception to Gilmore's grand statement that it is vital to teach
the idea that the law is an imperfect tool or technique and that there are many more questions which can be asked than there are questions which can be answered … and that it is usually folly to think that you can successfully predict how the next case is going to be decided. We deal in a range of possibilities, not in easy answers to hard questions.
Even so, this revolving jurisprudential door didn't stop there, with agreement. For by the time that Death was published the ever restless Gilmore was questioning the very idea of a rule-bound contracts casebook, or any casebook. (pp. 19, 30, 61.)After all, if "every rule is eaten up by its own exceptions,"is not the very certainty of the Langdellian case method significantly undermined? This, obviously, was not a point on which the coauthors could agree. And there were other points as well. It was thus enough for the two friends to concede:
Differences of emphasis and detail will no doubt be apparent between this essay and the Introduction to these Notes written by Professor Gilmore in 1971. On the other hand, it is believed that the fundamental coincidence of views represented by these two essays is more significant than the occasional minor discrepancies. Between the 1950's and the 1970's a great deal of water has passed over the dam, but the river is still demonstrably the same river.
Beyond the circles of agreement or disagreement, pesky questions remained: Could it be that Gilmore tendered his teaching notes as an indirect way of subverting the text of his coauthor's book? And if there was a kernel of truth in this suggestion, was it likewise possible that The Death of Contract extended this attempt beyond the Kessler casebook, to all casebooks, especially contracts casebooks? Admittedly, this is a bold (though duly respectful) inquiry. It may, nevertheless, be worth pursuing; therefore, I will return to the matter shortly. For now, a few words about upsetting applecarts may further help to set the stage for the daring inquiries to come.
If you go around upsetting applecarts,goring oxen and tilting at windmills,you must expect to be attacked. Theowners of the applecarts, oxen andwindmills will declare your work tobe perverse, indeed unsound.Grant Gilmore, "For Arthur Leff" (1981)
As far as I may report, no one as of 1981 had ever really referred to the late Arthur Leff's work on contracts in all the uncharitable ways Gilmore suggested, at least not in print. But such terms, and such characterizations, had been used in connection with The Death of Contract.For example:
Robert Braucher (Harvard law professor, reporter for Restatement (Second) of Contracts, and state high court justice, circa 1976): The idea that "Contract is Dead" is a "perverse dictum."
Richard Danzig (associate professor, Stanford Law School, from remarks delivered at 1976 annual conference of the Association of American Law Schools' section on commercial law, contracts, etc.): In his book, The Death of Contract, "Professor Gilmore has been imprecise, injudicious, or just plain mistaken."
These and other like statements "absolutely astonished"Gilmore, reported Professor Anthony Jon Waters. Evidently, Gilmore was surprised by "the extent and the vehemence of the response provoked by The Death of Contract."Curious. Had he really not expected to be attacked when he upset doctrinal applecarts, gored Harvard oxen, and tilted at jurisprudential windmills? One answer, though seemingly contrary, was offered by Professor Richard Speidel in his 1975 review essay of the little book: "I confess to an instinctive feeling that [Gilmore] will be amused by all of the reviewers who take him so seriously."(Similarly, Gilmore's Chicago students recalled that "no one spins a tale like Grant Gilmore.") Even granting Speidel's warranted speculation, how could Gilmore be "amused" by the "vehement" attacks that came to be leveled against him?
The amusement might reside in the fact that so many of Gilmore's critics read him simply at face value, as if he were deadly serious with the literary license he sometimes employed. Too often these critics took the playful as serious; and they just as often mistook the serious as frivolous. Watching learned men (and they were men) engage in such shadow scuffles can be laughable. And maybe Gilmore thought so … at first.
When, however, such misunderstandings burgeoned into scholarly ridicule, the attention ceased to be amusing and became astonish-ing. Gilmore's mistake, if we can brand it so, was in thinking it possible to be playful (and thus poetic) about things deemed serious (and thus "Truthful"). Harvardly speaking, writing The Death of Contract was akin to a professional death wish; hence, the not infrequent "critical reaction"to The Death of Contract.
Yet when the academic dust had settled over him, the impious Gilmore would not repent: "Despite the book's many shortcomings, I have not been persuaded by my critics that my reconstruction was fundamentally in error."Was the Yale Sterling Professor of Law being stubborn? Unsound? Was he, as today's jargon has it, in a state of denial? Or was he suggesting - just maybe - that a more careful reading of his Death might evoke (more than provoke) salutary images of how we view the law's applecarts, oxen, and windmills?
*****It's a timeless book.The Death of Contract … is sure to become- as it deserves to be - one of the staples of theliterature of the common law… [It] is one ofthose few books that deserve our most carefulthought and attention.[il11.]Richard Epstein (1994, 1976)
More important than the accolade is the idea that Gilmore's little book "deserves our most careful thought and attention." If this famous monograph deserves such attention, it is presumably because it was written with some careful reflection. The attentive scholar deserves the thoughtfulness of the attentive reader. That is as true in legal circles as in philosophy or literature departments. In fact, it is precisely such kinds of old-fashioned attention that stand to elevate the intellectual state of the legal mind above the occasional barren craters of historical and doctrinal scholarship. And if indeed, as some maintain, The Death of Contract is ultimately unpersuasive, then it must be so duly mindful of Professor Gilmore's ultimate goals as best as we can comprehend them. But surely, care must be taken to discern those goals. Otherwise, such characterizations are unreliable, even when made by Gilmore's friends (a few of whom were unsettled by his unorthodox monograph).
In Death, Gilmore sometimes wrote for the mind's eye of the "attentive reader," (e.g., p. 78); in other works, he wrote heedful of that same reader,or the "astute reader,"or the "careful and determined reader."In fact, Gilmore had long been familiar with the importance of forms of writing directed to "a hierarchy of readers."This, obviously, came all too naturally for a talented writer of Gil-more's stripe, and especially to anyone who, like him, had examined the peculiar weave of the poetic webs spun by Stephane Mallarme.
Mindful of the introductory evidence just presented, ask yourself: Is it reasonably possible that The Death of Contract had a meaning beyond what was "easily comprehensible,"a meaning discernable only by "close and careful study"?Just what is that meaning(s), and how can one (like a lawyerly Columbus) discover it? Let us begin by noting, if only at a passing glance, the largely unexplained impressions of others, namely, contracts scholars:
P.S. Atiyah: "Since Gilmore's thesis was so exaggerated, it was presumably not intended to be taken too seriously."
Ralph Mooney: Perhaps Gilmore "intended that The Death of Contract be read like an historical novel, for its broad themes rather than its specific details. Or perhaps [as Professor Speidel] has suggested, Gilmore wrote the book in a deliberately provocative way to ignite scholarly controversy."
John P. Dawson: Gilmore's accounts that both bargain consideration and Contract are dead seem "exaggerated"(echoed by E. Allan Farnsworth).
John Edward Murray, Jr.: Gilmore's suggestion that "the bargain theory of consideration can be traced only as far back as 1881, i.e., to the alleged creator of this revolutionary concept, O.W. Holmes, Jr." is an "amusing view" not at all consistent with "compelling" evidence to the contrary.
Next, consider the following two similar-sounding, but more developed observations:

questions.question: Whether the classical/formalist model of contract law has broken down and become irrelevant to contemporary legal decisionmaking and scholarship.
Whether provocative critiques asserting the 'death' of a legal doctrine produce lasting conceptual influence on legal scholarship, pedagogy, and practice.
Whether the themes and arguments of such a doctrinal critique have meaningful applicability beyond their immediate area (for example, to other fields of law or to broader social and legal thought).

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
How do casebook selection practices and pedagogical choices (e.g., using multi-issue appellate cases or emphasizing litigation realities) shape students' understanding of contract law and practice?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

papers.abstract:
There can by now be little doubt that the idea of civil society has become an overused concept in the past decade. Indeed, just as the slogan arose in Eastern Europe in the 1980s as a cudgel to batter the totalitarian state, it has emerged in the 1990s in Western Europe and in the United States as a method by which critics of the existing political order press home their claims. Interestingly, in a way which should be a warning to us all, the idea of civil society is used by political groups and thinkers on both the right and the left. And though in Europe, in general, it is most often the province of the left, in the United States it has been appropriated by both groups to advance their political agendas.
Thus, for right of center thinkers, as well as for libertarians, the quest for civil society is taken to mean a mandate to deconstruct many of the powers of the state and replace them with intermediary institutions based on social voluntarism. For many liberals, civil society is identified with social movements, also existing beyond the state. Many of the former refuse to recognize that voluntary organizations can be of a particularly nasty nature and based on primordial or ascriptive principles of membership and participation that put to shame the very foundations of any idea of civil society. Similarly the latter are blind to the fact that the Achilles heel of any social movement is its institutionalization which-one way or the other-must be through the state and its legal, and coercive, apparatus. In the meantime, both communitarians and liberals continue to couch the idea of civil society in their own terms, invest it with their own meanings, and make of it what they will. Right, left, and center, north, south, east, and west, civil society is identified with everything from multiparty systems and the rights of citizenship to individual voluntarism and the spirit of community.
That any concept could be invested with such varied and often contradictory meanings should make us suspect its usefulness within the social sciences, if not in politics. One way to ensure this concept's usefulness, I suggest, would be to distance it from its normative moorings in political philosophy and

Whether and how the institutionalization of social movements and voluntary associations produces contradictions in their relationship with the state, including reliance on legal and coercive mechanisms.

Whether the multiplicity of normative meanings attached to 'civil society' undermines its usefulness as an analytic concept and how the concept can be reframed or operationalized for empirical social-scientific study.

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW'S UNITY - AN ESSAY FOR THE MASTER CONTORTIONIST
papers.abstract:
. A Preface About Grant
Actually, we called him Mr. Gilmore, in that summer of 1981 in Madison, Wisconsin, when we were very young. We were attending the Association of American Law Schools conference on teaching contracts and the central figure quickly became Grant Gilmore, whom we watched from a distance and then timidly approached. The High Exalted Personages who were running the conference all called him Grant, and they clearly weren't that impressed with him. After all, he wasn't really a contracts scholar. He was a great authority on secured transactions,but he had always been overshadowed in contracts by his colleagues like Corbin, Kessler, and Malcolm Sharp. And the High Exalted Personages really didn't think much of The Death of Contract.
But to us relative beginners it was a shining path, and not because we took The Death as gospel. Most of us knew enough even then to know its faults, to recognize the hyperbole and inaccuracies and oversimplifications, to know that Gilmore was describing his own project when he wrote of The Common Law that "Holmes amused himself by dressing his lectures in a deceptive overlay of history,"and that hewas referring to himself when he wrote that "Holmes, like any revolutionary, merely sought to sugar over his more startling heresies with a frosting of antique learning."
We knew that there was more to Gilmore than elegant prose and intellectual pie throwing. He cared about law and legal thought; his writings about Holmes, Cardozo, and Corbin showed his passion. In his last years he was pessimistic, perhaps even despondent, about the future.I think he also was hurt and angry at his treatment by some of the institutions and people with whom he had been associated for many years. Let us hope that he got some solace from the enthusiasm that he inspired in the young.
What has survived for me is a matter of substance - his thesis that tort and contract have collapsed into one another. I don't know when I first started thinking about the overlap, but his famous "contorts" discussioncertainly spurred me on. When the Yale Law Journal organized a festschrift for Arthur Corbin's ninetieth birthday, Gilmore contented himself with one page of reminiscence about Corbin. His real tribute was a first-rate substantive article, The Assignee of Con-tract Rights and His Precarious Security.I don't know that I am up to Gilmore's standards, but I offer the following essay as a token to his memory.

papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: IAN MACNEIL'S CONTRIBUTION TO CONTRACTS SCHOLARSHIP.
papers.abstract:
Macneil has been both prolific and distinctive.  He has devoted a career to developing and marketing his relational contract theory.  Although I hope and expect that Macneil will have many additional productive years in which to further develop and market his theory, his work is now rich and unique enough to justify an attempt at overall assessment of its impact.In this comment I will discuss the impact of Macneil's writings on the work of other academics writing about contract law.
The reader should be aware that Macneil himself conceives of his work as much broader than anything most other contract scholars recognize as contract law.  His relational contract theory encompasses all exchange, and because Macneil sees exchange occurring almost everywhere, his theory becomes in effect a general theory of the social order.  It is a provocative theory at that level of generality and deserves to beevaluated on those terms.Nonetheless I limit my review, as indicated, to the impact of his work on contracts scholarship.
