papers.abstract:
It is extremely pleasant to be handed the task of commenting on a paper by Ian Macneil at a conference called in appreciation of the work of Stewart Macaulay.  The occasion seems a good one on which to speculate upon -- and simply to celebrate -- the contribution that these two extraordinary Scotsmen have made to contracts scholarship in our time.
That contribution -- the development of a "relational" perspective on contracting -- has been, I believe, fundamental, in the literal sense of altering the foundations of the subject.  You would never know this, unfortunately, from reading ordinary contracts scholarship, which the work of Macneil and Macaulay, as contrasted to law-and-economics, has as yet scarcely dented.  That is not an accident.  Most law-and-economics scholarship emerged from the "transactional" models of exchange and the highly individualist ideological assumptions central to straight common law doctrinal scholarship, and so has been readily assimilated to that scholarship.  The "relational" view poses a much more radical set of challenges: contracts scholars who took it seriously would really have to change their thinking about the field.  Let me try to explain why.
One way of looking at Macneil-Macaulay "relationalism" -- to compress for the moment into a single slogan the approaches of thesetwo quite different thinkers -- is as the continuation of two scholarly projects embraced, but then prematurely abandoned, by the Legal Realists of the 1920s and 1930s.  One of those projects was chiefly destructive, the other constructive.  Let's call the destructive project "critique, through contextualization, of classical-formalist contract law" and the other, "reconstruction, also through contextualization, of the actual operating norms and conventions of contracting."
(1) The project of critique was, of course, to take apart the magnificent doctrinal Crystal Palace that Langdell, Anson, Pollock, and Williston had built; the favored critical technique was to examine how courts actually operated the classical rules in different fact-situations stated in decided contracts cases.  The result was a vast body of contracts scholarship, reaching its Summa in Corbin's great treatise, showing how rules framed in abstract general terms ("performance of a pre-existing duty is not consideration sufficient to support a promise") could lead, as actually applied, to quite opposite results in different settings.
(2) The other project was to try to build a new contract law on the ruins of the old, a law that would be more solidly founded on the empirical regularities observed in the decided cases, and that would make articulate their hitherto unstated but implicit bases in ethics, policy, and social function.  The result was a body of distinguished work (the rollcall of soldiers in this cause includes the names of Corbin, Llewellyn, Kessler, Patterson, Fuller, and Dawson among many others) showing that contextual considerations -- such as the severity of the fault of the breaching party, the relative good faith of the parties, their relative sophistication or bargaining power, the degree of their deterimental reliance upon one another, the harshness of contract terms or the tiny standard-form type in which such terms appeared -- both did and shouldinfluence judicial decisions whether contracts had been formed, modified, breached, or excused, and what remedies should be given.
This kind of work, radically disruptive though it undoubtedly once was (it has since become the normal-science staple crop of the contracts field), was quite modest in its methods: it stuck to appellate contracts cases, and drew its contextual data from the facts as related in those cases.  Some of the Realists had been more ambitious about the reconstructive project: they planned to go beyond the cases to discover what the relation was between legal and social norms, and, if there were disparities between the two, to use the social norms (e.g., the best commercial customs) as the basis for reforming the legal ones.For various reasons -- resistance of traditional lawyers, frustration with the difficulty and inconclusiveness of empirical research, diversion into New Deal politics, inability to theorize beyond naive functionalism or behavioralism about law-society relations-- the Realists never took these ambitions very far off the ground.  Some of their successors bravely struggled onwards, producing remarkable work that was almost completely ignored in mainstream scholarship.  Dawson studied contract decisions in periods of high inflation in the United States and Germany.Kessler looked closely at auto dealer franchises as an instance of contract relationships within a vertically-integrated industry.Hurst and Friedman studied hundreds of contracts cases in the historical context of a developing Wisconsin society and economy.A few scholars, notably Reitz and Speidel, carried on the project of relating legal decisions, and evaluating them by their functional contribution to particular commercial contexts.Danzig thoroughly researched the background of some well-known contracts cases, locating the appellate decisions within great tangled complexes of emotional, social, and economic purposes as well as the labyrinths of lebal bureaucracies and professionalstrategies.Whitford produced seminal studies of consumer protection law, fully situated in regulatory and social contexts.There were a few empirical studies of contracting practices in specialized trades which were very useful but modestly refrained from trying to generalize from their conclusions.  Within the vast ocean of common law contracts scholarship, these social-contextual studies made up a forlorn and isolated archipelago.  After 1970, the main tendencies of new work on contracts turned away from Realist conextualism altogether.  In their efforts to reconstruct what looks remarkably like the old formal-classical rule-system (with some pieces missing, such as the "consideration" doctrine or the policy against stipulated penalties) on the basis of economic efficiency or Kantian moral autonomy, both the law-and-economics and contract-as-promise scholarsstuck mostly to the appellate cases, and used them not as the Realist tradition had, as rich storehouses of contextual data, but largely as statements of rules, and rather barebones statements at that.
Macaulay and Macneil paid no attention to these trends, and went their own way.  Their way, as it turned out, lay in the close inspection of the norms and practices of the commercial users of contract law, the contracting parties themselves.  Supplementing their own observations of contracting practices with materials from anthropology and sociology, they painted a stunning series of real-world contractual landscapes.  The shock value of this work, as so often with the best of the avant-garde, lay partly in its dramatic announcement of underground truths in public -- perceptions widely shared by business people and their lawyers, but never beforegiven utterance in the polite society of formal discourse about law.  As I see it, the new work challenged the salon jurists of the old establishment in three fundamental ways.
1.  Organic Solidarity. Classical contract law, like classical political economy, assumed a social world populated by self-constituting, self-reliant subjects, each pursuing his individual projects, and viewing other people either as threats or as means to realizing those projects.  A contract represented one of the carefully circumscribed occasional interactions that joined some of these isolated beings together for analienated moment of mutual exploitation.This Hobbesian individualism is not at all the only mode even of classical contract law, as Duncan Kennedy has shown,but it is the dominant mode of that law and of the modern economism that now seeks to resurrect it.
What Macneil and Macaulay brought to surface awareness was that the images of classical contract law described at best a small and residual body of contract dealings: "discrete transactions" (in Macneil's phrase) between strangers.  The common type of commercial exchange was among participants in continuing relations, members of interactive communities whose projects themselves, as well as expectations about how they will be carried out, are partially created by the community.  In classical contract, individuals have no obligations to each other save those created by the coercive rules of the state or their own promises:if contract law outcomes are therefore to be rationalized on the preferred grounds of consent rather than those of public policy, the outcomes must appear to flow from the parties' promises, from their ex ante allocations of performance obligations and risks, or at least from a plausible implication (or transaction-cost-saving legal approximation) of such promises.  In the "relational" view of Macaulay and Macneil, parties treat their contracts more like marriages than like one-night stands.  Obligations grow out of the commitment that they have made to one another, and the conventions that the trading community establishes for such commitments; they are not frozen at the initial moment of commitment, but change as circumstances change; the object of contracting is not primarily to allocate risks, but to signify a commitment to cooperate.  In bad times parties are expected to lend one another mutual support, rather than standing on their rights; each will treat the other's insistence on literal performance as willful obstructionism; if unexpected contingencies occur resulting in severe losses, the parties are to search for equitable ways of dividing the losses; and the sanction for egregiously bad behavior, is always, of course, refusal to deal again.
The work of Macaulay and Macneil thus picks up a recurrent if usually muted contrapuntal theme in liberal social science:that certain kinds of cultural-social understandings and institutions, to maintain them, have been important conditions of the successful operation of capitalist economies.  To put it another way, expectations of mutual advantage (narrowly conceived), reinforced only by coercive state enforcement of property-and-contract rights, fashion insufficiently durable bonds to induce cooperative social action on any large scale.  Something else must be at work to create the foundations of mutual trust and solidarity upon which economic planning depends.  Macneil's work in particular is close to Durkheim's in its emphasis upon the norms of solidarity and reciprocity, "organic solidarity," that can emerge from continuing relations.I don't mean to trivialize their achievement by trying thus to pigeon-hole it in the social science tradition.  It is one thing to have an insight at this general level of abstraction; it is another thing to have thoroughly analyzed, as Macneil and Macaulay have done, the particular ways in which the insight is played out in actual economic relations.
2.  Domination. Classical contract law solves the Hobbesian problem of power by trying to give the parties only the most circumscribed rights in one another's future conduct: rights bargained for through formally specified contracting procedures.  In the messy and open-ended world of continuing contract relations, where the contours of obligation are constantly shifting, the effects of power imbalances are not limited to the concessions that parties can extort in the original bargain.  Such imbalances tend to generate hierarchies that can gradually extend to govern every aspect of the relation in performance.  This is the potential dark side of continuing contract relations, as organic solidarity is the bright side: what starts out as a mere inequity in market power can be deepened into persistent domination on one side and dependence on the other.  This is not slavery, since the parties are legally free to exit; but the whole perspective of relational contract suggests that sunk costs can matter tremendously, that the trauma of abandoning a relationship around which a company has structured all its operations, hiring, investment, and planning decisions, can keep it tied into a dependence that its members experience as all the more corrupting because it is in some sense voluntary.
Modern contracts scholars tend to see such relations of domination as aberrational situations, which, for good or evil (depending on whether one is liberally or conservatively inclined) contract law has evolved various curative doctrines to police.  In other words, there is not that much of a problem, and contract law can take care of what problem there is.  Macaulay and Macneil, like the Critical Legal Studies scholars, follow the lead of the more unsparingly cold-eyed Realists such as Hale, Kessler, and Dawson,who find coercion and domination to be pervasive in market relations.  Their reactions to this knowledge differ somewhat.  Macaulay's reaction (which I feel more confident that I can describe than I do Macneil's)is to assimilate continuing contract relations to a general conception of political struggle.  In Macaulay's view, contract parties -- such as the automobile manufacturers and their suppliers or dealers, or the oil companies and gas-station franchisees -- appear both as social groups locked into relations of hierarchy and as political interest-groups trying strategically to manipulate outside institutions (including courts) to improve their basic bargaining positions.  On the whole, Macaulay is a depressed liberal; he wishes that the weaker parties to these relationships could transform them into more egalitarian ones, but is very pessimistic about their ability to do so, because he delieves that most of the institutional structures through which the struggle is carried on tend to work to the advantage of wealth and power.(More on this issue in a moment.)
3.  Discontinuity and Marginality of "Contract Law." All their other challenges to standard contracts work might have been forgiveable, if Macneil and Macaulay had not implacably insisted upon demonstrating, over and over again, the relative insignificance for contracts-in-action of the traditional materials of legal scholarship, the decisions of common law contracts courts.  This demonstration has two aspects:
(a) The marginality of state-enforced norms and sanctions in the governance of contract relations.  This was of course the theme of Macaulay's famous 1963 article which described businessmen who did not rely on legal norms to define or sanctions to enforce their relations because they had their own, more effective, norms and sanctions.Macneil's approach has been somewhat different.  It has been to contrast the detailed normative premises in traditional contract law with those emerging from relational contracting, and show that despite limited concessions to relationalism, modern contract law remains wedded to unrealistic models of the discrete transaction.Both men picture contract law and its enforcement as a world removed from, and only indirectly rleated to, the normal expectations of contracting parties (except in one-shot high-risk transactions between strangers where the Hobbesian assumptions of contract law may become the practical realism of the situation).  Macaulay in particular pictures the occasional resort by private parties to formal legal sanctions as mostly opportunistic and tactical: by going to law, the parties are not appealing to shared values embodied in legal rules, or seeking moral vindication of their position or a just settlement of their disputes; they are usually engaged in maneuvers to improve their bargaining positions.  The "law", to such parties, its norms, rules, procedures, costs, etc., appears in a completely alienated form as a set of games, strategies and hurdles.From this point of view, the only thing that matters about a legal form is whether it can help give one leverage or slow the other side down.  Parties with a lot of resources, for example, do not mind general equitable standards even if the substance of such standards cuts against them because they cannot practically be enforced without a lot of expensive evidence.  Such parties also like nice points of law -- jurisdictional objections, conflicts-of-laws issues, and the like -- because their lawyers are likely to be more practiced in arguing them than are the opposition's.Macaulay's point, I should stress, ought not be confused with the economist's reduction of all human choice to "rational" maximizing behavior.  Macaulay doesn't believe contracting parties think like Holmesian "bad men" about all norms, and certainly not the norms of their interest group or relational-contract community; but they often do think like "bad men" with respect to specifically legal rules and procedures.  Macaulay's businessmen may be seen as inhabiting overlapping and to some extent mutually contradicting moral universes of contracting rules, one of which (their private order) supplies the norms that they actually internalize, the other (the legal order) furnishing an arsenal ofstrategic weapons in case the relation breaks down.  His work reveals, then, a radical discontinuity between official ways of thinking about law, as a repository of values and sanctions controlling social behavior, and the expectations of the inhabitants of the "semi-autonomous social fields" (in Sally Moore's phrase) that the law is supposed to affect.  Even more interesting and disturbing, it reveals that quite often the professionals of the legal system themselves adopt the outsiders' rather than the official view: Macaulay shows lawyers, and even sometimes judges, accepting the chilling and amoral vision of the law as nothing but a storehouse of bargaining chips.
(b) The marginality of the common law of contract within the body of state-enforced norms and sanctions.  Macneil and Macaulay go well beyond the familiar point that general contract law has fallen from its nineteenth century primacy in the governance of private ordering to the relatively trivial status of a body of law employed to fill in the interstices left by the big new systems of specialized legislative and administrative regulation.  Macneil points out that from the relational perspective, any body of law that helps to structure contracting behavior ought to be considered as part of contract law: this would include corporation law and labor law, for example.  Macaulay's view of contract relations as periodic political conflict, sees common law contract courts as simply one among the many institutional battlegrounds on which the parties carry on their struggle.  The perspectives of both men suggest that even those who think legal scholarship should be confined to the study of state-enforced norms, are not looking at enough of the contract law that matters if they stick to the common law (and UCC) alone.
Now perhaps it will be clear why, if contracts scholars were to take seriously the challenges posed by Macneil and Macaulay, they would have to write very differently about their subject.  Contracts scholarship rests upon the essentially liberal premise that the terms of social interaction ought to be, and in our society mostly are, instituted by consent -- either the actual voluntary choices of the parties, or by means of state rules enacted and enforced by their constitutionally chosen representatives.  Liberals on the right want most terms to be of the former kind, liberals on the left are more favorable to the latter kind; but they both share this notion that social life is, both ideally and (almost) in practice, the product of voluntary individual choice.  If there is coercion, it should be defended as necessary to police deviations from consensuallyfixed terms, or else as an unfortunate but necessary minimum of control that people in any society would have to endure.
With their discovery of relational contract-in-action, Macneil and Macaulay imported a new element into contracts discourse, the element of society, which cannot be accounted for entirely as the product of individual or constitutional-democratic-state choices, but which exists in some respects prior to such choices, and which helps to condition both what is chosen and the structures within which choices are played out.  To express this in another way, their work shows how economic purposes and actions are deeply embedded in social fields, in densely woven webs of local customs, conventional morals, bonds of loyalty and entrenched power hierarchies.  Of course, nobody could claim that Macneil and Macaulay discovered contracting societies.  Mainstream contract law, especially in its post-Realist froms, repeatedly recognizes the existence of social background conditions to contracting.  For example, consider the "course of dealing, course of performance, and usage of trade" or the "commercial reasonableness" that may be consulted as supplementary guides to contractual intent, or the sometimes pervasive inequalities between parties in information, bargaining skill, or market alternatives that make up what the courts like to call "unequal bargaining power." But in mainstream contract law, such conditions only occupy the background; they are what will govern the transaction only until the parties or the state choose otherwise; they are canvases which individual intent or state policy may paint over at discretion.  Macneil's and Macaulay's accomplishment has been to bring contracting societies into the foreground, and by so doing to show that you cannot even begin to understand contractual expectations without understanding the social conditions of their generation, change, and termination.  Moreover, they demonstrate that such conditions are not supplementary, but primary, sources of contracting norms and sanctions.  Finally, not only are those social conditions not readily trumped by the state-enforced norms and sanctions of contract law, but they are often simply not affected by contract law at all.
want to make clear that I am not attributing to Macneil and Macaulay a kind of conservative Burkean organicism, some notion that contracting societies arise spontaneously and reproduce mysteriously, resistant alike to rational understanding and deliberate alteration.  On the contrary, they can be understood, and Macneil and Macaulay have gone a long way toward understanding them.  They are built with human intentions and purposes, and can be changed, like any other social arrangements, through politics, including but not at all limited to politics whose strategy is to make use of the instrumentalities of the state and legal system.  As Macaulay has shown, however, any groupthat tries to change the social structure of contract relations through political struggle must be prepared for a lot of frustration and unexpected consequences.
If contracts scholars were to accept the relational revolution, and shift their focus accordingly, what would be the fate of the traditional materials of contracts -- the common law and UCC cases and the commentaries on them?  At some moments in their work both Macneil and Macaulay have seemed to say that the relational perspective reveals that traditional contracts materials are an academic museum of quaint curiosities, a law of law professors bearing but slight resemblance to the law-in-action known to contracting parties and their lawyers.  In this view the marginality and discontinuity of mainstream contracts results from nothing more significant than an academic deformation professionelle, the narrow parochialism of the case-law tradition persisting through sheer inertia.  Clearly there is something to this; but it is not the whole story, as Macneil and Macaulay have also recognized on other occasions.As I have been arguing in this Comment, the relational perspective's revelation of a social world of semi-autonomous contracting cultures, governed by relations of cooperative organic solidarity and of pervasive hierarchical domination, is deeply upsetting to the core premises of our liberal social order.  Contract law has traditionally been one of the theatres -- a small, elite theatre, to be sure, compared to television or Chamber of Commerce lunches -- in which those premises are given public expression.  Contract law has, arguably, been filled with ideological purposes; and the manner in which it suppresses or relegates to the background conditions of the social element in contracting have not been just incidental consequences of professional parochialism, but important to its vindication of those purposes.
If you accept this account, if you stop thinking of contract law as a pathetically inadequate attempt by legal academics to structure the dealings of the commercial world and think of it instead as a (relatively modest) platform for the expression of ideology, then its doctrines become interesting again for what they can reveal about the society's official values.  (Of course, at least as interesting if not more so for the same purpose, would be less elevated, "field-level" manifestations of legal ideology, such as advice given in lawyers' offices; but these are obviously a lot harder to study.) This has been the focus of the fascinating work of some of the scholars associated with the Conference on Critical Legal Studies, who have tried to show, working with doctrinal materials alone, how contracts doctrine tries to suppress, deny, or mediate its own internal contradictions.  For example, every time mainstream contracts courts or commentators approach a full recognition of relationalist insights (as when relationalism raises reliance-based obligations, or paternalistically protects the weak from consenting to their victimization, or enforces a "socialism-of-the-transaction" by dividing unexpected losses by need and ability to pay), they will find some device to keep the implications of relationalism from threatening their liberalindividualist core premises.  They will use contract interpretation to disguise the relationalist result as the individualist intent of the parties.  They will saturate the reasons for the result in the peculiar facts of the case at hand.  They will classify the relational doctrine as belonging to an exceptional body of remedies available only in special and unusual situations.  They will rhetorically celebrate the core values of freedom of contract in dicta while doing freehanded equitable redistribution in the case before them.
If persuasive, the hypothesis just offered for the discontinuity between doctrine and law-in-action -- that doctrine is ideologically committed to denying certain relational realities -- might also furnish someguidelines for a task that both Macneil and I are very interested in: writing the history of contract relations.  If the hypothesis is right, it would be futile to try to write the history of contract law doctrine as if it were a functional adaptation by the legal system to the underlying needs of commercial parties.  I share, for example, what I take to be Macneil's skepticism that most of the changes in contracts doctrine over the last two centuries can be completely accounted for as functional responses to changing modes of structuring business transactions.  The two leading histories of nineteenth century contract law, Horwitz's and Atiyah's, seem most convincing to me when they treat doctrinal history as part of the more general history of shifts in ideological discourse (e.g., changing ideas of political economy), and least so when they treat it as a set of practical responses to the desires of businessmen.
Indeed, if we are prepared to take to heart the Macneil-Macaulay discovery of discontinuity between individualist-transactional doctrine and solidary-hierarchical-relational practice, we should probably discard completely some of the functionalist background assumptions that have tended to inform our views of the role of law in economic change.  I would speculate that most lawyers and law teachers who think about the matter at all would tell something like the following story about the evolution of contracts in recent times.  It has been, roughly speaking, a three-stage evolution.
The first stage is that of mercantilist regulation and community custom: local hierarchical relations of primary social groups (the manor, the town, the extended-family household production unit), tempered by equitable norms of community, set the basic terms of economic relations.  Contract law is the law of the primary group or of the local jury; there is also supplemental regulation of prices, wages, and production by mercantilist state policies, monopolies, or guilds.
In the second stage, economic actors win their freedom from status hierarchies, local customs, and state control to become free exchangers of land, labor, and capital in a laissez-faire market.  Contract law becomes the abstract, formal, classical system; anything (within the limits of public law) can be commodified and its exchange contracted for, on any terms the parties can extract; and the law will blindly enforce the exchange.
In the third stage, several things happen simultaneously.  First, discrete market transactions between strangers increasingly give way to continuing relations -- within firms, within increasingly specializedtrades, within increasingly solidary associations (trade associations, unions, etc.).  Second, regulation increasingly cuts into freedom of contract, to repair "market failures" or to redistribute power and wealth to increasingly organized and politically potent interest groups.  The private law of contracts increasingly recognizes both relational realities and regulatory policies.
Again, if Macneil and Macaulay are right, the far-reaching implication of their insight is that this entire story is in need of serious revision.  This whole notion that economic dealings started out embedded in hierarchical organic communities, then got disembedded as individuals dug out and formed their own free-floating relations in markets, and finally got re-embedded in specialized firms, trades and regulatory systems, is at best a set of very rough and inadequate generalizations.  Economic relations are always embedded; markets are always structured by a complex of local, ethnic and trading cultures, and by varying regimes of non-state and state regulation.  Dealing between "strangers" cannot regularly take place -- e.g., one cannot trade on bills of exchange outside trading communities that recognize bills of exchange.  The imagery behind the account of Stage Two in the standard story is supplied not by any close attention to the structure of economic dealings in nineteenth century England or America.  (Such attention, I agree with Macneil, would yield a richly "relational" historical sociology -- of plantation slavery, factory organization, networks of planter-factor, farmer-merchant-creditor, entrepreneur-banker, wholesaler-retailer -- and nothing remotely like a world of discrete transactions between strangers.) This imagery is rather the product of certain conventions of ideological discourse, conventions most definitely embodied in contract law among other places, which encouraged even people who dealt with one another in socially-embedded solidary and hierarchical continuing contract relations to think of one another as strangers and equals.  In short, the law embodies a set of fantasies about the world that become real when people act upon them as if they are real: when, for example, people accept the terms of a deal imposed upon them by powerful others as the product of circumstances and their own volition rather than simply of the power of others, or when they abandon a lifelong trading or business partner because the relation is no longer profitable.  Freedom of contract means, among other things, never having to say you are sorry.
Some theorists have even advanced a bold hypothesis of a specific historical causal relationship between the fantasy world of political-legal ideological discourse about contracts and the social world of contracting: they contend that encouraging people to deal with one another as strangers progressively erodes the underlying relations of solidarity, reciprocity and trust upon which capitalist economies essentially depend.If there is anything at all to this view, it suggests an urgent set of practical reasons -- if reasons are required beyond inherent intellectual fascination -- for lawyers interested in contract law to overcome their traditional resistance and to open their understandings to the remarkable, if up until now rather lonely, accomplishments of Macneil and Macaulay.

questions.question: Whether and how commercial contracting is governed in practice by informal, relational norms arising from continuing relationships rather than by formal, state-enforced contract rules.

Whether and how continuing contractual relationships create sustained patterns of solidarity and mutual support versus persistent power imbalances and domination that affect parties' choices and outcomes.

Whether formal legal doctrines and institutions function to mask, reproduce, or reshape the social realities of contracting (for example by promoting a model of discrete, voluntary transactions that diverges from embedded relational practice).

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
Does treating a series of successive discrete contracts differently from a single continuing contract leave parties vulnerable to opportunistic behavior in follow-up contracting?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
How do systemic institutional changes (deregulation, litigation costs, ADR, transnational codes) affect contracting behavior and the relation between law and practice?
How do social, economic, and cognitive contexts (power asymmetries, informational biases, gender and race dynamics) affect the substance, interpretation, and enforceability of contracts?
How does conceptualizing contracting as an ongoing social exchange (relational contracting) change doctrinal questions, methods, and conclusions?
How has historical doctrinal and institutional change shaped which promises are considered binding-specifically the shift from equitable/restitutionary grounds to market-style, bargained exchanges?
How do informal relational norms and repeated interactions govern commercial contracting in practice, and when do these norms supplant formal state-enforced rules?
Do appellate judges systematically shape factual narratives in published opinions in ways that influence doctrinal placement and case outcomes?
To what extent should background power asymmetries, bargaining inequality, race, and gender influence contract doctrine and judicial intervention?
How do parties in ongoing exchange relationships use relational contracting-informal, repeated-interaction arrangements-to govern performance and adapt to change?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
How and why did doctrinal reasoning shift historically from subjective/will-centered models toward objective, balancing, or institutional approaches in contract and agency law?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?
Should courts assess and remedy breaches of cooperative ADR or settlement agreements through a contextual, good-faith/relational analysis rather than a rigid formalist contract approach?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.topic: when and how courts should apply restitutionary/equitable doctrines (quantum meruit, unjust enrichment) instead of strict contract enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a two-tier analytic framework that tells courts when to award quantum meruit or restitution (distinguishing requested from unrequested performance), while Paper B repeatedly examines how courts and scholars invoke equitable or reliance-based remedies to accommodate relational realities that formal contract doctrine does not address.

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of contextual facts and background expectations (requests, course of dealing, continuing relations) in deciding entitlement and remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers its framework on the factual element of whether the defendant requested performance and derives different entitlements accordingly; Paper B foregrounds course-of-dealing, usages of trade, and the social norms of continuing relationships as primary inputs that should shape contract outcomes and remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of fairness and power imbalances in determining whether recovery is appropriate
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes categories like plaintiffs in breach, discharged or illegal contracts, and third‑party recoveries to determine when justice requires denying or limiting recovery, while Paper B explores how domination and hierarchical dependencies in continuing relations affect bargaining and why doctrine must consider substantive inequalities when allocating relief.

shared_topics.topic: the inadequacy of orthodox doctrinal approaches and the need for a reformed, more coherent analytic framework that fits contracting practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A criticizes inconsistent, jargon-laden case law and proposes a unified, two-tier doctrine to produce predictable results, and Paper B critiques mainstream transactional/formalist contract doctrine as disconnected from law-in-action and calls for scholarship and law to be reconceived to reflect relational contracting.

shared_topics.topic: how remedies should be measured (market value, unjust enrichment, or equitable division of losses) in non‑standard contract situations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A prescribes measuring recovery by market value in requested-performance quantum meruit cases and by the defendant's unjust enrichment in unrequested-performance cases, and Paper B discusses courts' tendency to redistribute losses, rely on equitable standards, or mask redistributive outcomes within doctrinal categories when addressing relational or unexpected contingencies.

shared_topics.topic: relational versus discrete (spot) transactions and their legal significance

papers.node_id: 1985wislrev483!!SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: WHAT WE DO AND DO NOT KNOW.
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: WHAT WE DO AND DO NOT KNOW.
papers.abstract:
We must know who "we" are before we can talk about what "we" do and not know about anything, including relational contract.  My students, for example, all know that I invented relational contract, and I daresay Stewart Macaulay's students all know that he invented relational contract.  Charles Fried knows that relational contract was invented by the Devil.  Any good classical neoclassical microeconomist knows there is no such thing as relational contract.  All these "wees" happen to be wrong.  Or are they?  Perhaps for their own purposes, each of these "wees" is correct.
Once we have established the correct "we", we must explain what we mean by "know".  Everyone "knows," for exam ple, of the explosion of litigation in this country.  But Marc Galanter's article, Reading the Landscape of Disputes: What We Know and Don't Know (And Think We Know) about Our Allegedly Contentious and Litigious Societyshows they are wrong.  Or does it?  It depends upon what we mean by "know;"the very fact that we think we know is itself a form of knowledge,a fact not changed by our preference for some other -- and possibly contradictory -- form of knowledge about the basic phenomenon allegedly known.Moreover, the very way we organize our thinking is a form of knowledge -- one often overlooked, even by lawyers whose stock-in-trade consists largely of such "organizational" knowledge.  To take a famous example, Albert Einstein became more knowledgeable about the physical world when he understood the laws of relativity, as did everyone who understood him.  This was true as soon as he understood, even though it was many years, if not decades, before "hard" knowledge existed in the form of either physical experiments or pragmatic uses of that knowledge.Similarly, we know more about some aspects of human behavior as a result of the development of neoclassical economics than we did before.
With these thoughts in mind we can proceed cautiously to talk about our -- that is, your and my, dear reader -- knowledge, or what we think we know, about relational contract.  Nevertheless, before we can take stock of relational contract scholarship or suggest directions for future research,we must relate that scholarly dimension to other relational contract dimensions, and delineate various categories of such scholarship.
The relational contract dimensions important in our inquiry are first, the everyday working of exchange relations and transactions, or contract behavior (the behavioral dimension); second, the positive law of the sovereign relating to that behavior (the legal dimension); and third, legal scholarship relating to that behavior (the scholarly dimension).

questions.question: How do parties in ongoing exchange relationships use informal, repeated-interaction arrangements (relational contracting) to govern performance, resolve disputes, and adapt to change?

What are the main conceptual and empirical gaps in our scholarly understanding of relational contracting, and which research methods and frameworks are best suited to fill those gaps?

papers.node_id: 9wmmarybuslrev419!!SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: A PRAGMATIST'S VIEW OF PROMISSORY LAW WITH A FOCUS ON CONSENT AND RELIANCE
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: MORALITY, MARKETS, AND CONTRACT LAW: A PRAGMATIST'S VIEW OF PROMISSORY LAW WITH A FOCUS ON CONSENT AND RELIANCE
papers.abstract:
"Contract law is multidimensional."By this, I mean that no unitary theory can fully explain contract law. Instead, contract law is comprised of many theories, including promise, reliance, consent, formalist, contextual, critical, economic, and relational theories.I believe we should be wary of unified theories that purport to account for the entire subject, despite the false appeal of theory to clarify and tame a subject. Instead, in my view, the only persuasive theory is that "contract law is a plausible, if not perfect, reflection of various normative choices of the surrounding society."
Nathan Oman's excellent new book,The Dignity of Commerce, makes an impressive case for how markets can produce "desirable" outcomes for society.In addition to a comprehensive account of what he calls "virtues" of markets, such as their tendency to produce cooperation, trust, and wealth, the book is full of useful and persuasive supporting information and discussions.Oman is indeed an erudite analyst and, in the process of making his case for markets, the book is rich in additional references.Further, Oman is not reluctant to challenge analysts with different perspectives than his own, while at the same time shedding light on their theses.
An additional strength ofThe Dignity of Commerceis that Oman is not a dogmatic advocate of his position. He sensibly recognizes the darker side of markets: "[O]ne cannot deny that markets can lead to morally monstrous results."Oman insists that his claim is "modest" that "certain kinds of well-functioning markets are sufficiently desirable to be a fit object of the law's concern"and that "markets can sometimes be bad."In a chapter on boilerplate largely advocating a diminished role for the principle of consent, he admits that "consent is not irrelevant[,]"and usefully discusses its various contributions.
Still, Oman writes that markets are the key to an integrated solution to some of the great contract law issues and he goes pretty far in placing markets as the core and foundation of contract law at the expense of other theories.In testing his theory, I will focus on the role of consent in boilerplate cases and the function of reliance in the enforcement of promises to show that in my view much more is at work than Oman's "market argument."First, inPart I, I will briefly describe Oman's thesis and raise some concerns. Then I will discuss two issues in Part II. First, has Oman done enough to convince that markets are what he calls the "centerpiece" of contract law? Second, does his effort to present what is essentially a unitary, integrative theory of contract handcuff his analysis of particular contract issues and doctrines? I will argue that markets are important and contract law should and does play an important role in supporting markets. However, we should not demote other visions of contract law, but see them all as important ingredients in understanding the subject. By largely espousing a unitary, integrative theory of contract law,Oman boxes himself into a corner that leads to some debatable propositions, including with respect to consent to boilerplate and reliance on promises.

questions.question: Whether market considerations should be the primary organizing principle of contract law.
Whether a market-centered account justifies reducing the legal importance of assent in standardized (mass-market) contracts.
What normative role reliance should play in justifying the enforcement of promises.

matched_themes: How have intellectual movements, jurisprudential methods, and broader institutional shifts influenced the content and development of contract doctrine and scholarship?
How should courts measure damages-expectation versus reliance versus restitution-when enforcing promises?
When and on what grounds should courts enforce non-bargained promises-should enforcement depend on detrimental reliance, reasonable expectations of performance, injustice, or other criteria?
Does the proliferation of competing theoretical approaches to contract law reflect a substantive crisis in the doctrine, and what are the underlying sources?
Should contract law adopt substantive, context-sensitive, individualized, complex, and dynamic rules rather than formal, standardized, objective, binary, and static rules?
Do no-binding-effect clauses (express statements that parties do not intend legal obligations) prevent courts from finding enforceable agreements in practice?
When should promises that lack a bargained-for exchange be legally enforceable, and should enforceability rest on promisor intent, promisee reliance, or mutual exchange?
When should courts supply implied contractual terms or default rules because doing so increases net joint gains in the face of transaction costs and behavioral frictions?
How should courts choose between reliance-focused relief and expectation-focused relief in particular cases, and what normative role should reliance play in justifying enforcement of promises?
Do doctrines emphasizing mutual agreement function mainly as evidentiary/timing devices rather than independent substantive requirements for contract formation?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

Which normative model should underlie contract law - the promise model, an exchange/consent model, reliance-focused theories, or a pluralistic framework - and what are the moral and practical consequences of each?
Should the enforceability of promises be grounded on mutual exchange/consideration or on foreseeable reliance?
Should enforcement of relied-upon promises incorporate distributive justice and power-dynamics considerations (e.g., bargaining power, social context)?
How have doctrinal categories, labels, and classifications influenced legal reasoning, interpretation, and substantive outcomes in contract law?

shared_topics.justification: Both papers probe how parties' mental states and manifestations of consent should control whether promises are enforceable — Paper A develops an 'expanded intent' account (volitional, cognitive, contextual purposive intent) to analyze defenses like mistake, while Paper B interrogates the continuing normative weight of consent (especially in boilerplate) within a broader account of promissory law.

shared_topics.topic: the function of reliance and expectation as justifications for enforcing or excusing promises (and related defenses)
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the justificatory role of reliance or expectation interests — Paper A examines how failures of basic assumptions (mistake, frustration, impracticability) affect parties' reliance and thus excuse enforcement, while Paper B analyzes the role of reliance in promissory enforcement and questions how reliance interacts with market-based justifications.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law should be organized around a single unifying principle or by multiple, coexisting theories
shared_topics.justification: Both take up methodological questions about doctrinal organization — Paper A argues for collapsing artificial doctrinal distinctions into a unified, intent-based analysis to improve consistency and accommodate modern transactions, while Paper B resists unitary, market-centered theories and defends a pluralist, multi-theoretical approach to explain different contract problems.

shared_topics.topic: how traditional doctrines (mistake, reform, boilerplate consent) should operate in modern markets and online contracting contexts
shared_topics.justification: Both address application of classic doctrines to contemporary market practices — Paper A uses an Internet house-sale vignette to show how mistake and changed circumstances play out with online representations and proposes an intent-based solution, while Paper B focuses on boilerplate and standardized market forms (and their consent deficits) to question how doctrines should treat mass-market contracting.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 76cornelllrev197!!ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF RELIANCE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE ROLE OF RELIANCE IN CONTRACT DAMAGES.

shared_topics.topic: whether promissory estoppel/reliance should cap contract damages at the reliance measure rather than the expectation measure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly critiques the 'estoppel-exception' view that promissory‑estoppel cases should be limited to reliance damages rather than expectation damages, tracing its doctrinal origins and arguing against it; Paper B treats the function of reliance in enforcement of promises and evaluates claims (from market‑centered theories) that would downplay reliance relative to other remedies, thereby engaging the same question of whether reliance should constrain recovery.

shared_topics.topic: the normative/economic arguments for privileging expectation damages versus reliance (efficiency concerns)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages explicitly with law‑and‑economics critiques that expectation damages produce excessive assurance and inefficient reliance and rejects those critiques; Paper B critiques unitary, market‑driven explanations of contract law that would subordinate reliance, assessing the adequacy of economic/market justifications for privileging certain doctrines.

shared_topics.topic: the proper relationship between consent/consideration doctrines and reliance-based enforcement (e.g., boilerplate and promissory estoppel tensions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the distinction between contracts resting on consideration versus estoppel and how that affects remedial choice between expectation and reliance measures; Paper B focuses on the tension between consent (especially in boilerplate) and reliance, arguing that reliance remains a crucial, distinct justificatory strand that must be balanced against consent/market rationales.

shared_topics.topic: doctrinal history and authoritative formulations (Restatements, case law) shaping reliance and promissory estoppel
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes the historical development of promissory estoppel and reliance doctrine in the Restatement (First) and (Second) and subsequent case law; Paper B situates contemporary debates about reliance and consent within broader doctrinal and scholarly developments, engaging with how authoritative accounts shape present doctrinal choices.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 32indlrev1247!!ARTICLE: Feminists & Contract Doctrine
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Feminists & Contract Doctrine

shared_topics.topic: the contest between formalist/abstract doctrines and contextual/relational approaches in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly catalogs and defends the plurality of theories (formalist vs contextual, relational, etc.) and criticizes unitary market-centered accounts for overlooking contextual concerns like boilerplate consent; Paper B criticizes contract law's preference for abstraction, rationality, and objectivity and argues feminist theory favors contextualization and attention to relational and situational factors.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract law is neutral/objective or instead reflects social values and biases
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues contract law should be understood as a reflection of the surrounding society's normative choices rather than a single neutral theory; Paper B argues contract doctrine is gendered—shaped by male perspectives—and thus is not neutral but embodies social biases.

shared_topics.topic: critique of dominant or unitary theoretical frameworks and the case for theoretical pluralism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A objects to Oman's attempt to make markets the 'centerpiece' of contract law and urges retaining multiple theoretical lenses (promise, reliance, consent, economic, critical, etc.); Paper B challenges claims that contract law is immune to social bias and promotes feminist perspectives as an essential corrective to dominant (implicit) frameworks.

shared_topics.topic: the proper definition and scope of contract doctrine (what the 'game' includes and how rules should be understood)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates how different theories should be applied to particular doctrines (e.g., boilerplate consent, reliance) rather than subsuming them under a single market theory; Paper B analyzes both the definition of the 'game' of contract law and the 'rules of the game,' asking whether those definitions and rules reflect a male-centered viewpoint and how feminism has or should reshape them.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 20seattleulrev45!!ARTICLE: The Four Phases of Promissory Estoppel
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: The Four Phases of Promissory Estoppel

shared_topics.topic: the role of detrimental reliance in enforcing promises
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes promissory estoppel as a doctrine built around detrimental reliance (including its evolution into reliance-based remedies), and Paper B directly questions and defends the function of reliance in enforcing promises versus market- or consent-based justifications.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract/promise law admits a unitary theory or requires pluralism
shared_topics.justification: Paper A presents promissory estoppel as a syncretistic doctrine that straddles estoppel, contract, tort, and equity rather than fitting a single doctrinal box, while Paper B rejects a unitary, market-centered theory of contract law and argues for a multidimensional or pluralistic approach (promise, reliance, consent, economic, etc.).

shared_topics.topic: the tension between bargained-for consideration/consent and reliance-based promise enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces the historical displacement of 'reliance consideration' by bargained-for consideration and situates promissory estoppel as a remedy when classical bargain/consent rules fail, and Paper B interrogates the limits of consent (especially in boilerplate) and whether reliance should justify enforcement where consent/consideration is weak.

shared_topics.topic: the normative grounding of promissory/promise enforcement (equity, tort, contract, or market rationales)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines promissory estoppel's roots in equity and its interactions with contract and tort doctrines to justify enforcement, while Paper B evaluates market-based normative accounts of contract law and questions whether markets alone suffice to ground doctrines that protect reliance and promise-expectations.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:CORBIN AND FULLER'S CASES ON CONTRACTS (1942?): THE CASEBOOK THAT NEVER WAS

shared_topics.topic: the function of remedies (expectation vs reliance) in contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques how reliance is used in enforcing promises and challenges market-centered accounts that may underplay reliance; Paper B foregrounds remedies by presenting the remedies-first pedagogical approach and discusses the expectation/reliance distinction (including Restatement Second §90) as central to understanding what contract law enforces.

shared_topics.topic: the doctrinal and pedagogical primacy of formation/consent versus remedies as organizing principles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates the normative weight of consent (especially in boilerplate) versus other values like reliance and market-supporting goals; Paper B documents the longstanding pedagogical dispute (Corbin vs. Fuller) over whether a Contracts course should begin with formation/consent or with remedies, showing competing ways to organize the subject.

shared_topics.topic: pluralism versus unitary theories as frameworks for understanding contract law
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues for a multidimensional, pluralistic view of contract law and criticizes unitary integrative theories (specifically Oman's market-centric account); Paper B illustrates pluralism in practice by recounting multiple, divergent pedagogical frameworks (formation-first, remedies-first, hybrid) that reflect different theoretical emphases about what contract law is about.

shared_topics.topic: the influence of leading scholars and canonical texts on doctrine and teaching
shared_topics.justification: Paper A engages directly with Nathan Oman’s book and the effect of adopting a scholar's thesis as a central organizing account of contract law, while Paper B examines historical correspondence between Corbin and Fuller and shows how prominent figures and their casebooks (and Langdell’s legacy) have shaped how contract doctrine is taught and conceptualized.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 27setonhalllrev490!!ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CONSIDERATION AS THE COMMITMENT TO RELINQUISH AUTONOMY

shared_topics.topic: the role of consent/voluntariness in creating contractual obligations (including boilerplate)
shared_topics.justification: Both papers interrogate how voluntary assent functions as a prerequisite for enforceable promises: Paper A debates the proper weight of consent (especially in boilerplate contracts) in Oman's market-centered account, while Paper B treats contractual formation as necessarily tied to certain voluntary acts and reconceives consideration as the operative voluntariness that justifies state enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: whether consideration or reliance should ground enforcement of promises
shared_topics.justification: Both engage the dispute over what doctrinal mechanism should make promises enforceable — Paper A directly contrasts reliance and consent in enforcement and critiques an overly market-driven account, and Paper B analyzes consideration versus reliance/modification doctrines (e.g., Restatement 90) arguing consideration operates as a commitment mechanism distinct from reliance.

shared_topics.topic: the function of contract doctrine in supporting market and social relations
shared_topics.justification: Both locate contract law within a broader social/economic order: Paper A questions Oman's claim that markets should be the centerpiece of contract doctrine and argues multiple normative theories matter, while Paper B explains consideration as a social mechanism (relinquishment of autonomy) that constructs the interdependent autonomy necessary for market reproduction.

shared_topics.topic: evaluation of doctrinal reform proposals and limits of doctrinal explanations
shared_topics.justification: Both papers assess reformist claims about contract doctrine: Paper A critiques a unitary market-based reforming impulse and its implications for boilerplate/consent, and Paper B evaluates calls for abolition or modification of consideration (and explains why some reforms like Restatement 90 and UCC 2-209 succeeded while abolitionist calls failed).

compared_to.partner_node_id: 33sandiegolrev175!!ARTICLE: Living Without the Avoidable Consequences Doctrine in Contract Remedies
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Living Without the Avoidable Consequences Doctrine in Contract Remedies

shared_topics.topic: how remedial doctrines (like the avoidable consequences rule) relate to the expectation interest and how damages should be calculated
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that the avoidable consequences (duty to mitigate) rule is best understood as a corollary of the expectation interest—an internal offset for benefits of breach that prevents overcompensation—while Paper B engages the broader question of how doctrinal rules (including remedies) should be justified by competing contract theories such as promise, reliance, and market-oriented accounts.

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of reliance versus expectation principles in enforcing promises and awarding damages
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers the expectation interest in explaining offsets for avoidable losses and how plaintiffs' choices reveal valuations relevant to damages, and Paper B directly interrogates the function of reliance (and promise) doctrines in promissory enforcement, weighing reliance against other justificatory frameworks for when and how promises should be enforced.

shared_topics.topic: whether contract rules should be framed as duties (e.g., a duty to mitigate or duties of consent) versus as corollary consequences of other normative principles
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques duty-based characterizations of mitigation (arguing the duty language misleads and that mitigation is better seen as implementing the expectation interest), while Paper B examines the normative status of consent (especially in boilerplate) and warns against treating single-duty or unitary duty constructs as the sole basis for contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism toward unitary, integrative theories of contract law and the need to situate doctrines within multiple normative frameworks
shared_topics.justification: Paper A challenges readings that treat mitigation as an exception to expectation compensation and instead reinterprets it within the expectation framework (with implications for alternative fault-based accounts), and Paper B explicitly rejects monolithic theories (such as market-central accounts) and argues contract law must be understood as multidimensional, drawing on promise, reliance, consent, economic, and other perspectives.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: MACAULAY, MACHEIL, AND THE DISCOVERY OF SOLIDARITY AND POWER IN CONTRACT LAW.

shared_topics.topic: relational/contextual approaches versus market-centered/transactional theories of contract
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops and defends a relational, context-sensitive critique of transactional law-and-economics models, arguing that continuing relationships and social norms drive contracting; Paper B criticizes a unitary, market-centered account (Oman's thesis) and argues for a pluralist view that keeps contextual, relational, and other theories in play.

shared_topics.topic: the role of consent and reliance in modern contracting (especially with boilerplate and continuing relations)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the classical emphasis on ex ante consent—showing how obligations in continuing relations often evolve beyond initial promises and rely on communal expectations—while Paper B directly analyzes consent's diminished normative force in boilerplate and scrutinizes reliance as an alternative or complementary justificatory ground for enforcing promises.

shared_topics.topic: the gap between formal legal doctrine and law-in-action / private ordering
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the marginality of common-law/UCC doctrines relative to private norms and sanctions governing commercial communities, arguing courts and doctrine often misrepresent contracting practice; Paper B engages with empirical market phenomena (e.g., boilerplate) and critiques theories that fail to account for how market practices and private ordering actually shape enforcement and normative judgments.

shared_topics.topic: whether markets generate trust/cooperation or foster domination and moral harms in contractual relations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights both 'organic solidarity' (markets and continuing relations as sites of trust and mutual support) and the risk of entrenched domination from power imbalances in long-term contracts; Paper B surveys Oman's claim that markets produce virtues like trust and cooperation while also acknowledging and probing markets' darker, morally troubling outcomes.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: PRECONTRACTUAL LIABILITY AND PRELIMINARY AGREEMENTS

shared_topics.topic: enforceability of promises or agreements when consent or complete terms are lacking
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the significance of consent (especially in boilerplate contexts) for binding promises, and Paper B examines when preliminary negotiations or incomplete agreements create enforceable commitments (intent to be bound, binding preliminary commitments) and what relief is appropriate.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether markets should be the centerpiece of contract law and how law supports market virtues like trust and cooperation, while Paper B argues that courts can promote efficient commercial behavior by giving legal effect to preliminary agreements and protecting investment-backed expectations.

shared_topics.topic: normative and theoretical foundations of contract law (economic vs pluralist/other theories)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques unitary, market-centered theories and urges a pluralistic view incorporating promise, reliance, consent, and economic accounts, whereas Paper B develops an economic/behavioral model to derive normative rules for precontractual liability and evaluates doctrinal fit.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Opportunism and Trust in the Negotiation of Commercial Contracts: Toward a New Cause of Action

shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates contract law as serving market functions (cooperation, predictability) and critiques overreliance on a market-centered account, while Paper B argues explicitly that legal rules should deter opportunistic behavior in negotiation and contracting to enable transactions that would otherwise be thwarted by temptation to renege.

shared_topics.topic: protection of reliance and transaction-specific investments outside classic postcontractual settings
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes the normative importance of reliance as a distinct justificatory basis (contrasted with consent and market arguments), and Paper B documents and defends legal protection for precontractual and negotiation-stage reliance in the form of transaction-specific investments that courts already compensate or should protect.

shared_topics.topic: skepticism toward unitary law-and-economics explanations of contract doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A objects to a single, market-centric theory of contract law and urges pluralist approaches, while Paper B challenges dominant law-and-economics assumptions (e.g., that precontractual parties do not make significant specific investments) and proposes doctrinal adjustments informed by empirical and social-psychological evidence.

shared_topics.topic: the role of trust in commercial contracting and how law should support it
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses markets as producers of trust among other virtues and questions reducing consent too far in boilerplate, whereas Paper B centers trust as a psychological precondition for complex commercial coordination and argues that legal regulation (including a new cause of action) is justified to reinforce trust-building in negotiations.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CULTURAL CONCEPTIONS OF COMPETITION: NOTE: TAX ABATEMENTS AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL: A MATCH NOT MADE IN YPSILANTI

shared_topics.topic: the interaction between economic incentives/market considerations and equitable contract doctrines
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes tax abatements as market/economic incentives and argues for using an equitable doctrine (promissory estoppel) when those incentives produce reliance harms; Paper B critiques market‑centered accounts of contract law and examines when market reasons should yield to other normative doctrines like reliance and consent.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines whether the Township's reliance was reasonable and discusses the economic necessity defense to enforcement of promises in the plant‑closure context; Paper B engages substantively with the scope and function of reliance as a constraint on enforcement of promises and how reliance interacts with other justificatory claims.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Rethinking Promissory Estoppel

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: "W(H)ITHER THE RELIANCE INTEREST?"+:Remedies for Imperfect Transactions in Contracts and Torts

shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues against a single, market‑centered unified theory of contract law and urges recognizing multiple normative strands (promise, reliance, consent, economic, relational), while Paper B begins from the premise that there is no unified remedial theory for imperfect transactions and develops multiple remedial approaches (contract expectation, reliance, tort responses) to address different defects.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: DANCING AROUND GENDER: LESSONS FROM ARTHUR MURRAY ON GENDER AND CONTRACTS

shared_topics.justification: Paper A foregrounds Williston's personal illness and its influence on his life and work, and Paper B centers morality and normative choices (e.g., consent, reliance, market virtues) as driving forces in how contract law should be understood and applied.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: A TRIBUTE TO PROFESSOR JOSEPH M. PERILLO: DEDICATION A TRIBUTE TO A GIANT

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: CONTEMPORARY POLITICAL THEORY AND PRIVATE LAW: ESSAY: CONTRACT THEORY ON AND OFF THE GRID

shared_topics.topic: the normative justification and legitimacy of adopting particular contract institutions
