papers.node_id: 103nwulrev615!!SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: ORIGINAL IDEAS ON ORIGINALISM: THE MISCONCEIVED ASSUMPTION ABOUT CONSTITUTIONAL ASSUMPTIONS
papers.abstract:
Whether or not they are originalists, most constitutional scholars and observers assume that the basic assumptions held at the time the Constitution was enacted or amended are relevant to ascertaining its original meaning. Some originalists use constitutional assumptions to constrain judges in their interpretations of the more abstract passages of the text. Others reject originalism precisely because they object to the outmoded assumptions thatprevailed at the time of enactment, and they assume that these assumptions must shape the original meaning of the text.
For example, some claim that because of widespread concern about the continued vitality of the militia, the original meaning of the Second Amendment's right to keep and bear arms is limited to those who are in service to the militia. Others think that because many in the Thirty-Ninth Congress and elsewhere assumed the continued existence of segregated government schools or the inferiority of women, the original meaning of the Fourteenth Amendment must be consistent with segregated schools and the common law rules of coverture. Still others claim that because people assumed at the time the Fourteenth Amendment was adopted that laws regulating private morality were within the police power of the states, such laws must be consistent with its original meaning.
In this Article, I challenge this misconceived assumption about the constitutional status of basic assumptions, which derives from a mistaken conflation of constitutions and contracts. Because the shared background assumptions of the parties are relevant to the enforcement of written contracts, it seems natural to treat written constitutions the same way. This equation of contracts and constitutions is further invited by the widespread and often unexamined assumption that, like contracts, constitutions are legitimate if and only if they are the product of consent. Because the shared background assumptions shape the scope of the parties' consent to written contracts, so too it is assumed that background assumptions shape the meaning of written constitutions.
But constitutions are not contracts. Contracts are consensual agreements between identifiable persons that provide a private law to govern their relationship. Constitutions inevitably lack the consent that legitimates contracts. Unlike contracts, from the time they are enacted into an indefinite future, constitutions purport to bind countless numbers of persons who do not consent. Or more precisely, statutes enacted pursuant to constitutions purport to bind members of the public who have not themselves consented to be bound. Therefore, if such statutes are binding, it is because of something other than the literal consent of the governed. And, unlike contracts that can "fail" when their basic assumptions turn out to be untrue, with constitutions failure is not an option.
Constitutional scholars have yet to examine systematically the lessons that can be learned from a close comparison of the important similarities and equally important differences between written constitutions and contracts. In this Article, I begin to fill this gap. Doing so requires recognizing three fundamental distinctions that are often overlooked in constitutional theory and practice: (1) the difference between express and implied-in-fact terms, (2) the difference between ambiguous and vague terms, and (3) the difference between constitutional interpretation and constitutional construction.
In Part I of this Article, I explain how express and implied-in-fact terms provide the meaning of both written contracts and written constitutions. In Part II, I distinguish the express and implied meaning of the text from the background assumptions that can condition the enforceability of a contract. Although background assumptions cannot vary this meaning, they can be relevant to interpreting the meaning of genuinely ambiguous terms in both contracts and constitutions. Most sustained disputes over constitutional terms concern terms that are vague, rather than ambiguous. Whether background assumptions may also be used to add specificity to vague terms in constitutions, as they can when construing contracts, will depend on one's theory of constitutional construction.
In Part III, I explore how one's approach to constitutional construction will depend on one's theory of constitutional legitimacy. That the legitimacy of constitutions, unlike contracts, is not based on original consent entails that original background assumptions do not affect the construction of constitutions the way they do contracts. Finally, in Part IV, I apply this analysis to three different background assumptions: (1) that there are background unenumerated natural rights, (2) that there is an unenumerated police power of the states, and (3) that the original meaning of the Constitution includes the interpretive methods that those who approved the Constitution assumed would be used.

questions.question: Whether the shared background assumptions held at the time a constitution is enacted should be used to determine the constitution's original meaning.
Whether written constitutions should be treated like private contracts such that the parties' background assumptions shape the scope and enforceability of constitutional text.
Whether and to what extent background assumptions may be used to resolve vague or ambiguous constitutional terms, and how different theories of constitutional legitimacy affect that use.

matched_themes: When should courts supply terms or liability rules for incomplete contracts rather than leaving gaps to private bargaining?
Should written constitutions be interpreted or treated analogously to private contracts so that background assumptions and parties' expectations influence scope and enforceability?
Should courts take parties' social, cultural, and identity backgrounds into account when interpreting and enforcing contracts to better protect reasonable expectations?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?

compared_to.partner_node_id: 93washlrev1609!!ARTICLE: REVERSING THE RELIANCE REVOLUTION IN CONTRACT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: REVERSING THE RELIANCE REVOLUTION IN CONTRACT

shared_topics.topic: the proper role of historical background assumptions in interpreting legal instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that background assumptions at enactment should not be conflated with the textual original meaning of constitutions the way they are used to interpret contracts, while Paper B traces how twentieth-century reliance-focused assumptions reshaped contract doctrine and questions whether those historical assumptions should govern modern enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: consent and consideration as foundations of enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts constitutions (which bind many nonconsenting persons) with contracts (enforced on the basis of parties' consent), and Paper B defends mutual consideration and party exchange as the traditional basis for contractual liability against reliance-based doctrines that sidestep consent.

shared_topics.topic: tension between classical/formalist doctrines and modern doctrinal innovations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines the divide between originalist/textualist meaning and later modes of constitutional construction that incorporate background assumptions, while Paper B frames promissory estoppel and the 'reliance revolution' as a modern departure from classical contract principles and argues for restoring the older framework.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction and doctrinal significance of express versus implied terms (and interpretation versus construction)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a tripartite distinction—express vs implied-in-fact terms, ambiguous vs vague language, and interpretation vs construction—for constitutional texts, and Paper B engages analogous issues in contract law by analyzing implied unilateral contracts, the definiteness of promises, and when courts should infer obligations absent explicit terms.

shared_topics.topic: use of legal and intellectual history to resolve contemporary doctrinal disputes
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for a systematic historical comparison between constitutions and contracts to inform interpretation and legitimacy questions, while Paper B conducts a detailed historical and intellectual survey of contract doctrines to justify reverting to traditional principles.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 73tullrev497!!ARTICLE:"Why Infer"? What the New Institutional Economics Has to Say About Law-Supplied Default Rules
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE:"Why Infer"? What the New Institutional Economics Has to Say About Law-Supplied Default Rules

shared_topics.topic: role and justification of implied (law‑supplied) terms in legal texts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes express versus implied‑in‑fact terms and treats implied terms as a shared interpretive mechanism in contracts and constitutions; Paper B develops a framework for when and why courts should supply implied obligations (default rules) in assent‑based relations.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling for vague or incomplete clauses (when courts should supply terms)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes ambiguous from vague constitutional terms and asks whether background assumptions may add specificity to vague provisions; Paper B interrogates courts' varied gap‑filling practices in contracts (e.g., quantity terms, long‑term contracts) and seeks criteria for when judicial supplementation is appropriate.

shared_topics.topic: normative legitimacy of judicial or legal intervention in supplying terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A grounds its argument about whether background assumptions should shape constitutional construction in a theory of constitutional legitimacy distinct from contract consent; Paper B asks the foundational question 'Why infer?' and seeks normative justification (efficiency/net benefit) for law‑supplied obligations in contexts where parties did not agree.

shared_topics.topic: use of background or behavioral assumptions to guide interpretation/default rules
shared_topics.justification: Paper A examines how original background assumptions have been used (and misused) to infer constitutional meaning and how such assumptions differ from contract contexts; Paper B emphasizes realistic behavioral assumptions (strategic behavior, bounded rationality, asset specificity) as central inputs to deciding whether a law‑supplied rule is warranted.

shared_topics.topic: need for a systematic comparative/institutional methodology to decide whether to supply terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A calls for systematic comparison of constitutions and contracts and links interpretive choices to broader theories of construction and legitimacy; Paper B proposes a comparative net‑benefit/new institutional economics methodology to compare feasible alternatives and justify imposing default rules.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 45wakeforestlrev641!!ARTICLE: REASONABLE EXPECTATIONS IN SOCIOCULTURAL CONTEXT
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: REASONABLE EXPECTATIONS IN SOCIOCULTURAL CONTEXT

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of background social and cultural assumptions to legal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that courts should consider parties' social identities and cultural backgrounds when determining reasonable expectations in contracts, while Paper B systematically examines whether and how background assumptions present at a founding should affect the original meaning or construction of constitutional text.

shared_topics.topic: the tension between consent-based legitimacy (individual autonomy) and societal interests in enforcement
shared_topics.justification: Paper A frames contract enforcement as protecting individual autonomy (consent) but balances that against societal objectives like credit reliability, and Paper B contrasts contracts' consent-based legitimacy with constitutions' lack of individual consent to explain why background assumptions should play a different role in constitutional construction.

shared_topics.topic: objective (reasonable person) versus contextual/subjective approaches to meaning and ambiguity
shared_topics.justification: Paper A critiques the objective theory of contract that substitutes a reasonable-person standard for parties' subjective intent and advocates a dynamic, contextual approach, while Paper B distinguishes ambiguous from vague constitutional terms and explores when contextual background assumptions may permissibly inform interpretation versus when construction is required.

shared_topics.topic: the role of implicit or unexpressed (implied-in-fact) assumptions or terms in determining meaning and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights how modern contracting often reveals implicit or unexpressed assumptions that courts should weigh in assessing intent and expectations, and Paper B analyzes express versus implied-in-fact terms and the circumstances under which background assumptions can influence the enforceability or specification of written terms.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 58ucinlrev1283!!ARTICLE: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF CONTRACT THEORY
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: THE SIGNIFICANCE OF CONTRACT THEORY

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of contract theory for understanding other legal forms (especially constitutions)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly uses concepts from contract law to critique common assumptions about how background assumptions should affect constitutional meaning, while Paper B surveys and defends the importance and diversity of contract theories—treating contract theory as a formative framework that shapes how legal doctrine is understood and reformed.

shared_topics.topic: the role of background assumptions and social/contextual facts in legal interpretation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates whether shared background assumptions at enactment should influence original constitutional meaning or construction, and Paper B treats relational, empirical, and critical contract theories as challengers to neoclassical doctrine by foregrounding social context and background practices in interpreting and applying contract law.

shared_topics.topic: normative foundations and legitimacy of legal instruments (consent vs other bases)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the consent-based legitimacy of contracts with the different, nonconsensual legitimacy claims of constitutions to argue this affects interpretive practice, while Paper B situates competing contract theories as expressions of underlying political and professional ideologies, debating what normative commitments should ground contract doctrine.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between explicit/textual terms and implied or contextual terms in legal documents
shared_topics.justification: Paper A develops a taxonomy distinguishing express versus implied-in-fact terms and ambiguous versus vague language in constitutions, and Paper B engages with similar issues through critiques of neoclassical contract doctrine (and promotion of relational/empirical approaches) that emphasize implied obligations, background expectations, and the limits of purely textualist contract models.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2001wislrev777!!CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PETER LINZER'S "ROUGH JUSTICE"
compared_to.partner_title: CONTRACTS SYMPOSIUM:COMMENTARY PETER LINZER'S "ROUGH JUSTICE"

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and role of background assumptions or context in interpreting legal texts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes whether shared historical background assumptions should inform the original meaning or construction of constitutional provisions, distinguishing when such assumptions can inform ambiguous versus vague terms; Paper B criticizes minimalist/textualist statutory and contractual interpretation and urges attention to legislative history, social context, and the parties' circumstances when construing statutes and contracts.

shared_topics.topic: gap‑filling and implied terms in incomplete legal instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes express terms from implied‑in‑fact terms and explores when background assumptions may be used to add specificity to vague constitutional provisions; Paper B treats courts' use of doctrines (reliance, unjust enrichment, tort) as a pragmatic ‘patchwork’ to fill gaps in incomplete contracts and relationships where precedent or text is insufficient.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of consent and bargaining power for legitimacy and enforceability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes that constitutions differ from contracts because constitutions bind non‑consenting future persons and thus background consent assumptions cannot ground constitutional legitimacy the way they can for contracts; Paper B focuses on disparities in bargaining power (e.g., employment arbitration) and how lack of meaningful consent should affect the enforceability of contractual terms.

shared_topics.topic: critique of formalist/textualist theories in favor of pragmatic, context‑sensitive adjudication
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that treating constitutions like contracts (a formalist consent‑based model) is a mistaken conflation and that construction must account for legitimacy concerns and practical consequences; Paper B condemns judicial formalism and economic/textual minimalism that ignore social context, advocating flexible doctrinal synthesis to achieve ‘rough justice.’

compared_to.partner_node_id: 2wmmarybuslrev73!!ARTICLE: FINGERPRINTS OF EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL ON THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: FINGERPRINTS OF EQUITABLE ESTOPPEL AND PROMISSORY ESTOPPEL ON THE STATUTE OF FRAUDS IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the tension between textual/formal requirements and equitable doctrines that excuse them
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes how the Statute of Frauds' writing/formality requirements conflict with equitable estoppel and promissory estoppel and when reliance or fraud justifies overriding formalities; Paper B interrogates whether background assumptions should alter the apparent textual meaning of constitutions and when non-textual considerations may legitimately modify or constrain a text's application.

shared_topics.topic: the role of reliance or consent in legitimizing enforcement of written instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A centers on promissory estoppel's requirement of reasonable reliance to enforce otherwise unenforceable oral agreements, while Paper B contrasts contractual consent (and background assumptions that affect consent) with the lack of literal consent underlying constitutional legitimacy and how that affects enforceability.

shared_topics.topic: the admissibility and limits of background assumptions or contextual evidence in construing written legal texts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A treats factual contexts (fraud, misrepresentation, inducement) as decisive in applying equitable doctrines to the Statute of Frauds; Paper B systematically examines when background assumptions can inform the meaning or construction of constitutional (and contract) text, and distinguishes their proper role for ambiguous versus vague terms.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between interpretation (textual meaning) and construction/enforcement (remedial or practical application)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts the statutory text of the Statute of Frauds with equitable remedies that alter practical enforceability, and Paper B explicitly separates constitutional interpretation from constitutional construction and links different remedial or pragmatic commitments to theories of legitimacy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 68cornelllrev617!!ARTICLE: AN ANALYSIS OF THE CESSATION OF CONTRACTUAL RELATIONS.
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN ANALYSIS OF THE CESSATION OF CONTRACTUAL RELATIONS.

shared_topics.topic: the distinction between express and implied-in-fact terms
shared_topics.justification: Paper A identifies and analyzes the legal-theoretical difference between express constitutional provisions and implied-in-fact constitutional terms, while Paper B repeatedly treats whether rights (e.g., to terminate) are expressly reserved or must be supplied implicitly, using that distinction to structure cessation remedies.

shared_topics.topic: the role of consent/assent and its limits in enforcing legal instruments
shared_topics.justification: Paper A contrasts constitutions (which bind many nonconsenting persons) with contracts (whose legitimacy depends on consent) to argue limits on using background assumptions, and Paper B centers freedom of contract and assent as the starting point for enforcement while explaining doctrinal and public-interest limits when consent cannot justify enforcement.

shared_topics.topic: judicial gap‑filling/construction when parties or texts fail to allocate rights
shared_topics.justification: Paper A addresses how courts must move from interpretation to constitutional construction when background assumptions or text leave gaps, and Paper B analyzes how courts determine cessation rights when contracts fail to allocate risks or intentions, employing gap‑filling doctrines and normative judgment.

shared_topics.topic: how ambiguity or vagueness in texts is resolved and when extra‑textual assumptions apply
shared_topics.justification: Paper A draws a sharp distinction between ambiguous and vague constitutional terms and explains when background assumptions can be used to add meaning, while Paper B confronts unclear or unspecified contractual provisions about termination and explains how courts use intent, reasonableness, and fairness to resolve such indeterminacy.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 146upalrev1235!!ARTICLE: AN EXPRESSIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT: FROM FEMINIST DILEMMAS TO A RECONCEPTUALIZATION OF RATIONAL CHOICE IN CONTRACT LAW
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: AN EXPRESSIVE THEORY OF CONTRACT: FROM FEMINIST DILEMMAS TO A RECONCEPTUALIZATION OF RATIONAL CHOICE IN CONTRACT LAW

shared_topics.topic: the relevance of background or shared social assumptions to legal meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates how socially mediated values and the expressive content of choices (per Anderson) affect what a choice means in contract law, while Paper B analyzes when and how background assumptions at enactment should (or should not) inform the original meaning or construction of constitutional text.

shared_topics.topic: whether individual choice or consent alone grounds binding legal obligations
shared_topics.justification: Paper A questions the conventional doctrine that a party's choice to contract by itself justifies enforcement and argues for supplementary justificatory reasons, and Paper B contrasts contracts and constitutions to argue that the consent-based rationale that supports contractual obligations cannot be uncritically applied to constitutional obligations.

shared_topics.topic: the need to justify enforcement or construction by normative reasons beyond the bare text or act
shared_topics.justification: Paper A proposes relying on considerations like reliance interests and the instrumental value of conventions to justify enforcing particular contracts, while Paper B contends that constitutional construction must be guided by theories of legitimacy and cannot simply import private-law background assumptions to justify binding interpretations.

shared_topics.topic: distinguishing categories and tailoring interpretive or remedial responses to context
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes commercial contracting from other forms and argues for differentiated enforceability and remedies depending on context, and Paper B draws fine-grained distinctions (express vs implied terms; ambiguous vs vague terms; interpretation vs construction) to show that different textual categories and doctrinal contexts warrant different interpretive approaches.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 36wmmarylrev1379!!ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS
compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: CARDOZO AND POSNER: A STUDY IN CONTRACTS

shared_topics.topic: judicial interpretive methodology and its normative grounding
shared_topics.justification: Paper A directly compares Cardozo's capacious, balancing doctrinal method with Posner's efficiency-driven, narrower framework, while Paper B analyzes how competing interpretive theories (originalism, construction) and theories of legitimacy determine how judges should construe constitutional text.

shared_topics.topic: when and whether judges should imply terms or obligations into written texts
shared_topics.justification: Paper A focuses on Cardozo's invention of implied duties (e.g., the covenant of good faith) versus Posner's reluctance to imply obligations, and Paper B treats the distinction between express and implied-in-fact terms and whether background assumptions may be used to supply implied content to constitutional provisions.

shared_topics.topic: the role of background assumptions and extra-textual values in fixing meaning
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates whether contract law should incorporate values like good faith, reasonable expectations, or solely efficiency, whereas Paper B critiques the use of historical background assumptions to determine original constitutional meaning and explores when such assumptions legitimately inform interpretation.

shared_topics.topic: consequences of judicial approaches for doctrinal development and legal practice
shared_topics.justification: Paper A emphasizes how differing judicial philosophies (Cardozo v. Posner) would reshape contract doctrine and legal education if one approach predominates, and Paper B examines how differing theories of construction and legitimacy produce divergent long-term effects on constitutional doctrine and governance.

compared_to.partner_node_id: 41loyuchilj175!!Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power
compared_to.partner_title: Article: Contract Formation and the Entrenchment of Power

shared_topics.topic: consent and voluntariness as the basis for legal obligation and legitimacy
shared_topics.justification: Paper A interrogates the widespread assumption that constitutions derive their meaning and legitimacy from the original consent of the governed by analogy to contracts, arguing that constitutions lack the consensual legitimacy of private agreements; Paper B centers mutual assent (voluntary consent) as the core source of contractual bindingness and examines how coercion undermines that legitimacy in private contracting.

shared_topics.topic: the primacy of initial formation/assent over later interpretive or remedial interventions
shared_topics.justification: Paper A distinguishes express/implied terms and argues for a clear separation between original meaning (interpretation) and construction informed by legitimacy, while Paper B identifies contract formation—particularly mutual assent—as the 'seat of power' that once established largely immunizes agreements from later policing doctrines, making formation determinative of outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the role of background circumstances or bargaining conditions in shaping enforceability (versus textual meaning)
shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes when background assumptions may appropriately inform ambiguous constitutional terms or affect enforceability, and Paper B analyzes how bargaining context (unequal power, duress, misrepresentation) affects whether courts should void or police contracts, treating background conditions as relevant to enforceability rather than pure textual content.

shared_topics.topic: the limits of interpretive or policing doctrines to remedy deeper structural problems
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that theories of constitutional construction are constrained by questions of legitimacy and thus cannot simply import contemporary background assumptions to resolve vagueness, while Paper B argues that modern contract policing doctrines (unconscionability, duress, misrepresentation) fail to correct the coercion problem because they leave the core formation rules intact—both papers critique remedial doctrines as inadequate to address foundational defects.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: REFLECTIONS ON FULLER AND PERDUE'S THE RELIANCE INTEREST IN CONTRACT DAMAGES: A POSITIVE ECONOMIC FRAMEWORK

shared_topics.justification: Paper A analyzes Fuller and Perdue's 'measure versus motive' claim—that courts may use one doctrinal measure of damages while actually aiming to protect reliance—and generalizes how one damage rule can approximate another; Paper B similarly interrogates whether background assumptions held at enactment should determine constitutional meaning, arguing that judges' underlying assumptions and motives must be distinguished from the formal textual measures used in interpretation.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A shows that reliance, expectation, restitution (and a proposed fourth) can serve as substitute measures for one another in practice, so the nominal doctrine need not match the substantive aim; Paper B distinguishes express vs implied terms and interpretation vs construction to show that formal doctrinal categories (e.g., background assumptions used to construe vague terms) can functionally operate to achieve different normative ends.

shared_topics.justification: Paper A separates Fuller and Perdue's descriptive claim (courts historically protected reliance) from their normative claim (courts should protect reliance), and explores how accepting the descriptive account affects the normative debate; Paper B similarly evaluates descriptive assumptions about original background beliefs and then links those empirical claims to differing theories of constitutional legitimacy and how constitutions ought to be constructed.

shared_topics.topic: use of contract doctrine (reliance, consent, enforceability) as a conceptual touchstone
shared_topics.justification: Paper A is centrally about contract-damages doctrines (reliance, expectation, restitution) and their economic functions; Paper B repeatedly uses contract concepts—consent, background assumptions, implied-in-fact terms, and enforceability—to compare and contrast how written constitutions should be interpreted and why constitutional texts differ from ordinary contracts.

compared_to.partner_title: SYMPOSIUM: LAW, PRIVATE GOVERNANCE AND CONTINUING RELATIONSHIPS: RELATIONAL CONTRACT: COMMENT: MACAULAY, MACHEIL, AND THE DISCOVERY OF SOLIDARITY AND POWER IN CONTRACT LAW.

compared_to.partner_title: ARTICLE: Evolving Business and Social Norms and Interpretation Rules: The Need for a Dynamic Approach to Contract Disputes

papers.node_id: 2000utahlrev223!!SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: Response: The Values of Legal Archaeology (c) 2000, Judith L. Maute.
papers.abstract:
I. Introduction: Historical Reconstruction as an Archaeological Dig
At its best, the study and practice of law is a passionate and untiring pursuit of justice. In the hustle of daily demands for our time and attention, we often lose sight of that goal, and lawyers' essential role in achieving just results. By pausing long enough to reflect on one case--intricately weaving together the facts, law, and historical context--one's passion and commitment to the ends of justice can be revitalized. To the extent that law is taught and received as a set of abstract legal rules, one can safely remain at a distance from the significance of a legal ruling to the parties, the greater community, and the legal system as a whole.
Professor Debora Threedy has suggested that historical reconstruction of noteworthy cases be viewed using the metaphor of an archeological dig.
"A reported case does in some ways resemble those traces of past human activity . . . . Cases need to be treated as what they are, fragments of antiquity, and we need, like archaeologists, gently to free these fragments from the overburden of legal dogmatics, and try, by relating them to other evidence, which has to be sought outside the law library, to make sense of them as events in history and incidents in the evolution of the law."
This metaphor captures what is involved in doing historical reconstruction, the value to those who get their hands dirty laboring in the field, and the resulting contributions to a deeper understanding of the law.
Historical reconstruction is invaluable to understanding legal processes: how cases are presented, take shape through the adversary process, and are finally decided by a court of last resort. The term "legal archaeology" is bothelegant and accurate. The process it describes is labor-intensive and thus can only be done by those who are willing to get their hands dirty, who are passionately motivated by a detective-like curiosity to understand, and who are willing to sift patiently through piles of sand until they find a coherent story take shape by piecing together broken shards.
Another possible metaphor is that of pathology done in the coroner's office. I suspect that everyone recalls a sense of outrage in response to studying a case at some time during their law school experience. The facts seemed compelling, providing a strong moral and legal basis for the claim. According to the law student's sense of justice, the case was wrongly decided.
During the process of legal education, many students and lawyers learn to shrug off outrage, and transfer their attention to a higher level of abstraction. They focus upon identifying the legal principle articulated by the court, and how that principle fit within the legal framework of this substantive area of law. As is so often true, if one does not accurately understand what transpired factually, a correct resolution to the problem is practically quite difficult. Law students and practicing lawyers must be vigilant toward the facts as stated, and constantly ask whether the court's decision was based upon assumptions about the facts which could not withstand careful scrutiny.

questions.question: Whether reconstructing the historical facts and context of reported cases (a "legal archaeology" approach) improves understanding of how cases are presented, shaped through the adversary process, and ultimately decided by courts, leading to more accurate interpretations of judicial outcomes.

Whether teaching and treating law primarily as a set of abstract rules causes students and lawyers to neglect factual and historical context, thereby diminishing their ability to evaluate the justice or correctness of court decisions.

matched_themes: Do appellate judges systematically shape factual narratives in published opinions in ways that influence doctrinal placement and case outcomes?
How do doctrinal classification and methodological choices (e.g., formal/systematic versus holistic/contextual) shape legal reasoning, interpretation, and outcomes?
How do historical inaccuracies or omitted factual background in appellate opinions affect the justification and legitimacy of resulting legal rules?

shared_topics.topic: normative concern with achieving just outcomes through careful fact and doctrine analysis
shared_topics.justification: Paper A debates which damage measure is 'just' in promissory estoppel contexts and ties remedy choice to policy and fairness (commercial vs donative cases), while Paper B frames historical reconstruction as a way to recover the moral and practical stakes of a case so that law students and lawyers can pursue more just results.

shared_topics.topic: normative concern with justice and the social significance of legal rules

papers.node_id: 90nwulrev49!!SYMPOSIUM: THE AFTERLIFE OF CONTRACT
papers.title: SYMPOSIUM: THE AFTERLIFE OF CONTRACT
papers.abstract:
Contracts can seem like a field where nothing ever happens,which indeed would make it a dead subject. We sometimes appear condemned to rehearse dualisms - classicism versus romanticism, independence versus interdependence - ad infinitum and ad nauseam. Lecturing in 1970, Grant Gilmore had the good fortune to believe that something had happened, although he named the event a "Death."He at least pretended to believe that classical contract doctrine had died with laissez-faire thinking.He also professed to think that an ethos of interdependence had prevailed in law as in economics.If so, one might think some modest celebration appropriate, rather than mourning, but that would have spoiled the drama of Gilmore's title,and what he believed in most of all was the value of telling a good story.
In The Death of Contract, Gilmore struck a musty and slightly stodgy pose. He wistfully looked back to "the idea of unrestricted freedom of contract, which was surely one of the master concepts of nineteenth century thought."He was confident that we had moved beyond such thinking, perhaps too far beyond:
As we look back on the nineteenth century theories, we are struck most of all, I think, by the narrow scope of social duty which they implicitly assumed. No man is his brother's keeper; the race is to the swift; let thedevil take the hindmost. For good or ill, we have changed all that. We are now all cogs in a machine, each dependent on the other. The decline and fall of the general theory of contract and, in most quarters, of laissez-faire economics may be taken as remote reflections of the transition from nineteenth century individualism to the welfare state and beyond.
Left out of Gilmore's story is the whirlwind of reaction soon to sweep over the land. The gathering storm can be spotted on Gilmore's radar screen if one examines his footnotes,but Gilmore blithely underestimated its potential force. For example, he derided Richard Posner as an anachronism, belittling what Posner might have to say about contract law before he could even say it:
Professor Posner feels that nineteenth century negligence theory was economically as well as legally sound and that the gradual erosion of the theory in this century is to be deplored. If he turns his attention to contract, his conclusions will no doubt be the same.
This dismissal in a footnote may have been deserved, but Gilmore can hardly be credited with foresight in predicting Posner's academic and professional fortunes. At the end of his book, Gilmore guessed that a "resurrection" of formalism might lie ahead, that "some new Langdell" might "summon us back to the paths of righteousness, discipline, order, and well-articulated theory."Although he was familiar with the nascent law and economics movement,he did not consider it a contender for the central role in the second coming. Amen.
Many different answers are possible to the question: exactly what was The Death of Contract about? One is that Gilmore was using classical contract as an illustration of the realist point that myriad cases cannot be neatly reduced to "doctrine." This point may seem obvious and dated now, but it was less so when Gilmore made it, and he did it so entertainingly that the book still seems fresh.
With 20/20 hindsight, we can see Gilmore's myopia concerning his own historical moment most clearly when he states, "We have witnessed the dismantling of the formal system of the classical theorists. We have gone though our romantic agony...."Agony? Who are the wild-eyed romantics of Gilmore's account who "deny the existence of any rules" and "churn around in an ecstasy of self-expression" in a period "confused, sprawling, formless and chaotic"?In 1970,Duncan Kennedyhad not yet begun his teaching career, and Jay Feinmanand Clare Daltonwere still in school. Gilmore's nihilistic, self-indulgent vanguard consists of none other than Lon Fuller, Friedrich Kessler, and Arthur Corbin!Of course, Gilmore was demonstrating his flare for dramatic exaggeration here. His serious point seems to have been to reveal that case holdings had been manipulated or mangled to build a grand, unified theory of contract.Furthermore, he made the telling observation that Fuller, Kessler, and Corbin had only to focus on all the cases that did not fit, indeed that contradicted, classical doctrine in order to begin to undermine the contrived construct.
While Gilmore mostly looked back, he was impressively prescient in some ways. He foresaw a central thesis of Critical Legal Studies before the movement was even conceived.Gilmore wrote:
It seems apparent to the twentieth century mind, as perhaps it did not to the nineteenth century mind, that a system in which everybody is invited to do his own thing, at whatever cost to his neighbor, must work ultimately to the benefit of the rich and powerful, who are in a position to look after themselves and to act, so to say, as their own self-insurers.
Gilmore also could be bafflingly obtuse. He utterly failed to appreciate the power of Stewart Macaulay's sociological research and practical realism as a perspective on late twentieth century law in action.Gilmore willfully misunderstood Macaulay,who deserves the last laugh. Gilmore's preoccupation with doctrine seems quaint today, and he offered no direction for the future. But, as I discuss below, it is Macaulay who has given the most satisfying, nuanced answer we have to an important question that Gilmore posed but did not attempt to answer. That is: How can we teach contracts, let alone write in the field other than as historians, after its "death"?
This essay examines three aspects of the state of contract and contract law today, a generation after The Death of Contract. First, if we doubt the continuing power of contract rhetoric and its association with laissez-faire economics, we need look no further than "The Contract With America," as the Republican Party dubbed its 1994 congressional election platform. In Part II, I examine this revival of laissez-faire thinking and begin to explore its connection to contract law. Second, if we doubt that classical contract doctrine lives as one important strand among others in current law, we need only read the advance sheets from the United States Supreme Court. In Part III, I analyze two recent Supreme Court cases to develop further the impact of free market ideology on contract, particularly the way in which this ideology seems to obscure market failure. Finally, in Part IV, I discuss an approach to teaching contracts that offers release from a purgatory of dualistic thinking. Some hope of escape from repetition of conflicts - between self and other, freedom and control, self-reliance and duties of care - can be found in Contracts: Law in Action, edited by Macaulay and his University of Wisconsin colleagues John Kidwell, William Whitford, and Marc Galanter.Their book weaves the history, philosophy, sociology, and doctrine of contract into a vibrant iftroubling picture, confronting students with the conflicts, complexities, and above all, the limits of the subject. They challenge students to become "skeptical idealists"in the practice of law. Their approach is both theoretically sophisticated and thoroughly practical.
. The Contract With America and the Revival of Laissez-Faire
Fittingly, as an emblem of what "contract" means today, the Contract With Americais unenforceable, relational, and a contract of adhesion. The Contract is also a slickly packaged revival of laissez-faire thinking that caught on, at least to some extent. I examine what seems to be its appeal, as well as its connection to contract law.
The Contract has provided some interesting political theater. As its proponents set out to govern for the long term according to market-tested but unnegotiated terms, we were treated in political life to some rhetorical twists previously used only in litigation of ordinary contract disputes. Although the Contract boasts that it contains no fine print, we quickly heard arguments along these lines: All we promised was a vote on these proposals, not to pass them.This argument draws upon weasel words buried well into the document, in an introduction to a list of legislative initiatives.
The most obvious reason for using contract rhetoric was to attempt to make a skeptical electorate more trusting of political promises.House Speaker Newt Gingrich made this point directly: "Believing that a campaign promise is one thing but a signed contract is quite another, House Republican candidates signed The Contract With America last September [in 1994]."Some critics had scoffed that the Contract was not binding, not a real contract (and never mind that "real" contracts might not be enforceable as a practical matter,either). The use of contract language to emphasize fidelity carried a risk of only deepening public cynicism at the first need to back away from the Contract's promises. This need materialized in the first week of the congressional session, when Gingrich expressed a willingness to be flexible on some of the Contract's provisions, saying: "We don'thave to adopt the things we talked about adopting. We are not going to get trapped into doing something dumb just so you all [members of the media] can say we're consistent."Republicans attempted to justify this Gingrich gyration with what amounted to a breathtaking extension of the idea of a "duty to read" as applied to the Contract, saying in essence, "The voters didn't read it, so we aren't bound by it."
In addition to dependence on the hobgobblin of consistency, a potentially bigger problem with contract rhetoric - if the object was just to underscore a spirit of zealous commitment - was that it might seem a pale imitation of Bill Clinton's New Covenant. This was the name Clinton gave to his vision, first in his acceptance speech after receiving the Democratic presidential nomination in 1992and repeated in his 1995 State of the Union Address.By a covenant, of course, Clinton did not mean a contract under seal.Clinton's New Covenant evoked the mystical bond between God and the chosen people, forged out of Abraham's dogged, awe-inspiring demonstrations of faith to a terrible, testing deity.Surely "covenant" carries a stronger message of commitment than a mere "contract."
President Clinton's difficulties may be primarily other than rhetorical in origin. But it is worth pondering why the Contract caughton in a way that the Covenant did not. Much of the appeal of the Contract is as a target:
The style of the contract makes it difficult to take seriously. It is a good - that is to say terrible - example of late-twentieth-century political rhetoric. There is banality raised to the level of torture, self-congratulation, certitude where only uncertainty is possible, straw myths refuted by fake facts and the inevitable ten - not nine, not eleven - points. Probably the worst of all are the greeting-card names attached to ordinary pieces of legislation: The Fiscal Responsibility Act (budget legislation), The Taking Back Our Streets Act (crime bill), The American Dream Restoration Act (tax reduction) …
This criticism comes not from the left, but from establishment figure Herbert Stein, who was chairman of the Council of Economic Advisers in the Nixon and Ford Administrations. Stein criticized not only the "stylistic slush" of the Contract, but also its substance:
The contract bases itself on five principles: individual liberty, economic opportunity, limited government, personal responsibility and security at home and abroad. I suppose no one in America would reject these principles. Some people might, however, want to add others, such as justice, equality, compassion, community or even culture.
The Contract's currency may be notoriety as much as popularity, but at least it has been noticed.
Why has the Covenant been largely ignored? One reason may be that much of the public does not really get a biblical allusion. The allusion seems to have had the most meaning to those who found it offensive. After the 1995 State of the Union address, U.S. Representative Robert K. Dornan (R-CA) took to the House floor to accuse the President of sacrilege for using the term "New Covenant."
Another problem with the Covenant may be that it is too complicated. President Clinton explained the Covenant in terms of a balance between free enterprise and opportunity, on the one hand, and responsibility, community, and justice, on the other.Although theCovenant brings back into the picture the values Herbert Stein found were left out of the Contract, it has received much less attention and seems to lack much appeal.
More fundamentally, does a balanced vision lack resonance today? Of course the problem may not be so much with the vision as with a failure to pursue it. Alternatively, the idea of a covenant, with its overtones of faith and community, may have less appeal than the idea of a contract. If we have moved to the welfare state, we do not seem to have moved "beyond," as Gilmore thought. Rather, it seems possible that we are moving back to a revival of laissez-faire thinking, to "the devil take the hindmost."
The real point of the Contract is not merely to emphasize commitment to its specific promises. It is to bring the aura of the marketplace to the political arena. Here I will borrow Arthur Leff's analysis of Richard Posner's "tunnel vision,"which applies with equal force to the Contract:
One is struck by the picture of American society presented … For it seems to be one which regulates its affairs in rather a bizarre fashion: it has created one grand system - the market … which is almost flawless in achieving human happiness; it has created another - the political process … which is apparently almost wholly pernicious of those aims.
The Contract, both in rhetoric and most of its content, waves the banner of freedom of contract and hails market regulation of human affairs. Its message is, "Let's get the government out of the way of the market." The urgent question remains: Is this point of view really prevailing? In the hope that it is, the Contract promised a "Job Creation and Wage Enhancement Act" to cut back dramatically on much federal regulation and a "Common Sense Legal Reform Act" to limit access to civil justice.
There is an alternative to the possibility that laissez-faire thinking is ascendant in 1995. This world view may be "dying a lingering death"that should not be mistaken for a complete recovery. Thedeath may be operatic, with the tragically flawed hero rising to sing again and again, and yet a little more, before finally expiring, much to the audience's ultimate relief.
Indeed, there are several signs that laissez-faire rhetoric needs to be cloaked in community spirit to be acceptable. For example, House Speaker Newt Gingrich felt compelled to purge the word "market" from his standard stump speech.Instead, early in 1995, he talked about the need to "replace the welfare state" with voluntarism, community spirit, charity, and good Samaritanism.On the day he was sworn in as House Speaker, he stated, "You can't believe in the good Samaritan and explain that as long as business is making money, we can walk by a fellow American who's hurt and not do something."Apparently, redistribution should be left to individual as opposed to collective political choice (although charitable organizations themselves have stressed that they cannot make up for large cuts in social welfare programs). For another example of a sign that laissez-faire rhetoric is not risk free, consider that a communications strategist advised the Republican Party in early 1995 that it is perceived as "mean" and "uncaring" and that it must sell its limited government message in terms of securing "the American dream" for "our children's future."That the Contract caught on as much as it did shows that the idea of limited government has at least surface appeal, but the real test will be whether the public will allow it to be implemented.
What does the state of thinking about questions of political economy have to do with the state of contract doctrine? Gilmore noted that there seems to be a connection,but he did not really explore the nature of it. The relationship is indirect. Contract law is not an effective device for redistribution. The wealth effects of changes in con-tract law are small and generally temporary, lasting only until powerful parties disfavored by legal rules figure out how to plan around them or pass on their costs.
Although the relationship between thinking about political economy and contract law is indirect, it is nonetheless significant. To understand the connection between the two, it is helpful to return to the last heyday of laissez-faire and to hear from Samuel Williston. In Gilmore's book, Williston is both a central character in the development of classical contract doctrine and a figure to be mocked along with Christopher Columbus Langdell.Gilmore describes Langdell as "an industrious researcher of no distinction whatever either of mind or … style" and credits him with "the idea that there was - or should be - such a thing as a general theory of contract."Gilmore adds: "The theory itself was pieced together by his successors - notably Holmes, in broad philosophical outline, and Williston, in meticulous, although not always accurate, scholarly detail."Williston is portrayed as a plodding scrivener. Elsewhere in Gilmore's book, Williston is described as one who can be counted on to "pursue [a] rule to its ultimate abstraction."In short, Gilmore paints Williston as the ultimate formalist. Gilmore gives us an entertaining caricature,and he thus succumbs to the sin of inaccuracy that he ascribed to Williston. Gilmore "impressionistically" presents "the Holmes-Williston construct"of classical contract:
The courts should operate as detached umpires or referees, doing no more than to see that the rules of the game were observed and refusing to intervene affirmatively to see that justice or anything of that sort was done. Courts do not, it was said, make contracts for the parties… Contract liability, furthermore, was to be sharply differentiated from tort liability and there was to be no softening or blurring of the harsh limitations of contract theory by the recognition of an intermediate no-man's-land between contract and tort; the idea which later flourished as "quasi-contract" was no part of the Holmesian theory.
If we turn to Williston's treatise after reading Gilmore, we will be surprised to read:
When it is now said that courts "will neither make nor modify contracts, nor dispense with their performance," if it is meant that such power will not be exercised except in accordance with legal principles, the statement is sound; but if the meaning is that parties to contracts are always liable in accordance with their terms, it is far too narrow a limitation of the functions of the common law, and a court which insists upon such a statement obliges itself in various situations to use the confusing language of fiction in order to achieve correct results. Under the name of implied contracts (quasi-contracts) courts have wisely imposed obligations on parties to contracts which they never agreed to assume; and because of fraud, mistake, duress, impossibility and illegality, have modified contracts or dispensed with their performance, simply because justice required it.
This is hardly distilled formalism; there is even a hint of realism in the scorn for fiction and the praise for wise judges openly doing justice. Williston had his rigid impulses (note the phrase "correct results"), but he saw a need for the policing of contracts to achieve justice in the equitable sense.
What did Williston think of laissez-faire ideology and its impact on contract law? In matters of political economy, he had a strong progressive streak. He lived and wrote about contract law in an era when "freedom of contract" was treated as a constitutional right, but he took a dim view of this state of affairs. In a remarkable address given at Cornell Law School in 1921, Williston said, "Observation of results has proved that unlimited freedom of contract, like unlimited freedom in other directions, does not necessarily lead to public or individual welfare and that the only ultimate test of proper limitations is that provided by experience."Williston criticized Lochner v. New Yorkin this address, chiding the Supreme Court for not giving greater scope in that case to the states' police powers in order to allow for "reasonable social experiment."He seized upon Muller v. Oregonas showing the way back to more reasonable protection of health, morals, and general welfare through restrictions on freedom of contract such as wage and hour legislation.
Most significantly, Williston linked the need for restrictions on freedom of contract to the policy underpinnings of contract doctrine.An extreme dogma of individualism, he believed, had led to an "exaggerated endeavor to find some warrant in the intention of the parties"for various contract rules really based on "policy and justice."These rules, he said, produce results sometimes "wholly beyond the range of thought of the parties"and occasionally "counter even to [their] expressed intentions"in order to further such policies as protection of reasonable relianceor prevention of punishment of a breacher.This example of his reasoning fits with Learned Hand's nuanced appraisal of Williston. In a forward to Williston's autobiography,Hand described him as skeptical of "consent" as an excuse for imposing harsh results on contracting parties.Hand also said that Williston was "not overawed by authority," "had no interest in subtleties for their own sake," but had "enough interest in formal symmetry" to reject sophistry as "a facile handmaiden to authority."
Before, during, and since Williston's time, "freedom of contract" rhetoric has had an impact on contract law in its tendency to overstress the importance of the "intention of the parties." Williston said the quest to see the law as fulfilling the intention of the parties had thrown a "blinding fog" about some contracts questions.To put this point in the economic terminology of today, free contract and free market rhetoric obscures market failures. The term "market failure" sounds technical, but it involves a number of value judgments.Once the judgment is made that a market is not operating in a sociallydesirable fashion, the problem can be addressed to some extent through contract law or, better yet, related administrative approaches, if only an ideological fog does not obscure the realities of market limitations and prevent development of approaches that hold some hope of improving allocative efficiency as well as fairness. Unfortunately, the fog is currently thick in Washington, in the House of Representatives, and also at the Supreme Court.

shared_topics.topic: access to civil justice and the consequences of enforcing arbitration or legal reform that limits remedies
shared_topics.justification: Paper A discusses political/legal reforms (e.g., 'Common Sense Legal Reform Act') and Supreme Court trends that limit access to civil justice as part of a market-oriented agenda; Paper B examines Circuit City and the expansion of FAA coverage over employment contracts, showing how arbitration enforcement can deprive employees of judicial remedies and meaningful litigation access.

shared_topics.topic: the proper aim of contract law: enforcing party expectations versus policing fairness
shared_topics.justification: Paper A traces debates over whether contract doctrine should prioritize autonomous party intent or intervene for justice, criticizing laissez-faire reverence for 'freedom of contract' and endorsing judicial policing where markets fail; Paper B directly contrasts a will/expectations theory with a fairness-oriented approach, arguing that substantive unfairness must remain central and that evidentiary inquiry can reconcile the two aims.

shared_topics.topic: the role of social practice and factual/evidentiary inquiry (versus formal rules) in determining assent and contract formation
shared_topics.justification: Paper A highlights Macaulay's sociological, law-in-action approach as an alternative to doctrinal formalism, while Paper B advocates restoring a social-practice, fact-based basis for assent (including U.C.C. §2-207 revisions) so courts assess evidence of agreement rather than rely on rigid formal rules.

shared_topics.topic: historical evolution of contract doctrine and the influence of key figures (e.g., Williston, Holmes, Gilmore) on contemporary theory
shared_topics.justification: Both papers map doctrinal history—Paper A by reading Gilmore's Death of Contract and reassessing Williston and Langdell, and Paper B by recounting the defeat of consensualists and the rise of Holmes/Williston objective theory—to explain how past debates shape present uncertainty over assent, fairness, and judicial roles.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of political economy and market ideology (laissez-faire) on contract law and its handling of market failure
shared_topics.justification: Paper A explicitly links the revival of laissez-faire rhetoric (e.g., The Contract With America) and Supreme Court trends to a diminished willingness to acknowledge market failures in contract law; Paper B situates doctrinal choices in nineteenth-century political economy (Adam Smith, subjectivity of value) and shows how commercial practices and market changes forced legal adjustments to address unfairness and evidentiary realities.

shared_topics.topic: whether mutual promises (reciprocal commitments) should be the baseline for imposing legal liability
shared_topics.justification: Paper A argues that mutual promises — an exchange of commitments — should be the standard that justifies conspiracy liability, and Paper B engages the normative and doctrinal status of promises in contract law (via Williston, Holmes, and critiques), asking when courts should enforce or modify obligations grounded in promises.

shared_topics.topic: the costs of vague or ad hoc doctrinal definitions and the need for clearer, doctrinally coherent standards
shared_topics.justification: Paper A documents how ambiguous definitions of 'agreement' produce ad hoc rules, jury confusion, and convictions for mere presence, advocating a clearer standard; Paper B similarly criticizes grand or illusionary doctrinal constructs in contract law and calls for more realistic, transparent approaches to avoid misleading or unjust outcomes.

shared_topics.topic: the impact of political, ideological, and rhetorical forces on the formation and application of legal doctrine
shared_topics.justification: Paper A situates conspiracy doctrine against justificatory rationales (and touches on First Amendment constraints) and shows how doctrinal choices reflect policy aims, while Paper B documents how political rhetoric (e.g., the Contract With America) and laissez-faire ideology have shaped contract doctrine and judicial attitudes, demonstrating non-legal influences on what rules prevail.

shared_topics.topic: judicial response to ambiguously understood terms / mutual misunderstanding

shared_topics.topic: subjectivist (party intent) versus objectivist/formalist versus realist approaches to contract interpretation

shared_topics.topic: preservation of reasonable expectations and reliance as a remedial goal

shared_topics.topic: efficiency and policy considerations in designing contract doctrines and remedies

shared_topics.topic: how speaker intention and illocutionary force affect interpretation and the law of contracts/statutes

shared_topics.topic: how changing market practices, commercial complexity, and ideological shifts demand doctrinal adaptation or reform
